skeptics.reframe: Synthetic-only training now matches real data for body pose and shape (BEDLAM) but fails when hands handle objects. What remains open is which parts of the interaction distribution renderers fail to capture, and whether modelling each one closes the gap. Candidate parts are contact geometry, the grasp approach and the arm, hand-object occlusion, and RGB-D sensor artifacts at close range. Two contributions would count as significant. One is a controlled study that measures how much of the gap each factor accounts for, also checking whether reported sim-to-real gains reflect domain randomisation tuned to each dataset. The other is an interaction-aware synthesis method that reaches real-only accuracy on real HOI benchmarks without real training images.

research_questions.question: If the 3D state is held fixed by re-rendering the exact annotated frames of public RGB-D hand-object datasets (DexYCB, H2O, HO-3D v3, HO-Cap), how much of the gap between synthetic-only and real-only training in joint hand-object estimation comes from each of five factors? The metrics are hand MPJPE, hand-held object ADD-S and BOP AR, contact F1 and penetration, and bimanual relative pose. The five factors are: (a) RGB appearance; (b) depth-sensor artifacts; (c) forearm and scene context; (d) contact-geometry error in the training grasps; (e) annotation error in the real ground truth. Do the gains survive across datasets, or do they reflect domain randomisation tuned to one dataset?
research_questions.why_top_venue:
Verified state of the field:
- The only systematic gap study is Zhao et al., CVPR 2025 (arXiv 2503.19307), checked against its HTML.
  - Setup: RGB only, measured on hand pose only. It composites real arm and object segments cut from real images, and takes poses from FreiHAND and DexYCB.
  - Result: near parity on DexYCB (0.87 vs 0.86 cm PA-MPJPE) and 1.02 vs 0.99 cm on FreiHAND.
  - It states that depth and contact were not studied, and that stronger backbones overfit synthetic data more.
- The verified gap that remains is on the object and contact side, the core of P05 as all three skeptics narrowed it.
  - BOP 2024 report (arXiv 2504.02812): 6D detection of hand-held objects on BOP-H3 scores 31.2 AP, versus 50.4 AP on BOP-Classic-Core.
  - AnyHand (arXiv 2603.25726, 2026) lists no contact realism and no depth-noise model among its limitations, and reports that synthetic-only training underperforms mixed training.

Why a paired design adds something new:
- Each frame exists both as a capture and as a render with the same pose, so pose distribution is no longer a confound.
- It enables modality swaps that unpaired studies cannot do: real RGB with twin depth, and twin RGB with real depth.
- That turns the vague claim 'synthetic cannot replace real' into a measured breakdown by factor. It is the reframe all three skeptics asked for, and none of the evidence papers does it.
- It tells the field whether to spend on renderers, on contact simulation or on sensor models.

Caveat: as pure analysis it may be read as an RGB-D and object extension of Zhao et al. or sent to a Datasets and Benchmarks track. A main-track paper needs the breakdown plus one constructive fix (RQ2 or RQ3).
research_questions.data_and_hardware:
Public data:
- DexYCB: RealSense RGB-D, multi-view, MANO and YCB 6D labels, about 119 GB, CC BY-NC 4.0.
- H2O: five RGB-D cameras, two hands plus object 6D poses (ICCV 2021).
- HO-3D v3.
- HO-Cap: multiple RGB-D cameras plus HoloLens, bimanual handovers (arXiv 2406.06843).
- YCB meshes, MANO, and HDRI sets.

Software: Blender Cycles or SAPIEN, including its active-stereo simulator.

Hardware: one 24-48 GB GPU workstation. Estimated cost, not measured:
- rendering about 1-4 GPU-days per 200k-frame condition;
- training about 1 GPU-day per run;
- about 40-80 GPU-days in total;
- 2-4 TB of disk.

No new capture, motion capture or robot is needed.
research_questions.risks:
1. Novelty. Reviewers may call it an extension of Zhao et al., CVPR 2025, or a Datasets and Benchmarks paper. Mitigation: lead with the object and contact metrics and the paired modality swap, and attach the RQ2 or RQ3 fix.
2. Annotation error. DexYCB, H2O and HO-3D ground truth carries annotation error of unquantified size (not verified here). It may swamp the contact factor, and real contact labels are derived from that same noisy ground truth.
3. Asset artifacts. Scanned YCB textures have baked lighting, itself a named P05 cause, and this confounds the appearance factor.
4. Possible null result. The gap may turn out to be mostly RGB appearance, which is publishable but weaker.
5. Competition. Groups with AnyHand-scale or PAM-scale pipelines could publish a similar analysis first.
6. Licensing. DexYCB is non-commercial (fine for academic work).

research_questions.why_top_venue:
Prior work, verified from abstracts:
- Depth is where synthetic-only transfer has the strongest precedent.
  - HOTrack (arXiv 2209.12009) trains only on synthetic data generated with depth simulation and tests on HO3D and DexYCB without fine-tuning. Its venue was not verified here.
  - DREDS (ECCV 2022) simulates active stereo for specular and transparent objects.
  - The physics-based active-stereo simulator (T-RO, arXiv 2201.11924) is open-source in SAPIEN.
- The newest large hand-object RGB-D set, AnyHand (2026), applies no sensor-noise model. Its depth combines SAPIEN ray-traced foreground with a MoGe-2-estimated background, and it names the missing noise model and mismatched intrinsics as limitations (verified from the paper HTML).
- No verified work models hand-specific depth artifacts.
- No verified work reports synthetic-only parity with real data for hand-object RGB-D.

Why it would matter: a parity result would be the first counterexample to P05 in the interaction setting, a headline-level finding for the field.

Caveat: without the parity result, the noise model alone is an ICRA or RA-L contribution.
research_questions.method_sketch:
1. Paired data. In DexYCB (RealSense) and H2O or HO-Cap (different RGB-D sensors), render clean depth of the annotated hand, object and static background for each frame. The pair is (clean depth, real depth).
2. Geometric physics prior. Compute projector-camera shadow masks from the known baseline, which captures the hand shadowing the object, plus a boundary mask at depth discontinuities.
3. Learned residual. Train a conditional generative corruption model, either a mixture-density U-Net or a small conditional diffusion model, that outputs a missing-pixel mask and a residual distribution. Inputs: clean depth, normals, per-pixel material class (skin, object, table, sleeve), range, viewing angle, and a sensor embedding.
4. Robustness to label error. Use robust losses and drop frames whose ground-truth residual says the annotation is off.
5. Intrinsic evaluation:
   - per-material error histograms;
   - missing-pixel F1 at hand-object boundaries;
   - a real-versus-synthetic discriminator accuracy.
6. Downstream evaluation. Train HOTrack-style and AnyHandNet-D-style depth-fusion models synthetic-only under four depth conditions: clean, heuristic Gaussian plus dropout, SAPIEN active-stereo simulation, and the learned model. Test on real DexYCB, HO-3D v3 and H2O.
7. Cross-sensor test. Fit on one sensor family, evaluate on another, and add a few-shot adaptation from about 100 paired frames.
research_questions.minimum_experiment:
Noise model: train on DexYCB, 4 subjects, one camera; test on 2 held-out subjects.

Downstream: render 100k synthetic hand-object frames with grasps taken from the DexYCB training split (to remove pose-distribution confounds). Train one point-cloud hand-plus-object pose network under the four depth conditions, 2 seeds each.

Metrics on real DexYCB test: MPJPE and object ADD-S, compared with the same network trained on real data.

Success criterion: the learned model closes most of the clean-to-real gap and beats the SAPIEN physics simulator.

Estimated effort: about 8 weeks.
research_questions.data_and_hardware:
Public data:
- DexYCB, plus H2O or HO-Cap for a second sensor family;
- HO-3D v3 for testing;
- YCB meshes and MANO.

Optional: the author's own consumer RGB-D camera with the ArUco-marked object. It gives a small paired probe at a metrically known pose, with and without hand occlusion, for cross-sensor validation.

Hardware: one 24-48 GB GPU.
- Noise-model training: about 2-4 GPU-days.
- Downstream runs: about 1 GPU-day each.
- SAPIEN simulation: CPU and GPU, within the same workstation.
research_questions.risks:
1. Annotation error contaminates the learned noise. DexYCB and H2O ground-truth error makes the real-minus-render residual partly label error, which the model may learn as noise. Filtering and robust losses help but do not remove it.
2. Existing baseline. The physics-based active-stereo simulator already exists, and reviewers will require beating it. If it already gives parity, the contribution shrinks to an analysis finding.
3. Limited reach. Depth matters only in RGB-D settings; many current hand-object benchmarks are RGB or egocentric, so impact on the wider field is limited.
4. Gap may not close. Parity may fail because RGB appearance or contact dominates; in that case RQ1 tells you so early.
5. Venue. Without parity the work lands at ICRA, RA-L or 3DV rather than CVPR.
6. Unverified details. The sensor models of H2O and HO-Cap (stereo versus time-of-flight) were not verified here; confirm them before claiming cross-family transfer.
target_venues: CoRL (if framed for robot demonstration capture)

research_questions.question: Synthetic-trained 6D pose drops sharply on hand-held objects: the BOP 2024 report gives 31.2 AP on BOP-H3 versus 50.4 AP on BOP-Classic-Core. Is that drop caused by the absence of grasping hands in the training renders? If so, does it matter whether the rendered hands grasp with physically consistent contact, forearm and approach, rather than appearing as random occluders? Does giving the model an explicit hand estimate as input recover the rest?
research_questions.why_top_venue:
Why this is open:
- The hand-held drop is the largest verified remnant of P05 on the object side. The BOP report measures it but does not diagnose its cause.
- Expensive contact-faithful synthesis efforts assume that contact realism matters for perception: DexCanvas (arXiv 2510.15786, 7,000 hours generated from 70 hours of real data), Policy-as-Data, and PAM (CVPR 2026). Nobody has shown with a controlled dose-response that it does.

What an answer is worth: a clean positive or negative result informs both the BOP and the hand-object community.

Caveat: top-venue value depends on a strong effect that holds across datasets. Otherwise this is workshop or analysis material.
research_questions.minimum_experiment:
Objects: 5-8 frequently grasped YCB objects.

Training: one multi-object GDRNPP-style model on about 50k renders per condition, for conditions (a), (b) and (d), 2 seeds each.

Test: DexYCB S0 test frames.

Metrics: ADD-S AUC and BOP AR, binned by occlusion.

Success criterion: condition (d) beats (b) by a margin larger than seed variance in the high-occlusion bins.

Estimated effort: about 6 weeks.
research_questions.risks:
1. Possible null on contact. Random occluders may close most of the gap, which reduces the contribution.
2. Dataset fit. BOP-H3 data are largely egocentric headset captures with object sets different from YCB, so cross-checks there may be weak.
3. Annotation noise. DexYCB object ground-truth noise limits how finely the high-occlusion bins can be resolved.
4. Competition. The BOP community may already be adding hand occluders to its 2025-2026 training data (not verified).
5. Reimplementation burden. The training-code gaps for unseen-object models force reimplementation if the study is extended beyond seen objects.

fit.thesis_assets_help:
Small edge overall, mainly for RQ2.

Assets that help:
- The single consumer RGB-D desk setup with an ArUco-marked object at metric pose. It gives a cheap paired probe: rendered versus real depth of a known object at a known pose, with and without the holding hand occluding it. That is a useful extra sensor for RQ2's cross-sensor test and a sanity check for RQ1.
- The Unity twin. It is a working digital-twin pipeline for re-rendering the author's own captures. Its rasterized output is not photoreal, so training renders should come from Blender Cycles or SAPIEN instead.
- The measured/held/constrained honesty labels. They map conceptually onto RQ1's annotation-error factor (separating measured from inferred labels), which is a small methodological carry-over.
- The object-conditioned recovery of an occluded holding arm. It relates to the forearm and arm factor that Zhao et al. (CVPR 2025) found matters, but only as background knowledge.

Assets that do not help:
- The causal 30 fps chain is irrelevant to this data question.
- The 28 recordings of one subject are too small and too homogeneous to train on or to serve as a benchmark. At most they are a qualitative cross-sensor test.
fit.what_a_small_lab_cannot_do_here:
The main routes the field is taking are out of reach for a small lab:
- Building synthetic data at large scale. AnyHand-scale sets (2.5M single-hand plus 4.1M hand-object ray-traced RGB-D images) and BEDLAM-style asset libraries are beyond one workstation.
- Training generative sim-to-real video engines such as PAM (CVPR 2026) or HVG-3D.
- Running physics and reinforcement-learning interaction generators at the scale of DexCanvas (7,000 hours generated from 70 hours of real capture) or Policy-as-Data.
- Retraining foundation 6D pose models (MegaPose, FoundationPose) from scratch. Their training code is not released per the GitHub READMEs, and the compute is large.
- Capturing new multi-view, contact-accurate ground truth. With one RGB-D camera, no motion capture and no robot arm, benchmark-grade labels cannot be produced.
- Showing synthetic-only parity across many backbones and benchmarks. Zhao et al. found that stronger backbones overfit synthetic data more, so a convincing parity claim at the state-of-the-art end needs many expensive training runs.

The feasible small-lab niche is narrower: a paired, factor-level analysis on public RGB-D hand-object datasets with ground truth, plus one targeted fix (a sensor-faithful depth model, or contact-consistent hand occluders for object pose). Proving synthetic-only parity in general is not feasible.

painpoint.name: Metrics hide absolute error, contact, physics and task tolerance

evidence.latest_state: Absolute placement is being addressed in egocentric hand tracking: world-space metrics (W-MPJPE, WA-MPJPE, jitter, acceleration error) are now routinely reported on HOT3D and ARCTIC. HaWoR (CVPR 2025) reports W-MPJPE 33.20 mm on HOT3D (number from a search snippet, not checked against the paper). StableHand (arXiv 2605.18553, May 2026) claims a 20-25% W-MPJPE reduction over the strongest baselines on HOT3D and ARCTIC. Contact is still scored with proxy metrics (intersection volume, penetration depth, jerk). GraspHOI (arXiv 2608.28386, Aug 2026) shows how these proxies mislead: its new CPP metric gives 72.83% on ARCTIC and 78.15% on ProciGen-GRAB, against 1.35% and 1.31% for TeHOR, so TeHOR's low penetration came from missing contact rather than better grasps. Per-frame contact ground truth is starting to come from tactile-glove datasets: HandSense in Glove2Hand (CVPR 2026 Highlight), OpenTouch (5.1 h of synchronized video, touch and pose, 2,900 clips) and TactiDex (tactile signals with object 6D pose; success and physical-realism metrics for single-hand and bimanual tasks). None is yet a standard benchmark for tracking or reconstruction. Physics checks have moved into methods: RePHO (CVPR 2026) refines poses with RL in a simulator, and HA-HOI ('Real2Sim in HOI', 2605.14462) targets 'simulation readiness'. CHOIR (2605.20992) reports reference-free physical and temporal metrics because in-the-wild video has no 3D ground truth. On task tolerance, Burde, Burget and Sattler (arXiv 2602.17101, Feb 2026) ran about 18.8M simulated grasps on 21 YCB-V objects with 9 grippers. They found that pose error, mainly spatial (translation) error, dominates grasp success, with FoundationPose at 89.9% and MegaPose at 59.4%; the grasps are simulated only, with no real-robot validation. BOP 2025 (ICCV 2025) still ranks by AR over VSD, MSSD and MSPD, adding only multi-view evaluation for BOP-Industrial. Overall no benchmark combines absolute error, instantaneous contact, physics and task success.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: Benchmarking the Effects of Object Pose Estimation and Reconstruction on Robotic Grasping Success
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Physics-based simulated grasp benchmark linking pose and mesh error to grasp success: 21 YCB-V objects, 9 grippers, about 18.8M grasps. Finds spatial (translation) pose error dominates success; FoundationPose 89.9% vs MegaPose 59.4%. Probably the same work as source paper 836.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: GraspHOI: Full-Body 3D Human-Object Reconstruction with Finger-Level Grasps from a Single In-the-Wild Image
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Defines the Contact-Penetration Plausibility (CPP) metric: the share of near-surface hand vertices with -2 to 10 mm signed distance. Shows IV and penetration depth reward detached hands (ARCTIC CPP 72.83% vs TeHOR 1.35%; ProciGen-GRAB 78.15% vs 1.31%).

evidence.crowdedness: MEDIUM: many 2025-2026 method papers now report their own world-space, penetration, jitter or simulation-plausibility numbers, but only a handful of groups build shared evaluation infrastructure: the Burde/Burget/Sattler grasp benchmark, tactile-glove datasets (HandSense, OpenTouch, TactiDex) and the BOP organizers. None of them provides a unified contact, physics and task-success benchmark.
evidence.trend: rising: robot learning from human video and the 2026 physics-focused venues (CVPR 2026 PhysHuman workshop, simulation-readiness claims, tactile-glove datasets) push the field to measure absolute placement, contact and task success. W-MPJPE has become routine in egocentric hand work, while contact, physics and task-tolerance metrics remain proposed one paper at a time and are not yet standardized.

skeptics.reasons:
No 2025-2026 work I found solves P06 or turns it into engineering. Several pieces have moved, so the pain point should be narrowed.

(1) Per-frame contact ground truth now exists from tactile gloves: OpenTouch (arXiv 2512.16842, Dec 2025, 5.1 h in-the-wild egocentric video-touch-pose data), TouchAnything (arXiv 2605.13083, 2026, 1,891 bimanual episodes with pressure maps and 3D hand pose, Contact IoU metric) and EgoTactile (arXiv 2606.09243). This weakens the "no instantaneous contact ground truth" part, but these datasets have clear limits:
- The contact is measured on the hand side only.
- The gloves change hand appearance.
- None provides absolute world-frame object pose plus measured contact on the HOI capture benchmarks that methods are ranked on (BEHAVE, InterCap, ARCTIC, DexYCB, HO3D).
- Their benchmarks are retrieval, classification or contact IoU, not tracking accuracy.

(2) EgoPHI (arXiv 2608.13014, listed as ECCV 2026) gets dense per-vertex force labels from physics simulation of existing datasets. Its real validation covers only two instrumented objects and eight participants, so the force ground truth is still mostly synthetic.

(3) The task-success link exists only for rigid-object 6D pose with parallel-jaw grasping in simulation: "Benchmarking the Effects of Object Pose Estimation and Reconstruction on Robotic Grasping Success" (arXiv 2602.17101). Its YCB-V numbers (MegaPose 59.4 percent vs FoundationPose 89.9 percent) are already in the P06 record as paper 836, and it is open-loop and not physically validated. It does not cover tracking of human hands or bodies with objects.

(4) The 2026 HOI work on physical plausibility (Real2Sim in HOI, arXiv 2605.14462; CVPR 2026 "Recovering Physically Plausible HOI from Monocular Videos", arXiv 2606.05359; the 1st PhysHuman Workshop at CVPR 2026) still reports penetration, contact ratio, acceleration and rollout criteria against BEHAVE's fitted pseudo ground truth. Each paper uses its own rollout criteria. This confirms the problem is active and that no shared standard exists.

(5) TactiDex (arXiv 2607.09190, Jul 2026) brings tactile-aligned human demonstrations into a dexterous robot benchmark. It evaluates policy learning, not whether capture or tracking is accurate enough for the task.

No saturated metric or released product resolves the core gap: hand-object tracking benchmarks still rank methods by root-relative or Procrustes-aligned error against fitted or pseudo ground truth. They do not check absolute placement, measured contact or task outcome together.

Caveat: an evaluation-only contribution is a harder sell at top venues unless it comes with a dataset or a protocol others adopt. The tactile-glove dataset line is growing fast and would be the nearest competition.

skeptics.reframe: Tactile gloves now supply per-frame hand-side contact, and simulated grasp tests now link rigid-object pose error to grasp success. What no benchmark offers yet is a single evaluation of hand-object or bimanual tracking for manipulation capture that combines three things: absolute world-frame hand and object pose against measured (not fitted) ground truth, contact measured on both the hand and the object, and a task-outcome test (simulated or real replay success of the captured demonstration). Without that, methods ranked by Procrustes-aligned or root-relative error and penetration proxies cannot be shown to produce demonstrations or digital twins accurate enough to reproduce the task.

skeptics.reasons:
P06 is not the artifact of one dataset or one group. Its 50 supporting papers come from many groups and venues, including CVPR, ICCV, ECCV, NeurIPS, ICLR, ICRA, T-RO, TPAMI, IJCV, SIGGRAPH Asia and the HANDS workshops. As stated, though, the pain point is largely a convention artifact plus a bundle, for four reasons.

(1) Much of the evidence is off-field. Limb-deficient pose (273, 521), privacy metrics (477), dashcam pedestrians (433), sign language (345), piano playing (578, 629), clinical and sports kinematics validation (1231, 1255), sEMG hand pose (418), text-conditioned motion-generation R-precision (8), a one-off evaluation bug in TRACE (1261) and 3DPW body saturation (1262) all concern body pose or generation conventions. None of them concerns tracking hands manipulating objects. The breadth of the paper count therefore overstates the core signal.

(2) The headline claim is that standard metrics do not check absolute placement, contact, temporal stability or physical plausibility, and that no fix is standard. Neighbouring subcommunities have long treated each of these as addressed:
- 6D object pose: BOP has used MSSD and MSPD since its 2019-2020 challenges, explicitly motivated by grasping and AR tolerances. Its VSD metric is built for visible-surface tasks.
- Hand-object reconstruction: penetration depth and volume, and simulation displacement under gravity, have been standard plausibility metrics since ObMan (Hasson et al., CVPR 2019). They are routinely reported on DexYCB, HO3D and HOI4D.
- World-grounded body recovery: since EMDB and WHAM (2023-2024), the standard metrics include W-MPJPE, WA-MPJPE, root translation error, jitter and foot sliding. These are absolute and temporal metrics.
- Bimanual hand-object tracking: ARCTIC (CVPR 2023) defines absolute and relative root error (MRRPE), contact deviation, motion deviation and acceleration error. These metric names are recalled from the paper; the leaderboard pages I fetched did not list them.

So the complaint mostly reflects one community's leaderboard habit: ranking monocular hand-mesh methods by PA-MPJPE on FreiHAND and HO3D. It is not a field-wide absence of metrics.

(3) The statement merges at least three distinct problems that have different status:
- metric choice (largely solved by existing metrics that some authors do not report);
- ground-truth availability (real and open);
- the perception-to-task link (real but thinly evidenced). The direct evidence is one ICRA 2026 simulated-grasp study (836), plus the T-RO 2024 position paper (1020) and the HANDS 2026 challenge reports.

(4) What survives is narrower. Real captured interaction data lacks per-frame contact, force and in-the-wild 3D ground truth: DyTact (1535) has only accumulated contact, and BEHAVE, InterCap and HOI-M3 have fitted pseudo ground truth. As a result, the existing contact and physics metrics are computed against proxies, or only on synthetic data or in simulation. Nobody has validated whether low tracking error on captured human demonstrations predicts downstream robot or digital-twin task success.

That residual problem is genuine and relevant to the author's field. It is an evaluation and ground-truth problem, not a "metrics are blind" problem. It should be restated, not kept in its current form.

skeptics.reframe: Real captured hand-object and bimanual interaction data has no per-frame ground truth for contact, force or absolute 3D pose; BEHAVE, InterCap and HOI-M3 rely on fitted pseudo ground truth, and DyTact records only accumulated contact. As a result, the existing contact, penetration, absolute-error and stability metrics are computed against proxies or only in synthetic or simulated settings. No benchmark has tested whether tracking error on captured human demonstrations predicts whether a robot can reproduce the task, or whether a digital twin is accurate enough for its use. The open problem is the missing link between the capture's ground truth and downstream task success, not a lack of metrics.

skeptics.reasons: Refutation attempt: much of P06 is a wish for better ground truth (per-frame contact, in-the-wild absolute 3D) and for a unified benchmark that is "proposed but not built". The parts that are only data collection (more tactile gloves, more mocap) or bug fixing (the PA-MPJPE bug in 1261) are not research questions. Partial fixes also exist: BOP MSSD/MSPD/VSD, penetration and simulation-displacement metrics, ARCTIC-style contact metrics, and the 2026 physics-based grasp benchmark by Burde, Burget and Sattler (arXiv 2602.17101). That benchmark already links object pose and mesh error to grasp success and finds that spatial or translation error dominates. Physics-replay success metrics also appear in recent retargeting work such as C2Dex (arXiv 2608.07045, RA-L submission). So the narrow object-pose-to-grasp question is partly answered, and a plain metric proposal risks reading as incremental. The refutation still fails, because at least one significant question remains open and top-venue reviewers value this kind of question. (1) Do hand-object tracking errors, measured as absolute, temporal or contact errors and not root-relative or PA errors, predict the success of transferring a human demonstration to a robot (retarget, replay in physics, then run on a real robot)? Can a task-calibrated error measure be learned or derived, with its uncertainty, so that it ranks bimanual RGB-D trackers the way downstream outcomes do? Existing studies cover rigid-object grasping with parallel-jaw grippers, not hand-object or bimanual trajectories, and the open-loop simulation they use has not been physically validated (stated in the P06 attempted fixes). (2) Can per-frame contact and absolute placement be evaluated without dense ground truth, using physics-consistency or cross-modal checks validated against sparse tactile ground truth? Tactile-glove ground truth is now reaching CVPR, for example EgoPressure (CVPR 2025) and Glove2Hand (CVPR 2026), which makes such a validation feasible. (3) How sensitive are leaderboard rankings to the alignment protocol? A rank-reversal analysis of Procrustes-aligned versus absolute versus task metrics would be an evaluation contribution of the kind NeurIPS Datasets and Benchmarks and CVPR accept. Risks are that venue fit may lean to the benchmark track or to RA-L/ICRA rather than the main CVPR track, that real-robot validation is costly, and that the area is getting crowded in 2026. The question survives, but only if it is framed as "which error predicts task outcome, and why" and not as "we need more annotation".

skeptics.reframe: For one-camera or RGB-D hand-object and bimanual tracking, no validated error measure is known to predict whether a tracked demonstration transfers into a successful robot or digital-twin execution. Standard root-relative and Procrustes-aligned metrics, and centimetre tolerances, have never been calibrated against downstream outcomes (physics replay, retargeted robot execution) or against per-frame tactile contact ground truth. The open question is which components of absolute, temporal and contact error govern task success, and whether a task-calibrated metric, checked against real-robot outcomes and sparse tactile ground truth, ranks trackers differently from current leaderboards.

research_questions.question: RQ1 (go option). Which components of hand-object tracking error decide whether a captured single-hand or bimanual demonstration can be reproduced in physics and on a robot? Does a task-calibrated error measure built from those components rank public trackers differently from PA-MPJPE, root-relative MPJPE, MRRPE and ADD(-S)? Fix the scope first: monocular RGB or RGB-D input, rigid and articulated objects, and two outcome protocols (open-loop physics replay and retargeted robot execution).
research_questions.why_top_venue: Robot learning from human video is one of the main 2026 themes at CoRL, RSS and CVPR, yet practitioners still choose trackers by PA-MPJPE leaderboards. The verified evidence shows that tracker quality changes downstream outcomes, but no study controls for it in the hand-object setting. (a) Burde, Burget and Sattler (arXiv 2602.17101, verified) link pose and mesh error to grasp success. They find spatial (translation) error dominates, but only for rigid objects, simulated grippers and open-loop grasps, with no human hand and no real-robot validation. (b) HumanEgo (arXiv 2605.24934, Appendix H.1, verified to exist) changes only the hand tracker and finds stereo Aria MPS (95% real success) well ahead of monocular trackers. Two reads disagreed on the monocular figures (27.5-80% versus 'at most 45%'; a depth bias of 5-11 cm versus about 15 cm), so treat those numbers as unverified. It is a coarse tracker swap with no breakdown by error type. (c) ManipTrans (CVPR 2025) tested robustness only to i.i.d. Gaussian hand noise of 0.5-1.5 cm; the success numbers come from a search snippet and are unverified. (d) Grasp-and-Lift (arXiv 2601.18121) and other physics-in-the-loop methods optimize executability but each defines its own success criterion. A controlled answer to which error matters, plus a released metric and a demonstrated rank reversal, would be useful to both the vision and the robotics communities. That is the profile of evaluation papers that NeurIPS Datasets and Benchmarks and CoRL accept.
research_questions.method_sketch:
Step 1, metric audit. Run at least six public methods with released weights on ARCTIC, DexYCB, HO3D v3 and HOT3D, which have mocap or multi-view ground truth and, for HOT3D, world-frame ground truth. Candidate methods: ARCTIC baselines, HaMeR, WiLoR, HaWoR, a HOLD-style per-video reconstructor, and FoundationPose or BundleSDF for the object. Compute one metric battery for every method: PA-MPJPE; root-relative and absolute or world MPJPE; MRRPE; ADD(-S) and MSSD; the hand pose expressed in the object frame, split into the component along the contact normal and the tangential component; contact onset and release timing error (ground-truth contact from mocap distance); jitter and acceleration. Report per-sequence bootstrap confidence intervals and Kendall tau between metrics.
Step 2, outcome oracles. (a) Open-loop physics replay in MuJoCo/MJX or Isaac Lab. A MANO-shaped collision hand is driven by PD control to the tracked targets, and the object is a free body starting at its ground-truth state. Success means the object follows the ground-truth trajectory within a tolerance and is not dropped. (b) Retargeted execution: map the hand to a dexterous hand or to a parallel-gripper grasp frame and run it under a closed-loop tracking controller. Keep only sequences whose ground-truth replay succeeds, and report the share removed.
Step 3, controlled error injection. Fit a structured error model to the real tracker residuals: global bias (depth offset), low-frequency drift, high-frequency jitter, wrist rotation, finger articulation, hand-object relative error split into normal and tangential parts, contact-timing shift, and occlusion dropouts. Inject each factor in a factorial design onto the ground-truth trajectories. Real tracker errors are correlated, so injection is the step that separates the causal effect of each factor.
Step 4, task-calibrated error (TCE). Fit a monotone GAM or logistic model of success on the error components, with Shapley attribution. Validate leave-one-tracker-out and leave-one-dataset-out. Compare Kendall tau(TCE, success) against tau(PA-MPJPE, success).
Step 5, actionable result. Show that a cheap correction aimed at the dominant component outperforms a method with lower PA-MPJPE on success. Example corrections: contact-frame relative alignment, or fixing the depth bias with RGB-D.
Step 6 (optional). A small real-robot check of the sim-predicted success curve.
research_questions.minimum_experiment: Run a 6-8 week pilot as a go/no-go gate. Data: DexYCB grasp-and-lift sequences (rigid objects, simplest to replay) plus a subset of ARCTIC bimanual sequences; 6 trackers; about 300 sequences whose ground-truth replay succeeds; open-loop replay only. Measure Kendall tau between each standard metric and replay success, with bootstrap confidence intervals. Go if tau for PA-MPJPE is clearly below the tau of a simple contact-frame or absolute error, and at least one rank reversal occurs among the top methods. Full minimum paper: the pilot plus factorial injection (8 factors x 4 levels x 300 sequences, about 9,600 replays per protocol, cheap on one GPU), TCE with leave-one-tracker-out validation, the second protocol (retargeted execution), and one actionable fix. Optional: a real check on a borrowed arm with a parallel gripper, covering 3 YCB objects x 4 injected error levels x 20 trials, comparing the real success curve to the simulated one.
research_questions.data_and_hardware: Data: public datasets only (ARCTIC, DexYCB, HO3D v3, HOT3D), released tracker checkpoints, MANO, and YCB/ARCTIC object meshes. Compute: one 24 GB GPU. Tracker inference takes roughly 2-4 GPU-weeks across the datasets (estimate). Open-loop replay in MJX or Isaac Lab is cheap. Avoid per-sequence RL training (ManipTrans-style residual fine-tuning) at scale; use it on a small subset at most. Hardware: no new capture is needed. A borrowed 6-DoF arm with a parallel gripper is optional, for the real check. No motion capture and no dexterous robot hand are required.
research_questions.risks: (1) Protocol dependence. Closed-loop policies absorb errors that open-loop replay does not, so which components matter can change with the pipeline. Mitigate by reporting both protocols and claiming only conclusions that hold in both. (2) Ground-truth replay failures: mocap ground truth can penetrate or float. Cleaning it can bias the sample, so report the filtered share. (3) A rigid MANO collision hand ignores soft-tissue contact area, so grasp stability is underestimated. (4) Evaluation-only papers draw 'so what' reviews at the CVPR main track. The actionable fix in Step 5 and a released metric and toolkit are needed. (5) Scoop risk is medium. The Burde/Burget/Sattler group could extend to hands, robot-learning groups already run tracker ablations, and HANDS or BOP organizers could add task metrics. (6) Some cited numbers (ManipTrans noise results, HumanEgo monocular figures, ARCTIC metric names) are unverified or were recalled and must be checked before writing.

research_questions.question: RQ2. Can per-frame, object-side contact be measured cheaply on bare-hand bimanual manipulation using objects with capacitive electrodes? Measured against it, do the current contact and physics proxies agree with real contact? The proxies are penetration depth, intersection volume, the GraspHOI CPP score, ARCTIC-style contact deviation, and reference-free physical-plausibility scores.
research_questions.why_top_venue: The pain point survives mainly as a ground-truth problem. BEHAVE, InterCap and HOI-M3 rely on fitted pseudo ground truth, and DyTact records only accumulated contact. Several tactile datasets measure contact on the hand side only, through gloves that change hand appearance: OpenTouch, TouchAnything, HandSense/Glove2Hand and EgoPressure (EgoPressure and part of the set are unverified). EgoPHI has real force ground truth on only two instrumented objects and eight participants. GraspHOI (arXiv 2608.28386) shows that penetration and intersection-volume metrics reward detached hands: CPP of 72.83% versus 1.31-1.35% for TeHOR. That argument still lacks real measured contact. A bare-hand, object-side, per-frame contact reference with metric object pose would test the proxies directly, and could settle how contact should be scored. That makes it a credible dataset-plus-analysis paper.
research_questions.method_sketch: Build 6-8 non-conductive objects, some 3D-printed and YCB-like, some household. Apply 8-24 electrode patches of conductive paint or copper tape to each, wired to MPR121-class capacitive controllers on a microcontroller sampling at 100 Hz or more. Synchronize to the RGB-D camera with an LED or hardware trigger. Track object pose with fiducial markers plus depth refinement. Characterize the sensor before capture: the hover-versus-touch threshold (calibrated with force-sensitive resistors on a subset of patches), latency and cross-talk. Capture 10-15 participants doing single-hand and bimanual tasks, including handovers. Evaluate HOI reconstruction methods and touch detectors by turning their reconstructed hand-object geometry into per-patch contact. Score per-patch contact F1 and onset and release timing error. Then test whether each proxy metric ranks methods, and orders sequences, the same way as measured-contact accuracy.
research_questions.minimum_experiment: 4 objects, 8 participants, about 1 hour of synchronized data, 4 reconstruction methods. Outcomes: (a) a sensor validation table with hover distance, latency and false-contact rate against the force-sensitive resistors; (b) per-patch contact F1 and timing error for each method; (c) rank correlation between each proxy metric and measured-contact F1. The headline result would be that penetration or intersection-volume metrics rank methods differently from measured contact. That would confirm GraspHOI's claim, or overturn it, with real ground truth.
research_questions.data_and_hardware: The existing consumer RGB-D camera. 2-4 capacitive controller boards, a microcontroller, conductive paint or copper tape, and a few force-sensitive resistors, about USD 100-300 in total. A 3D printer, or printed parts from a service. Markers for object pose. An ethics approval for human participants. One GPU for running the public methods. No motion capture and no gloves.
research_questions.risks: (1) Capacitive sensing fires on near-touch at 1-5 mm, varies with skin moisture, and suffers cross-talk, so 'contact' must be defined with a calibrated tolerance. (2) Spatial resolution is the patch size, about 1-4 cm, much coarser than vertex-level contact. (3) There is no hand pose ground truth; reviewers may ask for it, and the scope must say plainly that the dataset is object-side only. (4) Painted patches are visible in RGB. This is acceptable for evaluation but blocks training use without inpainting. (5) A small dataset may read as niche next to glove datasets that are growing fast. (6) Ethics approval and capture take months of the 12-18 month window. (7) Marker-based object pose is not mocap-grade, so its error must be measured and reported.

research_questions.question: RQ3 (secondary; depends on RQ1). Can an RGB-D hand-object tracker certify, frame by frame and in real time, that its estimate is within a task tolerance? Given a target coverage, does filtering or segmenting demonstrations by such certificates raise downstream replay success more than filtering by raw detector confidence or not filtering at all?
research_questions.why_top_venue: Hiding failures is the core of P06. A tracker that reports calibrated, task-tolerance bounds per frame turns a single benchmark number into a usable quality signal for demonstration curation, which robot-learning-from-video pipelines currently lack. Evidence that tracker errors cost policy success (HumanEgo's tracker ablation; Burde et al.) motivates this. Uncertainty-aware hand pose exists, but task-calibrated coverage guarantees evaluated against downstream success appear new. This is unverified beyond the searches made here.
research_questions.method_sketch: Predict the RQ1 task-calibrated error from per-frame features: detector confidence, occlusion ratio, depth validity, temporal residuals, contact state, and a provenance tag saying whether the value was measured, held from an earlier frame, or inferred from constraints. Wrap the predictor in conformal calibration suited to time series (split conformal plus adaptive conformal inference) to output per-frame upper bounds at a target coverage. Evaluate empirical coverage under dataset shift (calibrate on DexYCB, test on ARCTIC and HOT3D), with risk-coverage and AURC curves under the task tolerance. Downstream: keep only certified spans of demonstrations, run them through the RQ1 replay protocols, and compare success at a fixed data budget. Run the certifier online in a causal 30 fps chain to report latency.
research_questions.minimum_experiment: 3 trackers. Calibration and test sets drawn from two datasets. A target coverage of 90%. Report empirical coverage, and AURC compared with raw confidence. One downstream result: replay success of certified-only spans versus all spans versus confidence-filtered spans, on about 300 sequences from RQ1.
research_questions.data_and_hardware: The same public datasets and simulation pipeline as RQ1, and one GPU. The author's RGB-D desk chain serves as an online demonstration case. No new capture.
research_questions.risks: (1) Temporal dependence and dataset shift violate exchangeability, and coverage can collapse out of distribution. (2) It may be read as 'conformal prediction applied to pose' (incremental) unless the task-tolerance calibration and the downstream gain are clear. (3) The gain may be small if the replay policies already absorb errors. (4) It cannot start until RQ1 has defined the task-calibrated error.

fit.thesis_assets_help: Modest, and only in specific places; none for the core of RQ1. Helpful: (1) The per-frame labels marking each estimate as measured, held or constrained are the kind of provenance signal RQ3 uses as a reliability feature. They also support a small evaluation point: report error separately for measured and inferred frames. (2) The ArUco-marked object with metric pose and the working RGB-D synchronization chain shorten RQ2's capture setup. Object pose for the instrumented objects can reuse this pipeline, though its accuracy (45 mm marker scale) must be quantified and is not mocap-grade. (3) The causal 30 fps chain gives RQ3 a real-time demonstration case. Little or no help: the Unity twin (PhysX in Unity is not the usual validated engine for contact-rich MANO replay; MuJoCo or Isaac is the norm); the object-conditioned recovery of the occluded holding arm (the public RQ1 benchmarks have no arm or body ground truth to score it, though it can serve as one example of a tracker whose outputs are constrained rather than measured); and the 28 recordings of one subject (too small and single-subject for any benchmark claim, usable only as an RQ2 protocol pilot).
fit.what_a_small_lab_cannot_do_here: A small lab cannot do the following. (1) Build a multi-subject benchmark with measured hand ground truth: that needs optical motion capture or multi-view rigs at the ARCTIC or HOT3D scale. (2) Collect tactile-glove or force ground truth at the scale of OpenTouch (5.1 h), HandSense or EgoPHI. (3) Validate on dexterous robot hands at scale, with many tasks and hundreds of trials; at most it can run a borrowed arm with a parallel gripper on a few tasks. (4) Train RL-based transfer policies for each sequence (ManipTrans-style) across thousands of sequences on one GPU; it must use open-loop replay or small subsets. (5) Compete on W-MPJPE by training large world-space trackers of the HaWoR or StableHand kind. (6) Make a metric a standard alone: adoption needs a partner such as the HANDS workshop or the BOP challenge organizers, or a released toolkit that other groups pick up. The worth-pursuing verdict is MAYBE. RQ1 alone is feasible from public data, and the 6-8 week pilot (rank correlation between PA-MPJPE and replay success on DexYCB and ARCTIC) is the gate. Upgrade to YES if it shows a clear rank reversal; otherwise drop the direction. Unverified numbers to check before relying on them: ManipTrans noise results, the HumanEgo monocular figures, the ARCTIC metric names, and the venue and code release of Burde et al. Five web searches were used.

painpoint.name: Camera ego-motion and sensor drift corrupt world-frame trajectories

evidence.latest_state: Drift is smaller in 2026 but not solved. The newest egocentric hand result is InfiniHand (arXiv 2609.35743, Sep 2026). It is a streaming feed-forward model that runs at 11.19 FPS and estimates camera and hand together. Its world-space hand error (W-MPJPE) is 59.21 mm on ARCTIC, 87.37 mm on HOT3D and 28.77 mm on EgoDex. HaWoR scores 95.39, 93.70 and 103.85 mm on the same three sets, and WiLoR+DROID-SLAM scores 65.86, 106.77 and 96.02 mm. InfiniHand's authors still list missing metric scale and temporal scale drift over long sequences as open limitations. MINT (arXiv 2609.04958) predicts camera trajectory, field of view and hands jointly on HOT3D, with camera RPE-T 4.69 mm and RPE-R 0.284 deg. StableHand (arXiv 2605.18553) reports 20-25% lower W-MPJPE than the strongest baseline on HOT3D and ARCTIC, mainly on long spans where hands are out of view. For full bodies, DuoMo (CVPR 2026) reports 16% lower world-space error on EMDB and 30% lower on RICH; I did not check absolute numbers (an earlier search snippet quoted WA-MPJPE about 66 mm on EMDB). WildHSR (arXiv 2609.29106) is the first feed-forward method to beat optimization-based baselines on EMDB-2 WA-MPJPE and RTE, at 10.1 fps. Portable robot-demonstration rigs mostly avoid drift through hardware rather than solving it. HiFi-UMI (arXiv 2607.25895) uses offline head-mounted stereo-inertial SLAM and claims 3 mm workspace-local end-effector accuracy. Other systems swap VIO for Vive trackers, because wrist-camera VIO still fails under fast motion, weak texture and occlusion by the hand. Three things remain open: metric, drift-free, online world-frame trajectories over minute-long manipulation; joint hand-object world tracking when the manipulated object breaks the static-scene assumption; and RGB-D or rigid-scene anchoring for bimanual object handling.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: HaWoR: World-Space Hand Motion Reconstruction from Egocentric Videos
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Separates hand motion in the camera frame from camera trajectory in the world frame. Uses an adaptive egocentric SLAM for the camera and a motion infiller to fill frames where a hand leaves the view.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: Dyn-HaMR: Recovering 4D Interacting Hand Motion from a Dynamic Camera
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Optimizes two-hand 4D motion in the world frame from a moving camera, using SLAM camera motion and hand priors. It is the baseline cited for ego-motion drift.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: InfiniHand: Streaming World-Space Hand Motion Estimation from Egocentric Video
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Streaming feed-forward model (11.19 FPS) that jointly estimates MANO hands, camera trajectory and hand location. W-MPJPE is 59.21 mm on ARCTIC, 87.37 mm on HOT3D and 28.77 mm on EgoDex, against HaWoR's 95.39, 93.70 and 103.85 mm. The authors state that scale drift over long sequences remains.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: MINT: A Unified Model for World-Space Camera and Hand Motion Estimation from Scalable Egocentric Pipeline Supervision
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Single model that predicts camera trajectory, field of view, hand state and hand visibility, trained on 1,021 hours of pseudo-labelled egocentric video. On HOT3D, camera RPE-T is 4.69 mm and RPE-R is 0.284 deg.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: StableHand: Quality-Aware Flow Matching for World-Space Dual-Hand Motion Estimation from Egocentric Video
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Flow-matching motion prior for both hands in the world frame, weighted by per-channel observation quality, aimed at long out-of-view and occluded spans. Reports 20-25% lower W-MPJPE on HOT3D and ARCTIC.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: EgoFound3R: End-to-End Egocentric Hand Reconstruction in World Space with Point-Wise Interaction Attributes
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Reconstructs world-space hands end to end, together with visibility, contact and distance attributes. Reports lower MPJPE on OakInk-v2 (-43.2%), TACO (-22.4%) and HOI4D (-11.6%) at about 6 times the throughput.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: DuoMo: Dual Motion Diffusion for World-Space Human Reconstruction
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Two diffusion models, one for motion in the camera frame and one that lifts it to a globally consistent world frame. Reports 16% lower world-space error on EMDB and 30% lower on RICH.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: WildHSR: Metric Feed-Forward 4D People-Scene Reconstruction from a 3D Foundation Model
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Feed-forward reconstruction of people and scene at metric scale with a learned scale head. Its abstract says it is the first feed-forward method to beat optimization-based baselines on EMDB-2 WA-MPJPE and RTE, and it runs at 10.1 fps.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: Human3R: Everyone Everywhere All at Once
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: One forward pass estimates metric-scale scene, world-frame human motion and camera poses from monocular video.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: OnlineHMR: Video-based Online World-Grounded Human Mesh Recovery
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Online world-frame human mesh recovery that reports EMDB results comparable to chunk-based methods. Only the search snippet was seen.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: HiFi-UMI: Learning Deployable Manipulation Policies from High-Fidelity UMI Data Alone
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Replaces drifting wrist VIO in UMI-style capture with offline head-mounted stereo-inertial SLAM and GPIO-synchronized sensors. Claims 3 mm workspace-local end-effector accuracy without external tracking.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: Zero-shot Reconstruction of In-Scene Object Manipulation from Video
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Reconstructs hand-object manipulation consistent with the scene rather than in hand-centric coordinates, so the result is metric and world-anchored. Numbers not checked.

evidence.crowdedness: HIGH: at least 10 papers from 2025-2026 attack world-frame drift directly. They come from large groups (Meta Reality Labs with CMU/Penn on DuoMo, Shanghai AI Lab/Zhejiang on InfiniHand, Imperial/TUM on StableHand, Daniilidis/Liu at Penn), and the body-centric EMDB/RICH line is especially saturated. The narrower case of jointly tracking hands and the manipulated object in the world frame from RGB-D or a wearable sensor is much less covered.
evidence.trend: rising: five or more egocentric world-space hand papers appeared between May and October 2026 alone (StableHand, MINT, InfiniHand, EgoFound3R, Hand-4DGS). They are driven by demand for human video as robot training data and by 3D foundation models (DROID-SLAM, then feed-forward joint camera-and-hand prediction). The field is moving from offline SLAM-plus-optimization to streaming feed-forward models.

skeptics.reasons: Not refuted, but it needs narrowing. Most of the 2025-2026 work I found reduces the problem without saturating any metric. (1) Vision-only egocentric hands: InfiniHand (arXiv 2609.35743, Sept 2026, streaming at 11 FPS) is the newest state of the art I found. It still reports W-MPJPE of 87.4 mm on HOT3D and 59.2 mm on ARCTIC, against WA-MPJPE of 35.8 and 43.6 mm. That gap means global camera and trajectory error still dominates. Its authors say the backbone lacks metric scale and that monocular pipelines inherit time-varying scale drift. HaWoR, Dyn-HaMR (CVPR 2025), EgoGrasp (2601.01050) and StableHand (2605.18553) report gains of roughly 10-25% over HaWoR, not a solved metric. MINT (2609.04958) reports low relative camera error on HOT3D (RPE-T 4.7 mm per step) but no absolute drift over long takes. (2) World-frame bodies: Human3R (2510.06219) runs online at 15 FPS, but EMDB-2 W-MPJPE is still 175-276 mm for JOSH, TRAM, GVHMR and Human3R, so this is far from saturated. (3) Robot demonstration rigs: here the pain point is largely being reduced to engineering by swapping the tracking hardware. FastUMI Pro fuses lighthouse tracking with visual-inertial odometry for millimetre-level pose; a search result attributes this to the FastUMI-100K line, and I did not open that paper. UMI-3D (2604.14089) uses wrist LiDAR SLAM and shows qualitative robustness but no numbers. YUBI (2606.10244) tracks Quest 3S controllers from a fixed rig. These fixes trade drift for infrastructure, weight or occlusion dropouts: YUBI filters untracked episodes and UMI-3D is single-arm and heavier. None of them publishes drift numbers that would show the problem is gone. Device SLAM such as Aria MPS also gives good head poses on instrumented headsets, so the instrumented-headset case is largely engineering. The open research problem is uninstrumented or wrist-mounted cameras that mostly see the hands and the manipulated object. Note for this author: a static RGB-D rig avoids ego-motion entirely, so the pain point matters to the thesis only if the work moves to head-worn or wrist-mounted capture.

skeptics.reframe: With instrumented capture (Aria MPS, VR or lighthouse trackers, wrist LiDAR), drift is now mostly a hardware and engineering trade-off. The open problem is uninstrumented monocular egocentric or wrist-camera video, where the view is dominated by the moving hands and object. There, world-frame hand error is still about 2-2.5x the trajectory-aligned error: W-MPJPE 87 mm vs WA-MPJPE 36 mm on HOT3D for InfiniHand (2026). Metric scale also drifts over time. Streaming methods do not yet keep drift bounded and metric over minute-long manipulation without loop closure or added sensors.

skeptics.reasons: The statement says the field cannot separate device motion from hand, body and object motion. As written, it holds only by bundling three different problems, each of which leans on a narrow or out-of-domain setup. (1) The headline number is undercut by its own source. ACE-Data-0 (arXiv 2607.28625, Table 5/6, fetched) reports world trajectory errors of 102.1 mm for HaWoR and 98.2 mm for Dyn-HaMR, both run with their own estimated SLAM. The exocentric HaPTIC baseline, from a static camera with no ego-motion at all, already reaches 63.0 mm. Most of the world-frame error is therefore monocular hand-to-camera depth and scale ambiguity, and ego-motion adds roughly 35-40 mm on top. The ACE rig itself measures head poses that 'do not drift', so the dataset shows that device pose is solvable with instrumentation. (2) The 'metres of drift' evidence comes from long-range, outdoor or broadcast body trajectories that are not manipulation settings: WorldPose (a soccer pitch, broadcast cameras), EMDB (81 m walks) and the LiDAR/IMU line HSC4D, SLOPER4D, HiSC4D, ClimbingCap and likely RELI11D. That line comes largely from one group, the Xiamen University LiDAR-capture group, and its distance-proportional drift is the textbook dead-reckoning result the SLAM and inertial navigation communities have treated for decades. (3) The robot-capture evidence rests on specific hardware. The T265 jumps and scale distortion come from FastUMI-100K using a discontinued 2019 Intel sensor, and published T265 studies attribute the jumps to relocalization or loop-closure corrections. The Vive dropouts come from one sanding study with 21 users. (4) Other communities treat device pose at manipulation scale as largely solved. Aria MPS closed-loop trajectories are documented at no more than about 1.5 cm global RMSE at room scale, and XR headsets (Quest, Vision Pro) ship robust 6-DoF tracking. HOT3D, Nymeria and Ego-Exo4D all supply such device poses, so 'cannot separate device motion' does not hold when device SLAM is available. What survives is narrower but real. Methods that get only raw monocular egocentric video (internet or Ego4D-style video, no device SLAM) must estimate camera motion when hands and the manipulated object dominate a narrow or fisheye view. They then also have to fix metric hand depth, which is why HaWoR, Dyn-HaMR and the MINT/EgoPipeline pseudo-labelling work exist. The supporting groups are genuinely diverse (Meta, MPI, ETH, Bristol, Chinese robotics labs), so this is not a one-dataset artifact. However, the causal claim (ego-motion as the main error) and the magnitude claims (decimetres to metres) are artifacts of setup choices. For a fixed RGB-D or exocentric rig, like the author's, the pain point does not apply.

skeptics.reframe: When only raw monocular egocentric video is available, with no device SLAM or IMU poses (internet, Ego4D-style or legacy footage), current methods cannot recover metric, world-frame hand and object trajectories. The camera has to be estimated from views that hands and the manipulated object dominate, and those views break static-scene odometry. Even with a perfect camera, monocular hand-to-camera depth and scale leave about 60 mm of trajectory error, as the static exocentric baseline on ACE-Data-0 shows. When device poses exist (Aria MPS, XR headsets, mocap), drift is at the centimetre level and is not the bottleneck.

skeptics.reasons:
I tried to refute P07 as a problem with no research question, and the refutation fails for the core part. Some sub-claims do fit the refutation: T265 VIO jumps, Vive tracker dropouts under tool vibration, headset tracking loss under fast motion, and IMU-suit drift over tens of metres are hardware or integration problems. Those are fixed with better sensors, more anchors, offline bundle adjustment, or discarding bad clips. Metres-scale drift of whole-body trajectories over 81 m also lies outside the author's field.

The remaining core still poses a research question. When the camera is worn by the person doing the manipulating, much of the image is hands and a moving object. These break the static-world assumption behind SLAM and loop closure. The ACE-Data-0 benchmark (arXiv 2607.28625, July 2026) reports that ego-motion, not finger articulation, dominates egocentric world-frame hand error: about 98-102 mm against 63 mm for the best exocentric method. That error does not go away with more annotation money or better hardware, because no static landmark constrains the object.

Reviewers at top venues already treat this as significant. HaWoR (CVPR 2025 Highlight) and Dyn-HaMR (CVPR 2025 Highlight) are both about separating camera motion from hand motion. Several arXiv papers from Aug-Oct 2026 are still working on it: MINT, EgoFound3R, ACE-Ego-Hand and MEgoVista. MINT states that staged pipelines prevent joint modelling of camera and hand motion and that paired world-space labels are scarce.

Research questions that should survive review:
(a) Can the manipulated rigid object and hand-object contact act as constraints on ego-motion, rather than being masked out as outliers? This means estimating camera, hands and object jointly, with rigidity and contact.
(b) Can drift in world-frame hand-object tracking be bounded causally, in real time, when no loop closure is available?
(c) How should world-frame accuracy be evaluated when the ground truth itself drifts? For example, EMDB's reference trajectory drifts 23.4 cm over 81 m.

The weaknesses are real. The area is crowded, with strong groups and foundation-model pipelines. Incremental SLAM-plus-hand-regressor papers will look derivative. Part of the stated pain is better framed as data scarcity than as method. The question has to be framed around hand-object interaction, not general camera drift, to be novel.

skeptics.reframe: When the camera is worn by the person manipulating an object, the hands and object fill much of the view and break the static-scene assumption behind visual odometry. Current methods therefore mask the hands and object out as outliers and accept 10 cm-class world-frame drift. The open question is whether estimating camera, hands and rigid object jointly can bound world-frame hand-object drift causally, in real time, without loop closure. The joint estimate would use object rigidity, hand-object contact and inertial cues, and would need an evaluation protocol that does not trust drifting world-frame ground truth.

research_questions.question: When a head-worn or wrist-worn depth camera (or RGB plus a metric-depth model) films a person manipulating a known rigid object, can a causal estimator bound world-frame drift of the camera, both hands and the object? The object and its support surface would be treated as switching landmarks: a static anchor while the object rests, and a body rigidly attached to the grasping hand while it is held, with the switch driven by an estimated contact state. The alternative it is compared against is the current practice of masking the hands and object out of odometry as outliers.
research_questions.why_top_venue: Masking is what current pipelines do. HaWoR (CVPR 2025) and Dyn-HaMR (CVPR 2025) run SLAM on the background with the hands masked out, and the newest streaming models (InfiniHand, arXiv 2609.35743; MINT, arXiv 2609.04958) still leave a large gap between world-frame and trajectory-aligned error. InfiniHand reports W-MPJPE 87 mm against WA-MPJPE 36 mm on HOT3D. Its authors list scale drift over long sequences as unsolved. World-grounded hand-object work is all offline or takes the camera as given. WHOLE (arXiv 2602.22209) takes Aria metric-SLAM poses as input and is optimization-based. EgoGrasp (arXiv 2601.01050) and the Penn zero-shot in-scene manipulation paper (arXiv 2512.19684) are multi-stage offline pipelines. None of them uses the manipulated object as an ego-motion constraint, and none runs causally. Dynamic SLAM (DynoSAM, arXiv 2501.11893) does estimate camera and rigid-object motion jointly, but it has no hand coupling and no contact-gated switch between landmark and dynamic body. Three 2026 skeptics independently converged on the same open core: joint camera-hand-object estimation, causal, without loop closure. A clean result there with stratified evidence would be a CVPR/ICCV/ECCV paper.
research_questions.method_sketch: A sliding-window factor graph, for example GTSAM iSAM2, with these nodes per frame: camera pose T_wc, object pose T_wo, and the global pose of each hand. Articulation comes from an off-the-shelf regressor (WiLoR or HaMeR) and is not optimized. Factors: (1) RGB-D or dense learned odometry on background pixels only, using masks from a hand and object segmenter; (2) camera-to-object pose factors from a model-based tracker in the FoundationPose style, using the object mesh; (3) hand-to-camera factors whose translation is fixed by sensor depth or metric depth, which removes the monocular depth ambiguity; (4) a contact-gated object motion factor. When the object is not in contact, a strong static prior T_wo(t) = T_wo(t-1) makes the near-field object, which gaze keeps in view, act as a high-parallax landmark. When it is grasped, a soft rigid-attachment factor holds T_wh^-1 T_wo constant, so the hand and object constrain each other through occlusion. (5) A support-plane factor for the table, which is static and in view throughout. Contact state comes from a small classifier over hand-object distance and from whether the object's motion agrees with the background flow. A robust kernel and a switch variable let a wrong contact label be rejected. Novelty claim: the role switching is driven by contact and coupled to the hand. Plain dynamic SLAM has neither, and feed-forward hand models have no object anchor.
research_questions.minimum_experiment: Evaluate on HOT3D (Aria and Quest 3 sequences, which have motion-capture ground truth for the device, hands and objects, plus object meshes) and on the ARCTIC egocentric view (motion-capture ground truth, object meshes). Neither has a depth sensor, so depth comes from a metric-depth model. Add a real-depth check on HOI4D and H2O, which are egocentric RGB-D; their camera poses come from reconstruction or calibration, so report them as secondary results. Ablations on one pipeline: masked background odometry only; plus object factors without contact gating; plus contact gating; plus the support plane. Context baselines: published HaWoR, Dyn-HaMR, WiLoR+DROID-SLAM and InfiniHand numbers on the same splits. Metrics: camera ATE and RPE, drift per minute, W-MPJPE, WA-MPJPE, object world-frame ADD, and hand-object relative error. Stratify everything by the fraction of the image covered by hands and object, by background texture and by head angular velocity. Success criterion: a 20-30% lower camera drift and W-MPJPE on the hard strata than masked odometry, with no loss on easy clips, running causally at 5 fps or more on one GPU. A small self-captured validation set is optional (see the assets field).
research_questions.data_and_hardware: Public data only for the main claims: HOT3D, ARCTIC, HOI4D and H2O, all with object meshes. Whether HOT3D's test-split ground truth is publicly released was not checked; it may be held for challenges, in which case the work uses the train and validation splits. Compute: one 24 GB GPU for inference with off-the-shelf models, plus training of a small contact classifier; no large-model training. Optional: one consumer RGB-D camera (a short-range RealSense, Orbbec or Azure Kinect class) on a head strap or wrist mount, about 0.5-1 TB of storage, and GTSAM or a similar solver on the CPU.
research_questions.risks: (1) On HOT3D and ARCTIC the background may carry enough texture that masked odometry is already adequate. The gain would then appear only on a small hard stratum, and the paper would read as incremental, so the stratification has to be planned from day one. (2) Feed-forward models trained on 1,000-5,000 hours of video (MINT, InfiniHand) are improving quickly. EgoFound3R (arXiv 2610.01210) already predicts contact attributes, and a big group could add object tokens within months. (3) Requiring a known mesh limits scope, and reviewers will ask for a model-free variant. (4) Contact-label errors inject drift. (5) The DynoSAM, VDO-SLAM and object-level SLAM prior art must be cited and clearly separated, or the work will be seen as an engineering combination of DynoSAM, FoundationPose and WiLoR. (6) A pipeline of three heavy networks may not reach real-time rates, so the claim should be made about causality, not frame rate.

research_questions.question: Where does world-frame error in egocentric hand-object reconstruction actually come from: camera ego-motion drift, the metric hand-to-camera depth and scale ambiguity, or infilling while hands are out of view? And can a metric that needs no motion-capture ground truth, built on self-consistency, rank methods the same way motion-capture ground truth does, so that drift can be measured on in-the-wild and RGB-D footage?
research_questions.why_top_venue: The published evidence disagrees about the dominant error source. ACE-Data-0 (arXiv 2607.28625; device pose measured by OptiTrack markers) reports ego trajectory errors of 98.2 mm for Dyn-HaMR and 102.1 mm for HaWoR, and blames ego-motion. A skeptic read a static exocentric baseline (HaPTIC) at 63 mm in the same paper, which implies that much of the error remains even with no camera motion; that figure was not re-checked here. WHOLE (arXiv 2602.22209) is given Aria metric-SLAM camera poses and still reports a hand W-MPJPE of 10.41 cm on HOT3D-CLIP. InfiniHand shows a gap of about 50 mm between W-MPJPE and WA-MPJPE. World-frame ground truth itself drifts as well: EMDB's reference drifts 23.4 cm over 81 m. No paper decomposes the error with oracle substitution, and none offers a ground-truth-free drift metric for manipulation. A careful, reproducible decomposition plus a validated metric would steer a fast-moving subfield. That makes it a credible NeurIPS Datasets and Benchmarks paper, or a CVPR or ECCV analysis paper if paired with a simple strong baseline.
research_questions.method_sketch: Oracle-substitution study. For each public method with released code (HaWoR, Dyn-HaMR, WiLoR+DROID-SLAM, and InfiniHand, MINT or WHOLE if released), swap in one ground-truth component at a time on HOT3D and ARCTIC: ground-truth camera trajectory, ground-truth metric hand-root depth, and ground-truth visibility infill. The error that each swap removes is attributed to that component, with bootstrap confidence intervals and a split by clip length so error growth over time can be measured. Ground-truth-free metrics: (a) rest-pose closure, meaning that an object placed back where it started, or a hand returning to rest, should return to the same world pose; (b) consistency of the static support plane, meaning the table plane should stay fixed in the world; (c) consistency of a static object on re-observation, meaning that a resting object seen again after a camera excursion should not have moved. Validate each metric by rank correlation with motion-capture W-MPJPE and camera ATE across methods and clips. Then apply the metrics to HOI4D, H2O and self-captured footage that has no motion-capture ground truth.
research_questions.minimum_experiment: Run four or more methods on HOT3D and ARCTIC with three oracle swaps each, and produce an error-attribution table per dataset and per clip-length bin. Compute Kendall tau between each ground-truth-free metric and the motion-capture errors over at least 200 clips, and set a pass bar such as tau of 0.6 or more. Report one demonstration of the metrics on non-motion-capture RGB-D footage. A positive outcome is a clear ranking of the error sources that differs between datasets or clip lengths, together with a metric that tracks motion-capture error.
research_questions.data_and_hardware: HOT3D and ARCTIC for the motion-capture side; HOI4D, H2O and optional self-capture for the side with no ground truth. One GPU for inference only. Released code is needed for the baselines: HaWoR and Dyn-HaMR are public. Code availability for InfiniHand, MINT and WHOLE was not verified.
research_questions.risks: (1) Analysis papers are hard to place at CVPR without a method, so a baseline should come out of the study, for example using RQ1 as its demonstration. (2) If closed-source 2026 methods cannot be run, reviewers may call the study dated. (3) Rest-pose closure needs clips in which objects are returned, which may make up a small fraction of HOT3D. (4) The degree of disagreement between datasets is unknown in advance, and if one source dominates everywhere the finding may look obvious. (5) Protocol differences between papers, such as clip length and the alignment used for W-MPJPE, must be harmonized carefully.

research_questions.question: Can a wrist-mounted consumer RGB-D camera produce end-effector and object trajectories for robot demonstrations with bounded drift and no external tracking, by anchoring on the manipulated object and the support surface instead of on the background, which hand occlusion hides? How close can it come to lighthouse or headset-SLAM rigs?
research_questions.why_top_venue: Portable demonstration rigs currently avoid drift with extra hardware rather than solving it. FastUMI adds lighthouse fusion (claim seen only in a search snippet, not verified). HiFi-UMI (arXiv 2607.25895) uses offline head-mounted stereo-inertial SLAM and claims 3 mm workspace-local accuracy. YUBI uses Quest controllers. UMI-3D adds a wrist LiDAR and reports no drift numbers. Several of these papers also report that wrist VIO fails under hand occlusion, weak texture and fast motion. A vision-only, wrist-only rig with measured drift would interest ICRA, RA-L and possibly CoRL, but only if the trajectories are shown to matter downstream.
research_questions.method_sketch: Reuse the RQ1 graph with no articulated hand. The gripper or hand pose comes from fixed extrinsics; the object factor is again switched by contact state, and the support plane is a factor. A cheap IMU is optional if the camera has one. Ground truth without motion capture: a static RGB-D camera with ArUco markers on the desk and on the object gives a drift-free reference for the object's world trajectory, and for the wrist camera when its own marker is visible to the static camera. Desk markers are masked out of the wrist stream so they cannot leak into the estimate.
research_questions.minimum_experiment: Record about 30-60 pick, place and handover clips of 1-3 minutes, varying speed and texture. Compare wrist RGB-D VO with masking, ORB-SLAM3 or DROID-SLAM in RGB-D mode, and the object-anchored graph. Report drift per minute and object-pose ADD against the static ArUco reference, and quantify the reference's own error with a repeated static-placement test. A downstream check needs a borrowed arm: replaying trajectories, or a small policy-learning comparison. Without it the paper is RA-L or ICRA at best.
research_questions.data_and_hardware: One wrist-mountable RGB-D camera, the existing static RGB-D camera, printed ArUco markers, and one GPU. A borrowed robot arm is needed for any CoRL or RSS claim. Self-collected data is required, because no public wrist RGB-D dataset with drift-free reference poses was found.
research_questions.risks: (1) ArUco reference accuracy, likely a few millimetres at desk range but not measured here, may not be clearly better than the method being tested. (2) Reviewers will ask why not add a headset or lighthouse, as HiFi-UMI and FastUMI do, so cost and robustness have to be argued explicitly. (3) A single subject and a single desk limit generality. (4) Without robot results, CoRL and RSS are out of reach. (5) The approach overlaps RQ1 and should be framed as its application track, not a separate paper, unless the robot results are strong.

fit.thesis_assets_help: Small edge, mostly indirect. The thesis's static RGB-D desk rig has no ego-motion, so P07 does not arise in the thesis itself; pursuing it is a pivot to head-worn or wrist-worn capture. Four assets carry over. (1) The ArUco-marked object with metric pose, seen by a fixed camera, gives a drift-free world-frame reference without motion capture. Adding a second, moving camera to the existing desk gives a small self-made validation set for object world drift and wrist-camera drift (RQ1 optional check, RQ3 ground truth, RQ2 metric validation). This is the most useful asset. (2) The measured/held/constrained provenance labels are conceptually close to the switch, driven by contact state, between an object as a landmark and an object as a dynamic body. They also suit evaluation that states confidence honestly when reference poses are inferred rather than measured. (3) Experience with a causal 30 fps chain and the object-conditioned recovery of an occluded holding arm transfer to the rigid-attachment factor between hand and object during a grasp. (4) The Unity twin could display world-frame drift qualitatively, but it adds no evidence. The 28 recordings of one subject come from a static camera and have no value as a benchmark for this problem.
fit.what_a_small_lab_cannot_do_here: The lab cannot train the streaming feed-forward camera-and-hand models that now lead the vision-only egocentric line. MINT trains on about 1,021 hours of pseudo-labelled video and InfiniHand on about 5,000 hours of aggregated egocentric data, so the lab should not try to beat them on raw W-MPJPE leaderboards. Without motion capture or instrumented headsets (Aria with MPS, OptiTrack-marked devices as in ACE-Data-0), the lab cannot build a new egocentric dataset with drift-free ground truth for hands. It cannot address metre-scale global body drift (EMDB, RICH, WorldPose, LiDAR-IMU suits), which is crowded and needs outdoor or large-space capture. It also cannot build or validate UMI-class rigs at scale with lighthouse, Vive or headset SLAM, or show policy-learning gains without a borrowed robot arm. Searches for this analysis were limited: the WebSearch budget was exhausted, and the new evidence came from arXiv abstract, HTML and search pages via WebFetch. Code availability for InfiniHand, MINT and WHOLE, the public release of HOT3D test ground truth, and the FastUMI lighthouse claim remain unverified.

painpoint.name: Metric depth and placement from monocular RGB

evidence.latest_state: The 2026 papers I could check improve camera-space hand error, but the gap between absolute and aligned error is still large. ScaleHP (arXiv 2606.25619, June 2026) adds a scale token and a perspective-constrained least-squares solve. It reports CS-MPJPE 35.8 mm on FreiHand against PA-MPJPE 5.0 mm, and PA-MPJPE 4.6 / 5.9 mm on DexYCB / HO3Dv3. So metric placement error is still roughly seven times articulation error. EgoForce (SIGGRAPH 2026) uses the forearm as a metric cue and a ray-space closed-form solver, and cuts camera-space MPJPE by up to 28% on HOT3D. CS-ViT (arXiv 2609.24424) reports up to 37.1% lower CS-MJE than the prior best on HO3D. In video and world space, HandFlow (arXiv 2607.11221) reports about 30% lower world-space pose error than the strongest baseline on DexYCB/HOT3D. MINT (arXiv 2609.04958) still headlines an aligned metric: 13.6 mm PA-MPJPE-p on HOT3D, plus camera RPE-T 4.69 mm. This confirms that evaluation by alignment persists. ESTHER (arXiv 2609.34817) takes the stereo route and claims to keep metric scale when collapsed to one view, which is an implicit admission that monocular-only training does not. For RGB-only category-level object pose, YOPO (ICRA 2026) reports 54.1% at 10deg10cm on REAL275; I did not verify a matched RGB-D comparison number. For TAPVid-3D, a September 2026 SSM tracker reports mean metric AJ 0.256 on minival, and ARROW (Oct 2026) claims state of the art. The joint hand-to-object metric placement error that robot retargeting needs is still mostly unmeasured: WHOLE and ViDiHand give no such numbers in their abstracts.
