evidence.crowdedness: HIGH: I verified more than 15 papers from 2025-2026 that target metric hand or hand-object placement from monocular or egocentric RGB. They come from many groups (DFKI/MPI, IDEA, Stanford, NTU, CAS, robot-learning labs), and one appeared at SIGGRAPH 2026, one at CVPR 2025 and one at ICRA 2026. Joint hand-to-object metric placement for robot labels, with a metric (unaligned) benchmark, remains less crowded.
evidence.trend: rising: arXiv submissions from May to October 2026 on camera-space, world-space and metric hand pose keep increasing, driven by robot data engines built on egocentric and internet video. Stereo smart-glasses work (ESTHER) and metric foundation priors (MoGe-2, Metric3D) feed into it.

skeptics.reasons: I found no 2025-2026 work that solves P08 or turns it into engineering. The best recent methods are much better than older ones, but their absolute (non-aligned) errors are still several times their aligned errors and stay at the centimetre level. That is the gap P08 describes. The web search budget was already used up, so I made no WebSearch calls. All evidence below comes from WebFetch of the arXiv API and arXiv HTML pages. (1) Hands. EgoForce (arXiv 2605.12498, May 2026) has the best camera-space MPJPE: 43.9 mm on HOT3D, 25.0 mm on H2O and 49.5 mm on ARCTIC. Its Procrustes-aligned error is 6.6 mm on HOT3D, so the absolute error is about 7x the aligned one, and the authors say it 'remains sensitive to camera intrinsics' and needs calibrated 3D training data. In the same table, the HaMeR-with-depth baseline is off by metres (4493.7 mm on HOT3D). EgoFound3R (arXiv 2610.01210, Oct 2026) reports raw MPJPE of about 47-52 mm on OakInk-v2, TACO and HOI4D, against about 17-23 mm after Sim(3) alignment; its world-frame error on HOI4D is 159.7 mm. ESTHER (arXiv 2609.34817, Sep 2026) was trained with stereo on 194 h of its own data and still has a 32.5 mm wrist error in monocular mode, against 21.3 mm with stereo. It gets its metric scale from a learned, camera-specific prior rather than from geometry. (2) Objects. The BOP 2024 report (arXiv 2504.02812) gives 68.2 AR for the best RGB-only unseen-object 6D localization on BOP-Classic-Core, against 82.1 AR for RGB-D (FreeZeV2.1), so the modality gap is still about 14 AR. (3) 3D point tracking. A Sep 2026 state-space-model tracker (arXiv 2609.34035) claims the 'highest absolute metric accuracy' with a metric AJ of only 0.256 on the TAPVid-3D minival split, so the benchmark is far from saturated. (4) Products. Shipping hand tracking (headsets with several cameras, Vision Pro with stereo and depth) avoids monocular metric hands rather than solving it; I did not verify this against a source in this task. What weakens P08 is not a solution but crowding. At least six 2026 preprints (EgoForce, EgoFound3R, ESTHER, Hand3R, InfiniHand, StableHand) target world-space or metric hands, and world-scale foundation models (MoGe-2, VGGT-style reconstruction) are being used as metric stages. The generic claim 'monocular hands lack metric depth' is therefore a crowded line of work. The parts that remain open and are measured poorly are: hand-to-object and hand-to-hand relative placement at contact precision (about 1 cm or better), and metrics that do not align the error away. On the evidence for P08, RGB-D or stereo closes much of the gap, which fits the author's RGB-D setting as a teacher or as a source of ground truth.

skeptics.reframe: Metric hand pose from monocular RGB is now a crowded line of work, and in 2026 it still stalls at camera-space errors of about 25-50 mm on HOT3D, H2O and ARCTIC, against aligned errors of about 6-9 mm. What stays open and unmeasured is metric relative placement between hand and object, and between the two hands, at contact precision (about 1 cm or better). Today's metrics hide this error through root-relative, Procrustes or Sim(3) alignment, or through ground-truth rescaling. Calibrated RGB-D or stereo capture is the natural source of ground truth and of supervision for a contact-level placement benchmark and a matching method.

skeptics.reasons:
Artifact test, overall: P08 survives as a field-level problem, but several of its sharper claims are artifacts and should be cut.

Breadth of support (argues against an artifact). I mapped the 46 paper ids through w3_digest/all.json. The paper ids in field_papers.json do not match, so that file cannot be used for this lookup. The supporting papers come from unrelated groups and settings:
- hand-object datasets: ARCTIC, MPI/ETH, CVPR 2023; HOT3D, Meta, CVPR 2025; AssemblyHands; Ego-Exo4D; RenderIH;
- object pose: the T-RO 2024 monocular 6D survey, BOP 2023 and Omni6DPose;
- generic 3D point tracking: TAPVid-3D, Google DeepMind, NeurIPS 2024;
- human placement: BEV, CVPR 2022;
- robot-learning data engines: HuRo, RoboEdit and MINT/EgoPipeline;
- HANDS 2024/2025 challenge reports.

Each group reports the same failure in its own setting:
- ARCTIC: relative root error of 28-52 mm from a single view.
- HOT3D: 3D-lifting recall at 5 cm is 11.1% with MonoDepth against 42.6% with stereo, and the lifting error lies mostly along the optical axis.
- TAPVid-3D: 3D-AJ of 9.3 against 2D-AJ of 59.1.
- T-RO survey: RGB-only category-level pose trails RGB-D on REAL275, and the gap appears to be widening.
- MINT: hand translation error of 0.196 m on HOT3D, and the trajectory is mis-scaled by a factor of 0.47 to 1.41.

No single dataset or lab drives it.

What is an artifact or overstated:
1. The claim that "standard metrics align the error away, so the gap is neither measured nor penalized" reflects the hand-pose community's habits (PA-MPJPE on FreiHAND and HO3D), not the field's. ARCTIC and InterHand2.6M already report MRRPE, the hand-to-hand and hand-to-object placement error; RenderIH still reports 14.15 mm MRRPE. HaWoR (CVPR 2025, fetched) reports W-MPJPE, WA-MPJPE, RTE and ATE-S with estimated scale. The body community standardised world-frame metrics on EMDB. BOP has always scored metric errors. The gap is measured; it is simply not the headline metric on some hand benchmarks.
2. Some evidence does not support the claim:
   - SimpleHand on DexYCB (12.4 vs 5.5 mm) compares root-relative MPJPE with PA-MPJPE. Both remove root depth, so the gap is rotation and scale, not placement along the viewing ray.
   - The Ego-Exo4D comparison of MPJPE with PA-MPJPE (24.8 vs 8.3 mm) is likely the same kind of comparison.
   - TAPVid-3D's DriveTrack figure comes from outdoor driving scenes, so it says nothing about near-range hands.
   The "absolute error is two to three times aligned error" framing is therefore partly mismeasured.
3. Other communities treat the underlying ambiguity as solved by the sensor:
   - Single-view scale and depth ambiguity is a textbook fact.
   - Capture systems choose stereo, multi-view, RGB-D or ARKit and SLAM headsets for exactly this reason; the pain point's own fixes list stereo, triangulation and RGB-D as closing much of the gap.
   - In the robot-learning group, the problem exists mainly because those pipelines choose uncalibrated internet video (HaMeR or HaWoR plus learned metric depth); sensor-equipped capture setups avoid it.
4. Progress is fast:
   - HaWoR cuts world-space hand W-MPJPE on HOT3D from 119-156 mm to 33.2 mm by combining SLAM with Metric3D.
   - MegaSaM and foundation metric-depth models such as Metric3D, UniDepth and MoGe-2 are shrinking the problem. I have not verified their near-range accuracy for hands.

What survives: for monocular hand-object input, absolute and especially relative near-range placement is still tens of millimetres off: 33 mm W-MPJPE at best on HOT3D, 28-52 mm MRRPE on ARCTIC and 196 mm translation error for MINT. That is too coarse for contact-accurate labels, and robot-learning pipelines report missed contacts and penetration after retargeting.

Narrow it to monocular hand and object placement at contact accuracy; drop the "unmeasured" and "PA hides it" framing.

Relevance to this thesis: the thesis uses RGB-D, which the field already treats as the fix, so this pain point is mainly an opportunity to supply metric reference data. It is not a gap the thesis's own sensing setup suffers from.

Limits of this check: the WebSearch budget was already used up (200 of 200 for the session) when this task ran, so I made no searches. Checks were limited to WebFetch and the local digest. ARCTIC's MRRPE figures come from the digest records; the CVF page returned 403.

skeptics.reframe: From monocular RGB, the relative and absolute 3D placement of hands and objects at near range is still tens of millimetres off: 33 mm world-space MPJPE at best on HOT3D (HaWoR), 28-52 mm relative root error on ARCTIC, and about 0.2 m hand translation error in video-to-robot pipelines. That is too coarse for contact-accurate metric labels. Stereo, multi-view or RGB-D capture removes most of the error, so the open problem is calibration-free, contact-accurate monocular placement. It is not a problem that the field fails to measure.

skeptics.reasons:
Refutation attempt. Part of P08 really is a known solution waiting for resources. Stereo, multi-view triangulation and RGB-D already close most of the gap (pinned evidence: paper 578 drops HaMeR depth and triangulates instead; about 5 mm MRRTE gain from RGB-D on OphNet-3D). Several sub-complaints are bookkeeping rather than science: Procrustes alignment hides absolute error (1118), and evaluations rescale with ground-truth scale (444). Reporting absolute MPJPE alongside PA-MPJPE is a reporting fix, not a paper. The general-purpose monocular metric-depth line is crowded and moves fast. I verified MoGe-2 (arXiv 2507.02546, metric-scale point maps from one image), HaWoR (arXiv 2501.02973, world-space egocentric hand motion via adaptive SLAM plus an infiller) and Dyn-HaMR (arXiv 2412.12861, global 4D hand motion from a moving camera via SLAM plus priors). So 'add a metric-depth stage to a hand pipeline' is already done, and an incremental version would read as engineering. For this author, who owns an RGB-D sensor, the deployment problem is largely bypassed by the sensor, which weakens P08 as their own core problem.

Why it is not refuted. The evidence shows the problem is unsolved even with these tools, and the failure is specific and measurable. Monocular metric-depth stages mis-scale in opposite directions on different datasets (under on HOT3D, over on ARCTIC). Absolute hand error is still 2-3x the aligned error (DexYCB 12.4 vs 5.5 mm; Ego-Exo4D challenge winner 24.80 vs 8.31 mm). TAPVid-3D 3D-AJ is 9.3 against a 2D-AJ of 59.1. Depth regularisation and bundle-adjustment fixes leave 20-43 mm wrist and fingertip residuals. Video-to-robot data engines built on HaMeR or HaWoR produce missed contacts and penetration after retargeting (1382). The error persists for a structural reason: one view cannot fix depth along the viewing ray, generic depth priors are trained on room- and scene-scale content rather than the 0.2-0.8 m range where hands operate, and hand and object scale are coupled. Neither more annotation money nor more compute fixes that. At least three questions are significant enough for a top-venue reviewer:

(1) Can the joint near-field metric placement of two hands and an object be identified from monocular video by combining known physical rulers? Candidates are the anthropometric hand-shape prior, contact and non-penetration constraints, known or estimated object size, and parallax from multiple frames. If so, with what identifiability and uncertainty along the ray?

(2) Does ray-aware, uncertainty-calibrated placement measurably reduce failures in downstream robot retargeting compared with aligned-metric-optimal estimators? This links a vision metric to a robotics outcome (CoRL, RSS, ICRA).

(3) What evaluation protocol, without alignment, predicts usefulness as action labels?

An RGB-D rig such as the author's can supply metric ground truth to supervise or evaluate the monocular setting. A paper built only on that benchmark would be weaker than one built on (1).

Residual risk: the window is closing quickly. HaWoR, Dyn-HaMR and the MoGe/Depth-Pro class of models, plus work from 2025-2026 that I could not search (the search budget was exhausted), may already target metric hand-object placement. The novelty of (1) is therefore unverified. The author would also be working in the monocular setting rather than their RGB-D one.

skeptics.reframe: Generic monocular metric-depth priors mis-scale the 0.2-0.8 m range where hands work: under on HOT3D, over on ARCTIC, with 2-3x absolute-to-aligned error and 20-43 mm residuals after refinement. The research question is whether the metric placement of two hands relative to an object can be identified and certified from monocular video. The approach would combine physical rulers (an anthropometric hand-shape prior, contact and non-penetration, object size, parallax from multiple frames) in a joint estimator that is uncertainty-calibrated along the viewing ray. It would be evaluated without alignment, by how well it predicts robot retargeting success, with RGB-D or multi-view capture supplying metric ground truth.

research_questions.question: RQ1 (main). Is the centimetre-level camera-space error floor of monocular hand estimators mostly one unresolved per-sequence metric scale factor, with a spread close to population hand-size variation? If so, can a joint estimator that fuses independent physical rulers bring metric hand-to-object placement along the viewing ray to contact precision (about 1 cm) and give calibrated uncertainty along the ray? The rulers are a known or estimated object size transferred to the hand through contact and non-penetration, a metric-depth foundation prior with a learned near-range bias, multi-frame parallax, and the anthropometric hand-shape prior. The estimator should work even when absolute scale stays ambiguous.
research_questions.why_top_venue: The 2026 state of the art still has camera-space errors several times the aligned errors. EgoForce reports 43.9 mm camera-space MPJPE against 6.6 mm PA on HOT3D. ScaleHP reports 35.8 mm CS-MPJPE against 5.0 mm PA on FreiHand. HaWoR reaches 33.2 mm W-MPJPE at best. Robot data engines report missed contacts and penetration after retargeting. Under a pinhole camera, scaling the whole scene about the camera centre is an exact ambiguity, so only metric priors can fix it. The field has added priors one at a time: hand scale (arXiv 2210.11384, 2022), the forearm (EgoForce), a scale token (ScaleHP), stereo-taught scale (ESTHER), and object scale through contact (ArtHOI 2603.25791). None of these accounts for where the error comes from. That accounting is the novel part: a falsifiable error-floor hypothesis (error roughly equal to depth times the hand-size coefficient of variation, about 25-40 mm at 0.5 m), an identifiability argument for which rulers fix which unknowns, and calibrated posteriors along the ray. This is an analysis-plus-method contribution that CVPR, ICCV and ECCV reviewers reward, and it is not a leaderboard race. I could not verify by search that the error-floor decomposition has not been done; the arXiv abstract queries in this task found no direct match.
research_questions.method_sketch: (1) Error accounting. Run 3-4 public estimators (HaMeR or WiLoR, a camera-space method such as EgoForce or ScaleHP if code is released, HaWoR for video) on DexYCB, HO3Dv3, HOT3D and ARCTIC. Split the unaligned error into three parts: a per-sequence scale s (best similarity about the camera centre), residual error along the ray, and lateral and articulation error. Add oracle ablations: GT MANO shape (beta), GT scale, and GT ray depth. Regress the error on depth and on the subject's deviation from mean hand size. (2) Ruler fusion. Build a small probabilistic factor graph per sequence on top of frozen front ends. Unknowns: s, per-frame hand root depth along the ray, object 6D pose and scale, and optional camera motion. Factors: the hand-shape prior (anthropometric distribution, not a point estimate); an RGB model-based object pose (FoundationPose, GigaPose or MegaPose with CAD) or a category size prior when the object is model-free; a MoGe-2, Depth Pro or UniDepth depth prior with a near-range scale and shift bias learned on the training split; contact and non-penetration terms between the hand and object meshes; and temporal smoothness and parallax from MegaSaM or VGGT camera poses when the camera moves. Solve with Gauss-Newton or Levenberg-Marquardt. Use a Laplace approximation or sampling to get the posterior along the ray, and report which ruler dominates each frame as a provenance label. (3) Learn the per-cue noise models on training splits and check calibration on held-out data.
research_questions.minimum_experiment: Four tables on public data. T1: error decomposition of 3-4 baselines on DexYCB, HO3Dv3 and HOT3D (ARCTIC optional). It shows how much of the unaligned error is the scale term, and how error scales with depth and with hand-size deviation. T2: oracle ablations, with the error left over after GT shape, GT scale and GT ray depth. T3: the fused estimator against the strongest available camera-space and world-space baselines. Metrics are unaligned: hand-to-object relative root error (an MRRPE-style measure), signed contact-distance error at GT contact frames, absolute root error, CS-MPJPE, and PA-MPJPE as a sanity check. Ablate each ruler, and cover both the known-CAD and model-free object settings. T4: uncertainty calibration along the ray (coverage at 68 and 95 percent, NLL) against ensembles or MC-dropout baselines. Success means hand-to-object relative ray error at contact frames of about 10 mm or less with a known object, and absolute error near the measured anthropometric floor without one. If the scale term does not dominate T1, the hypothesis is refuted, and the paper becomes a negative-result analysis plus a fusion method.
research_questions.data_and_hardware: Public data only: DexYCB (multi-view RGB-D, YCB CAD, MANO GT), HO3Dv3 (RGB-D, YCB), HOT3D (egocentric Aria and Quest 3 with mocap GT, both hands, 33 objects), ARCTIC (multi-view plus egocentric with mocap GT, bimanual, articulated objects), and optionally HOI4D or OakInk2 for the model-free setting. A standard anthropometric hand-length table supplies the scale prior. All are downloadable; check each licence. Compute is one 24 GB GPU for frozen-model inference (hand, object pose, depth foundation model) and per-sequence optimization; no training of large models. No camera capture or mocap is needed. Effort is about 9-12 months for one student, plus a second student for the baselines and the data pipeline.
research_questions.risks: Crowding is high: at least 15 papers in 2025-2026 target metric or world-space hands, and a large lab could publish a similar fusion or a scale-aware foundation model first. Joint hand-object optimization with contact is old (for example Hasson et al. 2020, Cao et al. 2021, from memory and not verified here), so the contribution has to be the accounting, the identifiability and the calibrated uncertainty, not the use of contact. The scale term may not dominate. Errors may instead come from intrinsics mismatch, which EgoForce reports sensitivity to, or from occlusion. The paper then changes shape. Known-CAD results can look like they rely on object pose; the model-free setting has to show real gains. Baseline code for the newest 2026 methods may not be released.

research_questions.question: RQ2. Which parts of 3D hand and object placement error predict failure when human demonstrations are retargeted to a dexterous robot hand? The candidates are absolute against hand-to-object relative error, error along the ray against lateral error, and temporal jitter. Does a placement-aware evaluation metric, together with an uncertainty-aware retargeter that uses RQ1-style ray posteriors, predict and reduce those failures better than PA-MPJPE or MPJPE?
research_questions.why_top_venue: P08 matters mostly because robot data engines (HaMeR or HaWoR plus SLAM or metric depth) turn misplacement into missed contacts and penetration. The arXiv queries in this task found no paper that measures how placement error, broken down by direction and by absolute against relative, maps to retargeting or policy success. MEgoHand reports large wrist-translation error reductions without linking them to robot outcomes. A controlled study that links a vision metric to a robotics outcome, and then proposes a task-predictive metric, is the kind of cross-community result CoRL, RSS and ICRA value. It also gives P08 a principled evaluation protocol in place of 'report MPJPE too'. A real-robot experiment is not required to make the point.
research_questions.method_sketch: (1) Start from GT hand and object trajectories in DexYCB, ARCTIC, OakInk2 or HOT3D. Retarget them to a simulated dexterous hand (Allegro, LEAP or Shadow) in Isaac Lab, Isaac Gym or MuJoCo. Use kinematic retargeting plus physics replay, and optionally a residual-RL tracker in the style of ManipTrans or DexMachina (public code, not verified here). (2) Controlled error injection: add structured perturbations of known size along the camera ray and laterally; as a global scale and as relative hand-object offsets; and as static bias or temporal jitter. Then measure task success (object reaches its target pose), contact recall, penetration depth and object drift. (3) Fit sensitivity curves and learn or derive a scalar task-predictive placement error (for example a weighted relative error along the ray at contact frames). Validate its rank correlation with success on trajectories from 4-6 real estimators, including RQ1's. (4) Make the retargeter uncertainty-aware: inflate contact tolerance along the ray in proportion to the posterior, or sample retargets from the posterior, and measure the change in success.
research_questions.minimum_experiment: Use 50-100 sequences from two datasets and one simulated hand, with error-injection sweeps along about 3 error axes at 5 magnitudes each. Then run the trajectories of 4-6 existing estimators through the same pipeline. Report rank correlation (Spearman or Kendall) between each metric (PA-MPJPE, MPJPE, MRRPE-style relative error, the proposed metric) and task success, plus the gain in success from uncertainty-aware retargeting. A borrowed arm with a dexterous or parallel gripper running 2-3 tasks would strengthen the case for a top-venue submission but is optional.
research_questions.data_and_hardware: Public datasets as above, plus open simulation tooling (Isaac Lab or MuJoCo; robot hand URDFs are public). One RTX-class GPU with 24 GB is enough for kinematic replay and modest RL per sequence; keep the sequence count bounded, because residual-RL tracking can take hours per sequence. No robot is required; one borrowed arm for a small real check is optional. Effort is about 6-9 months for one student; it can share the RQ1 data pipeline.
research_questions.risks: Residual-RL trackers may absorb moderate placement error. The result could then be that placement matters less than claimed. That is still publishable as an analysis, but the method half weakens. Sim-to-real gap: reviewers at CoRL or RSS may want real-robot evidence. Setting up dexterous-hand RL in Isaac is engineering-heavy and costs months. Concurrent robot-learning papers (DexImit, DexMan, the RGB-to-LEAP-Hand pipeline 2602.09013) may add their own sensitivity analyses.
target_venues: NeurIPS Datasets and Benchmarks (if framed as an evaluation protocol)

research_questions.question: RQ3 (smaller scope). How little metric information is needed to bring a whole monocular hand-object video to contact-precision placement? Candidates for a metric anchor are one known-size or fiducial-marked object, a single RGB-D frame, a few sparse depth pixels, or a camera IMU. How should that anchor be propagated through contact and rigid object tracking to frames where it is not visible, while keeping uncertainty along the ray honest?
research_questions.why_top_venue: Low-cost demonstration capture (phones, glasses, one webcam) is the deployment setting for robot data engines. MonoEgo (arXiv 2609.34512, Sept 2026) shows interest in passive markers plus sparse anchors, but it states that residual geometric uncertainty and dynamic accuracy remain open. A metric-budget curve (accuracy against anchor type and amount) with a principled propagation method is a clean systems-and-analysis contribution. It fits ICRA, RA-L or T-RO more than CVPR, unless it is folded into RQ1 as its anchored variant.
research_questions.method_sketch: Reuse the RQ1 factor graph and add anchor factors: a fiducial or known-CAD object pose, depth samples at sparse pixels, a one-frame RGB-D scale, or IMU gravity and acceleration. Propagate metric scale over time through object tracking and through hand-object contact when the anchor leaves view, and model anchor dropout explicitly. Simulate each anchor budget on public RGB-D or mocap data by withholding information. Then validate on a small real set captured with a consumer RGB-D camera, using the depth stream only as held-out ground truth.
research_questions.minimum_experiment: Anchor-budget curves on DexYCB, HO3Dv3 and HOI4D (RGB-D available for sparse-depth simulation): unaligned hand-to-object relative error and absolute error against anchor type and density, and against the time since the anchor was last seen. Compare with an unanchored RQ1 estimator and with full RGB-D. Add a small real held-out set (a few subjects and objects) captured on one RGB-D camera, with its depth reserved for evaluation.
research_questions.data_and_hardware: Public RGB-D hand-object datasets plus one consumer RGB-D camera for a small real validation set; printed ArUco or AprilTag markers; one GPU. About 4-6 months if built on RQ1.
research_questions.risks: This could be seen as incremental engineering next to MonoEgo and fiducial-based capture systems, so top-venue odds are lower unless the propagation or uncertainty part is principled. Ground truth from a consumer RGB-D camera is noisy at hand-object boundaries and at very short range, so it should be reported as a reference with stated error and not as mocap-grade truth. A small, single-site real set limits generalization claims.
target_venues: T-RO (if extended with a real-robot study)

fit.thesis_assets_help:
The edge is small and secondary. The author's work is RGB-D, and the field already treats RGB-D as the fix for P08, so the thesis does not suffer the problem itself; the assets serve evaluation and RQ3. What actually helps:
(a) The calibrated single RGB-D desk setup with an ArUco-marked object of known metric pose gives an independent real-world reference for unaligned hand-to-object placement. This is a small held-out test with depth reserved as ground truth, and it can be the real validation set in RQ3, where the marked object is literally the metric anchor.
(b) Object-conditioned recovery of an occluded holding arm is a working instance of passing metric placement from an object to a limb through contact. That is the mechanism RQ1 and RQ3 formalise, so the code and intuition carry over.
(c) The measured/held/constrained honesty labels map directly onto the per-frame provenance and uncertainty-along-ray labels proposed in RQ1 and RQ3.
(d) The causal 30 fps chain and the Unity twin are marginally useful: the twin could render controlled synthetic error-injection cases, but MuJoCo or Isaac are better for RQ2's physics.
Limits: one subject, 28 recordings and one desk are not a benchmark, and give no mocap-grade ground truth. Consumer depth is noisy at contact boundaries and short range. The main experiments must therefore run on DexYCB, HO3Dv3, HOT3D and ARCTIC.
fit.what_a_small_lab_cannot_do_here:
- Train or pretrain metric-scale hand or foundation models on very large data. MINT used 1,021 hours of pseudo-labelled video, ESTHER 194 hours of stereo capture, and MoGe-2 or Metric3D-class depth models need comparable data. A small lab must build on frozen front ends.
- Collect a new mocap-grade multi-view benchmark with many subjects to compete with HOT3D, ARCTIC or ESTHER3D.
- Win a raw CS-MPJPE leaderboard race against several well-funded groups releasing monthly (EgoForce, ScaleHP, CS-ViT, HandFlow, StableHand, InfiniHand, EgoFound3R, ViDiHand).
- Run large real-robot policy studies across many tasks; at most a few tasks on a borrowed arm.
- Run broad novelty scans in this session: the WebSearch budget was exhausted, and the arXiv abstract queries run here (which found ArtHOI 2603.25791, DexImit 2602.10105, Hand3R 2602.03200, MEgoHand 2505.16602, MonoEgo 2609.34512 and the 2022 hand-scale depth paper 2210.11384) are not exhaustive. Novelty of the error-floor decomposition in RQ1 and of the sensitivity study in RQ2 is therefore unverified and must be re-checked before committing.
Realistic small-lab niche: analysis plus a principled fusion and uncertainty method on frozen models, unaligned relative-placement evaluation at contact precision on public data, and downstream sensitivity in simulation.

painpoint.name: Two hands and close bodies are confused with each other

evidence.latest_state: Per-hand accuracy on interacting-hand benchmarks is now close to saturated, but the relative placement of the two hands still is not. The strongest verified 2026 result is A2P (Han et al., CVPR 2026, arXiv 2503.17788). It reports MPJPE 5.36 mm and MRRPE 21.60 mm on InterHand2.6M, against 4DHands at 7.49 / 24.58 and InterWild at 7.85 / 26.74. On HIC it reports MPJPE 6.67 mm and MRRPE 22.24 mm. The relative-root error between the hands is therefore still about four times the per-joint error. The authors say extreme occlusion and motion blur remain open and suggest temporal modelling. On egocentric video, StableHand (arXiv 2605.18553, May 2026) cuts world-space W-MPJPE on HOT3D and ARCTIC by 20-25 percent over the strongest baseline, with the largest gains on the heavily occluded ARCTIC sequences. ViDiHand (arXiv 2606.30308) moves dual-hand 4D recovery onto video-diffusion features and drops the hand detector. On the body side, close contact is still handled by interaction priors and optimization, not solved. InterMesh (arXiv 2605.04554) cuts MPJPE by only 8.2 percent on Hi4D, CloseApp (arXiv 2507.02565) states that SAM-style segmentation fails to separate people in close contact, and HUG3D (CVPR 2026) still targets overlaps and distorted contact from a single image. MAMMA (CVPR 2026) reaches marker-level quality only with multi-view rigs. I found no 2025-2026 result that removes identity swaps or depth-ordering errors under heavy overlap from a single view. Caveat: the web-search budget was already spent, so this evidence comes only from arXiv listing pages and abstract/HTML pages. CHI3D and FlickrCI3D contact numbers newer than those in the pain-point record were not found.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: From 2D Alignment to 3D Plausibility: Unifying Heterogeneous 2D Priors and Penetration-Free Diffusion for Occlusion-Robust Two-Hand Reconstruction (A2P)
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Single-image two-hand reconstruction. It fuses foundation-model keypoints, segmentation and depth, and adds a penetration-free diffusion step. InterHand2.6M: MRRPE 21.60 mm, MPJPE 5.36 mm. HIC: MRRPE 22.24 mm, MPJPE 6.67 mm.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: StableHand: Quality-Aware Flow Matching for World-Space Dual-Hand Motion Estimation from Egocentric Video
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: A per-hand, per-channel observation-quality network drives a flow-matching bimanual motion prior. W-MPJPE drops 20-25 percent on HOT3D and ARCTIC, most on heavily occluded sequences.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: ViDiHand: The Surprising Effectiveness of Video Diffusion Models for Hand Motion Reconstruction
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Uses pretrained video-diffusion features to recover metric-scale two-hand 4D pose from egocentric video, without a detector or test-time optimization. Evaluated on ARCTIC, HOT3D and HOI4D.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: BIGS: Bimanual Category-agnostic Interaction Reconstruction from Monocular Videos via 3D Gaussian Splatting
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Reconstructs two hands and an unknown object from monocular video under severe inter-hand occlusion, using diffusion priors and Gaussians shared across both hands.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: Dyn-HaMR: Recovering 4D Interacting Hand Motion from a Dynamic Camera
attacking_papers_2025_2026.venue_year: CVPR 2025 (arXiv 2412.12861; venue from memory, not shown on the abs page)
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Multi-stage optimization that combines SLAM with an interacting-hand prior to recover global 4D two-hand motion from moving monocular cameras.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: VM-BHINet: Vision Mamba Bimanual Hand Interaction Network
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Models bimanual hand interaction with state-space (Mamba) layers. Reports a 2-3 percent MPJPE and MPVPE reduction on InterHand2.6M.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: Single-Query Person-Centric Bimanual Hand-Object Interaction Detection
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: One query per person predicts the body, both hand boxes, hand states and interaction targets. This targets hand-ownership ambiguity in multi-person scenes.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: Reconstructing Close Human Interaction with Appearance and Proxemics Reasoning (CloseApp)
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Dual-branch optimization with a proxemics diffusion prior, 3D Gaussian appearance, 2D keypoint and penetration constraints for close two-person interaction in the wild. Releases pseudo-ground-truth data.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: HUG3D: Human Interaction-Aware 3D Reconstruction from a Single Image
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Group-instance multi-view diffusion plus physics-based interaction priors to remove overlaps and distorted contact when reconstructing several people from one image.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: InterMesh: Explicit Interaction-Aware End-to-End Multi-Person Human Mesh Recovery
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Adds an interaction encoder and an interaction-guided refiner to DETR-style multi-person HMR. MPJPE drops 8.2 percent on Hi4D and 9.9 percent on CMU Panoptic; also evaluated on CHI3D.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: MAMMA: Markerless and Automatic Multi-Person Motion Action Capture
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Multi-view markerless SMPL-X capture of two-person close interaction, using mask-conditioned dense contact-aware landmarks trained on synthetic data. Claims quality competitive with commercial marker mocap.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: PromptHMR: Promptable Human Mesh Recovery
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Promptable HMR that takes interaction labels as prompts to model person-person interactions.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: Multiview Multi-Person Human Mesh Recovery Under Large Scenes with Occlusions (MVMP-HMR)
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Synthetic benchmark with up to 30 interacting people and 50 views, plus a feature-volume method. It reports that existing state-of-the-art HMR methods struggle under severe occlusion.

evidence.crowdedness: HIGH: at least 13 verified 2025-2026 papers attack this from both the hand side (A2P, BIGS, Dyn-HaMR, StableHand, ViDiHand) and the body side (PromptHMR, MAMMA, HUG3D, InterMesh, CloseApp), several at CVPR 2025/2026 and ECCV 2026, from strong groups such as MPI/Meshcapade (Black), NUS (Lee) and Imperial (Zafeiriou). Generic two-hand or two-person pose papers therefore face heavy competition.
evidence.trend: Rising. The method focus is shifting from single-image two-hand regressors to egocentric world-space dual-hand video models built on generative priors (flow matching, video diffusion; StableHand and ViDiHand in May-June 2026). Multi-person contact papers keep landing at CVPR 2026 and ECCV 2026. Robot-learning and teleoperation demand for bimanual capture is also pulling in attention.

skeptics.reasons:
I could not find 2025-2026 work that solves P09 or turns it into engineering. The WebSearch budget was already used up, so these results come from WebFetch of arXiv search and abstract or HTML pages. The openaccess.thecvf.com proceedings pages returned 403, so CVPR and ICCV 2025 listings could not be checked.

Partial progress does exist:
(1) WiLoR (CVPR 2025) provides real-time multi-hand detection and reconstruction trained on more than 2M in-the-wild images. This reduces missed and duplicate hand detections. Its abstract makes no claim about left/right identity or joint two-hand reasoning.
(2) Dyn-HaMR (arXiv 2412.12861; its CVPR 2025 venue was not confirmed on the abstract page) adds an interacting-hand prior. It is a multi-stage optimization pipeline, so it is slow, which matches the "slow optimization" caveat in the record.
(3) InfiniHand (arXiv 2609.35743, Sept 2026) reaches 7.72 mm PA-MPJPE on ARCTIC at 11 FPS, and StableHand (arXiv 2605.18553, May 2026) cuts W-MPJPE by 20-25%, with its largest gains on occluded ARCTIC sequences. So per-hand, camera-space articulation under occlusion is improving quickly. However, InfiniHand reports no two-hand relative-root, swap or penetration metric. Its authors also state that egocentric data with complex two-hand interaction remain scarce, which limits generalization under severe occlusion and intermittent hand visibility.
(4) At body scale, the abstract of "Reconstructing Close Human Interaction with Appearance and Proxemics Reasoning" (arXiv 2507.02565, July 2025) states that existing methods cannot recover plausible close interactions. SocialMirror (arXiv 2604.13581, 2026) still reports 83.6 mm RE and 47.5 mm PA-MPJPE on Hi4D. Its penetration score of 2380 is in the paper's own units, which I did not check. On zero-shot Harmony4D it reports 198 mm RE, 412 mm GE and 246 mm interaction error. These numbers are far from saturated.
(5) A Sept 2026 retargeting paper (arXiv 2609.24093) reports a lower starting success rate for dual-hand tasks (16.0%) than for single-hand ones (7.3% to 59.3%). It does not isolate perception error.

Taken together: no benchmark for hand-hand relative placement, identity under swaps, or contact consistency is saturated, and no released model provides real-time, identity-consistent, penetration-free joint two-hand (plus object) tracking.

Caveats on the record itself:
- Single-hand articulation inside each hand crop is close to engineering. The open problem sits in the relative and world-space placement of both hands, identity, and contact.
- The TeleOpBench 0% result reflects a whole teleoperation system, not the state of the art in estimation.
- The body-scale half (CHI3D, Harmony4D) is less central to a bimanual RGB-D thesis.
- I did not verify whether HIC or Re:InterHand numbers were reported in 2025-2026 papers.

skeptics.reframe: Per-hand articulation inside a crop is now close to solved on ARCTIC (PA-MPJPE about 7-8 mm, real-time detectors such as WiLoR). The open problem is the joint state of both hands: the placement of the two hands relative to each other and in metric world space, left/right identity kept through crossings and handovers, and contact that is consistent and free of interpenetration between the two hands and the shared object. This joint state has to be held during bimanual manipulation under hand-hand and hand-object occlusion, at interactive rates, without dense rigs or slow per-sequence optimization, and with metrics that report these quantities directly (relative root error, swap rate, penetration and contact) instead of per-hand PA-MPJPE.

skeptics.reasons:
The artifact attack works on parts of P09 but not on its core.

What survives:
- The two-hand half rests on datasets and benchmarks from several independent groups and capture setups.
  - Hands: ARCTIC (1121, MPI/ETH, multi-view dome with mocap), AssemblyHands (1122, Meta, egocentric), RenderIH and Re:InterHand (1186, 1185, synthetic and relit dome), TACO (88), HOH and CORE4D handover (1125, 121), and the HANDS 2024/2025 challenge reports (1528, 1529, 1536).
  - Teleoperation: TeleOpBench (1392, a robotics simulator).
- The body half also comes from separate groups: CHI3D/FlickrCI3D (1060), Hi4D (1250, ETH), Harmony4D (1249), EgoHumans (1248) and HHI-Assist/OpenRoboCare (813, 999, caregiving).
- So the failure under proximity does not come from one dataset, one lab or one convention. Two headline items were checked:
  - TeleOpBench Table 2 gives ball_bimanual success of MoCap 100%, exoskeleton 80%, vision 0% and VR 0%. For VR, the paper's stated reason is that "hand-over-hand occlusion breaks pose estimation".
  - Harmony4D reports that state-of-the-art mesh recovery has significant limitations under close contact, and that it needed fine-tuning on contact data to improve.

What the artifact attack does weaken:
1. The cluster joins two different problems. One is two-hand interaction; the other is multi-person close contact, which overlaps with the long-studied tracking topics of crowd occlusion and identity switches. Merging them inflates the count of 42 papers. Several listed papers barely support either half: ProGait (274), BANZ-FS (531), WorldPose (1197), SLOPER4D (1241), LiDAR-aid Inertial Poser (1244), Human-M3 (1245), HiSC4D (1036), HandsOnWorld (1483) and two generic pose surveys (1265, 1266).
2. Left-right and identity swaps are mainly a symptom of particular pipelines, not a field-wide wall.
   - The left-right claim comes from one challenge report, where SAM-Track swaps hands (1529), and from an AssemblyHands remark on refinement accumulating error after a wrong initialization (1122).
   - Modern hand detectors that predict handedness, together with standard multi-object tracking association, are widely used and long studied for this. The record gives no field-wide statistic on swap rates.
3. The core accuracy gap is modest on the main benchmark: InterHand2.6M MPJPE is 10.53 mm for two hands against 7.94 mm for one hand. Large gaps appear mainly in two places:
   - relative root placement and in-the-wild transfer (HIC RRVE of 23.6-67 mm; 28.9 mm on the Re:InterHand egocentric split);
   - multi-person contact (CHI3D errors above 50 mm; translation errors of 676-3158 mm).
4. The pain point is tied to single-view RGB.
   - Multi-view headset tracking (such as UmeTrack and commercial headset hand tracking) and dense-rig capture largely cope.
   - Depth sensing reduces the depth-ordering ambiguity the record blames.
   - TeleOpBench's 0% is one simulator benchmark using one monocular-vision pipeline and one VR device, so it does not show that all vision-based capture fails.
5. Several fixes already exist as dedicated work: two-hand tokenizers, interaction priors, relit synthetic data and contact signatures. "Persists" means the problem is still open, not that it has been neglected.

Limits of this check:
- The web search budget was used up, so recent two-hand methods (2025-2026) could not be searched. Only TeleOpBench, Harmony4D and an OmniHands abstract were fetched.
- I could not check whether newer two-hand transformers have closed the relative-root gap on HIC or ARCTIC.

Verdict: the pain point is real and comes from diverse sources. It is not refuted, but its framing is broader than the evidence. The robust core is relative placement and contact-consistent joint estimation of two hands under hand-over-hand occlusion from a single viewpoint. Identity and handedness swapping, and multi-person body contact, are weaker, setup-specific or older problems.

skeptics.reframe: From a single RGB or RGB-D view, current estimators cannot recover the relative placement and contact of two hands, and of the object they share, with physical consistency when one hand occludes the other. Each hand reaches near single-hand accuracy (InterHand2.6M MPJPE 10.5 mm against 7.9 mm for one hand). However, relative root error stays at about 24-67 mm in the wild and on egocentric data, and hand-over-hand handovers break vision and VR teleoperation (TeleOpBench ball_bimanual: 0% success). Handedness and identity swapping, and close contact between two bodies, are secondary problems that depend on the setup.

skeptics.reasons: Refutation attempt (no research question): parts of P09 are engineering. Left/right swaps in detectors and SAM-style segment trackers, mocap suits for teleoperation, and "more contact-rich data" are fixes that only need resources or better tracking glue. The record itself names lack of training data as a main cause, and the listed fixes include data collection (relighted synthetic interacting hands, dense domes). The field is also crowded. Interacting-hand recovery and close-contact human reconstruction have had a steady run of top-venue papers: IntagHand (CVPR 2022, verified), InterWild (CVPR 2023, verified), Hi4D (close-human-interaction dataset with alternating optimization, verified on arXiv; CVPR 2023 venue from memory) and Dyn-HaMR (4D interacting hands from a moving camera with an interacting-hand prior, verified on arXiv; CVPR 2025 venue from memory). So "two hands are confused" alone is a known, actively attacked problem, not an untouched one. Why the refutation fails: the remaining ambiguity is not a data-volume problem. Two near-identical articulated instances under overlap have an inherently multimodal posterior over identity, depth order and relative translation. The record's own numbers show that this does not close with training data. On Re:InterHand the egocentric relative-root error is still 28.89 mm after training on it. HIC relative-root error is 23.59 mm for the best method, against about 20 mm on InterHand2.6M. Iterative refinement compounds identity errors made at initialization. Vision and VR teleoperation score 0 percent on a bimanual handover. Questions a top-venue reviewer would treat as significant and that are not settled: (1) How to represent and propagate a calibrated multi-hypothesis posterior over hand or person identity and relative depth through overlap, so that a tracker commits only when evidence disambiguates instead of locking in a swap. (2) Whether jointly modelling the shared object as a physical coupling (both hands constrained by one rigid body, contact and non-penetration) removes the relative-translation ambiguity that per-hand estimators such as HaMeR cannot resolve. (3) Whether metric depth from a single RGB-D sensor removes the depth-order and relative-root ambiguity, and what residual error the self-occluded side keeps. That would give a measurable bound rather than another architecture. (4) Self-supervised or test-time consistency (temporal plus contact plus penetration) as a substitute for ground-truth contact labels, which the attempted fixes depend on. Downgrades: the body-scale half (CHI3D, multi-person tracking) is a separate, crowded subfield and dilutes the point. The detector-level left/right swap is engineering. Novelty risk is high, because each of questions 1 to 4 has partial prior work: interacting-hand priors, BUDDI-style social contact priors and diffusion multi-hypothesis hand methods. A paper here must show a clear gain under heavy overlap with an object, not on InterHand2.6M averages.

skeptics.reframe: When two hands share one object and overlap, which hand is which, which is in front, and how far apart they are can no longer be read from the image. The question is whether a tracker that carries a calibrated distribution over those three ambiguities, and is physically coupled through the shared rigid object (contact and non-penetration), avoids committed left-right swaps and lowers the relative-root error under heavy overlap. A second question is what residual ambiguity a single RGB-D depth channel leaves on the self-occluded side.

research_questions.question: RQ1 (main bet). When two hands share a rigid object and overlap, can a tracker keep a calibrated posterior over three things: which hand is which, which hand is in front, and the relative SE(3) between the hands? The posterior would be coupled through the shared object by contact, non-penetration and rigid co-motion. The tracker commits only when the evidence settles the ambiguity. Does this lower relative-root error (MRRPE) and committed left/right swaps on the most-overlapped frames, compared with per-hand estimators and single-estimate two-hand models, while running causally at interactive rates?
research_questions.why_top_venue: Per-hand accuracy is close to saturated, but the joint state of the two hands is not. A2P (CVPR 2026, arXiv 2503.17788, verified) reports InterHand2.6M MPJPE 5.36 mm but MRRPE 21.60 mm, and HIC MPJPE 6.67 mm but MRRPE 22.24 mm. The 2026 methods (A2P, StableHand 2605.18553, ViDiHand 2606.30308, InfiniHand 2609.35743) each output one estimate. From their abstracts, none reports a swap rate, overlap-stratified relative error, or calibrated uncertainty over identity and depth order. ARCTIC already defines MRRPE and contact-deviation style metrics, so the novelty has to come from three things together: an explicit model of the multimodal ambiguity, object coupling as the disambiguating evidence, and commit/abstain behaviour that downstream robot-demonstration pipelines can use. TeleOpBench (2505.12748; the skeptic verified Table 2) shows vision and VR teleoperation at 0 percent on a bimanual handover, so this has a concrete application. If the gain is clear on the hardest overlap stratum, CVPR/ECCV reviewers would see this as a principled contribution, not another backbone.
research_questions.method_sketch: (a) Front end: off-the-shelf per-hand detection and regression (WiLoR or HaMeR), plus 2D keypoints and hand masks. (b) Hypothesis generator: a small conditional flow-matching prior over the joint two-hand state (both MANO poses and the relative SE(3)), conditioned on per-hand features. It is trained on MANO parameters pooled from ARCTIC, InterHand2.6M, GigaHands and OakInk2, and sampled K = 16-64 times per frame. On top sit explicit discrete modes: handedness assignment (2) x depth order (2). (c) Object coupling: the object 6D pose (ARCTIC ground truth as an oracle first, then an estimated pose) enters three likelihood terms: fingertip-to-surface contact consistency, signed-distance non-penetration (hand-hand and hand-object), and rigid co-motion for a hand judged in contact. This lets the visible hand and the object constrain the occluded hand. (d) Temporal inference: a Rao-Blackwellised particle filter or multiple-hypothesis tracker. The discrete modes are sampled and the continuous state is refined per mode. A commit/abstain rule uses the mode-posterior entropy; when ambiguous, the output is a flagged state with intervals on relative translation. (e) Causal design, target 15-30 fps on one GPU.
research_questions.minimum_experiment: Step 0, prevalence audit (4-6 weeks, a go/no-go gate). Run WiLoR+HaMeR with a simple IoU tracker, InterWild, and any released 2025-2026 two-hand model on ARCTIC (allocentric and egocentric val), InterHand2.6M test, HIC and Re:InterHand. Stratify frames by the 2D overlap of the projected ground-truth hand masks into deciles. Report MRRPE, swap-frame rate, identity-recovery latency and penetration per decile. Go only if top-decile MRRPE is at least about 2x the bottom decile, or swaps are non-negligible (more than a few percent of frames) in the top decile. Otherwise reframe around relative placement only. Step 1: on ARCTIC val, compare (i) per-hand plus tracker, (ii) the multi-hypothesis prior without object, (iii) plus oracle object coupling, (iv) plus estimated object pose, and (v) full model against the single-estimate argmax of the same model. Metrics: MRRPE (hand-hand and hand-object), swap frames, recovery latency, penetration volume, contact F1 against ARCTIC contact, mode-posterior ECE and interval coverage, and FPS. All metrics are reported on the top two overlap deciles as well as overall. Also run InterHand2.6M/HIC as a no-object check, so the object term is not credited with gains it did not cause.
research_questions.data_and_hardware: Public data only. ARCTIC (2.1M frames with hand and articulated-object meshes and contact; verified abstract) is the main benchmark. InterHand2.6M, HIC and Re:InterHand are no-object references. HOT3D, GigaHands and OakInk2 supply extra MANO parameters to train the prior. One workstation GPU (24-48 GB) is enough: the prior is small, training takes about 1-3 GPU-days, and inference uses off-the-shelf backbones. No capture rig, mocap or robot is needed. A consumer RGB-D camera is only for qualitative real-world demos. Code availability for A2P, StableHand, InfiniHand and ViDiHand baselines is unverified; HaMeR, WiLoR and InterWild code is public from memory.
research_questions.risks: (1) Novelty overlap: diffusion multi-hypothesis hand methods, StableHand's quality-aware flow prior and Dyn-HaMR's interacting-hand prior cover parts of this. The paper wins only on the overlap-stratified, swap and calibration results plus object coupling. (2) Step 0 may show that swaps are rare in egocentric data, where hands enter from fixed sides. Then the swap story shrinks to allocentric and crossing scenes. (3) When the object is also occluded, object-pose error may cancel the coupling gain. ARCTIC has only 11 objects, so generalisation to unseen objects is weak evidence. (4) Calibration claims need careful protocol design, or reviewers will dismiss them. (5) Well-resourced groups (Meta, MPI, ETH) can add a similar module quickly, so time to submission matters.
target_venues: CoRL (if paired with the demonstration-transfer result of RQ3)

research_questions.question: RQ2 (measurable bound). In bimanual hand-object manipulation, how much of the error in relative placement between the hands and in depth order does one metric depth channel remove? Compare real consumer-sensor depth with monocular metric depth from foundation models. What residual error stays on the hand occluded by the other hand or the object, and does visibility-aware fusion with an object anchor close it?
research_questions.why_top_venue: A2P already fuses foundation-model depth priors, and headsets and phones increasingly carry depth sensors. Robot demonstration rigs are mostly RGB-D (RealSense, Azure Kinect class). Yet I found no 2025-2026 paper that quantifies sensor depth against foundation depth for two hands plus an object under overlap. The latest single-RGB-D two-hand methods found are the 2019 single-depth-camera tracker (Mueller et al., arXiv 2106.08059) and PDFNet (arXiv 2307.06038, TCSVT 2024), and neither isolates the occluded hand. A clean bound answers a design question every capture-system builder faces. Top-venue odds are realistic at ICRA/RA-L/CoRL. CVPR/ECCV would need a surprising general finding, for example that sensor depth adds nothing beyond foundation depth on the occluded hand, plus the fusion method.
research_questions.method_sketch: Build a depth-augmented bimanual evaluation set. Real data: H2O (arXiv 2104.11181, verified as multi-view RGB-D with both hands and the object 6D pose annotated; view and subject counts not verified). Rendered data: ARCTIC allocentric views rendered to depth from the ground-truth hand and object meshes, then degraded with a time-of-flight or structured-light noise model (edge flying pixels, dropouts, depth-dependent noise). The noise model is calibrated against noise statistics measured on the lab's own RGB-D recordings. Inputs: RGB only; RGB plus monocular metric depth (current models such as Depth Pro, MoGe or UniDepth; names from memory, verify versions); RGB plus sensor depth. Fitters: (a) naive fitting of depth residuals over the whole hand box; (b) visibility-aware fitting, where depth residuals apply only to mask pixels of the visible hand surface and the occluded hand is constrained by the object anchor and the RQ1 prior.
research_questions.minimum_experiment: Run 3 input conditions x 2 fitters on rendered ARCTIC and real H2O. Report MRRPE, depth-order error rate, and per-hand error split by visible versus occluded hand, all as a function of the overlap decile. As a single-hand reference, use DexYCB (real RGB-D, one hand), so the bimanual-specific residual can be separated out. Headline deliverable: a table and curve showing how much of the bimanual gap each depth source closes on the top-overlap stratum, and what remains on the occluded hand.
research_questions.data_and_hardware: H2O, ARCTIC (rendered depth), DexYCB; one GPU for rendering and inference; one consumer RGB-D camera only to measure sensor-noise statistics and to record a small qualitative set. No new ground truth needs to be captured.
research_questions.risks: (1) Render-to-real gap: simulated noise may miss sensor failures on skin and at hand edges (multipath, flying pixels between fingers), which could flip the conclusion. (2) H2O ground truth comes from a multi-view fit, and its error may be several millimetres, comparable to the differences being measured. (3) Reviewers may call it an analysis paper. (4) Foundation depth models improve fast, so the sensor-versus-foundation verdict may date quickly. (5) A2P-style depth-prior fusion may already capture most of the gain.
target_venues: CVPR or ECCV (stretch, only with a strong general finding)

research_questions.question: RQ3 (error budget for robotics). Which joint-state errors actually break transfer of a bimanual human demonstration to robot hands: relative-root offset, left/right swap events of a given duration, hand-object penetration, or per-joint articulation error? And what accuracy specification should a vision capture system therefore meet?
research_questions.why_top_venue: TeleOpBench reports 0 percent for vision and VR on a bimanual handover, and the contact-anchored retargeting paper (arXiv 2609.24093, unverified beyond its listing) reports low dual-hand success. Neither separates perception error from retargeting or control error. A controlled tolerance study would link the vision field's metrics (MPJPE, MRRPE) to manipulation success. The bimanual demonstration-capture community lacks this, and CoRL/RSS reviewers value it. It also tells RQ1 which error to minimise.
research_questions.method_sketch: Take ground-truth bimanual demonstrations (ARCTIC, OakInk2, or the DexManipNet data released with ManipTrans, arXiv 2503.21860, CVPR 2025 verified; code release unverified). Inject controlled errors drawn from the distributions measured on real estimators in RQ1 Step 0: relative-root offsets, swap events of varying length, penetration, jitter, and per-joint noise. Transfer to dual dexterous hands in simulation with a ManipTrans-style kinematic retargeting plus residual RL policy, or a simpler kinematic retargeting with a fixed controller. Measure task success, object-pose error and contact stability. Produce tolerance curves per error type. Then check that outputs of real estimators land where the curves predict.
research_questions.minimum_experiment: About 2 task families (handover/regrasp and a two-hand articulation task) x 5 error types x 5 magnitudes x 3 seeds in simulation. Add one real-estimator condition per task, using the RQ1 Step 0 outputs on the same sequences. Deliverable: tolerance curves and a ranked error budget, for example that X mm of relative-root error costs as much success as a Y-frame swap.
research_questions.data_and_hardware: ARCTIC or OakInk2 or DexManipNet trajectories; IsaacGym or IsaacLab on the single GPU (residual-RL training per trajectory may cost several GPU-days in total, so budget for it); no physical robot is needed. A borrowed arm and hand could add a few real trials, but that is optional.
research_questions.risks: (1) The retargeting and RL pipeline may dominate the result, because residual RL absorbs perception error. That would be a finding in itself, but a weaker paper. (2) A sim-only result invites the sim-to-real objection. (3) ManipTrans code and compute needs are unverified. (4) Reviewers may call some results obvious (a swap breaks the task), so the value lies in the quantitative crossover points. (5) The outcome depends on the task; two task families may not generalise.

fit.thesis_assets_help: The edge is small to moderate, and it is in framing and real-sensor demos, not in evaluation. (1) The ArUco-marked object with metric pose gives a near-oracle object anchor on real RGB-D. This lets RQ1 test object coupling on real data without object-estimation error, mirroring the oracle-object ablation on ARCTIC. (2) Object-conditioned recovery of an occluded holding arm is the same idea as RQ1/RQ2's object-anchored inference for the occluded hand, but at arm level rather than finger level. It is a natural thesis-to-paper bridge, though not a result that transfers directly. (3) The measured/held/constrained honesty labels are a discrete precursor of RQ1's commit/abstain output. They could become the reported state vocabulary, and they differ in spirit from StableHand's learned quality weights. (4) The causal 30 fps chain matches the online requirement in RQ1. (5) The Unity twin could render controlled-overlap synthetic RGB-D and visualise multi-hypothesis states, and it is useful for RQ2 noise-model studies. (6) The 28 recordings of one subject have no hand ground truth, one subject and one desk. They serve only for qualitative figures and for calibrating sensor-noise statistics in RQ2; they cannot be a benchmark. None of these assets helps the body-scale half of P09.
fit.what_a_small_lab_cannot_do_here: Out of reach for this lab: (1) Capture a new contact-rich bimanual ground-truth dataset at ARCTIC or GigaHands scale; that needs a multi-view dome or mocap, and marker ground truth breaks down at hand-hand proximity anyway. (2) Train video-diffusion-scale or egocentric-foundation models (the ViDiHand or Aria-data route) or compete on the per-hand InterHand2.6M MPJPE leaderboard against A2P-style foundation-prior fusion. (3) Work on the body-scale half (Hi4D, Harmony4D, CHI3D close contact), which needs multi-view capture and is crowded by MPI/Meshcapade, ETH and others. Drop it from scope. (4) Run real dual-arm dexterous teleoperation evaluation without borrowed hardware; RQ3 must stay mostly in simulation. (5) Solve multi-person identity in crowds. Also drop detector-level left/right swaps as a standalone topic; skeptics judged it engineering (handedness heads plus standard tracking association). Evidence caveat: the WebSearch budget was exhausted, so the checks here used arXiv listing and abstract pages only. H2O view and subject counts, baseline code availability (A2P, StableHand, InfiniHand, ViDiHand, ManipTrans), the depth foundation model names, and the venue of arXiv 2609.24093 are unverified.

painpoint.name: Consumer depth is noisy, holey and device-specific at hands and objects

evidence.latest_state: Note on method: the shared WebSearch budget was already used up (both search attempts were refused), so this evidence comes from arXiv API listings and arXiv abstract and HTML pages fetched directly. Since 2025, general-purpose RGB-D depth refinement has moved quickly by putting foundation-model priors on top of raw sensor depth. Prompt Depth Anything (CVPR 2025) uses iPhone LiDAR as a prompt and reports state-of-the-art results on ARKitScenes and ScanNet++. FoundationStereo (CVPR 2025) is a zero-shot stereo model. Camera Depth Models (arXiv 2509.02530, ByteDance) train one model per camera. On the Hammer dataset, the D435 model cuts L1 error from 0.055 (raw) to 0.026 and RMSE from 0.146 to 0.040, against 0.043 L1 for PromptDA. Real-robot kitchen and canteen tasks go from 0/30 successes with raw depth to 26/30 and 22/30. LingBot-Depth (arXiv 2601.17895) releases 3M RGB-depth pairs, about 2M of them real. It reports more than 40% lower RMSE than PromptDA and OMNI-DC under extreme masking (NYUv2 0.181 vs 0.324). On transparent and steel cups, grasping rises from 12-13/20 with raw depth to 16-17/20. DEPTHOR++ reports a 22% gain over RealSense L515 depth on Hammer. Many depth-completion papers for transparent or specular objects appeared in 2025-2026 (HDCNet, DCIRNet, DidSee, TransDiff, AISPO). The unsolved parts are the ones this pain point names. The fixes are still device-specific (CDM ships one model per camera; DEPTHOR++ targets dToF only). Authors still list highly transparent surfaces and misleading prompt depth as failure cases. None of these papers evaluates on hands or hand-held objects, or on HO-3D, DexYCB, BEHAVE or DTTD-Mobile. Hand and HOI papers instead avoid sensor depth: AnyHand (arXiv 2603.25726) trains on synthetic RGB-D with aligned depth, and Hand2Bot uses a heuristic morphology-based sensor-noise model. I found no 2025-2026 paper that reports a sensor-to-sensor transfer result for hand, body or object pose (for example Kinect to iPhone LiDAR, or ToF to stereo).

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: Prompting Depth Anything for 4K Resolution Accurate Metric Depth Estimation (Prompt Depth Anything)
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Uses low-cost iPhone LiDAR depth as a multi-scale prompt to Depth Anything, giving 4K metric depth. Trained with simulated LiDAR noise and pseudo ground truth. State of the art on ARKitScenes and ScanNet++, with grasping demos.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: FoundationStereo: Zero-Shot Stereo Matching
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Stereo foundation model trained on 1M synthetic pairs with a vision-foundation side-tuning backbone. Used to replace active-stereo depth from RealSense-class sensors.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: Manipulation as in Simulation: Enabling Accurate Geometry Perception in Robots (Camera Depth Models)
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Trains one RGB plus raw-depth denoiser per camera (RealSense D405/D415/D435/D455/L515, ZED 2i, Azure Kinect, Lucid Helios) on a sensor-noise data engine. Hammer D435 L1 drops from 0.055 to 0.026 (PromptDA 0.043). Sim-trained policies go from 0/30 to 26/30 real-robot successes.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: Masked Depth Modeling for Spatial Perception (LingBot-Depth)
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Treats missing and erroneous sensor depth as masked tokens for depth completion and releases 3M RGB-depth pairs (2M real). More than 40% RMSE reduction over PromptDA and OMNI-DC under extreme masking. Grasping of transparent and reflective objects improves from 12-13/20 to 16-17/20.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: DEPTHOR++: Robust Depth Enhancement from a Real-World Lightweight dToF and RGB Guidance
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Combines realistic dToF noise simulation, parameter-free anomaly detection and RGB-plus-monocular-prior completion. 22% average gain over RealSense L515 on Hammer; 22% RMSE gain on ZJU-L5.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: AISPO: Enhancing Depth Reliability for Robotic Manipulation of Non-Lambertian Objects via Affine-Invariant Shape Prior
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: RGB-D depth completion with an affine-invariant shape prior for transparent and specular objects; reports better grasping success.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: DidSee: Diffusion-Based Depth Completion for Material-Agnostic Robotic Perception and Manipulation
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Diffusion depth completion with a rescaled noise scheduler and semantic enhancement for non-Lambertian objects.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: HDCNet: A Hybrid Depth Completion Network for Grasping Transparent and Reflective Objects
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Transformer-CNN-Mamba depth completion; reports a 60% increase in grasp success on transparent objects.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: Geometry-Aware Sparse Depth Sampling for High-Fidelity RGB-D Depth Completion in Robotic Systems
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Normal-guided, reliability-aware sparse sampling with Marigold-DC, so that completion training mimics real sensor behaviour at edges (NYUv2).

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: AnyHand: A Large-Scale Synthetic Dataset for RGB(-D) Hand Pose Estimation
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: 6.6M synthetic RGB-D hand and hand-object images with aligned depth. Works around noisy, quantized real sensor depth (HO-3D) by training on clean synthetic depth; likely the source of the HO-3D RGB-D 1.09 cm AnyHandNet-D result.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: RGB-D Video Generation for Improving Human-to-Robot Object Handover Prediction (Hand2Bot)
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Generates RGB-D handover videos and applies a morphology-based depth edit to imitate real sensor noise for sim-to-real hand-object handover prediction.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: FounRef: Robust, Structure-Preserving, and Fast Metric Refinement of Frozen Monocular Foundation Priors with Sparse Anchors
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Training-free metric refinement of monocular foundation depth with sparse LiDAR anchors; reports 24% lower error and 15x faster inference than completion networks.

evidence.crowdedness: MEDIUM: general RGB-D depth refinement is crowded, with 12 or more 2025-2026 papers including CVPR 2025 work from NVIDIA (FoundationStereo) and ZJU/ByteDance (PromptDA, CDM), large tech reports (LingBot-Depth) and many transparent-object completion papers, but the hand and hand-held-object part, and cross-device transfer for hand, body and object pose, have almost no dedicated attackers.
evidence.trend: rising: robot learning needs metric depth that works across sensors, and foundation depth and stereo models made prompt-style refinement cheap, so 2025-2026 output (CDM, LingBot-Depth, DEPTHOR++ and the transparent-object completion line) is growing; HOI papers, however, mostly route around sensor depth with synthetic data or RGB-only methods rather than fixing it.

skeptics.reasons: Not refuted, but the general form is being turned into engineering fast. Several released 2025-2026 models clean up or replace consumer depth. Camera Depth Models (arXiv 2509.02530, Sept 2025) take RGB plus raw depth and output denoised metric depth. They are trained per camera on simulated noise from a neural data engine, and a policy trained on clean simulated depth transfers to the real robot with little loss on reflective and slender objects. LingBot-Depth (arXiv 2601.17895, Jan 2026) is a masked-depth-modeling completion model that claims to beat top RGB-D cameras on both precision and pixel coverage; its code, checkpoint and 3M RGB-depth pairs are released. Prompt Depth Anything (CVPR 2025) produces 4K metric depth from a low-cost LiDAR prompt. FoundationStereo (CVPR 2025) gives zero-shot stereo depth. Together these weaken three parts of P10 for static tabletop scenes: holes, specular and thin-object failure, and the sim-to-real depth gap. The core claim for this field still survives, for three reasons. (1) CDM explicitly excludes dynamic scenes, moving objects, hands and occlusion. Only its D435 and L515 models are tested quantitatively; the D405, Azure Kinect and ZED models are only visualized because no ground-truth depth exists. Its own limitations section says large regions of wrong metric depth mislead the output. (2) The reported CDM error on HAMMER (L1 about 2.6 cm, RMSE about 4 cm, AbsRel 3.1 percent) is on static objects, and is still larger than the 1-2 cm MPJPE and STA-MPJPE scale at which hand and hand-object methods now compete (HO-3D RGB-D 1.09 cm). So refined depth is not yet shown to be accurate enough for hands. (3) None of these works gives a benchmark with ground-truth depth or ground-truth 3D for close-range, fast, self-occluding hands and held objects across several devices. The device-specific gap (Kinect to iPhone: 83 to 256 mm) and motion-induced misalignment between RGB and depth, both in P10, are not addressed. I found no 2025-2026 hand-object paper showing that a depth foundation model closes the HO-3D, DTTD-Mobile or HuMMan gaps. Caveats: only six searches were allowed and the shared search budget was already used up, so the evidence comes from arXiv API listings and abstract or HTML fetches. GeoHand (arXiv 2605.17354) and an RGB-D handover-generation paper (arXiv 2608.13028) with a realistic sensor-noise model appeared in listings but were not read in full.

skeptics.reframe: The open problem is no longer depth cleanup in general. Released depth foundation models already handle that for static tabletop scenes: CDM, LingBot-Depth, PromptDA and FoundationStereo. What remains open is depth that is consistent over time, works across devices, and is accurate to about 1 cm at close range on moving, self-occluding hands and the objects they hold. That includes motion-induced misalignment between RGB and depth. There is also no multi-device benchmark with ground-truth depth or 3D for hands that would show whether refined depth actually helps hand-object tracking compared with RGB-only estimation.

skeptics.reasons: The artifact test mostly fails, so P10 is not refuted, but it comes out narrower and less new than stated. Breadth is real. The 40 supporting papers span hand-object (HO-3D, HOI4D, HOH, ADL4D, POV-Surgery, OphNet-3D, AnyHand, a hand-pose survey), object pose (PACE, HouseCat6D, PhoCaL, Omni6DPose, DTTD) and body (BEHAVE, InterCap, HuMMan, HARPER). They cover Kinect ToF, RealSense structured light and active stereo, iToF, iPhone LiDAR and LiDAR at range. They come from many unrelated groups, and the underlying physics (multipath, speckle, stereo failure on thin, dark, specular or moving surfaces) does not depend on any one dataset. Three problems inflate the record, though. (1) The count is padded. PACE appears twice (348, 1316) and DTTD/DTTDNet (1318, 1319) come from one group. About six papers (SLOPER4D, HSC4D, HiSC4D, LiDARCap, LiDAR-aid Inertial Poser, RELI11D) come from one wearable/long-range LiDAR community whose problem is sparse returns on people at 10+ m, not consumer depth at hands. Human-M3 and the in-bed pose dataset are also off-topic. (2) The headline numbers each rest on one dataset or one method. The 0.25 m iPhone error and the 25-40 point ADD-S drop come only from DTTD-Mobile. The 83-to-256 mm cross-device collapse is one baseline (VoteHMR) on HuMMan. The 'estimated depth beats sensor depth' result is HO-3D, whose depth is known to be heavily quantized. (3) Other communities have long treated this as known and are actively shrinking it. Kinect noise modelling dates to about 2012. The BOP 2023 report shows real consumer depth improving 6D pose by about 10-13 AR points (GPose2023 85.6 RGB-D vs 72.9 RGB; GenFlow 67.4 vs 57.0), so depth is clearly usable for tabletop objects. HIM2017 depth-based hand pose reached about 10 mm mean error on a single hand in frontal views. FoundationStereo (CVPR 2025) and Prompt Depth Anything (CVPR 2025, low-cost LiDAR as a prompt, with grasping shown) replace raw sensor depth outright. What survives is the close-range, contact and fast-motion case, where depth fails at the hand-object boundary, together with cross-device shift. As a broad 'consumer depth is noisy' claim, it is closer to a long-standing engineering constraint than an open research gap.

skeptics.reframe: Raw consumer depth is usable for tabletop objects and for isolated hands (about +10 AR on BOP; about 10 mm hand error in HIM2017). It breaks down in one specific regime: at the hand-object contact boundary at close range, under fast motion, and when the depth device changes. In that regime no benchmark measures how sensitive HOI trackers are to the depth source (raw ToF, structured light or stereo vs learned stereo or LiDAR-prompted depth), so nobody knows whether stereo foundation models or prompted depth already remove the problem for bimanual manipulation capture.

skeptics.reasons:
Refutation attempt. Much of P10 is engineering or hardware. The attempted fixes in the record (spray-painting objects, boundary removal, hole filling, switching sensors, multi-view fusion) are workarounds, not research. The generic problem of "make consumer depth clean" is being taken over by depth foundation models that refine or replace sensor depth. Three were verified: Prompt Depth Anything (CVPR 2025) uses low-cost iPhone LiDAR as a prompt for metric 4K depth. FoundationStereo (CVPR 2025) gives zero-shot stereo. Camera Depth Models (arXiv 2509.02530, 2025) refine noisy depth-camera output so that sim-trained manipulation policies transfer. Earlier, DREDS/SwinDRNet (ECCV 2022) did physics-plus-domain-randomized depth simulation and restoration for specular and transparent objects. A reviewer could therefore say: "fine-tune a CDM or Prompt Depth Anything style refiner on hand-object data". That is a known recipe that awaits data, which is the refutation case. Purely hand-specific denoising papers are rare (an arXiv API query for hand plus sensor depth plus RGB-D returned nothing), which is consistent with it being treated as preprocessing, not as a research topic.
Why it is not fully refuted. At least three questions survive that a top-venue reviewer would find significant.
(1) Sensor-agnostic hand-object pose and shape. The record shows a 3x error increase across devices (Kinect-trained 256 mm vs iPhone-trained 83 mm, paper 1438) and ADD-S AUC drops of 25-40 points on iPhone LiDAR (paper 1319). Learning representations, or doing test-time adaptation, so that one model works across ToF, structured light, stereo and LiDAR without per-device data is a generalization question with measurable benchmarks. It is not a request for annotation money.
(2) The value of raw active depth now that monocular and stereo foundation depth exist. On HO-3D, estimated depth already beat sensor depth (paper 1130), yet clean depth measurably helps (OphNet-3D, 17.66 to 15.97 mm). The open question is when and where sensor depth adds information beyond RGB plus foundation priors. Near-range thin fingers, contact regions and motion are the hard cases. This is a field-level question about the RGB-D modality, and a careful controlled study plus a method could be a CVPR/ICCV contribution.
(3) Joint inference that treats sensor depth as a device-specific, heavy-tailed, physics-driven observation inside articulated hand and object tracking. Examples are ToF multipath and phase ambiguity under motion and structured-light dropout at boundaries. This would replace hole-filling preprocessing. Generic refiners are scene-level and ignore articulated priors, contact and temporal coupling.
Residual weakness. Question (1) risks being an incremental "apply depth foundation model to HOI" paper. Question (3) needs physically validated noise models, which the record itself says are scarce. A small lab with one RGB-D sensor can only partly test cross-device claims, and needs a second device at minimum. Score: moderate, not refuted.
