skeptics.reframe: Generic depth foundation models now refine or replace consumer sensor depth at scene level. What is still open is how a hand-object tracker should use raw active depth at close range (thin fingers, contact boundaries, fast motion), where those generic refiners fail. The research question is how to combine device-specific sensor physics and noise with articulated hand and object priors, so that one model estimates hand-object pose and shape across sensors and reliably beats an RGB-plus-foundation-depth baseline.

research_questions.question: For hands and held objects at manipulation range (about 0.3-1.5 m), at contact boundaries and under fast motion, how much information does raw consumer depth still add over RGB plus metric foundation depth? And do the released learned refiners (Camera Depth Models, Prompt Depth Anything, LingBot-Depth) close the gap to oracle depth on each device?
research_questions.why_top_venue: Every hand-object capture system and every robot-demonstration pipeline chooses between RGB-D and RGB, yet nobody has measured that choice in the regime that matters. The refiner papers evaluate static tabletop scenes only. CDM, as checked on arxiv.org/html/2509.02530, tests D435, L515 and Lucid Helios quantitatively on static HAMMER scenes, and its own stated limitation is large regions of wrong metric depth. HOI papers, meanwhile, avoid sensor depth: AnyHand trains on synthetic depth, and on HO-3D, estimated depth beat sensor depth. The evidence for this pain point is single-source: 83 vs 256 mm cross-device on HuMMan, and ADD-S drops of 25-40 points on DTTD-Mobile. A controlled, multi-device answer stratified by region and motion settles a field-level question about the modality, and the robotics community already cares (CDM goes from 0/30 to 26/30 real-robot successes). There is also a hook nobody has used: HOI4D recorded a Kinect v2 (ToF) and a RealSense D455 at the same time, and its authors name 'knowledge transfer across different depth sensors' as an opportunity (verified on ar5iv 2203.01577). If the answer turns out to be 'refiners already fix it', that is itself a citable negative result. If a gap remains at fingertips and contact, it motivates the method below.
research_questions.method_sketch: 1) Protocol. Run a fixed set of downstream estimators against interchangeable depth sources and devices. Estimators: (a) a model-based object 6D tracker that takes RGB-D plus a mesh, such as FoundationPose; (b) an RGB hand-mesh regressor (HaMeR or WiLoR class), followed by metric placement and MANO fitting against the depth; (c) a joint MANO-plus-object render-and-compare fitter with contact and penetration terms and a swappable depth term. Depth sources: raw sensor; the per-camera CDM where one is released (D415, D435, D455, Azure Kinect, but not Kinect v2); Prompt Depth Anything; LingBot-Depth; RGB-only metric or video depth (Depth Anything V2 metric, UniDepth or MoGe class); FoundationStereo or Fast-FoundationStereo on the IR pair, for the lab's own D435 data only; and oracle depth rendered from ground-truth meshes. 2) Stratification. Score errors within k pixels of the hand-object contact boundary vs elsewhere, fingertips vs palm, by hand-speed bin from the ground-truth trajectories, by distance bin and by device. 3) A small method so this is not an analysis-only paper: reliability-gated fusion inside the depth term. A light head predicts per-pixel trust between sensor depth and foundation depth, conditioned on a device token and on hand and object masks. It is trained on one device and tested leave-one-device-out. 4) A small new real test set: the lab's D435 plus one or two borrowed devices (an Orbbec Femto Bolt or Azure Kinect, an iPhone Pro LiDAR) recording hand-held objects tagged with markers. The object pose reference comes from multi-marker RGB PnP, so it is independent of depth. It is used only for object pose error and held-object surface depth error under occlusion and motion.
research_questions.minimum_experiment: Use the DexYCB test split (8x RealSense D415, from memory, not re-verified), the H2O test split (5x Azure Kinect, verified) and an HOI4D subset, with paired Kinect v2 and D455 streams if both are annotated. Run {raw, CDM, PromptDA, LingBot-Depth, metric monocular, oracle} x {FoundationPose, HaMeR + depth fit}. Report absolute and root-relative MPJPE, ADD-S AUC, and depth AbsRel inside the hand mask and in the contact band. Compute is small: CDM measures 0.151 s per frame on an RTX 4090, so 100k frames take about 4 h per depth source. Go/no-go at month 3: if refined depth is within noise of oracle at the contact band on all devices, P10 is solved for HOI; publish a short analysis and pivot. If a gap of 30% or more of the raw-to-oracle difference remains at fingertips and contact, which is expected, build the gating method and the marker-referenced real set.
research_questions.data_and_hardware: Public data: DexYCB, H2O, HOI4D (CC BY-NC 4.0, verified), HO-3D, and ARCTIC meshes for rendered synthetic depth. Released checkpoints: CDM (the paper states that the models are released), PromptDA, LingBot-Depth (code, checkpoint and data stated released per the evidence). Hardware: the existing D435; borrow one ToF device (a Femto Bolt is about USD 400) and an iPhone Pro if possible. One 24 GB GPU is enough because the work is mostly inference. No motion capture is needed. One student, about 9-12 months.
research_questions.risks: (1) Ground-truth circularity. The DexYCB, HO-3D and H2O annotations were fitted partly to sensor depth, which biases evaluation toward raw depth. Mitigations: ARCTIC-rendered depth (motion-capture ground truth) with simulated noise, 2D reprojection checks on held-out views, and marker-referenced object poses in the lab's own data. (2) Device is confounded with dataset (scenes, subjects, distance) everywhere except the paired HOI4D streams. Whether HOI4D annotations exist for both sensors is not verified; check this in week 1. (3) CVPR reviewers reject analysis-only papers, so the gating method has to show a real gain. (4) Refiners appear every few months, so the benchmark goes stale; ship it as a plug-in harness. (5) There is no CDM for Kinect v2. (6) A big lab (the CDM or HO-Cap groups) could run the same comparison quickly.

research_questions.question: Can a single RGB-D hand-object estimator be trained once and deployed on ToF, active-stereo or structured-light, and iPhone LiDAR depth without per-device labels or per-device refiners, and beat both refine-then-estimate pipelines and RGB-only estimators at fingertips and contact, at interactive frame rates?
research_questions.why_top_venue: The record's sharpest numbers are cross-device collapses: Kinect-trained VoteHMR goes from 83 to 256 mm on iPhone, and ADD-S drops by 25-40 points on iPhone LiDAR. The current fix is one model per camera (CDM), and CDM is scene-level, does not model hands, and runs at about 6.6 Hz on an RTX 4090. arXiv API queries in this session found no 2025-2026 hand or hand-object paper on cross-sensor or test-time adaptation of depth. Keyword search is weak evidence of absence, but the evidence agent and three skeptics agree. One sensor-agnostic model with a clear leave-one-device-out protocol is a generalization result, not a data-collection request.
research_questions.method_sketch: Train on clean depth: render hand-object depth from public ground-truth meshes (ARCTIC, DexYCB, OakInk-class) and from AnyHand-like synthetic data if it is released. Pass the depth through a bank of parametric sensor simulators with randomized parameters. Active stereo: projector and second-camera occlusion bands, edge fattening, dropout on dark or specular surfaces, disparity quantization, minimum range. ToF: mixed and flying pixels at finger-object discontinuities, multipath in concave grasps, phase-motion artifacts. LiDAR: a sparse low-resolution grid with an upsampling halo. Architecture: an RGB foundation backbone (ViT, HaMeR style) with depth as a secondary token stream, gated by a predicted per-token reliability and conditioned on a device embedding. The embedding is inferred at test time from unlabeled frames by self-supervised render-and-compare against the observed depth under a learned heavy-tailed likelihood (test-time adaptation, with no labels on the target device). Check that the simulators are realistic against real D435 and ToF captures of static scenes with known geometry, such as a marker board and scanned objects.
research_questions.minimum_experiment: Leave one device out across D415 (DexYCB), Azure Kinect (H2O) and Kinect v2 vs D455 (HOI4D), plus a qualitative test on the lab's own D435 and on iPhone LiDAR. Primary metric: the cross-device degradation ratio, target-device error divided by source-device error, for MPJPE and ADD-S, reported in the contact band and at fingertips. Baselines: (i) the same network trained on raw source-device depth; (ii) CDM or LingBot-Depth refinement followed by the same network; (iii) RGB-only HaMeR or WiLoR plus metric monocular depth; (iv) a per-device fine-tuned oracle. Success means at least halving the degradation of (i), matching or beating (ii) at fingertips and contact, and running at 15 fps or more on one GPU.
research_questions.data_and_hardware: Public data only for training and quantitative testing: DexYCB, H2O, HOI4D, ARCTIC and OakInk meshes. One 24-48 GB GPU, training a ViT-B-scale model for a few days per run. The existing D435 plus borrowed ToF and iPhone LiDAR devices for qualitative tests and for checking simulator realism. One to two students, 12-15 months.
research_questions.risks: (1) Reviewers may call it 'domain randomization plus test-time adaptation, applied to hands'. Novelty has to come from hand-specific physics, such as concave-grasp multipath and finger-gap mixed pixels, and from the paired-sensor evaluation. (2) The noise simulators are not physically validated across devices, a scarcity the record itself notes. (3) RGB-only foundation estimators may already match RGB-D, which removes the motivation. RQ1 should run first and decide this. (4) Skin subsurface scattering affects ToF and is absent from mesh renders. (5) MANO and object conventions and annotation quality differ across datasets. (6) Real iPhone LiDAR hand data has no ground truth, so that claim stays qualitative.

research_questions.question: Are the holes and artifacts in consumer depth at the hand-object boundary evidence rather than noise? Can a hand-object tracker that models its device's image formation recover occluded finger and contact geometry better than hole masking, hole filling or learned completion? The image formation in question is the active-stereo projector and camera shadow bands and the ToF mixed pixels.
research_questions.why_top_venue: Every attempted fix in the record treats invalid depth as missing data: boundary removal, hole filling, and completion networks. For active IR stereo, however, the invalid band beside a finger or object edge comes from occlusion relative to the projector and the second camera. Its shape follows from the 3D configuration and the known baseline, so it carries negative evidence about the occluder's geometry. Exploiting that evidence inside articulated tracking would be a new idea, not a recipe. It speaks directly to the skeptics' reframe: device physics combined with articulated hand and object priors, which scene-level refiners ignore.
research_questions.method_sketch: Start from a render-and-compare MANO-plus-object tracker. Replace the masked L1 depth term with a device forward model. Given a candidate geometry, rasterize visibility from the projector and from both IR cameras (D4xx), plus disparity range and minimum range, to predict per-pixel validity. For ToF, predict mixed-pixel depth at discontinuities. Then score both the observed depth and the observed invalid mask under the predicted model, using a soft differentiable visibility and a small learned residual for effects the physics misses. Evaluate as a plug-in term on top of an existing tracker so the gain is isolated.
research_questions.minimum_experiment: Step 1 is cheap and is the go/no-go: on DexYCB (D415, same active-stereo family as the D435) and on new D435 recordings that save the native depth and IR streams, predict the invalid band from ground-truth or marker-referenced geometry. Measure its IoU with the observed invalid mask near the hand-object boundary. Stop if the IoU is below about 0.5 or the band covers too few hand pixels to matter. Step 2: add the term to the baseline tracker and report MPJPE on occluded joints, contact F-score and penetration, against hole masking, hole filling and CDM-refined depth. Step 3: H2O (Azure Kinect) as a second physics family, using the ToF mixed-pixel model.
research_questions.data_and_hardware: DexYCB and H2O for quantitative ground truth. The existing D435, with the IR streams recorded, for checking the formation model. Projector and camera layout from the Intel datasheets. One GPU; the work is optimization-based with little training. One student, 9-12 months.
research_questions.risks: (1) The released DexYCB and H2O depth may be registered to the color camera, which smears the native shadow geometry; check whether depth in the native IR frame is available before committing. (2) The invalid band may be too small a fraction of hand pixels to move the headline metrics. (3) A physics-based tracker runs below real time. (4) CVPR may see the topic as niche, making 3DV or ICRA more likely than CVPR. (5) The forward model is device-specific by design, which works against the cross-device story; frame it as a shared formation model with per-device parameters.

fit.thesis_assets_help: Small, with one real edge. (1) The single desk rig uses an Intel RealSense D435 at about 1.3 m (from the thesis text in writing/v9). A released per-camera CDM exists for the D435, and the D435 belongs to the same active-stereo family as DexYCB's D415. A pilot that runs CDM, PromptDA and LingBot-Depth on the existing recordings therefore costs weeks, not months. (2) The real edge is the ArUco-marked object with metric pose. It gives a reference for held-object pose and surface depth that comes from RGB PnP and so does not depend on depth, during hand occlusion and motion. That breaks the ground-truth circularity on the object side of RQ1 and supports the RQ3 invalid-band check. The marker pose error at 1.3 m and the 0.9 scale correction (50 mm declared to the detector vs the 45 mm print) must be carried into any error bars. (3) The measured, held and constrained honesty labels are conceptually close to the per-pixel trust gating in RQ1 and RQ2. That is framing, not data. (4) The causal 30 fps chain sets a real-time bar that CDM, at 6.6 Hz on an RTX 4090, does not meet, which is a fair systems argument for RQ2. (5) None for the 28 recordings of one subject as a benchmark: one device, one subject, no hand ground truth. None for the Unity twin or the object-conditioned recovery of the occluded arm on this pain point. It is not verified whether the recordings saved the native depth and IR streams or only depth aligned to color. If only aligned depth exists, the FoundationStereo-on-IR baseline and the RQ3 invalid-band analysis need new recordings. A D435 at 1.3 m is also a weak regime for finger-scale depth: expect roughly cm-level depth error there (not measured here), so new captures should be closer.
fit.what_a_small_lab_cannot_do_here: It cannot build a multi-device benchmark with motion-capture-grade ground truth for real, moving hands, which needs motion capture or a dense synchronized multi-view rig with many devices. It cannot measure true depth on skin, since subsurface scattering needs lab-grade reference scanning. It cannot produce physically validated noise models for many sensors, which needs each device plus precise reference geometry and a robot-moved camera, as HAMMER and CDM did. It cannot train foundation-scale depth refiners: LingBot-Depth uses 3M RGB-depth pairs, and CDM uses a neural data engine with per-camera models. So it should not compete on generic depth-refinement leaderboards (HAMMER, NYUv2, ARKitScenes) against NVIDIA, ByteDance or ZJU. It cannot run real-robot policy evaluations at CDM scale (30-trial tasks) without a robot arm. It cannot keep pace with the refiner release cadence, so any benchmark must be a plug-in harness rather than a fixed table. The viable niche is the narrow one: contact-band, fast-motion, cross-device evaluation and methods for hands and held objects, built on public multi-device data (DexYCB D415, H2O Azure Kinect, the paired HOI4D Kinect v2 and D455 streams) and released refiner checkpoints. That niche is open now, but a large group that already owns per-camera refiners or HOI capture rigs could close it within a cycle.

painpoint.name: Body parts hidden by occluders, self-occlusion or truncation

evidence.latest_state: Occlusion-robust body recovery is an active area that has improved but is not solved. VOccl3D (ICCV 2025) is still the clearest stress test: fine-tuning on it brings the hard split to 136.34 mm MPJPE and 175.92 mm PVE, and 3DPW error rises from 71.10 mm with ground-truth boxes to 116.52 mm with YOLO11 detections, so detection under occlusion remains a bottleneck. These figures come from the pain-point record and the paper's abstract confirms the approach, not the exact numbers. On standard benchmarks the gap is narrowing: DPMesh (2024) reached 70.9 mm MPJPE on 3DPW-OC. An April 2026 arXiv paper combining a ViT with a diffusion model reports 53.7 mm on 3DPW and 92.8 mm on AGORA (seen in a search snippet, not checked against the paper). MoPO (arXiv May 2026) adds motion priors and claims state of the art, but its abstract gives no numbers. SAM 3D Body (Meta, arXiv Feb 2026) is the strongest foundation-model step: it breaks results down by occlusion and truncation category and claims a large advantage under severe truncation. A search snippet suggests lower-body-truncated PCK is only about 39-62, but those numbers were not verified. SAM-Body4D builds on it with occlusion-aware completion of masks for video. In egocentric capture, hidden lower bodies remain the main failure. EgoPoseFormer v2 (CVPR 2026) beats the prior state of the art on EgoBody3M by 12.2% and 19.4% and improves wrist accuracy by 13.1%. Visibility-aware EvaPose with the Eva-3M dataset (CVPR 2026, 435K frames with visibility labels) and rear headset cameras (ICCV 2025, Ego4View, more than 10% MPJPE gain) attack the problem by adding sensors or labels rather than solving it from a single view. For bodies hidden by handled objects, the 2025-2026 work (amodal HOI completion on BEHAVE and InterCap, MILO at ECCV 2026) reports relative gains only. No result was found that closes the gap for close-range robot cameras or multi-person scenes with heavy object occlusion.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: SAM 3D Body: Robust Full-Body Human Mesh Recovery
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Promptable single-image body, hand and foot mesh recovery using the MHR body model, with mask and keypoint prompts; evaluation broken down by category, including occlusion and truncation.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: SAM-Body4D: Training-Free 4D Human Body Mesh Recovery from Videos
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Training-free video extension of SAM 3D Body; an occlusion-aware module recovers missing mask regions so the mesh stays consistent under occlusion.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: MoPO: Incorporating Motion Prior for Occluded Human Mesh Recovery
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Predicts which joints are visible and fills in occluded joints from past motion, then fuses the result with image features and refines it with inverse kinematics; claims state of the art on occlusion benchmarks.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: Discriminative-Generative Synergy for Occlusion Robust 3D Human Mesh Recovery
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Pairs a ViT pathway for visible regions with a diffusion pathway that fills in hidden body parts; a search snippet reports 53.7 mm on 3DPW and 92.8 mm on AGORA (numbers not checked against the paper).

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: Stable Diffusion-Based Approach for Human De-Occlusion
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Two-stage diffusion pipeline that completes the hidden body mask and appearance, which improves downstream 2D pose estimation and 3D reconstruction.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: Occlusion-Aware Temporally Consistent Amodal Completion for 3D Human-Object Interaction Reconstruction

evidence.crowdedness: HIGH: at least 13 papers from 2025-2026 were found with only six searches, including Meta (SAM 3D Body, EgoPoseFormer v2), MPI-INF (Theobalt), Berkeley/CMU-affiliated authors and UT Austin (Pavlakos), spread across generic HMR, egocentric and human-object interaction subfields, so general occlusion-robust HMR is crowded; narrower settings (low robot cameras, bodies occluded during bimanual object handling with RGB-D) are much less covered.
evidence.trend: rising: foundation human-mesh models (SAM 3D Body, SAM-Body4D) and diffusion priors drew a new wave of work on occlusion and truncation in 2026, and AR/VR industry labs keep publishing egocentric work where the lower body is out of view (two CVPR 2026 papers), while dedicated occlusion benchmarks (VOccl3D, Eva-3M) are still appearing.

skeptics.reasons: Not refuted, but the generic version is getting weaker fast and should be narrowed. Evidence that reduces it: (1) SAM 3D Body (Meta, arXiv 2602.15989, open-source model plus the MHR rig, 7M curated images) reports large gains on its SA1B-Hard categorical set for truncated lower bodies, very hard poses (114 PVE against 150-214 for baselines) and close interaction (54 PVE). It also reports 49.7/52.9 PVE on Ego-Exo4D and 63.5 PVE on Harmony4D. Generic single-image HMR under moderate occlusion and truncation is therefore turning into a released-foundation-model problem. (2) Occlusion-specialised single-image methods keep improving, e.g. Discriminative-Generative Synergy (arXiv 2604.21712, 2026): 3DPW-OC 67.2 mm, 3DOH 80.9 mm. Several of the pain point's worst-case numbers come from older baselines (HMR, SPIN, HybrIK, PARE, CLIFF at 309-332 mm; CLIFF on VOccl3D) and probably overstate the current gap. Evidence it persists: (a) the SAM 3D Body authors state that it processes each person separately and ignores human-object and multi-person interaction. That is exactly the object-occludes-body setting of this field, and they released no HOI-occlusion benchmark numbers. (b) Benchmarking 3D HPE under Occlusions (arXiv 2504.10350, v2 Feb 2026) finds that all nine lifting models degrade, diffusion models are unexpectedly worse, and distal joints (wrists, feet) are consistently the most vulnerable. These are the joints that matter for manipulation. (c) The 2026 occlusion SOTA still relies on detected 2D joints and fails under severe occlusion. By its own account it is too heavy for real time. (d) Egocentric invisibility is still an active CVPR 2026 topic (EvaPose/Eva-3M builds visibility labels because methods treat invisible joints like visible ones; EgoPoseVR targets inaccurate lower body from HMD views). EgoAllo improves on EgoEgo by 20-30% but still infers the unobserved body from priors. (e) HOI reconstruction (ScoreHOI 2025, the amodal-completion HOI work 2507.08137) still treats occlusion as a main open challenge on BEHAVE/InterCap. The core argument stands: parts with no image evidence are filled by priors, and neither data scale nor model scale yields observability. It is a research problem, not saturated engineering. It is, however, no longer a good standalone thesis direction framed as 'better occluded HMR', because foundation models are absorbing that framing.

skeptics.reframe: Generic occluded or truncated single-image body recovery is being absorbed by released foundation models (SAM 3D Body). The open problem is metrically accurate, uncertainty-calibrated recovery of the body parts that matter for manipulation during object handling. Those are the wrists, hands and forearms, plus the lower body seen from close-range, head-mounted or robot cameras, when the handled object or the other arm removes all image evidence. Foundation models process each person alone, ignore the object, and fill the hidden joints from priors without signalling it. A sharper target: use the interaction itself (object pose and contact, bimanual constraints, temporal context, RGB-D or sparse extra views) as evidence for the hidden parts, report per-joint visibility-conditioned error and calibrated uncertainty, and evaluate on real data from the actual capture placements rather than synthetic masks.

skeptics.reasons:
Artifact test, core claim: it survives. The 38 supporting papers come from many separate groups, venues and sensing setups. They include MPI and Tuebingen (BEHAVE, RICH/HOT, InterCap), ShanghaiTech (NeuralDome, HOI-M3), Meta (EgoBody3M, Nymeria, EgoHumans), UC Riverside (VOccl3D), IST Lisbon (BlendMimic3D and the Lino et al. benchmark), Verona (HARPER), Northeastern (SLP), and egocentric work from Akada and Wang at MPI. The settings span third-person HOI, egocentric fisheye, robot-mounted cameras, in-bed monitoring, clinical video and avatars, and the evidence covers 2022 to 2026. The problem is also older than the corpus: 3DOH50K (CVPR 2020) and PARE (ICCV 2021) already treated object occlusion and partial occlusion as open, and the 2025 benchmarks still find monotonic degradation, with distal joints (wrists, feet) the worst. No community treats single-view recovery of hidden parts as solved. Multi-view domes, marker mocap and RGB-D capture avoid the problem by adding viewpoints rather than solving it, and those are exactly the setups the practical use cases (head-worn, robot, one clinic camera) cannot have.

Where the artifact critique does land:
(1) The headline magnitudes depend on protocol. The 33 cm upper bound is the HOI-M3 Table 4 MPJPE for off-the-shelf HMR, SPIN, HybrIK, PARE and CLIFF (309.81 to 332.47 mm). I found no sign these models were fine-tuned on HOI-M3, and PA-MPJPE is also 127 to 188 mm, so the figure mixes domain shift, multi-person scale and root errors with occlusion. The 71 vs 116 mm VOccl3D gap is a detector-box effect, not an occlusion-recovery effect. The Lino et al. result is a synthetic noise-injection protocol on one synthetic dataset from the BlendMimic3D group. The "near-zero detection accuracy" claim is not traced to a verified source here.
(2) The pain point bundles distinct sub-problems that have different fixes: object occlusion in HOI, egocentric lower-body truncation, under-cover in-bed pose, self-occlusion in single-image avatar reconstruction, and robot-height truncation. Several items, such as NeRSemble, MVHumanNet++ and the avatar surveys, cite it only as a motivating limitation, not as a measured failure.
(3) For this author's setting (bimanual hand-object, RGB-D), body-level occlusion is adjacent. Hand self-occlusion and occlusion by the handled object are the relevant cases and are covered more thinly here.

Net: this is a real, field-wide, persistent problem, not an artifact of one dataset. But it is long-recognized and diffuse, its numbers are not comparable across protocols, and as stated it is too broad to serve as a novel research direction.

skeptics.reframe: From the viewpoints that interaction capture actually uses (head-worn, robot-mounted, a single RGB or RGB-D camera), body and hand parts hidden by the handled object or the person's own body stay hidden for longer than the temporal window of current lifters and priors. No benchmark has real annotations for this sustained, interaction-caused occlusion. Current figures (about 10 to 33 cm) mix detector failure, domain shift and protocol differences with true recovery error under occlusion, so the field cannot tell whether methods improve on the hidden parts or only on the visible ones.

skeptics.reasons: Attempted refutation: P11 is partly an observability limit (hidden parts give no pixels) plus a data-scarcity complaint ("real annotated data for practical camera placements is scarce"). The data-scarcity half is pure resource effort, and the generic "occlusion-robust HMR" framing is crowded and incremental; a new synthetic-occlusion set or a fine-tuned detector is not a top-venue question. The record is also diffuse, pooling in-bed monitoring, clinical reaching, clothed avatars and egocentric fisheye, which by itself states no question. The refutation still fails, because the field keeps publishing occlusion-specific research questions at top venues through 2026, and the open issues are conceptual rather than resource-bound. (1) Identifiability and posterior shape: hidden parts are fundamentally ambiguous, so the question is what the right output is (a calibrated distribution, not a point estimate) and how to evaluate it. The WACV 2025 probabilistic HMR paper states that current evaluation protocols do not detect wrong hypotheses for invisible joints, and FactorizedHMR (arXiv 2605.14854) argues for uncertainty-aware completion of ambiguity-prone variables. That makes "how to score hallucinated parts" an open methodological question. (2) In manipulation, the occluder is the handled object, whose geometry, pose, contact and physics constrain the hidden hand or body. Whether those constraints can collapse the posterior over unseen parts is a significant question that more labelled data does not answer. (3) Sensor and viewpoint design: egocentric and robot-mounted cameras make missing views the normal case. CVPR 2026 EvaPose (visibility-aware ego HPE), CVPR 2026 OcMotion (frequency-domain denoising prior for occluded mocap), EgoH4 (forecasting out-of-view hands from body pose) and REWIND (CVPR 2025) show reviewers accept these as research. The problem is not solved-awaiting-resources: the record says priors trained on lightly occluded data fail when the occlusion lasts longer than the model's temporal window, and masking-trained models do not generalize across occlusion patterns. Both are open generalization questions. The score is moderate rather than high for three reasons: the generic version is saturated; many fixes are engineering (fine-tuned detectors, synthetic data); and novelty depends on a sharp formulation tied to manipulation or RGB-D. For the author's bimanual RGB-D setting, depth gives the occluder's geometry explicitly, which supports the object-as-constraint framing.

skeptics.reframe: In hand-object and bimanual capture, the handled object both hides the hand or body and constrains it. The open question is whether the object's measured geometry and pose (available from RGB-D), contact and physical plausibility can make the hidden hand or body parts identifiable, and how to report them as a calibrated distribution instead of a prior-driven point estimate. Evaluation would score visible and hidden parts separately, so prior hallucination is no longer credited as accuracy, which current protocols cannot detect.

research_questions.question: In RGB-D hand-object and bimanual capture, how much of a hidden hand and forearm becomes identifiable when the posterior uses the handled object as evidence? The evidence is the object's measured geometry and pose, the occluder's depth free space (a hidden part must lie behind the observed surface, or it would have been seen), and contact with no penetration. Can the hidden parts then be reported as calibrated per-joint sets instead of a single estimate filled in from the prior?
research_questions.why_top_venue: Released foundation models are absorbing generic occluded body recovery. SAM 3D Body (arXiv 2602.15989, verified) processes each person alone and ignores the object. The 2026 occluded hand-object papers rely on learned or text priors from RGB and report aggregate error. These are GenHOI (arXiv 2603.19013, ECCV 2026 per its arXiv page, verified), the Affordance-Guided Diffusion Prior (arXiv 2510.00506, ECCV 2026 per its arXiv page, verified) and the occlusion-aware masked-autoencoder hand-object paper (arXiv 2506.10816, search result only). None of them separates hidden-joint error from visible-joint error or tests calibration. Pierzchlewicz et al. (arXiv 2210.11179, verified) show that min-of-K metrics favour miscalibrated distributions, especially for occluded joints. A paper that measures how much physical and geometric evidence shrinks the hidden-joint posterior, and gives hidden-joint sets with guaranteed coverage, makes a conceptual contribution rather than a leaderboard gain. Classic model-based RGB-D trackers used free-space and render-and-compare terms (Mueller et al. ICCV 2017, Oikonomidis et al. 2011). Modern generative hand and HOI priors drop them. Bringing these terms into the generative priors is the opening.
research_questions.method_sketch: (1) Train a small diffusion or flow prior over MANO articulation plus a short forearm and elbow chain (the SMPL-X upper limb), expressed in the object frame. Training data: ground-truth grasps from DexYCB, ARCTIC, GRAB and OakInk. (2) At test time, run guided posterior sampling (DPS-style, or score guidance as in ScoreHMR, CVPR 2024). The likelihood combines: (a) 2D heatmaps (WiLoR or HaMeR) and depth agreement for visible parts; (b) a free-space term that penalises any hypothesised hand surface point that projects onto a measured-depth pixel and lies more than tau in front of it, using the hand and object masks to separate occluder from hand; (c) object signed-distance penetration and contact terms, using a known object mesh or a BundleSDF reconstruction, with pose from FoundationPose; (d) kinematic consistency with the visible forearm and upper arm. (3) Calibrate per-joint sets with split conformal prediction, stratified by visibility class (visible, object-occluded, self-occluded, other-hand, truncated). (4) Ablate the evidence terms one at a time and report the shrinkage of the hidden-joint posterior per degree of freedom. This gives an identifiability profile: which hidden DoF the object fixes and which remain prior-driven.
research_questions.minimum_experiment: Use DexYCB (8 RealSense RGB-D views). The input is one view's RGB-D. Ground truth comes from the multi-view annotations. Per-joint visibility comes from z-buffer rendering of the ground-truth hand and object meshes in the input view. Compare: HaMeR and WiLoR (deterministic), SAM 3D Body hands, an RGB-only diffusion prior (HHMR-style), and the proposed sampler with each evidence term added in turn. Report, by visibility class: hidden-joint MPJPE of the sample mean; the radius of the 90% conformal set at fixed coverage; the energy score; and visible-joint MPJPE, which must not degrade. Pass criterion: on object-occluded joints, at least 20% lower error and at least 30% smaller 90% sets than the RGB-only prior, with empirical coverage within 2 points of nominal. Then repeat with object pose estimated by FoundationPose instead of ground truth, and on HO-3D v3 and H2O (two hands, RGB-D) to show transfer. About 2-3 months.
research_questions.data_and_hardware: Public data only for the core. Evaluation: DexYCB, HO-3D v3 and H2O (all RGB-D with multi-view ground truth). Prior training: ARCTIC, GRAB and OakInk. One 24 GB GPU: the small pose prior trains in hours to a day, and guided sampling runs at inference. Total downloads are several hundred GB, but subsets suffice. Optional: one consumer RGB-D camera for qualitative demos. No mocap and no robot.
research_questions.risks: (1) Novelty challenge: the classic RGB-D trackers already used render-and-compare free-space terms. The paper must lead with the calibrated identifiability analysis, not the constraint itself. (2) Reviewers favour RGB-only methods. Mitigation: add a variant that uses monocular depth and estimated object pose. (3) Gains may concentrate on object-occluded fingers, while self-occlusion stays prior-dominated. (4) Split conformal gives marginal, not conditional, coverage. (5) Ground-truth annotation noise in HO-3D and DexYCB (several mm, up to about 1 cm) limits the gain that can be measured on hidden joints. (6) The ECCV 2026 occluded hand-object groups may add depth or physics terms concurrently.

research_questions.question: Do current hand, body and hand-object estimators actually recover the parts they cannot see, or do they output what a prior would predict from the visible parts alone? This needs a benchmark and metric suite for occlusion caused by the interaction, stratified by visibility and occlusion duration, built from existing multi-view ground truth.
research_questions.why_top_venue: All three skeptics converge on this gap. Headline occlusion numbers (about 10-33 cm) mix detector failure, domain shift and protocol differences with real recovery error. No benchmark has real labels for sustained, interaction-caused occlusion, so the field cannot tell whether methods improve on hidden parts or only on visible ones. Nearby work does not fill it. EvaPose/Eva-3M (CVPR 2026, verified) labels visibility for egocentric bodies. Hand Visibility Detector (arXiv 2608.11574, August 2026, verified) classifies 2D keypoint visibility. Neither measures 3D accuracy or calibration on hidden parts across hand-object datasets. The headline finding would be that state-of-the-art hidden-joint error is no better than a blind prior that never sees the hidden pixels. That finding would be cited widely. If it turns out false, the benchmark still measures real progress. Compute is low, which suits a small lab.
research_questions.method_sketch: (1) For every camera in DexYCB, HO-3D v3, H2O, ARCTIC (egocentric view plus 8 allocentric views, SMPL-X arms), HOT3D, BEHAVE and InterCap, render the ground-truth hand, body and object meshes with a z-buffer. Label each joint and vertex in each frame as visible, object-occluded, occluded by the other hand or arm, self-occluded, or truncated. Add time since last visible and the length of the occlusion run. (2) Metrics: (a) MPJPE and PVE stratified by visibility; (b) a hidden-evidence gain, defined as the blind-prior error minus the method's error on hidden joints, where the blind prior is a conditional model trained to predict hidden joints from visible joints and object pose only; (c) for probabilistic methods, coverage, set size, energy score and NLL instead of min-of-K, following Pierzchlewicz et al. 2022; (d) error-versus-duration curves. (3) Evaluate 8-12 public models: HaMeR, WiLoR, SAM 3D Body, HOLD, DPMesh, plus GenHOI or MoPO if code is released, and the BEHAVE/InterCap baselines. (4) Optional real witness-camera split. One consumer RGB-D camera sits at the actual capture placement (close-range desk or robot height); a second camera sees the hidden side and is used only for evaluation. Witness ground-truth error is quantified with a marker-checked object.
research_questions.minimum_experiment: Visibility labels for DexYCB and ARCTIC (egocentric and allocentric) only. Evaluate four methods: HaMeR, WiLoR, SAM 3D Body hands and one hand-object method. Add the blind-prior baseline, trained in about a day. Key figure: hidden-joint error versus occlusion duration for each method and for the blind prior, split into object-occluded and self-occluded joints. Go/no-go: if a strong method's object-occluded joint error is within 10% of the blind prior, prior filling is shown and carries the paper. If every method beats the blind prior by a wide margin, pivot to a benchmark-and-calibration paper. About 6-8 weeks.
research_questions.data_and_hardware: Public multi-view datasets with ground-truth meshes (listed above). A differentiable or standard rasteriser (PyTorch3D or nvdiffrast) on one GPU. Storage for subsets: ARCTIC and HOT3D are large, so use their cropped or subsampled releases. Optional witness split: two consumer RGB-D cameras (about US$400-800 total) and 8-10 subjects under an ethics approval.
research_questions.risks: (1) The ground-truth meshes in HO-3D, BEHAVE and InterCap are fitted, so hidden-joint ground truth carries mm-to-cm error and must be reported as a floor. (2) Without a sharp blind-prior result, reviewers may call the relabelling incremental. (3) Dataset licences may block redistribution of derived labels; release scripts instead. (4) Rendered visibility can disagree with real silhouettes (sleeves, mesh-fit error). (5) Partial overlap with Hand Visibility Detector and EvaPose. (6) Benchmark adoption is uncertain.

research_questions.question: During bimanual handling, a hand or the holding forearm can stay hidden behind the object for longer than a motion prior's temporal window. In that case, can the tracked object serve as a proxy sensor for the hidden limb, by propagating the grasp while it stays locked and detecting regrasps explicitly? And does uncertainty that honestly grows with time unseen improve transfer from human demonstrations to robots?
research_questions.why_top_venue: The pain-point record shows motion priors collapsing once occlusion outlasts their window: about 302 mm MPJPE beyond an 81-frame window. Pipelines that learn robot skills from human video retarget hand poses that were filled in from priors, without flagging them. The object's motion stays observable while the hand does not, so during a stable grasp the hidden limb is partly observable through the object. The proposal treats this as a switching estimator with explicit observability states. It is evaluated with visibility-stratified error and physics replay, which links occlusion handling to the human-video-to-robot data problem that CoRL and RSS currently care about. AgenticFocus (arXiv 2607.08857, July 2026, found through the arXiv API, details not checked) reconstructs occluded hand motion for humanoid learning, which shows interest. No top-venue paper making the object-as-sensor observability argument was found (search limited to six queries).
research_questions.method_sketch: State per hand: the hand pose in the object frame T_ho, MANO articulation, a grasp mode (stable, regrasp or free) and a covariance. Object 6D pose comes from FoundationPose (markerless, RGB-D), with markers kept only as an oracle ablation. When the hand is visible, update from a per-frame estimator (WiLoR or HaMeR, refined with depth). When it is hidden and the grasp is stable, hold T_ho fixed (rigid attachment) with small process noise. Detect mode changes from evidence: object motion inconsistent with attachment given the visible arm, contact by the other hand, and depth free-space violations. In free mode, fall back to a learned bimanual motion prior conditioned on the object trajectory. The visible upper-arm and shoulder kinematics constrain the forearm and elbow. Covariance grows with time unseen and with mode uncertainty. The estimator is causal and runs in real time on one GPU. Downstream test: retarget the estimated hand trajectories to a simulated dexterous hand in MuJoCo or Isaac and replay them with the object trajectory. Measure object-drop rate, penetration and replay success against retargeting from per-frame estimates and from motion-prior infill.
research_questions.minimum_experiment: Use ARCTIC (two hands, egocentric and allocentric, mocap ground truth) and HOT3D (egocentric, mocap ground truth). Take segments with real object occlusion of a hand, plus synthetic long occlusions made by masking the hand for 1-5 s in the input view. Baselines: per-frame WiLoR or HaMeR with the last value held; a masked motion-infill transformer trained on GRAB and ARCTIC; offline smoothing as an upper bound. Metrics: hidden-wrist and hidden-hand MPJPE versus occlusion duration, and coverage of the predicted covariance. Pass criterion: beyond 1 s of occlusion, at least 30% lower hidden-wrist error than motion-prior infill during stable grasps, and at least 80% of regrasp events flagged (using ground-truth contact). Then run simulated replay on about 50 sequences, comparing object-drop rates. Finish with a qualitative real demo on a desk RGB-D setup with a witness camera. About 3-4 months.
research_questions.data_and_hardware: ARCTIC, HOT3D, GRAB, DexYCB and H2O. FoundationPose or BundleSDF for object tracking, which needs an object mesh or a reconstruction. One GPU. MuJoCo or Isaac with an open dexterous-hand model. One or two consumer RGB-D cameras. A borrowed robot arm is optional and only for a qualitative real-robot clip.
research_questions.risks: (1) Reviewers may see rigid attachment as engineering unless regrasp detection and the observability analysis are non-trivial. (2) ARCTIC's objects are articulated, and in-hand manipulation breaks the attachment assumption. (3) Object-pose error passes straight into the hidden-hand estimate. (4) CoRL and RSS reviewers expect real-robot results, and simulated replay alone may be judged insufficient. (5) Vision venues may read it as tracking engineering. (6) Physics-based hand-object tracking papers may overlap and need a closer novelty check. (7) Marker-based object pose would be discounted at review.

fit.thesis_assets_help: Moderate, concentrated in RQ3 and in the label design for RQ2; little for RQ1. The object-conditioned recovery of an occluded holding arm is already a working prototype of the grasp-locked propagation in RQ3, so the framing and a first pipeline exist. The measured/held/constrained honesty labels map directly onto the visibility and observability states that RQ2 and RQ3 need. The causal 30 fps chain supports a real-time claim, and the Unity twin can render z-buffer visibility labels and synthetic long occlusions. Hard limits: 28 recordings of one subject from one camera contain no ground truth for hidden parts, so they cannot carry quantitative claims at a top venue. ArUco markers on the object will be read as a crutch; headline results should use FoundationPose, with markers kept only as an oracle-object-pose ablation. The desk setup becomes a useful real split at the actual capture placement only if a second witness camera and roughly 8-10 subjects are added.
fit.what_a_small_lab_cannot_do_here: A small lab cannot compete on generic occluded body or mesh recovery (3DPW-OC, VOccl3D, AGORA, SA1B-Hard style leaderboards). Large groups dominate it, and foundation models trained on millions of images absorb it (SAM 3D Body used about 7M curated images); the lab cannot train or retrain models at that scale. It cannot build new mocap-grade data with ground truth for hidden parts at scale: no multi-view domes, optical marker capture or multi-person object-occlusion scenes like HOI-M3. It cannot own the egocentric hidden-lower-body problem, which needs custom multi-camera headsets and million-frame datasets (Meta EgoBody3M, Nymeria, Eva-3M, Ego4View). It cannot collect robot-mounted camera data at scale or run real-robot policy evaluations without a borrowed arm. It cannot validate the accuracy of its own hidden-part estimates from single-camera recordings: at least one extra witness view or public multi-view ground truth is required. The feasible niche is narrow: object-conditioned, calibrated recovery of hidden hands and forearms, plus visibility-stratified evaluation on existing public multi-view RGB-D data.

painpoint.name: Textureless, transparent, reflective, thin and small objects starve vision and depth

evidence.latest_state: Low texture alone is now close to solved in the easy setting, but transparent, reflective and small objects are not. PG-Pose (arXiv 2609.07231, IROS 2026) reports 94.2 percent ADD(S)@0.1d on OnePose-LowTexture. That benchmark is static and has no hand in it, and the pain point's 16.8 percent figure uses the stricter 1cm-1deg metric, so the two numbers do not compare directly. Reflective and metallic objects remain hard. On XYZ-IBD (arXiv 2506.00599, now a BOP-Industrial dataset in the BOP Challenge 2025), FoundationPose reaches 0.547 AP and SAM-6D 0.438 AP on unseen objects, while GDRNet (0.266) and SurfEmb (0.274) do worse on seen objects; the authors say all methods struggle. Depth Anything V2 has 26.4 mm MAE and 41.8 mm RMSE on XYZ-IBD, far from the millimetre accuracy small parts need. For transparent objects, recent work is mostly depth completion for robot grasping: DITR (diffusion inpainting), GAA-TSO (ClearGrasp, OOD, TransCG, STD) and HDCNet (up to 60 percent more successful grasps). HFF6DoF (Sensors 2026) reaches only 50.5 percent ADD on TDoF20-hard. The CVPR 2025 NTIRE challenge on depth from specular and transparent surfaces drew only 4 teams per track. In the 2025-2026 hand-object reconstruction papers found (ForeHOI, GHOST 2603.18912, Grasp in Gaussians, PhysHanDI), no abstract targets transparent or reflective objects. The two methods aimed at hand-held transparent objects are HADR (2024, handover depth restoration on synthetic TransHand-14K) and TransDex (2026, a visuo-tactile robot policy). ProxyPose (2607.06555) claims model-free 6-DoF tracking of textureless, transparent and reflective surfaces through video diffusion, but its abstract gives no numbers. Practitioners still fall back on markers: the quARtet fiducial (2610.01072, Oct 2026) exists because labware is transparent or reflective. No benchmark of hand-held transparent or reflective objects with ground-truth hand and object pose was found.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: ProxyPose: 6-DoF Pose Tracking via Video-to-Video Translation
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Fine-tuned video diffusion model turns the input video into a synthetic proxy polyhedron video, then recovers pose with classical solvers. Claims state-of-the-art tracking on textureless, transparent, reflective and deformable surfaces without CAD models, depth or masks; the abstract gives no numbers.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: Generalizable 6D Pose Estimation of Textureless Objects with Planar-based Gaussian Splatting (PG-Pose)
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Planar Gaussian reconstruction from reference images plus 2D-3D matching and geometric refinement for CAD-free pose of textureless objects; 94.2 percent ADD(S)@0.1d on OnePose-LowTexture, 2.1 points above the previous Gaussian-splatting state of the art.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: XYZ-IBD: High-precision Bin-picking Dataset for Object 6D Pose Estimation Capturing Real-world Industrial Complexity
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Benchmark of 15 reflective, textureless, mostly symmetric metal parts in bins (about 273k instances). FoundationPose 0.547 AP, SAM-6D 0.438, SurfEmb 0.274, GDRNet 0.266; Depth Anything V2 MAE 26.4 mm.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: NTIRE 2025 Challenge on HR Depth from Images of Specular and Transparent Surfaces
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Challenge report with stereo and monocular tracks for high-resolution depth on non-Lambertian surfaces; about 177 registrants and 4 teams per track. It names non-Lambertian surfaces and high resolution as open problems.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: GAA-TSO: Geometry-Aware Assisted Depth Completion for Transparent and Specular Objects
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Back-projects depth to a point cloud and uses gated cross-modal 2D-3D fusion for depth completion. Reports state-of-the-art results on ClearGrasp, OOD, TransCG and STD, plus better robot grasping.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: HDCNet: A Hybrid Depth Completion Network for Grasping Transparent and Reflective Objects
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Transformer-CNN-Mamba hybrid for depth completion on transparent and reflective objects; reports state-of-the-art results on public benchmarks and up to 60 percent more successful grasps.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: Diffusion-Based Depth Inpainting for Transparent and Reflective Objects (DITR)
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Two-stage pipeline: region proposal, then diffusion-based depth inpainting of the optical and geometric depth loss on glass and mirror-like objects.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: GHOST: Geometry-Guided Hallucination of Opaque Surface Textures
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Preprocessing that uses vision foundation models to turn transparent regions into opaque, textured images with consistent geometry, so off-the-shelf depth and reconstruction models work on them; no numbers in the abstract.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: TransBiolab: A Real-World Multi-View Dataset of Cluttered Transparent Biomedical Objects
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Multi-view RGB-D dataset of transparent lab plasticware: 161k frames, 98 scenes, 1.03M instances, 15 object types, with 6D pose, masks and depth; benchmarks and robot evaluation, but no numbers in the abstract.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: TransDex: Pre-training Visuo-Tactile Policy with Point Cloud Reconstruction for Dexterous Manipulation of Transparent Objects
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Self-supervised point-cloud reconstruction pre-training that fuses vision and touch to cope with depth noise and self-occlusion when a dexterous robot hand manipulates transparent objects.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: SDT-6D: Fully Sparse Depth-Transformer for Staged End-to-End 6D Pose Estimation
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Multi-view depth fusion with a sparse transformer for bin-picking pose under occlusion and reflections. Details come from the arXiv API listing only; the abstract page was not opened.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: 6DoF Pose Estimation of Transparent Objects: Dataset and Method (HFF6DoF, TDoF20)
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: New TDoF20 transparent RGB-D dataset (61,886 pairs, 20 objects) and a hierarchical-fusion keypoint method; 50.5 percent ADD on TDoF20-hard, 7.13 points above DenseFusion.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: quARtet Marker: A 3D-Printable Multi-Tag Fiducial for Robust Near-Frontal Pose Estimation
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Marker-based workaround for localising transparent or reflective labware: orientation error falls from 2.18 to 0.24-0.47 deg and position error from 1.50 to 0.17-0.20 mm. It shows that markers are still the practical fix.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: DeLTa: Demonstration and Language-Guided Novel Transparent Object Manipulation
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Learns long-horizon manipulation of novel transparent objects from one demonstration, combining depth estimation with vision-language planning. Seen only in the arXiv API listing; the abstract was not opened.

evidence.crowdedness: MEDIUM. The papers counted here, roughly 15 papers from 2025-2026, are robotics grasping (depth completion), industrial bin-picking (BOP-Industrial, XYZ-IBD) and low-texture CAD-free pose. Almost none target hand-held transparent, reflective or small objects in hand-object or bimanual tracking (HADR is 2024, TransDex is robot-side), so the intersection with the author's field is sparse.
evidence.trend: Rising. Attention is growing through new benchmarks (XYZ-IBD in the BOP Challenge 2025, TransBiolab at ACM MM 2026, the NTIRE 2025 specular and transparent depth challenge) and through foundation-model and diffusion methods (DITR, GHOST, ProxyPose). The growth is driven by industrial and lab robotics, not by hand-object capture.

skeptics.reasons: Not refuted, but one part of it is now largely solved, so the claim should be narrowed. The part that has been reduced to engineering is depth sensing on static transparent and reflective objects. LingBot-Depth (Masked Depth Modeling, arXiv 2601.17895, accepted to ECCV 2026, Apache-2.0, code, checkpoints and 3M RGB-D pairs released) treats missing sensor depth on specular, transparent and textureless surfaces as masked input and fills it in. Its authors say it beats top RGB-D cameras on depth precision and pixel coverage, and it has been shipped with Orbbec Gemini 330 cameras for grasping transparent objects; press reports a version 2.0 that ranks first on 12 of 16 depth-completion benchmarks. The source evidence item 'depth completion barely helps transparent pose' (ClearPose era) is therefore out of date. Other 2025-2026 depth fixes for transparent objects include SeeClear (arXiv 2603.19547, diffusion opacification followed by an off-the-shelf monocular depth model), HDCNet (2511.07081) and the stereo foundation-model approaches (ClearDepth, StereoAnything). For textureless objects with a CAD model, render-and-compare pose methods have steadily improved: BOP 2024 reports FreeZeV2.1 at +22% over the 2023 best on BOP-Classic-Core. On the other side, the evidence that the problem persists in the author's setting is direct. 3DReflecNet (CVPR 2026 oral, arXiv 2605.10204) states that state-of-the-art matching, SfM, novel-view-synthesis and relighting methods 'struggle to maintain accuracy' on reflective, transparent and low-texture objects. BOP 2025 added industrial datasets (XYZ-IBD, ITODD-MV, IPD) precisely because reflective metal parts in clutter remain hard. The BOP 2024 report names 2D detection of unseen objects as the main bottleneck, and that bottleneck is worse for small objects that the hand mostly covers. A July 2026 HOI foundation-model survey (2607.28394) does not treat material or size as solved; its abstract does not mention them at all. I found no 2025-2026 released model or benchmark that tracks a hand-held transparent, specular, thin or small object under hand occlusion and motion with saturated metrics. The depth-completion foundation models are shown on mostly static tabletop scenes and grasping, with no published evaluation on hand-held, moving and occluded objects. Ground truth for such objects in HOI capture still relies on coating or markers. What survives is the hand-held, dynamic, model-free, small or thin part of the claim, plus the shortage of ground truth, not the general 'depth sensors fail on glass' claim.

skeptics.reframe: Released RGB-D depth-completion foundation models (for example LingBot-Depth, ECCV 2026) now largely fix missing depth on static transparent and specular objects. The open problem is narrower: tracking and reconstructing, without a CAD model, hand-held objects that are transparent, specular, thin or small while the hand covers most of their few pixels and they move. This combines three gaps. Depth-completion priors have no published evaluation on such objects under hand occlusion and motion. Correspondence and detection collapse when the object takes up only a few unoccluded pixels. And there is no ground truth for these materials in HOI capture that does not change their appearance, such as coating or markers.

skeptics.reasons:
Diversity check: the 37 supporting papers come from many separate groups and settings, so P12 is not the artifact of one lab or one dataset. They include TUM (PhoCaL, HouseCat6D), UMich (ClearPose), ZJU (OnePose, OnePose++), HKU (Gen6D), Berkeley (DTTD), NVIDIA (HANDAL), Naver (SHOWMe), Meta (AssemblyHands), Tsinghua (HOI4D), Brown (GigaHands) and surgical groups (POV-Surgery, OphNet-3D), plus industrial benchmarks (XYZ-IBD, IndustryShapes). Other communities confirm the problem independently. The depth and robotics community has run dedicated work on transparent and specular depth since ClearGrasp and TransCG: the NTIRE 2025 challenge on depth of specular and transparent surfaces, D3RoMa (CoRL 2024), and DKT (arXiv 2512.23705, Dec 2025, which states that transparent objects "remain notoriously hard"). The hand-object setting also has a dedicated paper, HADR (arXiv 2408.14997), which says hand occlusion amplifies the depth failure on transparent objects. So the core material problem is real across the field, not an artifact.

The bundle is too broad, though, and several of its parts are artifacts of particular setups:
(1) Textureless. Model-based pose has long treated textureless objects as tractable: LINEMOD and T-LESS were built for them. In BOP 2024, the best unseen-object method (FreeZeV2.1) reached 75.5 AR on T-LESS and 74.2 on ITODD, against 91.5 on YCB-V. That is a real gap of about 16 points, but not a failure. The headline figure of 16.8 percent 1cm-1deg comes from OnePose-LowTexture, a protocol that is tied to keypoint SfM, CAD-free onboarding and a strict threshold. It reflects that pipeline choice, not a property of the field.
(2) Small objects. Dice ADD-0.1D 2.44 comes from one dataset (HOGraspNet) under a diameter-relative metric that is harsh for tiny objects under heavy hand occlusion. LM-O ape versus can is the well-known occlusion and pixel-count effect in a single benchmark. Gen6D's 1-2 pixel scale error is a property of that method's design. These are resolution and metric effects, not a material-sensing failure.
(3) Thin objects. Evidence rests mainly on HOSt3R and HOGraspNet, two papers.

What survives is narrower. Transparent and specular hand-held objects defeat active depth and correspondence. Depth-restoration methods are trained on static tabletop scenes. HOI benchmarks (DexYCB, HO3D, OakInk, ARCTIC, HOT3D) use mostly opaque objects, so the field's evaluations rarely test the case. That makes P12 partly a benchmark-convention gap (the objects are excluded, coated or taped) rather than a demonstrated failure of current HOI trackers on such objects. Recent foundation stereo (FoundationStereo, CVPR 2025) and diffusion depth (D3RoMa, DKT) are closing the static case quickly, which weakens the claim that the problem persists unchanged.

Score: 5. The problem is real and broadly recognized, but it is largely inherited from, and actively owned by, the depth-sensing community. The textureless and small-object strands are setup artifacts.

skeptics.reframe: Transparent and specular objects held in the hand break both active depth and correspondence-based tracking. Static-scene depth-restoration models do not handle hand occlusion and motion. HOI benchmarks leave these objects out or coat them, so the field has no measure of how far current hand-object trackers degrade on them. The textureless and small-object cases are better treated as known, partly addressed effects of model-free keypoint pipelines and pixel count.

skeptics.reasons:
I could not refute P12 as a problem with no research question. Part of it is engineering or data collection, and I set that part aside. That covers spray paint and tape, switching sensors, adding polarization or event cameras, and building larger datasets of glassware and metal. It also covers some of the small-object failures: dice at ADD 2.44 and a 1-2 pixel scale error on distant objects. These are partly an information limit, and more resolution or another camera view simply fixes them. On its own that part would not interest a top-venue reviewer. Transparent-object pose is also already its own subfield, and most of its output goes to robotics venues: ClearPose was published at ECCV 2022, ReFlow6D in RA-L 2024, and StereoPose and HADR are on arXiv (venue not confirmed). So 'transparent object pose' in isolation is not new.

Two research questions do survive, and both are specific to hand-object work. (1) When the object itself gives no reliable cue (no texture, invalid depth, or mostly covered by the hand), can the hand be the main observation of the object? That means using hand pose, contact and the physical feasibility of the grasp to infer the pose and shape of the held object, rather than treating the hand only as an occluder. The idea is barely explored. The only direct precedent I found is HADR (arXiv 2408.14997): it uses hand posture to guide depth restoration for hand-held transparent objects, but works on single frames, uses a synthetic dataset of 8 objects, and does not estimate pose or track over time. (2) Can render-and-compare trackers in the FoundationPose style be made material-aware, so that they model refraction and specular reflection while estimating pose and material together? Model-free tracking currently assumes Lambertian, textured objects. ReFlow6D and NeRF-based render-and-compare for transparent objects (arXiv 2410.13465) model refraction for static, single-object pose, but not with the hand occluding the object over time.

There is also a scientific question in evaluation: how to obtain ground truth without changing the object's appearance. Coating changes exactly the property being studied. That question is weaker and could be judged engineering.

Main risks. The topic is crowded at the object-pose level, and robotics venues absorb much of it. A hand-centric version has to show a real gain over FoundationPose-style trackers on real (not only synthetic) transparent, reflective and thin hand-held objects. Real ground truth for that evaluation is itself the bottleneck the pain point describes.
