skeptics.reframe: When a hand-held object gives no reliable appearance or depth evidence (transparent, specular, textureless, thin, or mostly covered by the hand), current trackers fail because they read the object's pose only from the object's own pixels. The open question is whether the hand's pose, its contacts and the physical feasibility of the grasp, combined with a render-and-compare model that accounts for refraction and specular reflection, can recover the object's 6D pose and shape over time. This has to be shown on real ground truth captured without coating the object.

research_questions.question: RQ1 (benchmark and diagnosis; do this first). If shape, size and grasp are held fixed and only the material changes (opaque, clear, mirror-specular), how much do current RGB-D object trackers and hand-object trackers degrade on hand-held objects? Which cue fails first: raw depth, segmentation, correspondence, or the hand seen through or reflected in the object? And do the 2026 depth foundation models (LingBot-Depth arXiv 2601.17895, single frame; DKT arXiv 2512.23705, video) close the gap once a hand covers the object and it moves?
research_questions.why_top_venue: There is no real benchmark of hand-held transparent or specular objects with ground-truth pose. HADR (arXiv 2408.14997, verified) is synthetic and depth-only (TransHand-14K). CHOC (arXiv 2211.10470, verified) is mixed reality, with rendered hands and 48 synthetic containers. ClearPose, TransCG, XYZ-IBD and TransBiolab are static or robot-side scenes. DexYCB, HO3D, ARCTIC and HOT3D use mostly opaque objects. DKT is evaluated on ClearPose and DREDS, and LingBot-Depth is single-frame; neither reports hand-held or occluded evaluation. A paired-material design makes material the only variable. That answers the artifact skeptic, because size and thinness also become controlled factors rather than dataset quirks. It also gives a falsifiable test of a claim the field now half-assumes: that depth foundation models have solved glass and chrome. A benchmark that overturns or confirms that claim fits NeurIPS Datasets and Benchmarks or 3DV. As a standalone CVPR main-track paper, a single-sensor, few-dozen-object dataset is borderline; it is strongest paired with RQ2.
research_questions.method_sketch: 1) Objects. Print each shape from one CAD file in three materials: matte opaque PLA (FDM); clear (SLA clear resin, sanded and clear-coated, plus a few off-the-shelf glass or acrylic items whose geometry matches a scan); and mirror (chrome spray or metallised film over PLA). Add two controlled factors: scale (100 percent and 50 percent) for small objects, and a thin-shape subset (spatula, ruler, pen-like). 2) Ground truth. A rigid marker tail: a multi-tag ArUco cube on a short rod at the end the hand does not grasp, calibrated once per object to the CAD frame. The tail is identical across materials, so its confound cancels in paired comparisons, and its image region is masked from tracker inputs. Optionally add one or two cheap USB RGB cameras so the markers can be triangulated across views. Validate the GT on the opaque twin against FoundationPose+ICP, and report GT error explicitly. 3) Protocol. 6-10 volunteers, scripted grasp and lift, in-hand rotation, two-hand handover and place. Pairing is by subject, shape and script, not by identical trajectory. 4) Evaluation. FoundationPose tracking on raw depth, on LingBot-Depth-completed depth and on DKT-completed depth; a model-free tracker (BundleSDF); RGB-only trackers where code exists (ComPose arXiv 2605.23523, ProxyPose arXiv 2607.06555); and a naive rigid-to-hand lock after initialisation. Hand trackers (HaMeR or WiLoR plus depth fit) are scored by contact and penetration plausibility against the GT object, since there is no hand GT. Metrics: ADD-S AUC, 2 cm / 5 deg success, track-loss rate, recovery time, and depth MAE inside the GT object mask.
research_questions.minimum_experiment: About 8 shapes x 3 materials at full size, plus 4 shapes x 3 materials at half size (36 objects). 6 subjects x 3 scripted actions x 1 take gives about 650 clips of about 15 s, roughly 290k frames at 30 fps; recording takes about 2 hours per subject. Deliverables: a GT accuracy report; a material x tracker x depth-preprocessing degradation table with paired statistical tests; and a per-cue failure attribution. Decision rule: if FoundationPose on completed depth comes within about 2 points ADD-S AUC of the opaque twin on clear and mirror objects, the material problem is effectively solved for this setting. That would be a publishable negative result, and the project would then narrow to the small and thin strand only.
research_questions.data_and_hardware: One consumer RGB-D camera. Ideally a second sensor of the other active type (ToF versus active stereo, about USD 300-400), because the failure modes differ and reviewers will ask about generality. One or two optional USB RGB cameras for multi-view marker GT. FDM printer plus SLA clear-resin printing (makerspace or print service), chrome spray, metallised film, ArUco cubes. One 24 GB GPU, enough for FoundationPose, LingBot-Depth inference and DKT 1.3B inference (the abstract reports about 0.17 s per frame, offline). Public opaque reference sets: DexYCB, HO3D, HOT3D. ClearPose and TransCG for checking the depth baselines. CHOC and TransHand-14K as synthetic pretraining sources if downloadable (availability not verified).
research_questions.risks: Clear SLA prints are hazier than glass, so reviewers may call them unrealistic; mitigate with a few real glass items. The tail changes the grasp and mass, and gives a cue if masking leaks. Single-view marker GT is likely 2-5 mm and 1-2 deg, which may be too coarse for the half-size objects; multi-tag or multi-view is needed (quARtet arXiv 2610.01072 reports 0.17-0.20 mm, but under near-frontal static conditions). The depth foundation models may already close the gap, leaving only a negative result. The dataset is small by CVPR standards. Someone with a mocap rig (the TransBiolab or HOT3D groups) could release a larger hand-held version first. Human-subject consent is needed even though only hands are recorded.

research_questions.question: RQ2 (main method). Can a causal tracker that treats the hand as the primary observation of a held object, and the object's own pixels and depth as evidence whose reliability depends on material, keep the 6D pose of transparent, specular, thin and small hand-held objects through in-hand rotation, regrasp and two-hand handover? Can it also report, calibrated against GT, whether each frame's pose was measured from the object, carried by the grasp, or inferred from contact?
research_questions.why_top_venue: Current trackers read object pose from the object's pixels, and those pixels are exactly what glass, chrome and hand occlusion destroy. Hand-as-cue tracking has begun, but every example verified this session stops short of the material dimension. ComPose (arXiv 2605.23523, May 2026) uses hand motion as a complementary cue in RGB; its abstract names no datasets or materials. GenHOI (2603.19013) and the in-the-wild egocentric HOI work (2606.30598) use hand priors for occlusion. HADR uses hand posture for depth restoration only, on synthetic single frames. None treats sensor failure as evidence, models material-dependent cue reliability, or certifies the provenance of each pose. A tracker that holds where all baselines fail, with calibrated provenance that robot-demonstration pipelines can use to filter frames, is a clear CVPR/ICCV method contribution with a CoRL application angle.
research_questions.method_sketch: State: the hand pose (from HaMeR or WiLoR plus depth fit; skin is roughly Lambertian, so the hand is the reliable signal) and the object-in-hand transform T_ho, with a slip and regrasp process model. Observation terms: (a) a video segmentation mask (SAM2-class) as a silhouette likelihood; (b) raw-depth validity, where holes or through-object background depth inside the predicted silhouette count as positive evidence that the object is there, learned per material class and sensor; (c) completed depth from LingBot-Depth or DKT with a learned per-pixel uncertainty; (d) contact and non-penetration terms from the hand mesh; (e) a FoundationPose-style render-and-compare score where reliable. A small gating network predicts each term's per-frame reliability. It is trained on the RQ1 train split plus Blender Cycles renders of glass and chrome objects in MANO grasps taken from DexYCB or ARCTIC. Output: the pose plus a provenance label (measured / held / constrained) with a calibrated error bound. Target speed: causal, 15-30 fps.
research_questions.minimum_experiment: RQ1 test split with held-out subjects and shapes. Baselines: FoundationPose (raw, plus LingBot-Depth, plus DKT), BundleSDF, the naive rigid-to-hand lock, and ComPose if code is released. Report ADD-S AUC and track loss by material and by segment type (stable hold, in-hand rotation, regrasp, bimanual handover). Show no regression on opaque DexYCB and HO3D. Ablate each observation term and the gating. Report provenance calibration as the expected calibration error of the label-implied error bound against true error. The critical test is to beat the rigid-to-hand lock on regrasp and handover segments, because on stable holds the lock alone is probably strong.
research_questions.data_and_hardware: The RQ1 data, public DexYCB, HO3D and HOT3D, and synthetic Blender renders (CPU or the single GPU; a few tens of thousands of frames are enough for a gating network). One 24 GB GPU for training the gate and running the foundation models offline; real-time operation needs lighter depth completion or a lower update rate for it. The same RGB-D camera as RQ1.
research_questions.risks: ComPose and its follow-ups may already cover the hand-cue mechanism, so novelty rests on the material-aware evidence and the provenance output; reviewers must be shown both matter. Gains may be confined to rare regrasp and handover segments. Hand pose itself degrades when fingers are seen through glass or reflected in chrome, which is circular. The depth-invalidity cue is sensor-specific, so two sensor types are needed to argue generality. A gate trained on few shapes may overfit. Code for ComPose and ProxyPose may not be available for comparison.

research_questions.question: RQ3 (higher risk; pursue only if RQ1 shows completion-then-track still fails). Can a tracker use a learned forward model of how a consumer RGB-D sensor corrupts depth on transparent and specular objects as its observation likelihood, instead of completing the corrupted depth and then tracking? The model would predict the hole pattern and the mix of front-surface and through-object background depth from pose, shape, material and background. Does this beat completion-then-track under hand occlusion and motion?
research_questions.why_top_venue: Every 2025-2026 fix found (LingBot-Depth, DKT, SeeClear, HDCNet, DITR, GAA-TSO) completes depth first and discards the information in how the sensor failed. Refraction-aware render-and-compare exists only for static single objects: the NeRF-based estimator in arXiv 2410.13465 (verified in the arXiv listing) and ReFlow6D (RA-L 2024). A learned generative sensor model inside analysis-by-synthesis tracking is a principled and general idea. Prior use of such sensor likelihoods for hand-held objects was not found in this session; that novelty is unverified.
research_questions.method_sketch: Training pairs come from the RQ1 captures. Inputs: the GT pose and CAD give rendered ideal depth and normals; an empty-scene capture gives background depth; plus the material label. The target is the observed raw sensor depth, holes included. A conditional U-Net or small diffusion model predicts a per-pixel distribution: invalid probability plus a mixture over object-surface depth and through-object background depth. In tracking, pose hypotheses come from FoundationPose's sampler or a particle filter around the RQ2 hand-anchored prior. Each hypothesis is scored by the likelihood of the actual raw depth under the predicted distribution, plus an RGB silhouette term. Optionally pretrain the model on simulated active-stereo depth (a DREDS-style IR-pattern simulation; DREDS, ECCV 2022, not verified this session).
research_questions.minimum_experiment: Held-out shapes and subjects. Compare three trackers on the clear and mirror subsets: raw-depth tracking, completion-then-track (LingBot-Depth, DKT) and sensor-model tracking. Report ADD-S AUC, track loss and runtime. Ablate the background term and the material conditioning. If two sensor types are available, train one model per sensor and show transfer across shapes.
research_questions.data_and_hardware: The RQ1 captures plus per-session empty-background frames. The model is small enough to train on one 24 GB GPU. A second sensor type is strongly recommended. No extra public data is required; ClearPose and TransCG raw-versus-GT depth could serve as extra pretraining pairs.
research_questions.risks: Highest risk of the three. The model is sensor-specific, so it may read as narrow. The through-glass term assumes a known static background, which a hand moving behind the object violates. Specular returns depend on room lighting and the environment, which the model sees only implicitly. It may end up only matching completion-then-track. Reviewers may answer with 'just use LingBot-Depth' unless the gain under occlusion and motion is large.

fit.thesis_assets_help: The assets give a small-to-moderate edge, mostly for RQ1 ground truth and RQ2 provenance; they are not a reason on their own to choose this direction. 1) The ArUco-marked object with metric pose, including the existing 45 mm marker and scale-correction chain, is close to the marker-tail ground-truth mechanism RQ1 needs. That saves perhaps a month of GT engineering. But a single marker seen by one camera is likely only a few mm and 1-2 deg accurate, so it must be upgraded to a multi-tag cube or an extra view before small objects can be evaluated. 2) The measured/held/constrained honesty labels map almost exactly onto the per-frame provenance output proposed in RQ2: measured from the object, carried by the grasp, or inferred from contact. This is the most distinctive carry-over, because no hand-cue tracker found (ComPose, GenHOI) reports calibrated provenance. 3) Object-conditioned recovery of an occluded holding arm is the same hand-object coupling run in reverse; its kinematic plumbing and the habit of inferring the hidden partner from the visible one transfer modestly to RQ2. 4) The causal 30 fps chain is a ready real-time harness and a baseline runtime budget. 5) The Unity twin is of limited help: Unity's real-time refraction and specular shading are not physically accurate, so synthetic training data should come from Blender Cycles. The twin is useful only for visualisation or demos. 6) The 28 recordings of one subject are presumably opaque objects with a single person. They are useful only to test the pipeline and as an opaque sanity set, not as benchmark data. The single desk RGB-D setup matches the small-lab constraint but cannot by itself answer the sensor-generality question; a second sensor type is recommended.
fit.what_a_small_lab_cannot_do_here: A small lab cannot build mocap-grade or dense multi-view ground truth (dozens of synchronised cameras and optical markers, as in ARCTIC or HOT3D), so its GT will be marker-tail based at a few mm, and that limits claims on small objects. It cannot capture hundreds of objects or dozens of subjects, so the dataset will be small next to CVPR dataset papers. It cannot train depth or video-diffusion foundation models: LingBot-Depth used 3M RGB-D pairs, and ProxyPose and DKT fine-tune large video diffusion backbones. The lab can only use and adapt them, and it should not compete on depth-completion or BOP-Industrial (XYZ-IBD) leaderboards. It cannot do physically accurate differentiable refraction and specular rendering at scale inside a tracker. It cannot run polarization, event or multi-sensor rigs at scale. It cannot replay identical trajectories across materials without a borrowed robot arm, so paired comparisons are statistical (same subject, shape and script) rather than motion-identical. Invisible-marker GT, such as UV-fluorescent paint under synchronised UV strobing (the LUV approach, not verified this session), is possible in principle but is a costly engineering detour. Not verified this session: whether ComPose and ProxyPose code is public, the venue of ComPose, and whether TransHand-14K and CHOC can be downloaded. WebSearch was unavailable (session budget exhausted); the additional checks used WebFetch of arXiv abstract pages and the arXiv API.

painpoint.name: Contact location and timing cannot be inferred from images

evidence.latest_state: Contact is still estimated only to the centimetre and only for some frames. On egocentric ARCTIC, HOPformer (Bansal et al., ECCV 2026, arXiv 2606.30598) reaches 31.9 mm contact deviation (CDev) and 82.4% SR@0.05. JointTransformer gets 35.0 mm and ArcticNet-SF 44.1 mm, so the state of the art moved only about 1 mm past the 32.56 mm HANDS23 figure. On the new in-the-wild EPIC-Contact set, HOPformer gets 20.7 mm CDev but only 29.8% SR@0.05, against 17.6% for JointTransformer. The contact ground truth in EPIC-Contact is still painted by hand on MANO and then fitted, not measured. For contact timing, TouchMoment/HiCE (CVPR Findings 2026, arXiv 2604.12343) is the source of the pain point's own numbers: exact-frame AP 14.25 on HOI4D and 24.25 on TACO. AP rises to 48.47 and 55.51 within 2 frames, and the mAP is 32.89 and 41.08. Exact-frame onset is therefore still mostly missed. For body-scene contact, the DECO successors (DecoDINO, arXiv 2510.23203; GRACE, arXiv 2505.06575; InteractVLM, CVPR 2025) report relative gains on DAMON: DecoDINO says +7% F1 and half the geodesic error. I could not verify any of them on out-of-domain BEHAVE, where DECO had F1 0.18. The newest trend, from August 2026, moves past binary contact to force and pressure: EgoPHI (ECCV 2026), HOPE (arXiv 2608.06192) and EgoTac (arXiv 2608.15060). EgoTac trains on 5.7M image-tactile pairs and reports in-domain force error below 0.06 N. These methods are supervised by simulated force or by data from tactile gloves and planar sensors, so the gap in per-frame contact ground truth on bare hands and arbitrary objects is narrowed but not closed.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: Towards in-the-wild Egocentric 3D Hand-Object Pose Estimation (EPIC-Contact dataset, HOPformer)
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Introduces EPIC-Contact (2.3K clips, 62.3K frames) with dense bijective hand-object contact correspondences annotated by hand, and a bimanual transformer. CDev 31.9 mm on ARCTIC-ego and 20.7 mm on EPIC-Contact; SR@0.05 29.8% in the wild.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: Detecting Precise Hand Touch Moments in Egocentric Video (TouchMoment, HiCE)
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Frame-level detection of contact onset. TouchMoment has 4,021 videos and 8,456 contact moments. Exact-frame AP is 14.25 on HOI4D and 24.25 on TACO, 48.47 and 55.51 within 2 frames. This is the source of the pain point's timing numbers.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: EgoPHI: Estimating 3D Hand-Object Contact and Force from Egocentric Vision
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Estimates dense contact maps and 3D force distributions on hand and object meshes from one egocentric RGB image plus the object geometry. Force supervision comes from simulation; validation uses test objects with embedded sensors.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: HOPE: Hand-Object Pressure Estimation from Monocular Videos
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: A vertex-anchored video transformer predicts per-vertex contact and pressure on the hand. It harmonizes tactile-glove, planar-sensor and contact-annotation data, is evaluated on OpenTouch and PressureVisionDB, and generalizes to bare hands.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: EgoTac: In-the-wild Tactile Prediction from Egocentric Vision
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Predicts tactile force and binary contact from egocentric video after training on 5.7M image-tactile pairs. In-domain force error is below 0.06 N, and it tracks the rise and fall of contact over time, which addresses contact timing.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: InteractVLM: 3D Interaction Reasoning from 2D Foundational Models
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Estimates 3D human and object contact from one image using VLMs and a Render-Localize-Lift module. Adds semantic human contact conditioned on the object type, with little 3D contact data needed.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: GRACE: Estimating Geometry-level 3D Human-Scene Contact from 2D Images
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: A point-cloud encoder-decoder maps geometry plus image features to per-vertex contact. Reports better precision and recall than DECO on DAMON and RICH.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: DecoDINO: 3D Human-Scene Contact Prediction with Semantic Classification
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: A DECO successor built on DINOv2 with a class-balanced loss. Reports +7% binary-contact F1 and half the geodesic error on DAMON, plus semantic contact labels.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: Visuo-Acoustic Hand Pose and Contact Estimation (VibeMesh)
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: A wearable rig with a bone-conduction speaker and piezo microphones, combined with RGB-D, to detect contact under occlusion and static contact. Provides a dataset with contact ground truth. This is a sensor-side fix, not a vision-only one.

evidence.crowdedness: MEDIUM-HIGH. I verified 9 papers from 2025-2026 working on this, including 2 at ECCV 2026, 1 in CVPR Findings 2026 and 1 at CVPR 2025, plus three force or tactile papers posted to arXiv within one month (August 2026). They come from strong groups: MPI-IS (Black, Tzionas), Bristol (Damen), SNU (Joo), ETH (Holz) and Tsinghua (Gao). Exact-frame contact timing and contact ground truth with real measurement remain thinner sub-niches.
evidence.trend: rising. Attention is moving from binary contact to force, pressure and tactile prediction from video, driven by robot learning demand. Three such arXiv papers appeared in August 2026 alone, and new benchmarks (EPIC-Contact, TouchMoment, OpenTouch) appeared in 2026.

skeptics.reasons:
Not refuted. The 2025-2026 work I checked cuts into one half of the pain point and leaves the other half standing. (Web search budget was exhausted, so evidence comes from arXiv API listings and abs/HTML pages fetched directly.)

(1) What has been weakened: the ground-truth and label side. The claim that "no per-frame contact ground truth exists and datasets rely on threshold labels" is out of date. Since late 2025, tactile-glove datasets that pair video with per-frame touch data have grown to scale:
- OpenTouch: 5.1 h of synchronized in-the-wild video, touch and hand pose (Dec 2025).
- EgoTouch / TouchAnything: 1,891 bimanual episodes with continuous pressure maps (May 2026).
- EgoTac: 5.7M image-tactile pairs (Aug 2026).
- TouchSight / HumanTouch: 500 h of pressure-glove data (Sep 2026).
- HT-Bench (7.8M tactile frames) and ACE-Data-0 (150 h): seen only as arXiv listing entries; their abstracts were not fetched.
Gloves instrument the hand, not the object, so the "arbitrary objects need instrumentation" argument is also weaker. HOPE (Aug 2026) maps glove, planar-sensor and threshold labels onto one shared set of hand-mesh vertices. Training-free and VLM methods also exist (ContactPrompt, May 2026; InteractVLM, CVPR 2025; Pi-HOC, Apr 2026 on DAMON and MMHOI). However, none of the abstracts I fetched gives absolute numbers that would show saturation.

(2) What remains unsolved: inferring contact from images, especially out of domain. The strongest 2026 vision-to-touch models still score low on unseen benchmarks for binary hand-vertex contact:
- EgoTac: F1 0.435 and IoU 0.285 on OakInk2; F1 0.290 on FPHA. HACO gets 0.400 and 0.268, DECO 0.243 and 0.075.
- TouchSight on OakInk2: F1 0.373, IoU 0.230. Temporal Pearson correlation of predicted force is 0.567.
- In domain, EgoTac reaches F1 0.71 to 0.85 on HOT3D, H2O and ARCTIC. The labels behind those in-domain scores were not identified.
- Exact-frame contact timing is still low: TouchMoment (CVPR Findings 2026) reports a relative gain of +16.91 AP at a two-frame tolerance over very low baselines (the record's paper 192 gives 14 to 24 AP).
- EgoTac states its own limits: a domain gap from glove appearance; it predicts hand-vertex contact rather than the contact location on the object surface; and temporal dynamics depend on data scale.
- I found nothing that brings 3D contact deviation in reconstructions (ARCTIC CDev of about 30 to 45 mm) below a centimetre, or that fixes out-of-domain body-object contact.

So the problem is not reduced to engineering. Its framing should move away from "no ground truth" toward "ground truth now exists, but only for gloved hands and on the hand side".

skeptics.reframe: Large tactile-glove video datasets (2025-2026) now give per-frame contact and pressure ground truth on the hand. Even so, contact inferred from images is still poor out of domain: the best 2026 models score F1 0.29-0.44 on OakInk2 and FPHA, and exact-frame touch-moment AP stays low. The open problem is to recover contact that is accurate to the frame, located on the object surface, and metric in 3D, for bare hands and unseen objects. That contact also has to be consistent with the reconstructed 3D hand and object, whose contact deviation is still 3-4 cm. Two routes look worth testing: geometry-aware fusion with RGB-D, or multi-view, and using glove-supervised priors to correct the reconstruction instead of predicting contact only on the hand mesh.

skeptics.reasons:
Artifact test, mostly survived. Checked the 36 paper ids against field_papers.json in the scratchpad. The support is wide. It covers hands (ARCTIC and its HANDS 2023-2026 challenge reports, OakInk, AffordPose, ContactArt, HMDO, SHOW3D, DyTact, TouchMoment, FEEL, EgoTactile, TactiDex, FurElise), bodies (BEHAVE, COUCH, InterCap, RICH, DECO, PICO, Open3DHOI, MMVP, TRUMANS, OMOMO, BEDLAM2, NymeriaPlus), human-human contact (CHI3D/FlickrCI3D, TPAMI 2025) and robotics (GLOVER++ CoRL 2025, Lakshmipathy RSS 2026). Sensing ranges over monocular, egocentric, multi-view, RGB-D, stereo, tactile gloves, pressure insoles and MIDI. Venues run from CVPR/ICCV/ECCV to SIGGRAPH Asia, TPAMI, IJCV, NeurIPS, CoRL, RSS and ICML, 2022-2026. The papers come from many groups: MPI-IS/ETH, Pons-Moll's Tuebingen group, Sminchisescu, SJTU, Stanford, CMU, Meta, BIGAI and the HANDS challenge teams. About 7 of the 36 come from the MPI-IS/SMPL ecosystem (DECO, PICO, RICH, InterCap, BEDLAM2, ARCTIC and its challenge report), around 20 percent. That share is not enough to call it one lab's artifact. No neighbouring community has solved this. Robotics avoids the problem by instrumenting the gripper or hand with tactile sensors; it does not infer contact from images. Measured-contact datasets such as ContactPose (thermal) and the paint and pressure setups listed in the record give only accumulated contact or contact in special setups, which supports the claim. Even InteractVLM (CVPR 2025), the most recent image-based contact method I checked, says that the scarcity of 3D contact annotations limits scalability and generalisation.

Where the artifact lens does bite:
(1) The headline numbers cannot be compared and are often benchmark-specific. CDev is an ARCTIC metric. Interaction-field error comes from the HANDS 2026 SHOW3D stereo challenge reports. Exact-frame AP 14-24 comes from one paper (TouchMoment) with a deliberately strict metric. Accumulated-contact mIoU 0.226 comes from one workshop paper (DyTact). The record treats these as one consistent signal of failure, which they are not.
(2) Several low scores partly measure label noise rather than inference failure. DECO's F1 0.18 out of domain on BEHAVE is scored against BEHAVE's distance-threshold labels taken from SMPL fits, and CHORE/PHOSA F1 is scored the same way. The record itself concedes that threshold labels inherit pose and scan errors.
(3) Dense per-vertex contact on SMPL/MANO is a convention of the parametric-model community. Coarse contact is routinely inferred from images: binary hand contact state has been detected at internet scale since 100DOH (CVPR 2020). The word "cannot" therefore overclaims; the problem is precision, timing and the lack of ground truth.
(4) "Needed precision" is never defined for a downstream task. The record does not show that centimetre contact error breaks robot retargeting or digital twins.

Net: the evidence is not narrow, so I do not refute it. The defensible core is narrower than the statement: no per-frame measured contact ground truth exists for uninstrumented objects, so contact estimation is trained and scored against derived labels whose errors are as large as the quantity being measured, and contact onset and release timing is barely benchmarked. Limits on this check: the WebSearch budget was exhausted, so counter-evidence came only from WebFetch of arXiv abstracts. I could not confirm the exact 100DOH accuracy figures, or ContactPose's thermal and accumulated capture details, from the abstract pages; those details are from memory.

skeptics.reframe: No sensor gives per-frame contact ground truth on uninstrumented objects. Contact on hands, bodies and objects is therefore trained and scored against derived labels (distance thresholds on fitted MANO/SMPL, manual painting, or accumulated thermal or paint imprints) whose errors are as large as the contact quantity itself. Dense contact estimators cannot be validated across datasets, and contact onset and release timing is almost unbenchmarked. The open problem is how to measure and supervise frame-accurate contact, not whether coarse contact can be seen in images.

skeptics.reasons:
Refutation attempt: part of P13 is a data wish, namely the call for per-frame contact ground truth on arbitrary objects. Gloves, insoles, instrumented objects and wet paint are known fixes that mostly need money and rigs. Large capture efforts are already filling this gap (EgoPressure, the 2026 ACE-Data-0 tactile and contact capture). A "collect more contact labels" thesis would therefore fail this lens. Part of the benchmark gap (ARCTIC CDev at about 3 cm, DECO F1 0.18 out of domain) also comes from upstream pose and shape error rather than from a contact-specific question.

The refutation does not hold for the core of the pain point. The record states that contact is an occluded relation at millimetre scale, and that the labels models learn from have errors as large as the quantity being measured. That is an identifiability and supervision problem, not a resource problem. Instrumenting objects changes their appearance and does not scale to arbitrary objects, so more money does not close the gap. At least three research questions would interest a top-venue reviewer:

(1) Can contact onset and release be inferred as a latent variable from what contact causes, rather than from appearance? Examples are object motion onset, physical consistency of the object's motion, and the RGB-D depth gap with a model of sensor noise. This would give self-supervised contact timing without tactile ground truth.

(2) Can cheap signals from other modalities (audio, vibration, thermal residue) teach contact to a vision-only model? Each acts as a weak per-frame label that the vision model must learn to do without at test time. This is a question about learning with privileged information.

(3) Is per-frame contact identifiable from monocular or RGB-D input at all? Where it is not, can a model output calibrated uncertainty that separates near-touch proximity from contact that transmits force? The record names exactly this ambiguity: geometric metrics do not establish contact, and threshold labels teach models to predict contact almost everywhere.

Top venues have published closely related questions: PressureVision (ECCV 2022 oral), DECO (ICCV 2023), S2Contact (ECCV 2022), ManiWAV (CoRL 2024), ContactDB (CVPR 2019), and TouchMoment (CVPR Findings 2026, which reports exact-frame AP of 14 to 24). Contact quality also matters for applications: when robot demonstrations are retargeted, wrong contact timing breaks grasp transfer.

Caveats. The area is getting crowded, and big labs hold the advantage on capture. A thesis-scale entry needs the latent-variable or physics framing rather than a new dataset. My web search budget was exhausted, so I verified papers through the arXiv API only; venues for EgoPressure and DECO come from memory.

skeptics.reframe: Hand-object contact is a latent state that is mostly not observed, and current methods learn it from distance-threshold or reconstruction-derived labels whose error is as large as the contact itself. Three questions follow. Can contact onset, release and location be identified from what contact causes, such as object motion onset, physical consistency and the gap measured in RGB-D depth? Can cheap signals from other modalities (audio, vibration, thermal) supervise vision-only training as privileged information? And where vision cannot identify contact, can a model give calibrated uncertainty that separates near-touch from contact that transmits force, rather than relying on more instrumented capture?

research_questions.question: Can the moments of hand-object contact onset and release be recovered to within one frame without any contact labels? The idea is to treat each event as a latent time that is interval-censored by what contact physically causes. Object motion onset is an upper bound on contact onset. A metric hand-object gap in depth that is visible and larger than sensor noise is a lower bound. Object settling, followed by the gap reopening, brackets release. A temporal hazard model would then learn from appearance and RGB-D where inside each interval the event falls.
research_questions.why_top_venue: Contact timing is the thinnest and least benchmarked part of P13. The best exact-frame AP is 14.25 on HOI4D and 24.25 on TACO (TouchMoment/HiCE, CVPR Findings 2026, arXiv 2604.12343, verified). Video LMMs fail to find the contact and release frame on a 20K-event Something-Something annotation set (arXiv 2511.20162, verified). Every current method learns from manual frame labels or from glove data (EgoTac 2608.15060, TouchSight 2609.20414, HOPE 2608.06192, all verified). A third supervision route is principled and scales to any RGB-D or pose-annotated HOI video: censored bounds derived from physics. It comes with an identifiability argument: with non-informative censoring and interval endpoints that vary across samples, the event distribution is identified on the union of endpoints, as in the Turnbull estimator. That argument directly answers the artifact skeptic's point that the labels are as noisy as the quantity being measured. The closest prior work I found is HOCALT (arXiv 2606.10743, under review, verified). It uses hand articulation plus category-agnostic object motion as a heuristic to localize contact intervals for robot transfer, but it neither trains nor evaluates frame-accurate onset. The other is Zampogiannis et al. 2018 (arXiv 1807.04870, verified), a bottom-up RGB-D contact detector with only qualitative evaluation. Neither formulates censored learning or measures against real timing.
research_questions.method_sketch: (1) Bound extraction, automatic and category-agnostic. Use the object 6D pose where the dataset provides it (HOI4D, DexYCB, HO3D, ARCTIC, TACO); otherwise use point tracks on the object mask (for example CoTracker), compensated for ego-motion. These give the motion-onset time t_m. From depth (HOI4D, DexYCB, HO3D, H2O) or from the GT meshes, compute the per-frame hand-to-object surface gap and a visibility mask, with a depth-noise model per camera. The last frame with a visible gap above k sigma gives t_g. Onset then lies in (t_g, t_m]. Release lies between object settling and the gap reopening. A missing bound becomes a right-censored or open interval; this covers touches of fixed objects and fully occluded gaps. (2) Model: a frozen video backbone (VideoMAE-v2, V-JEPA or DINOv2 features) plus hand-pose tokens and gap and motion features, feeding a discrete-time hazard head per hand-object pair. It is trained with the interval-censored negative log-likelihood -log sum_{t in I} h(t) prod_{s<t}(1-h(s)). Optionally, a few exact manual labels are added as uncensored events. The output is a calibrated distribution over the onset frame, not a single spike. (3) Ablations: motion bound only, gap bound only, RGB-only versus RGB-D, the distribution of interval widths (to show the identifiability effect empirically), and a causal (online) versus offline head. (4) Downstream payoff: gate contact constraints in an existing reconstruction refiner (for example on DexYCB or ARCTIC) with the predicted onset and release, and report the change in penetration, CDev and temporal contact stability. Alternatively, segment robot demonstrations and compare against HOCALT-style heuristics.
research_questions.minimum_experiment: 6-8 weeks, falsifiable. (a) Bound validity: on HOI4D, compute automatic intervals and check what fraction of TouchMoment manual onsets fall inside them. Target above 95%. Also report the median interval width; if most intervals are wider than about 10 frames, the signal is too weak. (b) Train the hazard head with the interval loss only (no manual labels) and evaluate on the TouchMoment HOI4D split at the exact frame and at +-2 frames, against HiCE's 14.25 and 48.47 AP. Kill criterion: drop this RQ if label-free training stays more than about 5 AP below fully supervised HiCE at +-2 frames, or if more than 10% of the bounds are violated. (c) Pilot measured set: 1-2 hours from 3-5 people on conductive objects, with an electrical-continuity or capacitive touch circuit sampled at 1 kHz or more and synchronized by an LED in the camera view. Report onset error in milliseconds and the noise floor of the manual labels. If manual labels already sit within +-1 frame of measured onset, reframe the paper around the cost of labels rather than their noise.
research_questions.data_and_hardware: Public data: HOI4D (2.4M egocentric RGB-D frames; RGB-D confirmed from the arXiv 2203.01577 abstract), DexYCB and HO3D (RGB-D with object pose, from memory), H2O (egocentric RGB-D, from memory), ARCTIC and TACO (mocap object pose, so motion bounds only), the TouchMoment labels on HOI4D and TACO (release status unverified), the Something-Something contact/release set (arXiv 2511.20162), and glove datasets with measured timing used only as test sets: OpenTouch (2512.16842), EgoTouch (2605.13083) and HandSense from Glove2Hand (CVPR 2026 Highlight, 2603.20850, re-rendered bare hands with synchronized tactile and IMU signals). Hardware: the existing consumer RGB-D camera at 30 fps; an Arduino-class board plus a wrist electrode and conductive or metal objects, or a piezo contact microphone, under 100 USD; one LED for synchronization; one 24-48 GB GPU (backbone frozen, only the temporal heads trained). Optionally 8-10 participants for a 3-4 hour validation capture.
research_questions.risks: Bounds can be wrong. An object can be pushed by another object; contact can happen without motion (fixed objects, light touches); articulated parts move; ego-motion leaks into the motion estimate. The preload lag between contact and lift is roughly 0.1-0.4 s in grip-lift studies (Johansson and Westling, from memory, unverified), so motion bounds may be 3-12 frames wide. Gap bounds disappear exactly when the contact side is occluded. TouchMoment data or code may be unreleased, which forces a re-annotation. Glove-trained models (EgoTac, TouchSight) may already track contact rise and fall well. They must be run as baselines, and their code availability is unverified. The topic's only recent venue was CVPR Findings, a sign that pure timing is seen as niche; the downstream 3D or robotics payoff in step (4) is therefore needed for a main-track paper. At 30 fps, frame quantization limits exact-frame claims to 33 ms.

research_questions.question: How far do derived contact labels (distance thresholds on fitted MANO and object meshes, manual frame labels, hand-painted correspondences) deviate from measured contact, and does scoring against them change which methods rank best? Can a contact estimator give calibrated, visibility-aware uncertainty, with conformal coverage under measured truth, that separates near-touch from force-transmitting contact instead of hallucinating contact in occluded frames?
research_questions.why_top_venue: The artifact skeptic's surviving claim is that contact is trained and scored against derived labels whose error is as large as the quantity itself. Nobody appears to have quantified this against measured ground truth in one study; I found none in arXiv API queries, though the search was limited. Glove datasets now give measured hand-side contact: OpenTouch, EgoTouch, EgoTac's 5.7M pairs and TouchSight's 500 h. EgoPHI (ECCV 2026, 2608.13014, verified) built two sensorized objects. Measured references are therefore available for the first time. If the ranking of published contact methods flips, or the 2-10 mm threshold choice moves F1 by more than the gaps between methods, the finding changes how the field evaluates. A calibrated, abstaining estimator answers the rq skeptic's third question: where is contact identifiable at all?
research_questions.method_sketch: (1) Audit: on sequences that have measured contact plus hand pose, and object pose where available, compute threshold labels at several distances and contact-onset lags. Measure their agreement with measured contact: per-vertex precision and recall, and onset and release lag in frames. Then re-score published estimators (HACO, DECO-style, EgoTac or HOPE outputs if released) under measured versus derived labels and report Kendall tau of the rankings. (2) Visibility-aware calibration: add a per-region visibility score (from depth and the hand and object masks) to a contact head, then apply split-conformal or selective prediction so that per-frame contact sets reach target coverage conditioned on visibility bins. Report coverage-versus-abstention curves under measured truth. (3) An identifiability map: bin frames by visibility of the contact region and by gap size, and show where even an oracle on fitted geometry cannot separate contact from near-touch.
research_questions.minimum_experiment: 6 weeks. On one public dataset that has measured touch and 3D hand pose (OpenTouch or EgoTouch), plus the small own capture from RQ1 that has metric object pose: compute threshold labels at 2, 5 and 10 mm. Report agreement with measured contact and the onset lag distribution. Re-rank at least three released contact estimators. Go criterion: label disagreement with measured contact at least comparable to the F1 gaps between methods, or a ranking change (Kendall tau below about 0.6). Stop or fold into RQ1 if derived and measured labels agree to within the differences between methods.
research_questions.data_and_hardware: OpenTouch (video, touch and pose), EgoTouch (pressure plus 3D hand pose, multi-view RGB), HandSense, and EgoPHI's sensorized-object recordings if released (unverified). TactiDex and EgoTactile are listed in the P13 record as glove-plus-mocap sets; their release was not checked. Own capture: the RGB-D desk rig with an ArUco-marked object for metric object pose and a touch circuit for measured onset. Compute: one GPU for inference of released models plus light head training.
research_questions.risks: Few public datasets carry measured contact together with an accurate object pose, so the threshold-label audit may rest mostly on a small in-house set from one lab, and reviewers may call it narrow. Glove-measured contact covers only the parts of the hand with sensors and changes the hand's appearance. Conformal calibration of contact is incremental on its own; the paper stands or falls on the audit finding. Released checkpoints for EgoTac, TouchSight and HOPE are unverified.

research_questions.question: Can hand-side tactile priors from glove-trained vision-to-touch models (which predict contact only on the hand mesh) be lifted, with single-view RGB-D geometry, onto the object surface? The goal is metric, object-side contact location, used to gate a hand-object refinement that pushes contact deviation from the current 3-4 cm toward 1 cm on RGB-D benchmarks.
research_questions.why_top_venue: EgoTac states as its own limit that it predicts hand-vertex contact rather than the contact location on the object surface (skeptic evidence). Reconstruction CDev remains 31.9 mm even for HOPformer on ARCTIC-ego (ECCV 2026, verified). Joining the new tactile priors to metric object-side contact and better 3D reconstruction is the reframe the solved-lens skeptic proposed.
research_questions.method_sketch: Run a released tactile predictor, or a HACO-style contact head, to get per-hand-vertex contact probabilities over time, gated in time by the RQ1 onset and release estimates. Track the object with depth plus model-based or model-free pose. Optimize the hand-object relative pose so that high-probability contact vertices lie on the observed or completed object surface within the depth-noise model, low-probability vertices stay outside, and penetration is penalized. Transfer contact to the object surface through nearest-surface correspondence, accumulated in the canonical object frame. Evaluate CDev, penetration, contact F1 against GT-mesh thresholds, and temporal contact stability on DexYCB and HO3D (RGB-D), plus ARCTIC with predicted depth.
research_questions.minimum_experiment: 4-6 weeks. On DexYCB, take an off-the-shelf hand-object reconstruction and add contact-gated refinement using (a) oracle GT contact, (b) predicted hand-side contact and (c) none. If even oracle contact does not cut CDev by more than about 30%, the bottleneck is upstream pose error, and this RQ should be dropped.
research_questions.data_and_hardware: DexYCB, HO3D and HOI4D (RGB-D with object meshes), ARCTIC; released vision-to-touch checkpoints if available; one RGB-D camera for qualitative demos; one GPU.
research_questions.risks: Crowded with strong 2026 entries: CHOIR (2605.20992, contact-aware 4D HOI reconstruction), C2Dex (2608.07045, stable object-side contacts for retargeting, submitted to RA-L), EgoPHI (ECCV 2026, contact and force on hand and object meshes) and arXiv 2604.09100 (ECCV 2026, touch-conditioned reconstruction under occlusion); all verified on arXiv. A single view rarely sees the contact side of the object. The tactile models may not be released or may transfer poorly to the RGB-D domain. The likely result is an incremental gain, which suits ICRA or RA-L better than CVPR. This is the lowest-priority RQ.

fit.thesis_assets_help:
The assets give a modest edge, and only for building test sets, not for training.
- The fixed single RGB-D desk rig is a ready-made capture station for the small set of measured contact timings that RQ1 and RQ2 need, once a cheap touch circuit and a sync LED are added.
- The ArUco-marked object with metric pose gives exactly the two physical bounds RQ1 relies on: precise object-motion onset, and a metric hand-object gap against a known object surface. It also gives the accurate object pose that most glove datasets lack, which the RQ2 threshold-label audit needs. The markers change the object's appearance, so this data is valid for evaluation only.
- The measured/held/constrained honesty labels are conceptually the same idea as RQ2's visibility-aware, abstaining contact output, so the thesis framing carries over.
- The causal 30 fps chain supports an online variant of the RQ1 hazard model, with a reportable detection latency.
- The occluded-arm recovery is marginal; it may help keep a hand estimate when the gap bound is lost. The Unity twin is useful for visualization only.
- The 28 recordings of one subject cannot serve as a benchmark or as training data, only as a pilot. Reviewers would require several participants and conductive objects with measured touch.
fit.what_a_small_lab_cannot_do_here:
- Cannot compete on scale-driven vision-to-touch. The leading 2026 work uses 500 h of pressure-glove data (TouchSight), 5.7M image-tactile pairs (EgoTac) or multi-view egocentric capture with wearable pressure sensors (EgoTouch). It comes from well-resourced groups (MPI-IS, Bristol, SNU, ETH, Tsinghua per the evidence).
- Cannot build sensorized objects with dense per-vertex contact and force, as EgoPHI did.
- Cannot capture mocap-grade hand and object pose for its own data.
- Cannot run crowd-scale dense contact painting for bodies (DAMON-style) or multi-site in-the-wild collections.
- Cannot measure per-frame contact ground truth on arbitrary, uninstrumented objects. A cheap electrical or capacitive touch circuit only works on conductive objects, gives onset and release rather than location, and stays a small validation set.
- Cannot pretrain large video backbones on one GPU. It can only fine-tune heads on frozen features.
- Body-scene and body-object contact (DECO out of domain on BEHAVE) is out of reach without new body capture; the realistic entry is hand-object contact timing and label validity (RQ1, RQ2), not dense contact location or force.

painpoint.name: Articulated and deformable handled objects

evidence.latest_state: Articulated objects have moved quickly in 2025-2026. Pipelines built on foundation models now reconstruct 4D hand-articulated-object interaction from monocular RGB, but they are slow, work offline, and use small evaluation sets. ArtHOI (CVPR 2026) reports articulated-object Chamfer distances of 3.3-8.1 mm on its own 5-video ArtHOI-RGBD set, against 13.8-282 mm for RSRD and 171-649 mm for EasyHOI. It needs about one hour per 100-frame video, and heavy hand-part and part-part occlusion is still hard. AgentSTAR (arXiv, Sep 2026) tracks ARCTIC articulated objects at 5.59 cm 3D EPE against 7.65 cm for V-DPM, and gets 3.36 cm Chamfer, but its optimisation budget is up to 10 hours. On HOT3D its mean rotation error is still 37.6 deg. Estimating articulation from egocentric hand-object video remains weak. With a 15 deg axis threshold and a 0.25 m pivot threshold, PAWS reaches only 0.20 full-parameter accuracy on HD-EPIC (ArtiPoint: 0.00) and 0.34 on Arti4D (ArtiPoint: 0.47). Category-level articulated pose and tracking work (PPF-Tracker, DICArt, CAP-Net, YOEO) still relies on category priors and depth. I found no 2025-2026 result that reported closing the PACE articulated tracking gap (10.1 vs 38.1 ADD(-S) AUC); this could not be confirmed because web search was unavailable. Deformable hand-object interaction is much less mature. PhysHanDI (ICML 2026) simulates deformation from hand-induced forces using three-view RGB-D capture. On PhysTwin-dense it reports 8.32 mm Chamfer on dynamic regions against 10.78 mm for PhysTwin, on a 19-sequence DenseHDI set. Neither area has a monocular, real-time, category-agnostic tracker, and there is still no common pose definition or metric.

evidence.crowdedness: MEDIUM-HIGH. I found about 15 relevant 2025-2026 papers on arXiv, several at CVPR 2026, ICML 2026 and CoRL 2025. Most attack articulated objects, from groups working on foundation-model HOI, egocentric articulation (Freiburg ArtiPoint/Hoi!, Aalto PAWS) and real-to-sim articulation. Deformable hand-object interaction is still LOW: PhysHanDI and DeformMaster are the only direct works I found, and both use multi-view RGB-D or physics simulation.
evidence.trend: Attention is rising. Articulated hand-object reconstruction became a named task in 2026 (ArtHOI, AgentSTAR, Track-Articulate-Act, PAWS), driven by foundation models (SAM3D, 3D point tracking, VLMs) and by demand for real-to-sim digital twins of robot demonstrations. Deformable hand-object interaction is emerging slowly through physics-based twins (PhysTwin follow-ups).

skeptics.reasons:
I found no 2025-2026 work that solves P14 or turns it into engineering, but 2026 work has weakened its strongest claims. Three such papers were checked; each has the limits P14 describes.

(1) ArtHOI (CVPR 2026, arXiv 2603.25791) reconstructs hands with articulated objects from monocular RGB video using foundation-model priors. It needs no pre-scanned template and no category prior. This contradicts the claim that articulation methods need category-specific priors and depth. However, it is offline optimization, about 1 hour per 100-frame clip on an A6000. It is evaluated on its own new datasets (5 objects in ArtHOI-RGBD, Chamfer distance 3.3-8.1 mm) plus small RSRD and ARCTIC subsets. The paper itself notes difficulty under heavy occlusion.

(2) PhysHanDI (ICML 2026, arXiv 2605.09538) reconstructs hands with deformable objects through physics-based inverse simulation. It needs 3-view RGB-D and an image-to-3D rest-state template, and is evaluated on PhysTwin plus 19 new sequences. Its own limitation is that large deformations, such as 180-degree twisting, are not covered. This matches P14's "small deformations only".

(3) Track, Articulate, Act (arXiv 2609.19119, Sep 2026, under review) builds simulation-ready articulated objects from casual monocular video via 3D point tracks. It covers revolute and prismatic joints only, and its abstract reports no numbers.

Related items: DeformMaster (2605.09586), Grasp in Gaussians (2604.12929), Interaction-Aware 4DGS (2511.14540) and RSRD (2409.18121; it needs a scan).

None of these reports progress on PACE articulated tracking, which stood at ICG 10.1 ADD(-S) AUC in P14's evidence. None defines a common pose definition or metric for articulated or deformable objects held in the hand. None runs online or in real time. No saturated benchmark or product exists.

Caveats: the WebSearch budget was exhausted (0 searches available), and the arXiv API returned 429 after two queries. Coverage is therefore one arXiv keyword listing for articulated objects and one for deformable objects, plus abstract and HTML checks of the three papers above. A 2025-2026 novel-object articulated tracker on PACE or HOI4D may exist that I could not find. The claim that it is unsolved holds; the wording should be narrowed because offline monocular template-free articulated HOI reconstruction now exists.

skeptics.reframe: Template-free articulated reconstruction of hand-object interaction from monocular video now exists, but only as offline optimization: ArtHOI, CVPR 2026, takes about 1 hour per 100 frames and is evaluated on a few one-joint objects. Deformable-object reconstruction with the hand still needs multi-view RGB-D and covers only small deformations (PhysHanDI, ICML 2026). The open problem is narrower: online or real-time causal tracking, from one RGB or RGB-D camera, of previously unseen objects whose shape changes (multi-joint articulated or large-deformation), while one or two hands occlude them. It also lacks a shared pose definition, metric and benchmark. Model-based trackers still fall from rigid to articulated objects on PACE, and no common evaluation exists for deformable objects held in the hand.

skeptics.reasons:
Artifact test, overall: mostly survives. The pain point is not an artifact of one dataset or one group. The 36 supporting works come from independent groups and settings: HOI4D (egocentric RGB-D), ARCTIC (multi-view bimanual studio), PACE (cluttered object pose), HANDAL and BOP (6D pose), PhoCaL, HMDO (10-camera deformable capture), ContactArt (category priors), Hoi! (articulated furniture with force), OphNet-3D surgical instruments, and DexGarmentLab, Bi-DexHands and UMI-style systems (robotics). The strongest template-free hand-object reconstructor is HOLD (CVPR 2024, verified on arXiv 2311.18448), and it assumes a rigid object; the articulation it models is the hand's. Every major in-hand benchmark either treats objects as rigid or allows one degree of freedom (ARCTIC). So the core capability gap, tracking hand-held articulated or deformable objects from one camera or RGB-D without a template, is a field-level problem.
Parts that are artifacts:
(1) The claim that there is 'no common pose definition, canonical pose or metric' reflects the rigid 6D-pose (BOP) community's conventions. Other communities defined these years ago. ANCSH (Li et al., CVPR 2020, verified) defines a canonical articulated object and part space with joint-parameter and joint-state metrics. GAPartNet (CVPR 2023, verified) defines cross-category part poses for 9 part classes over 27 categories. GarmentTracking (Xue et al., CVPR 2023, verified) defines a category-level canonical (NOCS) pose for garments and tracks it under large deformation. What is missing is a link between those definitions and hand-object benchmarks, not the definitions themselves.
(2) The headline evidence that 'every tested tracker nearly fails' is narrow. It rests mostly on one benchmark, PACE, which appears as a duplicate record pair (348/1316), plus HOI4D baselines. The trackers tested there (ICG, RBOT, BundleTrack, ICP) are rigid trackers applied to articulated parts, so their collapse is expected by design rather than a measured ceiling. Many other supporting papers (OnePose, Gen6D, HANDAL, the BOP reports) only state 'rigid objects only' as a scope boundary. That is a convention, not evidence that anyone tried and failed.
(3) Deformables merge two largely separate communities: garment and cloth manipulation in robotics, and hand-object vision. Each has its own active methods, for example Reconstruction of Manipulated Garment with Guided Deformation Prior (NeurIPS 2024) and TPAMI 2025 work on textureless deformable tracking.
(4) The method line is active and growing, so 'cannot be captured' is overstated. The inventory holds verified 2024-2026 work: ArtHOI (CVPR 2026, monocular 4D hand-articulated-object reconstruction), Clay-to-Stone (CVPR 2026, monocular articulated hand-object), Articulat3D (ECCV 2026), Robot See Robot Do (CoRL 2024), Articulated Object Estimation in the Wild (CoRL 2025), PokeNet (ICRA 2026), category-level articulated pose in TPAMI 2026, and the HANDS 2024 ARCTIC challenge entries.
Net: the capability gap is real and recognized by diverse groups. The 'no definitions or metrics' sub-claim and the 'all trackers fail' framing are artifacts of the 6D-pose community's evaluation setup. The WebSearch budget was exhausted, so evidence came from arXiv abstract fetches and the verified local inventory.

skeptics.reframe: No method tracks a hand-held articulated or deformable object of an unseen category, template-free, from one RGB or RGB-D camera under heavy hand occlusion, and no in-hand benchmark tests it. Hand-object benchmarks hold rigid or one-DoF objects (ARCTIC, HOI4D), and the leading template-free reconstructors such as HOLD assume rigidity. Canonical articulated and garment pose definitions and metrics already exist (ANCSH, GAPartNet, GarmentTracking) but have never been joined with hand pose, contact and occlusion in a shared evaluation. The open problem is that missing joint hand-plus-articulation and hand-plus-deformation capture and evaluation, not a lack of definitions.

skeptics.reasons:
Refutation attempt, under the no-research-question lens: part of P14 is resource-bound engineering and survives no better than a funding request. Datasets that treat articulated tools as rigid (HANDAL), annotation tools built around one 6D pose, deformable boxes that break labelling (PhoCaL), and unstable PBD/FEM simulators (Isaac Gym, ManiSkill3) are tooling or data-collection gaps. The missing "common pose definition and metric" is mostly a convention problem, and on its own it would be a benchmark-track paper, not a method contribution. If P14 were only "we need more articulated and deformable labels", it would be refuted.

The core does not reduce to money, though. The record's own numbers show that known methods fail for structural reasons, not because data is scarce: ICG falls from 38.1 to 10.1 ADD(-S) AUC on PACE, CAPTRA from 12.9 to 4.4, and ArtiPoint has 47-64 deg axis errors on Hoi!. Category articulation priors (ContactArt, CAPTRA, ANCSH) fail by construction on novel categories, and template-plus-ten-camera deformation graphs (HMDO) do not transfer to one camera. No solution is known that just needs more resources.

At least three research questions would interest top-venue reviewers:
(1) Can the hand itself, through its contact locations and its trajectory, act as the supervisory signal? The idea is to infer the unknown kinematic structure (part segmentation, joint type and axis) or the deformation field of a novel, unscanned object from a single RGB or RGB-D view, while the hand hides the object. Today articulation is either assumed from a category prior or estimated from clean depth that ignores the hand.
(2) Can a physically grounded deformable model be identified from a hand-driven interaction video alone, without a template or a multi-camera rig, and then used as a predictive digital twin? This would take PhysTwin-style system identification (spring-mass parameters fitted to a video) into the hand-occluded, monocular setting.
(3) What state representation and error metric make tracking comparable across rigid, articulated and deformable handled objects? This is publishable only if it is tied to a method or a benchmark analysis.

Venue evidence shows reviewers treat this area as significant. Verified on arXiv: ArtHOI (monocular 4D reconstruction of hand-articulated-object interaction, arXiv 2603.25791, accepted to CVPR 2026) and iTACO (articulated digital twins from casually captured hand-interaction RGB-D video, arXiv 2506.08334, 3DV 2026). Also verified: PhysTwin (arXiv 2503.17973), a physics-informed deformable reconstruction from video. The arXiv abstract does not frame PhysTwin around hands, and its venue was not confirmed on the arXiv page.

These same papers show the area is active and getting crowded. That lowers the novelty margin, but it does not remove the existence of open questions: ArtHOI is RGB-only and leans on foundation-model priors, and iTACO does not claim novel-category generalization. Deformable hand-object tracking with a single camera remains thinly covered, with only small deformations and uniform materials so far.

Score 7 rather than higher, for three reasons: the data and simulator half of P14 is engineering; the field is crowding at CVPR 2026; and a small lab cannot easily build the ground truth needed to evaluate deformable objects. Constraint: WebSearch was unavailable because the shared session budget was exhausted, so verification used WebFetch of arXiv pages plus the local GitHub paper lists in the scratchpad.
