skeptics.reframe: When the object is novel and unscanned and the hand hides it, can the hand's contacts and motion serve as the supervisory signal for the object's unknown extra degrees of freedom: its articulated joints, or a physically parameterized deformation? The goal is to recover them from one RGB or RGB-D view, without category priors or templates, and to evaluate them under one state metric that covers rigid, articulated and deformable objects. The dataset, annotation-tool and simulator-stability parts of P14 are engineering and do not form the research question.

research_questions.question: Can a causal tracker on a single RGB-D stream track a previously unseen hand-held articulated object at 15 fps or better on one GPU, with no category prior and no pre-scan? It must recover part poses, joint type, joint axis and joint state. The method uses the tracked hands as a kinematic probe while they hide the moving part. The hand cues are stable contacts, grasp persistence and, in bimanual use, the relative motion of the two hands.
research_questions.why_top_venue: Every 2025-2026 template-free articulated hand-object method found is offline or post-hoc. ArtHOI (CVPR 2026) needs about 1 h per 100-frame clip. AgentSTAR (arXiv Sep 2026) uses up to 10 h. iTACO (3DV 2026), Track-Articulate-Act (arXiv Sep 2026) and Track2Art (arXiv 2609.27675, RGB-D, 0.695 point IoU on a 20-object PartNet-Mobility suite, hands not mentioned) all analyse finished videos. Online alternatives either fail or need priors. Rigid trackers applied per part collapse: on PACE, ICG falls from 38.1 to 10.1 ADD(-S) AUC; on HOI4D laptop parts, BundleTrack scores 24.2 and 12.2 at 5deg5cm and ICP scores 0.9 and 1.5. Category-level trackers (PPF-Tracker, CAPTRA, DICArt) need category priors; CAPTRA drops to 4.4 on PACE articulated objects. Egocentric axis estimation stays weak: PAWS reaches 0.20 full-parameter accuracy on HD-EPIC, and ArtiPoint has 47-64 deg axis errors on Hoi!. A causal, category-agnostic tracker that shows an accuracy-latency trade-off approaching offline axis accuracy would be a clear first. It feeds online demonstration capture and real-to-sim, which CoRL, RSS and ICRA reward; CVPR and ECCV would need strong numbers. Caveat: WebSearch was exhausted, so coverage comes from arXiv title and abstract listings fetched on 2026-10-02. A concurrent online method may exist unseen.
research_questions.method_sketch: (1) Front end, every frame: video masks for the object and both hands (SAM2-class); hand meshes from a single-image regressor (WiLoR or HaMeR) snapped to depth; online 2D point tracks (CoTracker3 online mode) lifted to 3D with depth. (2) Online part discovery: in a sliding window, cluster 3D tracks by rigid-motion consistency (RANSAC over SE(3) hypotheses). Spawn a new part when the single-rigid-body residual stays above a threshold for N frames. Grow a per-part TSDF or Gaussian model incrementally (BundleSDF-style, but one per part). (3) Hand-as-probe factors: while a hand's contact patch stays on one part (hand-mesh-to-depth proximity plus mask overlap), tie that part's pose increment to the hand's pose increment, with a slip-robust kernel. In bimanual holds, the relative motion of the two hands observes relative part motion directly, so the joint state stays observable while the part is occluded. (4) Back end: an incremental factor graph (iSAM2 in GTSAM) over part poses. Online model selection chooses rigid, revolute or prismatic by BIC over the window. Joint state is a latent variable with a smoothness prior, and per-part marginal covariances are exported. (5) Keyframe-only heavy steps (part-model refinement, re-segmentation, loop closure) run in a background thread, so the foreground loop stays causal. Optional learned initialiser: a small network trained on PartNet-Mobility renders with MANO hands to predict joint type and axis from short track windows.
research_questions.minimum_experiment: Benchmarks: HOI4D articulated categories (egocentric RGB-D, part-pose ground truth); Arti4D (egocentric RGB-D, axis ground truth); ARCTIC as the bimanual stress test (RGB only, so run with monocular metric depth, and report this as a separate RGB setting). Optional: the PACE articulated split and a Hoi! subset. Baselines: per-part FoundationPose or BundleSDF, BundleTrack and ICP; PPF-Tracker or CAPTRA where code runs; ArtiPoint as the offline axis estimator; ArtHOI or iTACO as offline upper references on a small subset only. Metrics: per-part 5deg5cm and ADD(-S) AUC; axis angle error; axis or pivot distance; joint-state error; frames-to-lock, meaning frames after motion onset until joint type is correct and the axis is within 15 deg and 0.25 m (the PAWS thresholds); end-to-end latency and fps. Ablations: remove the hand factor; remove the bimanual relative-motion factor; remove the kinematic constraint; bin results by the hand-occlusion ratio of the moving part. Paper-level pass bar: at 15 fps or better, clearly beat the per-part rigid trackers on HOI4D. The method should also narrow most of the gap to offline axis accuracy on Arti4D. The hand factor should give its largest gain in the high-occlusion bin. A small held-out real set adds 10-20 hand-held tools and containers with per-part metric ground truth from 3-5 subjects.
research_questions.data_and_hardware: Public data: HOI4D, Arti4D, ARCTIC, PartNet-Mobility with MANO for synthetic pretraining; optionally the PACE articulated split and Hoi!. Hardware: the existing consumer RGB-D camera; one 24-48 GB GPU, enough for the causal pipeline and small learned parts, while offline baselines such as ArtHOI (about 1 h per 100 frames on an A6000) run only on subsets; printed ArUco markers, one per part, for the held-out set. A borrowed second RGB-D camera, used only for ground truth, avoids markers being visible to the tracker. No motion capture is needed. A borrowed arm is needed only for an optional real-to-sim replay demo. Timeline: about 9-12 months to a first submission.
research_questions.risks: High scoop risk: the ArtHOI, AgentSTAR, iTACO, Track2Art and PAWS groups each have the parts for an online variant, so speed matters. Joint type and axis are genuinely unobservable until enough motion has occurred, so early-frame errors are unavoidable and the metric must expose them rather than hide them. Hand estimates degrade exactly under heavy hand-part occlusion; PAWS reports failure when hand tracking fails. HOI4D articulated labels and monocular depth on ARCTIC add ground-truth and input noise. Running a SAM2-class segmenter, a point tracker and a hand regressor together on one GPU may cap the rate near 10 fps. If accuracy stays well below offline methods, the paper drops from CVPR or ECCV to ICRA or RA-L. A method claim built on fewer than about 10 object types will be read as narrow.

research_questions.question: Can a physically parameterised digital twin of a deformable object (spring-mass or MPM) be identified from a single RGB-D view of a hand manipulating it? The tracked hand serves as the known actuator, and physics fills in the hand-occluded and back-facing surface. How close does the result come to three-view systems on held-out-view reconstruction and future-state prediction?
research_questions.why_top_venue: Deformable hand-object reconstruction is the least crowded part of P14. The direct works found all use several views. PhysHanDI (ICML 2026) uses three-view RGB-D and reports 8.32 vs 10.78 mm Chamfer on dynamic regions against PhysTwin, on 19 DenseHDI sequences; it says large deformations such as 180-degree twisting are out of scope. DeformMaster (arXiv May 2026) and PhysTwin learn from multi-view interaction video. The P14 record also notes that monocular hand-object reconstruction fails on deformable objects, and that HMDO needs 10 cameras and a template. A single-view, hand-actuated version is a well-posed question with built-in ground truth: the views that were dropped. It serves real-to-sim for robot learning, which CoRL, RSS and CVPR value.
research_questions.method_sketch: Rest shape: initialise from the first frame with an image-to-3D model completed against the observed depth. Actuation: per-frame hand meshes act as kinematic colliders and control points (as recalled, PhysTwin drives its spring-mass model with hand control points; verify). Identification: two stages. A gradient-free search over topology and stiffness (CMA-ES, as in PhysTwin) is followed by differentiable refinement. Losses are computed from one view only: a depth residual on the visible surface, mask and silhouette loss, and 2D point-track loss. A visibility mask stops surfaces hidden by the hand from being penalised. A cross-object prior over material parameters reduces non-identifiability, and the posterior spread of the identified parameters is reported. An optional Gaussian appearance layer adds rendering. Evaluation focuses on prediction (rolling the twin forward under new hand motion), not only on fitting.
research_questions.minimum_experiment: Use the public PhysTwin data: multi-view RGB-D hand interactions with ropes, plush toys and cloth. As recalled it has three views; verify the release contents. Input is one view; ground truth is the other views' depth and tracks plus future frames. Compare four systems: PhysTwin with all views (upper bound); PhysTwin restricted naively to one view; a non-physical single-view dynamic reconstruction (4D Gaussian or deformation-field baseline); and the proposed method. Metrics: Chamfer distance on held-out views; 3D track error; future-prediction Chamfer at 0.5 s, 1 s and 2 s horizons; consistency of identified parameters across clips of the same object. Pass bar: recover most of the gap between naive single-view and three-view PhysTwin on prediction, not only on reconstruction. Second evaluation: DenseHDI if released (availability unverified), plus 10-20 own clips with a borrowed second camera used only as ground truth.
research_questions.data_and_hardware: Public data: PhysTwin dataset; DenseHDI (release unverified); HMDO for comparison where applicable. Hardware: one GPU is enough for spring-mass simulation and the identification loop; the existing RGB-D camera; a borrowed second RGB-D camera for ground truth on own clips; cheap deformable props (rope, plush, cloth, sponge). No motion capture and no robot are needed.
research_questions.risks: Material parameters may be non-identifiable from one view under hand occlusion; the paper could end up showing a better visual fit with no gain in prediction. The PhysTwin and PhysHanDI groups are best placed to publish a single-view version and may already be working on it. Large deformations such as folding and twisting stay out of reach, which limits the claim. Public multi-view deformable hand-interaction data amounts to tens of sequences, so statistical power is thin. Errors in the image-to-3D rest shape propagate into the identified physics. None of the author's thesis assets help here, so the ramp-up cost is the full learning curve.

research_questions.question: When is the state of a hand-held articulated object observable from one RGB-D camera? Can a tracker report, per part and per frame, whether its estimate is measured, propagated, or inferred from kinematic or hand constraints, with calibrated uncertainty? Does a shared state metric that joins canonical articulated pose definitions (ANCSH, GAPartNet) with hand contact and occlusion change how existing methods rank?
research_questions.why_top_venue: The skeptics showed that canonical articulated and garment pose definitions already exist (ANCSH, GAPartNet, GarmentTracking). What is missing is their link to hand occlusion and contact in an in-hand evaluation. Hand-object articulated benchmarks report only averaged errors. This RQ is publishable at a top venue only when tied to a method, namely the RQ1 tracker with its exported covariances, or to a benchmark analysis. For example, it could show that offline and online methods both concentrate their errors in hand-occluded, low-motion segments, and that calibrated self-reports allow safe gating for robot use. Alone it is a benchmark-track contribution, viable at NeurIPS Datasets and Benchmarks only at meaningful scale.
research_questions.method_sketch: Define per-part, per-frame state labels automatically from ground-truth meshes. Labels are measured (part visible above a threshold), constrained (part occluded, but a hand contact or the kinematic chain fixes it) and propagated (neither; the estimate is coasting). Compute them on HOI4D and ARCTIC by rendering part and hand meshes. Define a unified state error: per-part SE(3) error plus joint-parameter and joint-state error in the ANCSH canonical frame, and a rigid object as the zero-joint special case. Evaluate calibration with coverage of 90 percent intervals, risk-coverage curves (AURC) and label-classification accuracy for trackers that self-report. Compare stratified errors of the RQ1 tracker and the available baselines.
research_questions.minimum_experiment: Run the label generator on HOI4D and ARCTIC. Stratify the errors of the per-part rigid baselines, the category-level baselines and the RQ1 tracker by label. Report coverage and AURC for the RQ1 covariance outputs against a heuristic confidence baseline. Paper-level pass bar: rankings or conclusions change materially under stratification, and calibrated self-reports cut high-error frames at a fixed coverage. Add the RQ1 held-out marker set with hand-labelled states as a real-capture check.
research_questions.data_and_hardware: Same as RQ1: HOI4D and ARCTIC ground-truth meshes for automatic labels, the RQ1 own capture with per-part markers, and one GPU for rendering visibility. No extra hardware.
research_questions.risks: Reviewers may see it as evaluation hygiene rather than a contribution, so it is safest folded into the RQ1 paper. The dataset will be too small for a NeurIPS Datasets and Benchmarks submission: Hoi! has 3048 sequences and 381 objects, and iTACO has 784 videos. Label quality depends on ground-truth mesh accuracy. Extending it to deformable objects has no ground truth from one camera.

fit.thesis_assets_help: The assets help modestly with RQ1 and RQ3 and not at all with RQ2. (1) The single RGB-D desk setup and the causal 30 fps chain are the exact input and latency regime of RQ1. Capture, synchronisation, the causal loop and latency logging can be reused, which saves perhaps one to two months. (2) The ArUco metric-pose machinery extends directly to one marker per part. That gives cheap metric per-part ground truth for a small held-out set of hand-held tools, a real gap in public data. The markers would be visible to the tracker, though, so they should face a second camera used only for ground truth, or be inpainted. (3) The measured/held/constrained honesty labels map almost one-to-one onto RQ3's per-part observability states, which gives a ready evaluation idea. (4) Object-conditioned recovery of an occluded holding arm is the inverse of RQ1's hand-as-probe coupling. There the object constrains the arm; here the hand constrains the part. The idea and possibly some optimisation code transfer; the model does not. (5) The Unity twin is useful only for a real-to-sim replay demo of a recovered articulated asset. (6) The 28 recordings of one subject handling a rigid object have no value as data for this direction. Overall the edge is in infrastructure and ground-truth method, not in results or data, and it does not offset the scoop risk.
fit.what_a_small_lab_cannot_do_here: A small lab cannot build ground truth for hand-held articulated or deformable objects at the scale reviewers now expect, whether multi-subject, multi-view or motion capture. For comparison, Hoi! has 3048 sequences of 381 objects, iTACO 784 videos of 284 objects, and ARCTIC and HOI4D were captured in studios. It cannot capture dense deformable ground truth beyond a borrowed second camera: HMDO uses 10 cameras, and PhysTwin and PhysHanDI use three-view RGB-D. It cannot train large feed-forward 4D models or VLM-agent pipelines on massive synthetic articulated data. On one GPU it cannot match offline foundation-model pipelines on accuracy, or even run them over full benchmarks: ArtHOI takes about 1 h per 100 frames and AgentSTAR up to 10 h per clip. Without instrumented grippers it cannot do force-grounded evaluation as in Hoi!. Without a borrowed arm it cannot validate twins on a robot. It should not race the ArtHOI, AgentSTAR, iTACO, PAWS or PhysTwin groups on their own offline or multi-view terms. The viable lane is online, single-camera, category-agnostic tracking, with public data supplying most of the ground truth. Coverage caveat: WebSearch was exhausted, so the novelty checks rest on arXiv listing fetches and local paper lists dated 2026-10-02.

painpoint.name: Finger pose of the grasping hand under occlusion

evidence.latest_state: Single-view finger pose of a grasping hand under heavy occlusion is still unsolved as of late 2026. Papers keep reporting it as the main failure mode. Recent work has narrowed the gap on benchmarks but has not removed it. The strongest recent monocular video result is ViDiHand (arXiv 2606.30308; its arXiv HTML page says CVPR 2026, which I did not cross-check). It adapts a pretrained video diffusion model and needs no hand detector. On HOT3D it reports PA-MPJPE 11.4 mm against 20.0 mm for WiLoR, and MPJPE 21.5 mm against 31.0 mm. On ARCTIC it reports PA-MPJPE 9.8 mm against 11.9 mm, and on the held-out HOI4D set 14.0 mm against 14.9 mm. It runs at 5.5 fps on four A100 GPUs, so the authors present it as an offline annotation tool, not a real-time tracker. StableHand (arXiv 2605.18553) learns which frames to trust and uses a flow-matching prior; it cuts world-frame W-MPJPE by 20-25 percent on HOT3D and ARCTIC, with the largest gains on heavily occluded ARCTIC sequences. On single images, the ECCV 2026 papers GenHOI (text-prompted masked modelling) and the Affordance-Guided Diffusion Prior (hand-pose refinement conditioned on vision-language-model descriptions of how an object is grasped, tested on HOGraspNet) claim state of the art on DexYCB, HO3Dv2 and HOGraspNet. Their gains are incremental, and the abstracts give no occlusion-binned numbers. HOPformer (ECCV 2026) reaches an 82.4 percent success rate on ARCTIC and introduces the in-the-wild EPIC-Contact dataset, on which earlier methods roughly halve. Sensor fusion is still where the large gains come from. AVI-HT, which fuses glove IMUs with egocentric vision on DexGloveHOI, cuts keypoint error by 16.1 percent over the baselines. A fiber-optic glove reaches 4.9-7.2 mm fingertip error against motion capture. That confirms the pain point's claim that vision alone has not closed the gap. Calibrated multi-camera rigs remain the reliable option: an 8-camera biomechanical setup still had a 15 percent non-convergence rate with the two-stage baseline. HGGT starts to relax the calibration requirement by inferring the camera poses together with the hand mesh. A study with HoloLens 2, WiLoR, HaMeR and people with cervical spinal cord injury found similar error with and without hand impairment, and only about 0.1 mm difference between clear and opaque objects. That suggests the open problem lies in heavy, prolonged occlusion and hands missing from view, not in moderate object contact.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: The Surprising Effectiveness of Video Diffusion Models for Hand Motion Reconstruction (ViDiHand)
attacking_papers_2025_2026.venue_year: arXiv 2026 (the arXiv HTML page says CVPR 2026; not cross-checked)
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Adapts the features of a pretrained video diffusion model to recover metric 4D pose of both hands from full frames, with no hand detector, no infilling step and no test-time optimization. Reported PA-MPJPE: 11.4 mm on HOT3D vs 20.0 mm for WiLoR; 9.8 mm on ARCTIC vs 11.9 mm; 14.0 mm on HOI4D vs 14.9 mm. Runs at 5.5 fps on four A100 GPUs (offline).

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: StableHand: Quality-Aware Flow Matching for World-Space Dual-Hand Motion Estimation from Egocentric Video
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: A learned network scores how reliable each frame's wrist and finger observations are, and a flow-matching prior over both hands rebuilds the unreliable spans. Reports 20-25 percent lower W-MPJPE on HOT3D and ARCTIC, with the largest gains on heavily occluded sequences.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: GenHOI: Generalized Hand-Object Pose Estimation with Occlusion Awareness
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Single-image hand-object pose estimation that uses hierarchical text prompts plus masked modelling over the image, a predicted point cloud and the text, so it can reason about occluded parts. Claims state of the art on DexYCB and HO3Dv2.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: Affordance-Guided Diffusion Prior for 3D Hand Reconstruction
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: A diffusion prior over hand poses, conditioned on vision-language-model descriptions of how the object is typically grasped, refines heavily occluded hand regions. Tested on HOGraspNet, a dataset with severe occlusions.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: Towards in-the-wild Egocentric 3D Hand-Object Pose Estimation (EPIC-Contact, HOPformer)
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Releases EPIC-Contact, an in-the-wild egocentric dataset of 62.3K frames with dense 3D contact labels, and HOPformer, a single-pass transformer that predicts both hands and the object. Reports 82.4 percent success on ARCTIC (+6.2 points) and roughly doubles the success rate on EPIC-Contact.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: AVI-HT: Adaptive Vision-IMU Fusion for 3D Hand Tracking
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Fuses egocentric vision with 6-DoF IMUs on a glove through cross-sensor attention, for hand-object interaction with heavy occlusion. On DexGloveHOI (100K+ samples) it cuts mean keypoint error by 16.1 percent (24.2 percent wrist-aligned) against UmeTrack- and MANO-based baselines.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: Occlusion-Aware 3D Hand-Object Pose Estimation with Masked AutoEncoders (HOMAE)
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Masked-autoencoder training that hides the hand-object contact region, combined with a signed-distance-field plus point-cloud representation, to reason about occluded structure. Claims state of the art on DexYCB and HO3Dv2.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: MaskHOI: Robust 3D Hand-Object Interaction Estimation via Masked Pre-training
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Masked-autoencoder pretraining that masks fingertips and whole fingers more often, to imitate grasp occlusion, plus a masked signed-distance-field objective. Claims state of the art on hand-object benchmarks.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: Cascaded Diffusion Framework for Probabilistic Coarse-to-Fine Hand Pose Estimation
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: A diffusion model samples several possible joint configurations, then a mesh latent diffusion model reconstructs the hand mesh from one sample. Claims state of the art on FreiHAND, HO3Dv2 and DexYCB and stability under occlusion.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: DF-Mamba: Deformable State Space Modeling for 3D Hand Pose Estimation in Interactions
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: A deformable Mamba backbone that aggregates global context for occluded joints. Evaluated on five hand-only, two-hand and hand-object datasets, in RGB and depth; beats VMamba and Spatial-Mamba at about ResNet-50 speed.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: HandMCM: Multi-modal Point Cloud-based Correspondence State Space Model for 3D Hand Pose Estimation
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: A Mamba model over depth point clouds, with correspondence modelling and fused image features, aimed at self- and object occlusion. Reports the largest gains in severe-occlusion cases on three benchmarks.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: AnyHand: A Large-Scale Synthetic Dataset for RGB(-D) Hand Pose Estimation
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Synthetic RGB-D data with occlusion: 2.5M single-hand and 4.1M hand-object images. Adding it to the training data gives gains on FreiHAND and HO-3D, and a depth-fusion variant beats earlier RGB-D methods.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: HGGT: Robust and Flexible 3D Hand Mesh Reconstruction from Uncalibrated Images
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Feed-forward model that infers the hand mesh and the camera poses together from uncalibrated multi-view images. Aims to get multi-view robustness to occlusion without a calibrated rig.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: DeltaDorsal: Enhancing Hand Pose Estimation with Dorsal Features in Egocentric Views
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Reads finger pose from skin deformation on the back of the hand, contrasted against a relaxed-hand baseline. Cuts mean per-joint angle error (MPJAE) by 18 percent when fingers are 50 percent or more occluded.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: Fiber Optic Sensing Glove for High Performance Dexterous Manipulation Capture
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Glove with shape-sensing optical fibers and an inverse-kinematics solver at 60 Hz, free of occlusion. Reaches 7.2 mm mean fingertip error, 4.9 mm after calibration, against motion capture over 2 hours of manipulation by 5 subjects.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: Impact of Hand Impairment and Occlusions on Hand Pose Estimation Accuracy in Augmented Reality Applications
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Clinical benchmark of HoloLens 2, WiLoR, HaMeR, WildHands and MediaPipe against multi-camera triangulation, with 13 people with cervical spinal cord injury and 15 controls handling clear and opaque objects. Finds small differences: 0.1 mm between clear and opaque objects, and WiLoR and HaMeR about 2 mm better than HoloLens 2.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: Biomechanics-aware Multi-view Markerless Motion Capture of Dexterous Hand Movements
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Fits a biomechanical hand model end to end to an 8-camera recording. It handles object occlusion better than triangulating 2D keypoints and then solving inverse kinematics, which failed to converge on 15 percent of recordings.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: GraspHOI: Full-Body 3D Human-Object Reconstruction with Finger-Level Grasps from a Single In-the-Wild Image
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Single-image full-body human-object reconstruction that uses occlusion-aware palm correspondences and contact-aware optimization to refine finger articulation against the reconstructed object.

evidence.crowdedness: HIGH: I found at least 18 papers from 2025-2026 aimed at this problem, including at least four at ECCV 2026 and one listed as CVPR 2026. They come from the main hand-object groups working on ARCTIC, HOT3D, DexYCB, HO3D and HOGraspNet, plus wearable-sensing and clinical teams, so incremental monocular work here is heavily contested.
evidence.trend: rising: attention is growing because egocentric hand capture is now a data source for robot learning. Video diffusion and flow-matching priors (ViDiHand, StableHand), large synthetic RGB-D data (AnyHand) and wearable fusion (AVI-HT, fiber-optic glove, wristband pressure sensing) are all 2026 entry points. Reliable finger pose under heavy, prolonged occlusion, at real-time speed, without a calibrated rig is still open.

skeptics.reasons: I found no 2025-2026 work that solves finger-level pose of a grasping hand under heavy occlusion or turns it into engineering. The newest work makes it smaller, not gone. (1) WiLoR (CVPR 2025) and other scaled ViT regressors in the HaMeR line made detection and reconstruction strong in the wild. Their headline gains are on Procrustes-aligned, all-joint averages, and these do not isolate hidden fingers. I could not verify any occlusion-stratified numbers for them, and my web-search budget was used up, so this part comes from the arXiv abstracts I fetched. (2) The 2026 occlusion-targeted methods give only relative gains of about 20 percent, which matches the record's 'each fix gives small gains'. StableHand (arXiv 2605.18553) reports a 20-25 percent W-MPJPE reduction, largest on heavily occluded HOT3D/ARCTIC sequences. DeltaDorsal (CHI 2026, arXiv 2601.15516) reports an 18 percent MPJAE reduction when fingers are at least 50 percent occluded. EgoForce (arXiv 2605.12498) reports 28 percent lower camera-space MPJPE on HOT3D. EgoEV-HandPose (arXiv 2605.12297) still reports 30.54 mm MPJPE. HOPformer (ECCV 2026, arXiv 2606.30598, Bansal/Black/Damen) still calls severe occlusion and ambiguous contact challenging and says that learning-based methods do not generalise in the wild. (3) New sensing modalities show that the field itself treats vision-only as insufficient: EgoEMG (arXiv 2605.05712) uses EMG for articulation under occlusion, and Visuo-Acoustic (arXiv 2508.00852) adds acoustic sensing. (4) Generative and temporal priors (Dyn-HaMR, WHOLE arXiv 2602.22209, AGILE arXiv 2602.04672) fill in hidden joints that look plausible. None of them shows these joints are accurate, because ground truth during grasps is itself degraded (the EgoExo-Hands dome P90 is 12.53 mm with interaction vs 7.31 mm without, in the record). No benchmark measures per-finger error of occluded joints during contact, so nothing can be shown to be saturated. Two parts are weaker as research targets. First, the clinical sub-claim (three ad-hoc webcams give no finger kinematics) is closer to deployment and engineering than to an open research problem. Second, average-joint metrics on HO3D/DexYCB are near saturation, with only sub-millimetre backbone gains. The pain point should therefore be narrowed rather than dropped.

skeptics.reframe: Average-joint, Procrustes-aligned hand pose on HO3D/DexYCB is close to saturated. What stays open is the metric (camera-space) accuracy of the specific finger joints the object hides during contact, from one RGB or RGB-D view or a headset. Current temporal and generative priors fill these joints with plausible poses but cannot show they are correct. That is because ground truth is least accurate during grasps, and no benchmark reports error stratified by occlusion and contact. A sharper target: finger pose under occlusion that is verifiable and constrained by contact and geometry (for example, RGB-D depth of the object surface plus contact consistency), together with an occlusion-stratified evaluation protocol that has trustworthy labels during the grasp. The clinical few-camera sub-claim should be treated as an application, not as the research core.

skeptics.reasons:
Artifact lens verdict: P15 is not an artifact of one dataset, one group or one community's conventions, so it is not refuted. Some parts of it are artifacts, though, and the statement claims more than the evidence shows.

(1) The support is diverse. The paper ids resolve, through the w3_digest records, to papers from independent groups, sensing setups and venues:
- Meta egocentric work: HOT3D lineage, AssemblyHands (CVPR 2023), Ego-Exo4D (CVPR 2024), SHOW3D (CVPR 2026).
- Apple EgoDex (ICLR 2026).
- ETH and MPI ARCTIC-based benchmarking (ECCV 2024, Fan et al.).
- The UTokyo IJCV 2023 annotation survey.
- A MICCAI 2023 surgical RGB-D paper (POV-Surgery).
- EPFL Smart Kitchen (NeurIPS 2025).
- Glove, IMU and EMG papers (Glove2Hand, AVI-HT, EgoEMG).
- A single-image mesh baseline (CVPR 2024).
- HANDS 2024-2026 challenge reports.
The settings range from monocular crops to headsets, domes and clinics.

(2) The problem predates the 2022-2026 window. The HANDS'19 report (Armagan et al., ECCV 2020) already found that sampling and generalisation problems are worse under hand-object interaction and with RGB input. The ECCV 2024 egocentric benchmark still lists heavy occlusion and close two-hand-object contact as open. Neither the hand-pose community nor the egocentric community treats it as solved.

(3) The one community that does get good finger kinematics does it with exactly the hardware the pain point says is missing: marker or glove mocap and calibrated multi-camera domes. That supports the statement rather than refuting it. Meta's HOT3D (CVPR 2025) reports that multi-view methods clearly beat single-view ones, consistent with the multi-view clause.

Where the artifact charge partly lands:
- (a) The clinical sub-cluster (TULIP, the ARAT clinical-room study, OpenCap-style monocular reach) is mostly an artifact of off-the-shelf MediaPipe/MMPose triangulated from 1-3 ad-hoc webcams. The rehab-biomechanics community already reaches this accuracy with marker labs. Those papers inflate the count and should be dropped or made secondary.
- (b) Several benchmark numbers mix up occlusion with other factors. HO3D vs FreiHAND P-MPJPE (7.89 vs 5.01 mm) also reflects domain and label-quality differences. The dome P90 numbers (12.5 vs 7.3 mm) measure how annotation degrades, not how methods fail.
- (c) Part of the measured error at grasps may be label noise: ground truth is weakest exactly during grasps on the few benchmarks used (HO3D, DexYCB, ARCTIC, HOT3D). So the size of the gap is uncertain, even though its existence is not.
- (d) The wording "the field cannot recover" overstates it. Recent single-view models give usable finger pose under moderate occlusion. What fails is contact-critical accuracy at the thumb and fingertips under heavy occlusion.

The main risk this lens finds is not artifact but crowding. It is an old, heavily attacked problem where most fixes give incremental gains.

The score is 7 because the core is broad and long-standing, while about a quarter of the support (clinical, plus confounded metrics) is narrow or setup-specific. Verification: only the four external papers below were fetched and checked, and only at abstract level; the corpus paper identities come from the local digest files and were not re-fetched.

skeptics.reframe: With one RGB or RGB-D view, or body-worn cameras, no method recovers the thumb and fingertips accurately enough for contact while they are hidden by a grasped object, and this cannot be measured reliably either: benchmark ground truth is least accurate exactly during grasps. Better finger accuracy and better ground truth during grasps are the coupled open problem. Today, reliable finger kinematics during grasps still need markers, gloves or a calibrated multi-camera dome.

skeptics.reasons:
Refutation attempt. Large parts of P15 are not research questions. The clinical half (three webcams that exceed a reprojection standard, a six-camera room needed for finger tapping, a proposed five-camera rig that has not been tested) is a hardware and deployment problem whose known fix is more calibrated views, so it only waits on resources. The monocular half is a crowded, long-attacked target. Occlusion-robust hand mesh estimation has been a named CVPR topic since at least HandOccNet (CVPR 2022, verified). Large transformer regressors (HaMeR, verified on arXiv), video-based joint hand-object reconstruction (HOLD, verified on arXiv) and egocentric multi-view datasets (HOT3D, CVPR 2025, verified) followed. The record itself says new backbones give sub-millimetre gains and synthetic data gives 2-3 percent. Another backbone or another occlusion dataset would read to reviewers as incremental. The physics side is also stubborn: a hidden joint produces no image evidence, so a single view cannot remove the ambiguity, and a probabilistic output only restates it.

Why it still survives. At least three questions would interest a top-venue reviewer, and none of them is "collect more labels". (1) Evaluating without circular ground truth. The record shows that visual annotation is worst exactly during grasps: dome P90 MPJPE is 12.53 mm with interaction versus 7.31 mm without (paper 1534). Current occlusion benchmarks therefore score models against labels that fail the same way the models do. One question is whether non-visual sources (EMG, as in emg2pose at NeurIPS 2024 D&B, verified, or a tactile or IMU glove) can serve as independent ground truth or supervision for hidden fingers. That is a benchmark-validity question, not a request for annotation money. (2) Object-conditioned inference. In RGB-D, the tracked surface of the grasped object is observed even where the fingers are not, and a grasping finger must touch that surface without passing through it. Can contact and non-penetration constraints from the tracked object turn the hidden-joint problem from prior-limited into geometry-limited, and by how much does that reduce thumb and fingertip error beyond about 80 percent occlusion (paper 1543)? (3) Calibrated uncertainty for hidden joints. Diffusion hypotheses exist, but best-of-N scoring needs ground truth. An open question is whether a method can produce per-joint uncertainty that is calibrated against an independent sensor and can be consumed downstream, for example to decide which finger joints are safe to retarget to a robot hand. Each question is specific and testable, and would fit a CVPR/ICCV or CoRL paper. The approach of question (2) partly overlaps prior contact-aware HOI work. The novelty would have to come from the evaluation protocol and calibration, not from the constraint idea alone.

Net. The pain point is not refuted, but only a narrow reframed version survives, at a mid score. As stated, it bundles an engineering deployment gap with a crowded accuracy race. Search budget was exhausted, so I could not check for 2025-2026 papers that already tackle non-visual ground truth for occluded fingers. That would be the decisive novelty check.

skeptics.reframe: When a hand grasps an object, the hidden fingers are under-determined by the image, and the visual labels used to train and benchmark models are least accurate exactly then. The research question: in RGB-D, can contact and non-penetration constraints from the tracked object surface, together with an independent non-visual reference (EMG, tactile or IMU glove), give finger poses for the occluded thumb and fingertips that are both more accurate and calibrated in their uncertainty? The test is against that independent reference, not against visual annotations that fail the same way.

research_questions.question: How much of the reported 3D error on object-occluded finger joints in public hand-object benchmarks is label error rather than method error, and do method rankings and the recent claims of occlusion robustness still hold when the evaluation uses only occluded joints whose labels have independent support?
research_questions.why_top_venue: Recent claims of occlusion robustness all use unstratified, mostly Procrustes-aligned all-joint averages. This includes StableHand (arXiv 2605.18553, largest gains claimed on heavily occluded sequences), ViDiHand (arXiv 2606.30308), GenHOI (ECCV 2026) and HOMAE/MaskHOI. The labels they are scored against are least accurate during grasps: the record cites a dome P90 of 12.53 mm with interaction versus 7.31 mm without, paper 1534. Occluded-joint evaluation exists only in 2D. HaMeR's HInt annotates per-keypoint occlusion and reports PCK for visible and occluded joints separately (verified on the arXiv HTML). A 3D protocol with three properties would be a reusable community asset in a crowded area: (a) per-joint visibility in the input view, (b) a label-support tier for every joint, and (c) a measured label-noise floor. Reviewers at NeurIPS Datasets and Benchmarks and CVPR reward benchmarks that change how a crowded field measures progress, but only with a non-trivial finding: rankings that flip, or a stated fraction of occluded-fingertip error that falls inside label noise. Novelty caveat: my search budget ran out, so the absence of a 3D occlusion-stratified hand benchmark is unverified. One arXiv API query (hand, joint, visibility, occlusion, benchmark) returned none.
research_questions.method_sketch: 1) For each test frame, render the ground-truth MANO mesh and the object mesh into every calibrated view. Mark each joint and fingertip vertex as visible, hidden by the object, hidden by the hand itself, or out of view, using a z-buffer test against the observed depth where depth exists. 2) Assign a label-support tier to each labelled joint. On visual-annotation datasets (DexYCB, HO3D v3, HOGraspNet) the tier is the number of other views in which the joint is visible. On the marker-mocap datasets (ARCTIC, HOT3D) the label comes from markers, not from images. 3) Estimate a label-noise floor per tier with two checks. First, a leave-one-view-out test: triangulate 2D keypoints detected in the views where the joint is visible, then compare against the released label. Second, on ContactPose, measure the distance from the ground-truth fingertip to the measured contact region on the object surface. 4) Run public checkpoints inference-only: HaMeR, WiLoR, HandOccNet, one SDF-based hand-object method, one depth-based method, and one temporal or world-frame method if code is available. Report camera-space and PA-MPJPE per finger, per visibility bin and per support tier. 5) Report Kendall tau between the full-set ranking and the trusted-subset ranking, and the fraction of occluded-fingertip error that falls inside the noise floor. 6) Release the visibility and support labels plus an evaluation script.
research_questions.minimum_experiment: DexYCB s0 test (8 calibrated RGB-D views, visual labels) plus the ARCTIC validation split (marker-mocap labels). Five public checkpoints, inference only. Deliver per-finger, per-visibility-bin camera-space error tables, the leave-one-view-out label-noise floor on DexYCB, and ranking stability between the full and trusted subsets. Then add HO3D v3 (multi-camera RGB-D; test labels are held on a server, so use a held-out training-sequence protocol and state it) and HOT3D. Estimated effort: about 3-4 months for one student, mostly data handling and rendering.
research_questions.data_and_hardware: Public data only: DexYCB, HO3D v3, HOGraspNet (multi-view RGB-D, visual labels), ARCTIC and HOT3D (marker-mocap labels), ContactPose (RGB-D grasps with contact maps; the abstract confirms contact plus RGB-D but not the thermal sensor, which I recall from the paper and did not verify). The downloads are large, so plan for multi-terabyte storage or use per-split subsets. One workstation GPU with 24 GB is enough because the work is inference plus pyrender-style rasterisation. No capture hardware is needed.
research_questions.risks: 1) Null result: rankings may stay stable, and the paper then reads as an analysis note. Mitigation: state the label-noise floor as the main result, and pair the protocol with the method in RQ2. 2) The joints hidden in every view, which matter most, cannot be validated by cross-view support. The protocol can only report their coverage, which reviewers may call circular. Mitigation: use the marker-based ARCTIC and HOT3D as the independent tier. 3) Marker-mocap labels also degrade under occlusion, and the protocol cannot measure that without the raw marker data. 4) Some recent methods (ViDiHand, StableHand, GenHOI) may have no public code, which limits the model zoo. 5) Big labs that own these datasets could release similar stratified splits first.

research_questions.question: With a single RGB-D camera and a tracked rigid object, can a learned grasp prior be sampled under explicit geometric evidence (depth free-space carving, object non-penetration, fingertip contact on the observed object surface, and reprojection only for visible joints) so that error on object-occluded thumb and fingertip joints drops measurably and the per-joint uncertainty is calibrated, while the method runs at interactive rates?
research_questions.why_top_venue: Single-view RGB-D finger tracking during manipulation is underserved compared with monocular RGB. An arXiv API listing of 30 recent RGB-D hand-object pose papers had no single-camera RGB-D tracker of articulated fingers during manipulation; this listing is not exhaustive. Current priors fill hidden joints with plausible poses but cannot say which joints are supported by evidence. The closest work, all at abstract level: Follow My Hold (arXiv 2508.18213, monocular RGB, diffusion with depth and normal guidance), CHOIR (arXiv 2605.20992, monocular video, contact-aware optimisation), EgoAERO (arXiv 2606.08057, egocentric RGB-D, contact-consistent trajectories aimed at robot learning, no reported hand-pose accuracy), and the BMVC 2025 per-joint aleatoric uncertainty head (arXiv 2509.01242, no calibration evaluation in the abstract). Three things together would be new: measured depth used as negative evidence on the hidden joints, a per-joint evidence provenance (observed, constrained or prior-only), and coverage-calibrated uncertainty checked on the RQ1 trusted subset. The constraints themselves are old: free-space, contact and penetration terms were used in 2014-2016 generative RGB-D hand-object trackers and in ContactOpt and TOCH. Reviewers will therefore accept the work only if the paper shows a measured occluded-fingertip gain and calibration, not just more plausible contacts.
research_questions.method_sketch: 1) Visible structure comes from an off-the-shelf RGB regressor (WiLoR or HaMeR) plus a hand segmentation mask. 2) Object 6-DoF pose comes from a model-based tracker such as FoundationPose, or from the dataset ground truth in an oracle ablation. Build the object SDF from the known mesh. 3) Train a conditional flow-matching or diffusion prior over MANO finger articulation, conditioned on the wrist pose relative to the object and on an object shape code. Train it on public grasp data: DexYCB-train, OakInk, GRAB and ARCTIC grasps, plus DexGraspNet for scale. 4) At test time, sample from the prior with guidance from: (a) depth free-space, so no hand surface point lies in front of an observed depth pixel outside the hand mask; (b) object non-penetration through the SDF; (c) soft contact attraction for fingertips the prior predicts to be in contact; (d) 2D reprojection for visible joints only; (e) a causal temporal term. 5) Draw K samples and use their spread per joint. Calibrate with split-conformal prediction on a held-out split, and label each joint observed, constrained or prior-only according to which guidance terms are active for it. 6) Distil the sampler into a few-step model for interactive speed.
research_questions.minimum_experiment: DexYCB s0, one camera at a time (RGB-D), with oracle object pose and then FoundationPose object pose. Baselines: WiLoR, WiLoR plus a ContactOpt-style post-hoc refiner, one SDF-based hand-object method, and one depth-based method if code is available. Metrics, using the RQ1 bins: camera-space error on object-occluded fingertips and thumb joints, penetration depth, contact agreement on ContactPose, empirical coverage of the 90 percent intervals, and frames per second. Proposed success target, not a measured number: at least 15 percent lower object-occluded fingertip error than WiLoR plus the refiner, with coverage within 5 points of nominal. Add a synthetic RGB-D test set with exact finger labels (rendered or AnyHand) to separate method error from label error. Estimated effort: about 6-9 months.
research_questions.data_and_hardware: Public data: DexYCB and HO3D v3 (RGB-D evaluation), ContactPose (contact check), HOGraspNet (additional RGB-D), and OakInk, GRAB, ARCTIC and DexGraspNet grasps (prior training). Optional synthetic data: AnyHand (licence CC BY-NC-ND per its arXiv page, so check redistribution terms) or self-rendered scenes. One 24-48 GB GPU is enough to train a small conditional prior over MANO parameters, which is far cheaper than video diffusion. The lab's consumer RGB-D camera is needed only for qualitative real-world demos. Optionally, a phone-mounted thermal camera (a few hundred dollars) could record fingertip contact imprints on the lab's own objects as a cheap independent check; this is untested here.
research_questions.risks: 1) Ambiguity remains: a hidden finger often has several configurations that satisfy contact and non-penetration, so the constraints may narrow the distribution without lowering mean error. The calibration result then carries the paper. 2) The method needs the object model and pose, which rules out category-agnostic objects unless a reconstruction step is added. FoundationPose errors under heavy hand occlusion propagate to the fingers. 3) There is strong overlap with contact-aware HOI refinement (ContactOpt, TOCH, GraspTTA, Follow My Hold, CHOIR), so the novelty has to come from measured gains on depth-evidenced occluded joints and from calibration. 4) The RGB-D sensor's own error near the hand-object boundary (flying pixels, sensor misalignment between the colour and depth cameras) can corrupt the free-space term. 5) The best monocular systems (ViDiHand) may already match the RGB-D gain without depth, which would undercut the motivation. Always include them as baselines where code exists.

research_questions.question: When human grasps captured from single-view RGB-D are retargeted to a dexterous robot hand, does per-joint calibrated uncertainty with evidence provenance for the occluded fingers (from RQ2) raise grasp success compared with retargeting the point estimate of a state-of-the-art monocular hand model?
research_questions.why_top_venue: Egocentric and third-person hand capture is now a main data source for robot learning: EgoDex at ICLR 2026, plus EgoAERO, UniDex and RoboWheel on arXiv. In these pipelines the occluded fingers are exactly the contact-critical joints that get retargeted. A controlled study showing that knowing which finger joints to trust changes downstream manipulation success would be the first measurable link between hand-pose uncertainty and robot outcome. CoRL and ICRA reviewers value that link over millimetre-level pose gains.
research_questions.method_sketch: Take the grasps from DexYCB, ContactPose and the lab's own RGB-D recordings, and run three hand estimates: raw WiLoR, the RQ2 constrained point estimate, and the RQ2 samples with per-joint uncertainty. Retarget each to a simulated LEAP or Allegro hand in MuJoCo or Isaac. The uncertainty-weighted retargeter weights joint-angle matching by the calibrated confidence, and lets object contact and force closure govern prior-only joints. Execute lift-and-hold and small-disturbance tests in simulation physics with the object mesh, under several friction values.
research_questions.minimum_experiment: 300-500 DexYCB and ContactPose grasps with known YCB object meshes. Retarget them to the LEAP hand in simulation. Compare lift-and-hold success and slip for the three estimates, stratified by how much of the source hand the object occluded (RQ1 bins). Add a small real-robot check only if a LEAP hand or another dexterous hand can be borrowed. Estimated effort: about 3 months after RQ2.
research_questions.data_and_hardware: Public grasp data with object meshes (DexYCB, ContactPose), an open-source simulator, and the open LEAP hand model. Needs one workstation GPU and no robot. A real-robot validation needs a borrowed dexterous hand and arm; a LEAP hand is low-cost but still a purchase or loan.
research_questions.risks: 1) Simulated grasp success may depend more on the retargeting optimiser and the contact model than on finger accuracy, which would hide the effect. 2) Robotics reviewers may want real-robot results, which the lab may not have. 3) Kinematic mismatch between the human and robot hands can cancel the finger-level differences. 4) This question depends on RQ2 producing calibrated uncertainty, so it is a follow-on paper or a section, not an independent first project.

fit.thesis_assets_help: The thesis assets give a small edge, mainly infrastructure and framing; they add no scientific evidence. (1) The measured/held/constrained honesty labels match the per-joint evidence provenance (observed, constrained, prior-only) in RQ2 and RQ3. This is the most useful carry-over: the framing and some code transfer directly. (2) Object-conditioned recovery of an occluded holding arm, using an ArUco-marked object with a metric pose, follows the same pattern as RQ2 one level up the kinematic chain. It shows the author already has object-pose-conditioned reasoning and a working object-pose source for live demos, but it gives no finger-level component. (3) The causal 30 fps chain supports the interactive-rate claim and gives a live demo path. (4) The Unity twin could render synthetic RGB-D of the same desk setup with exact finger labels, giving a small sim-to-real validation set with perfect labels that is useful for separating method error from label error in RQ1 and RQ2. (5) The 28 recordings come from one subject and have no finger-level ground truth, so they cannot serve as benchmark evidence. They are useful only for qualitative figures and for testing RQ3 retargeting. Estimated benefit: perhaps one to two months of saved setup. The core contributions (the RQ1 protocol and the RQ2 prior and calibration) must be built from public multi-view datasets.
fit.what_a_small_lab_cannot_do_here: A small lab cannot win the monocular accuracy race. The leading results come from video-diffusion backbones run on several A100s (ViDiHand reports 5.5 fps on four A100s) and from large-scale pretraining. Another backbone or another synthetic-data paper would read as incremental, at several times the compute. It cannot produce new independent ground truth for dynamic manipulation. Marker motion capture (as in ARCTIC and HOT3D), calibrated multi-camera domes (as in EgoExo-Hands), mocap-validated sensing gloves (the fiber-optic glove, DexGloveHOI from AVI-HT) and EMG wristbands with mocap (emg2pose) are all big-lab or industry assets, and an off-the-shelf glove would change the hand's appearance anyway. It cannot generate synthetic RGB-D at AnyHand scale (6.6M images) or train video-generative hand priors from scratch. It cannot run clinical studies with patient cohorts and ethics approval, and that sub-claim is closer to engineering anyway. It cannot collect egocentric headset data at scale. It cannot build or evaluate multi-camera rigs that generalise across layouts. In short, the lab's viable entry points are evaluation validity on existing public multi-view and marker-labelled data, geometry- and depth-constrained inference with calibrated uncertainty, and downstream robot-retargeting tests in simulation. It should not compete on headline PA-MPJPE.

painpoint.name: Whole-body capture loses the hands and the handled object

evidence.latest_state: Single-image whole-body mesh recovery has nearly closed the hand-resolution gap. SAM 3D Body (Meta, arXiv 2602.15989, CVPR 2026 poster) uses a separate hand decoder whose wrist output prompts the body decoder. On FreiHAND it reaches PA-MPVPE about 6.2 mm, PA-MPJPE 5.5 mm and F@5 0.735 without training on FreiHAND, against 5.1 mm and 0.825 for the hand-only WiLoR. The authors still state that it does not beat hand specialists and that it ignores human-object and multi-person interaction. Video methods are adding stable hands as well: DanceHMR (arXiv 2605.18102) fuses body and hand residuals to remove jittery SMPL-X hands. In egocentric video, EgoH4 (arXiv 2504.08654) uses body pose to infer out-of-view hands on Ego-Exo4D, improving trajectory and pose errors by 3.4 cm and 5.1 cm over baselines. The object-in-hand part remains largely open. Monocular whole-body HOI reconstruction papers from 2025-2026 focus on body-object placement and physical plausibility: RePHO (arXiv 2606.05359, CVPR 2026), Real2Sim in HOI (arXiv 2605.14462) and 4DHOISolver/Open4DHOI (arXiv 2512.00960). None of their abstracts claims finger-level grasps. GraspHOI (arXiv 2608.28386, Aug 2026) is the first explicit attack on finger-level grasps inside full-body HOI. It reports gains in hand accuracy and contact plausibility on four benchmarks against six baselines, but only from single images, and the abstract gives no numbers. On the data side, HUMOTO (ICCV 2025) and ACE-Data-0 (arXiv 2607.28625: 150 h, 17M frames, 50 participants, body plus articulated hands plus object geometry) capture all three jointly. However, HUMOTO is mocap cleaned by artists, and ACE splits capture into a table-level setup for hands and a room-level setup for the body. InterAct (CVPR 2025) still has to correct hand motions in its aggregated data with optimization. I found no 2025-2026 number that replaces the OMOMO/FullBodyManip result in the record (12.42 cm with predicted hands vs 7.01 cm with ground-truth hands). I also found no real-time RGB-D method that tracks body, fingers and object together.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Promptable single-image whole-body HMR on the new MHR rig, with a dedicated hand decoder whose wrist output prompts the body decoder. FreiHAND PA-MPVPE about 6.2 mm vs WiLoR 5.1 mm. States that it ignores human-object interaction.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: Fast SAM 3D Body: Accelerating SAM 3D Body for Real-Time Full-Body Human Mesh Recovery

Uses depth-based metric registration plus occlusion-aware palmar correspondence and contact optimization. Reports gains on four benchmarks against six baselines.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: DanceHMR: Hand-Aware Whole-Body Human Mesh Recovery from Monocular Videos
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Recovers temporally coherent SMPL-X video meshes, using residual body-hand fusion against jittery hands and close-up-aware augmentation. Does not model objects.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: The Invisible EgoHand: 3D Hand Forecasting through EgoBody Pose Estimation (EgoH4)
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: A diffusion transformer that uses egocentric body pose to estimate and forecast 3D hand trajectories and articulation, including out of view. Improves trajectory and pose errors by 3.4 cm and 5.1 cm on Ego-Exo4D.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: Recovering Physically Plausible Human-Object Interactions from Monocular Videos (RePHO)
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Refines kinematic whole-body HOI estimates with RL in a physics simulator to remove interpenetration and floating objects. The abstract claims no finger-level hands.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: Real2Sim in HOI: Toward Physically Plausible HOI Reconstruction from Monocular Videos
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Recovers human motion first, then refines the object in a physics simulator for simulation-ready HOI. The abstract does not say whether hands are articulated.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: Efficient and Scalable Monocular Human-Object Interaction Motion Reconstruction (4DHOISolver, Open4DHOI)
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: A data engine for 4D HOI from internet video using sparse contact annotation, giving the Open4DHOI dataset (135 object types, 133 actions). The abstract claims no finger-level hands.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: EgoAllo: Estimating Body and Hand Motion in an Ego-Sensed World
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Estimates body and hand motion from head-mounted device signals, with hand estimates improved by body conditioning. Does not model objects.

evidence.crowdedness: MEDIUM: about 10 verified 2025-2026 papers attack pieces of it. Large labs (Meta with SAM 3D Body; Bristol and Keio with EgoH4) are closing the hand-in-body pose gap. Only GraspHOI (single image) and a few capture datasets (HUMOTO, ACE-Data-0) target body, fingers and object together, and I found nothing doing it in real time or from RGB-D video.
evidence.trend: Rising. Foundation-scale whole-body HMR (SAM 3D Body and its fast variant) made hands inside body models a hot topic in 2026, and the demand for humanoid and robot demonstration data is pushing whole-body HOI datasets and physics-plausible reconstruction (CVPR 2026 RePHO, ACE-Data-0). Finger-level grasps of the handled object inside whole-body video reconstruction were attacked explicitly only in Aug 2026 (GraspHOI).

skeptics.reasons:
Not refuted, but 2025-2026 work has removed part of it.

What is now largely solved:
(a) Recovering fingers inside a whole-body estimate from a single image. SAM 3D Body (CVPR 2026, open source, built on the MHR rig) reports hand accuracy on FreiHAND comparable to specialist hand models. It gets there with a separate optional hand decoder, and its authors describe a conflict between body and hand optimization. That supports the pain point's mechanism (resolution and camera mismatch) even as the model engineers around it.
(b) Joint full-body, finger-level and object reconstruction from one image. GraspHOI (arXiv 2608.28386, stated as accepted to CVPR 2026) chains SAM 3D Body, WiLoR and Hunyuan3D, then refines them jointly. It reports hand PA-MPJPE of 7.69 mm on ARCTIC (best baseline TeHOR 10.07 mm), contact plausibility of 72.83% and penetration of 2.91 mm on PICO-db. The single-image hand-object case is therefore moving to engineering by composition.
(c) The claim that no dataset covers body, fingers and object together is now false as stated. HUMOTO (ICCV 2025) is full-body plus hand mocap with 63 objects. ParaHome covers body, hands and articulated objects. ACE-Data-0 (arXiv 2607.28625) has 150 h, 75k episodes and 50 participants, with full-body and articulated-hand motion plus 6-DoF objects.

What persists:
(1) GraspHOI is single-image only. It needs an object mask and category prompt, assumes the object is substantially visible, handles rigid objects only, and says upstream errors propagate. Its headline hand number is Procrustes-aligned, so it hides the wrist-anchor and global translation and rotation errors the pain point is about (EMDB lower-arm MPJAE above 23 degrees; EgoBody3M out-of-view wrist 12.2 cm).
(2) Video and 4D whole-body HOI work (Open4DHOI arXiv 2512.00960, RePHO arXiv 2606.05359) focuses on body-object physics and plausibility. Neither abstract showed finger-level output; this was not checked in the full papers.
(3) ACE-Data-0 itself captures at two separate scales: a table rig for fine hand-object interaction and a room rig for the full body. That is the resolution tradeoff, solved by splitting the capture rather than by one joint system. Its abstract also reports large gaps for current methods under contact, occlusion and egomotion.
(4) HUMOTO has a single performer and needed heavy manual cleaning, so scaled capture with object interaction is still costly.

Net: the image-level, Procrustes-aligned version of the problem is close to engineering. The temporally consistent, metric, world-anchored version (wrist, fingers and object together from a body-framed camera under contact and occlusion) is not.

skeptics.reframe: Single-image whole-body plus finger plus object reconstruction is now done by stacking models (SAM 3D Body + WiLoR + Hunyuan3D in GraspHOI), and mocap datasets with body, hands and objects now exist (HUMOTO, ACE-Data-0). What remains open is temporally consistent, metric, world-anchored recovery of the wrist, fingers and handled object together from a body-framed camera (monocular or RGB-D) under contact and occlusion. Today's systems either report Procrustes-aligned hand error, which hides wrist-anchor and global error, or split capture into a separate table-scale hand rig and room-scale body rig. No benchmark scores body-anchored, unaligned hand and object error over time.

skeptics.reasons:
Artifact test, step one: is the evidence narrow? No. The 35 supporting papers come from many separate groups and setups: MPI/Tuebingen (BEHAVE, InterCap, BEDLAM, BEDLAM2.0), ETH (EMDB), Stanford (OMOMO, 1154), Meta Reality Labs (EgoBody3M, Codec Avatar Studio, NymeriaPlus), CUHK-SZ (MVHumanNet, MVHumanNet++), Hi4D, AthletePose3D, clinical groups (Care-PD, ARAT upper-limb), and humanoid/VLA benchmarks (Mimicking-Bench, SABER). They cover multi-Kinect RGB-D, optical body mocap, VR headsets, domes, synthetic renders and monocular video, so this is not one dataset's quirk. The weakness that HMR methods have at the wrist and lower arm (EMDB: more than 23 deg MPJAE for all methods; EgoBody3M: out-of-view wrist error of 12.2 cm against 5.18 cm overall) also shows up independently in the expressive whole-body literature, such as SMPL-X regressors, where hand accuracy lags behind dedicated hand models.

Step two: is part of it artifact or convention? Yes, in three ways.
(1) The pain point merges at least three separate problems. These are pixel density and primitive budget in full-body avatar domes (1430, 1439, 1440), forearm and wrist rotation error in body HMR (1238, 329, 1193), and dataset design choices in body-object HOI capture (BEHAVE, InterCap, MVHumanNet, BEDLAM). Several items are deliberate design choices, not barriers the field cannot overcome. MVHumanNet left out object interaction to scale. BEDLAM pasted GRAB hands onto bodies because it is a synthetic body dataset. BEHAVE and InterCap chose Kinect depth. OMOMO's 12.42 cm vs 7.01 cm figure comes from a motion-synthesis paper that predicts hands from object motion, not from a capture system.
(2) The why_it_persists claim that 'no dataset or model covers body, fingers and object together' is false. The mocap and graphics community has captured all three together for years. I verified GRAB (ECCV 2020: markers, SMPL-X with articulated hands, object pose, contact), ParaHome (IMU body suit plus hand mocap gloves plus 70 RGB cameras for articulated objects in a home) and HUMOTO (ICCV 2025: mocap plus cameras, full body with fingers and 63 objects). ARCTIC (CVPR 2023) captures hands and articulated objects with Vicon; I recall it also releases SMPL-X body fits, but the abstract I fetched does not confirm that, so it stays unverified. With instrumented rigs (markers, suits, gloves), joint body-finger-object capture is effectively solved.
(3) Some sources are off-core for this author: clinical gait (Care-PD), piano EMG, sign language, relighting (HumanOLAT), and Hi4D human-human interaction. They inflate the paper count without bearing on hand-object handling.

What survives: no markerless capture from a few consumer cameras (monocular RGB, egocentric, a few RGB-D views) recovers body, finger articulation and the handled object jointly at the fidelity of dedicated hand capture. The wrist and forearm, which anchor any hand-object estimate built on a body estimate, are where body estimators are weakest. This holds across communities and is relevant to robot demonstration capture, but it is narrower than the stated pain point and is a well-known open topic (expressive whole-body HMR), not a field-blind spot.

Searches used: 0 WebSearch, 4 WebFetch.

skeptics.reframe: Instrumented mocap (markers, suits, gloves: GRAB, ParaHome, HUMOTO) already captures body, fingers and objects together. What remains open is markerless capture from a few consumer cameras (monocular, egocentric or sparse RGB-D). Such capture cannot jointly recover the body, finger articulation and the handled object at the fidelity of dedicated hand capture. The main reason is that body estimators are least accurate at the wrist and forearm, the very joints that anchor the hand and the object. So a hand-object reconstruction placed on a body estimate inherits centimetre-level wrist error and lower-arm rotation error above 20 degrees.

skeptics.reasons:
Default refutation fails, but only in part. About half of P16 is data or resource cost and gives no research question. That half covers three things: domes lack pixel density on hands, scaled capture leaves out object interaction to stay tractable, and datasets paste GRAB or ARCTIC hands onto bodies. These are budget and logistics problems with a known fix: high-density hand cameras plus finger mocap plus object tracking in one session. Datasets of that kind keep appearing, for example HUMOTO (2025), and Contact4D (3DV 2026, unverified). A paper that only says "capture body, fingers and object together" is a dataset paper whose novelty is shrinking. The other half has real modelling questions:
(a) Kinematic coupling: how to estimate the wrist so that it agrees with both the arm chain and the hand-object contact. The record's own numbers show the size of the problem: OMOMO full-body MPJPE is 12.42 cm with predicted hands versus 7.01 cm with ground-truth hands, wrist and forearm rotation error is above 23 deg on EMDB, and out-of-view wrist error is 12.2 cm on EgoBody3M. Reviewers clearly count this as significant: Moon's Hand4Whole++ / CHAM (CVPR 2026) is a top-venue paper on exactly the hand-body wrist inconsistency.
(b) Joint body, finger and object inference from one camera, where the object and contact constrain the arm, not just the fingers. GraspHOI (arXiv, Aug 2026) is a first attempt from a single image. It reconstructs body, hands and object separately and then aligns them, so the bidirectional and temporal versions are still open.
(c) Learning a joint body-hand-object model without joint capture. The question is how to combine supervision from separate hand-object datasets (ARCTIC, GigaHands) and body-object datasets (BEHAVE, OMOMO) into a model that generalises across all three. This is a real learning question, not a request for more annotation money.
Weaknesses that keep the score from going higher:
- The method space is crowded. SMPLer-X, Multi-HMR, Hand4Whole, Hand4Whole++ and GraspHOI already exist, so plain "better hands in whole-body capture" is incremental.
- Some parts of the record (relighting artifacts on HumanOLAT, clinical ARAT capture) are off-core.
- The clean benchmark gap depends on datasets that do not yet exist at scale.
A publishable question survives only in narrower forms, such as wrist-consistent coupling or compositional learning across datasets. The broad complaint does not.
