skeptics.reframe: The wrist is where body capture and hand-object capture meet. A body estimator gets it wrong by more than 23 deg in forearm rotation and up to 12 cm in position. A separate hand estimator gets it right locally but cannot keep it consistent with the arm. The open question: can whole-body, finger and object state be estimated jointly from one RGB or RGB-D view, with hand-object contact constraining the arm chain and the arm chain constraining the grasp? And can such a model be trained by combining separate hand-object and body-object datasets instead of a joint capture that does not exist? The target is wrist-rotation, contact and full-body error close to what ground-truth hands give, on held-out objects.

research_questions.question: When a person holds a rigid object, can the object's 6-DoF track (from RGB-D, or from RGB with metric depth) act as a third anchor next to a body estimator and a hand specialist? The aim is to fix the forearm twist and wrist translation of whole-body video estimates, so that body, fingers and object are recovered together in the camera or world frame without Procrustes alignment, at close to the accuracy obtained with ground-truth hands.
research_questions.why_top_venue: The verified 2025-2026 state leaves exactly this cell empty. SAM 3D Body (CVPR 2026) and Hand4Whole++/CHAM (CVPR 2026, verified) make the wrist coherent with the arm, but they work on images and model no object. GraspHOI (arXiv 2608.28386, Aug 2026, verified) adds finger-level grasps, but only from a single image. It reports Procrustes-aligned hand error and needs a visible object. THO (arXiv 2603.14435, verified) reconstructs 4D HOI at 31.5 fps on one RTX 4090, but it uses SMPL on BEHAVE and InterCap with no finger articulation. WHOLE (arXiv 2602.22209, verified) recovers world-grounded hands plus object from egocentric video but has no body. The record already quantifies the gap reviewers care about: OMOMO full-body MPJPE is 12.42 cm with predicted hands versus 7.01 cm with ground-truth hands, forearm rotation error on EMDB is above 23 deg, and out-of-view wrist error on EgoBody3M is 12.2 cm. The core insight is general rather than another model stack: a held object is a measurable rigid extension of the hand, and it constrains the joints where body estimators are weakest.
research_questions.method_sketch: (1) Off-the-shelf per-frame front ends, each with a confidence. Body: Fast SAM 3D Body or a world-grounded video body model; which one fits is unverified. Hand: WiLoR or HaMeR, or HaWoR for video. Object 6-DoF: FoundationPose with a template or a generated mesh, using depth when it is available. (2) Grasp-phase segmentation: find held intervals from hand-object proximity and stable relative motion. Inside a held interval, model the hand pose in the object frame as a near-constant latent grasp variable shared across the interval. (3) A causal sliding-window optimizer (factor graph or differentiable) over the arm chain, MANO, the object pose and the latent grasp. Its terms are 2D keypoints, depth residuals, body-hand wrist agreement, forearm pronation and supination limits, bone lengths, contact and non-penetration, temporal smoothness and the object track. When the object hides the hand, the object pose plus the grasp drives the hand. When the hand hides the object, the hand drives the object. (4) Optional learned refiner: a small temporal transformer, a temporal and object-aware analogue of CHAM, that predicts corrections and per-component uncertainty. It is trained with masked losses on ARCTIC (SMPL-X + MANO + object), DexYCB/HO3D (hand-object) and BEHAVE/InterCap/OMOMO (body-object). (5) Per-component provenance output (measured vs inferred from a constraint), so downstream robot or digital-twin users know which wrist frames to trust.
research_questions.minimum_experiment: Main testbed: a single allocentric ARCTIC view on held-out subjects, plus HUMOTO rendered to RGB-D with a Kinect-like noise model if its license allows. Baselines: SAM 3D Body or Fast SAM 3D Body alone; the same with a WiLoR wrist swap; Hand4Whole++ if code is public; per-frame GraspHOI if code is public; THO for the body-object part. Metrics, all without Procrustes alignment: camera-frame wrist position error (cm), forearm twist error (deg), full-body MPJPE, root-relative hand MPJPE, object translation and rotation error or ADD-S, hand-in-object-frame error, contact and penetration, and acceleration error. Oracle: the same pipeline with ground-truth hands, which defines the gap to close. Ablations: no object; object without depth; object with depth; no grasp latent. Success criterion: close a clear share (target: half) of the gap to the ground-truth-hand oracle on wrist and forearm error, keep root-relative hand error at least as good as the hand specialist, and report the fps of the causal variant on one GPU. Add a real RGB-D demonstration on the author's own recordings, where marker-based object pose gives a quantitative check of the object anchor.
research_questions.data_and_hardware: Public data. ARCTIC (verified: SMPL-X, MANO and articulated-object ground truth; 8 allocentric plus 1 egocentric RGB views; leaderboard). DexYCB and HO3D (RGB-D hand-object). BEHAVE and InterCap (multi-Kinect RGB-D body-object). OMOMO (body-object mocap). HUMOTO (ICCV 2025: mocap body, fingers and 63 objects; rendering rights unverified). ParaHome (body, hands and articulated objects; access and venue unverified). Hardware: one GPU with 24-48 GB for the front ends and the optimization, and one consumer RGB-D camera for the real-world demonstration. No mocap and no robot are needed. Compute: days of fine-tuning, not foundation-scale training.
research_questions.risks: (1) No public dataset has real RGB-D together with body, finger and object ground truth. The RGB-D claim therefore rests on synthetic depth (a HUMOTO render) or metric monocular depth on ARCTIC, and reviewers will press on this. (2) ARCTIC is table-top. It is unverified whether the full body and lower arm are visible enough in the allocentric views; if not, the whole-body claim narrows to the upper body. (3) Scoop risk is real: a video version of GraspHOI, or Meta extending SAM 3D Body to objects, could appear within 6-12 months. (4) Reviewers may call it composition engineering unless the object-anchored twist correction gives a large, clearly attributed gain in the ablations. (5) The method depends on a template or reconstructed mesh, and the rigid-grasp latent breaks for articulated or deformable objects and for in-hand regrasping. (6) Upstream front ends change fast; pin versions and report them.

research_questions.question: How much of the error in whole-body hand-object reconstruction comes from the wrist anchor, from finger articulation and from the object pose? And do Procrustes-aligned hand metrics rank methods differently from unaligned, temporal and downstream (robot retargeting) metrics?
research_questions.why_top_venue: All three skeptics converge on one point: the surviving gap is hidden by evaluation convention. Hand accuracy is reported after Procrustes alignment: GraspHOI 7.69 mm PA-MPJPE on ARCTIC (skeptic-reported) and SAM 3D Body about 6.2 mm PA-MPVPE on FreiHAND. That alignment removes exactly the wrist and global error that robot demonstration capture and digital twins depend on. The skeptics found no benchmark that scores body-anchored, unaligned hand and object error over time; this was not exhaustively verified. A protocol that shows rank reversals between aligned and unaligned metrics, and ties unaligned wrist error to downstream grasp success, would change how the field reports results.
research_questions.method_sketch: Build an evaluation suite from public data with joint ground truth: ARCTIC (SMPL-X + MANO + object); HUMOTO and GRAB rendered to video; ParaHome if accessible; ACE-Data-0 if released. Define an error decomposition: (a) wrist anchor position and twist in the camera and world frames; (b) root-relative fingers; (c) object pose; (d) hand-in-object relative pose and contact; (e) temporal jitter. Tag each frame by visibility state (visible, occluded by the object, out of view) so errors can be split by provenance. Run 8-12 public pipelines. Whole-body HMR: SAM 3D Body, Fast SAM 3D Body, SMPLer-X, Multi-HMR, Hand4Whole++. Composition: body + WiLoR/HaMeR + FoundationPose. HOI: GraspHOI and THO, plus WHOLE on egocentric clips. Downstream test: retarget each output to a simulated dexterous hand on a simulated arm, replay the object trajectory, and report grasp and lift success with a fixed retargeting procedure. Report rank correlations between each metric and downstream success.
research_questions.minimum_experiment: ARCTIC plus one rendered dataset (HUMOTO or GRAB), at least six pipelines, the full decomposition, and Kendall tau between PA hand error, unaligned wrist error and simulated grasp success over a few hundred held-object clips. Publishable result: PA and unaligned rankings disagree, or unaligned wrist error predicts downstream failure better than PA error. Either can be checked within 3-4 months.
research_questions.data_and_hardware: Public datasets only. One GPU, and an open-source physics simulator on the same workstation. No capture and no robot.
research_questions.risks: A benchmark without new data is a hard sell at the CVPR main track; NeurIPS Datasets and Benchmarks fits better, or pair it with the first question. Dataset licenses may forbid redistributing renders, so release code and scripts only. The aligned-versus-unaligned finding may be judged unsurprising unless the downstream link is strong. Retargeting choices could dominate downstream success, so hold them fixed and ablate them. Fast model churn can date the leaderboard; release it as a living evaluation.

research_questions.question: Can a joint body-hand-object motion prior be trained compositionally on datasets that each annotate only two of the three components (body-object, hand-object, body-hand)? And can it match a prior trained on scarce joint capture when used for reconstruction on held-out objects and subjects?
research_questions.why_top_venue: This is a learning question, not a budget problem. Joint capture stays expensive and narrow. HUMOTO is mocap with a single performer and manual artist cleanup. ACE-Data-0 (arXiv 2607.28625) splits capture into a table-level setup for hands and a room-level setup for the body. InterAct (CVPR 2025) still has to correct hand motion in its aggregated data by optimization. If composition across partial annotations works, it unlocks the much larger two-component corpora. The masked multi-source formulation (generative modelling with missing modalities) is general enough for NeurIPS or ICLR as well as CVPR.
research_questions.method_sketch: Factorized per-frame state: body (SMPL-X), two MANO hands, object 6-DoF plus a shape code, and a contact map. Train a diffusion or flow-matching motion model with per-dataset availability masks, so loss falls only on the annotated components. Add consistency losses at the shared interfaces: the wrist joint between body and hand, and contact between hand and object. Sources: OMOMO, BEHAVE and InterCap for body-object (hands masked); ARCTIC, DexYCB, HO3D, OakInk and GigaHands for hand-object (body masked, or arm only); Ego-Exo4D, Nymeria and BEDLAM2 for body-hand (object masked). Use the trained model as a test-time guidance prior inside the optimizer of the first question, via score-guided refinement.
research_questions.minimum_experiment: Compare three variants: the compositional prior; a prior trained on joint data only (the ARCTIC train split or a HUMOTO subset); and no prior. Evaluate on held-out HUMOTO objects and ARCTIC subjects on three tasks. (a) Reconstruction gain when the prior is used in the first question's pipeline. (b) Completion of masked components, for example predicting hands given body and object, on the FullBodyManip protocol against OMOMO's 12.42 cm predicted-hand figure. (c) Physical plausibility: penetration, foot skating and contact consistency.
research_questions.data_and_hardware: Public mocap and capture datasets; licenses must be checked for each. One GPU with 24-48 GB. Training takes a few days to a week per model.
research_questions.risks: Large joint datasets (ACE-Data-0 if publicly released, HUMOTO) could weaken the motivation; frame the work as scaling with partial annotations. Unifying conventions across sources is laborious: SMPL vs SMPL-X vs the MHR rig, different frame rates and skeletons. The result may be negative, with composition not beating a small joint set. HOI motion generation is crowded (InterAct and the diffusion HOI line), so the contribution must be the reconstruction use and the partial-supervision result, not generation quality.

fit.thesis_assets_help: The help is modest and mostly for the first question. The thesis's object-conditioned recovery of an occluded holding arm is an arm-level prototype of that question's core idea, that a held object constrains the arm chain. The author therefore starts with working intuition and code at the arm level, though not for fingers or forearm twist. The ArUco-marked object with metric pose gives real RGB-D object-pose ground truth at the author's desk. No public body-finger-object dataset offers that, so it supports a quantitative real-depth check of the object anchor and a convincing demonstration. The measured/held/constrained honesty labels map directly onto the per-component provenance output of the first question and the visibility-tagged metrics of the second, a small but distinctive evaluation idea. The causal 30 fps chain and the Unity twin support a real-time and digital-twin demonstration. Limits: the 28 recordings come from one subject at one desk, have no body or finger ground truth, and probably frame only the upper body. They cannot serve as a benchmark or a training set. Estimated head start: a few months on the first question, little on the second and third.
fit.what_a_small_lab_cannot_do_here: A small lab cannot build joint body, finger and object capture with ground truth at scale; that needs optical mocap, gloves or dense camera domes, as in HUMOTO, ParaHome and ACE-Data-0. It cannot produce finger ground truth from its own single RGB-D camera. It cannot train or retrain foundation-scale whole-body HMR (SAM 3D Body-class data and compute), and it cannot compete with Meta on single-image whole-body hand accuracy. It should not race GraspHOI-style single-image composition, which is already close to engineering. It cannot run large-scale physics RL refinement over many objects (RePHO-style) on one GPU in reasonable time. Without a borrowed arm it cannot validate on a physical robot, so downstream claims stay in simulation retargeting. The lab should compete on the unaligned, temporal evaluation protocol, on object-anchored wrist coupling in video and on compositional learning from public data, not on data scale or backbone scale. Unverified points: whether full-body visibility in ARCTIC is adequate, HUMOTO rendering rights, ParaHome access and venue, ACE-Data-0 release status, and whether GraspHOI and Hand4Whole++ release code.

painpoint.name: Single-hand, single-object, single-agent scope

evidence.latest_state: The two-hands-plus-one-object case has moved well past single-hand scope. Monocular bimanual reconstruction from video is now an active benchmark problem on ARCTIC and HOT3D. BIGS (CVPR 2025) reconstructs two hands and an unknown object with Gaussian splatting. ACE-Ego-Hand (arXiv 2608.20308) reports about 30 percent lower MPJPE-p on occlusion-heavy ARCTIC and 40 percent on HOT3D, with 46-61 percent gains when out-of-sight hands are counted. StableHand (arXiv 2605.18553) reports 20-25 percent lower W-MPJPE for world-space dual-hand motion on HOT3D and ARCTIC. The gains come from tracking hands; the 6DoF object track and contact for each hand are still weak spots. Data has grown: GigaHands (CVPR 2025 Highlight) has 34 h, 56 subjects and 417 objects, but it is still a markerless lab rig. The less-covered settings are only beginning to get work. RHINO (CVPR 2026) jointly reconstructs body, hands, object and scene from monocular video. GraspHOI (arXiv 2608.28386) adds finger-level grasps to full-body HOI. HAT-4D (ECCV 2026) handles multiple objects but needs a human in the loop. Dex2HOI (arXiv 2605.30444) generates bimanual two-object interactions rather than reconstructing them. InterVLA (ICCV 2025) adds an egocentric human-object-human dataset. Many headline 2026 reconstruction and retargeting methods are still single-hand or single-person: Grasp in Gaussians, the real-time 4D HOI transformer at 31.5 FPS (2603.14435), and C2Dex at 57.78 percent success on DexYCB and 26.67 percent on TACO. I found no method that reconstructs or tracks two-person handovers or several agents sharing an object with contact for each agent. On the robot side, bimanual transfer from human video is growing: DexMan reports 19 percent higher success on OakInk-v2. Those numbers come from simulation or a few tasks, not from a measured bimanual success gap closing. A July 2026 foundation-model HOI survey (2607.28394) still frames the field largely around single hand-object interaction.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: Perceiving and Acting in First-Person: A Dataset and Benchmark for Egocentric Human-Object-Human Interactions (InterVLA)
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Two-person, multi-object, egocentric plus exocentric dataset (11.4 h, 1.2M frames, 2 ego and 5 exo views, hybrid RGB-MoCap) with benchmarks for ego motion estimation, interaction synthesis and prediction.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: RHINO: Reconstructing Human Interactions with Novel Objects from Monocular Videos
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Joint reconstruction of human body, an unseen manipulated object and static scene in a common world frame from monocular video with contact priors; new dataset with volumetric 4D ground truth. Addresses the missing body and scene context, but with a single person and one object.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: HAT-4D: Lifting Monocular Video for 4D Multi-Object Interactions via Human-Agent Collaboration
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: VLM-driven agentic pipeline with human-in-the-loop feedback that reconstructs several interacting objects from one video; introduces the MVOIK-4D benchmark. Covers multiple objects but is not automatic.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: ACE-Ego-Hand: Repurposing Video Diffusion Models for Occlusion-Robust Egocentric 3D Hand Motion Recovery
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Recovers continuous metric bimanual hand trajectories from egocentric video via a video-diffusion geometry encoder; reports about 30 percent lower MPJPE-p on ARCTIC and 40 percent on HOT3D, 46-61 percent with out-of-sight hands. Hands only, no object pose.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: StableHand: Quality-Aware Flow Matching for World-Space Dual-Hand Motion Estimation from Egocentric Video
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: World-space dual-hand motion estimation under hand-object occlusion and out-of-view hands; reports 20-25 percent lower W-MPJPE than the strongest baseline on HOT3D and ARCTIC.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: Dex2HOI: Dexterous Bimanual Two-Object Interaction Generation
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Text-to-motion diffusion for two hands manipulating one or two objects (dual-stream diffusion with cross-attention), with up to 540x faster inference; generation rather than tracking.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: GraspHOI: Full-Body 3D Human-Object Reconstruction with Finger-Level Grasps from a Single In-the-Wild Image
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Single-image joint body, hands and category-agnostic object reconstruction in metric space with contact-aware finger optimization; improves on four benchmarks against six baselines.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: GHOST: Fast Category-agnostic Hand-Object Interaction Reconstruction from RGB Videos using Gaussian Splatting
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Fast monocular hand-object Gaussian-splatting reconstruction evaluated on ARCTIC and HO3D, an order of magnitude faster than prior category-agnostic methods; the abstract does not say whether both hands are modelled.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: DexMan: Learning Bimanual Dexterous Manipulation from Human and Generated Videos
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Converts human or generated videos into bimanual humanoid dexterous skills without calibration, depth or object scans; reports +0.08 ADD-S and +0.12 VSD in object pose on TACO and +19 percent RL success on OakInk-v2.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: End-to-End Spatial-Temporal Transformer for Real-time 4D HOI Reconstruction
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Real-time (31.5 FPS on an RTX 4090) monocular body-object 4D reconstruction; explicitly limited to a single person and a single templated object, so it shows how far the scope restriction persists.

evidence.crowdedness: MEDIUM: work on two hands plus one object is crowded. At least eight 2025-2026 papers from large groups (Seoul National University/UNIST, CUHK/Shanghai AI Lab, Imperial College London, MPI/Meta, Brown) target it on ARCTIC and HOT3D. Two-person handover, several agents sharing an object, and joint tracking of body, both hands and several objects have only a few datasets and one or two methods each.
evidence.trend: rising: bimanual and egocentric dual-hand tracking papers multiplied through 2026, and new datasets (GigaHands, InterVLA, MVOIK-4D) target bimanual, multi-object and human-object-human scope. Humanoid and dexterous robot learning wants bimanual human data, which pushes the trend up. Multi-person reconstruction with a shared object is still rarely attacked.

skeptics.reasons:
Partly refuted, but the full pain point stands. The claim that the field "assumes one, usually right, hand" no longer holds for 2025-2026 bimanual work. Bimanual data now exists at scale: ARCTIC, OakInk2 (CVPR 2024), GigaHands (CVPR 2025; 56 subjects, 417 objects, 2,034 minutes), HOT3D, and EgoDex (ICLR 2026; 829 h of Vision Pro egocentric video with 3D two-hand and upper-body pose, 194 tasks). Monocular bimanual hand-object reconstruction is an active benchmarked task: BIGS (CVPR 2025) and AGILE (arXiv 2602.04672, 2026) both report results on ARCTIC bimanual sequences. Bimanual human-to-robot transfer has released methods: ManipTrans (CVPR 2025, with DexManipNet), DexMachina (arXiv 2505.24853), DexMan (arXiv 2510.08475) and H-RDT (arXiv 2507.23523, bimanual robot pretraining on EgoDex). So the single-hand part is now an engineering and scaling problem, not an open research gap.

Bimanual is still not solved. On ARCTIC, AGILE (the best reported) gets left/right MPJPE of 25.0/23.8 mm, an object F@5 of 57.6, and hand-relative object Chamfer of 21.9/30.6 cm^2. HOLD and BIGS are clearly worse. These are per-sequence optimization methods, not causal or real-time ones, and AGILE is evaluated only on the rigid ARCTIC subset. The fastest 2026 4D HOI method, THO (arXiv 2603.14435, 31.5 FPS), is a single-object method; its abstract says nothing about two-hand handling (unverified beyond the abstract). EgoDex has no object pose labels as far as I could find (not confirmed from the full paper).

I found no 2025-2026 work that solves these:
- multi-person handover reconstruction with shared-object contact;
- multi-agent correspondence in human-to-robot transfer;
- joint whole-body plus articulated hands plus object recovery in the wild.

Open4DHOI (arXiv 2512.00960) scales body-object capture but does not claim articulated hands or multiple people. Its own abstract calls in-the-wild 4D HOI extraction "unsolved". My searches turned up no in-the-wild 3D benchmark for handover or multi-object bimanual tasks; GigaHands, OakInk2 and HOT3D are lab or instrumented captures.

Net: refuted for "single hand". It survives for multi-agent and shared-object interaction, real-time and causal bimanual tracking with the object, and in-the-wild ground truth.

skeptics.reframe: Bimanual hand-object capture is no longer the gap: there are released datasets (GigaHands, OakInk2, EgoDex), offline monocular methods (BIGS, AGILE) and bimanual retargeting methods (ManipTrans, DexMachina). Three things remain open. First, causal, real-time two-hand plus shared-object tracking under mutual hand-hand-object occlusion: the best methods are per-sequence optimizers at about 24 mm MPJPE on ARCTIC. Second, multi-agent interaction (handovers, two people sharing an object), which needs agent correspondence and contact tracking across agents. Third, 3D ground truth for these settings outside instrumented labs.

skeptics.reasons:
Source diversity is not the weakness. The 33 supporting papers (resolved through the w3_digest records) come from many groups and venues, including CVPR (HOI4D, Assembly101, Ego-Exo4D, CORE4D, ParaHome, EgoPressure), ICCV (AffordPose, HUMOTO), NeurIPS (HOH, EPFL-Smart-Kitchen), ECCV (HOGraspNet), ICRA (ATTACH, RH20T), CoRL (RoboTube), RSS (EgoVerse), IJCV and SIGGRAPH Asia. So this is not the artifact of one dataset. The headline statement is still overstated or outdated, for four reasons.

(1) The bimanual dataset gap has been closed at lab scale for some time. Examples: ARCTIC (CVPR 2023, bimanual with articulated objects), OakInk2 (CVPR 2024, bimanual complex tasks), GigaHands (CVPR 2025, 34 h, 56 subjects, 417 objects) and HOT3D (CVPR 2025, egocentric two-hand object tracking, 19 subjects, 33 objects). There are also H2O, TACO and InterHand2.6M/Re:InterHand. "Bimanual remains largely uncovered" is false for data.

(2) In robot learning, bimanual is the community default, not a gap. ALOHA (2023), UMI (RSS 2024, which states it targets bimanual and dynamic demonstrations), DexCap (RSS 2024), EgoMimic and Mobile ALOHA are all bimanual. The "right hand only" and "single arm" restrictions come from particular papers' setups (for example the 1482 and 305 items), not from the field.

(3) Some quoted evidence is stale or off-target. HOI4D's 2022 remark that single-hand manipulation is unsolved predates ARCTIC. The Ego-Exo4D ego body-pose number and the Assembly101 pose-vs-video recognition gap do not measure the cost of bimanual or multi-agent interaction. The only direct bimanual-vs-single comparison is one real-robot VaseWiping result (80 vs 100 percent OOD success), which is a tiny sample.

(4) The item bundles four different problems (bimanual, multi-object, multi-person, joint body-hand-object), which have very different coverage.

What survives this lens:
(a) Methods lag the data. Joint reconstruction or tracking of two hands plus a shared, possibly articulated, object from monocular RGB or RGB-D is still served mainly by offline per-sequence optimization: HOLD, the HANDS 2024 ARCTIC-track 3DGS winner, and BIGS (CVPR 2025). BIGS itself states there was no comprehensive pipeline for bimanual category-agnostic reconstruction from monocular video, and the HANDS ARCTIC challenge frames heavy occlusion and dynamic contact as the open difficulty.
(b) Multi-person handover and joint body-hand-object capture remain thin and lab-bound. HOH, CORE4D and ADL4D are lab captures; Harmony4D notes that multi-human datasets are mostly controlled indoor captures.

Verdict: the statement as written ("most assume one right hand; bimanual largely uncovered") is refuted as outdated and partly an artifact of specific setups. A narrower method-level gap survives.

evidence.title: HOLD: Category-agnostic 3D Reconstruction of Interacting Hands and Objects from Video

skeptics.reframe: Bimanual hand-object data now exist at lab scale (ARCTIC, OakInk2, GigaHands, HOT3D), and bimanual robot data collection is standard (ALOHA, UMI, DexCap). Methods have not caught up. Reconstructing or tracking two hands and a shared, possibly articulated, object from a single RGB or RGB-D stream is still done mainly by offline per-sequence optimization (HOLD, the HANDS 2024 ARCTIC-track 3DGS winner, BIGS). There is no causal or real-time tracker that resolves inter-hand and hand-object contact under mutual occlusion, and none that adds body context or a second person (handovers). Those settings are covered only by a few lab captures (HOH, CORE4D, ADL4D).

skeptics.reasons:
Most of P17 as written does not yield a top-venue research question. The record classifies it as problem_type "data", and the remedies it lists (more bimanual and multi-person datasets, more subjects, objects and sites) are capture effort and annotation money. The bimanual single-object part is also out of date and crowded. ARCTIC (CVPR 2023), OakInk2 (CVPR 2024), GigaHands (CVPR 2025, 56 subjects, 417 objects, about 2,034 minutes) and HOT3D already provide bimanual data. On the method side, BIGS (CVPR 2025) reconstructs two hands plus an unknown object from monocular video, HOLD (CVPR 2024) and Jiang et al. (CVPR 2025) handle objects held in one or both hands, and ManipTrans (CVPR 2025) and DemoBot do bimanual human-to-robot transfer. The record's claim that "no method handles two-hand ... correspondence with shared-object contact" is therefore false for the two-hands, one-person, one-object case. "Add the left hand" or "collect more bimanual data" would be judged incremental. The quoted numbers (bimanual 80 percent vs single-hand 100 percent out-of-distribution, and body-plus-hand recognition beating body-only) come from single-paper anecdotes, not field-wide benchmark gaps.

One narrower part survives: the multi-agent and ownership-transfer case. In my searches (the handover-reconstruction search included) I found datasets (HOH, CORE4D, Harmony4D) but no method that estimates hands, bodies and a shared object from one or few views while explicitly reasoning about which hand or person holds the object at each instant. That covers handovers, bimanual regrasps and passing an object between hands. Evidence item 1125 says single-person HOI findings, even bimanual ones, do not transfer to two-person handovers, which points to a modelling gap rather than only a data gap. A reviewer could find this significant: (a) can the object's time-varying contact graph (who supports it, when the grasp is handed off) be inferred jointly with pose and used as a structural constraint against severe mutual occlusion; (b) can that structure, plus physics and contact consistency, break the circular data-scarcity loop through self-supervised or test-time optimisation on unlabelled multi-agent video, so that progress is not just paid for with more annotation; (c) does a contact-graph representation transfer to dual-arm or multi-robot demonstrations better than per-hand retargeting does. The survey item 1399 on agent correspondence and disentangling overlapping motions supports (a) and (c).

The pain point therefore survives only after reframing. The broad "single-hand scope" wording is refuted as a research question, and the "no method handles two hands" premise is already contradicted. The score of 5 reflects one credible, narrower question inside a mostly data-collection complaint. I did not verify the absence of 2026 multi-person handover reconstruction methods beyond these few searches, so novelty risk remains.

evidence.title: DemoBot: Efficient learning of bimanual manipulation with dexterous hands from third-person human videos

skeptics.reframe: Two-hand, one-object reconstruction and bimanual data are no longer the gap: BIGS, HOLD, ARCTIC, OakInk2 and GigaHands already cover them. What remains open is changing grasp ownership on a shared object. When an object passes between hands or between people (handovers, regrasps, joint carrying), current monocular and RGB-D pipelines have no model of which hand or person supports the object at each instant. They therefore cannot resolve mutual occlusion or keep contact physically consistent across agents. The research question is whether this time-varying contact and support graph can be inferred jointly with hand, body and object pose, used as a constraint, and learned self-supervised from unlabelled multi-agent video. That would break the circular dependence between scarce bimanual labels and unreliable bimanual tracking, and give a representation that transfers to dual-arm and multi-robot demonstrations.

research_questions.question: Can an online tracker hold a discrete, time-varying support state for the object (free, left hand, right hand, both hands) and infer it together with both MANO hand poses and the object's 6DoF pose? The state is used to carry pose through occlusion: the object moves with its supporting hand while it is hidden, and a hidden holding hand is constrained by the visible object. The test is whether this lowers world-frame hand and object error during mutual hand-hand-object occlusion and hand-to-hand transfer, at about 30 fps from one RGB-D camera, compared with per-frame estimators and filters that have no discrete state.
research_questions.why_top_venue: Offline per-sequence optimizers still lead on two hands plus a shared object: HOLD (CVPR 2024), BIGS (CVPR 2025), and AGILE (arXiv 2602.04672, ARCTIC left/right MPJPE 25.0/23.8 mm, rigid subset only). The fastest 2026 HOI method, THO (arXiv 2603.14435, 31.5 FPS), handles one person and one templated object. On 2026-10-02 I ran three arXiv API keyword queries: bimanual+tracking+object+real-time, hand-object+RGB-D+tracking, and hand-object+online+tracking+hands. None returned a causal tracker for two hands plus a 6DoF object. The closest recent causal RGB-D work, EgoAERO (arXiv 2606.08057), does not say in its abstract that it handles two hands. The contribution would be a model, a hybrid discrete-continuous support state with calibrated outputs that report where each value came from, rather than a dataset. It targets the exact regime all three skeptics say is still open (causal tracking, mutual occlusion, contact switches), and it delivers what robot demonstration capture and digital twins need. Honest bar: this reaches CVPR/ECCV only with large, pre-registered stratified gains on at least two public datasets; otherwise it is an ICRA or RA-L systems paper. The novelty check was keyword-only because the WebSearch budget was used up, so a concurrent method may exist.
research_questions.method_sketch: 1) Frozen front ends: a per-frame MANO regressor (HaMeR or WiLoR), the model-based 6DoF object estimator and tracker FoundationPose (a BundleSDF-style variant for unknown objects), and SAM 2 masks. Depth anchors hand translation and gives object ICP residuals. These are standard tools, not re-verified in this session. 2) State: wrist SE(3) and articulation for each hand, object SE(3), a grasp transform T_hand->obj for each support mode, and a discrete mode m_t in {free, L, R, LR}, optionally extended with 'other person'. 3) Inference: a switching state-space model solved as a fixed-lag factor graph (GTSAM iSAM2, lag 5-10 frames, about 170-330 ms at 30 fps). An interacting-multiple-model filter or a Rao-Blackwellized particle filter over modes is the alternative. Factors: detector measurements with learned uncertainty, down-weighted by visible-pixel fraction; a support factor that ties the object to the supporting wrist frame with slip noise; contact and penetration factors from fingertip-to-object signed distance; a transition prior estimated from labelled support switches. 4) Mode evidence: a small classifier on geometric features (fingertip-object distances, agreement of relative velocities, mask overlap). It is trained on support labels derived from ground-truth meshes in DexYCB, HO-Cap and ARCTIC. 5) Every output value carries a provenance tag (measured / propagated through support / prior only) and a covariance, and the calibration of that covariance is evaluated. Ablations: no discrete mode, oracle mode, learned mode, lag 0 versus lag 10, rigid versus slip-tolerant support.
research_questions.minimum_experiment: (a) Go/no-go diagnostic, months 1-3. Run per-frame WiLoR + FoundationPose and FoundationPose tracking on HO-Cap and H2O (two-hand RGB-D). Bin frames by occlusion ratio and by time to the nearest support switch, with switches derived from ground-truth hand-object distances. Show whether error concentrates in those bins. If it does not, stop or reframe. (b) Months 3-8: implement the tracker and report world-frame MPJPE per hand, object ADD-S and rotation/translation error, hand-relative object error, mode F1 and switch-time error, FPS and latency on one GPU, and calibration (the fraction of errors inside the reported 2-sigma bound). (c) Baselines: per-frame estimators, a filter without a discrete mode, FoundationPose tracking and BundleSDF, with offline HOLD or BIGS on a subset as a non-causal reference. (d) Small real-world check: 20-40 sequences, 2-3 subjects, an ArUco-cube object, the owned RGB-D camera as input and one borrowed camera used only for ground truth. The set covers within-person hand-to-hand transfers and simple two-person handovers. Fix the success criterion before running: a clear error reduction in the occluded and switch bins, no loss on fully visible frames, at or near 30 fps. This is a target, not a measured number.
research_questions.data_and_hardware: Public RGB-D data with two hands and object pose. HO-Cap: several RGB-D cameras plus a HoloLens, and its abstract lists 'handovers between hands'. Its MANO and object label format and its venue were not checked. H2O, egocentric two-hand RGB-D with object 6D pose (Kwon et al., ICCV 2021): venue and labels from memory, unverified here. DexYCB: single hand, used for regression testing. RGB-only cross-checks: ARCTIC and HOT3D. Software: HaMeR or WiLoR, FoundationPose, SAM 2, GTSAM. Hardware: one 24 GB GPU (RTX 4090 class) is enough for inference and for training the small mode classifier. One consumer RGB-D camera, one borrowed camera for ground truth, a printed ArUco cube, and about 1-2 TB of storage. No motion capture and no robot. Dataset downloads over 1 GB need planning.
research_questions.risks: Gains may sit in a small fraction of frames, so averaged metrics barely move; pre-register the stratification bins so reviewers do not read them as cherry-picking. Semi-automatic labels such as HO-Cap's are least reliable near switches, so the metric is noisiest exactly where the method claims gains. FoundationPose needs an object mesh; the model-free variant is slower and weaker. Slip and in-hand rotation break the rigid-support assumption. Well-resourced groups working on dual-hand egocentric tracking (StableHand, ACE-Ego-Hand) could add object tracking first, and offline video-diffusion priors may stay more accurate. Reviewers may see 'detector plus filter', so the discrete support model and its calibrated provenance must clearly be the contribution.

research_questions.question: Can a two-person handover (giver, receiver, four hands, one object) be reconstructed in one shared metric frame from a single RGB-D view? The approach infers a time-varying ownership graph (giver holds -> both hold -> receiver holds) jointly with the poses and enforces support and contact consistency across the two people. The test is whether this beats running a single-person hand-object reconstructor on each person independently.
research_questions.why_top_venue: Datasets exist, but I found no reconstruction method for this setting. HOH (NeurIPS 2023 Datasets and Benchmarks, verified) has 2,720 handovers, 136 objects and 40 participants, with multi-view RGB and depth, skeletons, fused point clouds, hand and object segmentations, and aligned 3D object models. Other datasets: CORE4D (arXiv 2406.19353), InterVLA (ICCV 2025) and CoMind (ECCV 2026, ego and exo collaborative cooking with handover prediction; no 3D pose labels stated in its abstract). Two arXiv API queries, 'handover AND human-human' (newest 30, to 2026-09-30) and 'human-object-human OR two-person', returned only datasets, generators (HHOI 2511.20446, SynAgent 2604.18557, InterPhys 2605.01036, Sketch2Colab 2603.02190) and robot-side handover work. None estimates 3D hands and object 6DoF for both giver and receiver. The pain-point record (paper 1125) states that single-person HOI findings, even bimanual ones, do not transfer to two-person handovers, which points to a gap in modelling and not only in data. Robotics wants this capability: DUET (arXiv 2606.20990) pretrains dual-robot policies on human-human demonstrations, and human-robot handover is an active ICRA topic. A first method with an evaluation protocol on existing data is a typical CVPR/ECCV contribution if the cross-agent constraint clearly drives the gains. Novelty is supported by keyword queries only.
research_questions.method_sketch: 1) Front ends for each person: a SMPL-X body regressor, WiLoR or HaMeR hands assigned to people through body wrist proximity and tracking, and object 6DoF from FoundationPose with HOH's aligned models. 2) Ownership: a discrete per-frame state over {giver, both, receiver, none} with a mostly monotone left-to-right HMM prior, plus a contact flag for each hand. 3) Joint per-sequence test-time optimization on one GPU, alternating two steps. (a) Viterbi decoding of ownership given the poses. (b) Continuous optimization of all poses with support factors (the object is rigid in the supporting hand or hands), contact attraction, cross-person interpenetration penalties, depth alignment, temporal smoothness, and a no-floating term when the object is unsupported. 4) A causal, prefix-only variant aimed at robot receivers. 5) Ablations that test whether the ownership graph causes the gains: independent per-person reconstruction plus a naive merge, joint optimization without ownership, and oracle ownership.
research_questions.minimum_experiment: Go/no-go first: on HOH, show that independent per-person reconstruction fails inside the transfer window (object pose drift, a floating or doubly penetrated object). Main test: take one RGB-D view of HOH as input and build pseudo-ground-truth from the remaining views (fused point clouds, aligned object models, skeletons). First verify which views and labels HOH actually releases. Start with 200-400 handovers and 2-3 object categories. Metrics: object pose error and hand-surface-to-held-out-point-cloud distance across the transfer window; ownership accuracy and transfer-time error against HOH timing labels, if HOH provides them; interpenetration volume; the number of frames in which the object is unsupported. Supplement with a small own capture: 3-5 pairs, 30-50 handovers, an ArUco-marked object, the owned RGB-D camera plus one borrowed camera for ground truth. This needs ethics approval.
research_questions.data_and_hardware: HOH (NeurIPS 2023 Datasets and Benchmarks; the abstract does not mention MANO or per-frame object 6D labels, so the absence of MANO ground truth is not confirmed). The H2O human-human handover benchmark (Ye et al., arXiv 2104.11466): the abstract mentions hand and object pose annotations; the ICCV 2021 venue is from memory and unverified. CORE4D (body and object, collaborative; hand labels not checked). InterVLA (ICCV 2025, hybrid RGB plus motion capture, ego and exo views). One 24 GB GPU, since per-sequence optimization takes minutes per clip. One consumer RGB-D camera, one borrowed camera and an ArUco object. Ethics approval for two-person capture.
research_questions.risks: Evaluation credibility: there may be no per-hand MANO ground truth for both people, and pseudo-ground-truth built from other views can be challenged. A single view with four hands and two bodies has severe occlusion, and assigning hands to people can fail. Groups that own InterVLA or CORE4D, or larger HOI groups, could publish a method first. Reviewers may call it 'HOLD/BIGS with two people' unless the oracle-versus-learned-ownership ablation shows the graph is the source of the gain. A handover is a short, narrow event, so generality has to be argued: joint carrying, tool passing, bimanual regrasp. Human-subject capture adds logistics and delay.

research_questions.question: Can support consistency serve as a self-supervised test-time adaptation signal for per-frame hand and object estimators on unlabelled bimanual and handover video? The constraints are that the object stays rigid in its supporting hand's frame within each support segment, stays at rest or falls when unsupported, and never penetrates a hand. A second question is how much labelled-data-equivalent accuracy this buys. Pursue it only after the first question shows the support state can be inferred reliably.
research_questions.why_top_venue: The pain-point record names a circular gap: bimanual data are scarce because bimanual tracking is unreliable, and tracking is unreliable because labelled bimanual data are scarce. A label-free signal that breaks this loop is more general than another lab dataset, and a curve showing how many labelled sequences it is worth, measured across ARCTIC, HO-Cap and H2O, would interest CVPR, ICCV and possibly NeurIPS. The novelty case is weaker than for the first two questions, because contact and penetration losses are already common in HOI optimization. The new element has to be the discrete support segmentation used as self-supervision structure for feed-forward models, not another per-sequence optimizer.
research_questions.method_sketch: Teacher-student setup. The teacher is the fixed-lag tracker from the first question; it produces support segments with mode confidence and smoothed poses on unlabelled video. The student is LoRA adapters on HaMeR or WiLoR and on an object pose refiner. Losses: rigidity of the object-in-hand transform within each segment, contact and penetration through the object SDF, multi-frame depth reprojection, and confidence-weighted pseudo-labels. Segments with low mode confidence are dropped. Comparisons: plain temporal-smoothness self-training, and supervised fine-tuning on N labelled ARCTIC sequences, which gives the label-equivalence curve.
research_questions.minimum_experiment: Adapt on unlabelled subsets: HOH clips, a GigaHands subset and the author's own recordings. Evaluate on held-out labelled splits of ARCTIC, HO-Cap and H2O, reporting MPJPE and object error with and without adaptation. Report the label-equivalence curve and a failure analysis of drift caused by wrong support modes, including how often confirmation bias occurs.
research_questions.data_and_hardware: Unlabelled: a GigaHands subset (CVPR 2025), HOH, and an EgoDex subset (ICLR 2026; hand and upper-body pose only, no object pose found) for a hand-only variant. Labelled evaluation: ARCTIC, HO-Cap, H2O. One 24 GB GPU is enough for LoRA on a ViT-H-sized hand model at small batch sizes. Expect several TB of storage for video subsets, so the downloads need planning.
research_questions.risks: Confirmation bias: wrong modes reinforce themselves. Gains may be small next to supervised models trained on large data such as GigaHands. Video I/O and storage are a burden for one workstation. NeurIPS and ICLR reviewers may want broader scope than hand-object tracking. The question depends on the first one succeeding.

fit.thesis_assets_help: The assets give a modest edge, mainly for the first question (online support-state tracking) and the real-world part of the second (handover reconstruction). (1) The causal 30 fps RGB-D chain is already the skeleton of the online tracker in the first question. (2) Object-conditioned recovery of an occluded holding arm is a single-agent, arm-level case of the support factor, where pose is propagated from the visible object to the hidden holder. The first question generalizes it to finger-level MANO hands and to switching between holders. (3) The measured/held/constrained labels are a seed for the per-output provenance and the discrete support state: 'held' is a support mode, and testing whether those labels are calibrated is something reviewers value. (4) The ArUco-marked object with metric pose gives cheap object ground truth for a small real-world handover set, but only while a marker is visible, which is precisely not during occlusion; a second camera is needed for ground truth in the frames that matter. (5) The Unity twin helps with demos and perhaps synthetic switch sequences, not with evaluation. Limits: the recovery is arm-level, not finger-level; the data are 28 recordings of one subject from one camera on a 45 mm marker scale chain. That is not benchmark data, so a top-venue paper must stand on public datasets. Net: the assets save infrastructure time and supply a natural framing, but they give no competitive advantage in results.
fit.what_a_small_lab_cannot_do_here:
A small lab cannot do the following here:
- Build a capture setup at the scale of GigaHands, HOT3D or ARCTIC (dozens of synchronized cameras, motion capture, many subjects and objects), or produce in-the-wild 3D ground truth for several people. Datasets are the main lever the original pain point asks for, and they are out of reach.
- Train video-diffusion or foundation-scale hand and HOI priors of the kind used by ACE-Ego-Hand or built on EgoDex-scale data. At most, it can adapt existing models with LoRA on one GPU.
- Win the averaged ARCTIC or HOT3D leaderboards against large groups' offline optimizers with diffusion priors. The lab should compete on causal and real-time operation, on metrics stratified by occlusion and contact switches, and on multi-agent settings instead.
- Validate bimanual or dual-robot transfer on real hardware at scale, as DUET does with a humanoid and a mobile manipulator. Without a borrowed arm, robot claims stay in simulation.
- Run large human-subject handover studies; only small, ethics-approved captures are realistic.
- Rely on an exhaustive novelty check: this analysis used keyword arXiv API queries after the WebSearch budget ran out, so a concurrent 2026 method for causal bimanual-plus-object tracking or handover reconstruction may have been missed.

Not verified in this session:
- HO-Cap MANO and object labels, and its venue.
- H2O (Kwon et al.) RGB-D labels and venue.
- The venue of the H2O handover benchmark (Ye et al.).
- CORE4D hand labels and venue.
- Whether HOH lacks MANO ground truth.
- DemoBot.

painpoint.name: Reconstructed and generated interactions are not physically consistent

evidence.latest_state: The open question has moved on from whether outputs penetrate or float. In narrow offline settings, putting a simulator inside the reconstruction loop now largely removes the visible artifacts. What remains open is doing this for hands and deformable objects, in real time, under occlusion, and with unobserved mass and friction. On BEHAVE, Real2Sim in HOI (HA-HOI, arXiv 2605.14462) reports human-object penetration of 0.013 cm against 0.084 for CARI4D, plus lower acceleration error (Acc-h 0.52 vs 1.07). Its object Chamfer distance is worse (15.68 vs 11.93 cm), so physical plausibility is still bought with some visual accuracy. For single-image scenes, REST3D (SIGGRAPH Asia 2026) reports a 2.7% collision rate against 23.7% for the best baseline. Its stability rate is 94.9%, against 58.3% for the best baseline (DigitalCousins) and 2.5% for SAM3D, on Replica, ScanNet++ and 25 casual images, with geometry comparable to SAM3D (F-score 0.868). It is limited to rigid objects and relies on a VLM. MessyKitchens' Multi-Object Decoder (MOD), built on SAM 3D, still reaches object IoU of only 0.445 and contact F1 of 66.1. On hand-object datasets, Grasp-and-Lift (arXiv 2601.18121) states that DexYCB and HO3D annotations penetrate, miss contacts or give unstable grasps when replayed in a simulator. It repairs them offline with black-box CMA-ES search through the simulator. RePHO (CVPR 2026) and HSImul3R use a physics-trained RL tracking policy or physics-in-the-loop for body-object and human-scene interaction. For generated video, Physion-Eval (arXiv 2603.19607) finds a human-identifiable physical glitch in 83.3% of exocentric and 93.5% of egocentric generated videos. So world-model physics is clearly still unsolved. All these fixes are offline and per-sequence, and none estimates contact force or object mass from RGB-D. None runs at real-time rates.

evidence.crowdedness: HIGH. At least 14 papers from 2025-2026 attack this from reconstruction, scene lifting, generation and video world models. They come from strong groups, among them Pavlakos (UT Austin), Kitani (CMU), Joo (SNU), Liu (NTU), Gui and Wang (UIUC), Laptev (MBZUAI), Wu and Zou (Stanford) and T.-K. Kim (KAIST). Generic physics-in-the-loop refinement is therefore heavily contested.
evidence.trend: Rising attention. The demand for simulation-ready and Real2Sim assets for humanoid and robot learning, together with SAM 3D-era scene lifting and video world models, produced a cluster of physics-in-the-loop papers from March to September 2026 (REST3D, SimuScene, SAM3D-Phys, PhysOmni, RePHO, HA-HOI, HSImul3R, PhysHanDI). Video-physics benchmarks (Physion-Eval, PhyWorldBench, PhysicsLENS) appeared over the same months.

skeptics.reasons:
Partly refuted. P18 as written ("outputs are not physically consistent") is too broad. Several of its sub-claims were addressed in 2025-2026, but the whole problem is not solved.

(1) Static multi-object scenes from a single image. This is largely engineering now. CAST (SIGGRAPH 2025) adds a physics-aware correction step that enforces support, non-penetration and relation constraints. REST3D (SIGGRAPH Asia 2026) and PhysOmni (ACMMM 2026) refine image-to-3D outputs into simulation-stable scenes without floating or penetration. So the SAM 3D independent-object artifact has a known post-processing fix. Low object IoU (below 0.45) remains a geometry problem, not a physics problem.

(2) Mocap and monocular HOI artifacts. These are now routinely cleaned with simulation in the loop: InterMimic (CVPR 2025) uses teacher policies to refine imperfect mocap; RePHO (CVPR 2026) uses RL in a simulator on noisy kinematic estimates; Grasp-and-Lift (2026) uses CMA-ES to make DexYCB/HO3D trajectories executable; HA-HOI (2026) cuts penetration from 0.084 to 0.013 cm. The "hovering, penetration, floating" symptom therefore has standard remedies.

What these fixes do not solve:
- They are offline and slow (RL or CMA-ES per sequence).
- They assume a known object template and guessed mass and friction.
- They trade accuracy for plausibility. HA-HOI object Chamfer distance is 15.68 cm against a best prior of 11.93 cm, and its stated limits are heavy occlusion and sensing noise.
- They target single rigid objects. Bimanual, deformable and articulated cases are only starting (PhysHanDI 2026).
- No benchmark checks physical validity against measured contact force or ground-truth dynamics. Current metrics are penetration and simulator success, which can be gamed.

(3) Generative video and world models are far from solved. On PhyWorldBench (ICLR 2026 oral), the best model (Pika 2.0) is reported to satisfy both semantics and physics in 26.2% of clips. Many 2026 benchmarks (PhyGround, MechVerse, H2R-Bench, RoboTrustBench, Principia) still report physics and contact failures. That half of P18 survives, but it is far from a small-lab RGB-D tracking thesis.

Net: the generic claim is not refuted. The reconstruction sub-claim, "nobody enforces contact, support or non-penetration", is outdated and should be narrowed.

Verification caveats: the HA-HOI numbers come from its HTML page via a summarising fetch. The 26.2% figure comes from search snippets, not from the abstract itself. The RePHO, REST3D and PhysOmni numbers could not be read; only their abstracts were checked.

skeptics.reframe: The open problem is physical consistency in tracking, not avoiding penetration. Hand-object and bimanual reconstruction still lacks a way to be physically consistent and accurate at the same time, online, under occlusion, while object mass, friction and contact forces are not observed. Simulation-in-the-loop refinement (InterMimic, RePHO, HA-HOI, Grasp-and-Lift) removes penetration and floating, but it is offline, template-bound and limited to single rigid objects. It also costs geometric accuracy: HA-HOI object Chamfer distance is 15.68 cm against 11.93 cm for the best prior. No benchmark scores physical validity against measured contact or force ground truth.

skeptics.reasons:
Artifact test, overall: the evidence is not narrow. The 33 supporting papers come from many unrelated groups (MPI-IS: IPMAN 1251, InterCap 1563, COUCH 1151; Meta: Nymeria/NymeriaPlus 1247, emg2pose 418; ShanghaiTech and others: HOI-M3 37, InterAct 1134, OMOMO 1154, TRUMANS 79). They span venues from CVPR, ECCV, ICCV, SIGGRAPH Asia and NeurIPS to T-RO, IJCV, TPAMI and robot-learning surveys. They also span four settings: body-scene estimation, mocap HOI datasets, single-image multi-object reconstruction, and world-model video generation. Outside the corpus, the same failure is reported by communities with different conventions. Physics-IQ (Motamed et al., Google DeepMind, 2025) and Kang et al. (ICML 2025) find that video generators produce realistic pixels without physical consistency, and that scaling alone does not fix this. InterMimic (CVPR 2025, UIUC) independently names inaccurate contacts in mocap HOI data as a problem. Recent arXiv work keeps coming up in hand-object reconstruction, from groups other than the corpus authors: DynamicHOI (Sep 2026), PhysHanDI (May 2026), CHOIR (May 2026), C2Dex (Sep 2026) and the gravity-field diffusion bridge (2025). These papers attack the same problem, so it is not one dataset's quirk.

Where the artifact critique does hit:
(1) The record merges three clusters with different causes into one umbrella: kinematic penetration, missing gravity and support, and learned world models. Several headline numbers are specific to one paper's setup. The object IoU below 0.45 comes from the authors' own MessyKitchens benchmark (405), which promotes their method. The single-flat-floor limit belongs to IPMAN (1251, 2023). The 84.4 vs 90.7 percent imitation success comes from InterAct's own pipeline (1134). These should not be quoted as field-level facts.
(2) For the geometric half of the claim, non-penetration and contact between hand and object, the hand-object community has had standard fixes since ObMan (CVPR 2019, contact and penetration losses) and ContactOpt (CVPR 2021). Penetration volume and contact ratio are routine benchmark metrics. That part is closer to a known trade-off than an open field problem, and the hand-object papers (the author's core area) are notably absent from the evidence list.
(3) Graphics and physics-based character control (InterMimic, PhysHOI) gives physical consistency by construction, as robot simulation does. This is solved only in simulation, though: it needs known mass, friction and object models, and it gives up tracking fidelity.

Net: the umbrella statement survives as a field-wide, cross-community problem, but its geometric sub-claim is long-addressed and several of its numbers are local to one paper. What genuinely survives is dynamic consistency (support, gravity, contact forces) recovered from real noisy observations when the physical parameters are not observed, together with the lack of any force or physics ground truth to evaluate it.

skeptics.reframe: Geometric plausibility (no interpenetration, contact present) already has standard loss and post-processing fixes. What remains open is dynamic consistency: recovering support, gravity and contact forces for hand and body manipulation from real, noisy, occluded capture when mass, friction and contact state are not observed. No force or physics ground truth exists to evaluate it, so penetration and contact metrics serve only as proxies. Physics simulation enforces consistency only by giving up tracking fidelity, and only when it has known object models and parameters.

skeptics.reasons:
Attempted refutation: P18 could be read as engineering. On that reading, one either plugs a rigid-body simulator into the loop or adds penetration and contact losses, and the remaining gap is better mocap data. The record does not support that reading. It is typed "research", and its why_it_persists entry names an identifiability problem that more data or more resources do not solve. The quantities physics needs (mass, friction, contact state and force) are not observed in RGB or RGB-D. The known fixes fail in specific, documented ways: guidance losses add jitter, contact correction fails on large errors, intuitive-physics terms cover only one flat floor, and simulators are action-specific and fit poorly with diffusion models. The record also notes that the mocap HOI datasets themselves carry the artifacts (InterAct, paper 1134), so collecting more of the same data does not remove the problem. On my own reading, there is no known solution that only awaits resources.

The field is clearly active at top venues in 2026, which argues against "no research question". It also means novelty must be stated precisely, because the field is crowded. arXiv listings retrieved through the API show the following. DynamicHOI (2609.36454) couples hand inverse dynamics and object Newton-Euler wrenches for monocular HOI reconstruction. phi-Scene (2606.21596) settles image-to-3D scenes by support topology plus rigid-body simulation. CHOIR (2605.20992) uses contact as the coupling signal for 4D HOI. Physics-aware Gaussians are used for multi-view 4D HOI capture (2606.15908). "The Invisible Hand of Physics" (2606.05328) probes whether video diffusion models encode physical plausibility. Related papers that state venues in their arXiv comments: MOCHI (SIGGRAPH 2026), HAT-4D (ECCV 2026), AGILE (SIGGRAPH 2026) and MASIV (ICCV 2025). Because of this density, a generic "add physics to HOI reconstruction" paper would read as incremental. The density is also why the score is 7 and not 9.

Research questions a top-venue reviewer would find significant:
(1) Joint identification of unobserved dynamics (mass, friction, contact wrenches) and kinematic correction from monocular or RGB-D HOI. The input kinematics can be grossly wrong under occlusion, and the method must state when the physical parameters are identifiable. Today's physics refiners assume small errors.
(2) Bimanual handling is statically indeterminate: internal squeeze forces between two hands do not show up in object motion. A specific question is how to reconstruct physically consistent and executable bimanual grasps when vision cannot determine force sharing. One option is a learned or optimality prior on load sharing, evaluated against force or tactile ground truth.
(3) Evaluation validity. Penetration and floating metrics are proxies. Whether a reconstruction can be executed in a simulator or replayed on a robot (as in InterAct's 84.4 vs 90.7 percent imitation success, paper 1134) is a different and better criterion. A benchmark with force or tactile ground truth that tests whether proxy metrics predict executability would be a significant contribution.
(4) For generative world models: can physical consistency be enforced or decoded inside diffusion latents without an action-specific simulator?

Residual weakness. Parts of P18 are generic to graphics and generation (foot sliding, floating keyboards) and fall outside the author's tracking setting. The research value lies in the reconstruction side, specifically the bimanual and RGB-D part.

Web search budget was exhausted, so all lookups went through the arXiv API. Venues are taken from the authors' arXiv comment fields and were not checked against proceedings.
