skeptics.reframe: Hand-object and body-object reconstruction from one RGB or RGB-D view has no observable handle on the quantities physical consistency depends on: mass, friction and contact force. Current fixes are proxy losses, which add jitter and fail on large errors, or task-specific simulators, which assume small kinematic error. The open question is how to jointly infer the unobserved dynamics and correct the kinematics, with stated conditions for when those dynamics are identifiable, so that the output can be executed in a simulator or on a robot. This is sharpest in bimanual handling, where the internal force shared between the two hands is statically indeterminate from vision. Success should be measured by executability and agreement with force or tactile ground truth, not only by penetration and floating proxies.

research_questions.question: When two hands hold one rigid object, the squeeze force between them does not change how the object moves, so vision alone cannot determine it. Can this internal force be recovered from one consumer RGB-D view by combining object wrench consistency (Newton-Euler) with a friction safety-margin prior, while each output force component is flagged as either measured or prior-driven? Can it be validated against a measured internal force, run causally at 30 fps, and leave kinematic accuracy no worse than the input?
research_questions.why_top_venue: Every recent physics-plausible interaction method checked treats a single hand, or a body with one object, and validates only against proxies such as penetration, floating or simulator success, never against measured force. The methods checked are RePHO (CVPR 2026, 2606.05359), HA-HOI (2605.14462), Grasp-and-Lift (2601.18121), DynamicHOI (2609.36454, which derives hand forces and object wrenches by inverse dynamics, single hand, offline), CHOIR (2605.20992) and Hu et al., 'Physical Interaction' (SIGGRAPH Asia 2022, 2209.10833, which estimates contact forces in real time from one RGB-D view, for a single hand). An arXiv API search for physics-aware two-hand reconstruction found no paper that resolves the internal-force component for two hands. That search is not exhaustive: the session's web-search budget was used up, so only the arXiv API and abstract pages were checked. Bimanual holding is the case where force from vision is provably underdetermined. A method that states what is identifiable, recovers the rest with a validated prior, and avoids the accuracy loss HA-HOI shows (object Chamfer distance 15.68 vs 11.93 cm) answers the reframe on which all three skeptics converged. It also supplies the grip-force targets that bimanual robot-transfer work lacks: ManipTrans (CVPR 2025) and DexMachina transfer kinematics only.
research_questions.method_sketch: (1) Front end. Hand meshes per frame come from an off-the-shelf monocular hand tracker (a HaMeR or WiLoR-class model, MANO output). The object 6DoF pose comes from a model-based tracker; the object template is known, and that assumption is stated. Contact patches per hand come from hand-object proximity plus a contact classifier, each with a confidence. (2) Net external wrench. Compute w = [m(a - g); I*alpha + omega x I*omega] from a causal fixed-lag SE(3) smoother (lag of 3-5 frames). Mass is given, or taken from the RQ2 posterior. (3) Force distribution. Solve one small second-order cone program per frame. The variables are contact forces at the patch points of both hands, inside friction cones. The net-wrench equality is soft, because acceleration from 30 fps pose is noisy. The objective is a safety-margin prior: each contact's tangential-to-normal ratio is pulled toward mu/SM, with SM fitted on a calibration split, plus temporal smoothness. The key point to demonstrate is that min-norm or min-effort distribution, the robotics default, puts the internal force at the least squeeze the friction cones allow, so it systematically underestimates the squeeze. The prior is what selects the internal-force component. (4) Measurement-gated correction. When no feasible force set reproduces w, adjust contact locations and hand pose, but only for quantities the vision front end marked as unobserved or low-confidence; observed quantities stay fixed. This tests whether the plausibility-for-accuracy trade-off is avoidable. (5) Output. Per-hand contact forces, the internal force, and a flag per component (measured / derived from wrench / prior-driven). A per-frame SOCP of this size solves in milliseconds with an off-the-shelf conic solver, so the causal 30 fps claim is realistic and separates this from offline RL and CMA-ES refiners.
research_questions.minimum_experiment: Build three 3D-printed rigid objects (two boxes of different size and one bar), each split along its mid-plane. The two halves are joined through a single-axis compression load cell that reads the squeeze between the left and right grip plates. Each object has an internal IMU and a ballast cavity. Use two surface coatings per object, with friction coefficient measured by incline test, and two masses. Record 6-8 subjects doing 3 tasks (lift-hold-place, lift-and-rotate, carry) for 3 repetitions each, about 600-900 trials or 2-3 hours of RGB-D. Synchronize the camera and the microcontroller with an LED flash and timestamps. Metrics: internal-force MAE (N) and correlation against the load cell; net-wrench residual against IMU-derived wrench times the known mass; hand MPJPE and object ADD-S against a marker-based reference on the same frames; penetration and MuJoCo replay success, for comparison. Baselines: kinematic-only output; ContactOpt-style contact and penetration refinement; min-norm force QP; a CMA-ES simulator-in-the-loop refiner in the style of Grasp-and-Lift; DynamicHOI's actuation prior if its code is released (unverified). Ablations: no safety-margin prior, oracle vs estimated mass, gating on vs off, causal vs offline. Kinematic-only generalization check on ARCTIC (bimanual, verified) with proxy metrics, to show no loss of accuracy. Go/no-go at month 3: on a pilot with 2 subjects and 1 object, the prior must beat min-norm on internal-force error.
research_questions.data_and_hardware: One consumer RGB-D camera (RealSense D435/D455 class or Orbbec Femto class) and one workstation with a single 24 GB GPU; inference of the pretrained trackers plus a CPU conic solver is enough. Per object: a button or S-type load cell (10-50 kg range), a 24-bit ADC (HX711 or ADS1232), an ESP32 or Arduino, a BNO08x-class IMU, a 3D-printed shell and steel ballast. Calibration needs a kitchen scale for mass, CAD plus a bifilar pendulum for inertia, and an incline for friction. Total hardware is roughly 300-600 USD. Ethics-board approval for 6-10 volunteers is needed; allow 1-2 months. Public data for the kinematic checks: ARCTIC (verified to exist; bimanual, mocap-based, no force). OakInk2, GigaHands, HOT3D and TACO are widely used bimanual sets but were not re-verified in this session. EgoTouch (TouchAnything, 2605.13083) offers bimanual hand pose with pressure maps; its release status and whether it includes object pose are unverified. Replay test in MuJoCo or Isaac. No motion capture and no robot needed.
research_questions.risks: (a) Novelty pressure. DynamicHOI (Guo, Huang, Kong, Sep 2026) already does single-hand inverse dynamics with an actuation prior, and Hu et al. 2022 already does real-time single-hand RGB-D contact forces. A bimanual extension from either group within 12 months is plausible, so the contribution has to rest on the identifiability framing, the measured internal-force ground truth and the gating, not on 'adds physics'. (b) Reviewers may call the core a known grasp-force QP with a biomechanics prior. The vision side (contact under occlusion, gating, causal smoothing) has to carry measurable gains. (c) A split-object load cell measures one internal-force axis, and the grip design constrains how subjects hold the object, which narrows the tasks and draws an 'unnatural object' critique. (d) Acceleration from 30 fps pose is noisy. Any translation-scale error (the thesis chain already needed a 0.9 marker-scale correction) scales the wrench linearly. (e) A few rigid template objects may be judged too narrow for CVPR; RSS, CoRL or RA-L are more receptive. (f) Recent tactile benchmarks (EgoTouch 2605.13083, TactiDex 2607.09190, TouchSight 2609.20414) mean 'first force ground truth' cannot be claimed. The distinctive part is object-level wrench decomposition between the two hands, not pressure maps.

research_questions.question: Is the mass of an object held and moved by a person identifiable from a single RGB-D view, and only through the person's motor behavior since the object trajectory alone does not fix it? Does a calibrated mass posterior make reconstructed bimanual interaction more physically consistent than the default or guessed mass that current physics-in-the-loop refiners assume?
research_questions.why_top_venue: Every physics-in-the-loop interaction refiner reviewed by the skeptics (RePHO, HA-HOI, Grasp-and-Lift, InterMimic) assumes or guesses mass and friction, and the 'rq' skeptic named 'state when physical parameters are identifiable' as the sharp open question. For a hand-held object, mass has an exact scale ambiguity: object kinematics plus contact geometry fit any mass, because all contact forces scale linearly with it. Any identification must therefore come from human-side cues: lift timing, wrist and forearm kinematics, posture. A formal ambiguity statement, together with an empirical test of which cues break it and a calibrated estimator, is a clean question of the kind the field rewards. The closest work found, ViTacPhys (2608.21355), classifies mass and friction from human demonstrations but needs tactile sensing. The arXiv API search found no vision-only method for hand-held objects; this is not exhaustive.
research_questions.method_sketch: (1) Formal part. Write the Newton-Euler and friction-cone system for the held object and show the one-parameter scale family. Friction is identifiable only at slip onsets or through grip adjustments, and object motion alone gives no information on mass. (2) Estimator. Build a small temporal model (GRU or temporal convolution; also a Gaussian-process baseline) over features from the RQ1 front end: object SE(3) trajectory, wrist and forearm kinematics, hand aperture, lift-phase timing. It outputs a posterior over log-mass and is trained leave-one-subject-out. An object-only feature set is the control and should fail if the ambiguity argument holds. (3) Use. Feed the posterior into the RQ1 force program, either by marginalizing or by using its mode with an uncertainty flag. Compare against a default mass (for example 0.5 kg) and the oracle mass on force error and replay success. (4) Human reference. Run a short online observer study in which people rank or estimate weight from the same clips. Psychophysics work on judging lifted weight from kinematics exists (for example Runeson and Frykholm 1981, cited from memory and not verified in this session).
research_questions.minimum_experiment: Make hidden-ballast objects: identical-looking shells in 3 shapes with masses of about 0.2, 0.5, 1.0 and 1.5 kg. Record 8-10 subjects doing lift-and-place and carry, with randomized order and blinding to limit first-lift sensorimotor-memory effects, for about 500-800 trials of RGB-D plus IMU. Metrics: log-mass error, pairwise heavier/lighter accuracy, calibration (NLL and expected calibration error), cross-subject and cross-shape generalization, and the downstream change in the RQ1 internal-force error. Go/no-go pilot by month 2: 2 subjects, 2 masses (0.3 vs 1.2 kg), at least 80 percent pairwise accuracy from human-side features and chance level from object-only features.
research_questions.data_and_hardware: The same single RGB-D desk rig and single GPU (the models are small). 3D-printed shells with ballast cavities, steel weights, a kitchen scale, an optional IMU. Ethics approval for volunteers and for the online observer study. As far as found, no public hand-object dataset varies hidden mass within one object appearance, so this data must be collected. Public bimanual datasets serve only as unlabeled pretraining for the kinematic encoder.
research_questions.risks: (a) The signal may be weak for light household objects below about 0.5 kg, where human kinematics change little. The result could be negative or only coarse (light vs heavy). A rigorous identifiability analysis with a negative empirical result is harder to place at a top venue. (b) Subjects adapt after the first lift, so the cue is strongest on first contact; the protocol must control order. (c) Subject-specific style may dominate, and cross-subject generalization with fewer than 10 subjects may fail. (d) The heaviest masses change body posture, and a desk view may crop the body. (e) Neighbouring work exists: tactile-based property estimation (ViTacPhys) and robot inertial identification with force/torque sensors. Reviewers may ask why not add a cheap sensor, so the answer has to be the passive-capture use case (videos of demonstrations).

research_questions.question: Do the proxy metrics now used to claim physical plausibility actually predict force-level correctness of hand-object reconstructions? The proxies are penetration depth or volume, contact ratio, floating distance and simulator replay success. Can a sensor-free wrench-feasibility score, computable whenever object mass is known, predict force error better than these proxies?
research_questions.why_top_venue: Two skeptics independently noted that no benchmark scores physical validity against measured contact or force, and that penetration and simulator-success metrics can be gamed. Meanwhile the 2025-2026 papers (HA-HOI, RePHO, Grasp-and-Lift, REST3D) report progress on exactly those proxies. A meta-evaluation showing which proxies track force-level truth, and which reward unrealistic solutions, would change how the whole cluster is evaluated, at small cost. Tactile datasets now give pressure ground truth: EgoTouch (2605.13083, bimanual), TactiDex (2607.09190) and TouchSight (2609.20414). None of the abstracts found evaluates object-level wrench consistency or proxy validity.
research_questions.method_sketch: On the RQ1 and RQ2 recordings, run 5-6 reconstruction or refinement methods. Also apply a controlled perturbation grid to good reconstructions: contact dropout, hand-pose noise, object-pose noise, wrong mass, wrong friction, and penetration removal by pushing contacts apart. For every output compute (i) the standard proxies and (ii) the measured errors: internal force against the load cell, and net wrench against IMU times mass. Report Kendall tau and partial correlations between each proxy and each measured error, plus failure cases where a proxy improves while force error worsens. Propose a wrench-feasibility score: the minimal friction-cone-feasible residual of the RQ1 force program, which needs object mass and inertia but no force sensor. Test whether it ranks methods closer to the measured order. Release the data, protocol and scoring code.
research_questions.minimum_experiment: Reuse the RQ1 dataset (no new capture). Use at least 5 methods, about 6 perturbation types at 3 levels each, and all trials. The headline table gives per-proxy rank correlation with measured internal-force and net-wrench error, with bootstrap confidence intervals over subjects. Secondary: apply the wrench-feasibility score to a public bimanual set (ARCTIC, using its published object masses if available, unverified) to show that it can be computed at scale.
research_questions.data_and_hardware: No hardware beyond RQ1. A single GPU to run the baselines. MuJoCo for the replay-success proxy. Ethics approval is shared with RQ1.
research_questions.risks: (a) The dataset is small and narrow (a few rigid objects, desk tasks), which is weak for a NeurIPS Datasets and Benchmarks track. It may end up as a section of the RQ1 paper rather than a standalone paper. (b) If proxies correlate well with force error, the finding is less interesting, though still useful. (c) The new score assumes known mass and inertia, which the target in-the-wild settings lack (this ties to RQ2). (d) Any new metric invites gaming in turn. (e) Tactile benchmarks may become the accepted force ground truth before this lands.

fit.thesis_assets_help: The assets give a modest edge, mostly to RQ1 and RQ3; they give none to the learning side of RQ2. (1) The single RGB-D desk rig with an ArUco-marked object at metric pose is the measurement front end needed to turn a known-mass object's trajectory into a reference net wrench by Newton-Euler. This only holds if the pose is smoothed or an IMU is added: double-differentiated 30 fps marker pose is noisy. Translation-scale errors scale the wrench linearly, and the chain's 0.9 marker-size correction must be re-validated before force numbers are trusted. (2) The measured/held/constrained honesty labels are the most distinctive asset. They map directly onto the per-component identifiability flags (measured / derived from wrench / prior-driven) and onto measurement-gated correction in RQ1, which is the proposed answer to the accuracy-for-plausibility trade-off. (3) The causal 30 fps chain gives an online baseline and the scaffolding for the causal claim. (4) Object-conditioned recovery of an occluded holding arm helps place contacts for a hidden hand under occlusion in RQ1. (5) The Unity twin is useful for visualization and demos only; replay or executability tests should use MuJoCo or Isaac. (6) The 28 single-subject recordings have no force, mass or friction variation, so they serve only as a pipeline pilot, not as evidence. Net effect: perhaps 2-3 months saved on rig, synchronization and pose-pipeline work, nothing more.
fit.what_a_small_lab_cannot_do_here: A small lab cannot compete on generic physics-in-the-loop refinement at scale. Strong groups are working on this now (Pavlakos, Kitani, Joo, Gui and Wang, Kim, and others): RL tracking policies trained over thousands of sequences (RePHO, InterMimic, InterPrior-style), large simulation sweeps, and humanoid controllers. It cannot capture large bimanual datasets that need multi-view domes or optical motion capture (ARCTIC or GigaHands scale), or build whole-hand tactile and pressure-glove corpora at the scale of EgoTouch or TouchSight (the latter reports 500 hours of glove recordings). It cannot train or fine-tune video world models or physics-aware video generators, which is the Physion-Eval and PhyWorldBench half of P18. The single-image scene-stability strand (REST3D, SimuScene, CAST, PhysOmni) is SAM 3D- and VLM-heavy and crowded. Without a borrowed bimanual dexterous platform, executability cannot be validated on real robot hands; it can only be validated in simulation. Measured ground truth for deformable or articulated objects (the PhysHanDI direction) is out of reach within 12-18 months. Measured force ground truth is limited to cheap single-axis load cells and IMUs, so only object-level wrench and one internal-force axis can be measured, not dense contact pressure. Even modest human-subject studies require ethics approval, and the 1-2 months this takes must be budgeted. Verification note: this session's web-search budget was exhausted before this task. Novelty checks used the arXiv API and abstract pages only, so 'not found' means not found in those searches, not proven absent.

painpoint.name: Scaled in-the-wild data rests on unverified pseudo-labels and filtering

evidence.latest_state: The strongest 2026 response is to build portable ground-truth references that go out into the wild, instead of trusting monocular pseudo-labels. SHOW3D (CVPR 2026) uses a back-mounted 8-camera rig plus a Quest 3 headset. Its hand labels were checked two ways: against a 30-camera dome, median/P90 MPJPE is 6.28/7.31 mm without objects and 7.90/12.53 mm with hand-object interaction; against manual in-the-wild annotation, it is 5.65/12.35 mm and 6.36/16.48 mm. Its objects have sub-centimetre P50 translation error against MoCap. Even SHOW3D still keeps only 1.9M of 4.3M frames after confidence filtering, and it reports misses under heavy object or other-hand occlusion. ESTHER (arXiv, Sep 2026) first validates its stereo pseudo-label teacher against Vicon: 15.9 mm P-MPJPE, 9.3 mm PA-MPJPE and 19.1 mm wrist error. It then pairs an in-the-wild pseudo-labelled training set with a roughly 10-hour mocap test set (ESTHER3D: 17.7 mm P-MPJPE versus 19.4 mm for POEM-v2). Its authors say depth error of about 21 mm, not image alignment, limits the labels. The scaling side (MINT's 1,021-hour EgoPipeline pseudo-labels, InfiniHand's roughly 5,000-hour corpus, HumanNet's 1M hours, EgoInfinity, IronMind's 10,000-hour VLA pretraining) still trains on unverified estimator outputs. These works report only downstream benchmarks (MINT: 13.6 mm PA-MPJPE on HOT3D) or policy success, never the error of the released labels. JALA (CVPR 2026) and IronMind explicitly sidestep unreliable hand labels with latent or camera-space actions rather than measuring them. None of them provides a per-label confidence protocol, or a measurement of what filtering removes and how that affects downstream learning.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: SHOW3D: Capturing Scenes of 3D Hands and Objects in the Wild
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Mobile ego-exo multi-camera rig that labels 3D hands and objects in the wild, including outdoors. Labels are validated against a 30-camera dome, manual annotation and MoCap (6-8 mm median MPJPE); 1.9M of 4.3M frames survive filtering.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: Ego-Exo 3D Hand Tracking in the Wild with a Mobile Multi-Camera Rig
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Precursor to SHOW3D: a back-mounted 8-camera rig plus Quest 3 ego-exo pipeline that produces in-the-wild hand ground truth, with a rigorous quality evaluation.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: ESTHER: Egocentric Stereo Hand Estimation and Reconstruction in the Wild
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Calibrated stereo pseudo-label teacher checked against Vicon (15.9 mm P-MPJPE) before scaling. Releases the ESTHER3D benchmark: an in-the-wild pseudo-labelled training set plus a roughly 10 h mocap test set.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: MINT: A Unified Model for World-Space Camera and Hand Motion Estimation from Scalable Egocentric Pipeline Supervision
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Open-source EgoPipeline produces 1,021 h of pseudo-labelled camera and hand trajectories. The model pretrains on these labels, fine-tunes on a small high-quality set and predicts per-frame hand observability; it reaches 13.6 mm PA-MPJPE on HOT3D zero-shot.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: InfiniHand: Streaming World-Space Hand Motion Estimation from Egocentric Video
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Streaming feed-forward world-space hand and camera estimator pretrained on about 5,000 h of aggregated egocentric data. Reports 21.4% lower ARCTIC PA error than ViDiHand.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: Joint-Aligned Latent Action: Towards Scalable VLA Pretraining in the Wild (JALA)
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Names unreliable in-the-wild hand-tracking labels as the problem and avoids them with latent actions aligned to inverse dynamics and real actions, trained on the 7.5M-video UniHand-Mix corpus.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: IronMind: Scaling Humanoid Dexterous Manipulation via Camera-Space Ego-Centric Pretraining
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Treats noisy hand-pose tracking as a data-quality challenge and scales VLA pretraining to 10,000 h. Policy success reaches 55.0% versus 5.0% without pretraining; no label-error measurement.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: Do as I Do: Dexterous Manipulation Data from Everyday Human Videos
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Reconstructs and retargets monocular in-the-wild hand-object video to dexterous robot hands. Evaluates on datasets with ground truth and gives an efficacy playbook for human-data collection.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: EgoInfinity: A Web-Scale 4D Hand-Object Interaction Data Engine for Any-View Robot Retargeting and Video-to-Action Robot Learning
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Modular web-scale video-to-4D hand-object engine with no human in the loop. Uses cross-module metric calibration and interaction-aware refinement to reduce drift and contact inconsistency.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: HumanNet: Scaling Human-centric Video Learning to One Million Hours
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: One-million-hour human-centric video corpus that treats curation and filtering as a first-class design principle, with automatic hand and body signals; validated only through VLA ablations.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: Reconstructing Objects along Hand Interaction Timelines in Egocentric Video (ROHIT)
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Evaluates hand-held object reconstruction on 2.4K EPIC-Kitchens clips without 3D ground truth, using 2D projection error as a proxy. Illustrates the evaluation gap.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: RoboWheel: A Data Engine from Real-World Human Demonstrations for Cross-Embodiment Robotic Learning
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Monocular or RGB-D hand-object reconstruction refined by an RL physics optimizer, then retargeted. Label quality is judged by trajectory stability compared with teleoperation.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: Egocentric Whole-Body Human Mesh Recovery with Prior-Guided Learning
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Shows that optimization-based egocentric SMPL-X pseudo-GT is substantially more accurate than regression-based pseudo-GT; body-side evidence that pseudo-GT quality varies and matters.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: NymeriaPlus: Enriching Nymeria Dataset with Additional Annotations and Data
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: In-the-wild egocentric dataset with mocap-suit body ground truth upgraded to MHR and SMPL. This is the wearable-mocap route to measured ground truth outside the lab, for bodies but not fine hand-object contact.

evidence.crowdedness: MEDIUM. More than ten 2025-2026 works produce scaled pseudo-labels (Meta Reality Labs ego-exo, PKU HumanNet, Rice EgoInfinity, industry VLA groups), but only two or three (SHOW3D, ESTHER, partly MINT) measure label error against a reference. None studies label-confidence reporting or filtering bias as its main question.
evidence.trend: rising: the race toward VLAs pretrained on human video (1,000 to 1,000,000-hour corpora in 2026) keeps adding unverified pseudo-labelled data. Portable ground-truth rigs (SHOW3D, ESTHER3D) and mocap-validated teachers appeared only in 2026, which shows that label verification is starting to be recognised as a gap.

skeptics.reasons: Not refuted. No 2025-2026 work found that measures label accuracy on the released scaled data itself (internet video, headset-tracker or HaMeR/HaWoR labels), or that removes the bias from filtering out occluded, blurred and truncated frames. The pain point has been narrowed, though. The claim "no reference exists where the data is collected" is weakening for hands. Rim et al. (arXiv 2510.02601, Oct 2025) built a back-worn rig with eight exo cameras plus Quest 3 ego cameras that gives multi-view 3D hand ground truth outdoors and in the wild. The follow-up SHOW3D (arXiv 2603.28760, CVPR 2026) extends this to hands and objects in diverse real environments, and it says outright that it reduces the trade-off between realism and annotation accuracy. ESTHER (arXiv 2609.34817, Sep 2026) pairs a large in-the-wild stereo training set of model-generated labels with a mocap test set of metric ground truth. That is the "validate a subset" pattern the pain point already lists as an attempted fix, so it does not verify the released training labels. These works give portable, calibrated multi-view references outside the lab. But (a) their labels are still pipeline outputs from multi-view fitting, not independent measurement. (b) They cover only capture-rig data, not the internet or Vision Pro/Aria-scale corpora (EgoDex, HD-EPIC, Ego4D robotization) that drive scaling. (c) None reports error stratified by occlusion, or the downstream cost of the frames that confidence filtering discards. Do as I Do (arXiv 2606.19333, Jun 2026) reconstructs dexterous trajectories from online video and evaluates only on datasets that have ground truth, which supports persistence. No benchmark here is saturated. Downstream gaps such as AssemblyHands verb accuracy (54.7 from predicted vs 60.0 from annotated poses) and the 6.9-17.3 percent frame yields have not been shown closed. Limits of this check: the shared WebSearch budget was exhausted (0 searches run), so evidence comes from arXiv API listing queries and abstract fetches only. One API query hit HTTP 429. Glove-based in-the-wild capture (for example DexCap- or DexWild-style systems) could not be checked and may narrow the claim further.

evidence.title: Ego-Exo 3D Hand Tracking in the Wild with a Mobile Multi-Camera Rig (Rim et al.)
SHOW3D: Capturing Scenes of 3D Hands and Objects in the Wild (Rim et al.)
ESTHER: Egocentric Stereo Hand Estimation and Reconstruction in the Wild
Do as I Do: Dexterous Manipulation Data from Everyday Human Videos
Reconstructing Objects along Hand Interaction Timelines in Egocentric Video (evaluates EPIC-Kitchens with 2D projection error only, no 3D ground truth)

skeptics.reframe: Portable multi-view rigs now give 3D hand and object reference labels outside the lab (Rim et al. 2025, SHOW3D at CVPR 2026), but only for rig-captured data. The internet and headset-tracker corpora that actually scale still have no estimate of their label error, broken down by occlusion and motion. Nobody measures how much confidence filtering skews them toward easy frames, or what that bias and noise cost a pose estimator or robot policy trained on them. The open problem is narrower than "no ground truth in the wild". Use small portable-rig reference sets to calibrate and predict pseudo-label error on large unlabelled corpora, and keep the hard occluded frames in those corpora with calibrated confidence instead of discarding them.

skeptics.reasons:
The artifact attack mostly fails on breadth and partly succeeds on depth. Breadth: the 32 supporting papers are not one dataset or one community. They span at least three communities and many independent groups. Egocentric HOI and hand data: EgoDex (Apple, Vision Pro ARKit labels), AssemblyHands and Assembly101 (Meta and academic partners, tracker labels), HD-EPIC (Bristol, Aria MPS), EPFL-Smart-Kitchen, IndEgo, Hoi!, PianoMotion10M (MediaPipe plus HaMeR). Robot learning from human video: WIYH, HuRo, HumanNet, Open-AoE, EgoLive, EgoVerse, OpenEgo, Human Universal Grasping, Humanoid Policy ~ Human Policy, plus three independent surveys (Robot Learning from Human Videos, Data Pyramid, VLA datasets). Avatars and bodies: MVHumanNet/MVHumanNet++, Codec Avatar Studio, RenderMe-360, SmartPortraits. The label sources also vary: headset SDKs, monocular foundation models, and multi-view RGB fits. So this is not the convention of one lab or one sensor.

On the other side, the artifact critique holds in four places.
(1) Much of the support is boilerplate. Dataset papers routinely write "annotations may be imperfect under occlusion" in their limitations, and counting those as 32 independent confirmations inflates the evidence.
(2) The quantitative harm rests on single papers. One paper (WIYH*) shows that unverified labels give little pretraining gain. One paper (HuRo) gives the 6.9/17.3 percent retention figures. One 2023 benchmark (AssemblyHands) shows verb accuracy falling from 60.0 to 54.7 percent with predicted poses. One paper (1129) reports an 85 percent higher error for the original Assembly101 labels. None of these has been replicated across settings.
(3) The record merges three different problems into one pain point: noisy hand labels, missing measured geometry for avatars, and survivorship bias from filtering. The avatar-geometry part, with Sapiens normals and no depth sensor, is a separate issue from hand-object tracking.
(4) The body-pose community has treated pseudo-GT unreliability as a known problem for years. SMPLify-X pseudo-GT curation, EFT/NeuralAnnot-style pseudo-GT, and the shift to synthetic data such as BEDLAM all respond to it. This counts against novelty, not against existence: the problem is recognised and unsolved, not solved.

Partial counter-evidence on verification: mocap-grounded egocentric references do exist. For example, HOT3D (verified) uses optical-marker mocap with Aria and Quest 3. They are lab-bound, which confirms the stated mechanism: references exist only where the in-the-wild data is not collected.

Net: this is a real field-level problem, not a local artifact. But the claims of measured downstream harm and of filtering bias are narrow and should be presented as under-measured rather than established. For the thesis author, the defensible version is the absence of any protocol for measuring and propagating pseudo-label error, not a proven large harm.

evidence.title: EgoDex: Learning Dexterous Manipulation from Large-Scale Egocentric Video
HOT3D: Hand and Object Tracking in 3D from Egocentric Multi-View Videos
World In Your Hands: A Large-Scale and Open-Source Ecosystem for Learning Human-Centric Manipulation in the Wild (paper 1376, single source for the WIYH* little-gain result)
HuRo: Robotizing Human Videos for Scalable VLA Pretraining (paper 1381, single source for the 6.9/17.3 percent retention)
AssemblyHands: Towards Egocentric Activity Understanding via 3D Hand Pose Estimation (paper 1122, downstream verb accuracy 60.0 vs 54.7)
Efficient Annotation and Learning for 3D Hand Pose Estimation: A Survey (paper 1129)
MVHumanNet++ (paper 1435) and SmartPortraits (paper 1442): avatar/body geometry pseudo-GT, a different community from hand-object
Expressive Body Capture: 3D Hands, Face, and Body from a Single Image (SMPL-X; evaluation on curated pseudo-GT, an early sign that the body community already recognised pseudo-GT)

skeptics.reframe: In-the-wild hand-object datasets at scale have no protocol for estimating per-frame label error on the data they release, or for tracing how that error and confidence-based filtering (which drops occluded and fast frames) carry into downstream tracking and policy learning. Mocap-grade references exist only in the lab (HOT3D, AssemblyHands), so error is never measured where the data is collected. Evidence that this causes large downstream harm is still limited to single papers.

skeptics.reasons:
Skeptic case, which partly holds: as P19 is written, much of it asks for more data or more equipment. The obvious fix is to put mocap rooms, calibration rooms or multi-view domes where in-the-wild data is collected, or to pay for multi-view re-annotation of subsets (Assembly101 to AssemblyHands; EgoLive calibration room). Those fixes are known and mostly wait on resources. "Report label confidence" is a protocol or engineering wish, not a research question. Learning from noisy labels and uncertainty-aware pose estimation are also established areas. The study's own corpus has ProbPose (CVPR 2025), UPose3D (ECCV 2024), Weakly-Supervised 3D Hand Reconstruction with Uncertainty Guidance (ECCV 2024) and TokenHMR (CVPR 2024), whose loss tolerates biased pseudo-ground truth. So "pseudo-labels are noisy, so model the noise" is not new on its own.

Why I do not refute it: at least three questions survive that a CVPR, ICCV, NeurIPS or CoRL reviewer would find significant. Each is specific to scaled hand-object data and none is solved by money alone.

(1) Reference-free error estimation and certification of 3D hand and object pseudo-labels on the released in-the-wild data. Can label error be predicted with calibrated bounds where no mocap exists, using geometric self-consistency, physics or contact plausibility, cross-estimator disagreement, or sparse cheap sensing such as depth? Can those bounds then be validated on held-out multi-view or mocap subsets? The pain point records that nobody measures accuracy on the released data. SmartPortraits shows that a pseudo-GT error bound decides which methods can even be ranked.

(2) Selection bias from confidence filtering. Filtering keeps only 6.9 to 17.3 percent of Ego4D and EPIC frames (HuRo), and the frames it keeps are not a random sample: the hard frames are removed systematically. The question is whether this biases the estimators and policies trained on the data toward easy views, and whether uncertainty-weighted training, importance reweighting or label repair can recover the occluded and fast frames without poisoning training. This is a distribution-shift problem with measurable downstream effects: AssemblyHands verb accuracy is 54.7 percent from predicted poses versus 60.0 percent from annotated poses, and there is the WIYH* finding below.

(3) Data-scaling behaviour under label noise. WIYH reports that its unverified variant gives little gain over no pretraining. That makes the open question how label quality trades off against scale for manipulation pretraining. A further risk: when the student and the labeller share a model family (HaMeR or HaWoR labels used to train HaMeR-like models or VLAs), errors may be correlated and confirmation bias may set in, which would cap what scaling can achieve.

There is also top-venue precedent for treating pseudo-GT quality itself as a contribution: BioTUCH (ICCV 2025) refines pose pseudo-ground truth with bioimpedance contact sensing; the biomechanical-skeleton HMR paper (CVPR 2025) uses iteratively refined pseudo-labels; XR-Poser (CVPR 2026) uses auto-labelling at scale. The topic is therefore publishable, but only when framed as estimation or learning, not as building a dataset. Score capped at 6: the space is crowded with noisy-label and uncertainty work, and a weak submission would read as engineering.

skeptics.reframe: Scaled hand-object data is labelled by monocular estimators whose error on the released in-the-wild frames cannot be measured. The filtering step also removes the frames where those estimators fail, and these are not a random sample. The research question: can per-frame 3D hand and object label error be estimated, with calibrated and certifiable bounds, without a mocap reference? Bounds would be built from geometric, physical and contact self-consistency or sparse depth, and validated on held-out multi-view subsets. A second question is whether training on uncertainty-weighted labels that keep the hard frames does better than confidence filtering, measured on downstream pose estimators and manipulation policies.

research_questions.question: RQ1. Can the per-frame error of 3D hand (and known-model object) pseudo-labels be predicted, with calibrated and validated bounds, on in-the-wild frames that have no reference? Specifically: does an error estimator calibrated on lab mocap data keep its coverage on portable-rig in-the-wild ground truth (SHOW3D), and what does it say about the error of labels in released scaled corpora?
research_questions.why_top_venue: Every 2026 scaling effort trains on estimator outputs whose error on the released frames has never been reported. Examples are EgoDex ARKit labels, MINT's 1,021 h EgoPipeline, InfiniHand's roughly 5,000 h corpus, HumanNet's 1M h and IronMind's 10,000 h. These works report only downstream benchmarks or policy success (P19 evidence). The test of whether lab-calibrated error estimates transfer to the wild became possible only in 2026: SHOW3D (CVPR 2026, arXiv 2603.28760) is now public on HuggingFace (facebook/show3d-dataset, CC-BY-NC-4.0, checked 2026-10-02), with in-the-wild multi-view hand and 6DoF object references validated to 6-8 mm median. There is top-venue precedent for calibrated pose uncertainty: CUPS (arXiv 2412.10431, conformal uncertainty for human pose-shape, venue unverified) and CHAMP (arXiv 2407.06141, venue unverified). There is also precedent for treating pseudo-GT quality as a contribution (BioTUCH, ICCV 2025). arXiv listing queries found no paper that predicts per-frame 3D hand pseudo-label error without ground truth. The closest is keypoint self-consistency failure detection for 6D object pose (arXiv 2608.03516, Aug 2026). The contribution would be the first quantitative, validated quality statement about scaled hand data, plus a reusable label-confidence protocol, which is exactly the missing piece P19 names.
research_questions.method_sketch: (1) Teachers. Run 3-4 off-the-shelf hand estimators (HaMeR, WiLoR, HaWoR, Hamba) and, for objects with CAD models, FoundationPose on calibration sets and test sets. (2) Reference-free features per hand and frame. a) Cross-estimator disagreement in root-relative and camera space. b) Test-time-augmentation variance. c) Reprojection residual against an independent 2D hand-keypoint detector, and mask IoU against SAM 2 masks. d) Temporal residual against a smoothed trajectory (acceleration and jitter). e) Hand-object penetration and contact plausibility when the object model is known. f) Visibility cues: truncation, occlusion fraction from segmentation, blur. g) A depth or stereo residual where depth exists. (3) Learn a per-joint error regressor (gradient-boosted trees or a small MLP) that predicts MPJPE or a failure probability. (4) Calibrate with split conformal prediction. Use Mondrian (occlusion-binned) conformal for conditional coverage, and weighted conformal under covariate shift (Tibshirani et al., NeurIPS 2019) for the lab-to-wild shift. Model the reference's own noise floor explicitly. (5) Evaluation protocol: calibrate on lab mocap (HOT3D, ARCTIC, DexYCB), then test coverage and interval width on SHOW3D in-the-wild frames and on ESTHER3D's mocap test set if it is released. Compare against the confidence scores current pipelines filter on. (6) Audit: apply the calibrated estimator to released corpora (EgoDex, HD-EPIC, HOI4D, and HaMeR-labelled Ego4D/EPIC subsets). Report predicted error distributions stratified by occlusion, motion and grasp type, and validate the audit on any subset that has a reference.
research_questions.minimum_experiment: Three estimators (HaMeR, WiLoR, HaWoR) on HOT3D (calibration) and a subsample of about 100-200k SHOW3D frames (test), using features a, c, d and f only. Report: Spearman correlation of predicted versus true per-hand MPJPE; AUROC for detecting failures above 20 mm (chosen above SHOW3D's P90 reference error of 12-16 mm); and empirical coverage and width of 90 percent conformal intervals, overall and per occlusion bin. Compare naive lab-calibrated CP, Mondrian CP and weighted CP, against a baseline of thresholding the estimator's own detection or confidence score. Go/no-go gate at month 2: failure AUROC of at least 0.8 on SHOW3D, and a clear coverage gap that shift correction closes. If the gate fails, the result becomes the negative finding in RQ2's motivation, not a standalone paper.
research_questions.data_and_hardware: Public only. Calibration: HOT3D (Aria and Quest 3 with mocap), ARCTIC (bimanual, mocap), DexYCB and HO3D v3 (RGB-D), AssemblyHands. In-the-wild test: SHOW3D (public on HuggingFace, CC-BY-NC; total download size not verified, so plan for multi-TB and subsample); ESTHER3D (arXiv 2609.34817; release status unverified). Audit targets: EgoDex, HD-EPIC, HOI4D, Ego4D/EPIC clips. Models: HaMeR, WiLoR, HaWoR, Hamba, an RTMPose or MediaPipe hand 2D detector, SAM 2, FoundationPose. Hardware: one 24-48 GB GPU. Inference over about 0.5-1M subsampled frames per teacher takes days, not weeks. 5-10 TB storage. No capture rig, mocap or robot needed. MINT's EgoPipeline is reported open-source, but its code availability was not verified.
research_questions.risks: (1) Reference noise floor. SHOW3D labels are themselves multi-view fits (6-8 mm median, up to about 16 mm P90), so bounds tighter than about 15 mm cannot be validated. Certify failures at coarser thresholds, or use a noisy-reference conformal formulation. (2) Survivorship bias in the reference. SHOW3D released only the 1.9M of 4.3M frames that passed its own confidence filter, so the hardest occlusions are under-represented in the in-the-wild test. Hard-case calibration must lean on HOT3D and ARCTIC, and this caveat must be stated. (3) Correlated teacher errors. HaMeR, WiLoR, HaWoR and Hamba share training data and ViT backbones, so ensemble disagreement can collapse exactly on hard frames. Mitigate with signals that do not depend on the teachers (2D detector, masks, physics, depth). (4) Weighted conformal needs density-ratio estimates in a high-dimensional feature space, so guarantees may be loose under strong shift. (5) Novelty perception: reviewers may read this as 'conformal prediction applied to hands'. The audit of real corpora and the downstream use in RQ2 are what clear the bar. (6) Competition: the SHOW3D (Meta) and ESTHER groups own the references and could publish a similar analysis. Speed matters, so target the next CVPR or NeurIPS cycle. (7) The audit of unlabelled corpora is a prediction, not a measurement, and must be worded that way.

research_questions.question: RQ2. Does confidence-based filtering of hand(-object) pseudo-labels bias the trained models toward easy views? Can keeping the hard frames with calibrated per-frame uncertainty weights, or repairing them, beat filtering on occluded and fast-motion test cases? Is there an error ceiling when student and teacher come from the same model family?
research_questions.why_top_venue: Video-to-robot pipelines keep only 6.9-17.3 percent of EPIC-Kitchens and Ego4D frames (HuRo, arXiv 2609.10706). SHOW3D keeps 1.9M of 4.3M frames. HumanScale (arXiv 2606.20521) credits a 'carefully designed filtering and labeling pipeline' without measuring label error. Yet no work measures what filtering removes or what that costs downstream: all three skeptics say this is under-measured, and the harm evidence rests on single papers (WIYH* little gain, AssemblyHands 54.7 vs 60.0 verb accuracy). A controlled study with ground-truth references answers a design question that every data engine faces. A positive result (uncertainty weighting recovers hard-bin accuracy) would be a method contribution, and a characterized trade-off curve between retention and hard-bin error would be a benchmark contribution. Both fit NeurIPS Datasets and Benchmarks or CVPR, and CoRL if the downstream proxy is a policy.
research_questions.method_sketch: (1) Build controlled pseudo-labelled training corpora from datasets that do have references: the SHOW3D train split, HOT3D, ARCTIC and AssemblyHands. Replace the GT labels with teacher outputs (WiLoR or HaMeR). (2) Label policies: A, keep all pseudo-labels; B, confidence-threshold filtering at retention 10, 25 and 50 percent (matching the published 6.9-17.3 percent); C, keep all with heteroscedastic or inverse-variance weights from the RQ1 error estimator; D, label repair for flagged frames (temporal smoothing and multi-teacher fusion, plus object-conditioned constraints when the object pose is known); E, oracle GT labels as the upper bound. (3) Train an identical student (HaMeR-style with a ViT-S or ViT-B backbone) under each policy, with 3 seeds. (4) Evaluate on held-out GT (SHOW3D test, HOT3D test, ESTHER3D test if released), stratified by occlusion fraction (rendered from the GT meshes), truncation, motion speed and grasp type. Also measure the distribution shift that filtering itself causes: viewpoint, pose, occlusion and object-category histograms of kept versus removed frames. (5) Teacher-student coupling: compare a student from the same family as the teacher with one from a different family, and measure how much the student's errors correlate with the teacher's. (6) Downstream proxies. a) Pose-based action recognition on AssemblyHands (the 54.7 vs 60.0 setting). b) Physics replay or a small behaviour-cloning policy in simulation (IsaacGym or MuJoCo) on hand-object trajectories retargeted from ARCTIC or OakInk2 sequences, labelled under each policy.
research_questions.minimum_experiment: One teacher (WiLoR) and one student (ViT-S, about 1M crops) on one reference dataset (HOT3D, or the SHOW3D train/test split). Policies A, B (three retention levels), C and E, with 3 seeds each, so about 18 runs at about 1-2 days each on one GPU. Primary metric: MPJPE and PA-MPJPE in the top occlusion tercile, versus the bottom tercile. Success criterion: B is significantly worse than A or C on the hard tercile and not better on the easy one, with non-overlapping seed confidence intervals; or else a clear retention-versus-hard-error trade-off curve. Add the AssemblyHands action-recognition proxy only once this effect is shown.
research_questions.data_and_hardware: Public datasets as in RQ1 (HOT3D, ARCTIC, SHOW3D, AssemblyHands, OakInk2 for sim trajectories). One 24-48 GB GPU. Budget about 1-2 GPU-months for 20-40 student runs at reduced scale (ViT-S/B, about 1M crops). IsaacGym or MuJoCo for the simulated downstream proxy. No robot needed; a borrowed arm would only add an optional real-robot sanity check.
research_questions.risks: (1) Null result. If filtering costs little at this scale, the paper weakens. Report it as a characterized trade-off curve, and pre-register the hard-tercile metric to avoid fishing. (2) Scale transfer. Reviewers will ask whether 1M-crop ViT-S results hold at the 1,000-hour, ViT-H scale. A small lab cannot answer this directly, so show trends across 2-3 data and model sizes. (3) Confounds: filtering changes both noise and dataset size. Include a random-subsampling control at matched retention. (4) Robotics reviewers may dismiss the sim downstream proxy as not policy-relevant, which caps CoRL chances without a real robot. (5) Hard-frame definitions need GT occlusion masks, which exist only where meshes are given. (6) Depends on RQ1's error estimator for policy C. Use a simpler disagreement weight first, so the RQ2 timeline does not depend on RQ1.

research_questions.question: RQ3 (optional, lower tier). How much does one consumer RGB-D view tighten the certified error of monocular hand-object pseudo-labels, separately for visible and occluded joints? Does a per-frame provenance label (measured by sensor / inferred from object or kinematic constraint / held from the past / estimator-only) predict label error better than estimator confidence?
research_questions.why_top_venue: Consumer RGB-D is the cheapest independent sensor a capture pipeline can add, and the pain point says no per-label confidence protocol exists. ESTHER (arXiv 2609.34817) reports that depth error of about 21 mm, not image alignment, limits its stereo labels, so whether metric depth certifies or merely shifts the error is an open question. On its own this is more likely an ICRA or RA-L contribution than a CVPR one. It strengthens RQ1 as one feature family plus a provenance taxonomy, and gives robot-demonstration capture a cheap verification recipe.
research_questions.method_sketch: On public RGB-D datasets with GT (DexYCB, HO3D v3, HOI4D, H2O), compute the depth residual between rendered pseudo-label meshes and the sensor depth on the visible hand and object surface. Separate joints into visible, self-occluded and object-occluded. Fit the RQ1 error estimator with and without depth features, and with and without provenance labels assigned by rule (sensor-supported, constraint-inferred, temporally held, prior-only). Measure the change in coverage and interval width per visibility class. Add a small real pilot with one consumer RGB-D camera and an ArUco-marked object, which gives an independent metric object-pose reference.
research_questions.minimum_experiment: DexYCB and HO3D v3 with two teachers (HaMeR, WiLoR). Compare the error estimator with no depth, with a depth residual, and with depth plus provenance labels. Report failure AUROC and conformal interval width separately for visible and occluded joints. The expected and reportable outcome is that depth tightens bounds on visible joints but not on occluded ones, and that provenance labels capture part of the occluded-joint error.
research_questions.data_and_hardware: DexYCB, HO3D v3, HOI4D, H2O (public RGB-D with hand GT). One consumer RGB-D camera, already owned, for a pilot. One GPU. No other hardware.
research_questions.risks: Limited novelty as a standalone paper. Consumer depth is noisy on thin fingers (flying pixels, holes), so the depth residual may itself be unreliable within about 1 m. Depth carries no information about occluded joints, which is where the labels fail. A single-subject pilot cannot support generalization claims. Best published as an ICRA or RA-L paper, or folded into RQ1.

fit.thesis_assets_help: Small edge, mostly conceptual, and limited to RQ3 plus parts of RQ2. (1) The measured/held/constrained honesty labels are already a working per-frame provenance protocol. This is exactly the 'per-label confidence protocol' P19 says is missing, so the thesis gives a ready taxonomy and the practical experience to generalize it (the RQ3 provenance-label ablation and the RQ1 feature design). (2) The ArUco-marked object with metric pose is a cheap independent reference for object labels on the author's own RGB-D recordings, useful for a pilot check of FoundationPose-style object pseudo-labels and of depth residuals. (3) Object-conditioned recovery of an occluded holding arm maps directly onto the 'label repair' policy D in RQ2: constraint-based recovery of occluded frames instead of discarding them. (4) The causal 30 fps chain and the Unity twin are not relevant here. (5) The 28 recordings of one subject are far too small and homogeneous to serve as a reference set or benchmark, and are at most a qualitative demo. RQ1 and RQ2 rest entirely on public datasets (HOT3D, ARCTIC, SHOW3D, AssemblyHands), so the thesis assets do not change the feasibility or the venue odds of the core paper.
fit.what_a_small_lab_cannot_do_here: A small lab cannot build or deploy the references that would measure released labels directly: a SHOW3D-style back-mounted 8-camera rig plus headset, an ESTHER-style 10-hour Vicon test set, a multi-view dome, or a multi-view re-annotation campaign on a scaled corpus. It cannot process 1,000-10,000-hour corpora end to end; tens of TB and multi-GPU inference rule out labelling all of EgoDex, Ego4D or HumanNet, so only subsamples can be audited. It cannot retrain HaMeR-scale (ViT-H) students on millions of frames many times, so its scaling conclusions are trends at reduced model and data size. It cannot pretrain VLAs or measure real-robot policy success across label policies, so policy-level harm can be shown only through simulation or an action-recognition proxy, which weakens a CoRL or RSS submission. It also cannot collect new in-the-wild ground truth to test the hardest occlusions that SHOW3D's own filtering removed. Verification note: the shared WebSearch budget was exhausted in this session (0 searches ran). Novelty was checked with arXiv API listing queries and abstract fetches only. They found no work on per-frame error estimation for 3D hand pseudo-labels or on a controlled study of filtering bias. The closest work found was CUPS (arXiv 2412.10431), CHAMP (arXiv 2407.06141), keypoint self-consistency failure detection for 6D object pose (arXiv 2608.03516), UST-Hand (arXiv 2605.17742) and HumanScale (arXiv 2606.20521). SHOW3D's public availability was confirmed on its project page and HuggingFace. ESTHER3D's release status and MINT's code release are unverified.

painpoint.name: Jitter, drift and unrecoverable track loss over time

evidence.latest_state:
The verified 2025-2026 work treats track loss as an engineering problem to bolt on, not a solved one. On the rigid-object side, several trackers now add explicit failure detection and re-acquisition on top of FoundationPose-style render-and-compare:
- RRTrack (arXiv 2607.23669) reports gains of 66.3% in equal-subset mean ADD-S AR and 65.7% in ADD-S AUC over FoundationPose, at 55.2 FPS, on its own synthetic RGB-D benchmark with fast motion and complete disappearance.
- Opra et al. (RA-L, arXiv 2607.23468) monitor divergence and globally re-detect, at 57.6 FPS. They match state-of-the-art accuracy on standard benchmarks and introduce a new occlusion and fast-motion dataset.
- Point2Pose (arXiv 2604.10415) recovers model-free tracking after complete occlusion using 2D point trackers and an online TSDF. The authors state that this costs single-object accuracy.
- GRC-Pose (arXiv 2609.39116) reports 58% better motion retention than prior methods on HOT3D.

Hand-aware tracking (ComPose, arXiv 2605.23523), haptics (V-HOP, RSS 2025; KineFuse, arXiv 2607.14842) and inertial or event sensing (DynamicPose, arXiv 2508.11950; Event6D, arXiv 2603.28045) are used to bridge occlusion and fast motion. On the human side:
- HaWoR (arXiv 2501.02973) infills hand motion when the hands leave the egocentric view.
- Multi-THuMBS (arXiv 2607.01626) keeps identities across shot cuts.

The key point is that each recovery paper evaluates on its own new dataset. No 2025 or 2026 BOP report adds a tracking or temporal task: the latest report found is BOP 2024 (arXiv 2504.02812), which is still per-image. No shared long-horizon loss-and-recovery metric was found. No result could be confirmed that closes the original gaps on PACE (best model-free 5deg5cm under 13%) or on EgoHumans ID switches. The problem is therefore partly attacked, mostly for rigid objects with known models, and still open for model-free bimanual hand-object tracking and for standardised evaluation.

Caveat: the WebSearch budget was already exhausted (0 searches ran), so all evidence comes from WebFetch of arXiv title-search listings and abstract pages. Venue labels come from the arXiv pages. HaWoR's CVPR 2025 venue is not confirmed. No numbers were found for PACE, EgoHumans, EMDB or RHOBIN in the 2025-2026 papers checked.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: RRTrack: Robust and Recoverable Object 6D Pose Tracking for Dynamic Scenes
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Training-free tracker that recovers after fast motion and complete disappearance, using a closed loop between 2D segmentation and 6D pose, geometric verification and DINOv2 dual-bank template re-detection. Reports +66.3% ADD-S AR and +65.7% ADD-S AUC over FoundationPose at 55.2 FPS on a new synthetic benchmark.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: Robust 6-DoF Object Pose Tracking with Built-In Recovery under Occlusions and Rapid Object Motions
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: RGB-D tracker combining learned keypoint matching with optimisation. It monitors reliability, detects divergence, re-detects globally and verifies the recovered pose. Runs at 57.6 FPS and matches state-of-the-art accuracy on standard benchmarks, plus a new occlusion and fast-motion dataset.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: Point2Pose: Occlusion-Recovering 6D Pose Tracking and 3D Reconstruction for Multiple Unknown Objects Via 2D Point Trackers
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Model-free, causal, multi-object RGB-D 6D tracking with an online TSDF. Uses 2D point trackers to recover instantly after complete occlusion. Contributes a new multi-object dataset with motion-capture ground truth and states that it trades single-object accuracy for generality.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: GRC-Pose: Generation-Reconstruction Correspondence for Prior-Free 6D Object Pose Tracking
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Prior-free RGB-video 6D tracking that uses uncertainty-weighted correspondences and sequence-level inference with a memory for occlusion. Reports state of the art on HOT3D with 58% better motion retention, and stays competitive on YCBInEOAT and LINEMOD.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: ComPose: When to Trust Hands for Object Pose Tracking
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: RGB 6DoF object tracking that uses hand motion from foundation models as a complementary cue, with adaptive joint selection and temporal-consistency refinement, so tracking stays stable under severe hand occlusion.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: RGBTrack: Fast, Robust Depth-Free 6D Pose Estimation and Tracking
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: RGB-only tracker built on FoundationPose, using XMem 2D tracking, a Kalman filter and a state machine to recover the pose under occlusion and fast motion.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: DynamicPose: Real-time and Robust 6D Object Pose Tracking for Fast-Moving Cameras and Objects
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Retraining-free tracker that uses visual-inertial odometry, depth-informed 2D tracking and Kalman-filter multi-hypothesis refinement for scenes where the camera and the object move fast at the same time (a stated FoundationPose failure mode).

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: V-HOP: Visuo-Haptic 6D Object Pose Tracking
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Transformer tracker that fuses vision with a unified haptic representation to stay on track through in-hand occlusion. Reported to beat visual trackers by a large margin on challenging real sequences and on Feelsight.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Event-plus-depth tracking of novel objects at 120+ FPS, aimed at the large inter-frame displacements under rapid motion. Seen in the arXiv listing only.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.venue_year: arXiv 2025 (2501.02973); reported as CVPR 2025, venue not confirmed on the page
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: World-space hand motion from egocentric video, with adaptive SLAM and a motion infiller network that completes frames where the hands leave the view, targeting track loss for hands.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Keeps multi-person 3D mesh identities and motion continuity across shot changes by reconstructing boundary frames in a shared 3D frame. Reports gains in identity tracking, mesh recovery and camera pose.

evidence.crowdedness: MEDIUM: at least eight verified 2025-2026 papers attack object-track recovery, but most come from robotics groups (Stachniss, Sangbae Kim at MIT, Srinath Sridhar at Brown, Jingjin Yu at Rutgers) publishing at RA-L, IROS, RSS or on arXiv, each with its own dataset and no shared benchmark; work on hand-object and multi-person long-horizon recovery is thinner.
evidence.trend: Rising. Recovery-focused 6D tracking papers grew from about 2 in 2025 to at least 5 by September 2026. Three drivers push this: FoundationPose's known failures under occlusion and fast motion, the robot-learning demand for long manipulation trajectories from human video, and new egocentric hand-object benchmarks (HOT3D). Evaluation standards have not kept up.

skeptics.reasons:
Not refuted as stated, but the generic object-side claim "trackers cannot re-acquire an object once lost" is now being taken apart quickly and is close to engineering. Several 2026 papers build in failure detection and re-acquisition. Point2Pose (arXiv 2604.10415) is model-free and multi-object, and claims instant recovery after complete occlusion by using 2D point trackers. RRTrack (arXiv 2607.23669) closes a loop between video segmentation and 6D refinement and re-acquires lost targets by DINOv2 template matching. It reports about +66% ADD-S AR over FoundationPose at 55 FPS. An RA-L paper by Opra, Ghafari, Stewart and Stachniss (arXiv 2607.23468) adds a module that watches pose reliability, detects divergence or occlusion, and re-detects globally, at 57.6 FPS. DynamicPose (arXiv 2508.11950) fixes FoundationPose's failure under joint camera and object motion with VIO and a Kalman filter. ComPose (arXiv 2605.23523) uses hand motion as a cue during severe grasp occlusion and adds temporal-consistency constraints instead of external smoothing. On the human side, CoMotion (ICLR 2025) tracks multiple people online through occlusion by updating poses from new images instead of matching detections. So the recipe (foundation-model segmentation, template or keypoint re-detection, filtering) is now widely available.

Three reasons the pain point is not refuted. First, none of these results is on a shared, saturated benchmark. Each recovery paper brings its own new dataset: RRTrack's is synthetic, and Point2Pose and the RA-L paper each introduce a new one. Point2Pose says outright that it gives up single-object accuracy to gain recovery. Second, evaluation is still per-image: the BOP 2025 challenge page lists only 6D localization and detection tracks, with no sequence-level tracking task. So the record's claim that no standard metric exists for loss detection, re-acquisition latency or long-horizon drift still holds. Third, most of these papers are on rigid objects with free or mildly occluded motion. Bimanual and hand-object settings remain open: grasp occlusion lasts long, the object is held and moving, and the camera may move. So do body-object identity switches and the collapse of interpolation windows (the EgoHumans and DTF evidence). No 2025-2026 work I found reports these solved at scale.

The pain point is too broad as written. The jitter part is largely an engineering problem (filtering, motion priors). The re-acquisition part is crowded: three or more recovery papers appeared in July 2026 alone.

Limits of this check. The web-search budget was used up, so I collected evidence only through arXiv API listings, arXiv abstract pages and the BOP challenge page. I read abstracts only, not full papers.

skeptics.reframe: Generic jitter smoothing and rigid-object re-acquisition after full occlusion are close to engineering as of 2026 (Point2Pose, RRTrack, the RA-L built-in-recovery tracker, DynamicPose). Two parts stay open. The first is failure-aware tracking during hand-object and bimanual interaction: the object is held and occluded by one or both hands for long stretches, often under camera motion. This needs calibrated loss detection, re-acquisition that uses the hand state, and identity-consistent hand, body and object tracks across long sequences. The second is the lack of a shared sequence-level benchmark and metric to measure it. Such a metric would cover time-to-detect-loss, time-to-recover, the fraction of frames tracked within tolerance, and drift per minute, starting from detection rather than from a perturbed ground-truth pose. BOP 2025 still scores per image, and each 2026 recovery paper evaluates on its own new dataset.

skeptics.reasons:
Group diversity: the 31 paper ids (30 distinct; PACE appears twice as 348 and 1316, and Khirodkar/Meta contributes both EgoHumans and Harmony4D) come from many unrelated groups and settings: MPI/Tuebingen (InterCap, COUCH, RHOBIN), ETH (EMDB, WorldPose), Meta (EgoHumans, Harmony4D), the BOP organisers, PACE, Omni6DPose, DynOPETs, EgoXtreme, OmniPose6D, KAIST event data, two clinical prosthesis datasets, and several surveys. So it is not an artifact of one dataset or one lab. It survives the artifact test only partly, for four reasons.

(1) It bundles four problems, and other communities already own or have largely addressed three of them. Person identity switches (EgoHumans, EHPT-XC, MuPoTS HOTA) are the generic multi-object tracking problem with its own long literature. Body-mesh jitter is mostly a pre-2024 complaint. TRACE (paper 1261, CVPR 2023) is itself cited as evidence, yet WHAM (CVPR 2024, verified) reports acceleration error of about 5-6.6 m/s^2 on 3DPW, RICH and EMDB, against 18-25 for per-frame HMR2.0 and CLIFF. On EMDB-2 jitter it reports 21.5 for WHAM against 2987.6 for TRACE. Temporal regressors have largely closed the jitter gap for bodies. Hands and prolonged occlusion remain open.

(2) The 'why it persists' claim that there is 'no mechanism or metric for detecting loss and re-acquiring the target' is false at field level. 2D single-object tracking has had a long-term tracking protocol with target-absence sequences, image-wide re-detection, and tracking precision, recall and F-score since 2018 (Lukezic et al., 'Now you see me', verified). That protocol was integrated into the VOT toolkit and its long-term challenge. The gap is only that this protocol has not been carried over to 6D object or hand-object tracking.

(3) For 6D object tracking, drift on established benchmarks is near-saturated. FoundationPose (CVPR 2024, verified) reports 96.42 ADD-S AUC and 93.09 ADD AUC on YCBInEOAT with no re-initialisation after loss. It reports 97.5 ADD-S model-free on YCB-Video, and can re-acquire by re-running its own pose estimator. The dramatic failure numbers (PACE ADD-S AUC 38.1, under 13% at 5deg5cm, BundleTrack 6.4) come from new datasets built to be hard: clutter, a moving camera, extreme egocentric conditions. Those papers state that existing methods fail on their data in order to motivate themselves. This is a known selection effect of a corpus made of dataset and benchmark papers, not independent evidence of a field-wide wall.

(4) Several specific numbers come from one paper's own setup. The 302 mm DTF collapse depends on an 81-frame window under synthetic occlusion in a single arXiv benchmark. The 741 ID switches are EgoHumans-specific. The low-light event-camera and prosthesis-gait items are outside the hand-object core.

What survives is narrower and real. In hand-object and bimanual settings, 6D trackers are still scored per image (BOP) or started from a perturbed ground-truth pose. No benchmark measures loss detection, re-acquisition latency or long-horizon drift under hand occlusion and fast object motion. The FoundationPose authors themselves name texture-less objects, severe occlusion and missing detections as failure modes. The evaluation gap is the defensible pain point. A general claim that trackers cannot keep a stable track is not.

skeptics.reframe: In hand-object and bimanual manipulation, 6D object and hand trackers are evaluated per image or started from a perturbed ground-truth pose. No benchmark or metric measures loss detection, re-acquisition latency or long-horizon drift under prolonged hand occlusion and fast object motion. The long-term tracking protocol of the 2D tracking community (target absence, re-detection, tracking precision, recall and F-score) has not been carried over to 6D hand-object tracking, so methods that score near saturation on YCBInEOAT can still fail silently in real long manipulation sequences.

skeptics.reasons:
Case for refutation (partly holds): P20 bundles several problems with different statuses. Body-estimator jitter is mostly handled by known smoothing and motion priors (EKF/RTS, sequence priors), which is engineering. Person ID switches in egocentric multi-human tracking are a separate MOT problem with its own literature. The generic object-tracking fix is also known: detect divergence, re-detect globally, verify, then resume. A July 2026 RA-L paper (arXiv 2607.23468) does exactly this at 57.6 fps, and FoundationPose can already re-initialise by switching to its estimation mode. So 'add a failure detector and re-initialise' is a systems paper for RA-L or IROS, not a CVPR/ICCV/CoRL question. As stated, the pain point is too broad and has a partly known solution.

Case against refutation (decisive): in hand-object and bimanual manipulation, at least one significant research question survives. While a hand fully covers the object, or the object passes between two hands, its pose cannot be seen. Re-detection cannot help because nothing visible remains to re-detect. The field's attempted fixes (interpolation windows, which collapse to about 302 mm past 81 frames; propagating the previous pose; periodic re-initialisation) do not use the one signal that is still present, which is the grasp. That leads to two questions: (1) can an estimated contact or grasp state carry object pose through visual blackout, with calibrated uncertainty that rises with occlusion time and triggers verified re-acquisition when the object reappears? (2) how should continuity be measured? The record notes that BOP scores per image and tracking benchmarks start from a perturbed ground-truth pose. Long-term single-object tracking, by contrast, has loss, re-detection and time-to-recover protocols. Benchmark numbers back the gap: on PACE (ECCV 2024, verified), model-free tracking stays below 13% 5deg5cm (BundleTrack 6.4) and model-based ICG reaches 38.1 ADD(-S) AUC. Recent top-venue work treats drift in HOI video as a live problem (AGILE, SIGGRAPH 2026, verified, moves to anchor-and-track propagation to avoid SfM drift). A tracker that knows when it is lost and uses the hand to bridge occlusion, scored by a new continuity protocol, would be judged significant by a CVPR/ICCV/CoRL reviewer, especially for robot demonstration capture. Remaining risk: the method part could shrink to a filter plus a re-detector unless the contact-carried pose and the uncertainty calibration are learned and evaluated rigorously. Searches were limited (the shared WebSearch budget was used up), so related HOI-specific occlusion-bridging work from 2025-2026 may exist that I could not find.
