skeptics.reframe: In hand-object and bimanual manipulation, the object often cannot be seen for long stretches: a hand covers it, or it passes between two hands. Today's trackers fill this gap by interpolating, propagating the previous pose or re-detecting, and none of these work when nothing visible is left. Current benchmarks cannot detect the failure: they start from the ground-truth pose and score frame by frame. Research question: can the estimated grasp or contact state carry the object's pose through visual blackout, with calibrated uncertainty that grows during occlusion and triggers verified re-acquisition? And can a continuity protocol (fraction of frames tracked, time to detect loss, time to recover, error just after re-acquisition) show whether such a tracker beats detect-and-reinitialise baselines over long manipulation sequences?

research_questions.question: Do 6D object trackers fail silently during hand-object and bimanual manipulation, and does a sequence-level continuity protocol change how they rank? The protocol would start trackers from a detection, require a pose plus a lost/confidence flag every frame, and score tracking precision, recall and F-score, time to detect loss, time to recover, error just after re-acquisition, and drift per minute. Scores would be broken down by occlusion duration and grasp state (free, one-hand held, bimanual, handover).
research_questions.why_top_venue: All three skeptics agree on one evaluation gap, and the artifact skeptic calls it the defensible core. BOP 2025 has only per-image localization and detection tracks. I fetched the BOP challenge page and found no sequence or tracking task. Tracking benchmarks such as YCBInEOAT start from a ground-truth pose, where FoundationPose already reaches 96.42 ADD-S AUC. Each 2026 recovery paper (RRTrack 2607.23669, Opra et al. RA-L 2607.23468, Point2Pose 2604.10415) evaluates on its own new dataset, so none of them can be compared with the others. 2D tracking has had a long-term protocol with target absence and re-detection since 2018 (Lukezic et al., arXiv 1804.07056, adopted in the VOT long-term challenge), but nobody has carried it over to 6D hand-object tracking. If per-frame accuracy and continuity rank trackers differently, a shared protocol on existing motion-capture ground truth is a field-level contribution. Robot learning from human video now needs long, unbroken object trajectories, which raises the demand.
research_questions.method_sketch: (1) Per-frame object visibility and grasp-state labels from existing ground truth. Render the ground-truth MANO hands and the object mesh in each camera to get the visible fraction of the object. Derive grasp state from hand-object contact distance, and handover events from contact switching between the two hands. (2) Define 'lost' as an ADD-S or 5deg5cm error above a tolerance. Port the VOT long-term definitions to 6D: tracking precision over frames where the tracker claims the object, tracking recall over frames where the object exists, and F-score swept over the tracker's confidence. Add sequence-event metrics: time to detect loss, time to recover after the object reappears, post-recovery error, silent-failure rate (confident and wrong), and drift per minute on long sequences. (3) Protocol: initialise from a detector (FoundationPose's estimator or SAM-6D-style detection on the first visible frame), never from ground truth. Use a fixed causal budget and report fps. (4) Run 6 to 8 trackers with a uniform confidence interface. Where a tracker has no native score, use its render-and-compare score. (5) Analysis: rank correlation between per-frame and continuity metrics, failure taxonomy by occlusion duration bin and grasp state, and metric stability under different tolerances.
research_questions.data_and_hardware: No capture is needed. Public datasets: HOT3D, which needs a research-license download (storage is large but its size is unverified; plan a subset), HO-Cap, DexYCB, and optionally HO3D v3 and H2O (egocentric RGB-D, two hands). One 24 GB GPU (RTX 3090 or 4090 class) is enough for inference-only runs of all trackers. Running the full HOT3D set at about 30 fps would take several hours per tracker per camera stream, so use a subset stratified by occlusion events. You also need CPU rendering for the visibility labels: a pyrender or nvdiffrast pass over the ground-truth meshes. One graduate student for about 6 to 9 months.
research_questions.risks: Reviewers may call it 'VOT long-term ported to 6D' unless the analysis shows that per-frame metrics actually mislead. If no ranking inversion appears, the paper weakens to a toolkit. The BOP organisers or the HOT3D team (Meta) could add a tracking track first; this is the biggest scoop risk, and the window is roughly 2027. The 2026 recovery trackers (RRTrack, Opra et al., ComPose) may not release code, which leaves the comparison to older baselines. HOT3D has no depth images, which splits the evaluation into RGB and RGB-D tiers. The HO-Cap size and sequence lengths are unverified here; if its sequences are short, the long-horizon drift metric rests on HOT3D alone. Evidence limit: the WebSearch budget was exhausted, so prior art was checked only through arXiv API listings and abstract pages, and a 2026 hand-object tracking benchmark could exist unseen.

research_questions.question: Can the estimated grasp state carry a held object's 6D pose through full visual blackout in bimanual manipulation? The tracker would keep an explicit grasp mode (free, left-held, right-held, both, in transfer) and a per-hand hand-to-object transform. Its uncertainty would grow with occlusion time and with hand articulation change, and it would trigger verified re-acquisition when the object reappears. Would it beat detect-and-reinitialise trackers on continuity metrics while staying causal and real-time on one RGB-D camera?
research_questions.why_top_venue: While a hand covers the object, or the object passes from one hand to the other, re-detection has nothing to work with. Interpolation collapses past its window: the 302 mm DTF figure at 81 frames comes from the P20 record. Propagating the last pose freezes the object while the hand moves on. The one signal still present is the grasp. ComPose (arXiv 2605.23523, May 2026) shows the field is starting to treat hands as a cue, not just an occluder. Its abstract, however, claims no full-blackout carry, no calibrated uncertainty, no grasp-mode or handover switching and no loss/recovery metric. The other 2026 recovery papers treat rigid objects without hand reasoning, and visuo-haptic work (V-HOP, RSS 2025; ViTa-Zero) needs tactile hardware. A vision-only tracker that knows when it is guessing, and why, scored with the continuity protocol from the first question, targets the case robot demonstration capture needs most. Reviewers at CVPR, ICCV or CoRL would likely see it as significant.
research_questions.method_sketch: Causal state-space tracker on one RGB-D stream at at least 20 fps. Observation model: a FoundationPose-style render-and-compare refiner for the object, plus a per-frame hand estimator (HaMeR or WiLoR) refined against depth for both hands. State: object pose, grasp mode, and one hand-to-object relative transform per holding hand. When held and visible, update the relative transform from both observations. When held and occluded (visible fraction from mask times depth below a threshold), predict the object pose as hand pose composed with the relative transform. Covariance grows with occlusion time, plus a learned slip term: a small temporal network trained on public hand-object ground truth (DexYCB, HO-Cap, OakInk2, ARCTIC) that predicts how much the relative transform changes given the hand articulation sequence. A grasp-mode switch detects regrasps and handovers from contact proximity and articulation, and hands the carry to the receiving hand. Re-acquisition: when the object reappears, compare the carried hypothesis with global re-detection candidates. Accept only those that pass a render-and-compare score threshold calibrated by conformal prediction on held-out sequences, which also gives the 'lost' flag the first question needs. Symmetric extension: when the hand is occluded by the object, the tracked object pose constrains the hand (mutual bridging).
research_questions.data_and_hardware: Public training and evaluation data: DexYCB, HO-Cap, ARCTIC, OakInk2 (for relative-transform dynamics), HOT3D (evaluation). One consumer RGB-D camera, for qualitative live demos and a small unlabeled long-sequence stress set only; it gives no ground truth. One 24 GB GPU. The learned slip model is small, so training takes hours to days, not weeks. Pretrained hand estimators and FoundationPose weights are public. One to two graduate students for 12 to 15 months.
research_questions.risks: The method could collapse to 'Kalman filter plus re-detector' unless the learned slip model and the calibrated verification clearly beat simple rules in the ablations. Hand pose error carries into object pose through a lever arm: wrist rotation errors of 10 to 15 degrees at 10 cm offsets give centimetre-level errors. Depth refinement of the hand is therefore mandatory, and long objects remain hard. In-hand finger gaiting breaks the rigid-attachment assumption; restrict the claims to grasp-and-move and handover and report the failure cases. Scoop risk is high: ComPose (Jeon group, May 2026) and the July 2026 recovery wave mean a hand-aware recovery tracker could appear before the ICCV 2027 or CoRL 2027 deadlines. Release the first question's benchmark early to stake the evaluation ground. The code for most 2026 competitors is unverified. HOT3D lacks depth, so RGB-D claims rest on HO-Cap and DexYCB, whose sequence lengths may limit long-horizon claims.

fit.thesis_assets_help:
Small. The assets help with framing and engineering, not with evaluation.
- The measured/held/constrained per-joint labels are an early, hand-built version of the explicit uncertainty state and lost flag the second question formalises.
- The object-conditioned recovery of an occluded holding arm is the reverse half of the proposed mutual bridging, where the tracked object constrains the occluded hand. It is a usable prior result and a credible story for why the author is positioned for this.
- The causal 30 fps chain shows the author can build a real-time pipeline. The method contribution, however, sits on FoundationPose and a learned hand estimator, not on the thesis chain.
- The ArUco-marked object gives metric ground truth only while the marker is visible. It loses ground truth during exactly the blackout frames that matter, so it cannot serve as evaluation data, and a fiducial-based tracker would not be accepted as the method.
- The 28 recordings come from one subject and one object, so they cannot form a benchmark. At most they are a qualitative stress set.
- The Unity twin could render visualisations, or a few synthetic occlusion clips for illustration, but not benchmark data.
In short, the assets give a head start on the idea and on real-time systems skills, and nothing on data or ground truth.
fit.what_a_small_lab_cannot_do_here:
The lab cannot capture new ground truth for long bimanual or handover sequences. With one consumer RGB-D camera and no motion capture, it cannot label poses during occlusion, so a new dataset contribution is out of reach and both questions must rest on public ground truth (HOT3D, HO-Cap, DexYCB, ARCTIC, OakInk2).

It cannot run an official community challenge or set the standard by itself; the BOP organisers or Meta's HOT3D team could add a tracking track and overtake the first question.

It cannot match the engineering throughput of the groups now publishing recovery trackers (NVIDIA, Meta, MIT, Bonn/Stachniss, Brown, Rutgers), and it cannot train foundation-scale pose or hand models; it must build on public FoundationPose, HaMeR or WiLoR weights.

It cannot evaluate tactile, event-camera or inertial sensing (V-HOP, Event6D, DynamicPose) without new hardware.

It cannot show downstream robot policy gains on a real arm unless it borrows one; simulation replay is the realistic substitute.

The generic part of P20 is not worth a small lab's time: smoothing body-mesh jitter (largely closed by temporal regressors such as WHAM), person identity switches (the established multi-object-tracking literature) and rigid-object re-acquisition after full occlusion (crowded in 2026). Search caveat: the shared WebSearch budget was exhausted before this task, so prior art was checked only through arXiv API listings and abstract pages. An unseen 2025-2026 hand-object continuity benchmark or grasp-carried tracker remains possible.

painpoint.name: Estimators fail outside their training capture domain

evidence.latest_state: As of late 2026 the gap has narrowed but is still there. The best recent systems shrink it with large-scale or pseudo-labelled training and with explicit camera or geometry handling, not with domain-generalization methods. Stated cross-domain gaps remain, especially across camera modality and rig. ESTHER (arXiv 2609.34817, Sep 2026; egocentric stereo, trained on in-the-wild data with mocap ground truth) gets 17.7 mm P-MPJPE and 8.6 mm PA-MPJPE zero-shot on its own ESTHER3D test set. Zero-shot on HOT3D it gets 30.5 mm P-MPJPE (WiLoR 30.2 mm, HaMeR 36.3 mm), and wrist errors are 54-102 mm. The authors say small-scale fine-tuning on 10 percent of HOT3D is still needed because of the grayscale fisheye modality and the different focal length. MINT (arXiv 2609.04958) pretrains on pseudo-labels from public egocentric video, produced by an open labeling pipeline. It reports 13.6 mm PA-MPJPE for bimanual hands zero-shot on HOT3D, but that metric is Procrustes-aligned and so hides the metric and global error that dominates cross-rig transfer. New in-the-wild data sources also attack the root cause: SHOW3D (CVPR 2026) is the predecessor of the Meta Ego-Exo mobile rig (arXiv 2510.02601), and EPIC-Contact with HOPformer (ECCV 2026) reports 82.4 percent success on ARCTIC and roughly doubles the success rate on in-the-wild EPIC-Contact. On the synthetic side, Zhao et al. (CVPR 2025) show that synthetic hand data can match real data once the forearm, frequency statistics, pose and occlusion are modelled. On the human side, HAMSt3R (ICCV 2025) fine-tunes and distils MASt3R with a human-mesh-recovery encoder because object or scene point-map models fail on humans. That confirms target-domain (human) data is still the fix, not true generalization. I found no 2025-2026 paper that removes the cross-lab gap on DexYCB to TACO, HO3D or HOGraspNet without target data. I also found no 2025-2026 follow-up on the surgical or human-NeRF (MVHumanNet to HuMMan) cases.

evidence.crowdedness: MEDIUM. More than ten 2025-2026 papers from strong groups (Meta Reality Labs, Black/Damen, Yao, Naver and others) touch the gap, but almost all attack it indirectly through new in-the-wild datasets or data scaling. Few target cross-rig or cross-lab transfer without target labels as the primary problem.
evidence.trend: Rising. Foundation-model pretraining, pseudo-label pipelines over public egocentric video, and new in-the-wild capture rigs (SHOW3D, EPIC-Contact, ESTHER3D) made zero-shot cross-dataset evaluation on HOT3D and ARCTIC a common 2026 reporting practice. Robot-learning demand for hands captured on arbitrary headsets and cameras adds pressure.

skeptics.reasons:
I found no 2025-2026 work that removes the gap for hand-object interaction. Some parts of P21 are shrinking, though, and the broad statement is too general to stand as written.

(1) Partly reduced, single-person body and hand mesh recovery. SAM 3D Body (Meta, arXiv 2602.15989, released model) reports leave-one-out results on five new domains. On EE4D-Physical, PVE is 49.7 when that dataset is held out and 37.0 when it is in training, a ratio of about 1.34x. The record cites 2-4x for older models (cross-dataset root-relative MPJPE of 33-55 mm against 12-14 mm within dataset). The gap narrows a lot with scale, but it does not close. The same model reaches about 5.5 PA-MPJPE on FreiHAND without training on it. WiLoR and Fast-HaMeR follow the same trend: large multi-dataset training plus augmentation makes single-image hand mesh recovery in the wild usable.

(2) Being reduced to engineering, object-centric 3D models used on humans. HAMSt3R (ICCV 2025) and Human3R (arXiv 2512.06368) add human priors or human training data to DUSt3R/MASt3R. That fixes the specific failure the record cites. It is a data and fine-tuning recipe, not an open research problem.

(3) Not solved, hand-object interaction outside the lab and on new sensor rigs. HOPformer with the EPIC-Contact dataset (Bansal, Black, Damen et al., ECCV 2026, arXiv 2606.30598) measures a baseline dropping from 76.2% success on ARCTIC to 17.6% in the wild. Their model reaches 82.4% on ARCTIC and only "nearly doubles" the in-the-wild baseline (about 35%; I inferred this from the abstract wording, no exact number checked). That is still a gap of more than 2x.
- V-HPOT (WACV 2026, arXiv 2601.06537) needs camera-normalised depth plus test-time self-supervised refinement to cut cross-domain error by 41-71% on H2O and AssemblyHands. So camera-rig and intrinsics shift still breaks models unless they adapt.
- Egocentric foundation-style models (MINT, arXiv 2609.04958; InfiniHand, arXiv 2609.35743) scale pseudo-labels to 1-5k hours of egocentric video. MINT's abstract claims zero-shot generalisation to HOT3D and ARCTIC, but the HOT3D result it reports used HOT3D supervision. InfiniHand claims robustness in the wild only qualitatively. Neither shows the hand-object, contact or object-pose gap closed.

Overall: the trend (scaled pseudo-label pipelines, released foundation models) is turning the body-only and hand-only parts into engineering. The hand-object part (contact, object pose, occlusion by the manipulated object), new capture rigs or headsets and RGB-D sensors, and specialised domains stay open, mainly because there are no target-domain labels to evaluate or adapt with. As a direction, "domain gap" in general is crowded and hard to own. A narrowed version is more defensible.

skeptics.reframe: Single-person body and hand-only mesh recovery now generalise across datasets to within about 1.3x of in-domain error, by scaling data and pseudo-labels. Hand-object interaction estimation does not. That covers object pose, contact and hands occluded by the manipulated object, on a new capture rig, headset or RGB-D sensor, or in the wild: success still drops by roughly 2x or more (ARCTIC 82% vs EPIC-Contact about 35%). There is no labelled target data to measure or adapt with. Open problem: label-free adaptation or certification of hand-object trackers on a new rig, using cues the rig itself provides (multi-view or depth consistency, physical contact and penetration constraints). The goal is to detect and reduce the gap without collecting target annotations.

skeptics.reasons:
Artifact lens verdict: not an artifact of one dataset or one group, but too generic to stand as a field-specific pain point in its current form.

Against the artifact hypothesis (why it survives). I resolved the 30 paper ids through scratchpad w3_digest/*.jsonl. Note that field_papers.json uses a different indexing, so id 88 there is a different paper. The supporting works come from many unrelated groups and rigs: TACO (Tsinghua), EgoPressure (ETH), HOT3D and AssemblyHands (Meta), CORE4D, HOGraspNet (KAIST), OakInk (SJTU), POV-Surgery (ETH/Balgrist), the Ohkawa IJCV 2023 survey (UTokyo), MVHumanNet/MVHumanNet++ (CUHK-SZ), HumanOLAT (MPI), SHOW3D, ADL4D, EgoTactile, HANDS 2024 challenge reports, and clinical and fingerspelling datasets. It also matches an independent body-pose study I verified: PoseBench3D (arXiv 2505.10888) retests 18 lifting methods in more than 100 cross-dataset runs and reports "systematic generalization gaps". No community treats this as solved. Dataset bias (Torralba and Efros, CVPR 2011) and domain adaptation are long-standing open problems, not closed ones.

For the artifact hypothesis (why the score is not higher).
(1) Selection bias. About 25 of the 30 sources are dataset papers. A dataset paper's job is to argue that existing datasets do not transfer and that the new one fixes this, for example HOGraspNet to DexYCB at 42.65 mm versus HO3D-trained at 57.31 mm. These numbers are self-serving motivation, not a neutral measurement across the field.
(2) Some evidence is a rig artifact with a known fix. The 184.27 mm HOT3D collapse is a camera-extrinsic mismatch, and the same report removes it with extrinsic perturbation augmentation.
(3) The cluster mixes unrelated problems: hand MPJPE transfer, head and body NeRF domain gaps, DUSt3R on humans, relighting, and fingerspelling. What they share is only the general ML fact that test distributions differ from training distributions.
(4) Scaling has largely dealt with the 2D-aligned version of the problem. I verified this for SMPLer-X (arXiv 2309.17448: 32 datasets, 4.5M instances, "excellent transferability to even unseen environments") and HaMeR (arXiv 2312.05251: multi-dataset training plus ViT, large in-the-wild gains on HInt). Zhao et al. (CVPR 2025, arXiv 2503.19307) claim that synthetic-only hand training can match real-data accuracy once forearm, frequency statistics, pose and occlusion are modelled. That weakens the claim that target-domain labels are "the missing ingredient".

What remains is narrower. Metric 3D accuracy (absolute depth and scale, hand-object contact, object pose) across rigs and headsets has no shared cross-dataset protocol for hand-object interaction, unlike PoseBench3D for body lifting. The evidence for this residual is real but comes mostly from dataset-paper motivation sections.

skeptics.reframe: Large multi-dataset hand and body models now transfer well for 2D-aligned pose across capture domains, but their metric 3D hand-object accuracy (absolute depth and scale, contact, object pose) drops by an unmeasured amount when the camera rig, headset layout or depth sensor changes. Unlike PoseBench3D for body lifting, the field has no cross-rig protocol for hand-object interaction that separates rig-specific failures (extrinsics, sensor noise) from appearance shift.

skeptics.reasons:
P21 says that hand, hand-object and human reconstruction models lose roughly 1.5x to several-fold accuracy outside their capture domain. Reported cases include DexYCB to TACO 39.5 vs 76.2 mm, cross-dataset HMR 33-55 mm vs 12-14 mm, and a collapse on HOT3D when the headset camera layout changes.

Case for refutation. As P21 states it, the problem reads like a wish for more varied labelled data: its own "why it persists" says target-domain labels are the missing ingredient. There is also outside evidence that scale closes much of the gap. HaMeR (CVPR 2024) showed that a large ViT trained on many mixed 2D and 3D hand datasets generalizes in the wild far better than earlier models, which makes the single-hand part look like a resource problem. Generic domain generalization or adaptation for hand pose is an old, crowded topic, and recent entries mostly appear at mid-tier venues: CLIP-based image-free domain generalization (arXiv 2022, tested on STB/RHD), masked-reconstruction domain adaptation (arXiv 2025), and HandCLR contrastive pretraining (HANDS@ECCV24 workshop, gains of 4 to 15 percent). A paper that only says "our domain adaptation narrows the gap by X percent" would be judged incremental at CVPR or ICCV.

Why it survives. At least three questions are not just a matter of collecting more data, and a top-venue reviewer would plausibly see them as significant:
(1) Label-free test-time adaptation for hand-object interaction (HOI). Can physical and geometric self-consistency remove the cross-domain gap without any target labels? Candidate signals are hand-object contact and non-penetration, temporal smoothness, multi-view or depth agreement, and object rigidity. Earlier temporal self-training and contact-consistency test-time adaptation (for grasp generation) exist but were never shown to close cross-rig gaps on modern benchmarks such as HOT3D, TACO or HOGraspNet.
(2) Rig-agnostic estimation. Can multi-camera or egocentric trackers condition on camera intrinsics and extrinsics so that they transfer zero-shot to a new headset layout, instead of relying on augmentation? The HOT3D collapse to 184 mm is a measured failure with no principled fix.
(3) Diagnosing the gap. Which factors cause it (viewpoint and camera geometry, appearance, subject shape, interaction or grasp distribution, or bias in how ground truth was annotated), and does scaling fix each one? This could become a controlled benchmark contribution.
The HaMeR-style scaling answer covers single-hand appearance only. It does not address object pose, contact, extrinsics, or the human-versus-object-centric gap in DUSt3R-style and LRM models, so the problem is not already solved and waiting only on resources.

Score 5.5. The pain point yields publishable questions only after it is reframed away from "add data". In its raw form it is close to an engineering and data problem, and generic domain adaptation for hand pose is saturated.

skeptics.reframe: Can hand-object and bimanual trackers adapt to a new capture rig, camera layout or scene with no target labels? The idea is to use physical and geometric self-consistency at test time (contact and non-penetration, object rigidity, temporal smoothness, agreement with depth or multiple views) and to condition on camera parameters so that a new headset layout transfers zero-shot. The method should be validated on cross-rig benchmarks (DexYCB/TACO/HOGraspNet to HOT3D or in-the-wild), with a controlled breakdown of how much of the gap each factor causes (viewpoint, appearance, interaction distribution, annotation bias) that shows which parts data scaling fixes and which it does not.

research_questions.question: RQ1 (diagnosis and protocol; the other two questions reuse its outputs). When a hand-object estimator moves to a new capture rig, how much of the accuracy drop comes from each controllable factor? The factors are camera intrinsics and viewpoint, sensor modality and noise, appearance and background, grasp or interaction distribution, and ground-truth annotation noise. Which of these factors does data scaling (HaMeR- and WiLoR-class models) actually remove, when error is measured in metric camera space (root position, object pose, hand-object relative translation, contact) and not only with Procrustes-aligned PA-MPJPE?
research_questions.why_top_venue: Cross-dataset evaluation of hand-object models in 2026 is common but not controlled, and it hides the error that matters. MINT (arXiv 2609.04958) reports 13.6 mm PA-MPJPE on HOT3D. That metric is Procrustes-aligned, and one skeptic notes the run used HOT3D supervision. ESTHER (arXiv 2609.34817) reaches about 30 mm P-MPJPE zero-shot on HOT3D, yet its wrist errors are 54-102 mm. The HOPformer baseline (ECCV 2026, arXiv 2606.30598) drops from 76.2 percent success on ARCTIC to 17.6 percent in the wild. The DexYCB paper itself reports 1.4-1.9x more error from DexYCB to HO3D and 3.4-3.7x from HO3D to DexYCB. Body lifting has PoseBench3D (arXiv 2505.10888), a cross-dataset analysis framework; I found no counterpart for hand-object interaction that separates rig factors from appearance and annotation bias. A protocol that splits the gap into factors, reports metric and contact error, and shows which factors scaling leaves behind would change how the field reports zero-shot transfer. Venue fit is strongest for NeurIPS Datasets and Benchmarks. A CVPR or ECCV main-track paper needs one sharp, non-obvious finding, for example that most of the residual metric gap is intrinsics plus annotation bias rather than appearance.
research_questions.method_sketch: (1) Unify metric hand-object datasets in one evaluation frame: MANO convention, camera-space coordinates, a single crop protocol and one metric suite. The suite covers CS-MPJPE, root translation error, PA-MPJPE, object ADD-S and translation error, hand-object relative translation, contact F1 and penetration depth. Datasets: DexYCB (8-view RGB-D), HO3D v3 and HOGraspNet, which have metric MANO and object pose; ARCTIC and HOT3D are evaluation-only RGB and egocentric targets. HO3D and DexYCB share YCB objects, so object identity can be held fixed while the rig changes. (2) Factor interventions. (a) Hold out views within a dataset (train on some DexYCB cameras, test on the others). Appearance, subjects and annotation stay constant, so only viewpoint changes. (b) Warp images to virtual cameras whose intrinsics and distortion match other rigs (RealSense, Aria fisheye, Quest grayscale), which isolates intrinsics and modality. (c) Composite new backgrounds and relight, which isolates appearance. (d) Resample test sets by grasp taxonomy or contact pattern, which isolates the interaction distribution. (e) Audit annotation noise by rendering each dataset's ground-truth hand and object meshes into its own sensor depth and measuring the residual. This gives a per-dataset label-noise floor that no model can beat, and part of the apparent transfer gap may simply be disagreement between labels. (3) Fill a transfer matrix using frozen public models plus one small single-source model the lab trains itself (ViT-B on DexYCB only), so that the held-out targets are clean. Attribute the gap to factors with a Shapley-style or regression decomposition, separately for each metric. (4) Release the evaluation code and the conversion scripts, not re-hosted data.
research_questions.minimum_experiment: Three metric RGB-D source/target datasets (DexYCB, HO3D v3, HOGraspNet), three models (HaMeR, WiLoR, and the lab's DexYCB-only ViT-B), FoundationPose for object pose with CAD, and four interventions (view hold-out, virtual-camera warp, background swap, grasp-stratified resampling). Add the depth-residual audit of the ground truth on all three datasets. Deliverables: a 3x3 transfer matrix with CS-MPJPE, PA-MPJPE, object ADD-S and contact F1; a factor-attribution table; and a check of whether model rankings flip between PA metrics and metric camera-space metrics. Proposed success criterion: the factors explain most of the cross-dataset CS-MPJPE gap, and at least one finding contradicts current PA-only reporting. Mostly inference plus one mid-size training run, so about 4-6 months for one student.
research_questions.data_and_hardware: Public datasets only: DexYCB, HO3D v3, HOGraspNet, ARCTIC, HOT3D, plus optionally TACO and OakInk. Depth availability and sensor model for HOGraspNet and TACO are unverified and must be checked before committing. Storage needs are several TB (an estimate, not checked). One 24-48 GB GPU is enough for inference, for LoRA or mid-size training, and for differentiable depth rendering (PyTorch3D or nvdiffrast). No capture hardware is required; the lab's own RGB-D rig can serve as an extra unlabelled target.
research_questions.risks: (1) Factors are confounded across datasets (subjects, objects and rigs change together), so the attribution can be contested. Interventions within a dataset reduce this but do not remove it. (2) Benchmark papers succeed only through adoption. A Meta or HANDS-workshop group could publish a similar cross-rig protocol on HOT3D first. (3) Licenses on HOT3D, ARCTIC and others may prevent redistributing converted data, so only code can be released. (4) Virtual-camera warping cannot reproduce real fisheye blur or grayscale sensor noise. (5) The single-source model trained here is weaker than foundation models, so reviewers may question whether its gaps carry over to them. (6) Main-track reviewers may call it 'just analysis' without a striking finding; NeurIPS Datasets and Benchmarks is the safer target.

research_questions.question: RQ2 (method). Can a pretrained RGB hand-object estimator be adapted online to a new consumer RGB-D rig without any labels? The only supervision would be the sensor's metric depth plus hand-object physical consistency: non-penetration, persistent contact while the object moves with the hand, object rigidity, and temporal smoothness. Does adapting a small set of weights (LoRA or normalization layers) beat per-frame output optimization against the same signals in metric hand and object accuracy, especially on frames where the manipulated object hides the hand?
research_questions.why_top_venue: The skeptics agree that the gap still open in late 2026 is metric and global error plus object pose and contact on a new rig. Hand-only, 2D-aligned transfer is being closed by scale (SAM 3D Body leave-one-out PVE 49.7 vs 37.0 in-domain; HaMeR and WiLoR in the wild). Existing label-free routes are narrower. V-HPOT (WACV 2026, arXiv 2601.06537) adapts hands only, with pseudo-depth from DPT and a scale-consistency loss. CRISP (CVPR 2025, arXiv 2412.01052) adapts object pose and shape only. In my searches I found no work that adapts a joint hand-object model across rigs using real sensor depth plus physical constraints and evaluates it on modern metric benchmarks. This claim rests on six searches and is not exhaustive. Commodity RGB-D is the default sensor for robot demonstration capture and desk digital twins, so a label-free adaptation recipe matters to both CV and robotics audiences. Weight-space adaptation also has an argument output optimization lacks: it amortizes over the stream, so occluded frames, where the depth residual is uninformative, can still benefit from what was learned on visible frames.
research_questions.method_sketch: Base: a hand regressor (HaMeR or WiLoR, or the lab's DexYCB-only model from RQ1) plus a model-based object tracker (FoundationPose with CAD), coupled through a light joint refinement head. Trainable parameters at test time: LoRA adapters on the ViT plus normalization layers. A frozen source copy acts as an EMA teacher and anchor to prevent collapse, with periodic reset. Label-free losses: (1) a robust, truncated residual between rendered hand and object depth and observed depth, masked by SAM 2 segmentation and weighted by a per-pixel noise model for the sensor (larger noise at edges, thin fingers and specular objects); (2) SDF-based penetration between hand and object; (3) contact persistence: fingertips in contact keep their object-frame position while the object moves rigidly; (4) temporal smoothness and object rigidity; (5) 2D keypoint agreement with an off-the-shelf 2D detector as a weak appearance anchor. Run causally and online at camera rate with asynchronous adapter updates. Baselines: no adaptation; per-frame output optimization against the same losses (the classic model-based RGB-D fitting route); V-HPOT-style scale consistency; Tent-style normalization adaptation; and an upper bound of supervised fine-tuning on 10 percent of labelled target data, mirroring ESTHER's statement that 10 percent of HOT3D was still needed.
research_questions.minimum_experiment: Source: the DexYCB-only model, so that targets are guaranteed held out, plus off-the-shelf HaMeR only on targets confirmed absent from its training set. Targets: HO3D v3 and HOGraspNet, if the training-set check passes and their depth is usable, plus the lab's own desk RGB-D recordings, where only object pose can be scored. Report CS-MPJPE, root error, object ADD-S, hand-object relative translation, penetration and contact F1, all stratified by visible-hand fraction. Also report throughput in fps. Ablate each loss and compare weight-space against output-space adaptation. Proposed success criterion: weight-space adaptation recovers a substantial share (for example half or more) of the gap between zero-shot and 10-percent-labelled fine-tuning in CS-MPJPE and object ADD-S, beats output-only optimization on the heavily occluded stratum, and stays near real time.
research_questions.data_and_hardware: Public metric RGB-D hand-object datasets: DexYCB (verified RGB-D, 8 views), HO3D v3, HOGraspNet. HO-Cap is a possible extra target, unverified. One consumer RGB-D camera for an own-rig target and a live demo. One 24-48 GB GPU for online LoRA updates and differentiable rendering. Object CAD models (YCB) are needed for the model-based object branch.
research_questions.risks: (1) Novelty: fitting to RGB-D depth is a decades-old model-based technique, and test-time optimization with contact and penetration terms is standard in hand-object reconstruction pipelines. Reviewers will accept the paper only if weight-space adaptation clearly beats output optimization or brings something it cannot (amortization, gains on occluded frames). (2) Training-data contamination: HaMeR's training mix includes DexYCB and HO3D, so clean targets are scarce, and a lab-trained source model is weaker than state of the art. (3) Online adaptation can drift or collapse on long streams. (4) Consumer depth is unreliable on fingers and thin or specular objects, exactly where contact happens. (5) The method is RGB-D-only, which narrows its audience compared with egocentric RGB, and camera-conditioning approaches (ACE-Ego-Hand arXiv 2608.20308, MetricHMSR CVPR 2026, ScaleHP arXiv 2606.25619) may shrink the metric gap from the RGB side. (6) The model-based object branch needs CAD; model-free objects would need a different object prior.

research_questions.question: RQ3 (certification without labels). Can the per-sequence and per-frame metric error of a hand-object tracker on a new, unlabelled rig be predicted from label-free signals? Candidate signals are the depth-rendering residual, disagreement across models or views, penetration, contact flicker, temporal jerk and violations of object rigidity. The prediction needs to be good enough to rank candidate models for that rig, to give calibrated error bounds for downstream robot-demonstration or digital-twin use, and to decide when the RQ2 adaptation should be triggered.
research_questions.why_top_venue: The root cause of P21 is that the target domain has no labels, so today the gap can be neither measured nor managed on a new rig. Accuracy estimation under distribution shift is established for classification, but for structured metric 3D regression of hand-object interaction I found little. The closest recent work, 'Detecting Pose Estimation Failures via Keypoint Self-Consistency' (arXiv 2608.03516), handles object pose only and needs a small labelled calibration set from the target domain. Downstream users (imitation learning from human video, digital twins) need per-frame trust more than one more mm of average accuracy, which gives the work a CV-plus-robotics audience.
research_questions.method_sketch: Build a meta-dataset from the RQ1 transfer matrix: tuples of (model, dataset or rig, sequence, frame) mapped to the true CS-MPJPE, object ADD-S and contact error. Compute label-free features: depth residual statistics inside hand and object masks, spread across an ensemble of public models (HaMeR, WiLoR, the lab model) and across augmentations, penetration volume, contact on/off flicker, joint jerk, object-frame drift of contact points, and 2D reprojection disagreement with an independent 2D detector. Train a light error regressor with leave-one-rig-out splits so that it cannot memorize dataset identity, adding adversarial or grouped normalization if needed. Wrap it in conformal prediction weighted for covariate shift to get error intervals. Downstream use: filter or down-weight frames before kinematic retargeting to a simulated dexterous hand, and gate the RQ2 adaptation.
research_questions.minimum_experiment: Leave-one-dataset-out across 4-5 datasets (DexYCB, HO3D v3, HOGraspNet, ARCTIC, HOT3D, with depth features only where depth exists) and 3 models. Report Spearman correlation between predicted and true per-sequence CS-MPJPE, AUROC for frames above an error threshold, and empirical coverage of the conformal intervals on the held-out rig. Baselines: the model's own confidence, MC-dropout variance, ensemble disagreement alone, and an oracle trained with target labels. One downstream check: simulated grasp-retargeting success with and without filtering (MuJoCo or Isaac, single GPU).
research_questions.data_and_hardware: Same public datasets as RQ1. No new capture is needed; the lab's own rig can be a qualitative or object-pose-only held-out target. One GPU; the regressor itself is tiny, and the cost is running the models to build the meta-dataset.
research_questions.risks: (1) The fundamental limit: predictions that are consistent but wrong pass every self-consistency check. A shared global-scale or depth bias across ensemble members is exactly the cross-rig failure, and only the depth residual can catch it, so the RGB-only setting may fail. (2) Only a handful of rigs exist, so the meta-dataset has few independent domains and conclusions may not generalize. (3) The regressor may learn dataset identity rather than error. (4) The general ML area (accuracy estimation, conformal prediction under shift) is mature, so reviewers will ask what is specific to hand-object interaction. (5) The downstream robotics gain may be small if retargeting is already robust to noisy frames.

fit.thesis_assets_help: The thesis assets give a modest edge; they do not decide anything. (1) The single desk RGB-D rig is a genuinely different target domain: third-person desk layout and a consumer depth sensor, unlike the DexYCB or HO3D layouts and egocentric headsets. It is useful as an extra held-out rig for RQ2 and RQ3 and as a live demo. (2) The ArUco-marked object with metric pose gives real object-pose ground truth on that new rig without motion capture. Public data does not offer this in the same configuration, so object ADD-S on the own rig can be scored. There is no hand ground truth, so hand metrics there are unavailable. (3) The measured, held and constrained honesty labels are a conceptual precursor of RQ3's per-frame trust estimation and could serve as a weak signal for when depth is reliable. They are hand-designed for one setup, though, and not evidence by themselves. (4) The causal 30 fps chain is a ready testbed for online, streaming adaptation in RQ2. (5) The Unity twin could render controlled sweeps of camera placement and intrinsics for the RQ1 viewpoint and intrinsics factors, but it adds a synthetic-to-real confound and should support real-image interventions, not replace them. (6) Object-conditioned recovery of an occluded holding arm is only loosely related; it may supply occlusion-stratified test cases. (7) The 28 recordings of one subject are too small and single-subject for any generalization claim; they serve only as a qualitative or object-pose-only target. Overall, the assets save perhaps a few weeks of setup and give one honest extra rig. They do not create a competitive advantage over well-resourced labs.
fit.what_a_small_lab_cannot_do_here: The main 2026 attack on this pain point is data scale and new capture, and a small lab cannot compete on either. Specifically, it cannot: (1) capture new in-the-wild multi-view or mocap ground truth at the scale of SHOW3D, the Ego-Exo mobile rig, ESTHER3D or EPIC-Contact; (2) pretrain foundation models on 1-5k hours of pseudo-labelled egocentric video (MINT, InfiniHand), or retrain ViT-H HaMeR, WiLoR or SAM 3D Body-class models from scratch on one GPU; (3) acquire and calibrate several headsets (Aria, Quest 3) and rigs, so cross-headset work must rely on HOT3D and other public data; (4) collect labelled target data across many rigs, which is the fix the field currently uses; (5) reach the clinical and surgical domains (POV-Surgery, OphNet-3D) or train human-NeRF models at MVHumanNet scale, both part of the P21 cluster; (6) win a race on camera-conditioned, rig-agnostic architectures, a 2026 line already active (ACE-Ego-Hand arXiv 2608.20308, MetricHMSR CVPR 2026, ScaleHP arXiv 2606.25619, V-HPOT, HGGT arXiv 2603.23997). A small lab should therefore stay on label-free adaptation, metric diagnosis and certification, where public data plus one RGB-D camera and one GPU are enough, and should not frame its work as generic domain generalization, which is crowded and mostly gets mid-tier venues.

painpoint.name: Fast motion, motion blur and low light break RGB capture

evidence.latest_state: The problem is now better measured, but it is not solved for hand-object or RGB-D capture. On EgoXtreme (CVPR 2026, about 1.3M egocentric Aria frames covering maintenance, sports and smoke-filled rescue), zero-shot RGB object-pose estimators collapse under low light, blur and smoke. The pain-point record gives PicoPose ADD(-S) recall at 0.1d of 2.81 on sports, and 15.12 falling to 4.74 with dehazing on smoke. The authors confirm that deblurring does not help and that temporal tracking-based methods are the most promising. On the object side, event cameras now have working methods. EventTrack6D (Event6D, CVPR 2026, KAIST with Bowen Wen of NVIDIA) tracks novel objects at more than 120 FPS, was trained only on synthetic data, and transfers to real data without fine-tuning. A keypoint-based event tracker followed at ICRA 2026, and YCB-Ev 1.1 and YCB-Ev SD (50k synthetic event sequences) supply event ground truth. On the hand side there are now real event-hand datasets: EgoEVHands (stereo events, 5,419 sequences, 30.54 mm MPJPE, better than RGB stereo in low light and bimanual occlusion) and EEH-R in EventEgoHands++ (about 1M frames including low light, IEEE Access 2026). For the body, E-3DPSM reports up to 19% lower egocentric event MPJPE at 80 Hz, and FlashCap provides millisecond-accurate event, RGB, LiDAR and IMU ground truth. I found no 2025-2026 paper that jointly reconstructs hand and object (or bimanual hand-object contact) under fast motion, blur or low light with metric 3D ground truth. Also missing are any for blurred RGB-D (depth-RGB misalignment under fast motion) and for athletic body-object motion beyond AthletePose3D-style fine-tuning. Blur-robust RGB hand work such as HandFlow, ESTHER and Direction-Aware Hybrid shows robustness only qualitatively or as a side claim; I found no dedicated blurred hand-object benchmark.

evidence.crowdedness: MEDIUM: at least a dozen 2025-2026 papers attack pieces of the problem. The active groups are KAIST (EgoXtreme, Event6D with NVIDIA), IIT Genoa, Keio, Zhejiang and several robotics labs. Each paper covers only hands, only rigid objects or only bodies; I found none on joint hand-object or RGB-D capture under blur and low light.
evidence.trend: rising: CVPR 2026 accepted both a dedicated extreme-condition benchmark (EgoXtreme) and an event-based novel-object tracker (Event6D). 2026 also brought several real event-hand datasets (EgoEVHands, EEH-R) and event-augmented robot policies (E-VLA, ECHO). Attention is therefore growing fast, driven by egocentric AR and robot demonstration capture.

skeptics.reasons:
I found no 2025-2026 work that solves this pain point or turns it into plain engineering. Activity is growing quickly in one area: event-camera hand pose, especially egocentric hands.
- EventEgoHands (ICIP 2025) and EventEgoHands++ (arXiv 2609.17189, Sep 2026) add a real egocentric event dataset of about 1M annotated frames, including dark scenes and hand-object recordings.
- EgoEV-HandPose (arXiv 2605.12297, May 2026) adds a stereo event dataset of real bimanual hands, with low light.
- EvHand-FPV (arXiv 2509.13883) is another egocentric event hand tracker.

These works narrow the claim that events "lack accurate labels" for hands alone. Even so, the best reported event-only error is still about 30 mm MPJPE (EgoEV-HandPose 30.54 mm, consistent with EBH 28.6-30.8 mm). Image-plus-event methods reach 12-16 mm, so the metric is far from saturated.

Object pose with events has also moved forward, but the work is narrow:
- datasets: E-POSE (Scientific Data 2025), MTEvent (CVPR 2025 workshop), YCB-Ev SD (synthetic, arXiv 2511.11344);
- trackers: a learning-free event-based 6D tracker (arXiv 2603.08264, 2026) and event-flow-plus-frame 6-DoF tracking (arXiv 2508.14776).

These need known object models, are tested on rigid objects with no hands, and claim only parity with, or a modest gain over, existing methods.

The curated awesome-event-based-hands list (checked 2026-10) has no 2025-2026 paper that jointly reconstructs hands and objects from events. Its two hand-object entries cover hand-motion transfer and kitchen action recognition. I found no blur-robust hand-object or bimanual RGB-D method or benchmark in 2025-2026. Blur-aware hand-mesh work is still BlurHandNet (CVPR 2023) and EBH (ECCV 2024), plus video-temporal methods such as OmniHands and DanceHMR, which treat blur only as a nuisance.

The pain point's own benchmark evidence still stands as of 2026: EgoXtreme ADD(-S) recall below 25% under fast sports motion, preprocessing that hurts, and an AthletePose3D velocity correlation of 0.11. So the general pain point survives.

I would narrow it in two ways:
1. "Event-based hand pose lacks real labelled data" is no longer accurate. Two real datasets of about 1M frames exist, and the remaining gap is accuracy.
2. Body-only athletic motion and generic object pose are side issues for this field. The core unsolved part is the joint hand-object (and bimanual) reconstruction under fast motion, blur or low light, which has neither a method nor a ground-truth benchmark. That is because the RGB-D and marker pipelines used for ground truth fail on exactly those frames.

Event-camera work now has real labelled hand-only data (about 1M frames), but event-only error is still about 30 mm, and event object trackers need known object models and are tested without hands. skeptics.reasons:
Partly survives, partly an artifact. I checked P22's record in w3b_painpoints.json and matched its 28 paper ids to titles in w2b_part1.json and w2b_part2.json. The papers come from many groups and venues: body/sports datasets (AthletePose3D, WorldPose, HardMo, RELI11D, FreeMan), pedestrian and dashcam work (PVCP, pedestrian motion reconstruction), LiDAR mocap (LIP), robot-view forecasting (HARPER), event-based pose (EHPT-XC, EBH, YCB-Ev), object pose datasets (EgoXtreme, HANDAL, DTTD, HouseCat6D, PhoCaL, ClearPose, IndustryShapes), surveys, and InterCap. So the narrow claim that motion blur hurts RGB pose estimation is not one group's quirk. Outside the record, BlurHand (CVPR 2023, Seoul National University) and the event-hand line (EvHandPose TPAMI 2024, Ev2Hands 3DV 2024, EvRGBHand CVPR 2024) independently state the same problem for hands.

The pain point as stated is still largely an aggregate of artifacts.

(1) Most of the strong numbers are off-field for hand-object or bimanual capture. AthletePose3D's 234 mm MPJPE is a training-distribution shift (models trained only on Human3.6M), not an RGB sensing limit; it drops to 98 mm once athletic data is added. WorldPose, the pedestrian datasets and the 10 fps LiDAR evidence concern full bodies at stadium or street scale. EgoXtreme's collapse mixes smoke and extreme lighting with egocentric sports motion, which is a "we built an extreme-condition dataset" setup.

(2) Only about three items speak to the author's setting: InterCap avoiding very fast interactions with Kinect, EBH on blurred hands, and HANDAL on glare. The ground-truth-pipeline claim comes from projects that chose commodity sensors (Kinect, Aria). The mocap and high-speed-imaging community has long handled fast motion in the capture setup itself with global-shutter, short-exposure, high-fps and strobe-lit rigs. HOT3D, for example, takes ground truth from optical markers rather than from blurred frames.

(3) The sub-claim that event cameras "lack established pose algorithms" is false for hands and outdated for rigid objects. For hands: EvHandPose, Ev2Hands, EvRGBHand, EBH, EventEgoHands, and BlurHandNet for blurred RGB. For rigid objects: YCB-Ev, MTevent, line-based event 6DoF tracking (arXiv 2408.03225), Event6D (arXiv 2603.28045), and optical-flow-guided event 6DoF tracking (arXiv 2512.21053). The sub-claim reflects the object-pose papers' framing only.

(4) The claim that restoration hurts rests on essentially two papers: EgoXtreme for deblur, dehaze and low-light enhancement on zero-shot object pose, and EBH/BlurHand for deblur-then-estimate on hands.

What survives is narrower. Fast hand and tool motion during manipulation gets blurred, and RGB and depth fall out of alignment, on commodity RGB-D. Datasets avoid this regime, so no real benchmark with 3D ground truth covers fast hand-object interaction.

Metadata note: the field list gives AthletePose3D as ECCV 2022 (it is a CVPR 2025 workshop paper as far as I know) and EgoBody as arXiv 2026 (it is ECCV 2022). Both look like mislabels; I did not re-verify them.

skeptics.reframe: On commodity 30 fps RGB-D sensors, fast hand and tool motion during manipulation gets blurred, and the RGB and depth frames fall out of alignment. Hand-object datasets therefore exclude this regime through stop-and-go capture, blur filtering or marker-based ground truth. As a result, no real benchmark with accurate 3D hand and object ground truth covers fast, contact-rich interaction. Blur-aware and event-based methods exist for hands alone (BlurHandNet, EvHandPose, Ev2Hands, EvRGBHand) and for rigid objects alone (YCB-Ev, MTevent, Event6D), but I found none, unverified, for joint hand-object pose and contact under fast motion.

skeptics.reasons:
The skeptic case is partly right but does not hold for the whole pain point. Two parts of P22 have no research question in them. (a) "Real blurred datasets with 3D ground truth are rare" is a wish for more capture and annotation effort. (b) Part of the problem already has a known engineering fix that only needs resources: a high-frame-rate, short-exposure global-shutter camera under strong lighting, or a beam-splitter rig. Dataset builders already sidestep the problem with stop-and-go capture and blur filtering. If the pain point is read as "collect more blurred or dark data", it is refuted.

At least one research question survives, and top venues have accepted work on it. The evidence shows that the obvious fix, restoring the image first and then estimating pose, fails. In EgoXtreme (CVPR 2026, verified), deblurring, dehazing and low-light enhancement lower PicoPose ADD(-S) recall: 2.81 to 2.58 at 0.1d, and 15.12 to 4.74 under smoke. EBH (ECCV 2024, verified) reports that one blurry image is temporally ambiguous and that deblur-first does not work. That makes the issue a modelling question, not a resource question. The question: can blur be treated as a measurement of motion inside the exposure window instead of as noise? Concretely, a forward model of how a camera forms an image, including exposure-time integration, rolling shutter and time-of-flight depth motion artifacts, applied jointly to an articulated hand and a rigid object. Fitting that model would recover hand-object trajectories inside one exposure. The same forward model could produce self-consistency supervision for exactly the frames where human annotation is unreliable.

Top venues have accepted this framing for single entities: BlurHandNet (CVPR 2023) and EBH (ECCV 2024) for hands, Human from Blur for bodies, Shape from Blur and Motion-from-Blur for objects. Event-based 6DoF object tracking and event-based hand mesh work are active in 2025-2026. I found no joint hand-object (or bimanual) method or benchmark that models blur or uses events with 3D labels. The ryhara event-hands list tags only 4 hand-object papers, and from their titles they appear to be mostly action recognition and manufacturing datasets. Hand-object contact and grasp constraints are a plausible way to resolve the temporal ambiguity of one blurred frame. That is a significant question.

Points against a high score:
- Event-based hand pose is getting crowded.
- The hand-only blur problem is partly addressed, so novelty depends on the joint hand-object or RGB-D angle.
- Low light and smoke add little beyond the existing robustness literature.
- A reviewer may answer "just use a faster camera" unless the work targets commodity or egocentric sensors and automatic labelling.

Score 6.5: the pain point survives as a research question in narrowed form, not as stated.

skeptics.reframe: Commodity RGB and RGB-D sensors blend fast hand-object motion into blur, rolling-shutter distortion and time-of-flight depth artifacts during each exposure. Current tracking and labelling pipelines discard these artifacts as noise, and restoring the image first makes pose worse. The open question: can a forward model of image formation over the exposure window, applied jointly to hand and object (or used with events as a side channel), use contact constraints to resolve the temporal ambiguity of a blurred frame? The goal is to recover the hand-object trajectory inside one exposure and to produce self-supervised 3D labels for the fastest frames, which are exactly the ones existing datasets filter out.

fit.worth_pursuing: MAYBE. The gap is real and I checked it on 2026-10-02. Blur-as-signal and event methods exist for hands alone (BlurHandNet CVPR 2023, EBH ECCV 2024), for rigid objects alone (DeFMO CVPR 2021, Shape from Blur NeurIPS 2021, Motion-from-Blur CVPR 2022, Event6D CVPR 2026, which uses events plus depth) and for bodies (Human from Blur; venue not verified). arXiv API queries on blur, exposure, rolling shutter and events combined with hand and object found no joint hand-object method and no benchmark for this regime. Neither does the awesome-event-based-hands list: its 4 hand-object entries cover action recognition, motion transfer and manufacturing. The obvious alternative, restoring the image first, is known to fail (EgoXtreme: PicoPose 15.12 to 4.74 with dehazing, 2.81 to 2.58 on sports; EBH: deblur-first fails), so a model-based route is open. RQ1 becomes a YES only if three things hold. (1) A two-month pilot shows that 'drop blurred frames and interpolate from sharp neighbours' does not close the error gap on realistic fast manipulation. (2) The no-mocap ground truth described below is accurate to well under the effect size. (3) The work is fast enough to land before the well-resourced groups (SNU for BlurHand/EBH, KAIST with NVIDIA for EgoXtreme/Event6D, Meta for HOT3D) extend to hand-object. Low light and smoke are not worth pursuing for this author: they add little beyond robustness work, and they need capture conditions a small lab cannot produce safely or at scale.

research_questions.question: RQ1 (primary). Can motion blur in commodity RGB / RGB-D video be treated as a measurement of the hand-object trajectory inside each exposure? The idea is a joint, contact-coupled forward model of exposure integration that recovers 3D hand pose, 6D object pose and contact at sub-frame times, on exactly the fast frames that current pipelines fail on and that datasets filter out. A second part: can this be benchmarked with sub-exposure ground truth without motion capture?
research_questions.why_top_venue: Top venues have accepted blur-as-signal for each single entity: hands (BlurHandNet CVPR 2023, EBH ECCV 2024), rigid objects (DeFMO CVPR 2021, Shape from Blur NeurIPS 2021, Motion-from-Blur CVPR 2022) and bodies (Human from Blur, venue unverified). An extreme-condition object benchmark (EgoXtreme CVPR 2026) was also accepted, and it concludes that restoration hurts and temporal tracking is the way forward. No joint hand-object version or benchmark exists (checked 2026-10-02). The scientific claim is a new constraint, not engineering. A rigid known object held in a grasp shares its motion with the hand during the exposure. The object's blur streak is a well-posed rigid-motion measurement, so it can resolve the temporal-direction and speed ambiguity that makes a single blurred hand image ill-posed (the ambiguity BlurHandNet and EBH report). A first benchmark with sub-exposure 3D ground truth for fast hand-object interaction would also become a reference that datasets now avoid by design: InterCap avoided very fast interactions because of blur and RGB-depth misalignment.
research_questions.method_sketch: (1) State: per-frame continuous-time trajectories over the exposure window, chained across frames: MANO pose and global transform for each hand, and the SE(3) object pose for a known template (YCB or scanned), each as a low-order spline. (2) Forward model: render K = 8-16 sub-exposure samples with a differentiable rasterizer (nvdiffrast). Appearance comes from an object texture taken from the scan and a hand appearance model fitted on sharp frames (parametric texture or Gaussian hand avatar). Average in linear radiance after inverting the camera response, apply per-row rolling-shutter timing, and compare to the observed blurred RGB with photometric, alpha-matte and silhouette losses. A depth residual is evaluated at the depth exposure time, which is offset from the RGB exposure, so depth acts as a second time sample. (3) Priors: a grasp-rigidity term (the relative hand-object pose varies slowly while in contact), contact and penetration terms, and smoothness across frames. (4) Initialisation and amortisation: per-frame feed-forward estimates (WiLoR or HaMeR for hands, FoundationPose for the object) plus neighbouring sharp frames. A learned predictor extends BlurHandNet-style temporal unfolding (start/mid/end states) to hand plus object; it is trained on synthetic exposure-integrated data and refined by test-time optimisation. (5) Output: sub-exposure trajectories with uncertainty. The same optimiser can automatically label fast frames in existing recordings.
research_questions.minimum_experiment: (a) Go/no-go pilot, months 1-2: 10 self-captured fast sequences (shaking, hammer strikes, toss-and-catch, quick pour and flick, fast handover, i.e. sustained blur and direction reversals). Plot WiLoR/HaMeR and FoundationPose error against blur streak length, and run the 'discard blurred frames and interpolate' baseline. Continue only if errors on the sustained-blur segments clearly exceed what interpolation achieves. (b) Synthetic: synthesize blur by 8-16x frame interpolation and averaging of DexYCB, HO3D v3 and ARCTIC clips, with interpolated ground truth (the BlurHand recipe), plus rendered exposure-integrated hand-object scenes. (c) Real benchmark: 2-3 short-exposure global-shutter cameras at 200-500 fps under strong or IR lighting give sharp reference views. A consumer RGB-D camera at 30 fps on auto exposure records natural blur. Hardware or LED-flash sync to sub-millisecond. Ground truth is a multi-view MANO fit plus markerless object pose on the sharp frames, transferred to the blurred camera through extrinsics and timestamps, so every blurred frame has ground truth at its exposure start, middle and end. Report ground-truth error on a held-out sharp view. Target 6-10 subjects, 10-15 objects, 40-80 sequences, 20-40k blurred test frames. (d) Metrics: hand MPJPE and PA-MPJPE and object ADD-S at exposure start, middle and end; motion-direction accuracy; contact F1; penetration; all stratified by streak length. Baselines: WiLoR/HaMeR, BlurHandNet, deblur-then-estimate, FoundationPose tracking, a recent joint hand-object reconstruction method, and interpolation. Ablations: no grasp coupling, no depth timing, no rolling-shutter model, no amortised initialisation.
research_questions.data_and_hardware: Existing consumer RGB-D camera (the author's D435). 2-3 global-shutter USB3 machine-vision cameras that reach 200+ fps at reduced resolution; I estimate roughly USD 100-1500 each, prices not verified. LED or IR flood lights, an LED or trigger sync board, and a YCB object set (about USD 300). One 24 GB GPU is enough: optimisation is offline, minutes per sequence, and amortised training is ResNet/ViT-scale. Public data: DexYCB, HO3D v3, ARCTIC, HOT3D, BlurHand, InterHand2.6M. Ethics approval for human subjects. Total extra hardware is roughly USD 1.5-4k (estimate).
research_questions.risks: (1) Reviewers may say 'just use a faster camera'. The work must be framed around the cameras that actually record demonstrations and egocentric data (commodity RGB-D, headsets, wrist cameras) and around labelling existing footage. (2) The interpolation baseline may close most of the gap at normal manipulation speeds; the pilot gates this. (3) Pseudo ground truth from 2-3 cheap cameras may reach only about 5-10 mm for the hand (estimate), close to the effect size. Ground-truth error must be measured and reported. (4) Sub-millisecond sync across different cameras is fiddly. (5) A hand appearance model under blur (shading, skin texture) may be the bottleneck; silhouettes and alpha mattes are the fallback. (6) The method needs known object templates; template-free would be stronger but much harder. (7) Fiducials on objects for ground truth leak into the test images as a shortcut. Use markerless object ground truth, or markers only on faces the test camera cannot see. (8) Getting scooped: the SNU group (BlurHand/EBH), KAIST (EgoXtreme/Event6D) or Meta (HOT3D) could extend to hand-object quickly.
target_venues: NeurIPS (Datasets and Benchmarks track, for the benchmark alone)

research_questions.question: RQ2. In one commodity RGB-D device, RGB and depth are captured at different times. On the D435, colour is rolling-shutter with a long exposure, while depth comes from global-shutter IR imagers with a different exposure centre; the IR stream can also run faster at reduced resolution. This sensor detail is from general knowledge of Intel's datasheet and was not re-checked here. Can a causal tracker that places every measurement at its true capture time (per-row RGB time, depth exposure time, optional high-rate IR) and couples hands to the held object track fast bimanual manipulation? It would need lower error and lag than frame-synchronous fusion, so that robot demonstrations can be recorded at natural speed rather than slowed down.
research_questions.why_top_venue: Demonstration capture for robot learning is a stated application, and capture setups avoid fast motion (InterCap, record 1563: very fast interactions avoided because of blur and RGB-depth misalignment). Continuous-time, asynchronous, rolling-shutter-aware estimation is standard in visual-inertial odometry and SLAM. An arXiv API query on rolling shutter or exposure time with hand or grasp returned no hand-object tracker that models these timings (2026-10-02). For CVPR the fit is moderate. The fit is good for ICRA and RA-L. It reaches CoRL or RSS only with a downstream result: policies or retargeted trajectories from natural-speed demonstrations that match or beat those from slowed demonstrations.
research_questions.method_sketch: Fixed-lag sliding-window smoother with a continuous-time state: SE(3) B-splines for each wrist and the object, a spline over MANO articulation, and an explicit contact or attachment state. Measurement models: (1) 2D hand and object keypoints and masks from RGB, each stamped with its row time, with covariance inflated along the local blur direction estimated from the image; (2) depth point-to-model residuals at the depth exposure time; (3) optional global-shutter IR frames (emitter interleaved or off) as a sharp side channel; (4) a hand-object attachment constraint while in contact; (5) online estimation of the RGB-to-depth time offset and rolling-shutter readout time, as in Kalibr-style temporal calibration. Must run in real time on one GPU.
research_questions.minimum_experiment: Use the RQ1 sharp-reference rig as ground truth. Compare (a) a frame-synchronous causal baseline, (b) per-frame offline state of the art, and (c) the continuous-time tracker, ablating each timing component (row time, depth offset, IR side channel, coupling). Plot hand and object error and latency against hand speed, up to the fastest motions in the pilot. Measure the actual RGB-depth offset and its effect on contact and penetration errors. Test at least two sensor types (active stereo such as the D435, and a time-of-flight camera if one can be borrowed) to show the timing model generalises. Optional downstream test: retarget natural-speed and slowed demonstrations to a simulated or borrowed arm and compare trajectory fidelity and task success.
research_questions.data_and_hardware: The D435 the author already owns, a borrowed time-of-flight RGB-D camera if possible, the RQ1 reference cameras and sync, and one GPU. Public hand-object datasets do not expose per-row timing or raw IR, so the data must be self-captured: a few subjects and about 20-40 sequences are enough for a robotics paper. A borrowed arm or a simulator is needed for the CoRL/RSS version.
research_questions.risks: (1) The effect may be small at typical manipulation speeds, since 30 fps readout skew is a few to tens of milliseconds; the pilot must show it matters. (2) The work can be read as engineering or device-specific. (3) A CVPR-class venue is unlikely without RQ1's forward model. (4) The robot result needs a borrowed arm. (5) Firmware and SDK timestamp quirks can hide the true exposure times and need careful measurement, for example with an LED timing board.
target_venues: CoRL or RSS (only with a downstream policy or retargeting result)

research_questions.question: RQ3 (conditional on buying an event camera). One event camera is added to an RGB-D desk rig, and hand and held object are coupled through contact. Can this track a fast-moving object and its holding hand or hands jointly through blur and low light? The test is whether the coupling closes the gap between event-only hand error (about 28.6-30.8 mm MPJPE in EBH; 30.54 mm in EgoEV-HandPose) and image-plus-event error (12.0-16.4 mm in EBH). Object-only event trackers (Event6D: events plus depth, more than 120 FPS) ignore the hand.
research_questions.why_top_venue: The field is moving fast here: Event6D and EgoXtreme at CVPR 2026, real event-hand datasets in 2026 (EgoEVHands, EEH-R). Every paper still covers either hands or objects, never both. A first joint event hand-object tracker with a ground-truth evaluation would be a recognisable contribution. The contact coupling gives it scientific content beyond merging two trackers.
research_questions.method_sketch: Object branch: event-plus-depth novel-object tracking in the style of Event6D (whether its code is released is unverified). The tracked high-rate rigid motion drives the global motion of the grasping hand through an attachment constraint. Hand articulation is updated from events plus RGB (EvRGBHand/EBH-style features) at a lower rate. Joint optimisation or a learned fusion head adds contact and penetration terms. Training uses simulated events (v2e/ESIM) from synthetic hand-object renders and from the RQ1 high-fps reference footage, which narrows the simulation-to-real gap. Low-light tests keep ground truth valid by lighting the reference cameras with IR, which the event and RGB cameras can be filtered against.
research_questions.minimum_experiment: Capture 20-40 sequences with the event camera, the RGB-D camera and the RQ1 reference cameras, at normal light and at controlled low lux. Compare with Event6D (object), EvRGBHand/EBH-style hand baselines, RGB-D baselines and RQ1. Ablate the coupling. Metrics: hand MPJPE, object ADD-S, contact F1 and latency. Also report results on the public event-hand sets (EBH, EvRealHands, EEH-R) to show the hand branch is competitive.
research_questions.data_and_hardware: One event camera, roughly USD 1-6k depending on model (unverified estimate). Event-to-RGB-D extrinsic and temporal calibration with blinking patterns. The RQ1 rig and one GPU. Public data: EBH, EvRealHands, EventEgoHands++ EEH-R, YCB-Ev and YCB-Ev SD, and the Event6D benchmarks.
research_questions.risks: (1) Crowded and fast-moving: KAIST with NVIDIA, MPI (Ev2Hands line), Keio and SNU already hold event data and pipelines. (2) It can look incremental, as 'Event6D plus an event hand tracker'. (3) The event simulation-to-real gap and calibration take time. (4) Real ground truth is the same bottleneck as RQ1. (5) The hardware cost is real for a small lab. Pursue only after RQ1's rig and benchmark exist, as an extension that reuses them.

fit.thesis_assets_help:
The assets give a small to moderate edge, mostly for RQ2 and for the pilot.
(1) Sensor. The author already uses a RealSense D435, which has exactly the timing structure RQ2 exploits: rolling-shutter RGB, global-shutter IR stereo for depth, and a faster IR mode. This is from general knowledge of Intel's datasheet and was not re-checked here. Existing capture, calibration and transport code saves roughly 1-2 months.
(2) Honesty labels. The measured/held/constrained labels already flag frames where marker measurement failed. Cross-tabulating them against hand and object speed in the 28 recordings gives a quick motivating statistic: how often fast motion forces 'held' frames. It is pilot evidence only, since it comes from one subject.
(3) Occluded-arm recovery. The object-conditioned recovery of the occluded holding arm is the same idea as the grasp-coupling prior in RQ1 and RQ3 (the held object's pose constrains the holding limb), so the concept, and possibly code, carries over.
(4) ArUco object pose. The marker-based metric object pose is useful only as ground truth on the sharp reference views. ArUco fails on blurred frames, and markers visible to the test camera become a shortcut, so they cannot label the blurred stream.
(5) Causal chain. The causal 30 fps chain is a ready frame-synchronous baseline for RQ2.
(6) Unity twin. It could render exposure-integrated synthetic frames by accumulating sub-frame renders, a minor help; Blender or Kubric-style pipelines are the usual choice.
(7) Recordings. The 28 recordings of one subject are not a benchmark and would not satisfy reviewers. Use them as pilot data only.

painpoint.name: Embodiment gap: human hand motion does not map to executable robot actions

evidence.latest_state: The field has moved from pose-level kinematic retargeting toward contact-, interaction- and physics-preserving retargeting, and a single cross-embodiment success rate around 55-65 percent in simulation is now the frontier. The best reported number is Contact-Anchored Retargeting with Residual Policy Learning (arXiv 2609.24093, Sept 2026). It raises single-hand mocap transfer from 7.3 to 59.3 percent over 25,454 trajectories and dual-hand success from 16.0 to 62.4 percent over 25 tasks across four robot hands, with zero-shot real bimanual execution. SPIDER (arXiv 2511.09484, Meta/CMU/Berkeley) applies physics-informed sampling to GigaHands, OakInk2 and ARCTIC: 9 embodiments, 6 datasets, a gain of 18 percent over standard sampling, and 10x faster than RL. ManipTrans (CVPR 2025) learns residual policies for bimanual transfer and released DexManipNet with 3.3K episodes. From monocular video, C2Dex reaches end-to-end success of 57.78 percent on DexYCB and 26.67 percent on TACO, against baselines of 17.78 and 10.00. DexMan gains 19 percent on OakInk-v2. TopoRetarget improves Pen-Spin training success by 40.6 points on ContactPose-based retargeting. Touch2Robot puts the robot hand's contact back into the collection loop and raises real replay completion from 37.9 to 72.1 percent. ReForce (Xiaolong Wang group) adds force-aware retargeting, and OmniRetarget and ContactMimic bring interaction-preserving retargeting to humanoid whole-body work. Still open: success stays near 60 percent even in simulation and lower from video (TACO 27 percent). Bimanual transfer still trails single-hand transfer in most reports. Contact and force are mostly inferred through physics refinement rather than measured from human data. No paper resolves the strategy mismatch, where the human method does not suit the robot (two hands versus one gripper, workspace limits), and there is no shared benchmark for comparing methods.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: Dexterous Robot Manipulation from Human Demonstrations via Contact-Anchored Retargeting and Residual Policy Learning
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Three stages: physics refinement with a simulated MANO hand to recover contacts and forces, contact-anchored retargeting, then a residual RL policy. Single-hand success rises from 7.3 to 59.3 percent (25,454 trajectories), dual-hand from 16.0 to 62.4 percent; transfers to four hands and runs zero-shot on real bimanual tasks.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: SPIDER: Scalable Physics-Informed Dexterous Retargeting
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Physics-based sampling with curriculum virtual-contact guidance turns kinematic human demonstrations (GigaHands, OakInk2, ARCTIC and others) into dynamically feasible trajectories. Covers 9 embodiments and 6 datasets, gains 18 percent over standard sampling, runs 10x faster than RL, and releases a large feasible robot dataset.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: ManipTrans: Efficient Dexterous Bimanual Manipulation Transfer via Residual Learning
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Pretrains a generalist hand-motion imitator, then fine-tunes a residual module under interaction constraints to transfer bimanual human manipulation to dexterous hands. Releases DexManipNet (3.3K episodes, including pen capping and bottle unscrewing).

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: C2Dex: Contact-Consistent Reconstruction and Retargeting for Dexterous Manipulation from Monocular Video
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Contact-consistent hand-object reconstruction from monocular video followed by retargeting. End-to-end success is 57.78 percent on DexYCB and 26.67 percent on TACO, against 17.78 and 10.00 for baselines; validated by real-robot replay.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: TopoRetarget: Interaction-Preserving Retargeting for Dexterous Manipulation

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: ReForce: Learning Force-aware Retargeting for Dexterous Manipulation
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Learns a retargeting that maps human motion and forces to robot actions reproducing the intended contact. Reports lower force-tracking error on paper-cup grasping and tongs tasks; the abstract gives no numbers.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Shows the predicted robot-hand contact to the demonstrator during collection, with contact-aware RL retargeting. Real replay completion rises from 37.9 to 72.1 percent, and Diffusion Policy improves by 29.1 points.

Beats object-aware replay by more than 55 percent and imitation learning by more than 68 percent.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Interaction-mesh retargeting that preserves agent-object-terrain relations under kinematic constraints, with augmentation across morphologies. Trains RL loco-manipulation policies that transfer zero-shot to a Unitree G1.
