evidence.crowdedness: HIGH. At least 12 papers from 2025-2026 attack the problem directly, many appearing month by month in mid to late 2026, from strong robotics groups: Meta FAIR with CMU and Berkeley (SPIDER), Xiaolong Wang at UCSD (ReForce), BIGAI (ManipTrans), Stanford Bohg/Liu (Human2Sim2Robot), Hang Zhao at Tsinghua (TopoRetarget), and several Chinese robotics labs.
evidence.trend: Rising. Large hand-object mocap datasets (OakInk2, GigaHands, ARCTIC, TACO) and the push to scale dexterous VLA data from human video have made retargeting a bottleneck. The contact- and force-preserving retargeting the pain point proposed is now being built, with several papers posted on arXiv in June to September 2026 alone.

skeptics.reasons:
Partly reduced, not solved. The narrow claim that kinematic retargeting yields non-executable motion (self-collision, penetration, air grasps) has been largely turned into an engineering recipe in 2025-2026. Physics-in-the-loop retargeting now exists with released code: SPIDER (Meta, arXiv 2511.09484, 9 embodiments, 6 datasets, 2.4M feasible frames, open-loop real Franka+Allegro execution), DexMachina (2505.24853, bimanual functional retargeting on ARCTIC with code and a benchmark), OmniRetarget (2509.26633, interaction-mesh retargeting for humanoids with a released dataset), TopoRetarget (2606.16272), REGRIND (2607.11874, retargeting-guided residual RL from one demo with sim-to-real), and Direct Dynamic Retargeting (2605.23762). Cross-hand latent action spaces (XL-VLA, 2603.10158) go after the "mapping tied to one hand" sub-claim.

The pain point as a whole still stands, for three reasons. First, the success metrics are far from saturated, and bimanual or long-horizon cases are still worst. SPIDER reaches 41.3-47.9% on OakInk2 and 42.0% on ARCTIC, against 70.6-87.9% on pick-and-place-heavy GigaHands. C2Dex (2608.07045) reaches 57.78% on DexYCB and 26.67% on TACO. Second, the strongest methods need per-task RL with privileged simulator state and have no real-robot validation: DexMachina says so explicitly, and DexMan reports simulation only. TopoRetarget is single-hand. Third, the strategy and workspace gap (a two-hand human strategy versus a one-gripper robot) and the absence of a functional correspondence across morphologies are not addressed by any of these papers.

Two of these papers also name upstream limits. SPIDER states that its performance depends on the quality of the reconstructed 3D hand-object interaction, and that noisy meshes and motion degrade its trajectories. C2Dex shows that contact-consistent reconstruction is what moves success from 17.78% to 57.78% on DexYCB and from 10.00% to 26.67% on TACO. So the remaining bottleneck is moving back into the thesis author's field: the quality of hand-object reconstruction, especially contact quality.

All numbers were checked against the arXiv abstract or HTML pages. Product-level human-video-to-robot pipelines (for example EgoMimic, Phantom and GR00T) were not checked because the search budget ran out.

skeptics.reframe: Kinematic infeasibility is now handled by physics-based retargeting (SPIDER, DexMachina, OmniRetarget). What remains open is turning bimanual, long-horizon, contact-rich human demonstrations into robot actions that run on real hardware without per-task RL on privileged simulator state. Success there is still about 26-58% (SPIDER on OakInk2 and ARCTIC, C2Dex on TACO and DexYCB). The two dominant causes are noisy, contact-inconsistent 3D reconstruction of the hand-object interaction and the human-to-robot strategy gap. For a tracking and reconstruction thesis, the open part is to capture bimanual hand-object interaction with physically consistent contacts, and to judge that capture by whether it can be executed after retargeting, not only by pose error.

skeptics.reasons:
Taken as a whole, the claim that human hand motion does not map to executable robot actions holds up as a field-wide problem. It is not an artifact of one dataset. The P23 record cites 41 paper ids from at least three communities. In hand-object interaction (HOI) datasets: OakInk and OakInk2, HRDexDB, UniFucGrasp and DexCanvas. In egocentric and VLA (vision-language-action) data: EgoDex, EgoVerse, HuRo, RoboEdit, HumanNet, SABER and Human2Robot. In humanoid and caregiving work: Mimicking-Bench, OpenRoboCare and robot-assisted bathing. The record also cites the UMI-style FastUMI-100K and HiFi-UMI and three surveys. The hardware is varied: Allegro, Shadow, Inspire, XHand, Panda and Unitree G1/H1. Two methods outside the cited set confirm that the gap is real and that separate groups are attacking it. ManipTrans (Li et al., BIGAI, CVPR 2025) moves human bimanual motion to dexterous robot hands with residual learning. DexMachina (Mandi et al., Stanford/NVIDIA, arXiv 2505.24853) proposes functional retargeting because kinematic transfer is not enough. Robotics has also discussed the underlying correspondence problem in imitation learning for over two decades without settling it (unverified in this pass). No community treats the problem as solved. Teleoperation retargeting such as DexPilot and AnyTeleop works only because a human closes the loop, so it does not answer offline transfer from demonstrations.

The artifact concerns apply to the sub-claims and headline numbers, not to the core problem.
1. The "bimanual transfer performs worst" clause rests mainly on one team's HANDS 2025 challenge report (1533: 52.8 vs 76.2 percent). That is a single protocol, and ManipTrans and DexMachina report workable bimanual transfer in simulation.
2. The numbers come from specific setups and do not generalise. The Allegro figure of 1.21 percent is a seed-level success protocol on HRDexDB. The 55.2 percent self-contact figure is from one audit of 288 HuRo trajectories. The 6/5 percent box-lifting result is for a humanoid without dexterous hands.
3. The paper-id count is inflated by duplicates. OakInk2 appears twice (67 and 1456), and the human-activity-video VLA pretraining paper appears twice (869 and 1489). Several entries are dataset papers that only state the gap in their limitations.
4. The "human strategy is wrong for the robot" evidence is anecdotal. It comes from one bag-grocery co-training example (696) and one study of sanding strategies (998).

For this author, the problem is adjacent. It sits in robotics and control, not in tracking and reconstruction. The part that belongs to tracking and reconstruction is narrower: human captures lack contact, force and object-state information, which is what effect-level retargeting needs.

skeptics.reframe: Human hand-object captures, including bimanual ones, record pose but not the contacts, forces and object-state transitions that effect-level (task-preserving) retargeting needs. As a result, retargeted trajectories pass on reconstruction errors such as penetration, floating fingers and self-contact as physically non-executable robot motion. Evidence for a specific bimanual penalty currently comes from a single challenge report and should be treated as provisional.

skeptics.reasons:
P23 does not reduce to an engineering task, a data-collection task, or a request for more annotation money. Its root cause is conceptual. The record notes that no pose-level correspondence preserves the effect on the object across hand morphologies, and that functional equivalence across morphologies is undefined (paper 1131). It also notes that the contact and force information that effect-level retargeting would need is missing from human data. More data alone does not fix this: HRDexDB already pairs human and robot grasps, and kinematic retargeting from those pairs still succeeds 1.21 percent of the time on Allegro. A bigger, better-funded version of the current pipelines would not close the gap either, because the pipelines that fail (kinematic IK, copy-rotation, OmniH2O) are mature already.

Three research questions survive that a top-venue reviewer would find significant:
(a) Representation. Which description of a demonstration stays invariant across embodiments: object-state trajectories, contact-transition sequences, or wrench-level task constraints? Can that description be estimated from monocular or RGB-D video of the human, rather than from mocap?
(b) Error budget. How do specific reconstruction errors (hand-object penetration, contact timing, object 6-DoF drift, bimanual relative pose) translate into robot execution failure? Which errors are tolerable? This asks the perception community to optimise physically meaningful targets instead of MPJPE.
(c) Bimanual transfer. How should two-hand coordination be transferred? The record cites 52.8 percent bimanual versus 76.2 percent single-hand success in the HANDS 2025 HO-Tracker (paper 1533), and states the framework lacks a bimanual coordination design.

The topic is also demonstrably publishable now. ManipTrans (bimanual human-to-dexterous-hand transfer via residual learning) is accepted at CVPR 2025, which I verified on its arXiv page. DexMachina (functional retargeting for bimanual dexterous manipulation; Mandi, Hou, Fox, Narang, Mandlekar, Song, 2025) and object-centric dexterous manipulation from human motion (Chen, Wang, Yang, Liu) frame the problem as a research question. However, I could not verify where either was published.

Points against P23, which lower the score but do not refute it:
1. Part of the pain point is genuinely engineering or hardware: joint-limit clamping, per-hand mapping matrices, and humanoids without dexterous hands.
2. The finding that the human strategy itself can be wrong for the robot may not be solvable from human data at all. It is an argument for robot data, not a perception question.
3. The core subproblem (RL or residual policies in simulation) is crowded and needs much compute. Well-resourced robotics labs dominate it.
4. For this author the relevance is adjacent. The part that fits a tracking and reconstruction thesis is narrower: perceiving the quantities that effect-level retargeting needs, and the error budget in (b). Policy learning is outside that part.

Verification notes:
- The quantitative evidence comes from the pain-point file. I did not re-check it at its sources.
- The WebSearch budget was exhausted, so I verified the papers by fetching their arXiv pages.
- The CVF page for ManipTrans returned 403. Its arXiv comments field states CVPR 2025.
- I recalled DexCap as RSS 2024, but its arXiv page shows no venue, so the venue is unverified.

Object-Centric Dexterous Manipulation from Human Motion Data
DexCap: Scalable and Portable Mocap Data Collection System for Dexterous Manipulation
HRDexDB (paper id 1131 in pain-point file): kinematic retargeting seed-level success 1.21 percent on Allegro
HuRo five-source audit (paper id 1381): 55.2 percent free of non-grasp self-contact
HANDS 2025 HO-Tracker report (paper id 1533): 52.8 percent bimanual vs 76.2 percent single-hand

skeptics.reframe: The research question is not retargeting itself; it is which embodiment-invariant description of a demonstration can be perceived. Robot hands cannot reuse human hand poses, so transfer must preserve the effect on the object: object-state trajectories, the order in which contacts form and break, and the forces involved (wrench-level task constraints). The question is whether these can be recovered from monocular or RGB-D video of bimanual handling, and how much reconstruction error of each kind (penetration, contact timing, object pose drift, relative pose between the hands) robot execution tolerates. That turns the tracking metric from MPJPE into executability and gives a reconstruction thesis a defensible bridge to robot demonstration capture.

research_questions.question: Which hand-object reconstruction errors make a human demonstration non-executable after retargeting, and how large can each one get before success collapses? Does a reconstruction score weighted by executability predict downstream robot success better than MPJPE, ADD-S and penetration depth, and does the error budget differ between bimanual and single-hand handling?
research_questions.why_top_venue: Hand-object perception methods are still ranked by MPJPE, ADD and penetration. Meanwhile at least eight video-to-robot pipelines from 2025-2026 say that reconstruction quality limits robot success, but none measures which error matters: C2Dex 2608.07045, SPIDER 2511.09484, RoboWheel 2512.02729, EgoInfinity 2606.17385, DexImit 2602.10105, Do as I Do 2606.19333, AGILE 2602.04672 and DynamicHOI 2609.36454. Two checks on arXiv pages support this. First, SPIDER's limitations section names upstream perception errors from HaMeR, FoundationPose and Trellis as a failure source, and the paper has no controlled noise-injection experiment (checked in its arXiv HTML). Second, C2Dex shows that contact-consistent reconstruction lifts end-to-end success on DexYCB from 17.78 to 57.78 percent and on TACO from 10.00 to 26.67 percent, but it does not break this gain down by error type. Five arXiv keyword searches found no paper that measures an error budget or validates a reconstruction metric against executability; with a search this limited, that does not prove none exists. A result that changes what the hand-object field optimizes is a contribution CVPR, ICCV, ECCV and NeurIPS Datasets and Benchmarks accept, and robotics readers at CoRL can use it directly.
research_questions.method_sketch:
1. Build an error model from real estimators. Run 2-3 public estimators on sequences that have ground truth (DexYCB, HO3D v3, ARCTIC, H2O): WiLoR or HaMeR for hands, FoundationPose with depth for objects, and one joint hand-object method. Fit residual distributions for each error type: object translation drift, object rotation jitter, global hand offset, finger articulation error, hand-object penetration, shifts in contact onset and offset, floating fingertips, error in the relative pose between the two hands, temporal jitter, and gaps from occlusion.
2. Inject each error type at graded magnitudes into mocap-quality references, alone and in realistic combinations.
3. Pass every reference through retargeters that span the design space: kinematic IK (the public dex-retargeting package from AnyTeleop), physics-based sampling (SPIDER, whose code a skeptic reports as released; not re-checked), and, on a small subset only, a residual-RL tracker (ManipTrans or DexMachina).
4. Execute in MuJoCo or Isaac on two robot hands, using both hands where the source is bimanual. Record object-tracking success, whether the contact mode is correct, and the failure type.
5. Fit a success model per retargeter (logistic or GAM). Report tolerance thresholds, interactions between error types, and which errors physics-based retargeters absorb and which they amplify.
6. Turn the fitted model into an executability-weighted error score. Test it on held-out real estimator outputs by rank correlation with simulated success, against MPJPE, ADD-S, penetration volume and contact F1.
7. Method payoff: a cheap test-time refinement that minimizes the weighted score, for example by putting contact timing and the relative pose between the hands ahead of absolute hand position. It should raise downstream success even when MPJPE stays the same or gets worse.
research_questions.minimum_experiment:
Use 60 sequences: 20 bimanual from ARCTIC or OakInk2, 20 bimanual from GigaHands or TACO, and 20 single-hand from DexYCB as a control. Test 16 conditions: 5 error types at 3 magnitudes each, plus clean. Use 2 retargeters (kinematic IK and SPIDER) and 2 robot hands. That is about 3,840 simulated executions. At an estimated few GPU-minutes each (per-run time not verified), this takes roughly 1-2 weeks on one GPU.

Pass criteria:
(a) At least one error type shows a sharp tolerance threshold, and that threshold differs between bimanual and single-hand references.
(b) On the outputs of two real estimators, the executability score's Kendall tau with simulated success beats MPJPE and ADD by a clear margin, with a bootstrap confidence interval that excludes zero.
(c) The refinement raises simulated success on real estimator outputs.

If (b) fails, the work shrinks to an ICRA or RA-L analysis paper.
research_questions.data_and_hardware:
Bimanual references with mocap ground truth: ARCTIC, OakInk2, GigaHands, TACO.

Single-hand RGB-D with ground truth: DexYCB and HO3D v3.

Bimanual egocentric RGB-D with object poses: H2O. This is from memory; check its license, ground-truth quality and depth availability.

Robot hand models come from MuJoCo Menagerie or vendor URDFs. The retargeting code is dex-retargeting, SPIDER, and ManipTrans or DexMachina. Check their licenses and confirm each runs on one GPU.

Hardware is one workstation with a 24-48 GB GPU. No robot or motion capture is needed. The consumer RGB-D camera is optional and only adds a qualitative real capture.
research_questions.risks:
1. High risk of being scooped. The groups behind SPIDER, C2Dex and EgoInfinity already report contact-consistency and kinematic-feasibility metrics, and could add a sensitivity ablation in a revision. Publish quickly and release the benchmark code.
2. The results may depend on the retargeter: physics-based retargeters absorb small errors, which weakens any claim of one universal budget. Report results per retargeter class and focus on errors that no retargeter recovers from, such as contact-mode errors and the relative pose between the hands.
3. Synthetic perturbations may not match real estimator errors. Sample them from the fitted real residuals and validate on real outputs.
4. Success in simulation is not success on a real robot, and there is no real dexterous hand to check against.
5. Computer-vision reviewers may see an analysis paper as low in novelty unless the metric and the refinement clearly deliver.
6. Third-party code may be hard to reproduce or tied to old Isaac Gym versions.

research_questions.question: Single-view RGB-D capture of bimanual object handling leaves many quantities occluded. Can it still become an executable robot reference if the retargeter is told which quantities were observed, which were inferred from constraints, and which are unknown? Does this provenance-aware reference raise executability over the point-estimate pipelines in use now, most of all in the occluded segments?
research_questions.why_top_venue: The current video-to-robot pipelines pass one point estimate downstream (C2Dex, RoboWheel, DexImit, EgoInfinity, Do as I Do, and SPIDER on in-the-wild video). SPIDER's limitations state that large misalignments push the retargeter into semantically wrong contact modes. Occlusion is worst in bimanual handling, where one hand hides the other hand and the object, and bimanual transfer still trails single-hand transfer: 52.8 versus 76.2 percent in the HANDS 2025 HO-Tracker report, a single-team figure not re-verified. An interface between perception and retargeting that carries uncertainty is a reusable, principled contribution rather than one more pipeline. Novelty is moderate. Acceptance depends on showing that the gains concentrate in occluded segments and that the uncertainties are calibrated.
research_questions.method_sketch:
1. From single-view RGB-D, estimate each frame: the object's 6-DoF pose with FoundationPose, using the depth residual as confidence; each hand with WiLoR or HaMeR refined against depth; contact states from hand-object signed distance plus depth consistency; and the relative pose between the hands.
2. Give each quantity a calibrated variance and a provenance label: observed; inferred from a temporal or physical constraint (for example, an object held rigidly by an occluded hand); or unknown.
3. In the retargeting objective (a SPIDER-style physics sampler), weight the tracking terms by inverse variance. In segments where the object is observed but the hand is not, stop tracking the hand and track object state plus contact-schedule constraints, so the physics sampler fills in the hand.
4. Compare four variants: the same pipeline with uniform weights (point estimate), provenance-weighted, an oracle occlusion mask, and published C2Dex or SPIDER numbers where the inputs match.
5. Report success split by occlusion level and by failure type, with calibration plots for the contact probabilities.
research_questions.minimum_experiment:
Run 40-60 sequences in simulation with a SPIDER-style sampling retargeter on 1-2 robot hands. Single-hand: DexYCB, using one RGB-D view chosen from its eight. Bimanual: H2O, or single-view depth rendered from ARCTIC ground-truth meshes with an added sensor-noise model.

The ablation compares point estimate, provenance-weighted and oracle. Pass criteria: a gain in success on high-occlusion segments with confidence intervals that exclude zero, and an expected calibration error showing the variances are meaningful.

Optional real-world check: replay in simulation the object trajectories of the author's RGB-D recordings, whose object pose is measured by ArUco. This works at object level only and is a qualitative sanity check, not a result.
research_questions.data_and_hardware:
Datasets: DexYCB and HO3D v3 (RGB-D with ground truth); H2O (bimanual RGB-D, needs checking); ARCTIC with rendered depth (whether ARCTIC or OakInk2 ship real depth is unverified).

Models: public weights for FoundationPose and WiLoR or HaMeR.

Hardware: one GPU and one consumer RGB-D camera for qualitative real captures. No robot is needed for the core claim. A borrowed or self-built low-cost open-source hand (LEAP class) would only serve a demo.
research_questions.risks:
1. The area is crowded. At least six pipelines from 2025-2026 target video-to-dexterous-robot transfer, from strong groups: Malik and Abbeel, Huazhe Xu and Jiangmiao Pang, Kaiyu Hang, and Meta with CMU and Berkeley.
2. Physics-based retargeters may already absorb most of the noise, which would make the gain small. Run the error-budget question above first to find out whether this headroom exists.
3. Bimanual RGB-D datasets with good ground truth are scarce, and rendered depth lacks real sensor artifacts.
4. Calibrated uncertainty for hand-pose estimators is a hard problem in its own right.
5. Without a real robot, CoRL and RSS reviewers may discount the result.

fit.thesis_assets_help:
The edge is small. The thesis tracks the body and arm (a Unity humanoid rig) and recovers an occluded holding arm conditioned on the object. A grep of the repository docs found no MANO finger tracking and no finger or contact ground truth, and both research questions need finger-level hands and contacts.

Three assets help:
(1) The ArUco-marked object with a metric 6-DoF pose gives measured object trajectories under real hand occlusion, captured on a consumer RGB-D camera. These can calibrate a realistic object-drift error model for the first question and serve as a small real sanity set for the second, at object level only.
(2) The measured/held/constrained honesty labels are a direct precursor of the observed/inferred/unknown provenance labels in the second question. They give the author prior design experience and a coherent narrative.
(3) Object-conditioned recovery of an occluded arm is the same idea as inferring an occluded hand from the observed object. The second question extends it to finger level.

Four assets do not help:
(1) The Unity twin: dexterous transfer work runs on MuJoCo or Isaac physics.
(2) The causal 30 fps chain: offline retargeting does not need it.
(3) The 28 recordings: they come from one subject and have no finger ground truth, so they cannot be a dataset contribution.
(4) The desk setup: it adds nothing beyond a qualitative demo.

Overall: low to moderate for the second question, low for the first.
fit.what_a_small_lab_cannot_do_here:
A small lab cannot compete on headline transfer success. Per-task RL or residual policies over thousands of trajectories and several robot hands need GPU clusters. Examples are ManipTrans, DexMachina, the contact-anchored method (25,454 trajectories) and SPIDER (2.4M feasible frames, as a skeptic reported).

It cannot validate on real dexterous or bimanual hardware such as Allegro or Shadow hands or dual arms unless it borrows them. Real zero-shot claims, which CoRL and RSS reviewers increasingly expect, are therefore out of reach.

It cannot collect a multi-subject bimanual dataset with mocap ground truth, tactile gloves or force sensors. The force half of effect-level retargeting (ReForce, Touch2Robot) cannot be measured.

It cannot study the strategy gap (two human hands versus one gripper, workspace limits), which needs robot-side demonstrations. Nor can it run web-scale data engines like EgoInfinity, DexImit or RoboWheel.

It cannot match the field's pace either. About a dozen relevant papers appeared between June and September 2026, so any pipeline-style contribution is likely to be scooped within months. The realistic opening is narrow: an analysis, metric and refinement contribution that sits upstream of retargeting (the first question), with the provenance-aware interface (the second question) as the follow-up.

painpoint.name: Interaction forecasting and synthesis do not generalize

evidence.latest_state: Search was limited: the shared WebSearch budget ran out before my first query, so all evidence below comes from WebFetch of arXiv search listings and abstract pages. In 2026, egocentric hand-motion forecasting still has errors of several centimetres. EMPIRE (arXiv 2608.22449, Aug 2026) adds an explicit manipulation-planning stage and calls itself state of the art at 84.53 mm MPJPE and 38.97 mm finger-relative error on its new 650,910-window, 111-task EMPIRE-651K set. That is the same error scale the pain point records for TACO and GigaHands (29 to 70 mm). In text-to-HOI generation, PAMI (arXiv 2609.38466, Sep 2026) reports 14.5 percent higher contact recall than the previous state of the art on InterAct. Its abstract names object drift, missed contact and penetration as open failure modes, so invalid contact persists. Other recent work claims better generalization: HO-Flow (2604.10836) on GRAB, OakInk and DexYCB; Dex2HOI (2605.30444), which handles bimanual two-object generation and claims up to x540 faster inference; LIGHT (2603.25734), which reports better generalization to novel objects; InfBaGel (ICLR 2026), which generalizes to unseen scenes; and GIRAF (CVPR 2026 HuMoGen workshop), which generalizes to unseen articulated-object configurations. These claims are qualitative or measured on small in-lab unseen splits. No abstract I found shows open-world generalization or reliable plans longer than five primitives. Fixes now move to new data sources: physics-simulated RL data (Policy-as-Data, 2606.22806, which reports better generalization to unseen objects and long-horizon generation), video-generation priors, and 3D interaction-trace world models trained on diverse video (mu0, 2606.13769). No 2025-2026 result found closes the data-scarcity root cause.

evidence.crowdedness: HIGH: at least 15 papers from 2025-2026 attack the problem directly. They come from many strong groups (Imperial/Zafeiriou-Potamias, Inria/Schmid, Tuebingen/Pons-Moll-Geiger, UIUC/Gui-Wang, Meta Reality Labs, Tsinghua/Yebin Liu, CAS/Shan-Chen, UMD/Huang) and appear across body-object, hand-object, video-generation and robot world-model communities.
evidence.trend: rising: September 2026 alone has new text-to-HOI (PAMI), forecasting (EMPIRE, HAP) and synthesis papers. Attention is moving away from mocap-only diffusion toward physics-simulated data, video-generation priors and 3D-trace world models that feed robot learning. That shift widens the audience but does not yet remove the generalization gap.

skeptics.reasons:
Not refuted, but the pain point needs narrowing. Work from 2025 and 2026 does go after one part of it: synthesis on unseen objects. Several methods now produce open-vocabulary, zero-shot hand-object or human-object interaction by distilling priors from video diffusion models, MLLMs or LLMs instead of relying only on small mocap sets. Examples are OpenHOI (NeurIPS 2025 oral; novel object categories, multi-stage tasks, physics refinement), InteractAnything, HOI-PAGE, AnchorHOI, InterPose (web-video scale), Target-Aware Video Diffusion, DeVI (physics-based dexterous HOI from synthetic video, zero-shot across objects) and InterMimic (zero-shot physics-based whole-body HOI control). This weakens the stated cause ("trained on small mocap sets"), and the field is clearly moving to video and foundation-model priors plus physics tracking for plausibility.
None of these works solves the metric problem the pain point describes. They are judged on plausibility, CLIP or text alignment, penetration statistics and user studies, not on 3D forecasting error over a held-out horizon of 1 to 3 seconds against real ground truth. I found no 2025-2026 result showing that the TACO, GigaHands, CORE4D or HHI-Assist forecasting errors (tens of mm, tens of degrees, growing with horizon and on unseen objects) have closed or saturated. Uni-Hand (Nov 2025) still lists modality gaps and limited downstream validation. Mu0 (2026), a 3D interaction-trace world model, reports beating baselines but no saturated held-out metric. Wh0 (2026) raises zero-shot success on unseen dexterous tasks only from 8.3 to 38.9 percent, so long-horizon multi-step manipulation is still far from solved.
Three things remain open: forecasting from noisy perceived states (as opposed to ground-truth mocap), physical and contact validity measured on held-out objects, and planning beyond about five primitives. No benchmark measures plausibility and metric accuracy together. Search caveats: the WebSearch budget was used up before this task started, so the evidence comes from the arXiv API listings and abstract pages only. Venues and numbers inside the full papers were not checked. For a tracking-focused thesis author, this pain point remains adjacent rather than core.

skeptics.reframe: Plausible zero-shot interaction synthesis is now addressed by distilling video and foundation-model priors. What remains unsolved is accurate 3D forecasting over 1 to 3 seconds of real hand-object (and bimanual) interaction on unseen objects, starting from noisy perceived states rather than mocap ground truth, with contact validity scored jointly with forecasting error. No current benchmark measures this, and published errors on TACO, GigaHands, CORE4D and HHI-Assist are still tens of millimetres and grow with horizon.

skeptics.reasons:
Artifact test, partly passed. The core claim is not an artifact of one dataset or one group. The 37 supporting papers come from many independent labs and settings: SJTU (OakInk, OakInk2), Tsinghua (TACO, CORE4D), Brown (GigaHands), Apple (EgoDex), the Ego4D consortium, MPI (COUCH), Stanford (OMOMO), BIGAI (TRUMANS), EPFL (HHI-Assist), Verona (HARPER), and two independent 2025 surveys (2503.12763, 2503.13120). They cover hands, full body, two-person and egocentric settings. All of them say that scarce, narrow interaction data limits generalization to unseen objects and tasks, and that generated motion has penetration and floating contact.

Much of the specific evidence, though, is a product of how papers are written and scored rather than a field-level finding:
(1) Almost every source is a dataset or benchmark paper. These papers have a built-in reason to build unseen-object or unseen-task splits and to show that off-the-shelf baselines (MDM and similar) fail on them. The quoted numbers (TACO 54.9-70.5 mm, GigaHands 69.3 mm, CORE4D 186.4 vs 170.8 mm, InterVLA 172.5 mm) measure untuned baselines on new splits. They are not the limits of the best current methods.
(2) "Generative forecasters are worse than predictive ones" is a scoring effect. Scoring one sample with deterministic MPJPE penalizes multimodal predictors, and the stochastic motion-prediction community has long handled this with best-of-K, diversity and realism metrics (BeLFusion, ICCV 2023).
(3) Error growing over a 1-3 s horizon is a known, irreducible property of an uncertain future. It has been treated that way since early human motion prediction work (Martinez et al., CVPR 2017, where a zero-velocity baseline was competitive). The 0.031 to 0.053 m growth in EgoDex is expected, not a defect.
(4) The statement bundles unrelated issues: hand and body forecasting, text-to-HOI synthesis, human-human assistance, LLM primitive planning (OakInk2's 36 percent), and video generation. "Does not generalize out of distribution" is the generic limitation of any learned model.
(5) Fixes are already appearing. Physics-based imitation claims zero-shot generalization and physically valid contact (InterMimic, CVPR 2025). Large-scale data aggregation and correction efforts are underway (InterAct, HandX, GigaHands, EgoDex). HandX itself reports that model scaling saturates, so data diversity, not model size, is the bottleneck.

The narrow claim that survives: HOI generation is short of data and lacks physics, on unseen objects. This claim is real and appears across the field. Most of the remaining evidence is metric, horizon or baseline-choice artifacts. Relevance to the author's tracking and reconstruction field is also only adjacent.

Caveats: the web search budget was exhausted after one search, so I verified only three external papers by fetching them directly. I did not re-read the full text of the 37 source papers; the per-paper summaries come from the stored step-2 extraction (w2b_part1.json).

skeptics.reframe: HOI generation and forecasting models trained on small mocap sets of single subjects interacting with single objects have no physical or contact model. They produce invalid contact (penetration, floating, sliding) and lose accuracy on unseen object geometries and tasks. Model scaling saturates. Under fair stochastic metrics, the gap is a shortage of diverse data and physical grounding, not the horizon length or the choice between generative and predictive models.

skeptics.reasons:
Refutation attempt: P24's own why_it_persists line says the cause is data. Interaction capture is costly, so mocap sets are small and narrow, and generators interpolate inside them. Read that way, the pain point is a wish for bigger mocap sets, and the field is already building them: GigaHands, HOI-M3, and InterAct (CVPR 2025), which aggregates and corrects existing sets. Part of the stated failure is also ill-posed. Losing MPJPE accuracy after one to three seconds is partly what any single-reference metric does when the future is stochastic, so not all of it is a model deficiency.

The refutation fails for three reasons:
(1) The record says model scaling saturates. Generative forecasters do worse than predictive ones on TACO: 54.9-70.5 mm versus 28.8-36.6 mm right-hand MPJPE. Error also rises on unseen tool geometry, unseen chair shapes (CORE4D 186.4 vs 170.8 mm) and an unseen task (HHI-Assist, 154.8 mm at 1 s). Gaps that persist and grow on held-out factors are not explained by sample count alone. They point to missing structure: contact, physics and composition.
(2) Top venues keep accepting papers on exactly this generalization gap, which a reviewer would not do for a solved problem waiting on funding. Examples from a local copy of a GitHub list: InterDiff (physics-informed diffusion, ICCV 2023), InterDreamer (zero-shot text-to-HOI, NeurIPS 2024), AvatarGO (zero-shot 4D HOI, ICLR 2025), PrimHOI (compositional primitives, ICCV 2025) and OpenHOI (open-world hand-object synthesis, NeurIPS 2025). The same list's own taxonomy names an object-zero-shot level, an interaction-zero-shot level and a level with no paired data at all, and calls the higher ones open.
(3) At least three research questions would interest a reviewer: (a) can contact and physical feasibility learned without paired mocap (simulation, video generative priors, affordance parsing) close the gap on unseen objects and tasks, measured on held-out splits with penetration and contact metrics; (b) forecasting on robot-estimated poses is several times worse than on ground truth, so can forecasting be trained jointly with perception noise and occlusion, with uncertainty passed from the tracker to the forecaster; (c) can hierarchical or compositional representations plan beyond the five-primitive point where LLM planning fails (36 percent overall success).

Residual weaknesses (why 7, not higher): the area is crowded with strong groups (UIUC, Stanford, BIGAI, ShanghaiTech). Relevance to the thesis author is adjacent: their strength is RGB-D tracking, not generation. Some of the long-horizon error is irreducible stochasticity, so a paper has to argue with distributional or physical-validity metrics rather than MPJPE alone. The opening most specific to this author is question (b), forecasting from noisy real-time RGB-D tracking. It connects to their perception work and is far less crowded than text-to-HOI synthesis.

Verification caveat: the web search budget was used up, and arXiv, dblp and CVF returned 429 or 403 errors. All five cited papers therefore come from a GitHub paper list already saved in the scratchpad (HungrySemiconductor_Awesome-Zero-Shot-3D-HOI_main.md), not from venue pages. The benchmark figures come from the P24 record.

skeptics.reframe: Hand-object and body-object forecasters are trained on clean, small mocap. They fail on unseen objects and tasks, and they fail on poses estimated from real RGB-D under occlusion (several times worse than on ground truth). Scaling does not fix either. The open question is whether forecasting can be learned and evaluated in a way that is robust to the uncertainty of tracking, and physically valid on held-out objects and tasks. That means propagating tracker uncertainty into the forecast, adding contact and physics priors that do not need paired mocap, and scoring with distributional and penetration metrics rather than single-future MPJPE.

research_questions.question: How much does 3D hand-object forecasting degrade when the observed past comes from a real single-view RGB(-D) tracker instead of mocap ground truth, and can a forecaster that takes per-frame tracker uncertainty and provenance (confidence, visibility, measured versus imputed) as input recover most of that gap while producing calibrated, contact-valid forecasts on unseen objects?
research_questions.why_top_venue: All three skeptics converge on this as the open, less crowded slice of P24. The P24 record states that forecasting from robot-estimated partial poses is several times worse than from ground truth, yet the hand-object forecasters checked here (EMPIRE 2608.22449, Uni-Hand 2511.12878, Poly-Autoregressive Prediction 2502.08646, Diff-IP2D 2405.04370, the TACO benchmark 2401.08399) do not, in their abstracts, address noisy tracked 3D inputs or uncertainty propagation. The closest precedent is body-only: Scriboora (arXiv 2511.15565, Nov 2025) builds a paired clean versus detector-noisy body-pose variant, reports substantial degradation and recovers only part of it by fine-tuning on detector poses. Other related body-only work: EgoCast (2412.02903) uses estimated current-frame poses, HARPER (2403.14447) uses partial robot-view observations, and Toward Reliable Human Pose Forecasting with Uncertainty (2304.06707) models uncertainty but starts from clean inputs. No equivalent was found for hands with objects, where errors are correlated with occlusion and contact. A paired benchmark with a joint metric (distributional accuracy, calibration and contact validity) plus a method that beats fine-tune-on-noise is a credible CVPR/ICCV/ECCV contribution. It also matters to the robot-demonstration and digital-twin audience, because deployed forecasters only ever see tracker output.
research_questions.method_sketch: (1) Paired benchmark. Run off-the-shelf single-view estimators (a MANO hand regressor such as HaMeR or WiLoR, and a model-based object pose tracker such as FoundationPose with the dataset meshes) on the RGB(-D) frames of public sets that have image and 3D ground truth (DexYCB, HO3D v3, ARCTIC, HOT3D). Store the per-frame confidence, visibility and failure flags. Pair each estimated past with the ground-truth future, using seen/unseen-object and seen/unseen-subject splits. (2) Learned perception-noise model. Fit a conditional model of estimator error (temporally correlated, conditioned on occlusion, contact and hand-object distance) on the paired data. Use it to corrupt image-free mocap sets (GRAB, OakInk2, TACO, GigaHands), so training scales beyond the datasets that have images. (3) Forecaster. Use an object-relative representation (hand joints in the object frame plus distances to the object SDF) with uncertainty and provenance tokens per input frame. Output either a sample set (diffusion or flow) or a heteroscedastic distribution, trained with an energy-score or NLL objective and a penetration/contact-consistency term. (4) Joint evaluation. Report the GT-to-perceived degradation ratio, best-of-K and energy score at 0.25-2 s horizons, interval coverage (calibration), penetration depth, contact recall against ground-truth contact, and hand-object relative drift, all binned by occlusion level. Baselines: constant velocity, a deterministic predictive transformer, a diffusion forecaster, filter-then-forecast (Kalman or learned smoother, then forecast), and fine-tune-on-detector-noise (the Scriboora remedy).
research_questions.minimum_experiment: Use DexYCB and HO3D v3 only, since both have RGB-D frames, MANO hand ground truth, YCB object poses and meshes. Use one hand estimator and one object tracker to build the perceived-input variant. Compare four forecasters (constant velocity, predictive transformer, diffusion forecaster, and the proposed uncertainty-conditioned forecaster), each trained on GT-only, GT plus synthetic noise, and real-noise fine-tuning, at 0.5 s and 1.0 s horizons on a held-out-object split. Success criterion, set as a target rather than a measured value: the proposed model recovers a clearly larger share of the GT-to-perceived gap than fine-tune-on-noise, keeps interval coverage near nominal, and does not raise penetration. Second stage: add ARCTIC or HOT3D for bimanual and egocentric coverage, plus a cross-dataset test (train with the noise model on GRAB/OakInk2, test on DexYCB perceived).
research_questions.data_and_hardware: Public data only. Datasets with paired images and ground truth: DexYCB, HO3D v3, ARCTIC, HOT3D (ARCTIC and HOT3D need license agreements). Image-free mocap for noise-augmented training: GRAB, OakInk2, TACO, GigaHands. One workstation GPU (24-48 GB) is enough. The dominant cost is a one-time precompute of estimator outputs over the image datasets, which takes days on one GPU and can be subsampled temporally. Forecaster training is small (sequence models over joints and 6D poses). The consumer RGB-D camera is optional and only needed for a small real-world qualitative test. No mocap and no robot are needed.
research_questions.risks: (a) Incremental-looking result: Scriboora already shows the body version, so reviewers may say that noise hurts and fine-tuning fixes it. The paper has to show that occlusion-correlated failures defeat plain fine-tuning and that uncertainty conditioning plus calibration change downstream outcomes. (b) Estimators improve quickly, so the gap measured with today's HaMeR/WiLoR/FoundationPose may shrink. Mitigation: make the benchmark estimator-agnostic and report the trend across estimator quality. (c) Long-horizon error is partly irreducible stochasticity (artifact skeptic), so single-future MPJPE alone will not convince; distributional and calibration metrics are required. (d) Scoop risk from the large forecasting groups (EMPIRE, Uni-Hand), which could add an estimated-input variant. (e) Adjacent to the author's core field: this is forecasting, not tracking, so the first paper needs a strong benchmark story. (f) The evidence base is thin: this assessment rests on abstracts fetched through the arXiv API, because WebSearch was unavailable. A hand-object paper on noisy-input forecasting may exist under different terminology and should be checked again before committing.

research_questions.question: Can a short-horizon (100-1000 ms) hand-object or arm-object interaction forecaster, used as a learned process model inside a causal real-time RGB-D tracker, bridge occlusion gaps and compensate pipeline latency better than hold-last-value, constant velocity or Kalman filtering? Can its predictive uncertainty decide when the tracker should trust the forecast and when it should trust the measurement?
research_questions.why_top_venue: Forecasting papers evaluate forecasting in isolation, and tracking papers use generic motion priors. P24's own evidence says forecasting inherits perception error, but nothing found closes the loop the other way, with interaction forecasts improving live tracking and teleoperation or digital-twin latency for bimanual object handling. For ICRA or RA-L, a clean system result counts: lower error inside occlusion spans, lower latency-compensated error, and downstream gains in simulated retargeting. This question is a robotics-venue result, not a CVPR one.
research_questions.method_sketch: A causal tracker emits per-frame state plus provenance (measured, held, constrained). The forecaster from RQ1, or a lighter variant, predicts a distribution over the next k frames. During an occlusion span or low-confidence period, the tracker propagates the forecast distribution instead of holding the last value. When measurements return, it fuses forecast and measurement as prior and likelihood (an EKF or particle-filter update with the learned process model and learned covariance). For latency, the digital twin or teleoperation target is rendered at t plus the measured pipeline latency from the forecast. Evaluation: (i) quantitative, on DexYCB, HO3D v3 and ARCTIC with synthetic occlusion masks of controlled duration and simulated latency, with error plotted against occlusion length; (ii) a real RGB-D case study in which the ArUco-marked object supplies metric object ground truth; (iii) a downstream test retargeting the forecast to a simulated robot hand (MuJoCo or Isaac), scoring grasp success or object-drop rate with and without forecasting.
research_questions.minimum_experiment: Run one public dataset (DexYCB) with synthetic occlusion spans of 0.1-1.0 s and simulated latencies of 33-200 ms. Compare five strategies (hold-last-value, constant velocity, Kalman, learned forecaster without fusion, learned forecaster with uncertainty-gated fusion) on error inside and just after occlusion spans and on latency-compensated error. Add one real-camera sequence set from the existing causal 30 fps chain, where object pose error is measured against the ArUco ground truth.
research_questions.data_and_hardware: Public: DexYCB, HO3D v3, ARCTIC (for arm/bimanual). Own: the consumer RGB-D camera and the existing causal pipeline for a real-time demonstration. One GPU, real-time inference at 30 fps. A simulator replaces the robot arm. More subjects (cheap to record with the consumer camera) would be needed for any real-data quantitative claim, but hand/arm ground truth would still be missing without mocap.
research_questions.risks: (a) Novelty: learned motion priors inside trackers are well known for bodies, and latency compensation by prediction is standard in teleoperation and VR. The contribution has to rest on interaction-aware (object-conditioned), uncertainty-gated fusion for bimanual handling, which reviewers may find incremental. (b) The real-data evaluation is weak: one subject and no hand/arm ground truth, so quantitative claims must come from public datasets with synthetic occlusion, which reviewers may call unrealistic. (c) Without a real robot, ICRA reviewers may discount the result, so a borrowed arm for a small handover or teleoperation demo would help substantially. (d) Depends on RQ1 producing a well-calibrated forecaster.
target_venues: CoRL (only with a real robot experiment)

research_questions.question: For observation-conditioned (not text-conditioned) bimanual hand-object forecasting, does an explicit object-frame contact constraint (predicted contact on the object surface plus a differentiable non-penetration and non-sliding projection at each forecast step) reduce invalid contact on held-out object geometries without hurting forecast accuracy, when accuracy and validity are scored together?
research_questions.why_top_venue: Invalid contact on unseen objects is the part of P24 that the artifact skeptic accepts as real. Recent synthesis work (PAMI 2609.38466, LIGHT 2603.25734, HO-Flow 2604.10836) attacks it for text-to-HOI and is scored on plausibility rather than metric error against real futures. PhysHanDI (ICML 2026, 2605.09538) uses physics for deformable hand-object reconstruction and prediction but, per its abstract, does not address noisy inputs. A joint accuracy-plus-validity result on held-out objects for forecasting fills a measurement gap. This is the weakest of the three as a standalone paper and is best used as the contact module and metric inside RQ1.
research_questions.method_sketch: Represent hands relative to the object SDF. Predict future per-vertex contact probabilities on the object surface. After each autoregressive or denoising step, project the hand pose with a few differentiable iterations that remove penetration and penalise tangential sliding at predicted contacts; optionally, step a lightweight rigid simulation for the object given hand contacts. Augment training with synthetic object geometries to widen shape coverage. Compare no constraint, guidance-style penalty, and hard projection on GRAB, OakInk2 and ARCTIC unseen-object splits, reporting MPJPE/energy score, penetration depth and volume, contact recall against ground truth, and hand-object relative drift together.
research_questions.minimum_experiment: Use one bimanual dataset with an unseen-object split (ARCTIC or OakInk2). Use one diffusion forecaster with three contact-handling variants at 0.5 s and 1.0 s horizons. Report the accuracy-validity trade-off curve rather than a single number.
research_questions.data_and_hardware: Public mocap with object meshes: GRAB, OakInk2, ARCTIC (TACO optional for tools). One GPU. No camera, mocap or robot needed.
research_questions.risks: (a) Crowded: physics-informed HOI forecasting already exists for body-object (InterDiff, ICCV 2023), and contact guidance is standard in 2025-2026 synthesis, so the standalone novelty is thin. (b) Projection can trade accuracy for validity, giving a mixed headline. (c) Unseen-object splits in current datasets are small, which limits how strongly generalization can be claimed. Recommendation: merge into RQ1 as its contact-validity component rather than run it as a separate paper.

fit.thesis_assets_help: Modest, and almost entirely for RQ2 (tracker-in-the-loop forecasting for occlusion and latency). The causal 30 fps RGB-D chain with measured/held/constrained honesty labels is a ready-made example of tracker output carrying per-frame provenance, which is exactly the input RQ1 and RQ2 assume. The object-conditioned recovery of an occluded holding arm is a concrete occlusion-bridging baseline that a learned forecaster has to beat. The ArUco-marked object provides metric object ground truth for a small real-noise test, and the Unity twin is a natural latency-compensation demo. Limits: the 28 recordings come from one subject and have no hand or arm ground truth, so they cannot train a model or support a quantitative top-venue claim; they are good only for a qualitative real-world case study. The author's system works at arm level and does not appear to track fingers (MANO), while P24's benchmarks are finger-level hand-object, so the overlap is partial. For RQ1 the assets supply only the provenance-label idea and a demo. For RQ3 they supply nothing.
fit.what_a_small_lab_cannot_do_here: A small lab cannot compete on the main thrust of P24, which is a data and compute problem. Specifically: (1) open-world text-to-HOI or video-to-HOI synthesis built on video-diffusion, MLLM or world-model priors (OpenHOI, mu0 2606.13769, Wh0 2606.22136, DeVI), which needs multi-GPU training and large video corpora; (2) a new large, diverse, multi-subject interaction mocap dataset, the stated root cause, because there is no mocap or multi-view rig; (3) physics-simulated RL data generation or physics-based imitation at scale (Policy-as-Data 2606.22806, InterMimic), which needs large simulation compute; (4) egocentric forecasting at EMPIRE-651K or Uni-Hand scale; (5) long-horizon planning beyond about five primitives with real robot execution (no arm); (6) claims about generalization across populations or subjects, which need many subjects with ground truth. What is feasible: the narrow perception-aware slice, meaning paired ground-truth versus tracker-estimated inputs on public datasets, uncertainty-conditioned and calibrated short-horizon forecasting, joint accuracy-plus-contact-validity metrics, and a real-time tracker-in-the-loop system result. Evidence caveat: the shared WebSearch budget was exhausted, so the novelty checks in this assessment come from arXiv API listings and abstract pages fetched with WebFetch (Scriboora 2511.15565, EgoCast 2412.02903, HARPER 2403.14447, 2304.06707, PhysHanDI 2605.09538 at ICML 2026, Poly-Autoregressive 2502.08646). The claim that no hand-object noisy-input forecasting paper exists is based on abstracts only and should be re-checked with full-text search before committing.

painpoint.name: Benchmarks are saturated, fragmented or unvalidated for real use

evidence.latest_state:
No single fix exists. Each sub-area is repairing its own benchmarks, and how far that has got differs a lot. For 6D object pose, the BOP Challenge 2024 report (arXiv 2504.02812) shows unseen-object methods closing on seen-object accuracy: FreeZeV2.1 is 22% above the 2023 best on BOP-Classic-Core and the best unseen-object 6D localization reaches 82.5 AR. Unseen-object 2D detection still trails seen-object detection by 35%. BOP 2025 then moved to new industrial sets (XYZ-IBD, IPD, ITODD-MV, single- and multi-view) and to the H3 sets (HOT3D, HOPEv2, HANDAL); results were presented at ICCV 2025 and no 2026 challenge is announced on the BOP site. Results on the harder sets still fall well short. XYZ-IBD (75 multi-view scenes, about 273k instances) reports clear drops against household benchmarks; per the pain-point record, SAM6D and FoundationPose score 0.578 and 0.564 AP there versus 0.70-0.73 on BOP-Core5. EgoXtreme (CVPR 2026) finds that generalizable pose estimators fail under low light, motion blur and smoke, and that deblurring does not help. Robot-learning evaluation is the most actively attacked part:
- Distributed or autonomous real-world evaluation: RoboArena (7 institutions, 600+ pairwise episodes), AutoEval and UMI-Bench 1.0 (June 2026).
- Real-to-sim and world-model evaluators that report correlation with real success: VISER (mean Pearson 0.92), SC3-Eval (0.929), WEAVER (0.870), and PolaRiS and Colosseum V2 (correlation reported, no figure captured here).
- A September 2026 study (arXiv 2610.00731) on a bimanual workspace: reconstruction quality alone moves the real-to-sim correlation from r = 0.51 to r = 0.90 and the mean error from 17.5 to 7.0 points. So evaluation fidelity depends on twin and reconstruction quality.

The clinical and markerless side is still unvalidated in pathological populations. A September 2026 scoping review of 117 studies finds lower-limb agreement of about 5 to 6 degrees, with gaps in pathological cohorts and kinetics. For hand-object and bimanual 3D tracking specifically, I found no 2025-2026 benchmark that validates its scores against downstream use (robot success, digital-twin fidelity). Recent hand-object benchmarks such as DynaHOI and HanDyVQA target new tasks rather than checking that existing metrics predict real use.

evidence.crowdedness: HIGH for robot-policy evaluation and benchmark validity, where I found more than ten 2026 arXiv papers (world-model and real-to-sim evaluators, distributed real-robot networks) from large groups (the DROID/RoboArena consortium and others). MEDIUM for 6D pose (BOP organizers plus one new dataset per gap). LOW for task-validated hand-object or bimanual 3D tracking benchmarks, where I found no paper that checks its metrics against downstream use.
evidence.trend: Rising. The September 2026 arXiv listing is dense with evaluation-validity work (world-model evaluators, real-to-sim correlation studies). BOP keeps moving to industrial and egocentric sets because the classic sets are close to saturated. CVPR 2026 accepted extreme-condition egocentric datasets (EgoXtreme). Attention on validating hand-object tracking metrics against digital-twin or robot outcomes has not yet risen.

skeptics.reasons: I could not refute P25 as a whole. Recent work has filled parts of it, but every fix I found is a curated response that shows the pattern repeating rather than a solution. (1) Fragmentation in object pose has largely become engineering work. BOP 2024 (arXiv 2504.02812) added model-free onboarding and the BOP-H3 hand-object and headset sets (HOT3D, HOPEv2, HANDAL). BOP 2025 brought the industrial sets the pain point names (XYZ-IBD, ITODD-MV, IPD) into one protocol, with a multi-view track. The evidence item from paper 402 (XYZ-IBD sits outside the household benchmarks) is therefore out of date as a "fragmentation" claim. The same report also confirms saturation and a lasting gap. BOP-Classic-Core unseen-object 6D localisation now reaches 0.844 AR on the leaderboard, and the report says 2D detection of unseen objects is still 35 percent behind seen objects. That supports the "saturated on controlled scenes, real gaps elsewhere" part. I could not read the BOP-Industrial or BOP-H3 leaderboard scores, so I cannot say whether the industrial gap has closed. (2) Fragmentation in robot evaluation is partly reduced by RoboArena (arXiv 2506.18123, June 2025): double-blind, crowd-sourced pairwise evaluation at seven institutions on DROID hardware. It covers one platform, has a little over 600 trials, and gives rankings rather than diagnoses, so the "non-diagnostic, confounded by hardware" claim stands. LIBERO-Plus (arXiv 2510.13626, Oct 2025) directly confirms the saturation point: VLA success drops from 95 percent to below 30 percent under modest camera and initial-state changes. (3) I found no 2025-2026 work that settles the avatar and clinical items (task-linked metrics, low inter-rater agreement, borrowed MCIDs) or the claim that intermediate metrics such as trajectory accuracy do not predict downstream quality. My search budget for this session was used up, so these rest on absence of evidence and are not verified. Overall, the pain point is real but very broad and only adjacent to the author's field. It is a meta-problem: each benchmark that fixes one gap saturates later. As a research direction it is weak unless narrowed. The large, well-resourced consortia behind BOP and RoboArena already hold the object-pose and robot-ranking parts.

skeptics.reframe: In hand-object and bimanual capture, no benchmark checks whether tracking accuracy predicts how well the capture works for its downstream use. Hand and object pose errors on HO3D, DexYCB, ARCTIC or HOT3D are not validated against robot retargeting or replay success, or against digital-twin physical plausibility. A method can rank well on MPJPE or ADD yet produce captures that fail when replayed on a robot or in simulation, mainly through contact and penetration errors and drift under occlusion. A small lab could build a replay-validated benchmark protocol that ties capture error to task success.

skeptics.reasons:
P25 holds up only as a generic statement about evaluation in machine learning as a whole. As a field-level pain point for hand-object, bimanual and RGB-D tracking it does not hold up, for five reasons.

(1) It is four unrelated clusters merged into one. The 37 papers are object-pose datasets (BOP, PACE, XYZ-IBD, HouseCat6D, DTTD, YCB-Ev), robot-learning data and benchmark papers (UMI-Bench, RH20T, RoboTube, H2R-Bench), head and body avatar capture (RenderMe-360, NeRSemble, ActorsHQ, SmartPortraits) and clinical markerless motion capture (TULIP, ARAT and reachable-workspace scoring). Each one has its own failure mode: saturation, fragmentation across labs, missing protocols, and clinical label validity (ICC, MCID). The groups behind them are genuinely diverse, so this is not the artifact of a single dataset. What diversity of groups really shows is that the complaint is generic.

(2) It is a convention of the dataset-paper genre. Almost every new dataset paper motivates itself by saying earlier benchmarks are saturated or constrained, and 30 or more of the 37 sources are dataset or benchmark papers that make exactly that self-serving argument. Ott et al. (Nature Communications 2022) found the same saturation dynamic across 3,765 vision and NLP benchmarks. So this is a property of AI benchmarking in general, not a problem specific to this field.

(3) The headline claim is contradicted, and fixes are already in place. The BOP Challenge 2024 report (Nguyen, Hodan et al.) says the best 2024 model-based method was 22% more accurate than the best 2023 method on BOP-Classic-Core, which is continued progress, not saturation. The same challenge already moved from lab-like setups to real-world scenarios with BOP-H3 (high-resolution and AR/VR headset captures, including hand-object egocentric data in the HOT3D style) and added model-free onboarding tasks. The object-pose community therefore treats this as an active, funded part of the benchmark cycle, not an open problem.

(4) None of the cited evidence comes from the author's core field. No hand-object or bimanual benchmark appears in the list (HO3D, DexYCB, ARCTIC, HOT3D, H2O, OakInk). The relevance tag is already "adjacent", and the benchmark numbers (XYZ-IBD AP, PACE AR, UMI-Bench score, UPDRS F1) all come from neighbouring tasks.

(5) The clinical sub-claim belongs to a separate community. Validity studies with ICC, Bland-Altman and MCID analysis are long-established practice in biomechanics and rehabilitation. That makes it a question of regulatory-style validation, not a vision research gap.

One narrower thread is relevant to the field and plausibly survives. Two papers (H2R-Bench 1393 and SmartPortraits 1442) report that intermediate accuracy metrics, such as trajectory or pose accuracy and video quality, rank-correlate poorly with downstream quality. That is evidence of a gap in validating metrics against their downstream use, not of saturation. Even this thread rests on only two papers, neither of which is about hand-object tracking.

skeptics.reframe: Tracking metrics for hand-object and bimanual work (per-frame MPJPE, ADD(-S), contact accuracy) have never been checked against the downstream uses they are meant to serve: success when a captured demonstration is replayed on a robot, and digital-twin fidelity. A method that ranks well on these metrics could still produce demonstrations or twins that fail. This version rests on only two adjacent papers (H2R-Bench, SmartPortraits), so it would need direct evidence from hand-object benchmarks (DexYCB, ARCTIC, HOT3D) before anyone builds on it.

skeptics.reasons:
Refutation case (strong for most of the record): P25 is a bundle of four unrelated evaluation complaints from object pose, robot learning, avatars and clinical scoring. Read as stated, most of it is not a research question. "Household 6D benchmarks are saturated, so build industrial, clutter, long-range or egocentric sets" (402, 348, 1020) is data collection that only needs money and capture effort, and the BOP organisers are already doing it: the BOP Challenge 2024 report (verified) added BOP-H3 headset and hand-object datasets plus model-free onboarding tasks. "Evaluation is fragmented across robots and labs" (1399, UMI-Bench 1372) is a coordination and hardware-standardisation problem. "Clinical cohorts are small and inter-rater ICC is 0.1-0.4" (1424) is a recruitment and labelling problem, and it is outside the author's field. Each new dataset fixes one gap, so another targeted dataset by itself is incremental at CVPR/ICCV main track. The fixes for these parts are known (more data, shared protocols, standard hardware) and mainly wait on resources. On these parts the skeptic position holds.
What survives: one sub-claim is a real scientific question, not a resource gap. It is metric validity, meaning whether the intermediate error a method optimises predicts the downstream outcome it is built for. Two evidence items in the record show it. In 1442, trajectory accuracy does not carry over to downstream reconstruction and synthesis quality, and the authors say explaining why is future work. In H2R-Bench (1393), the core score ranks methods only weakly in line with video-quality metrics. For hand-object and bimanual reconstruction, the two stated applications (robot demonstration capture, digital twins) need contact, relative hand-object pose and physical feasibility. Benchmarks such as HOT3D (CVPR 2025, verified) and DexYCB score MPJPE, ADD-S or Chamfer error instead. Nobody has shown that these per-frame geometric errors rank methods the same way as retargeted policy success or physics-replay success. Top venues have published this kind of evaluation-validity question. SIMPLER (verified arXiv 2405.05941) was published because it showed, with paired sim-real evaluations, that a cheap evaluation correlates with real-robot outcomes. Questions a reviewer would accept as significant: (a) Which hand-object reconstruction errors (contact F1, penetration, relative object-in-hand pose, temporal jitter) predict downstream success when the reconstruction is replayed in simulation or retargeted to a dexterous robot? Do current leaderboards keep their ranking under that criterion? (b) Can a reference-free physical-consistency score (simulation replay of the reconstructed grasp sequence) be validated as a stand-in for ground truth on in-the-wild, occluded bimanual video, where annotation is impossible? That would replace the "cheap-to-annotate controlled capture" bottleneck that the record names as the reason the problem persists. These need an experimental design and a new methodological claim, not only more annotation.
Why the score is only middling: the question is adjacent and sits in evaluation methodology. It fits a NeurIPS Datasets and Benchmarks or CoRL paper better than a CVPR main-track method paper. It needs a physics or retargeting pipeline and several baseline reconstructors. The negative result (metrics do not correlate) carries the paper only if the alternative metric is validated. Most of P25's 37 papers and its benchmark numbers (XYZ-IBD AP drop, PACE drop, UMI-Bench 55.84, TULIP F1 0.69) support the refutable "need more realistic data" reading, not the surviving question. I could not run the dedicated search for a 2024-2026 paper that already correlates hand-object reconstruction metrics with downstream robot or physics success, because the shared WebSearch budget was exhausted. Novelty against that possible prior work is therefore UNVERIFIED.
