skeptics.reframe: Hand-object and bimanual reconstruction methods are ranked by per-frame geometric error (MPJPE, ADD-S, Chamfer) on controlled captures. No one has shown that these rankings predict what the stated applications need: success when the reconstruction is replayed in a physics digital twin or retargeted to a dexterous robot. The research question is which metric or reference-free physical-consistency score predicts downstream utility. A second question is whether such a score can be validated, using paired downstream outcomes, to evaluate occluded in-the-wild bimanual video where ground truth cannot be annotated.

fit.worth_pursuing:
MAYBE. As stated, P25 is a NO. It merges four unrelated evaluation complaints (object-pose saturation, robot-evaluation fragmentation, avatar benchmarks, clinical validity). Most of those are data or coordination problems, and large consortia already own them: BOP (2504.02812, verified), RoboArena (2506.18123, verified), UMI-Bench (2606.10382, verified). One narrowed version is a YES: checking whether hand-object and bimanual tracking metrics predict downstream use. The case for it rests on three findings from this session:
(1) Video-to-robot pipelines published in 2026 already use simulated replay or retargeting success as their headline metric. All five were verified on arXiv: C2Dex (2608.07045, RA-L 2026), VideoManip (2602.09013), DexImit (2602.10105), FlowHOI (2602.13444) and AGILE (2602.04672, SIGGRAPH 2026).
(2) Reconstruction benchmarks (DexYCB, ARCTIC, HOT3D/BOP-H3) still rank methods by geometric error.
(3) Keyword searches of arXiv listings found no paper that correlates the two.
The verdict is MAYBE rather than YES for four reasons:
- The novelty check rests on keyword searches only, because the shared WebSearch budget was used up. It is partly verified, not exhaustive.
- The authors of those pipelines are one ablation away from this result. The work has to be submitted within about 6-9 months, not 18.
- The natural venues are CoRL, RSS and NeurIPS Datasets and Benchmarks. CVPR or ICCV main track is realistic only if RQ2's validated metric and a selection gain come with it.
- Without a robot, "downstream success" means simulated success. A September 2026 study (2610.00731, verified) shows that sim-to-real agreement itself depends on reconstruction quality (r = 0.51 versus 0.90).

research_questions.question: Do the per-frame geometric metrics used to rank hand-object and bimanual trackers predict whether a reconstruction succeeds when replayed in physics or retargeted to a dexterous robot hand? The metrics are MPJPE/PA-MPJPE, ADD-S, object Chamfer distance and relative hand-object pose error. Which error types dominate downstream failure: relative in-hand object pose, contact and penetration, temporal jitter, drift under occlusion, or global scale?
research_questions.why_top_venue:
Evaluation-validity papers backed by paired outcomes have top-venue precedent. SIMPLER (arXiv 2405.05941, verified) showed that a cheap evaluation tracks real-robot outcomes. The September 2026 real-to-sim study (2610.00731, verified) shows reconstruction quality moving sim-real correlation from r = 0.51 to 0.90.

In hand-object work, at least five 2026 video-to-robot pipelines report simulated success as their main number: C2Dex (2608.07045, RA-L), VideoManip (2602.09013), DexImit (2602.10105), FlowHOI (2602.13444) and AGILE (2602.04672, SIGGRAPH 2026). The benchmarks that rank the reconstructors underneath them (DexYCB, ARCTIC, HOT3D in BOP-H3) score geometric error only. Keyword searches of arXiv listings found no paper that tests whether those rankings predict downstream success.

Two outcomes would be reusable by both the vision and robotics communities: a documented ranking flip, and an error budget per error type. Neither needs new data capture.
research_questions.method_sketch:
1) Pipeline pool. Build combinatorial pipelines from public parts so that the method-level rank statistics have enough samples: 3 hand estimators x 3 object trackers x (raw or temporally smoothed / contact-refined) = about 18 pipelines, run on sequences that have ground truth.

2) Two downstream oracles of different cost.
- O1, physics replay: a collision MANO hand is PD-driven toward the reconstructed hand poses in MuJoCo or Isaac. The object is free under gravity and friction. Success means the object reaches the ground-truth end pose within thresholds without being dropped. Also log the residual external wrench needed.
- O2, dexterous retargeting: Allegro, Inspire or Shadow hands, using an open retargeter. Options are SPIDER (2511.09484, verified, sampling-based and reported 10x faster than RL), or ManipTrans (2503.21860, CVPR 2025, verified) and DexMachina (2505.24853, verified) on a subset. Success means object-trajectory tracking success.

3) Controlled perturbation on ground truth. Inject each error type alone, at matched magnitude (for example the same MPJPE increase), to trace per-type error-budget curves.

4) Statistics.
- Sequence-level Spearman correlation.
- Method-level Kendall tau with bootstrap confidence intervals.
- An explicit count of ranking flips.
- A mixed-effects regression of success on error components.
- A composite metric fitted on one dataset and tested on the others for transfer.
research_questions.minimum_experiment:
Data: DexYCB (single-hand grasp-and-lift) and ARCTIC (bimanual, articulated), 150-200 sequences each. Run 8-12 pipelines, oracle O1 on all sequences and oracle O2 on a 50-sequence subset. Ground-truth-input replay serves as the upper bound and the normaliser. Perturbation sweep: 5 error types x 4 magnitudes.

The study counts as informative either way, provided the confidence intervals are reported:
- (a) The downstream ranking differs from the MPJPE / ADD-S ranking, with Kendall tau clearly below about 0.8 and at least one documented flip; or
- (b) One or two error types (expected: relative in-hand pose and contact) explain most of the variance in success.

A held-out HOT3D subset tests whether the composite metric transfers.
research_questions.data_and_hardware:
Public datasets: DexYCB, HO3D v3, ARCTIC and HOT3D (CVPR 2025, 833 min, verified); OakInk2 optional (prior knowledge, not re-verified).

Software: public reconstructors such as HaMeR, WiLoR, FoundationPose, BundleSDF and HOLD (from prior knowledge, not re-verified this session); the MuJoCo or Isaac Gym/Lab simulator; the SPIDER, ManipTrans and DexMachina retargeters (papers verified, code release not checked).

Hardware: one workstation GPU with 24-48 GB for reconstruction inference and RL on a subset. Bulk replay runs CPU-parallel in MuJoCo. No robot and no motion capture are needed. An optional real spot check of 20-30 trials would need a borrowed or low-cost dexterous hand.
research_questions.risks:
1) Scoop. The 2026 pipeline papers are one ablation from this result; plan the first submission within 6-9 months.
2) Null-ish result. If MPJPE and ADD-S already rank methods correctly (tau above 0.8), the story shrinks to the error budget. The perturbation study is designed in advance so that it is informative either way.
3) Oracle dependence. Success depends on the controller, the retargeter and the simulator parameters (friction, mass). Use two oracles and report how far they agree.
4) Reviewers will ask whether simulated success predicts real success (see 2610.00731). Without a robot, claims must be scoped to simulated downstream use.
5) Ground-truth noise. DexYCB and HO3D ground truth contains penetration and jitter (prior knowledge), so replay of ground truth will not reach 100% success. Normalise by ground-truth success and weight the motion-capture ground truth (ARCTIC, HOT3D).
6) Few methods. Method-level n is small; mitigate with the combinatorial pipelines and sequence-level statistics.
7) Alignment conventions. Root-relative versus absolute frames, and Procrustes alignment, change the correlations; report both.
8) Novelty is only partly verified. It rests on about 8 arXiv keyword searches with no hit, because WebSearch was exhausted.

research_questions.question: Can a reference-free physical-consistency score stand in for ground truth when ranking or selecting hand-object reconstructions on occluded, in-the-wild bimanual video? The score is the residual external wrench a replay needs to make the object follow its reconstructed trajectory, given the reconstructed hand contacts and friction cones, combined with an observation-consistency term. It would be validated against paired ground-truth error and paired downstream outcomes.
research_questions.why_top_venue:
P25's stated reason for persisting is that benchmarks follow what is cheap to annotate, which means controlled captures. A validated label-free score would allow evaluation and test-time selection exactly where annotation is impossible: occluded, bimanual, in the wild.

Physics-plausibility terms already exist, but as training losses or descriptive metrics that have never been validated against downstream success or ground-truth error. Examples are penetration and contact losses (the ObMan line, 1904.05767, verified in the listing) and physics-aware 4D capture (2606.15908, verified in the listing).

Presenting the validation together with a measurable gain in downstream success from test-time selection is what turns an evaluation note into a CVPR or ICCV method paper.
research_questions.method_sketch:
1) Score. For each segment, solve a small inverse-dynamics QP: find the admissible contact forces at the reconstructed contacts (friction cones) that best explain the object's acceleration and the hand's grip. The score S combines the residual wrench, a penetration term, and a render-and-compare term against RGB-D silhouettes and depth. The observation term blocks trivially consistent but wrong outputs, such as a static object or a hand far from the object.

2) Validation. Correlate S with ground-truth error and with the O1/O2 downstream success from RQ1. Compare against baselines: penetration only, contact ratio, simulation displacement, estimator confidence, and per-frame provenance flags.

3) Uses.
- (i) Rank pipelines on unlabeled clips and check that ranking against a small manually annotated subset.
- (ii) Test-time selection among K pipeline outputs or hypotheses per segment, measured as gain in downstream success.
- (iii) Reject segments likely to fail, measured with risk-coverage curves.
research_questions.minimum_experiment:
Use the RQ1 pipeline pool on DexYCB and ARCTIC. Success requires all three of the following:
- S correlates with downstream success and with ground-truth error better than the penetration-only and simulation-displacement baselines, with bootstrap confidence intervals.
- Per-segment selection among 4 or more pipeline outputs raises O1 success above the best single pipeline.
- Risk-coverage curves show that rejection by S beats rejection by estimator confidence.

Out-of-distribution check: HOT3D held out with ground truth; then 50-100 occluded bimanual in-the-wild clips with light manual labels (2D keypoints, contact yes/no) to confirm that the ranking agrees.
research_questions.data_and_hardware:
Same as RQ1, plus the following:
- A CPU QP solver (for example OSQP).
- Object mass and friction from dataset metadata or sampled priors.
- About 1-2 student-weeks of light annotation for 100 clips.
- Optional: a consumer RGB-D camera and an ArUco-marked object, which give metric object pose under bimanual occlusion for a small real validation slice. Hand ground truth would be absent.

The single GPU is used only to run the reconstructors.
research_questions.risks:
1) Gaming. Physically consistent but wrong reconstructions can score well, so the observation term is essential and must be ablated.
2) Unknown mass and friction add noise. Report sensitivity sweeps.
3) Accelerations differentiated from 30 fps tracking are noisy, so the residual wrench may need smoothing. That smoothing then biases the score.
4) S may predict downstream success but not ground-truth error, or the reverse. The framing must follow the data.
5) Reviewers may see it as a known plausibility metric. The novelty claim must be the validation and the selection gain, not the term itself.
6) The work depends on RQ1's oracles, so it slips if RQ1 slips.

fit.thesis_assets_help:
Small to modest; none of the assets is decisive.
(1) The measured/held/constrained honesty labels are a ready-made per-frame provenance signal. They can serve as a baseline or feature in RQ2's failure-prediction and risk-coverage analysis. That is one ablation, and possibly a short subsection.
(2) The single RGB-D desk setup with an ArUco-marked object of metric pose gives a cheap real validation slice: metric object pose under bimanual occlusion, without hand ground truth. It is useful for RQ2's out-of-distribution check. The 28 recordings of one subject are far too narrow to be a benchmark and fit only as a small or qualitative slice.
(3) The causal 30 fps chain can be added to the pipeline pool as a realistic online entry.
(4) The Unity twin gives little edge. Dexterous replay should run in MuJoCo or Isaac to be accepted by the community, and Unity PhysX results would be questioned.
(5) The object-conditioned recovery of the occluded holding arm has no direct use, because the questions hinge on hand-object contact, not arm pose.
fit.what_a_small_lab_cannot_do_here:
The lab cannot do the following:
- Build a new large ground-truth hand-object benchmark with motion capture and many subjects at the scale of HOT3D, ARCTIC or DexYCB.
- Run distributed or large real-robot evaluation of the RoboArena, AutoEval or UMI-Bench kind, which needs several robots and institutions.
- Compete in curating BOP-style object-pose benchmarks or industrial capture (XYZ-IBD, IPD).
- Validate simulated success against real dexterous-robot success at scale. With no robot arm or hand, a borrowed hand allows at most a spot check of 20-30 trials, so claims must be scoped to simulated downstream use.
- Run per-trajectory RL retargeting (ManipTrans or DexMachina style) over thousands of sequences x many pipelines on one GPU. Bulk work must use a cheap physics-replay oracle, with RL or SPIDER-style retargeting on a subset only.
- Address the clinical and avatar parts of P25 (patient cohorts, inter-rater studies, multi-camera head rigs).
- Outpace the well-resourced groups behind the 2026 video-to-robot pipelines if they add this ablation. Speed and a clean experimental design are the only levers.

painpoint.name: Contact force is unobservable from vision and unmeasured in natural capture

evidence.latest_state: Between December 2025 and September 2026 the problem changed from "no data" to "mostly glove-supervised vision-to-pressure models", but nobody has measured, metric, general force from bare-hand video. The best reported hand-object numbers come from EgoPHI (ECCV 2026), the first method to estimate dense contact plus 3D force on both hand and object meshes from one RGB image. Its force labels come from simulation, not measurement. Hand force MAE is 4.03 N on ARCTIC in-distribution and 5.16 N on out-of-distribution H2O. Hand volumetric IoU falls from 2.2 to 0.6. Sim-to-real on two instrumented objects gives MAE 0.48 N (cube) and 1.35 N (cylinder). It still needs object meshes, assumes uniform stiffness, predicts only normal force and works frame by frame. On the pressure side, EgoTactile (ICML 2026 spotlight) and EgoPressDiff (ICASSP 2026) use video diffusion; EgoPressDiff reports more than 34 percent relative volumetric IoU gain on EgoPressure. EgoTac trains on 5.7M image-tactile pairs and reports in-domain force error below 0.06 N, but its out-of-domain transfer is only shown qualitatively or relative to baselines. TouchSight, HOPE and Glove2Hand (CVPR 2026 Highlight) attack the glove-appearance problem: they turn gloved recordings into bare-hand video or lift glove pressure onto MANO vertices. Their bare-hand in-the-wild results are mostly qualitative. On the body side, joint contact force from monocular video reaches 0.32 BW RMSE (hip) and 0.23 BW (knee) on OrthoLoad, leave-one-subject-out. Separately, video inverse dynamics is shown to amplify pose noise about 1000x. For robot learning, ForceBand (sEMG wristband) reports more than 50 percent lower force error than vision baselines and 87 percent task success. CHORD and Dex-X instead obtain wrench or tactile signals from simulated reconstruction of the human video. None of the 2026 work closes the original gap: there is no measured bimanual 3D force on arbitrary non-planar objects from bare-hand RGB(-D), and the out-of-distribution drop seen in EgoPressure remains.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: EgoPHI: Estimating 3D Hand-Object Contact and Force from Egocentric Vision
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Estimates dense contact maps and 3D force distributions on hand and object meshes from monocular RGB plus the object mesh. Training force labels come from a physics simulation pipeline. Hand force MAE is 4.03 N on ARCTIC and 5.16 N on out-of-distribution H2O; sim-to-real MAE is 0.48 to 1.35 N on instrumented objects.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: EgoTactile: Learning Grasp Pressure for Everyday Objects from Egocentric Video
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Benchmark of egocentric video paired with full-hand pressure on 3D everyday objects, with a bare-hand transfer subset. Proposes EgoPressureFormer and EgoPressureDiff, a diffusion model built on a pretrained video diffusion backbone.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: EgoPressDiff: Multimodal Video Diffusion for Egocentric UV-Domain Hand-Pressure Estimation
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Conditional video diffusion that predicts UV hand-pressure maps from RGB, depth, pose and MANO vertices. Reports more than 34 percent relative volumetric IoU gain on EgoPressure.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: Glove2Hand: Synthesizing Natural Hand-Object Interaction from Multi-Modal Sensing Gloves
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Translates sensing-glove HOI video into photorealistic bare-hand video while keeping the tactile and IMU signals (HandSense dataset). This supplies contact ground truth for bare-hand contact estimation.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: HOPE: Hand-Object Pressure Estimation from Monocular Videos
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Lifts glove pressure and contact annotations into MANO vertex space and uses a vertex-anchored video transformer with contact-gated pressure prediction. Evaluated on OpenTouch, PressureVisionDB and contact datasets, with bare-hand generalization.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: TouchSight: Bare-Handed Tactile Prediction from Egocentric Video via Generative Visual Augmentation
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Uses 500 hours of pressure-glove data, re-rendered to bare hands by generative video models (TwinTouch-20H), to predict dense full-hand contact force. Beats prior contact methods on OakInk2; transfer to bare-hand in-the-wild video is shown only qualitatively.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: EgoTac: In-the-wild Tactile Prediction from Egocentric Vision
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Trains on 5.7M image-tactile pairs to predict force and contact from egocentric video. In-domain force error is below 0.06 N; zero-shot results on in-the-wild video.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: TouchAnything: A Dataset and Framework for Bimanual Tactile Estimation from Egocentric Video
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Bimanual egocentric plus wrist-camera dataset with continuous pressure maps: 208 tasks, 1891 episodes. Adding wrist views gives up to 5.0 percent relative contact IoU gain.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: OPENTOUCH: Bringing Full-Hand Touch to Real-World Interaction
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: First in-the-wild dataset aligning egocentric video, full-hand glove tactile data and hand pose: 5.1 hours, 2.9K clips, single hand. Defines retrieval and classification benchmarks.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: ForceBand: Learning Forceful Manipulation with sEMG
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: An sEMG wristband estimates per-finger force synchronized with human video (10-hour dataset). More than 50 percent lower force error than vision baselines; 87 percent robot success on force-controlled pick-squeeze-place.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: Human-Centric Transferable Tactile Pre-Training for Dexterous Robotic Manipulation (H-Tac)
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: 160-hour egocentric human tactile-action dataset (135k episodes, more than 300 tasks) used to pretrain tactile representations for robot policies.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: ART-Glove: Articulated Tactile Glove for Contact-Grounded Dexterous Interaction Capture
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Tactile glove with 2048 taxels and 22-DoF joint sensing at 120 Hz for capturing contact-grounded demonstrations while preserving dexterity.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: Dex-X: Learning Visual-Tactile Dexterous Manipulation From Human Videos with Simulated Interaction
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Reconstructs HOI from monocular human video in simulation, which generates tactile supervision missing from the video. Real-robot success is 93 percent on cube picking and 53 percent on table cleaning.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: Learning Dexterous Manipulation Using Contact Wrench Guidance From Human Demonstration (CHORD)
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Object-centric contact-wrench representation of human demonstrations used to guide RL. 82.12 percent average success over 1831 simulated tasks.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: ReForce: Learning Force-aware Retargeting for Dexterous Manipulation
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Learns a residual on kinematic retargeting to track desired human contact forces, using a force tracker trained in simulation. The abstract does not say how the human force is obtained.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: From Pixels to Newtons: Predicting In Vivo Joint Contact Forces from Monocular Video

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: How Noisy Poses Break Inverse Dynamics: Analysis and Mitigation for Video-Based Joint Torque Estimation

evidence.crowdedness: HIGH. Over 15 papers from 2025 to 2026 attack this directly. They come from strong groups (Holz/ETH, MIT Matusik/Torralba, Joo/SNU, Ding/Tsinghua, Malik/Aloimonos, Xiaolong Wang, Meta Reality Labs) and reach CVPR 2026, ECCV 2026 and ICML 2026. Most are hand-pressure models with glove supervision and robot-learning tactile datasets.
evidence.trend: Rising. A burst of arXiv papers from May to September 2026 (more than ten found with six searches) follows the release of glove-video datasets: OpenTouch, EgoPressure, TouchAnything, H-Tac. Two forces drive it: robot learning wants force-enriched human demonstrations, and generative video models can turn glove footage into bare-hand footage.

skeptics.reasons: Not refuted, but the pain point as stated is too broad, and much of it is being worked on hard in 2025-2026. The claim that video datasets carry no measured force is being eroded quickly. OpenTouch (arXiv 2512.16842, Dec 2025) released 5.1 h of in-the-wild egocentric video synchronized with full-hand touch and pose. TouchAnything/EgoTouch (arXiv 2605.13083, May 2026) offers 1,891 bimanual episodes over 208 tasks with dense pressure maps and multi-view RGB. EgoTactile (arXiv 2606.09243, ICML 2026 spotlight) has full-hand pressure on everyday 3D objects, a diffusion predictor and a bare-hand transfer subset. TouchSight (arXiv 2609.20414, Sep 2026) uses 500 h of pressure-glove data plus generative glove-to-bare-hand rendering (TwinTouch-20H). That directly attacks the "gloves change hand appearance" objection. EgoPHI (arXiv 2608.13014, ECCV 2026) estimates dense 3D contact and force on hand and articulated object meshes from egocentric images. On the robot side, glove-based force-aware transfer is now routine: OSMO, Feel the Force, GIFT and ART-Glove. On the body side there is MonoMSK and Pixels-to-Newtons. The physical core is still unsolved, though, and none of this reduces it to engineering. (a) The new labels are normal pressure from gloves, not 3D force vectors with shear, object-side reaction forces or mass and friction. (b) EgoPHI's force supervision is simulated and needs known object geometry; real validation used only two instrumented objects and eight participants, and the authors say generalization is open. (c) Bare-hand transfer is shown only qualitatively (TouchSight, EgoTactile). No benchmark has measured force ground truth on bare, uninstrumented hands in the wild, so the stated failure to generalize to unseen views and objects cannot even be measured in the target setting. (d) Body force-from-video is still noisy; 2605.24776 documents that pose noise breaks inverse dynamics. No metric is saturated and no product exists. Caveats: the area is now crowded, led by groups with custom tactile hardware (Wenbo Ding/Tsinghua, Holz/ETH, MIT Matusik/Luo). The pain point is also adjacent to the author's tracking-and-reconstruction field, so the data-scarcity framing is a weak entry point for a small lab.

skeptics.reframe: Data scarcity for vision-to-pressure is being addressed quickly by in-the-wild tactile gloves and generative rendering from gloved to bare hands (OpenTouch, EgoTouch, EgoTactile, TouchSight). The open problem is narrower. No method recovers physically consistent 3D contact force vectors on both the hand and the object, meaning normal plus shear force, object reaction and a wrench balance against object motion. And no method is quantitatively validated on bare, uninstrumented hands. That gap exists because there is no benchmark with measured force ground truth on bare hands. Existing labels are either glove normal pressure, which changes appearance and has no shear, or simulation-derived forces that need known object geometry (EgoPHI). A tractable angle for a tracking and reconstruction lab is physics-consistency evaluation: check inferred forces against tracked object kinematics using known mass and an instrumented object. Collecting more glove data is not the angle.

skeptics.reasons:
Artifact test, partly passed. The evidence is not narrow. The 34 supporting papers (checked against w3_digest/all.json) span three communities: hand-object vision (EgoPressure ETH/CVPR25, Glove2Hand, FEEL, EgoTactile, HT-Bench), body capture and biomechanics (MMVP, MotionPRO, AddBiomechanics ECCV24, IPMAN CVPR23, Muscles in Time NeurIPS24, ImDy ICLR25), and robot learning (RH20T, VTDexManip, DexCanvas, Kaiwu, surveys and a position paper). They come from many groups, venues and sensors, so this is not one dataset's quirk. The core physical claim is also not a convention. Grip or internal squeeze force lies in the null space of the grasp map, so kinematics alone leave it statically indeterminate, and a sensor at the contact interface changes the contact. That is a structural observability limit.

Three things weaken the claim as written:
(1) Selection bias. Most of the supporting papers are force, pressure or tactile dataset papers. They state "force is missing" as motivation for their own contribution, so the count of 34 overstates independent confirmation.
(2) The statement bundles separable problems, and one of them is largely solved in another community. Biomechanics has long estimated ground reaction forces and joint moments from motion. OpenCap (PLOS Comp Biol 2023) gets about 6.2% bodyweight MAE in GRF from two smartphones, comparable to IMU suits. So "cannot be inferred from video outside the lab" does not hold for whole-body GRF in gait-like activities. It holds mainly for fast or atypical motions (the >25% bodyweight out-of-distribution error in 334 and the jumping failure in ImDy).
(3) "Unmeasured in natural capture" and "models collapse" are going out of date. Large in-the-wild glove-plus-egocentric datasets now exist: OpenTouch (MIT, Dec 2025, 5.1 h, 14 environments, measured force), EgoTac (Aug 2026, 5.7M image-tactile pairs, zero-shot on unconstrained video) and EgoTouch/TouchAnything (May 2026, bimanual, dense pressure). Prior vision-to-pressure work (PressureVision ECCV22, PressureVision++) generalized across participants.
The collapse numbers come from single setups: EgoPressure's own view split (36.8 vs 62.1 IoU) and one cross-dataset run of PressureVision++ (0.8 IoU). They are not field-wide benchmarks.

What survives: calibrated force magnitude for multi-contact, occluded hand-object and bimanual grasps from bare-hand video, validated without a glove that alters appearance. The rest is either solved elsewhere (body GRF) or under active data-scaling attack (hand contact and pressure). Relevance to an RGB-D bimanual tracking thesis stays adjacent.

skeptics.reframe: Video already gives contact location and, through biomechanics pipelines, whole-body ground reaction forces. What it still cannot give is calibrated force magnitude for multi-contact, occluded hand-object and bimanual grasps. Internal squeeze force is statically indeterminate from kinematics, and every way of measuring it (gloves, pads, instrumented objects) changes how the hand looks or how the contact behaves. The open problem is physically consistent bare-hand force estimation that transfers across views, objects and scenes, checked against ground truth that does not alter the interaction. Larger glove-video datasets such as OpenTouch, EgoTac and EgoTouch scale the training pairs but do not remove the appearance gap.

skeptics.reasons:
Refutation attempt. Half of P26 is a data-collection complaint. "Unmeasured in natural capture" and "human demonstration datasets omit force" are partly a wish for better sensors and more instrumented capture, and that half yields no research question by itself. The other half does survive. Force is not visible in images: it depends on mass, friction and stiffness. Any sensor placed at the contact changes the contact, and vision-to-force models lose about half their contact IoU on unseen views (EgoPressure: 36.82 percent on unseen views vs 62.11 percent on seen ones). This is an identifiability and generalization problem, not one that only awaits money. More data would not fix it, because the paired data can only be collected in ways that disturb what is measured.

Top venues treat it as a research problem. Verified examples: PressureVision (arXiv 2203.10385, ECCV 2022 venue from memory), PressureVision++ (WACV 2024, weak supervision from prompted pressure), EgoPressure (CVPR 2025), and EgoPHI (ECCV 2026, per its arXiv listing). EgoPHI predicts dense hand and object force from one RGB image, trains on physics-simulated force labels and validates sim-to-real on instrumented objects. Three 2026 arXiv preprints address the same gap; their venues are unknown. HOPE (Joo group) lifts glove, planar-sensor and mesh-distance contact labels into one hand-vertex space so bare-hand video can be used. EgoTac uses 5.7M image-tactile pairs. A third predicts contact force distributions from vision with geometry priors (Advanced Robotics 2026). The heavy 2026 activity shows reviewers find the question significant. It also shows the generic "predict pressure from RGB" framing is crowded, and a newcomer needs a sharper angle.

Research questions a reviewer would find significant:
(1) Identifiability. Tracked object kinematics plus a mass or inertia estimate fix the net external wrench on the object. The split of that wrench between two hands, and the internal squeeze force, lie in the null space of the grasp map. Which priors make the force split recoverable, with stated error bounds: friction-cone and equilibrium constraints, deformation of the hand and object surfaces, skin color change, temporal slip events?
(2) Supervision without interference. Can an instrumented capture that changes the contact still yield an unbiased model of bare-hand force? Possible routes are a learned glove-to-bare-hand correction and self-supervision from physical consistency.
(3) Evaluation without instrumentation. Can a physically consistent benchmark use only object-side sensing, such as load cells or IMUs inside objects, so that hands stay bare?

The author's RGB-D bimanual tracking fits (1) directly. Because P26 is listed as adjacent to the author's field, and the area is moving fast in 2026, the score is moderate rather than high.

skeptics.reframe: In bimanual handling tracked with RGB-D, the object's tracked motion plus its mass fix the net wrench on the object. How much of that wrench each hand applies, and how hard the hands squeeze against each other, cannot be read from the motion: these components lie in the null space of the grasp map. The research question is which visual and physical cues make that split identifiable, with stated error bounds: friction cones, equilibrium, hand and object surface deformation, slip events. A second question is how to supervise and evaluate such estimates without putting a force sensor between the hand and the object, which changes the contact.

research_questions.question: In bimanual holding and transport of a rigid object seen by one RGB-D camera, which parts of each hand's wrench can be identified from the tracked object kinematics, its known mass and the contact geometry? How tightly can the parts that cannot be identified (load sharing between the hands and internal squeeze) be bounded by friction-cone feasibility plus a grip-load coupling prior? The test is against bare-hand force ground truth measured inside the object.
research_questions.why_top_venue: This turns the over-broad pain point into a precise, falsifiable claim, and it targets the gap all three skeptics left open. There is no benchmark with measured force on bare hands that the sensor does not touch. Current evidence is thin. EgoPHI (ECCV 2026, arXiv 2608.13014) takes monocular RGB plus object geometry, trains on simulated force labels, and validates on only two instrumented objects with eight participants; its abstract does not mention bimanual grasps. TouchSight, EgoTactile and HOPE show bare-hand results mostly qualitatively. The closest prior work is Pham et al., CVPR 2015 (https://openaccess.thecvf.com/content_cvpr_2015/papers/Pham_Towards_Force_Sensing_2015_CVPR_paper.pdf) and TPAMI 2018. They used one hand, RGB-D at 30 fps, minimal forces from an SOCP plus a neural network for the internal forces, Honeywell FSG020WNPB sensors at fixed positions on a box, an Xsens IMU and three operators, and reported about 10-15 percent relative force error (verified from the PDF). Moving to two hands with palm contacts changes the identifiability structure: 12 wrench components against a 6-D Newton-Euler constraint, so load sharing itself becomes indeterminate except in special support configurations. Interval outputs with coverage checks answer the reviewer objection that force is unobservable instead of hiding it. The nearest bimanual measured-force result is outside top vision venues: a 2026 ergonomics paper (arXiv 2608.22586) regresses per-hand triaxial forces for 6-12 kg boxes from RGB plus known mass, with 35 subjects, RMSE 4.7-5.6 N horizontal and 10.6-11.0 N vertical, and no physics. Caveat: the novelty over Pham is moderate, so the measured bare-hand bimanual benchmark and the identifiability analysis have to carry the paper.
research_questions.method_sketch: (1) Tracking: 6-DoF object pose (fiducials for benchmark ground truth; a markerless FoundationPose-class tracker for the method) and two MANO hands (a HaMeR/WiLoR-class regressor refined with depth). Contact patches come from hand-object proximity plus a learned contact prior. (2) Kinematics: object linear and angular acceleration from fixed-lag smoothing (algebraic differentiation as in Pham 2015, or a Kalman filter with a jerk model), with a covariance, validated against an IMU inside the object. (3) Observable part: the net external wrench W = M(a - g) plus rotational inertia terms. The hand wrenches must sum to W. (4) Feasible set: contact forces at the patches are unilateral, inside friction cones with mu in an interval [mu_lo, mu_hi], and satisfy Newton-Euler within the acceleration covariance. This set is convex. Project it onto per-hand quantities (vertical load share, squeeze along the axis between the hands, per-hand torque) and solve LP/SOCP min and max problems to get a bound per frame. (5) Point estimate: a MAP solution inside the set under an internal-force prior. Option (a) is a grip-load safety-margin model from the motor-control literature (grip force tracks load force with a margin above the slip limit; Johansson and Westling 1984, cited from memory), calibrated on a held-out subset. Option (b) is a prior learned from public glove-pressure data. (6) Identifiability index: interval width divided by mg, plus an analytic classification of bimanual grasp configurations by the rank of the grasp map under the active unilateral constraints. For example, two palms under the object are nearly determinate by moment balance, while a side squeeze leaves the squeeze undetermined but the net wrench determined. (7) A causal 30 fps variant for online use.
research_questions.minimum_experiment: Build one instrumented box with adjustable mass (about 0.5-3 kg via inserts). Mount two large handle or side plates, each on a force sensor: a small 6-axis F/T sensor, or a 3-4 load-cell array that gives normal force and centre of pressure. Add an IMU and fiducials for pose ground truth, and synchronize with an LED flash or a hardware trigger. Hands stay bare. Record 8-12 subjects x 6 tasks (lift-place, carry, tilt or rotate, pass from hand to hand, squeeze-lift from the sides, carry with palms under) x 3 masses x 2 surface frictions, about 2-4 hours of RGB-D in total. Metrics: per-hand vertical load error (N and percent of mg), squeeze error, net-wrench error, interval coverage and mean width, and error against the identifiability index. Baselines: a constant 50/50 split; a Pham-style minimum-norm SOCP; a direct learned regressor in the style of arXiv 2608.22586; EgoPHI if its code is released. Ablations: marker vs markerless object pose, 30 vs 60 fps, width of the mu prior, type of prior. Example pass criteria: nominal 90 percent intervals cover at least 90 percent of frames, and per-hand vertical load error beats the 50/50 baseline clearly on asymmetric grasps.
research_questions.data_and_hardware: One consumer RGB-D camera (RealSense D4xx, Orbbec or Azure Kinect class) and one single-GPU workstation; no training of large models is required. Instrumented object, two options. Option 1: two small 6-axis F/T sensors (low thousands of USD each; price unverified). Option 2: single-axis load cells with a 24-bit ADC (tens of USD; normal force and centre of pressure only, no shear). Either option also needs an IMU, a microcontroller and a 3D-printed or machined shell. Public data: DexYCB and HO3D, whose YCB objects have published masses (from memory), to develop the markerless tracking path; ARCTIC, HOT3D or OakInk2 for bimanual hand-tracking priors (no force; object masses not known, unverified); OpenTouch or TouchAnything glove pressure for a learned internal-force prior (licences and calibration to newtons unverified). Requires human-subjects ethics approval.
research_questions.risks: (1) Reviewers may call it a bimanual extension of Pham 2015/2018. Mitigation: the measured bare-hand benchmark, the identifiability theory and modern baselines. (2) Internal squeeze is genuinely unobservable from kinematics, so prior-based squeeze error may stay large (perhaps 30-50 percent; my estimate, unverified). That reads as weak unless it is framed as calibrated bounds. (3) Acceleration noise: by a back-of-envelope sqrt(6)*sigma/dt^2, a second difference of 1 mm pose noise at 30 fps gives about 2 m/s^2 std before filtering. That is comparable to g in dynamic phases, so dynamic tasks need smoothing or the IMU; quasi-static phases dominated by gravity are fine. (4) Handle-mounted sensors fix where the hands touch, which partly brings back the critique that instrumentation shapes the interaction. (5) Scoop risk: the EgoPHI authors, the ETH Holz group, MIT and SNU Joo are active, and a bimanual, physics-consistent EgoPHI is an obvious next step. (6) Markerless hand tracking fails when a palm is under the box. Contact-position error propagates: Pham 2015 measured a 6.13 mm std in contact position, which gave a 1.55 N std in force. (7) Ethics approval and the build may consume months 1-4.

research_questions.question: Can consistency with tracked object dynamics (Newton-Euler with known mass, plus friction cones) serve as a test-time projection and as a self-supervised fine-tuning signal that makes glove-supervised or simulation-supervised hand-force predictors metric on bare hands? Which force components does it actually fix: the net-wrench subspace, the null space, or per-contact normal force?
research_questions.why_top_venue: Every 2026 route to bare-hand transfer (TouchSight, Glove2Hand, HOPE, EgoTactile) uses appearance translation or label lifting and reports bare-hand results mostly qualitatively. A model-agnostic physics route needs no extra force labels and would be evaluated quantitatively on measured bare-hand forces, making it a general add-on. The result is publishable even if it is partly negative, provided the error is split into the observable net-wrench part and the unobservable internal part, because that split is the honest analysis the field lacks. Reviewers value plug-in gains backed by real measured evaluation more than another pressure regressor.
research_questions.method_sketch: (1) Take released predictors that output per-vertex pressure or force on MANO or object meshes. Convert the outputs to contact forces (pressure x vertex area along the normal); tangential components stay free inside the cone. (2) Add a differentiable convex projection layer (cvxpylayers-style) onto the set {Newton-Euler with tracked acceleration and known mass, friction cones with mu in an interval, unilateral normals}, weighted by the prediction's confidence. (3) At test time, apply the projection only. (4) At training time, apply a consistency loss between the predicted and projected forces on unlabeled RGB-D video of objects with known mass (YCB objects in DexYCB/HO3D, plus the RQ1 rig recordings without sensors), anchored to the original predictions to avoid collapse. (5) Report error decomposed into the net-wrench subspace and the grasp-map null space, so that gains that hold by construction are separated from real gains. Mass cannot be identified from kinematics, so it must be known or taken from a category prior.
research_questions.minimum_experiment: Run 2-3 predictors with public weights x {raw, projected, fine-tuned}. Evaluate on (a) the bare-hand benchmark from RQ1 and (b) EgoPHI's real instrumented-object data if it is released. Metrics: per-hand and per-contact force error split into net-subspace and null-space components; contact IoU, which should not degrade; consistency of the decomposition across subjects. Control: random projection-weight perturbation. The key reported number is the change in null-space and per-contact error, because the net-wrench gain is largely tautological.
research_questions.data_and_hardware: The same RGB-D rig and instrumented object as RQ1, and one GPU, which is enough for projection and light fine-tuning (no diffusion training). Public weights are needed: availability for EgoPHI, HOPE, EgoTactile and EgoPressDiff is unverified, while PressureVision/PressureVision++ and EgoPressure baselines are older and more likely available (unverified). YCB object masses and the DexYCB/HO3D videos are used for unlabeled fine-tuning.
research_questions.risks: (1) The predictors may be unreleased, or may assume egocentric views and object meshes that do not match a third-person desk camera. (2) The net-subspace gain is partly guaranteed by construction, so reviewers will discount it. (3) The null-space gain may be near zero, which leaves an analysis-only contribution (better as a section of the RQ1 paper than a standalone paper). (4) Converting glove pressure to newtons is uncertain because glove calibration and drift are poorly documented. (5) Mass must be known. (6) Pressure predictors output normal force only, so shear stays unconstrained except through the cones.

fit.thesis_assets_help: The assets give a moderate-to-small edge, mostly for RQ1. (1) The ArUco-marked object with metric pose and the causal 30 fps chain supply exactly the object kinematics needed for the observable net wrench, the core of RQ1. My estimate is that this saves about 2-3 months of pipeline building. (2) The measured/held/constrained honesty labels map directly onto the observable / bounded / prior-filled split that RQ1 reports, so they can frame the paper. That is a real conceptual match, not decoration. (3) The object-conditioned recovery of an occluded holding arm helps decide which hand is on which side when the supporting hand is occluded. It recovers the arm, though, not finger-level contact geometry, so contact patches still need a MANO-class hand tracker. (4) The single RGB-D desk setup is the capture rig. (5) The Unity twin is useful only for showing force arrows; its physics engine is not a validated force reference. (6) The 28 recordings of one subject have no force ground truth and are pilot material only. Caveat: before any acceleration-based wrench, quantify the thesis pose chain's scale correction (45 mm printed marker, 0.050 m declared, rescaled by 0.9) and its 30 fps pose noise against an IMU, because force error scales directly with both. None of the assets measures force, and force measurement is the bottleneck.

painpoint.name: Fine-grained actions, phases and events cannot be inferred automatically

evidence.latest_state: The gap is narrowing on curated multiple-choice video QA but is still far from solved. On HanDyVQA (CVPR 2026; 11.1K QA on fine-grained hand-object interaction dynamics), the best model, Gemini-2.5-Pro, reaches 73 percent average accuracy against 97 percent for humans. On HD-EPIC VQA, Gemini Pro scored 37.6 percent overall in the original paper. The CVPR 2026 challenge entry EgoAdapt reaches 67.22 percent overall, with 64.03 percent on fine-grained action, 64.87 percent on 3D perception and 61.63 percent on object motion; the previous best entry, DeepFrames, had 44.21, 48.30, 42.59 and 30.17. EgoAdapt gets there with per-category prompt routing, calibrated scoring and test-time consistency adaptation, not with any new 3D hand or object state, and humans remain above 90 percent. EgoCoT-Bench (arXiv 2026-05) reports up to 87.8 percent on manipulation-state perception, but finds that models often give the right answer with evidence that contradicts it. That means the reasoning is not grounded. On the robot side, Automatic Labelling for Bimanual Mobile Manipulation (arXiv 2026-09) segments phases from kinematic signals (gripper, end-effector, force) and then runs vision-language reasoning on each phase. Human acceptance is 90.5 percent for the temporal divisions and 78.7 percent for arm labels, with 87.4 percent run-to-run consistency. This only works because robot logs supply the event signal. FEEL (arXiv 2026-03) uses force gloves to get contact segmentation without annotation. Neither is solved for vision-only, unscripted human video, and none of the work found jointly infers contact, grasp and release phase, and object state from 3D hand-object tracking.

evidence.crowdedness: HIGH. At least nine new 2025-2026 benchmarks and methods were found with only six searches. They come from large egocentric-video groups (the HD-EPIC/EPIC consortium, Tokyo/AIST for HanDyVQA, Ego-Exo4D users) and robot-learning labs (HKU, USC, Tsinghua/Zhipu for ProcVLM), plus a yearly CVPR challenge, so the video-QA framing is crowded. The narrower framing, inferring contact, phase and object state from 3D hand-object tracking, is much less occupied.
evidence.trend: Rising attention. In 2026, new benchmarks (HanDyVQA, EgoCoT-Bench, PIE-V), a CVPR 2026 challenge with large score jumps, and several robot-labelling and progress-reward papers appeared in September 2026 alone. The driver is demand for automatic labels and rewards for VLA and robot-learning data from human video.

skeptics.reasons: No 2025-2026 work I found solves P27 outright. Some parts have narrowed, though, so the claim as written overstates the gap. Progress: (1) On HD-EPIC VQA, a fine-tuned Qwen3-VL-8B (EgoAdapt, a CVPR 2026 challenge entry) reaches 67.2 percent overall, against 37.6 percent for Gemini Pro. By category it scores 64.0 on fine-grained action, 64.9 on 3D perception and 61.6 on object motion, against human scores near 90-94. The record's '20-35 percent' figures are therefore out of date, but the gap to humans is still about 25-30 points. (2) On HanDyVQA (Dec 2025, fine-grained hand-object dynamics, including state change and object parts), Gemini-2.5-Pro scores 73 percent against 97 percent for humans. The authors name spatial relations, motion and part-level geometry as the failure modes, and adding explicit hand-object interaction cues improves results. That supports the pain point's causal story: missing 3D hand-object state, not missing scale. (3) CFG-Bench (Nov 2025) reports that leading MLLMs remain weak at physical-interaction detail and at evaluative judgment, which covers completion and mistakes. (4) On the robot-learning side, VLM auto-segmentation is now routine: ProcVLM labels a 60M-frame corpus, and TREAD, LA4VLA, RoboSubtaskNet and the Dec 2025 proprioception-plus-VLM segmentation paper all segment automatically. Coarse subtask labelling is therefore becoming engineering. However, ProcVLM reports no accuracy against human labels, curates about 15k trajectories by hand, and states that its rewards are limited by boundary-localisation quality. So the human-verification dependence persists at fine granularity. (5) A CVPR 2026 Findings paper on detecting precise hand touch moments (TouchMoment, 8,456 contact moments) treats frame-exact contact onset as an open detection task, and its existence confirms that contact events are not solved. I could not read its numbers (HTTP 403). Net: caption-level and coarse-phase labelling has largely become engineering with VLMs plus light curation. What remains is frame-accurate, 3D-grounded detection of contact, grasp and release events, object state changes, per-hand bimanual actions, and completion or mistake judgement. These still lack automatic solutions and validated accuracy. This is adjacent to the author's field but connects directly: 3D hand-object tracking supplies the missing signal.

skeptics.reframe: Coarse action captions and subtask segmentation are now routinely produced by VLMs at corpus scale, with light human curation. What is still not automatic is frame-accurate, 3D-grounded event inference in hand-object and bimanual manipulation. That covers contact onset, grasp and release frames, per-hand simultaneous actions, object state changes, and completion or mistake judgement. Best models still sit about 25 points below humans on HanDyVQA and HD-EPIC, and VLM segmentation pipelines report no accuracy against ground truth. Benchmarks such as HanDyVQA find that explicit hand-object cues help. A tracker that outputs 3D hand-object pose and contact over time could therefore serve as the event-inference signal and as a validation reference for these labels.

skeptics.reasons:
Lens: is P27 an artifact of one dataset, one community's conventions, or a few setups? The core does not reduce to one artifact, but the pain point is broader than its support, and part of it is an artifact.

Why it survives (it is not one group's artifact):
(1) Weak verb, state-change and fine-grained action recognition is reported independently by many unrelated groups and setups: Ego4D (TPAMI), HD-EPIC (Bristol, CVPR 2025), Assembly101 and AssemblyHands (Meta, CVPR 2022 and 2023), HoloAssist (Microsoft, ICCV 2023), TACO and HOI4D (Tsinghua, CVPR), EPFL-Smart-Kitchen and IndEgo (NeurIPS 2025), ATTACH (ICRA 2023, multi-Kinect), the ICRA 2024 handover-failure dataset, ChildPlay-Hand (in-the-wild) and EgoHOIBench (ICLR 2025).
(2) Verified by WebFetch:
- The EgoHOIBench abstract (ICLR 2025) states that EgoVLMs find verbs harder than nouns.
- The HD-EPIC abstract (CVPR 2025) reports Gemini Pro at 38.5 percent overall VQA.
(3) Fine-grained egocentric action recognition has been an open challenge track since EPIC-Kitchens 2018. No neighbouring community treats it as solved.

Where it is an artifact or inflated (the reason for the 5):
(a) Contact, grasp and release events are not unsolved in instrumented 3D capture.
- GRAB computes contact from the fitted meshes (verified in its abstract).
- ARCTIC, OakInk and DexYCB derive contact or grasp states geometrically.
- Teleoperation logs give the gripper open and close state directly.
- So "pipelines rely on human labelling" for contact and phase events belongs to passive RGB and VLM-captioned video. It is not a field-wide condition, and least of all in the author's RGB-D 3D-tracking setting.
(b) Several sub-claims rest on single, mostly non-peer-reviewed sources:
- VLM completion verification near chance: WIYH only, arXiv.
- "No temporal segmentation method meets needs": H-RDT only, arXiv.
- Aligning video, mocap, tactile and robot logs to events: one position paper, arXiv 2026.
- Atomic-action label hallucination: Open-AoE, HumanNet and EgoLive, all arXiv 2026 data-engine papers with one shared convention, which is VLM auto-captioning of passive video.
(c) Some headline numbers come from how a benchmark was built, not from a field-wide ceiling:
- HoloAssist's roughly 35 percent fine-grained top-1 reflects a long-tailed taxonomy.
- ATTACH's view-split halving is tied to furniture occluding at least one view in its rig.
- VLM HD-EPIC scores are zero-shot general-purpose models, which is a moving target.
(d) The 29-paper list is padded with papers that do not support the claim:
- BANZ-FS fingerspelling.
- The PCIE_Pose challenge report.
- Ego4D's limitations concern geographic bias.
- AssemblyHands and AssemblyHands-X mainly say that pose quality limits action recognition.
(e) The statement bundles three distinct problems:
- Fine-grained verb recognition.
- VLM 3D and kinematic reasoning.
- Event segmentation for robot data.
Each has narrower support than the bundle suggests.

Net: the claim that verb, state-change and fine-grained action recognition from passive video is weak is field-wide and well supported. The contact-event and phase-labelling part is largely an artifact of RGB-only, caption-supervised pipelines. Relevance to the author stays adjacent.
