skeptics.reframe: Recognising verbs, object-state changes and contact events from passive RGB video stays weak across many datasets and groups, because caption-level supervision carries no 3D hand-object state. In instrumented 3D or RGB-D capture, the same events can be computed directly from geometry (contact, grasp, release). The open, field-wide gap is therefore narrower: carry those event labels and phases from 3D hand-object geometry over to unscripted monocular or egocentric video, at scale and without human verification.

skeptics.reasons:
Attempted refutation: parts of P27 are labelling logistics. The robot-learning half (VLM atomic-action labels hallucinate and need human-in-the-loop correction; fixed-interval segmentation; completion verification near chance) reads like a request for more annotation effort or a stronger VLM, and the egocentric-VLM half is the core turf of the large video-understanding community, which already attacks it with hard-negative objectives (EgoNCE++, ICLR 2025, verified: hard-negative verb captions raise verb accuracy by about 34 points, so part of the verb gap is a training-objective issue already being solved). Multimodal timestamp alignment (video, mocap, tactile, robot logs) is largely sync engineering. If the pain point is read as "label more video" or "wait for better VLMs", it yields no top-venue question.
Why the refutation fails: the evidence points to a structural cause that more caption data does not remove. Verbs, contact onset/release, grasp stages and object-state changes are defined by small 3D hand-object changes that object-centric, caption-level supervision does not carry. HD-EPIC (CVPR 2025, verified) shows Gemini Pro at 32.5 percent on 3D perception and 20.8 percent on object motion against about 93 percent for humans. ATTACH and the predicted-vs-annotated hand pose result tie recognition quality to 3D pose quality. That gives open, testable questions that a CVPR/ICCV/CoRL reviewer would find significant. (1) Can event segmentation (contact, grasp, release, hand-over, state change) be inferred self-supervised from reconstructed 4D hand-object trajectories, as discontinuities in relative pose, contact and support, rather than learned from labels? (2) Does jointly estimating 4D hand-object state and event/phase segmentation improve both, with events acting as priors on contact and physics for tracking under occlusion, and tracking acting as grounding for verbs? (3) Can 3D-kinematic tokens fed to a VLM close the verb/motion gap, and how robust is that to noise from monocular or RGB-D trackers? Recent work is moving in this direction (WHOLE, arXiv 2602.22209, world-grounded hand-object reconstruction with VLM contact localization; verified only as a search hit), which shows the question is live and publishable but also crowded. 
Limits: the pain point is tagged adjacent to the author's core field. Its labelling and timestamp-alignment parts are engineering. The pure VLM benchmark part is a crowded race against foundation-model scale. Only the 3D-grounded event-inference reframing fits the author's field (tracking and reconstruction, bimanual, RGB-D) and has a non-obvious research question.

evidence.title: Do Egocentric Video-Language Models Truly Understand Hand-Object Interactions? (EgoNCE++)
HD-EPIC: A Highly-Detailed Egocentric Video Dataset
WHOLE: World-Grounded Hand-Object Lifted from Egocentric Videos
Vision-Language Models for Egocentric Video: From Hand-Object Interaction to Embodied AI (survey)

skeptics.reframe: Manipulation events (contact onset and release, grasp phases, bimanual hand-overs, object-state changes) are defined by small 3D hand-object changes, but current recognisers learn them from 2D caption-level supervision. The open question is whether events and phases can be inferred jointly with 4D hand-object tracking, self-supervised from the kinematics and contact of the reconstruction, so that each task helps the other: events constrain tracking under occlusion, and tracking grounds the verbs. It should be measured against human event labels and stay robust to monocular or RGB-D tracking noise.

research_questions.question: Can frame-accurate bimanual manipulation events (per-hand contact onset and release, grasp, lift, place, hand-over, articulation state change) be inferred from estimated 4D hand-object trajectories, rather than from RGB appearance or VLM captions? And how does event accuracy degrade as the input moves from mocap-quality 3D, to RGB-D tracking, to monocular tracking?
research_questions.why_top_venue: The closest 2025-2026 work leaves exactly this gap open. I verified each of the following this session. EgoLoc (arXiv 2508.12349) already uses HaMeR plus depth to get a 3D wrist and a VLM to find contact and separation times. It reaches SR 0.819 within 5 frames and an MAE of 3.7 frames on EgoPAT3D-DT. Its authors say it handles only videos where one hand is visible, and they list bimanual transitions as future work. TouchMoment (CVPR 2026 Findings, arXiv 2604.12343) uses RGB only and detects only the contact onset of a single hand (AP within 2 frames). It has no release events and no two-hand interaction. Polyphony (CVPR 2026, arXiv 2605.31115) segments dual-hand actions on HA-ViD and ATTACH from video features, with no 3D hand-object state. Skeptics and HanDyVQA both say the missing ingredient is 3D hand-object state. No paper found asks how good the 3D tracking must be before the events it implies are reliable. A clear result on that question would be a requirements specification that both the tracking community and the robot-demonstration labelling community would cite.
research_questions.method_sketch: (1) Free labels. Define events geometrically on public mocap HOI datasets using the ground-truth meshes. Contact is a fingertip or palm signed distance below a threshold, held for k frames. Grasped means the object's rigid motion is explained by the hand transform, with a low co-motion residual, while in contact. Supported means the object is static and touching the scene. Release is the transition from grasped to free or supported. Hand-over means a bimanual grasp followed by a single-hand release. Articulation change comes from ARCTIC's articulation angle. Check these definitions against a small human-labelled subset (about 300 to 500 events) and report agreement. (2) Measure real tracker error. Run off-the-shelf estimators on the same sequences (for example HaMeR or WiLoR for hands, and FoundationPose with the known mesh for objects), using depth where the dataset has it. Fit an error model per error type (hand translation, fingertip, object rotation, dropouts under occlusion). (3) Event model. Per frame and per hand, use these features: distances from fingertips to the object surface, relative velocity, the hand-object co-motion residual, object velocity, and tracker uncertainty or visibility. Feed them to a temporal network with cross-hand attention. Train it on ground-truth tracks corrupted with the fitted error model, and decode with a semi-Markov or CRF layer that enforces the event grammar (contact before grasp, release only after grasp, hand-over needs two grasps). (4) Sensitivity analysis. Sweep each error type and report which one dominates event error.
research_questions.minimum_experiment: Use ARCTIC, or DexYCB plus HOI4D if storage is tight. Compute the geometric event labels. Run monocular and RGB-D trackers to get estimated tracks. Report event F1 at plus or minus 1, 2 and 5 frames, MAE in frames, and segment F1@k per hand for these inputs: (a) ground-truth tracks; (b) estimated tracks with a naive distance threshold; (c) estimated tracks with the noise-robust model; (d) an EgoLoc-style VLM prompt plus 3D wrist; (e) an RGB-only detector or a zero-shot open VLM. The idea is worth a paper if (c) clearly beats (d) and (e) on release and hand-over events and stays close to (a). This takes about 6 to 8 weeks.
research_questions.data_and_hardware: Data: ARCTIC (bimanual, articulated, meshes, 2.1M frames); HOI4D (2.4M egocentric RGB-D frames with 3D hand pose, object pose and action segmentation; verified); DexYCB (grasp sequences; from memory); H2O (RGB-D with 3D hands, object 6D pose and action labels; from memory, not re-verified); OakInk2 (bimanual, with primitive-task segments; from memory, not re-verified); and the KIT Bimanual Actions dataset (540 RGB-D recordings, 6 subjects, 9 tasks, per-hand frame-wise action labels; verified). The last one fits a desk RGB-D camera closely. EgoPAT3D-DT and TouchMoment allow head-to-head comparison with RGB methods. Hardware: one 24-48 GB GPU. Running HaMeR or WiLoR plus FoundationPose over a few hundred thousand frames takes days, not weeks. Plan for 2-4 TB of storage if raw ARCTIC images are used. The consumer RGB-D camera is needed only for a small real-world qualitative test. No mocap or robot is needed.
research_questions.risks: (1) Reviewers may call the ground-truth case trivial ('threshold the SDF'). The novelty has to come from noise robustness, bimanual grammar and the sensitivity analysis, not from the label definitions. (2) The EgoLoc group names bimanual as its next step, so the window may be 6-12 months. (3) On in-the-wild egocentric video (EPIC, HD-EPIC), current monocular hand-object trackers may be too poor for any 3D route to beat RGB detectors. A small hand-labelled in-the-wild set is needed to show where the crossover lies. (4) Contact onset is partly subjective, so geometric and human labels may disagree by several frames. (5) Licences for redistributing derived labels must be checked for each dataset.

research_questions.question: Does jointly inferring discrete interaction modes (free, approaching, grasped-rigid, supported-static, hand-over, articulating) together with continuous 3D hand and object pose improve tracking under heavy hand-object and bimanual occlusion, and improve event accuracy at the same time, compared with a decoupled pipeline that tracks first and segments second?
research_questions.why_top_venue: This is the 'each task helps the other' reframing that the rq skeptic proposed, and it sits inside the author's core field (tracking under occlusion) rather than next to it. Current HOI reconstruction uses contact as a per-frame or soft constraint, or as a learned generative prior. WHOLE (arXiv 2602.22209, verified) learns a generative hand-object motion prior and does not output events or phases. A causal hybrid model, whose discrete phase posterior is both an output (event labels) and a tracking prior, could show two-way gains. If it did, it would contribute both to 4D HOI tracking and to automatic demonstration segmentation, and that pairing fits CVPR/ICCV and RSS/T-RO.
research_questions.method_sketch: One mode variable per hand-object pair, with mode-dependent dynamics. When grasped, the object pose equals the hand pose composed with a slowly drifting relative transform. When supported, the object is static. When free, the object follows a constant-velocity model. When articulating, motion is constrained to the joint axis. Inference has two variants. The classical one is a causal interacting-multiple-model or switching factor graph over per-frame detections from off-the-shelf hand and object estimators, with depth when available. The learned one is a soft-mode mixture whose mode classifier is supervised with the free geometric labels from RQ1. Under occlusion, the posterior over the grasped mode carries the object with the hand, and a consistent hand-object trajectory in turn sharpens the event posterior. Compare against a decoupled tracker followed by the RQ1 event model, temporal smoothing, and a generative-prior method where code exists.
research_questions.minimum_experiment: On DexYCB or HO3D, and then the ARCTIC egocentric view, drop object-pose observations for windows of 5 to 60 frames, both with synthetic dropouts and with real occlusion masks. Compare object ADD-S or MSSD and hand MPJPE inside the occluded windows for three trackers: constant velocity plus smoothing, decoupled tracking, and mode-switching tracking. Report event F1 from the mode posterior against the RQ1 labels. The result is worth pursuing if error inside the occluded windows drops substantially and events improve, not just one of the two. This takes about 2 to 3 months once RQ1's labels and tracker runs exist.
research_questions.data_and_hardware: Data: DexYCB, HO3D and ARCTIC (from memory, not re-verified in this session), HOI4D (verified, egocentric RGB-D) and HOT3D (from memory) for egocentric occlusion. Hardware: one GPU, 24 GB is enough for inference-time estimators and a small mode network. The causal filter variant can run on CPU at 30 fps. An RGB-D camera and the author's desk setup are useful for a live causal demonstration, but not for the main numbers.
research_questions.risks: (1) Switching and interacting-multiple-model filters are old in robotics tracking, so the novelty has to show up as measured two-way benefit on hand-object benchmarks, not as the model class. (2) Diffusion or generative HOI priors (WHOLE and successors) may already absorb most of the occlusion gain. (3) Gains may be small on mocap datasets with little occlusion, so occlusion-heavy subsets have to be built and justified. (4) Mode errors cascade: a wrong 'grasped' carries the object away. This needs a recovery mechanism and an honest failure analysis. (5) Two-way gains may not hold at once, which would leave a weaker one-direction paper.

research_questions.question: How accurate are today's automatic event labellers at frame level when they are checked against geometry-derived ground truth from 3D hand-object capture? The labellers in question are zero-shot VLMs, EgoLoc-style VLM-plus-3D-wrist pipelines, RGB contact detectors and VLM subtask segmenters. And does giving them estimated 3D hand-object state, as structured text or as kinematic tokens, close the gap and make their reasoning consistent with the evidence?
research_questions.why_top_venue: VLM-based segmentation and labelling are now routine for robot-learning corpora. The skeptics found that ProcVLM-style pipelines report no accuracy against frame-level ground truth, and EgoCoT-Bench reports correct answers grounded in contradictory evidence. A benchmark that audits these labellers at frame level, using event ground truth computed from 3D mocap rather than from captions, answers a question the robot-learning and egocentric communities both need answered. It also tests the field-level causal claim ('missing 3D state, not missing scale') directly. Benchmarks of this kind fit the NeurIPS Datasets and Benchmarks track and CVPR.
research_questions.method_sketch: Reuse RQ1's geometric event labels, validated by humans on a subset, across ARCTIC, HOI4D, DexYCB and, where licences allow, OakInk2, HOT3D and GigaHands. Pose the task as temporal localisation of per-hand events plus phase segmentation with left/right attribution. Evaluate several groups: open VLMs (for example Qwen3-VL 8B), a small number of frontier-API VLMs on a capped subset, EgoLoc, a TouchMoment-style detector, and a VLM subtask segmenter. Then add three augmentations: (a) estimated per-frame hand-object distances, contact probability and object velocity as text time series in the prompt; (b) QLoRA fine-tuning of an 8B VLM with a small kinematic-token adapter; (c) an evidence-consistency check, where the cited frame must actually show the event in 3D. Report each augmentation with ground-truth 3D and with estimated 3D, to separate the value of the information from tracker noise.
research_questions.minimum_experiment: Pick one dataset (ARCTIC or HOI4D) and about 1,000 events. Compare zero-shot Qwen3-VL against Qwen3-VL with prompts that include ground-truth 3D state and with prompts that include estimated 3D state, reporting event F1 at plus or minus 2 and 5 frames and left/right attribution accuracy. If the 3D-augmented prompt closes most of the gap with estimated state, the benchmark has its headline finding. This takes about 4 weeks.
research_questions.data_and_hardware: Data: the same public 3D HOI datasets as RQ1. Optionally use HanDyVQA and HD-EPIC subsets for transfer, but only where 3D state can be estimated. Hardware: one 24-48 GB GPU, which is enough for 8B-model inference and QLoRA. Frontier-API evaluation is a paid cost and sends data off-machine, so it has to be capped and approved. No new capture is needed.
research_questions.risks: (1) The VLM benchmark space is crowded and dominated by large egocentric groups (HD-EPIC consortium, HanDyVQA, EgoCoT-Bench), and frontier models move fast, so absolute numbers age within months. The lasting contribution has to be the 3D-state ablation and the frame-level audit protocol. (2) A benchmark built only from derived labels may be judged thin unless the human validation is solid. (3) Mocap-lab footage (ARCTIC, DexYCB) is visually far from in-the-wild egocentric video, which limits how far conclusions transfer. (4) Licence terms may block redistribution of derived labels.

fit.thesis_assets_help: Small, and limited to RQ2. The thesis's measured/held/constrained honesty labels and its object-conditioned recovery of an occluded holding arm are a hand-written version of the mode-switching idea in RQ2: a 'held' state that ties object and hand during occlusion. That gives a working prototype and intuition for which failure modes matter. The causal 30 fps chain supports an online, causal event-and-tracking claim. The ArUco-marked object gives metric object trajectories, so lift and place events can be computed from object motion on the author's own recordings. They are not ground truth for hand contact, and the markers can also be occluded. The Unity twin is useful only as a demo of an event timeline replayed in a digital twin. The 28 recordings of one subject are too small and too homogeneous for any benchmark or training claim. Use them only as a qualitative real-world RGB-D desk test. For RQ1 and RQ3 the assets give essentially no edge: all main results must come from public datasets.
fit.what_a_small_lab_cannot_do_here: A small lab cannot compete on the VLM video-QA framing. Fine-tuning or pretraining large video-language models at corpus scale is out of reach: ProcVLM trains on a 60M-frame corpus, and EgoAdapt-style challenge entries rely on heavy compute and many iterations. So is chasing HD-EPIC or HanDyVQA leaderboards against groups that can retrain every quarter. A small lab cannot collect a new large multi-subject dataset with mocap, force gloves (FEEL, about 3M frames) or tactile sensing (OPENTOUCH), and so cannot produce its own instrumented event ground truth beyond public data. Without a robot, it cannot use robot logs (gripper state, end-effector, force) as the event signal, which is why the robot-side labelling work (Automatic Labelling for Bimanual Mobile Manipulation) succeeds. It cannot afford large human annotation campaigns for frame-level event ground truth on in-the-wild egocentric video, so any in-the-wild test set must stay small (hundreds of events). Frontier-API evaluations at scale are a cost and data-egress decision and must be capped. What remains feasible is the narrow, 3D-grounded, bimanual event problem on public mocap HOI datasets with free geometric labels, off-the-shelf trackers and a single GPU. This framing is less crowded but adjacent to the author's core field. The window is likely 6-12 months, because the EgoLoc group names bimanual extension as its next step.

painpoint.name: Novel objects in dense clutter

evidence.latest_state: Unseen-object 2D detection is still the weakest stage, read from the BOP leaderboards on 2026-10-02. On BOP-Classic-Core, the best unseen-object detection entry is 3PT-Detection at 58.0 AP (Oct 2025) and 57.9 AP (Nov 2025). The best seen-object detector, GDet2023 (2023), scores 79.8 AP, so the gap has narrowed from about 37 AP to about 22 AP but has not closed. Other recent entries are CLON at 55.2 (Jun 2026), MUSE at 53.3 (BOP 2025 winner, arXiv 2510.17866), NIDS-Net at 46.9 and CNOS-FastSAM at 42.8. The dense-bin dataset IC-BIN remains the worst case: 44.2 or 38.9 AP for 3PT-Detection and 33.7 AP for MUSE, against 73.1 AP for the seen-object GDet2023. On BOP-H3 (HOT3D, HOPEv2, HANDAL), 3PT-Detection reaches 54.8 AP, up from MUSE at 41.8 and CNOS at 30.3, with HOT3D at 48.4. On BOP-Industrial unseen detection, MUSE reports 34.3 AP in its paper (IPD 21.6, XYZ-IBD 32.3, ITODD-MV 49.0). The leaderboard shows 3PT-Detection at 57.9 there (IPD 63.4, XYZ-IBD 57.5), so a large jump happened in late 2025, but around 40 percent of instances in industrial bins are still missed. Unseen-object 6D localization, where instance counts are given and detection is partly bypassed, is much stronger: FRTPose-WAPR.v2 scores about 84.5 AR on BOP-Classic-Core and 75.2 AR on IC-BIN. That contrast supports the pain point that detection, not pose refinement, is the bottleneck in clutter. The industrial pose and 6D-detection figures were read by a page summarizer and look unusually high, so they are not cross-checked; the 2D detection figures match the MUSE paper. Occlusion-specific pose work stays incremental: WALDO (arXiv 2511.15874) reports about +5 percent on IC-BIN and about +2 percent on BOP and adds a visibility-weighted metric. New clutter datasets (XYZ-IBD, GraspClutter6D with 62.6 percent mean occlusion, IndustryShapes, MessyKitchens) document the degradation without fixing it. The 3PT-Detection, CLON and FRTPose/WAPR methods appear only as leaderboard entries; no paper for them was found.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: MUSE: Model-based Uncertainty-aware Similarity Estimation for zero-shot 2D Object Detection and Segmentation
attacking_papers_2025_2026.venue_year: arXiv 2025 (BOP Challenge 2025 first place in Classic-Core, H3 and Industrial detection)
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Training-free template-matching detector and segmenter on SAM-style proposals, with a joint absolute and relative similarity score and an uncertainty-aware prior. Reports 53.3 AP on BOP core, 41.8 on H3 and 34.3 on Industrial, and names cluttered backgrounds, hard negatives and occlusion as remaining failure cases.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: WALDO: Where Unseen Model-based 6D Pose Estimation Meets Occlusion
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Occlusion-focused unseen-object pose pipeline: visibility-focused dense sampling, multiple pose hypotheses, iterative refinement and occlusion augmentations, plus a visibility-weighted metric. Reports about +5 percent on IC-BIN, about +2 percent on BOP and 3x faster inference.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: BioDet: Boosting Industrial Object Detection with Image Preprocessing Strategies
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Improves unseen-object 2D detection in industrial bin picking with low-light enhancement and foundation-model background removal. Scores 37.9 AP on the BOP-Industrial leaderboard (XYZ-IBD 26.9).

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: NOCTIS: Novel Object Cyclic Threshold based Instance Segmentation
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Training-free instance segmentation of unseen objects that reports gains over RGB and RGB-D baselines on the seven BOP 2023 core datasets.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: Back to the Feature: Zero-Shot 6DoF Pose Estimation via Dense Local Features (B2TFPose)
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Training-free unseen-object pose from frozen DINOv3 dense features, with geodesic view NMS, render-guided re-correspondence and multi-mask scoring to handle uncertain segmentation. Reports 40.7 and 56.4 mean AR on BOP core.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: Accurate and efficient zero-shot 6D pose estimation with frozen foundation models (FreeZeV2)
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Zero-shot pose from frozen foundation features; BOP 2024 best overall, reported as 8x faster and about 5 percent more accurate than FreeZe.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: BOP Challenge 2024 on Model-Based and Model-Free 6D Object Pose Estimation
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Challenge report naming unseen-object 2D detection as the pipeline bottleneck and introducing the BOP-H3 practical detection tasks.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: XYZ-IBD: Benchmarking Robust 6D Object Pose Estimation under Real-World Industrial Complexity
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Industrial bin-picking benchmark with 75 multi-view scenes and about 273k instances under dense stacking and multi-instance ambiguity. Reports significant drops for state-of-the-art 2D detection and 6D pose versus household benchmarks.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: GraspClutter6D: A Large-scale Real-world Dataset for Robust Perception and Grasping in Cluttered Scenes
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: 1,000 cluttered scenes with 14.1 objects per scene and 62.6 percent occlusion. Benchmarks segmentation, pose and grasping, and shows pose accuracy falling with occlusion.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: AlignPose: Generalizable 6D Pose Estimation via Multi-view Feature-metric Alignment
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Multi-view feature-metric alignment across calibrated RGB views for unseen-object pose, one route around single-view ambiguity under occlusion.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: DA-Fusion: Deformable Attention-Based RGB-D Fusion Transformer for Unseen Object Instance Segmentation
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: RGB-D deformable-attention fusion for unseen object instance segmentation in cluttered bins; introduces the Object Clutter Bin Dataset (OCBD).

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: MooMIns: Monocular 3D Reconstruction and Object Pose Estimation from Multiple Instances
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Gaussian-splatting reconstruction of an unseen object from multiple identical instances in one monocular image, then geometric 6D pose, tested on synthetic and real bin picking.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: IndustryShapes: An RGB-D Benchmark dataset for 6D object pose estimation of industrial assembly components and tools
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Industrial multi-instance RGB-D pose benchmark with about 4.6k images and 6k poses.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: MessyKitchens: Contact-rich object-level 3D scene reconstruction
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Cluttered-kitchen dataset and method for object-level 3D reconstruction under heavy occlusion, targeting physically plausible, non-penetrating object layouts.

evidence.crowdedness: HIGH. BOP 2025 had dedicated unseen-object detection tracks on three dataset groups. At least seven teams submitted detection entries in 2025-2026 (3PT, CLON, MUSE, FOSOD, BioDet, NIDS-Net, CNOS variants). The groups include the BOP organizers (CTU Prague, TUM, Meta Reality Labs), industry teams and Korean labs (GraspClutter6D, MUSE), so the core detection-in-clutter problem is contested by well-resourced groups.
evidence.trend: rising. BOP 2024-2025 added the BOP-H3 and BOP-Industrial bin-picking tracks (XYZ-IBD, IPD, ITODD-MV) aimed at this bottleneck. Unseen-detection AP on industrial data jumped from about 34 to about 58 within late 2025, and new clutter datasets keep appearing (GraspClutter6D, IndustryShapes, MessyKitchens). However, this is an adjacent topic for hand-object work: attention sits in the bin-picking and robot-grasping community rather than hand-object tracking.

skeptics.reasons: I found no 2025-2026 work that solves this or turns it into engineering. The official BOP leaderboards, fetched on 2026-10-02, still show a large detection gap. On the model-based unseen-object 2D detection leaderboard for BOP-Classic-Core, the best entries are 3PT-Detection at AP 0.579-0.580 (Oct-Nov 2025), CLON at 0.552 (2026-06-11) and MUSE at 0.533. The equivalent seen-object leaderboard tops out at 0.885 (Synthetica) and 0.798 (GDet2023). Unseen detection has moved from 52.0 to about 58 AP in two years, but it still trails seen detection by roughly 22-30 AP points. The pain point's "about 35 percent" figure is slightly out of date, but the bottleneck itself is still there. MUSE (arXiv 2510.17866) ranked first in the BOP 2025 detection tracks without training, yet its leaderboard AP is only 0.533. 2026 papers still frame proposal sensitivity under occlusion and clutter as an open problem: L2G-Det (arXiv 2603.03577) says proposal-based methods often fail under occlusion and background clutter. DA-Fusion (arXiv 2607.17754) introduces another bin-picking segmentation dataset (OCBD) because RGB-only methods over-segment and depth-only methods under-segment. One part has narrowed. On industrial bins (XYZ-IBD unseen 6D detection), multi-view RGB reaches AP 0.816 (3PT-Pose, Nov 2025) and single-view RGB-D reaches 0.765 (SAM-FP, 2026-09-11). Bin picking with known CAD models and several cameras is approaching usable, so the claim that pose falls apart in bins is too broad. The occlusion-binned ADD(-S) numbers (GraspClutter6D, PACE) could not be rechecked against newer methods; I found no 2025-2026 result showing that drop closed. Fit for this author is weak. The pain point is about static clutter and the BOP pipeline, and well-resourced BOP teams compete hard on it. The author's field is hand-object tracking, where the main occluder is the hand, not a pile of other objects. My web search budget was used up, so the evidence comes from fetched BOP pages and the arXiv API, not a broad survey.

skeptics.reframe: Narrower version that still holds as of late 2026: detecting and correctly identifying novel objects from a single view, under heavy occlusion and with repeated identical instances, is still the bottleneck. Best unseen 2D detection AP on BOP-Classic-Core is about 0.58, against 0.80-0.885 for seen objects. Pose for well-separated objects, and multi-view industrial bin picking (about 0.82 AP), is close to solved. For this author, the open version is novel-object detection and identity under occlusion by the manipulating hand or hands over a video. Static piles are less relevant, and BOP-H3 (HOT3D, HANDAL) is the matching benchmark.

skeptics.reasons: Artifact test. The core claim (unseen-object 2D detection is the main bottleneck of novel-object 6D pipelines and degrades sharply in dense clutter) is not traceable to one dataset or one group. It is stated by the community benchmark itself (BOP 2024, arXiv 2504.02812, verified: 'the 2D detection accuracy for unseen objects is still -35% behind ... the main bottleneck'), whose author list spans CTU Prague, Meta, NVIDIA, MVTec, ENPC, TU Darmstadt, Niantic and others, and is independently echoed by GraspClutter6D (GIST, Korea; arXiv 2504.06866, verified, 62.6% occlusion scenes), XYZ-IBD (TUM plus XYZ Robotics; arXiv 2506.00599, verified: SOTA 2D detection and 6D pose show 'significant performance degradation compared to standard household benchmarks'), PACE (SJTU/Stanford; arXiv 2312.15130, verified title and authors) and IndustryShapes (a separate European group). Settings differ: household tabletops, industrial bins, transparent objects, moving camera. So it is not a single-dataset artifact. Weaknesses that lower the score: (1) Group concentration: three of the clutter datasets (HouseCat6D, PhoCaL, XYZ-IBD) come from the same TUM/Busam lineage, and roughly a third of the 27 listed paper ids (OnePose, OnePose++, Gen6D, 6D-Diff, DTTD, YCB-Ev, ClearPose, Omni6D, DTTDNet) are about model-free onboarding, depth noise, events or transparency rather than dense-clutter detection, so the 27-paper count overstates the support. (2) The headline gap numbers (35% AP, 37 mAP) come from BOP reports only and are a moving target measured on BOP's seven core datasets; they are a benchmark snapshot, not a field constant. (3) 'Pose accuracy falls with occlusion' (MegaPose 77.9 to 42.3) is generic and expected for any vision method; by itself it is not a distinctive pain point. (4) The PACE result (PPF 52.2 vs CosyPose 4.4 with GT detections) is very likely an artifact of PACE's training-data setup and domain gap, since learned instance-level methods beat PPF by wide margins on BOP; I could not verify the PACE training protocol, so this item should not be used as evidence. (5) The 'benchmarks hide detection via GT masks' complaint is partly a convention already corrected: BOP has used fixed default detections (CNOS) for the unseen tracks since 2023 and added 6D detection tasks in 2024. (6) Known-object bin picking in dense clutter has long been handled industrially by PPF/template matching (Drost-style), and class-agnostic unseen-object instance segmentation on cluttered tabletops is a mature subfield; what remains open is identity assignment among novel, similar, heavily occluded instances, not clutter segmentation as such. Relevance to the author's field is adjacent: hand-object and bimanual capture scenes rarely involve dense piles, and the hand-induced occlusion case is not what these benchmarks measure. Net: the problem is real and field-wide in the object-pose community, but its statement bundles a generic occlusion trend and one questionable dataset result with the genuinely documented novel-object detection and identification gap. WebSearch budget was exhausted, so BOP 2025 results (which could show the gap narrowing) were not checked.

skeptics.reframe: Under BOP-style default detections, novel objects are found but often given the wrong identity: when a model must tell apart many similar, heavily occluded instances it has never seen, segmentation and pose accuracy collapse. The measured gap is about 35% detection AP against seen objects on BOP-Classic-Core (BOP 2024), and it is larger on industrial bins. For hand-object capture, the open version of this is identifying and posing a novel object that the hands occlude heavily, which current clutter benchmarks do not measure.

skeptics.reasons:
Attempted refutation: much of P28 is data-bound or about benchmark protocol rather than an open scientific question. (a) "Benchmarks supply ground-truth masks" is an evaluation-protocol complaint. BOP already scores end-to-end detection and 6D localization, so this part needs no new research. (b) GraspClutter6D (arXiv 2504.06866, verified) reports that models trained on its 1,000 dense scenes (62.6% occlusion) beat models trained on other datasets. That supports the view that part of the clutter gap closes with more realistic training data, which is a resource fix. (c) The unseen-detection gap is a moving target. Proposal generators built on SAM/FastSAM plus DINO-style matching (CNOS, SAM-6D, MUSE) improve each year mostly from stronger foundation backbones and larger synthetic training sets. A thesis-level contribution risks being overtaken by the next backbone release. (d) Relevance to the author is only adjacent: in hand-object or bimanual capture the object of interest is usually isolated by the hand and tracked over time, not picked out of a static pile. So the single-image bin-picking framing sits outside the author's core field.
Why it is not refuted: at least one question remains that top-venue reviewers treat as significant and that is not solved by more annotation. The BOP 2024 report (arXiv 2504.02812, verified) names 2D detection of unseen objects as the main bottleneck of 6D pipelines, about 35% behind seen-object detection. On BOP-H3 the gap grows further (MUSE 39.0 versus 52.0 on classic core, as reported in the pain-point record from paper 1312; I did not check these numbers myself). Open research questions include the following.
1. How can unseen-object detection, instance identity and pose be inferred jointly, rather than in a cascade where proposal errors cannot be recovered? Examples are render-and-compare hypotheses that compete for pixels, or amodal reasoning shared across instances.
2. Why do learned instance-level networks fall below classical PPF matching in clutter even when given ground-truth detections (PACE, from the record; PACE itself is verified as arXiv 2312.15130, but the PPF figure was not checked)? What inductive bias, such as local geometric invariance or partial-evidence voting, closes that gap?
3. Can multi-view or temporal evidence resolve which of several stacked identical parts is which, a problem single images cannot settle? AlignPose (arXiv 2512.20538, multi-view, from a listing) suggests this line is active but not closed.
Papers in this line (SAM-6D, CNOS, FoundationPose, GigaPose) appear regularly at CVPR, ICCV and ECCV, so the topic is publishable. Net verdict: a real research problem, but crowded, close to the backbone race and only adjacent to the author's field. The publishable core is narrower than the full statement.

skeptics.reframe: Cascaded unseen-object 6D pipelines break in dense clutter because proposal errors (missed, merged or wrongly identified instances among repeated parts) cannot be recovered downstream, and learned pose networks fall below classical geometric matching when only a small part of each object is visible. The open question is how to infer detection, instance identity and pose of novel objects jointly from partial evidence. For this author's field, the angle is to use temporal and interaction evidence (multi-view motion, which instance a hand touched or moved) to resolve identity and occlusion ambiguities that single images cannot. Results should be scored end-to-end, with no ground-truth masks.

fit.worth_pursuing: MAYBE. NO for P28 as stated: static dense clutter in piles and bins, measured on BOP-Classic-Core or BOP-Industrial. YES-leaning MAYBE for the narrower version the skeptics converged on: novel-object detection and identity under hand occlusion in RGB(-D) video. That narrower version is less crowded. The BOP-H3 unseen 2D detection leaderboard, fetched 2026-10-02, has only five entries. The best is 3PT-Detection (Nov 2025) at 0.548 AP (HOT3D 0.484, HANDAL 0.536), then MUSE at 0.418 (HOT3D 0.438, HANDAL 0.357) and CNOS-FastSAM at 0.303. The H3 unseen 6D-detection board peaks at 0.587 (3PT-Pose, HOT3D 0.553), and its top entries take 6.5-72 s per image. Every entry is listed as single-image RGB or RGB-D. I found no entry that uses temporal or hand evidence, although HOT3D and HANDAL are video datasets. Temporal and hand-aware detection is still open, cheap to run (inference only on public data) and in the author's field. Single-object unseen tracking through hand occlusion is not open: GRC-Pose (arXiv 2609.39116, HOT3D), a RA-L 2026 tracker with failure recovery (arXiv 2607.23468), Point2Pose (arXiv 2604.10415) and ROHIT (arXiv 2512.07394, hand interaction timelines on HOT3D) already cover it. A paper must therefore target detection with no initialization, several objects and identity, not single-object tracking. It should also be merged with any hand-object occlusion pain point rather than pitched as P28.

research_questions.question: On hand-object RGB(-D) video, can a causal track-and-verify layer recover the novel objects that per-frame zero-shot detectors miss, and how much of the unseen-object detection gap does it close on hand-occluded frames at interactive frame rates? The layer models hand occlusion explicitly, builds up template-matching evidence over time, and keeps an object hypothesis alive while it is held.
research_questions.why_top_venue: Unseen-object 2D detection is the stated bottleneck of 6D pipelines (BOP 2024 report, arXiv 2504.02812). On the hand-centric BOP-H3 track it is still 0.48 AP on HOT3D for the best entry and 0.30-0.42 for public methods. Every leaderboard entry is single-image and takes 1-72 s per image. A training-free method that turns video and hand evidence into a large AP gain on heavily hand-occluded frames, at more than 10 fps amortized, is a clear and measurable step. The study also gives the first occlusion-stratified diagnosis of detection versus identity versus pose error on hand-object benchmarks with no ground-truth masks. CVPR, ICCV and ECCV regularly accept unseen-object detection and pose papers (CNOS, SAM-6D, FoundationPose, GigaPose).
research_questions.method_sketch: (1) Per-frame base. A public training-free detector (CNOS, or MUSE if its code is released): SAM or FastSAM proposals plus DINOv2/v3 template matching, run only on keyframes. (2) Hand layer. An off-the-shelf hand mesh estimator (HaMeR or WiLoR; ground-truth hands on HOT3D and DexYCB as an oracle ablation) renders a hand mask and depth. Template similarity is recomputed over the predicted-visible object pixels only, and templates are rendered with the same hand cut-out, so occlusion by the hand is not counted against the match. (3) Temporal layer. Each object hypothesis lives in a 3D track: depth on DexYCB, headset SLAM poses on HOT3D. It is propagated cheaply between keyframes with SAM2-style mask memory or a point tracker (CoTracker), and identity log-odds accumulate in a Bayesian filter. A hypothesis that disappears into a hand switches to a held state tied to the hand's motion (contact prior, as in the ROHIT interaction timeline). It is re-verified on reappearance with a render-and-compare score (FoundationPose refiner). (4) Output. Per-frame calibrated boxes and masks for BOP AP, plus 6D poses for end-to-end AR. Baselines: per-frame CNOS, MUSE and SAM-6D; SAM2 or SAM3 video propagation from first-frame detections; FoundationPose tracking with re-detection; Point2Pose; the RA-L 2026 recovery tracker; GRC-Pose if code is available.
research_questions.minimum_experiment: Weeks 1-6, diagnostic and go/no-go test. Run public CNOS-FastSAM and SAM-6D (plus MUSE if released) per frame on HOT3D clips and on the DexYCB test split. Bin AP by ground-truth hand-occlusion fraction, computed by rendering the provided MANO or UmeTrack hands and object meshes. Proceed only if AP in the high-occlusion bin (over 50 percent hidden) is at least 15 AP below the low bin. If not, there is no hand-specific story and the work falls back to generic temporal detection. Weeks 7-14: add (a) temporal score smoothing with SAM2 propagation and (b) hand-aware visible-region scoring with a held state. Success means +8-10 AP in the high-occlusion bins over both the best per-frame detector and the SAM2-propagation baseline, fewer identity switches, and at least 10 fps amortized on one GPU. Weeks 15-24: end-to-end 6D AR with FoundationPose on the recovered detections, ablations (oracle versus estimated hands, keyframe rate), and a short qualitative demo on a consumer RGB-D camera.
research_questions.data_and_hardware: Public data only for the quantitative results. HOT3D (egocentric multi-view video, 33 objects, mocap ground truth, used in BOP-H3). DexYCB (multi-camera RGB-D, several YCB objects on the table, one grasped). HANDAL (handheld objects, BOP-H3). HO3D v3 as a single-object sanity check. Object meshes come with all of them. Assumed, not verified here: the BOP-H3 HOT3D test images are drawn from short contiguous clips, so neighbouring frames are available. Hardware: one workstation GPU with 24-48 GB for inference-only foundation-model pipelines; about 1-2 TB of disk for HOT3D and DexYCB subsets (downloads over 1 GB need the user's approval under the repository rules). A consumer RGB-D camera is used only for the demo. No mocap and no robot.
research_questions.risks: (1) BOP rules may require single-image input, so a video method may not rank on the official leaderboard. That would force a self-defined causal-video protocol, scored with the BOP toolkit and reported next to single-frame numbers. (2) SAM3-class video segmenters with exemplar or concept prompts may close much of the gap on their own. That baseline is mandatory, and if it closes more than about 70 percent of the gap the contribution shrinks. (3) Backbone churn (new DINO or SAM releases) moves every baseline within months; the method must be backbone-agnostic and report gains over several base detectors. (4) Neighbouring work is active (GRC-Pose Sept 2026, the RA-L 2026 recovery tracker, Point2Pose, ROHIT). Novelty must rest on detection and identity of several objects with no initialization, not on single-object tracking. (5) HOT3D Aria streams have no depth, so the RGB-D claim rests mainly on DexYCB. (6) The 3PT entries have no paper and their method is unknown; they may already use cues this project plans to add.
target_venues: BOP / R6D workshop at ICCV or ECCV (early visibility)

research_questions.question: When one or two hands manipulate several identical or near-identical novel objects (swap, pick and put back, handover), can instance identity and 6D pose be kept by inferring which instance the hands moved, and how does this compare to appearance-based multi-object trackers and per-frame unseen-object pipelines? The inference uses contact-gated motion constraints (an object moves only while touched) and physical plausibility, not appearance.
research_questions.why_top_venue: Wrong identity among repeated identical parts is a documented failure of unseen-object pipelines in clutter: SAM-6D loses over 33 percent AP under repeated instances, and detections get wrong IDs in dense multi-instance scenes (from the P28 record; the skeptics' reframes agree). No hand-object benchmark measures it: HOT3D's 33 objects are all distinct and DexYCB, HO3D and ARCTIC show one object per grasp. Robot demonstration capture of assembly (identical blocks, screws, cups) and digital twins need persistent identity, and a robot replaying a demonstration with the wrong instance fails. A new task, a small but careful benchmark and a principled method fit CoRL, ICRA and RSS. CVPR or ECCV is possible if the benchmark is convincing.
research_questions.method_sketch: A scene-level multi-hypothesis tracker over per-instance 6D states with a static / held / released state machine. It extends the ROHIT interaction-timeline idea (arXiv 2512.07394) from single-object reconstruction to multiple instances with identity. Detection and coarse pose come from a training-free unseen-object pipeline (CNOS or SAM-6D proposals, FoundationPose refinement). The appearance term sets only the object class; when instances look alike it is flagged as uninformative rather than trusted. Identity is solved as online MAP data association, with likelihoods from (a) motion continuity in 3D using RGB-D depth, (b) hand-object contact probability from the hand mesh and depth proximity (only touched objects may move), and (c) physical plausibility: support, no interpenetration, static objects stay put. Lost instances stay in the scene graph, attached to the hand while held, and are re-associated on release. Ablations remove each cue. Baselines: per-frame unseen pipeline plus ByteTrack or OC-SORT, SAM2/SAM3 multi-object video segmentation, Point2Pose (multi-object, model-free), and FoundationPose per object with re-detection.
research_questions.minimum_experiment: (a) Synthetic set: about 200 sequences rendered with BlenderProc (or the author's Unity twin), with 2-4 duplicate copies of YCB or T-LESS meshes. Real hand motions come from DexYCB or ARCTIC MANO trajectories, retargeted to grasp the copies, and scripted swaps, handovers and full in-hand occlusions are added. (b) Real evaluation set: 30-40 single-RGB-D-camera desk sequences, 3-5 subjects, 2-4 identical objects per scene. Ground-truth 6D pose comes from ArUco markers on faces kept out of the method's input (marker pixels masked or inpainted), and every frame carries a measured, propagated or constrained label so the hard occluded frames are not scored against invented ground truth. Identity ground truth is annotated by hand from the video. Metrics: IDF1, ID switches, HOTA, per-instance 6D AR on measured frames, frames to recover after release. Success means a large cut in ID switches over SAM2-based and tracking-by-detection baselines on swap and handover segments, with no loss of 6D AR on easy segments.
research_questions.data_and_hardware: Public: YCB and T-LESS meshes, DexYCB, ARCTIC and HO3D hand trajectories for synthesis, HOT3D for a no-duplicates sanity check. New: about 40 short real RGB-D sequences captured on one consumer RGB-D camera at one desk, with printed ArUco markers and off-the-shelf duplicate objects. A second cheap RGB-D camera is strongly advised to improve ground truth under hand occlusion. One GPU (24 GB is enough). No mocap and no robot. A borrowed arm for a replay demo would raise the CoRL case but is optional.
research_questions.risks: (1) Reviewers may see the duplicate-instance hand task as artificial. Anchor it in real tasks: assembly demonstrations, sorting, cup and block games used in robot learning. (2) Single-camera marker ground truth is weakest exactly in the hand-occluded frames being studied, and a one-camera, few-subject set will be criticized next to mocap datasets. Mitigate with a second camera, the measured/propagated/constrained labelling, and scoring pose only on measured frames while scoring identity on all frames. (3) Slow, clean motions let simple trackers keep identity, so the benchmark must contain genuinely ambiguous events (simultaneous bimanual moves, full occlusion while held, handovers). (4) Markers make identical objects distinguishable, so masking them must be shown not to leak identity, for example by checking that the method scores the same with markers physically covered. (5) Recruiting subjects needs ethics approval and adds lead time.
target_venues: CVPR / ECCV (if the benchmark is strong)

fit.thesis_assets_help: The assets give a small edge, mostly for research question 2 and almost none for research question 1. (a) The single RGB-D desk setup and the ArUco-marked object with metric pose show the author can already capture a small real evaluation set with metric 6D ground truth for duplicate-instance sequences. Ground truth for research question 2 is the main cost item, so this is a real but modest head start. The markers must be masked from the method's input. (b) The measured/held/constrained honesty labels carry over almost directly as per-frame ground-truth provenance labels. They answer the obvious reviewer objection that ground truth is unreliable in exactly the occluded frames, and they match the static/held/released states the tracker reasons about. (c) Object-conditioned recovery of an occluded holding arm is the mirror image of hand-conditioned object reasoning (the hand explains the object's occlusion and motion). It is useful intuition and some reusable occlusion-reasoning code, not a technical advantage. (d) The causal 30 fps chain helps only the real-time framing (amortized detection with cheap tracking between keyframes) and as a demo harness. (e) The Unity twin could render the synthetic duplicate-instance hand sequences, but BlenderProc is the field standard, so the gain is convenience only. (f) The 28 recordings of one subject are not usable as a benchmark: one subject, no duplicate instances, and no hand-occlusion stratification. At most they serve as qualitative demos. Research question 1 runs entirely on public data (HOT3D, DexYCB, HANDAL) and gains nothing from the assets.
fit.what_a_small_lab_cannot_do_here: A small lab should not compete on the static-clutter core of P28. The BOP-Classic-Core and BOP-Industrial unseen-detection races are fought by well-resourced teams: the BOP organizers (CTU Prague, TUM, Meta), industry teams and the 3PT, CLON and MUSE groups. Their gains come from foundation-backbone upgrades, huge synthetic rendering, ensembles and heavy compute; the top 3PT entries take 6-72 s per image, and the industrial jump to about 0.82 AP uses multi-view bin rigs. A one-GPU lab cannot train or fine-tune foundation detectors at that scale, and cannot build a mocap-grade multi-view ground-truth dataset like HOT3D or a 1,000-scene clutter dataset like GraspClutter6D. It cannot validate grasp success at scale without a robot arm. It also cannot quickly settle the learned-versus-PPF question in clutter, which needs large retraining sweeps. Even the hand-centric niche is exposed: backbone releases (new SAM or DINO versions, SAM3-style video concept tracking) can erase a method's margin within one review cycle. Official BOP-H3 ranking may also be closed to video methods if the single-image rule applies; this was not verified. Not verified here: whether the BOP-H3 test images come from contiguous clips, whether MUSE and the 3PT, CLON and FRTPose methods have public code, and the PACE PPF-versus-learned figures.

painpoint.name: Multi-sensor synchronization, calibration and registration errors

evidence.latest_state: Generic camera-to-camera synchronization and calibration is close to solved: RocSync (arXiv 2511.14948, Nov 2025, Pollefeys/Fuernstahl group) uses an LED clock with red and infrared LEDs and reports 1.34 ms RMSE against hardware sync across more than 25 heterogeneous RGB and IR cameras in surgical recordings. Marker-free software methods recover time offsets and extrinsics from people moving in the scene. Spatiotemporal Multi-Camera Calibration using Freely Moving People (RA-L 2025) solves rotation, time offset and person association together from monocular 3D pose. Humans as a Calibration Pattern (arXiv 2412.19089, v2 Mar 2025) and Dynamic Gaussian Scene Reconstruction from Unsynchronized Videos (AAAI 2026, coarse-to-fine sub-frame offsets for 4DGS) handle unsynchronized, uncalibrated video. For LiDAR plus camera body capture, FreeCap (2025) and Sen-Cap (ECCV 2026, evaluated on Human-M3, FreeMotion, LiDARHuman26M and RELI11D) skip explicit cross-sensor calibration altogether. Feed-forward human-scene models such as HARMONI (arXiv 2603.12789, 2026; up to 64 percent better multi-view pose), Tele360 and HiReFF increasingly estimate cameras together with the human. None of these methods targets the case P29 names: sub-frame timing and calibration error on commodity RGB-D rigs (several Azure Kinects or RealSense units, headset plus Kinect, phone plus depth camera) during fast hand-object motion. I found no 2025-2026 paper or benchmark that measures hand or object error as a function of the time offset or calibration error. The InterCap-style floor of about 18-20 mm from Kinect sync remains unaddressed in the hand-object literature I could check. Caveat: the WebSearch budget was used up, so this picture rests only on arXiv listing and abstract pages. I could not check the CVF open-access pages for CVPR, ICCV or ECCV 2025 (HTTP 403).

evidence.crowdedness: MEDIUM: at least nine 2025-2026 papers attack generic camera synchronization and calibration, from robotics calibration groups, ETH and Balgrist, Kyoto, SNU and NAVER, and ShanghaiTech (LiDAR mocap). However, none I found targets the sub-frame timing floor of commodity RGB-D rigs for fast hand-object motion, which is uncrowded.
evidence.trend: Stable to rising attention. Calibration and synchronization are increasingly folded into feed-forward 4D human and scene models and unsynchronized 4DGS (2025-2026), and calibration-free LiDAR-camera mocap reached ECCV 2026. Most of this work is a byproduct of reconstruction pipelines rather than a standalone problem, and the hand-object timing question gets almost no direct attention.

skeptics.reasons: The source record already labels P29 problem_type "engineering", and 2025-2026 work closes most of it. (1) Temporal sync. RocSync (arXiv 2511.14948, Nov 2025) is a low-cost LED clock that encodes red and IR exposure windows. It reaches 1.34 ms RMSE against hardware sync across heterogeneous RGB and IR consumer and professional cameras, and was run on more than 25 cameras in surgical recordings. That is well below the one-Kinect-frame (about 33 ms) error the record cites for HuMMan, and it covers the IR modality the record says breaks chessboard methods. Software-only methods also give sub-frame offsets from scene content: VisualSync (NeurIPS 2025, arXiv 2512.02017) uses epipolar constraints on tracked points (median error below 50 ms in the wild); SyncTrack4D (arXiv 2512.04315) reaches below 0.26 frames on Panoptic Studio; Dynamic Gaussian reconstruction from unsynchronized videos (AAAI 2026, arXiv 2511.11175) does coarse-to-fine sub-frame offset estimation. (2) Calibration without targets. Spatiotemporal multi-camera calibration using freely moving people (RA-L 2025, arXiv 2502.12546) solves rotation, time offset and association jointly from off-the-shelf 3D human poses. SteerPose (BMVC 2025) calibrates extrinsics from articulated 2D poses, a 2026 sports method self-calibrates from human and stick poses (arXiv 2604.17567), and Hydra (arXiv 2504.20584) gives marker-free RGB-D hand-eye calibration with open code and ROS 2 integration. (3) Other record items are already handled by standard practice or vendor features. PTP or hardware triggers and multi-device sync hubs cover lab rigs, and the record itself lists PTP and 3D-pose calibration constraints as fixes. What survives is narrow: millisecond-level sync for fast hand motion with no added hardware, on mixed casual rigs (phone plus depth camera, headset plus external camera) with rolling shutter and clock drift. The software methods above report errors of tens of milliseconds or fractions of a frame, which is still coarse for fast finger motion, and I found no benchmark that measures hand or object pose error as a function of residual offset. That remainder is mostly careful system engineering plus a missing measurement, not a top-venue research problem in itself. It matters to this author mainly as a dataset-quality caveat. Limits of this check: the WebSearch budget was exhausted, so all evidence comes from arXiv API queries and abstracts. I did not open full papers, so venue claims come from arXiv comments.

skeptics.reframe: Narrow version: on casual, mixed capture rigs with no added hardware (phone plus depth camera, headset plus external camera, rolling shutter, drifting clocks), the residual sub-frame time offset and rolling-shutter error are neither estimated at millisecond level nor measured in terms of their effect on fast hand and object pose accuracy. A useful contribution would jointly estimate those offsets from the hand-object motion itself and benchmark hand error against residual offset. Lab rigs with hardware sync, an LED clock or human-based self-calibration no longer have this problem.

skeptics.reasons: Viewed as an artifact, P29 mostly comes from particular rigs. It is not a problem the field at large faces. (1) Narrow setting. The 26 supporting papers are almost all body-scale or scene-scale dataset papers: SLOPER4D, HSC4D, HiSC4D, Human-M3, RELI11D, WorldPose, EMDB, Nymeria, NymeriaPlus, EgoHumans, EgoBody, HuMMan, FreeMan, MVHumanNet++, MVP-Human and SmartPortraits, plus one survey. The record itself places them in G2 body-object and G5 avatar/clinical. They also cluster by lab: three come from Yudi Dai's LiDAR line (SLOPER4D, HSC4D, HiSC4D), two from Meta Nymeria, two from the ShanghaiTech dome line (NeuralDome, HOI-M3) and several from ETH/AIT (EgoBody, EMDB, WorldPose, EgoSim). The labs differ, but the cause is always the same: heterogeneous consumer devices with no shared trigger (iPhone, HoloLens, Aria, LiDAR, phone plus Kinect). (2) The hand-object core treats it as solved by rig design. DexYCB (CVPR 2021, 8 RealSense D415) states that its cameras are extrinsically calibrated and temporally synchronized. ARCTIC (CVPR 2023) synchronizes its color cameras with 54 Vicon cameras. Neither lists sync as a limitation (verified from the arXiv PDFs). (3) The magnitude claim does not survive scrutiny. InterCap says its 18-20 mm error is bounded below by Azure Kinect sync imperfections. Microsoft's multi-device documentation says hardware-synced Kinects align color exposures within 100 us, with depth deliberately offset by about 160 us per device to avoid laser interference. At a hand speed of 1-3 m/s, 160 us is about 0.2-0.5 mm, which is negligible against 18 mm. So the sync floor only matters when a lab chooses software sync or devices that cannot be synced (HuMMan's iPhone has up to one frame of error; EgoBody aligns HoloLens to Kinect with a flashlight). That is a rig choice, not a field-wide barrier. (4) Neighbouring communities have long-standing solutions. VIO and robotics treat camera-IMU temporal offset as a solved estimation problem: Qin and Shen, IROS 2018, estimate the time offset online, and the Kalibr and Li-Mourikis lines are older but not verified in this session. PTP or genlock hardware triggering is standard in mocap domes, and the record itself lists PTP sync as an existing fix. (5) The problem is engineering, not research. The record labels it problem_type engineering and relevance adjacent. Only two of its items mention hands at all (EgoBody's HoloLens-Kinect misalignment visible on fast hand motion, and InterCap's hand jitter), and EgoBody's flashlight alignment is a rig choice. Some research interest survives in the niche of unsynchronized casual or heterogeneous capture (egocentric headset plus exo phone, rolling shutter), but that is narrower than the stated pain point. Not verified: Sync-NeRF and other unsynchronized multi-view work, because the shared search budget was used up, and the Kalibr and Li-Mourikis references.

skeptics.reframe: Narrow survivor: in casual or heterogeneous hand-object capture, where an egocentric headset or phone is paired with exo RGB-D cameras that share no trigger, sub-frame time offsets and rolling shutter misalign fast hand motion. A method that estimates time offsets and calibration jointly from the hand-object observations would remove the need for sync claps and flashlights. This holds only for rigs that cannot be hardware-synced. Hardware-triggered rigs such as DexYCB, ARCTIC and daisy-chained Azure Kinects do not have the problem.

skeptics.reasons:
Most of P29 does reduce to engineering, and the record itself labels it problem_type "engineering". Hardware triggers, PTP sync, light-absorbent chessboards and better rigs already fix the dataset-building complaints (claps, flashlights, drift, IR over-exposure). Those are bought with money and care, not with a research idea, and no top venue would accept "we synchronized our Kinects better".

One part still holds up as research. In commodity rigs, unknown sub-frame time offsets, rolling shutter and ToF exposure timing set a floor on accuracy. InterCap gives about 20 mm vertex-to-point error, bounded below by Kinect sync. HuMMan reports up to one Kinect frame of software-sync error. EgoBody shows misalignment on fast hand motion. Fast hand motion falls below that floor, while slow body motion does not. That gives a real estimation problem: recover continuous-time motion when the cameras do not share a clock.

Top venues have accepted this kind of problem. Verified examples:
- Spatiotemporal bundle adjustment for unsynchronized human capture (TPAMI).
- Motion Capture from Internet Videos (ECCV 2020 oral).
- Sync-NeRF, with learnable per-stream time offsets (AAAI 2024).
- CasCalib (FG 2024).
- Humans as a Calibration Pattern (arXiv 2412.19089, Dec 2024; venue not verified).
So the question is publishable, but body-level and frame-level versions are already crowded. The open gap is narrower: sub-frame, rolling-shutter-aware and ToF-aware self-synchronization driven by articulated hand-object dynamics and contact constraints. A scoped arXiv query for hand-object synchronization (2026 results) returned no paper on sub-frame sync for hands. Recent hand-object datasets (SHOW3D CVPR 2026, RoboTacDex) still solve sync with hardware.

That narrowed version is a modest but legitimate question for a top venue. It also fits a single-lab RGB-D bimanual setting and its robot-demonstration use. The score stays mid-range for three reasons:
- The obvious practical fix (hardware trigger or PTP) exists, which weakens the motivation.
- Prior art covers the generic version of the problem.
- A reviewer may see the hand-specific version as incremental unless it shows clear accuracy gains on fast bimanual motion over hardware-synced ground truth.

Web search budget was exhausted, so evidence came from direct arXiv fetches only. The venue for 2412.19089 was not confirmed.

skeptics.reframe: Commodity multi-camera RGB-D rigs have no shared clock, so fast hand motion hits an accuracy floor that hardware sync fixes but self-calibration has not. Body-level methods estimate frame-level offsets from slow, large-scale motion. The open question is whether sub-frame time offsets, rolling-shutter and ToF exposure timing can be recovered together with continuous-time bimanual hand-object motion and extrinsics. The signals to use are articulated kinematics, object rigidity and contact constraints. The test is whether such a method matches hardware-triggered accuracy on fast bimanual manipulation without any trigger.

painpoint.name: Demonstration capture is costly, narrow and misses force-rich skills

evidence.latest_state: Force-aware handheld and wearable interfaces have multiplied in 2025-2026, and each fixes one slice of the problem. ForceMimic (ICRA 2025) reports a 54.5 percent relative gain on vegetable peeling over vision-only imitation. Feel the Force (tactile glove) reaches 77 percent across 5 force-sensitive tasks. FreeTacMan collected 10k visuo-tactile trajectories across 50 contact-rich tasks. ManipForce reports 83 percent average success on six assembly tasks. TAMEn raises bimanual success from 34 to 75 percent. UMI-FT, TacUMI, OmniUMI and PolyUMI add finger force/torque, tactile, wrench or audio sensing to UMI-style grippers. BRIDGE reports that handheld-only data still trails, with gains of up to 36.7 percent when targeted teleoperation is added. This supports the pain point's claim that handheld tools distort force-rich skills. An ICRA 2026 study of gripper design on medical demonstrations finds bare hands substantially outperform gripper tools, which reconfirms the bandage-opening evidence. On the scale side, egocentric bare-hand corpora have grown sharply: EgoDex (ICLR 2026, 829 h), EgoScale (20,854 h, +54 percent success on a 22-DoF hand), EgoSteer (9.6K h curated) and HumanVerse-500 (500 h whole-body). None of these corpora carries force. The newest line infers force from bare-hand video: EgoTactile (ICML 2026, video paired with full-hand pressure), EgoTac (5.7M image-tactile pairs, force error below 0.06 N in-domain), TouchSight (500 h of pressure-glove data used to predict contact from bare hands) and Glove2Hand (CVPR 2026 Highlight, glove video translated to bare hands with tactile labels kept). The open gap is exactly what the record's why_it_persists names: scalable bare-hand capture with accurate 3D hand-object tracking plus physically grounded force. That remains unsolved and is the closest entry point for a hand-object tracking and reconstruction researcher. Note: the WebSearch budget was exhausted, so all items above come from arXiv API listings and abstracts. Venue labels are as given in arXiv comments, and success numbers are the papers' own self-reported figures.

evidence.crowdedness: HIGH: more than 20 verified 2025-2026 papers attack it from several directions (UMI-style force/tactile grippers, tactile gloves, exoskeletons, bilateral teleoperation, egocentric video at scale, force-from-video prediction), many from large well-resourced robotics labs and companies (Apple's EgoDex, Columbia/Stanford UMI lineage, NVIDIA-scale egocentric pretraining). The narrower sub-problem of force-grounded 3D bare-hand-object capture is less crowded but filling quickly.
evidence.trend: Rising. The arXiv API returned new force/tactile handheld interfaces almost every month from 2025-09 through 2026-09, and 2026 adds a fast-growing bare-hand force-from-video line (EgoTactile, EgoTac, TouchSight, Glove2Hand) next to scaling of egocentric human data (EgoScale, EgoSteer, HumanVerse-500). The driver is demand for VLA and humanoid training data.

skeptics.reasons:
P30 is refuted as broadly stated. Its two main claims have both been addressed in 2025-2026.
(1) "Interfaces cannot record clean force-rich skills." This is now an active area of hardware engineering with released systems. UMI-FT (2601.09988, Jan 2026) puts six-axis F/T sensors on each finger of a handheld UMI. It does whiteboard wiping, skewering and lightbulb insertion, regulates both external and grasp force, and has open hardware and software. TacUMI (2601.14550) combines ViTac sensors with an F/T sensor. OmniUMI (2604.10647) records RGB, depth, tactile, internal grip force and external wrench in sync. ManipForce (2509.19047) and ViTaMIn-B (2511.05858, bimanual visuo-tactile) are further examples. Others: FreeTacMan (2506.01941), a wearable visuo-tactile gripper; a tactile-conditioned UMI with GelSight (2510.13324); PinFT (2607.10000), a tweezer with an embedded 5-axis F/T sensor; and the Koala co-designed gripper (2608.20546). DexUMI (2505.21864) uses a wearable exoskeleton so the demonstrator gets direct haptic feedback, with 86 percent average success on two dexterous hands. Bilateral force-feedback teleoperation keeps advancing (DITTO 2609.19196; Compliance for Free 2609.19976). The sources the pain point cites (UMI could not open bandage packaging; no force-sensing sander) describe the state of 2023-2024 devices. The fix is now an engineering pattern: add F/T or tactile sensing to a UMI-style device.
(2) "Datasets stay narrow, small and static." Generalist AI's GEN-0 (Nov 2025 blog, a product claim that has not been peer reviewed) reports 270,000 hours of real-world manipulation data from thousands of homes and workplaces, growing by more than 10,000 hours per week. EgoDex (2505.11709, ICLR 2026) has 829 hours across 194 tasks, with hand and finger poses tracked by Apple Vision Pro. For data volume, the bottleneck has moved from capture cost to industrial scale-up.
What survives is narrower. The force-capable devices are still grippers or exoskeletons placed between the hand and the task, and each is shown on about three tasks. The large datasets (EgoDex, GEN-0) mostly carry vision and pose, not contact force. The pain point's own why_it_persists line identifies the residual: natural bare-hand capture that recovers force and contact. That residual is the part relevant to the author's field (hand-object tracking). It overlaps with the field's core contact and physics-plausibility pain points more than it stands as a separate robot-learning data problem. The relevance label is adjacent, and the hardware part is handled by robotics labs with fabrication budgets, so the broad statement is not a viable direction for this author.
Caveat: the web-search budget was exhausted. All evidence comes from fetches of arXiv API/abs pages and the Generalist blog. The statements on limitations are taken from abstracts.

skeptics.reframe: Force and contact can now be recorded with an instrumented gripper or glove, and vision-and-pose data now reach hundreds of thousands of hours. What has not been demonstrated is recovering contact location, contact force and object state from natural bare-hand, bimanual demonstrations captured with one camera or RGB-D, without placing a device between the hand and the object. Instrumented UMI-FT/OmniUMI-style captures could provide the paired ground truth for evaluating that. Fine flexible-object handling is the case where an interposed device most distorts the skill.

skeptics.reasons:
P30 combines two claims, and they hold up differently under the artifact lens.

(a) Demonstration data is costly, slow and narrow. This is not an artifact. The 21 supporting papers come from many unrelated groups and settings: RH20T and other SJTU work, the UMI line (FastUMI-100K, UMI-Bench), the egocentric corpora (EgoVerse, EgoLive, Open-AoE, World In Your Hands, HumanNet), RoboTube, the generative-data work (Wh0), and two surveys (Data Pyramid 2607.24744, VLA datasets). The large-dataset efforts outside the list were built because of this same problem: Open X-Embodiment (2310.08864), DROID (2403.12945) and AgiBot World (2503.06669). No community treats this as solved.

(b) Interfaces cannot record force-rich or fine flexible-object skills. This part rests on a few small, setup-specific studies. 854 (Georgadarellis et al., ICRA 2026, arXiv 2603.17189) is an 8-participant study of one task, opening a sterile bandage package with UMI. The figures for 65.8 percent success, 200 demonstrations, twice the bare-hand time and the 780 g tool all come from that single study. 782 (Li, Cui, Sadigh, ICRA 2025, arXiv 2503.07017) compares only low-cost modalities on three tabletop tasks in one lab with a Franka; its kinesthetic-replay failure is one task, Push Sanitizer. 919 (simulation versus teleoperation) and 998 (a sanding tool) are narrow industrial setups. The general statement 'teleoperation without force feedback misses force' is old, accepted knowledge in the haptics and bilateral-teleoperation literature, not a new field-level finding.

The robot-learning community is also actively building interfaces that do capture force and touch: ForceMimic (ICRA 2025, 2410.07554, a robot-free force-motion capture rig that beat force-feedback teleoperation on zucchini peeling), FreeTacMan (2506.01941, a wearable visuo-tactile gripper), Adaptive Compliance Policy (2410.09309, a UMI-style rig with force sensing), DexUMI (2505.21864) and DexCap (2403.07788). The pain point lists some of these as attempted fixes, but this is better described as an engineering frontier than a capability the field lacks.

'Mostly tabletop pick-and-place' is partly dated for 2025-2026, given the in-the-wild and mobile corpora (DROID, AgiBot World, the egocentric datasets), although tabletop tasks still dominate the benchmarks.

The bridge to the author's field is the claim that bare-hand capture needs accurate hand-object tracking and force sensing the field lacks. That is the pipeline's own synthesis in 'why it persists'; none of the evidence items states it. The relevance is correctly labelled adjacent.

Net: the costly-and-narrow core survives across diverse groups. The specific force-rich claims and all the headline numbers are single-study artifacts, and the force-capture gap is being closed piecemeal by dedicated hardware. Search was limited: the WebSearch budget was exhausted, so I checked papers only through the arXiv API, and did not open the full texts of 919 and 998.

skeptics.reframe: Human demonstration data for manipulation is still costly to collect and narrow in its tasks and scenes; groups as different as the Open X-Embodiment, DROID, AgiBot World, UMI and egocentric-corpus teams all report this. Every capture interface makes a trade-off: it either sits between the hand and the object (grippers, teleoperation, kinesthetic teaching, gloves) and so distorts or slows the skill, or it records bare hands only through vision, which gives no reliable contact or force signal. Dedicated rigs (ForceMimic, FreeTacMan, DexUMI) recover force or touch for one tool or one gripper at a time. No method yet recovers accurate 3D hand-object state plus contact from natural bare-hand capture at scale. That last gap, not interface ergonomics, is where the author's field connects.

skeptics.reasons:
Large parts of P30 as written are not research questions. "Datasets are small, static, tabletop and geographically uneven" is a wish for more collection effort and money; "a 780 g gripper is heavy", "UMI fingers cannot open bandage packaging", "no powered sander with integrated force sensing exists" are hardware-engineering items whose fixes are known in kind (lighter tools, redesigned fingers, embedded F/T or tactile sensors) and only need building. A steady stream of interface papers (UMI 2402.10329, FastUMI 2409.19499, DexCap 2403.07788, DexUMI 2505.21864, ForceMimic ICRA 2025, TacUMI 2601.14550, OSMO glove 2512.08920, RealDexUMI 2606.06033) shows that "a better capture device" is an incremental systems line, publishable at CoRL/ICRA but not a distinct scientific question, and each one moves the same scale-versus-fidelity trade-off rather than resolving it. Haptic teleoperation transparency is an established, decades-old control topic. So the cost/narrowness half of the pain point is refuted under this lens.

What survives is the clause in why_it_persists: natural bare-hand demonstrations would avoid every interface's burden and distortion, but recovering the force/contact half of a skill from vision requires accurate hand-object tracking plus force inference that the field lacks. That yields a genuine research question a CVPR/CoRL reviewer would find significant: is interaction force (normal/shear, its timing and magnitude) identifiable from markerless hand-object 3D reconstruction (RGB or RGB-D, one or few cameras, with occlusion), what priors make the inverse problem well-posed (physics-consistent contact optimisation, deformation of the object or skin, learned visuo-tactile mappings), and does force recovered this way transfer to a robot policy better than force-free kinematic retargeting on contact-rich tasks? The question is non-trivial because force is not observable from kinematics alone under static equilibrium and grasp-force redundancy, and because the error budget of current hand-object trackers (penetration, jitter, contact misplacement) directly corrupts any dynamics-based estimate.

Caveats that lower the score: (1) the question is no longer about capture cost; it is a reframing into vision-based force/contact inference, which belongs to the author's core field rather than to P30's robot-learning framing; (2) the space is filling fast in 2026: TouchAnything (bimanual tactile estimation from egocentric video, 2605.13083), EgoTac (2608.15060), human-centric tactile pre-training from 160 h of egocentric video (2607.01067), and Chain-of-Modality using EMG armbands (2504.13351), so novelty would need a sharp angle (e.g., metric force with ground-truth validation under bimanual occlusion, or a physics-identifiability analysis) rather than another tactile-prediction network; (3) ground-truth force for evaluation itself needs instrumented objects or gloves, partly reintroducing the interface problem. The pain point survives only in this narrowed form.
