skeptics.reframe: Interface-free capture of force-rich skills: from markerless bare-hand (bimanual, occluded, RGB or RGB-D) hand-object 3D reconstruction, when is interaction force (normal and shear, timing and magnitude) identifiable, what physical or learned priors make the inverse problem well-posed given grasp-force redundancy and tracker error, and does force recovered this way, validated against instrumented ground truth, give better robot transfer on contact-rich tasks than kinematic-only retargeting?

research_questions.question: From a single consumer RGB-D view of bare-hand manipulation, often bimanual, which parts of the hand-object contact forces can actually be determined, and can a tracker report them as metric estimates where kinematics determines them and as calibrated intervals where it cannot (the internal squeeze force)? Validation is against low-cost instrumented objects.
research_questions.why_top_venue: Inferring force from vision is a 2026 topic with several new top-venue papers: EgoPHI (ECCV 2026, arXiv 2608.13014, verified), EgoTactile (ICML 2026 spotlight, 2606.09243), Glove2Hand (CVPR 2026 Highlight, 2603.20850), TouchSight (2609.20414), EgoTac (2608.15060), TouchAnything (2605.13083) and DynamicHOI (2609.36454, verified, 2026-09-29). From their abstracts, each one returns a single force value, either from a learned regressor or from physics supervision. None separates what object kinematics determine from what they cannot. Grasp-force redundancy means part of any vision-based squeeze-force estimate comes from a prior. The internal force between two hands holding a box does not appear in the object's motion at all. A method built around identifiability first, with calibrated intervals checked against real metric ground truth on bimanual holds, is a clear contribution that reviewers can verify. The closest older work is Pham, Kyriazis, Argyros and Kheddar, 'Hand-Object Contact Force Estimation from Markerless Visual Tracking', TPAMI 2018 (DOI 10.1109/tpami.2017.2759736, verified via Crossref). It covered single-hand RGB-D with 2017-era trackers. The 2026 contribution would add bimanual internal forces, occlusion handling, honest uncertainty and modern trackers. Paper type: method, a small real benchmark, and an error-budget analysis.
research_questions.method_sketch: (1) Tracking. Track the object's 6D pose on RGB-D with a model-based tracker of the FoundationPose class. Track both hands with a MANO regressor of the HaMeR/WiLoR class, refined against depth; these tool names are prior knowledge. Get contact points from hand-object mesh proximity, with a temporal filter on contact state. (2) The observable part. Fit a smooth trajectory (spline or Kalman) to the object pose. Newton-Euler with known mass and inertia gives the total external wrench; subtract gravity and any table support. Once the object is lifted, the net wrench from the hands is fully determined. (3) Distribution over contacts. Build the grasp matrix G with friction cones and solve a second-order cone program for the feasible set of contact forces. Report the null-space (internal) component as an interval. The lower bound is the minimum squeeze that keeps every contact inside its cone for a friction-coefficient interval. The point prior comes either from human grip-force safety-margin findings (Johansson and Westling style; prior knowledge, not verified here) or from an optional learned appearance cue such as fingertip deformation, in the style of PressureVision. (4) Label every output component as measured (fixed by dynamics), bounded (cone-constrained) or prior (physiological or learned), so users know which numbers to trust. (5) Propagate tracker pose uncertainty through acceleration into the wrench to calibrate the intervals, and publish the error budget. At 30 fps, a raw second difference turns 1 mm of position noise into about 2 m/s^2 of acceleration noise (sqrt(6)*sigma/dt^2), so the trade-off between smoothing bandwidth and force bandwidth must be stated explicitly.
research_questions.minimum_experiment: Build 4-5 instrumented objects. Two are split boxes for bimanual holds: two halves joined by a single-axis load cell that reads the squeeze between the hands, plus an IMU for ground-truth acceleration. One is a split cylinder for single-hand power and precision grips. One is a handle object carrying only an IMU. Vary mass with inserts and friction with surface covers. Record 8-10 participants doing 5-6 tasks (lift-hold-place, shake, pass between own hands, pour, press on a kitchen scale, rotate), 3 repetitions each: about 5-8 h of 30 fps RGB-D. Metrics: net-force RMSE in N against IMU acceleration times mass plus gravity; coverage of the internal-force interval (target 90 percent nominal) and its mean width against the load cell; contact onset and offset timing error. Ablations: RGB versus RGB-D, second hand occluded versus visible, markerless versus marker-based object pose. Baselines: kinematic minimum-norm force; a Pham-style physics optimization; a learned image-to-force head trained on the same data; and EgoPHI and DynamicHOI if their code is released. A scale check needing no new hardware: on DexYCB and HO3D, use the published YCB object masses (prior knowledge) to compute the net wrench from ground-truth poses as pseudo ground truth, and compare it with the wrench from estimated poses. Pass criterion: coverage within 5 points of nominal, with narrower intervals than the learned-only baseline on held-out objects and subjects. Rough timeline: hardware build in months 1-2, ethics approval in parallel in months 1-3, capture in month 4, method and analysis in months 4-10, submission around month 10-12.
research_questions.data_and_hardware: The existing consumer RGB-D camera and the single workstation GPU. A 24 GB card is enough to run off-the-shelf trackers and train a small force head; the cone program runs on CPU, for example with CVXPY. Roughly US$200-400 of load cells, HX711 ADCs (80 samples/s), IMUs, ESP32 boards and 3D prints; these prices are approximate and not verified. An optional borrowed 6-axis F/T sensor for a calibration rig. An LED or audio pulse to synchronise the camera with the sensors. Human-subjects ethics approval. Public data: DexYCB and HO3D (YCB masses), ARCTIC for bimanual kinematics, ContactPose (ECCV 2020) for contact maps, and EgoPressure (arXiv 2409.02224; venue CVPR 2025 per prior knowledge, not confirmed). EgoPHI, EgoTactile and TouchAnything data if released. The Hoi! dataset (2512.04884) has force ground truth for its grippers; whether its human-hand sequences carry force is unverified. No motion capture and no robot are needed.
research_questions.risks: (1) High risk of being scooped. EgoPHI (ETH, ECCV 2026) already estimates contact and force for a single hand from RGB, validated on instrumented objects with 8 participants. A temporal or bimanual follow-up from that group or from the DynamicHOI authors is likely within 6-12 months. (2) In slow, quasi-static tasks most of the force is internal and unobservable, so the 'measured' part may be mostly gravity. Reviewers may find that obvious unless the interval and prior layer clearly beats learned regressors on metric error and calibration. (3) 30 fps capture and depth noise limit how much acceleration bandwidth can be recovered, so impacts and fast transients will be missed. (4) Split instrumented objects constrain where people can grasp and limit object variety, so the benchmark may be judged small. (5) Friction coefficients are unknown, and the intervals may come out too wide to be useful. (6) Ethics approval and multi-subject capture can take 2-3 months. (7) Comparing against EgoPHI depends on its code being released.

research_questions.question: When force-sensitive tasks demonstrated with bare hands are retargeted to a robot, does contact force recovered from the RGB-D demonstrations (with its observability labels and intervals) make execution more reliable than kinematic-only retargeting? How much of the gap to retargeting with measured force does it close?
research_questions.why_top_venue: The core claim of P30 is that capture without an interface loses the force half of a skill. Force-transfer papers (ForceMimic ICRA 2025, Feel the Force 2506.01944, UMI-FT 2601.09988, VisTacAlign 2609.30959) all measure force with hardware. Papers that transfer from bare-hand video (EgoDex ICLR 2026, EgoScale 2602.16710, DexWild RSS 2025) have no force signal. A controlled three-way comparison on the same demonstrations (kinematic only, vision-recovered force, measured force as an oracle from the instrumented objects) answers that claim directly. CoRL and RSS reviewers value this kind of result, and it would be new.
research_questions.method_sketch: Reuse the RQ1 demonstrations. Build MuJoCo twins of the instrumented objects with known geometry and mass and a friction range. Retarget the hand trajectories to (a) a parallel-jaw gripper with grip-force control and (b) a simulated dexterous hand (LEAP or Allegro). Use a tracking controller, optionally with residual RL in the style of DexMachina or ManipTrans; both are prior knowledge, not verified here. Compare three variants: kinematic only; kinematic plus the recovered net wrench and grip-force interval used as impedance or force targets (a point inside the interval, such as the lower bound plus a margin); and kinematic plus the load-cell force (oracle). Tasks: lift and carry a compressible or fragile object (crush versus slip), a bimanual box carry that needs squeeze to hold, wiping with a normal force, and pressing to a target force on a scale. Run in simulation first, with randomised friction and mass, then a small real check.
research_questions.minimum_experiment: Simulation: 4 tasks x 3 variants x 100 episodes with randomised physics. Metrics: success, slip rate, crush or over-force rate, force-tracking error. Real robot: a borrowed low-cost arm (a LeRobot SO-101-class arm or a lab Franka; prior knowledge) with a parallel gripper, using the same load-cell objects to read force. Run 2 tasks x 3 variants x 20 trials. The claim holds if the vision-force variant closes at least half of the success gap between kinematic-only and measured-force retargeting, in simulation and on at least one real task.
research_questions.data_and_hardware: The RQ1 data and objects; MuJoCo on CPU or Isaac Lab on the single GPU; a robot arm with gripper borrowed for 2-4 weeks; no motion capture. Best scheduled for months 12-18, after RQ1.
research_questions.risks: Simulated contact models (soft or penalty contacts) reproduce real grip forces poorly, so gains in simulation may not transfer. The human-to-robot embodiment gap (finger-pad area, friction, compliance) breaks a one-to-one force mapping; if even the measured-force oracle fails, the comparison is inconclusive. On a few tasks, a hand-tuned constant grip force may match the vision-force variant. CoRL and RSS reviewers expect many real tasks, ideally a dexterous hand, which a small lab may not have. Robot access is not guaranteed.

research_questions.question: Do current hand-object trackers produce motions whose implied wrenches are physically feasible (Newton-Euler with known mass, contacts inside friction cones)? Does enforcing that feasibility at test time reduce pose and contact errors, especially when one hand is occluded?
research_questions.why_top_venue: This is weaker as a standalone top-venue paper. It works best as the public-data section of RQ1, or as a 3DV or WACV paper that de-risks RQ1 within 4-6 months with no new hardware. It could reach CVPR or ECCV only if the feasibility metric substantially re-ranks published trackers and the test-time correction gives clear gains on the occlusion splits of ARCTIC, DexYCB and HO3D. It overlaps with DynamicHOI (physics supervision for reconstruction) and with the field's physical-plausibility pain points, so the novelty has to come from the benchmark metric and the occlusion analysis.
research_questions.method_sketch: For each sequence with a ground-truth object pose and known mass, compute the wrench the hands must supply. Masses: YCB values for DexYCB and HO3D; for ARCTIC, estimates from mesh volume and an assumed density, flagged as approximate. For each tracker's output compute (i) the wrench error against the wrench from ground-truth poses and (ii) a feasibility residual: the smallest friction-cone violation that explains the motion given the predicted contacts. Then add that residual as a penalty or differentiable cone-program term in test-time refinement, and measure the change in pose, contact and penetration errors.
research_questions.minimum_experiment: Evaluate 4-6 public trackers, using released outputs or code, on DexYCB, HO3D and ARCTIC. Report the rank correlation between standard metrics (MPJPE, ADD-S, penetration) and the feasibility metric, stratified by occlusion. Apply the test-time correction to two trackers. Also check whether the ground-truth annotations themselves are physically feasible.
research_questions.data_and_hardware: Public datasets only, on the single GPU. No new hardware and no participants.
research_questions.risks: Ground-truth poses may themselves be physically inconsistent because of annotation jitter, which contaminates the pseudo ground truth. Contact labels in these datasets are proxies. ARCTIC masses are not published (to my knowledge). The work may be seen as incremental relative to physics-aware HOI reconstruction papers, and acceptance at CVPR or ECCV is unlikely without striking results.
target_venues: CVPR / ECCV only with strong results

fit.thesis_assets_help: The assets give a small but real edge. They save perhaps 2-3 months of pipeline work and supply a framing; they supply no usable data. (1) The honesty labels (measured / held / constrained) map almost one-to-one onto the force decomposition in RQ1: measured is the net wrench fixed by object dynamics, constrained is the internal force bounded by friction cones, and held/prior is what physiology or a learned model fills in. This is the most transferable asset, because the conceptual contribution is the same: say which numbers are observed and which are assumed. (2) The ArUco-marked object with metric pose gives exactly what the Newton-Euler term needs, a metric object trajectory, and serves as the reference for checking markerless object tracking. Markers can go on the instrumented objects without changing how people grasp them. The author's own 10 percent marker-scale correction (50 mm declared versus 45 mm printed) is a useful cautionary example: a translation scale error passes linearly into the inertial force term, though not into the gravity term. (3) Object-conditioned recovery of an occluded holding arm helps when one hand in a bimanual hold is hidden. Its contact location is still needed for the grasp matrix, so this addresses the occlusion ablation directly. (4) The single RGB-D desk setup is the right sensor class, so no new camera is needed. (5) The causal 30 fps chain is more a limitation than a help for force: raw second differences at 30 fps turn 1 mm of noise into about 2 m/s^2 of acceleration noise, and real-time operation is not what reviewers will judge here. (6) The Unity twin helps only for visualisation; force ground truth and retargeting should use MuJoCo or Isaac. (7) The 28 recordings of one subject have no force ground truth and cover one person, so they cannot serve as a benchmark; they are at most a qualitative demo.
fit.what_a_small_lab_cannot_do_here: The pain point as originally stated (capture cost, data scale, interface engineering) is out of reach. A small lab cannot build and run a fleet of force- or tactile-sensing handheld or wearable interfaces (UMI-FT, OmniUMI, TacUMI, FreeTacMan, DEXOP) or collect at their scale. It cannot gather hundreds to thousands of hours of egocentric data (EgoDex 829 h; EgoScale 20,854 h; GEN-0's 270,000 h, an unreviewed industry claim). It cannot train vision-to-touch models at EgoTac scale (5.7M image-tactile pairs) or TouchSight scale (500 h of pressure-glove data), and it cannot afford multi-subject pressure-glove capture across many objects. It cannot evaluate policies across many real tasks and embodiments, especially dexterous robot hands, and has no motion capture for ground-truth hand pose. Competing on data volume or on interface hardware against Apple-, NVIDIA- and Columbia/Stanford-scale groups is not viable. Only the narrow vision-side question fits a small lab: how much of the force is identifiable from a single RGB-D view, with honest intervals and cheap instrumented-object ground truth. The robot-transfer question (RQ2) is feasible only with a borrowed arm, and then on few tasks. Literature check note: WebSearch was unavailable (session budget exhausted). The closest competitors (EgoPHI ECCV 2026, DynamicHOI 2609.36454, Pham et al. TPAMI 2018) were verified through arXiv abstract pages and Crossref. Statements marked prior knowledge (DexMachina, ManipTrans, the Johansson and Westling grip-force results, YCB masses, the EgoPressure venue, hardware prices) were not verified in this session.

painpoint.name: Non-robot data does not reliably improve robot policies

evidence.latest_state: Since late 2025 the evidence has moved: positive transfer from human video is now well documented, but every positive result still depends on some form of alignment. Physical Intelligence (Kareer et al., arXiv 2512.22414) reports that human-to-robot transfer only appears once the VLA has been pre-trained on enough scenes, tasks and embodiments. In that regime, fine-tuning pi0.5 on head-plus-wrist-camera human data with a 50/50 robot mix roughly doubles performance on generalization settings seen only in human data. EgoScale (NVIDIA/UT/GT, arXiv 2602.16710) pre-trains on 20,854 h of action-labelled egocentric video, reports a log-linear scaling law against validation loss and +54% success on a 22-DoF hand, and still needs an aligned human-robot mid-training stage. HumanScale (arXiv 2606.20521) reports 52.5% (in-distribution) and 90% (out-of-distribution) higher success than an equal volume of teleoperated pre-training, but only after heavy filtering and labelling. Several 2026 papers confirm that naive mixing still fails. Li et al. (Agrawal/Du/Gupta, arXiv 2606.06627) find that hand-pose quality matters and that even accurate hands transfer only when the networks specialize per embodiment (+29.7% absolute in the low-robot-data regime, six tasks). ReWeight (arXiv 2609.13851) measures random human-robot mixing at 44% versus 39% robot-only versus 57% with optimal-transport retrieval weighting in simulation, and 68.8% in real-robot tests. For simulation, SimHum (CoRL 2026, arXiv 2601.19406) reaches 62.5% out-of-distribution success on four bimanual tasks with 80 real episodes, +53.7 points over real-only, while the mechanistic analysis of sim-and-real co-training by Lei et al. (Zhu lab, arXiv 2604.13645) attributes gains to representation alignment and importance reweighting rather than offering an a-priori exchange-rate predictor. Data valuation is starting to appear: ATHENA (arXiv 2606.16208) uses influence functions to match full-data RoboTwin 2.0 performance with 50% of demonstrations. No method yet predicts, before training, how much one hour of human video or simulation is worth for a given task, and the dependence on 3D hand-object reconstruction quality remains an open, partly measured factor.

evidence.crowdedness: HIGH: at least 10 verified 2025-2026 papers from large, well-resourced groups (Physical Intelligence, NVIDIA GEAR, Stanford/Berkeley/GT, MIT, UT Austin, CMU/UIUC, SJTU) attack human-video and sim co-training directly, with frequent arXiv releases through September 2026.
evidence.trend: Rising: egocentric human data is now treated as the main way to scale VLAs (EgoScale, HumanScale, EgoVerse, pi0.5 human transfer), and 2026 work is moving from showing that human or simulation data can help to explaining and controlling when it helps, through alignment, weighting, influence-based valuation and mechanistic analysis.

skeptics.reasons: The headline "non-robot data does not reliably improve robot policies" is clearly weaker in 2025-2026 than the record suggests, but it is not solved. Positive evidence against the pain point: (1) Kareer et al. (Physical Intelligence, arXiv 2512.22414, Dec 2025) report that human-to-robot transfer emerges once the VLA is pretrained on enough scenes, tasks and embodiments, and that a simple co-training recipe nearly doubles performance on generalization settings seen only in human data. (2) EgoScale (arXiv 2602.16710) pretrains on 20,854 h of action-labeled egocentric video, reports a log-linear scaling law between human data scale and validation loss, and a 54 percent gain over no pretraining on a 22-DoF hand. (3) HumanScale (arXiv 2606.20521) claims that at equal pretraining volume, filtered egocentric video beats robot-data pretraining (52.5 percent higher in-distribution and 90 percent higher OOD success). (4) The sim-and-real co-training recipe (arXiv 2503.24361) and a mechanistic follow-up (arXiv 2604.13645) make sim co-training a working, partly explained practice. Together these show that "human video lowers in-domain success" (the record's main benchmark item, paper 224) is regime-specific. It reflects small, non-diverse robot pretraining and naive mixing, and is not a law of the field. Why it is not refuted: every positive result still depends on conditions the record names. PI needs diverse robot pretraining first. EgoScale needs an aligned human-robot mid-training stage. HumanScale needs a careful filtering and labeling pipeline plus robot fine-tuning data. X-Diffusion (arXiv 2511.04671) still documents negative transfer from infeasible human demonstrations. Humanoid Policy ~ Human Policy (arXiv 2503.13441) finds human data has minor in-domain effect. The 2604.13645 authors state that when and why co-training works "remain poorly understood". The 2026 survey (arXiv 2606.00054) lists embodiment and viewpoint grounding, and evaluation that predicts transfer efficiency, as open. So the claim that the exchange rate cannot be predicted in advance survives. The claim that the data gives no gain does not. For this author the relevance stays adjacent: the field the author controls is the quality of 3D hand-object labels, and no work links reconstruction fidelity to downstream transfer value.

skeptics.reframe: Human video and simulation now improve robot policies at scale, when there is diverse robot pretraining or aligned mid-training. What is still missing is any way to predict, before training, how much a given non-robot demonstration set will help a target robot and task. In particular, no work measures how the accuracy of its 3D hand-object reconstruction (hand pose, object pose, contact, occlusion handling) controls that value. A field-relevant version for this author: build a benchmark or valuation method that ties reconstruction fidelity of bimanual human demonstrations to their downstream transfer value and negative-transfer risk.

skeptics.reasons:
The strong claim, that non-robot data gives no gain or lowers in-domain success, rests on very few measurements. Nearly all of the quantitative negative evidence comes from one benchmark paper (id 224, Data Utilization Law, CVPR 2026). That paper tested three bimanual tasks on one platform (Aloha-Agilex-2.0) with one teleoperation budget, and the headline drop (Pick Dual Bottles 0.70 to 0.45) is a single task-condition pair with unreported trial counts. The second quantitative source (709, TRI large-behaviour-model co-training study) is mostly simulation (TRI-Ramen) and tests latent-action and discrete-token encodings, so it shows that particular action-extraction schemes failed, not that human data is useless. The third source (782, How to Train Your Robots, ICRA 2025) compares kinesthetic teaching with teleoperation. It never tests human video or simulation, so citing it as evidence that non-robot data fails is a mis-attribution. Most of the other 16 papers are dataset or survey papers (HoloAssist, EgoExoLearn, EgoVerse, Open-AoE, HumanNet, World In Your Hands, two 2026 arXiv surveys, a 2026 arXiv position paper). They mention the issue as motivation or future work and do not measure it. The groups are diverse, but the measured evidence is narrow.

There is also a large positive literature from different groups that contradicts the strong form. EgoMimic (verified) reports clear gains from co-training on egocentric human data and finds that one extra hour of hand data is worth more than one extra hour of robot data. Sim-and-Real Co-Training (Maddukuri et al., NVIDIA/UT, verified) reports an average 38 percent real-world gain from simulation data despite a visible sim-real gap. MimicGen and DexMimicGen, GR00T N1, EgoVLA, Being-H0, Phantom and HAT (Humanoid Policy ~ Human Policy) all report gains from non-robot or synthetic data when it is aligned. Physical Intelligence reports that human-to-robot transfer appears with enough robot pretraining (could not be verified this session). So 'does not improve' reflects particular setups: naive pretraining on a small bimanual platform, and token encodings of latent actions.

What survives is the weaker claim. The size of the gain depends on alignment (viewpoint, embodiment retargeting, action-label quality, task overlap), and nobody can predict the exchange rate or the mixing ratio in advance. Other communities have not solved this either: data-mixture selection for LLMs (for example DoReMi) and negative transfer in domain adaptation are still set empirically. So this part is not an artifact, but it is a generic, long-standing transfer-learning question rather than a defined problem.

The link to the author's field, in the why_it_persists field (that it is unknown how much 3D hand-object reconstruction fidelity matters), is the most useful part. Even so, it is partly addressed: Phantom, HAT/PH2D and 'What Matters When Cotraining on Everyday Human Videos' (2026) already study how pose quality affects transfer, according to local scratchpad notes that were not web-verified. Relevance to tracking and reconstruction stays adjacent. The WebSearch budget ran out after one call, so most positive counter-evidence comes from scratchpad paper lists, not fetched pages.

skeptics.reframe: Non-robot data (human video, simulation) does help robot policies, but only when it is aligned in viewpoint, embodiment retargeting, action-label quality and task overlap. No one can yet predict in advance how much a given human or simulated dataset is worth to a target robot. For a 3D hand-object tracking researcher, the open question is how errors in the reconstructed 3D hand-object action labels (hand pose, object 6D pose, contact) lower that transfer value. This needs a controlled study where reconstruction fidelity is varied and downstream policy success is measured, which existing co-training papers only partly cover.

skeptics.reasons: The refutation fails. P31 is not a wish for more data money, and its answer is not already known and merely waiting on resources. The evidence is a set of contradictory, task-dependent results: human-video pretraining lowered in-domain bimanual success (Pick Dual Bottles 0.70 to 0.45), latent-action pretraining helped only when robot data was scarce, and mixing ratios are tuned by hand. That pattern points to a missing model of when and why non-robot data transfers, and building that model is a scientific question. Top robotics venues currently publish exactly this kind of work as research rather than engineering. Wei et al. 2025 (arXiv 2503.22634) report that some visual sim-real discrepancy helps and that physical fidelity matters more than visual fidelity; the fetched abstract gives the venue as IROS 2025, which is a strong venue but not on the target list. Li et al. 2026 (arXiv 2606.06627, Agrawal and Gupta groups) show that higher-quality triangulated hand labels transfer better than monocular estimates, and that an embodiment motion gap remains even with accurate hands. VideoManip 2026 reconstructs 3D hand-object trajectories from RGB video to train dexterous policies. At least three questions a reviewer would accept as significant survive. (1) Fidelity-to-utility: how do errors in 3D hand-object reconstruction (wrist pose, finger articulation, object 6D pose, contact, metric scale under occlusion) propagate into policy transfer value, and which error components dominate? (2) A priori valuation: can the exchange rate of a human or simulated demonstration be predicted before policy training from measurable properties of the reconstruction and its alignment with the robot? (3) For bimanual tasks, does reconstructing coordination and contact explicitly close the embodiment gap that hand pose alone does not? Question (1) maps directly onto the author's field and turns a robot-learning complaint into a perception research question. Score deductions: relevance to the author is adjacent; the area is crowded, with many well-resourced robot-learning groups running large co-training studies; and much published work is empirical ablation that is costly in robot hours, which a thesis author with one RGB-D setup may struggle to match. The surviving question is therefore narrower than the pain point as stated.

skeptics.reframe: The value of human demonstrations for robot policies depends on how accurately 3D hand-object interaction is reconstructed, and no one has measured or modelled that dependence. The research question: how do specific reconstruction errors (wrist and finger pose, object 6D pose, contact, metric scale, and bimanual coordination under occlusion) degrade co-training gains? Can a reconstruction-side alignment score predict a demonstration's exchange rate against teleoperated robot data before any policy is trained?

research_questions.question: Which parts of 3D hand-object reconstruction error decide how useful a human demonstration is to a robot? Does ranking reconstruction methods by standard accuracy metrics (MPJPE, object ADD/ADD-S, Chamfer distance) agree with ranking them by downstream usefulness, measured as physics executability and policy success in simulation? The error parts to separate are wrist translation and scale or depth bias, wrist rotation, finger articulation, object 6D pose, hand-to-object relative pose, contact onset and offset timing, high-frequency jitter versus low-frequency drift, frames lost or held stale under occlusion, and the relative pose between the two hands.
research_questions.why_top_venue: Nobody has measured this. The closest work is Li et al. (arXiv 2606.06627, Agrawal, Du and Gupta groups, verified). They added calibrated isotropic Gaussian noise to the triangulated hand joints only, at 0.5x and 1.0x, for a single-arm parallel-jaw Piper. A search summary of their HTML page reports mean success falling from 48.3 to 30.0 to 20.0 percent; I did not read that table directly. They did not vary object pose, contact or temporal structure, and they did not test bimanual or dexterous hands. Do as I Do (arXiv 2606.19333, Berkeley, Malik and Abbeel, verified) reports only an aggregate gap: retargeting success of 71 percent for monocular reconstructions against 81 percent for OakInk2 mocap, with position error 0.05 m against 0.03 m. It does not attribute the gap to error sources. The September 2026 HOI survey (arXiv 2607.28394, verified) says evaluation should separate reconstruction fidelity, action executability and downstream data efficiency, and it names no benchmark that does so. Two targeted searches found no benchmark that ranks HOI estimators by downstream executability. A result showing that standard metrics mis-rank methods for robot use would change how a whole CV subfield evaluates itself. That suits a CVPR, ECCV or ICCV paper or a NeurIPS Datasets and Benchmarks paper.
research_questions.method_sketch: (1) Start from ground-truth bimanual HOI sequences in ARCTIC and OakInk2, with DexYCB and HO3D as single-hand controls. (2) Collect real estimator outputs on the same clips: HaMeR, WiLoR or HaWoR for hands; FoundationPose or BundleSDF for objects; at least one joint HOI pipeline if its code is released. Fit a structured error model to the residuals: per-factor bias, temporal spectrum, and dependence on occlusion and visibility. (3) Build controlled perturbations that change one factor at a time at matched magnitudes, plus the real estimator outputs as the realistic condition. (4) Measure usefulness with probes of increasing cost. P1, executability: retarget each sequence and roll it out in a GPU simulator with a fixed physics tracker (ManipTrans, DexMachina or SPIDER, whichever releases usable code; not verified), and record object-tracking success and drop rate. P2, policy value: train a small diffusion or ACT policy in simulation on retargeted demonstrations for 3-4 tasks. Report success and an exchange rate against a ground-truth-retargeted baseline of the same size. Use both a parallel-jaw gripper and one dexterous hand to test whether finger error matters only for dexterous hands. (5) Analysis: a Shapley or ANOVA decomposition of usefulness over the error factors; Kendall tau between standard metrics and usefulness across estimators; then a usefulness-aligned metric (for example, hand-object relative pose in the contact frame plus velocity error), showing it ranks methods better.
research_questions.minimum_experiment: Use one bimanual dataset (ARCTIC or OakInk2), 5-8 objects and 100-200 clips. Run 3 real estimator pipelines plus 6 single-factor perturbations at 3 magnitudes, with probe P1 only and one pretrained or sampling-based tracker so that each rollout needs no per-clip RL training. Deliverables: usefulness-versus-error curves per factor, plus Kendall tau between MPJPE or ADD and executability across the estimators. If one factor, such as hand-object relative pose or depth bias, explains most of the variance and the standard metrics mis-rank at least one pair of estimators, the paper has its core. P2 on 3 tasks is the second step.
research_questions.data_and_hardware: Public data only: ARCTIC, OakInk2, DexYCB, HO3D, and optionally H2O for egocentric bimanual RGB-D. GPU simulation: Isaac Gym or Isaac Lab, MuJoCo or Genesis. One workstation GPU with 24-48 GB. Per-clip RL tracking would need cloud burst or a smaller clip count. No robot is needed for the minimum experiment. An optional real check needs a borrowed or low-cost 6-DoF arm with a parallel gripper, of the AgileX Piper class used by Li et al., running 2 tasks.
research_questions.risks: (a) The proxy may be invalid: simulation executability may track simulator contact artifacts rather than real transfer, so reviewers at robot venues will ask for at least a small real-robot check. (b) Compute: if the available trackers need RL training per sequence (DexMachina-style curricula), the factor sweep becomes intractable on one GPU. Check tracker code and cost in month 1. (c) Scoop risk is high. Berkeley (Do as I Do), the Agrawal and Gupta groups, NVIDIA (DexMachina, SimHum) and Meta (SPIDER) are each one step from this study. (d) The headline may look obvious, for example that object-relative pose matters most, unless the metric mis-ranking result is clear. (e) The fitted error models may not cover the failure modes of in-the-wild video.

research_questions.question: Can the value of a human demonstration, measured as its marginal contribution to robot policy success, be predicted before any policy training, using only signals from the reconstruction side? Candidate signals are estimator uncertainty or multi-hypothesis spread, per-frame provenance (measured, held or constrained), physical consistency (penetration, contact persistence, object support), visibility and occlusion ratio, and kinematic reachability for the target embodiment. Does weighting or filtering by this score beat random mixing, and does it come close to post-hoc influence-based curation at a small fraction of the cost?
research_questions.why_top_venue: Every skeptic agreed that no one can predict the exchange rate before training. Existing valuation is post-hoc and depends on the policy. ATHENA (arXiv 2606.16208) and other influence-function methods need trained policies and gradients. ReWeight (arXiv 2609.13851) retrieves by optimal transport against robot data at post-training time: 39 percent robot-only, 44 percent random mix and 57 percent ReWeight in simulation. Do as I Do keeps only 4-9 percent of internet videos through hand-tuned quality checks. A score that is cheap, independent of the policy, and comes from perception would move valuation upstream to capture and reconstruction time, where a perception lab has an advantage. CoRL and RSS publish data-valuation and curation work. NeurIPS publishes it when the predictor generalizes across estimators and embodiments.
research_questions.method_sketch: Ground truth for the targets comes from the RQ1 infrastructure: per-demonstration executability from P1, and per-demonstration influence on a small simulated co-training policy from P2, estimated with an off-the-shelf influence or leave-group-out method. Features are computed only from the reconstruction: ensemble or test-time-augmentation variance of hand and object pose, provenance flags for each frame, penetration depth, contact-flicker rate, acceleration energy, occlusion ratio, residual against measured depth when RGB-D is available, and inverse-kinematics residual and joint-limit margin for the target robot. Train a light predictor (gradient boosting or a small temporal transformer). Test generalization across estimators, objects and datasets held out of training. Then use the score to filter and weight in co-training with a fixed small robot-data budget. Compare against random mixing, a ReWeight-style retrieval baseline, and post-hoc influence curation, reporting success, compute cost and the predicted versus realized exchange rate.
research_questions.minimum_experiment: In simulation, use 3 tasks, one gripper embodiment, a fixed robot set of 20-50 demonstrations, and a pool of 300-500 reconstructed human demonstrations drawn from two estimators. Report Spearman correlation between predicted score and measured influence or executability on held-out estimators. Then compare co-training success with score weighting, random mixing and influence curation at equal human-data volume, using at least 3 seeds.
research_questions.data_and_hardware: Same as RQ1, plus enough GPU time for roughly 50-100 small policy trainings to estimate influence or ablations. That fits on one GPU over weeks if the policies are small; it does not fit for VLA-scale models. A real check is optional: a borrowed low-cost arm for one task, scoring the author's own RGB-D captures before training.
research_questions.risks: (a) The area is crowded: ReWeight, ATHENA, X-Diffusion (arXiv 2511.04671, which treats human actions as noisy robot actions) and EgoBridge all address weighting or alignment. Novelty rests entirely on pre-training prediction from perception signals. (b) Influence estimates for small simulated policies are noisy, which would cap the measurable correlation. (c) The predictor may collapse to one trivial feature, such as penetration or occlusion ratio. That is still useful but weaker. (d) A simulation-only result is weak at CoRL and RSS. (e) The exchange rate also depends on task overlap and visual domain gap, which reconstruction signals do not see, so the predictable share of variance may be modest.

research_questions.question: For bimanual demonstrations, how much downstream value does metric depth add over monocular RGB reconstruction? Does that added value come mainly from correct inter-hand and hand-object relative pose and contact timing under mutual occlusion? Does object-conditioned recovery of the occluded hand or arm close the gap?
research_questions.why_top_venue: The field is scaling monocular and egocentric RGB data: Do as I Do, EgoScale and HumanScale. Do as I Do names monocular depth ambiguity and the inability to tell contact from occlusion as its main failure modes. No one has priced, in terms of downstream usefulness, what a consumer depth camera buys for bimanual demonstrations. A clean answer, such as 'RGB-D halves the executability gap on coordination-heavy tasks but not on single-hand tasks', would tell dataset builders when depth is worth carrying. On its own this RQ is weaker than RQ1 and works best as a section or follow-up of it.
research_questions.method_sketch: Use RGB-D datasets with ground truth: H2O (egocentric bimanual RGB-D), and DexYCB and HO3D (single-hand RGB-D) as controls. Reconstruct each clip three ways: (a) a monocular RGB pipeline (HaWoR or WiLoR plus FoundationPose in RGB mode or a SAM 3D-style tracker); (b) an RGB-D pipeline (depth-fitted hands plus FoundationPose in RGB-D mode); (c) pipeline (b) plus object-conditioned recovery of the occluded hand or arm. Evaluate with the RQ1 probes, adding bimanual metrics: hand-to-hand relative pose error, synchrony of contact timing, and the rate of handover and bimanual-lift success in simulation. Stratify results by occlusion level.
research_questions.minimum_experiment: On H2O, take 50-100 bimanual clips with the three reconstruction variants and run P1 executability with one tracker. Report the executability gap, RGB against RGB-D against RGB-D with recovery, stratified by occlusion level. A small real test set comes from the author's own RGB-D recordings, where the ArUco-marked object provides metric object pose. Report it only as a qualitative or real-world sanity check.
research_questions.data_and_hardware: H2O, DexYCB and HO3D, all public. Optionally the author's own consumer RGB-D camera for a few new multi-subject recordings. One GPU. No robot for the minimum experiment.
research_questions.risks: (a) 'Depth helps' is the expected answer, so the paper needs a surprising stratified finding to clear top-venue review. (b) H2O annotation quality and object variety are limited, and depth noise on small objects may wash out the gain. (c) The trend toward RGB-only egocentric scaling may make reviewers see RGB-D as niche. (d) The result stays simulation-only unless the RQ1 real check is added. Likely venues are ICRA, IROS or RA-L unless it is folded into RQ1.
target_venues: CVPR (as part of the RQ1 study)

fit.thesis_assets_help: A modest help, mainly to RQ2 and RQ3; very little to RQ1. (1) The measured, held and constrained labels already form the per-frame provenance signal that RQ2 needs as a predictor feature, and 'held' frames are exactly the occlusion-related stale-value error that RQ1 should model. This is the most useful asset. (2) Object-conditioned recovery of an occluded holding arm is the intervention to test in RQ3. It works at wrist and arm level, which is what parallel-jaw policies consume: Li et al.'s policy outputs a tool-centre-point pose plus a grasp command. It says nothing about finger articulation for dexterous hands. (3) The single RGB-D desk setup with an ArUco-marked object of metric pose gives a small real-world check of object-pose and depth-bias errors, plus a demonstration of capture-time demonstration scoring running causally at 30 fps, which is a good application figure for RQ2. (4) The Unity twin does not help: the experiments need Isaac Gym, Isaac Lab, MuJoCo or Genesis physics with dexterous-hand and gripper trackers. (5) Twenty-eight recordings of one subject at one desk cannot be a dataset contribution and cannot carry a top-venue claim. Use them only as a qualitative real-world example. The core ground truth must come from ARCTIC, OakInk2, DexYCB, HO3D and H2O.
fit.what_a_small_lab_cannot_do_here: A small lab cannot compete on the pain point as written, which is the question of whether human video or simulation helps robot policies at scale. That question is decided by groups with fleets of robots and VLA-scale compute: Physical Intelligence (pi0.5 human-transfer co-training), NVIDIA (EgoScale, with 20,854 h of egocentric video; SimHum), HumanScale, and the Agrawal, Gupta and Du groups, whose controlled study ran 3,480 real-robot rollouts. Specifically, the lab cannot: pretrain or fine-tune VLAs on thousands of hours of video; collect a large multi-subject egocentric dataset; run hundreds of real rollouts per condition, across embodiments or with dexterous robot hands; or make credible scaling-law or exchange-rate claims about real robots. Without at least a borrowed low-cost arm, any downstream-value claim rests on simulation proxies that robot-venue reviewers will discount. Per-clip RL physics tracking over a large factor sweep may also exceed one GPU. The niche a small lab can hold is perception-side and runs on public data: controlled measurement of how hand-object reconstruction errors carry into downstream value, and cheap pre-training prediction of that value. It has to be done fast, because well-resourced groups are one step away from it.

painpoint.name: Bimanual robot policies fail on coordination and handover

evidence.latest_state: Under clean conditions, coordination and handover in simulation have improved sharply. On RoboTwin 2.0 Easy, Co-VLA (arXiv 2606.20285, June 2026) reaches 82 percent average against 76 percent for pi0, and 91 percent on Handover Block against 64 percent. M3 modality masking (arXiv 2608.22419, Aug 2026) raises the clean average from 41.0 to 62.7 percent and Handover Block from 27 to 74 percent. Under domain randomization the collapse that defines P32 remains. On RoboTwin 2.0 Hard, Co-VLA averages 22 percent against 21 percent for pi0, and Handover Block reaches only 12 percent against 7 percent. M3 reaches only 15.1 percent average in the Clean2Rand setting. Real dual-arm results are moderate and degrade out of distribution. On the AgileX Cobot Magic, in-distribution handover rises from 63 percent (pi0) to 73 percent (Co-VLA), but out-of-distribution handover reaches only 13 to 27 percent. The BiCoord benchmark (arXiv 2604.05831, Apr 2026) reports that DP, RDT, Pi0 and OpenVLA-OFT all struggle on long-horizon tasks with tight inter-arm coupling and role exchange. For human-to-robot handover, DexH2R (ICCV 2025) reports Easy to Hard drops of 71.1 to 26.6 percent for MotionNet, 39.4 to 8.3 percent for DP and 66.3 to 27.1 percent for DP3. The authors attribute the DP failures to occlusion and lack of explicit 3D information, and note that DP3 needs robust segmentation. In short, clean-simulation success has largely been solved by large VLA models with coordination priors. Robustness to realistic perception and clutter (Hard and randomized settings, out-of-distribution real scenes) is still near 10 to 25 percent.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: Co-VLA: Coordination-Aware Structured Action Modeling for Dual-Arm Vision-Language-Action Systems
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Splits each dual-arm action into a shared coordination intent plus an arm-specific residual and adds a controller at deployment time. On RoboTwin 2.0 the average rises from 76 to 82 percent Easy and from 21 to 22 percent Hard. Handover Block rises from 64 to 91 percent Easy and from 7 to 12 percent Hard. Real out-of-distribution handover rises from 13 to 27 percent.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: Robust Bimanual Vision-Language-Action Models via Embarrassingly Simple Modality Masking (M3)
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Randomly masks the wrist-camera views and action queries during training so the policy does not rely on spurious correlations between views. On RoboTwin 2.0 the clean average rises from 41.0 to 62.7 percent and Handover Block from 27 to 74 percent, but Clean2Rand reaches only 15.1 percent. Real out-of-distribution clutter success rises from 12.5 to 61.1 percent.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: BiCoord: A Bimanual Manipulation Benchmark towards Long-Horizon Spatial-Temporal Coordination
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: New benchmark with continuous dependence between the arms and dynamic role exchange, plus temporal, spatial and spatiotemporal coordination metrics. It shows that DP, RDT, Pi0 and OpenVLA-OFT struggle on long, tightly coupled tasks.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: CUBic: Coordinated Unified Bimanual Perception and Control Framework
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Frames bimanual coordination as a unified perception problem, using dual codebooks for two-way coordination and a unified diffusion policy. The abstract claims gains on RoboTwin but gives no numbers.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: CoWAM: Coordination Contracts for Selective Policy Intervention with WAMs
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Expresses synchronization, arm-role compatibility and collision convergence as coordination contracts that gate interventions on a world-action-model policy. Across eight simulated bimanual tasks it reports +16.7 points in coordination-valid selection and +9.6 points in closed-loop success.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: DexH2R: A Benchmark for Dynamic Dexterous Grasping in Human-to-Robot Handover
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Real ShadowHand handover dataset (4,282 trials, 39 participants, 56 objects) with a DynamicGrasp baseline. From Easy to Hard mode, success drops from 71.1 to 26.6 percent for MotionNet, 39.4 to 8.3 percent for DP and 66.3 to 27.1 percent for DP3. The authors cite occlusion and the need for segmentation.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: MobileH2R: Learning Generalizable Human to Mobile Robot Handover Exclusively from Scalable and Diverse Synthetic Data

evidence.crowdedness: HIGH. At least ten 2025-2026 papers attack the problem directly: ICCV 2025 (DexH2R, AnyBimanual, Imaginative Coordination), CVPR 2025 (MobileH2R) and several 2026 arXiv VLA, benchmark and coordination papers (Co-VLA, M3, CUBic, CoWAM, BiCoord, PassGen). Large Chinese robotics labs and industry groups (RoboTwin consortium, Samsung R&D, the Pi0 ecosystem) dominate, using big compute and shared benchmarks.
evidence.trend: Rising. RoboTwin 2.0 and its leaderboard (CVPR 2025 challenge, Aug 2026 evaluation update), new coordination benchmarks (BiCoord, 2026) and a steady flow of bimanual VLA papers in 2026 show growing attention. The focus is shifting from clean-simulation success, where scores are now 60 to 90 percent, to robustness under randomization and in real out-of-distribution scenes, where success is still 10 to 27 percent. That remaining gap is a perception problem: 3D state of both arms, the object and the partner's hand under occlusion.

skeptics.reasons: Partly refuted. The simulation half of P32 is out of date. The record says success is "well below 50 percent and near zero on handovers... even in noiseless simulation" and cites the RoboTwin 2.0 collapse from Easy to Hard (DP3 55.2 to 5.0 percent). Large pretrained world-action models released since late 2025 have nearly saturated that benchmark, randomized setting included. Motus (arXiv 2512.13030, code and checkpoints released) reaches 88.66 percent clean and 87.02 percent randomized across the 50 RoboTwin 2.0 tasks. Its per-task results (clean/randomized) are Handover Block 86/73, Handover Mic 78/63, Stack Blocks Three 91/95, Place Dual Shoes 93/87 and Lift Pot 96/99. Riemann-1.0 (arXiv 2608.27033, Aug 2026) reports 94.3 percent average on RoboTwin 2.0. So the claims about "near-zero handover in sim" and "collapse under domain randomization" no longer hold for current models. What changes the outcome is pretraining and scale, not a new idea, so for simulated coordination the remaining work is engineering. The pain point is not fully refuted. Three parts survive. (1) Benchmarks published in 2026 still report failure on long-horizon, tightly coupled coordination and in real-world settings. BiCoord (arXiv 2604.05831, Apr 2026) says DP, RDT, Pi0 and OpenVLA-OFT struggle with long-duration, highly coupled tasks. DuoBench (arXiv 2606.11901, Jun 2026) names early interaction, parallel arm execution and sim-to-real transfer as open failure modes. Neither abstract gives numbers. (2) Dynamic human-to-robot handover with real perception is still weak. DexH2R reports about 30 percent real-world success with human initialization and 0 percent without, and the HandoverSim-family benchmarks still assume perfect perception of the hand and object state. (3) The record's own root cause, that precise and timely 3D state of the partner's hand and the object under occlusion is not available outside simulation, is not touched by the RoboTwin saturation. RoboTwin evaluates arm-to-arm coordination from simulator renders, not perception of a human partner. Score is lowered because the headline numbers in the record are stale and the policy-side problem is moving fast in well-funded labs. The relevance to the author's field (perceiving hands and objects) is only in the handover perception part.

skeptics.reframe: Arm-to-arm coordination in simulation is close to saturated (RoboTwin 2.0 at about 87 to 94 percent average in the randomized setting, handover tasks at about 63 to 86 percent, for Motus and Riemann-1.0), so it is no longer a pain point. What remains is perceiving a human partner. Policies for human-to-robot handover and for close human-robot bimanual interaction still depend on perfect simulator state of the partner's hand and the object. When that state has to come from real RGB-D perception under mutual occlusion and motion, success drops sharply (DexH2R about 30 percent), and long-horizon, tightly coupled real-world coordination still fails on the 2026 benchmarks BiCoord and DuoBench. The open problem in the author's field is low-latency, occlusion-robust 4D tracking of the hand and object that is accurate and timely enough for a reactive policy to use, together with benchmarks that score policies on perceived state rather than ground-truth state.

skeptics.reasons:
P32 holds up mostly as an artifact of which baselines were reported and when. Its evidence is narrow and partly out of date.

(1) Who reported the failures. Almost all the evidence comes from benchmark papers reporting their own baselines. Benchmark papers have a structural incentive to design tasks that current methods fail. The low numbers are per-task DP, ACT and DP3 policies trained from about 50 demonstrations (RoboTwin 2.0 entries dated 2025-08; TWIN/RLBench2 with PerAct2-era baselines; HGen-Bench DP/DP3).

(2) The sources cluster in a few groups and setups. RoboTwin and RoboTwin 2.0 (1160, 1176) share a platform lineage. Bi-DexHands and its RL follow-up (1035, 1191) are the same benchmark line. The handover items (1188 HandoverSim, 257 DexH2R, 1183) come from one sub-community built around HandoverSim or DexYCB-style setups. Paper 1533 is a HANDS 2025 hand-object tracker challenge report, not a bimanual robot policy, so it does not support the claim. Several of the cited papers (RP1M piano, VTDexManip, DexGarmentLab, AgiBot World) are dataset or platform papers whose limitations are generic.

(3) The headline claims are contradicted by current results. The claim of failure "even in noiseless simulation", with handover "near zero", does not hold on the live RoboTwin 2.0 leaderboard (local mirror updated 2026-09-24; board re-fetched 2026-10-02):
- ME-Dex-1.0 scores Handover Mic 98/98 (clean/randomized), Handover Block 97/53, Lift Pot 100/65, Stack Blocks Two 100/89, and 89.6 easy / 68.1 hard on average.
- GigaBrain-0.7 scores 100/100 on Handover Mic.
- PatchWAM leads clean evaluation at 91.6.
- The cited collapse (DP3 55.2 to 5.0) is a 2025 baseline. Co-trained 2026 VLA and world-model policies keep 46 to 68 percent under randomization.

(4) Real dual-arm imitation also contradicts the "cannot reliably" wording. ALOHA/ACT (Zhao et al. 2023) reports 80 to 90 percent on six fine bimanual tasks. ALOHA Unleashed (CoRL 2024) reports 75 percent on shirt hanging, a task that includes an arm-to-arm handover.

(5) Human-to-robot handover from vision is an active line, not an open gap. GenH2R (CVPR 2024) learns handover from point clouds rather than ground-truth state, and MobileH2R extends it. The "baselines assume perfect perception" point is specific to the original 2022 HandoverSim baselines.

What survives:
- Real-world success stays low. The RoboDojo-real leaderboard (2026-09) has a top success rate of 24.4 percent. That board covers multiple embodiments and is not specific to bimanual coordination.
- Many policies still drop sharply from clean to randomized conditions (for example FastWAM 77.8 to 1.9).
- Dynamic dexterous handover under occlusion, which DexH2R targets, is still hard.

These survivors are general robot-learning robustness and sim-to-real problems, not a bimanual-coordination problem the field faces at large. The pain point is also only adjacent to the author's field (perception and tracking).

skeptics.reframe: The part that survives is narrower than P32. Reactive human-to-robot handover, and bimanual policies deployed in the real world, need low-latency 3D state of the partner's hand and the object under occlusion. Benchmarks either supply this as simulator ground truth (HandoverSim) or performance degrades in dynamic, occluded settings (DexH2R hard mode). Real-world success on dual-arm benchmarks is still about 24 percent or lower (RoboDojo-real). In clean simulation, coordinated tasks and handover are largely solved by 2026 co-trained policies, so this is a perception-for-handover gap, not a coordination-policy gap.

skeptics.reasons:
Refutation attempt. Much of P32 does reduce to engineering or resources. The record bundles three different failures. (a) Policies fail even in noiseless simulation with privileged state (PerAct2/RLBench2 handover 0-11 percent, BiGym stack_blocks 0 percent). Part of that comes from benchmark design, sparse demonstrations and the "coordinated demonstrations are scarce and noisy" explanation, and the obvious fix is more and better bimanual data. RoboTwin 2.0, HGen-Bench and LLM-generated simulation data are already pursuing that, which is a scaling effort rather than a question. (b) The RoboTwin 2.0 Easy-to-Hard collapse (DP3 55.2 to 5.0 percent) comes from visual randomization of clutter, lighting, background and table height. It is a robustness or sim-to-real gap, and the known fixes are domain randomization, pretraining and real-data co-training. (c) Handover benchmarks assume perfect perception of the hand and object. Taken alone, each of these is either a well-known open problem in policy learning or a call for more data. In addition, for this author the relevance is only adjacent: the policy-learning core belongs to CoRL/RSS/ICRA, not to tracking and reconstruction. The low success numbers will rise with scale, and a paper that raises RLBench2 handover success from 11 to 30 percent with a new architecture is a crowded, incremental contribution.
Why it is not refuted. Strip away the data and scaling part and at least one question remains that a top-venue reviewer would find significant and that sits at this author's boundary. Every handover and coordination benchmark either hands the policy perfect simulator state of the partner hand and object (HandoverSim, GenH2R, HGen-Bench) or reports a collapse when that state must be perceived (DexH2R hard mode, RGB-only failure under occlusion and depth ambiguity). Question: what 3D hand-object state representation, together with its uncertainty, should a real-time tracker hand to a reactive bimanual or handover policy so that the policy stays robust to the estimator's actual error distribution under mutual occlusion by two arms and a human hand? And can tracking accuracy metrics (MPJPE, ADD-S) be replaced by task-grounded metrics that predict downstream handover success? This is not known and does not merely await resources. Nobody has measured how policy success degrades with realistic tracker error profiles (jitter, latency, occlusion dropouts), as opposed to Gaussian noise. Nor is it established whether policies should consume uncertainty or whether trackers should be trained against a policy-aware loss. That is a CoRL/RSS/ICRA-level question with a CVPR/ICCV angle, as DexH2R at ICCV 2025 and GenH2R at CVPR 2024 show. A second, weaker question concerns representations of coordination itself (relative-pose or contact-graph action spaces between the two arms). It is mainstream policy-learning territory and not this author's strength. The score is held at 6 because the significant question is narrower than the pain point as stated, the field is fast-moving and crowded (RoboTwin challenge, AnyBimanual, VLA papers), and the author's contribution would be the perception-to-policy interface, not the policy failure itself.

skeptics.reframe: Handover and coordinated bimanual policies are trained and scored on perfect simulator state of the partner hand and object, and they collapse when that state must come from a real tracker under mutual occlusion. The open question is what the tracker-to-policy interface should be: which 3D hand-object state, with what calibrated uncertainty and latency budget, and evaluated by which task-grounded metric, so that downstream handover and coordination success can be predicted and preserved under realistic, rather than Gaussian, perception error.

research_questions.question: When a human-to-robot handover policy gets hand and object state from a real RGB-D tracker instead of simulator ground truth, how much success does it lose? Which error properties cause the loss: structured occlusion dropouts, temporally correlated drift, latency or segmentation leakage? Do the standard tracking metrics (MPJPE, ADD-S, BOP MSSD) rank trackers in the same order as closed-loop handover success, and if not, what task-grounded metric does?
research_questions.why_top_venue: Learned human-to-robot handover policies are trained and benchmarked on simulator state or on point clouds segmented with ground-truth labels. HandoverSim baselines use privileged state. GenH2R (CVPR 2024) builds its point clouds from the simulator's one-hot hand and object labels and reports no analysis of perception noise or latency; both points were checked in the arXiv 2401.00929 HTML. Real dynamic handover still collapses: in DexH2R (ICCV 2025) DP falls from 39.4 to 8.3 percent and DP3 from 66.3 to 27.1 percent between Easy and Hard mode, and the authors blame occlusion and the need for robust segmentation. Two arXiv sweeps run in this session (titles containing handover, 2026; human-to-robot handover, 2025-2026) found no paper that measures closed-loop handover success under the real error distribution of current hand and object trackers, or that tests whether tracking metrics predict it. Autonomous driving has a precedent: planner-centric metrics (Philion et al., CVPR 2020, recalled and not re-fetched here) reordered perception models by downstream impact. The hand-object field has no equivalent. The publishable finding is a reordering: if the tracker with the best ADD-S or MPJPE is not the best for handover, or if structured real errors hurt much more than Gaussian noise of the same RMS, every hand-object tracking paper that claims robotics relevance is affected.
research_questions.method_sketch: Build a perceived-state HandoverSim. HandoverSim replays DexYCB hand-object motions, and DexYCB holds the real 30 fps RGB-D frames of the same sequences. (1) Run 3 to 5 off-the-shelf trackers on the real frames of the HandoverSim test sequences. Candidates: FoundationPose with SAM2 masks for the object, HaMeR or WiLoR with depth alignment for the MANO hand, and one joint hand-object estimator. Use the camera closest to the robot viewpoint and log per-frame hand and object poses with timestamps and each tracker's measured compute latency. (2) DexYCB contains no robot, so it lacks the gripper occlusion. Composite a depth-rendered gripper into the real RGB-D frames along the policy's approach path using the z-buffer, and report results with and without it. (3) In simulation, physics runs on ground truth, but the policy observes a point cloud rendered from the hand and object meshes at the tracked poses, delayed by the measured latency. A second variant relabels the ground-truth cloud with the tracker's masks. (4) Controls: ground truth; iid Gaussian noise matched to each tracker's per-frame RMS; the tracker with temporal smoothing; a latency-only shift. (5) Build 8 to 12 tracker variants (backbone, frame rate, filter, mask quality) and compute Kendall tau between each standard metric and closed-loop success. Then fit a small task-grounded metric, for example object error in the grasp region during the final approach window, dropout fraction and latency-weighted error, and validate it on held-out trackers and held-out subjects (HandoverSim s1 split). Fold a latency sweep (0 to 300 ms, 5 to 30 fps) with simple forecasters (constant velocity, Kalman) into the same study.
research_questions.minimum_experiment: Two open policies: handover-sim2real (CVPR 2023; official code and pretrained models confirmed on GitHub) and GenH2R (evaluation scripts and pretrained models released, training code not yet released). Cross them with 4 observation conditions (ground truth, real tracker, RMS-matched Gaussian, real tracker plus measured latency) and 3 trackers on the official HandoverSim s0 test split. Report success, completion time and hand-contact failures. Then run the rank-correlation study over 8 to 12 tracker variants. Kill criterion: if a standard metric already ranks the variants with Kendall tau above about 0.9 against success, and RMS-matched Gaussian noise reproduces the success loss, the result is only a sensitivity note. In that case stop, or move to RQ2 only if the loss itself is large.
research_questions.data_and_hardware: Public data: DexYCB (a large download, roughly 100 GB; size not verified), HandoverSim (PyBullet, CPU-bound, so a many-core workstation matters more than the GPU), the handover-sim2real and GenH2R checkpoints, YCB meshes, and optionally HO-3D v3 as a second source of tracker error. One 24 GB GPU is enough to run the trackers over a few hundred short sequences. The core result needs no robot. A consumer RGB-D camera serves for a small real check of tracker latency and error. A borrowed Franka or UR arm with a parallel gripper, for 30 to 60 real handovers with an external camera, would strengthen a robotics submission.
research_questions.risks: (1) Viewpoint mismatch: DexYCB cameras are third-person, while the released policies were designed around a robot-mounted camera, so reviewers may say the error profiles do not transfer. Mitigation: frame the study as an external-camera setup and include the gripper compositing. (2) The 'of course noise hurts' critique: the paper stands only if metrics mis-rank trackers or structured errors differ clearly from Gaussian noise; otherwise it is incremental. (3) HandoverSim's giver is a non-reactive replay and the gripper is a parallel jaw, so the conclusions say little about reactive or dexterous handover. DexH2R would be the dexterous target, but whether its RGB-D data and code are released and usable was not verified. (4) Scoop risk: the groups that own HandoverSim, handover-sim2real, GenH2R and DexH2R (NVIDIA/ETH, Tsinghua) have robots and could run this quickly. (5) Simulation-only evidence is weak at CoRL, and CVPR or ICCV reviewers may see the paper as robotics; the metric-reordering result has to carry it.

research_questions.question: What interface should a hand-object tracker expose to a reactive handover policy: point estimates, or state with calibrated uncertainty and explicit per-entity validity labels (freshly measured, extrapolated or held, inferred from contact)? Does training the policy against a learned model of the tracker's real error, or fine-tuning the tracker with a policy-aware loss, recover the success lost under mutual occlusion by the object, the human hand and the gripper?
research_questions.why_top_venue: This is the surviving question from the strongest skeptic (rq lens, score 6). Learned perception-noise models from real camera data exist in legged robotics (a learned badminton policy for a legged manipulator, arXiv 2505.22974, found in this session's arXiv listing). Calibrated intervention for perception errors exists for imitation policies (AutoIntervene, arXiv 2608.07065, same listing). In learned human-to-robot handover, however, the policies take point clouds segmented from ground truth. The 2025-2026 arXiv sweeps run here (handover with uncertainty; human-to-robot handover) found no work that feeds tracker uncertainty or validity into a learned handover policy. The scattered precedents are planning-based: an aerial-vehicle risk analysis over human-pose uncertainty (arXiv 2509.10692) and closed-loop grasping with an uncertainty-aware estimate (arXiv 2310.18459). An answer to 'which interface' transfers to any policy that consumes perceived hand-object state: demonstration capture, teleoperation, digital twins. That bridge interests both the vision and the robotics communities.
research_questions.method_sketch: (1) From the RQ1 traces, fit a temporal generative model of each tracker's error, conditioned on visibility fraction, hand-object-gripper distances, hand speed and depth. A candidate is a small autoregressive GRU with a discrete dropout or coasting state. Validate it by checking that closed-loop success under sampled errors matches success under the real traces on held-out sequences. (2) Fine-tune the handover-sim2real point-cloud student under five observation regimes: (a) ground truth; (b) iid Gaussian domain randomization; (c) learned-error randomization; (d) regime c plus a per-entity validity token (measured, held, contact-inferred) and a per-point uncertainty channel; (e) regime d plus a tracker fine-tuned with a policy-aware loss. That loss weights each frame's tracking error by the policy's action sensitivity, estimated by finite differences in simulation or by the RQ1 success predictor. (3) Wrap the uncertainty in split conformal prediction so the policy sees intervals with valid coverage. (4) Evaluate on the perceived-state HandoverSim with a held-out tracker and held-out subjects. Report success, hand-contact failures as a safety measure, and uncertainty calibration. Add an ablation showing that the policy actually uses the uncertainty channel, for example by shuffling it at test time.
research_questions.minimum_experiment: The five-regime comparison on HandoverSim s0 and s1 with one held-out tracker and 3 seeds per regime. Bar for a paper: regime d recovers at least half of the gap between ground truth and perceived state, and beats RMS-matched Gaussian randomization by more than the variance across seeds. Optional real check: 30 to 60 handovers on a borrowed arm with an external consumer RGB-D camera, comparing regime b with regime d.
research_questions.data_and_hardware: The same data as RQ1, plus RL fine-tuning compute. Budget several days of many-core CPU and one GPU per regime and seed; the actual fine-tuning cost of handover-sim2real was not verified. Training and evaluation need no robot. A borrowed arm with a parallel gripper is strongly recommended for CoRL or RSS. The policy-aware tracker fine-tuning needs only the tracker's training code and the simulator.
research_questions.risks: (1) Gaussian randomization may close most of the gap, which makes the interface question moot; this is the kill criterion, and it can be checked early in RQ1. (2) The policy may learn to ignore the uncertainty and validity channels; the shuffle ablation must show they are used. (3) Policy-sensitivity weights estimated by finite differences can be noisy and expensive. (4) Without real-robot results, CoRL or RSS acceptance is unlikely; ICRA or RA-L is the realistic floor. (5) Once RQ1 is public, a well-equipped lab could add realistic perception noise to GenH2R-style training quickly. Submit RQ1 and RQ2 together, or RQ2 soon after.

fit.thesis_assets_help: Small. The measured/held/constrained honesty labels are a working prototype of the validity token in RQ2, so they give a head start on defining and producing per-frame validity flags. The causal 30 fps chain supplies a real, measured latency and jitter profile for the latency condition in RQ1. Object-conditioned recovery of an occluded holding arm targets the same occlusion of the partner's arm and could be one of the trackers evaluated. The ArUco-marked object with metric pose gives a cheap real check of object-tracker error under consumer-sensor noise. The 28 single-subject recordings contain no handover, no robot and no hand ground truth, so they cannot serve as the benchmark. The Unity twin adds nothing, because the established handover stack is PyBullet (HandoverSim, handover-sim2real, GenH2R). The core of both questions runs on DexYCB, HandoverSim and the released policies, not on the thesis data.
fit.what_a_small_lab_cannot_do_here: It cannot compete on the policy side of P32 as originally stated. Arm-to-arm coordination in simulation is close to saturated by large pretrained world-action and VLA models: Motus reports 88.66 percent clean and 87.02 percent randomized on RoboTwin 2.0, and leaderboard entries such as ME-Dex-1.0 and GigaBrain-0.7 are at or near 100 on Handover Mic. Matching them needs multi-node pretraining, which a lab with one GPU cannot do. Nor can it run real dual-arm platforms (ALOHA, AgileX Cobot Magic) at the scale needed for in-distribution and out-of-distribution evaluation, or attack the long-horizon, tightly coupled real-world failures that BiCoord and DuoBench report. Several data efforts are out of reach: a DexH2R-scale real handover dataset (4,282 trials, 39 participants, dexterous hand, multi-camera ground truth), MobileH2R-scale synthetic human motion, and large human-subject handover studies, which need a robot arm and ethics approval. The realistic contribution is on the perception side: measuring and shaping the tracker-to-policy interface in simulation on public data, with at most a small real check on a borrowed arm. Of the three skeptics, the artifact lens refuted P32 as stated (score 3), the solved lens judged it partly refuted (score 4), and the rq lens upheld only this narrowed interface question (score 6). Unverified items: Philion et al. CVPR 2020 was recalled and not re-fetched; the DexYCB download size and the DexH2R data and code release were not checked.

painpoint.name: Wearable and non-visual sensing drifts and does not transfer

evidence.latest_state: As of late 2026 nothing closes the gap; the 2025-2026 gains are partial and specific to one modality. Sparse-IMU capture improves mainly by adding extra signals. These include UWB inter-sensor ranging (UMotion CVPR 2025; Group Inertial Poser ICCV 2025; Ultra Diffusion Poser CVPR 2026, which reports up to 22% lower joint position error than prior work), insole pressure with a physics simulator (GRIP with the new PRISM dataset, arXiv 2026), egocentric cameras plus SLAM on consumer wearables (EveryWear and the Ego-Elec dataset, arXiv 2025), drift-simulating augmentation (MODA CVPR 2025) and label smoothing (AAAI 2026). None of these removes the need for an absolute reference. For wrist sEMG, emg2pose stays the reference benchmark. Hadidi et al. (arXiv 2026) report that a tuned position decoder beats velocity decoding on the Tracking task in all three generalization splits, which reduces integration drift, and they claim the best published streaming result. REACT (arXiv 2026) personalizes from under 45 s of per-user calibration but cuts angular error by only up to 3.9%, so the held-out-user gap remains. EgoEMG (41 users, bilateral EMG plus vision, submitted to NeurIPS 2026) shows EMG-vision fusion beating vision-only baselines. For RF sensing, cross-layout WiFi pose error falls by more than 60% with geometry-conditioned learning (PerceptAlign, MobiCom 2026: 21 subjects, 5 scenes, 7 layouts). RePos (arXiv 2026) cuts MM-Fi cross-environment MPJPE by 10-21%. Wave2Body (arXiv 2026) leads 7 of 8 M4Human cross-domain rows. The absolute errors still sit well above RGB or IMU-suit levels, though I found no exact cross-domain MPJPE numbers in the abstracts. Privacy is still not measured on non-RGB pose benchmarks. The only rigorous privacy benchmark I found is differentially private 2D RGB pose estimation (arXiv 2504.10190, reported as CVPR 2026, venue unverified).
