evidence.crowdedness: HIGH: I found at least 16 papers from 2025-2026 split across three active communities. They are IMU motion capture (Holz/ETH, Xu Feng's line at Tsinghua, Kitani at CMU, all at CVPR, ICCV, SIGGRAPH and AAAI), sEMG hand pose built on Meta's emg2pose (several groups), and RF/WiFi/mmWave pose (MobiCom and arXiv). The narrower sub-gaps are much less crowded: a privacy metric for non-RGB pose, and EMG or IMU fused with RGB-D for hand-object manipulation.
evidence.trend: Rising. Consumer wearables (smartwatch, earbuds, smart glasses, the Meta EMG band) and new multimodal datasets (emg2pose, EgoEMG, PRISM, Ego-Elec, M4Human) bring a steady flow of CVPR/ICCV 2025-2026 and arXiv 2026 papers. The dominant fix is extra sensors or calibration (UWB, pressure, cameras, few-shot personalization), not modality-only transfer. So drift and cross-user or cross-room transfer stay open, which keeps attention high.

skeptics.reasons:
I found no 2025-2026 work that solves this pain point. Some parts have been reduced, and the claim needs narrowing.
(1) sEMG. Meta's generic neuromotor interface (Nature 2025, code released, shipped as a product wristband in 2025) generalizes out of the box to unseen users. That success is for discrete gestures, cursor navigation and handwriting, not continuous hand pose. For continuous joint angles on emg2pose, the 2026 cross-user gains are small: REACT, a FiLM user-conditioning method needing under 45 s of calibration, cuts angular error by at most 3.9%. EMG-JEPA (OpenReview, title only verified) reports about 3.5-5.1% gains in the search snippet. DexEMG (arXiv March 2026) claims generalization without per-user recalibration, but its abstract gives no cross-user numbers. Cross-user continuous pose and drift therefore remain open, while the gesture-level problem is effectively solved by a product.
(2) Wi-Fi. Cross-environment error is still large in 2026. RePos (arXiv 2607.02986) reports 254-296 mm MPJPE on the MM-Fi unseen-environment protocol, against about 87 mm in-domain. WiFi-JEPA reports a leave-one-environment-out mean of 324 mm. This supports the pain point.
(3) Sparse IMU. Drift is being reduced by adding absolute or relative references rather than removed: UWB inter-sensor ranging (UMotion 2505.09393; Ultra Diffusion Poser 2606.02153, title only) and physics priors (2505.05010). This confirms that IMUs alone drift and need an extra reference.
(4) Wrist pressure arrays (arXiv 2609.16518, September 2026) reach 4.6 deg single-user joint error. Across four users, per-finger contact force reaches only R2 = 0.57, rising to 0.75 when external pose is supplied. The authors position the wristband as a complement to vision, not a replacement.
(5) I found no standard privacy metric for non-visual pose estimation. This sub-claim was searched only indirectly, so it is unverified rather than refuted.
Overall the pain point stands, but it bundles too many modalities. The 'cannot replace cameras' framing is close to consensus and is now pursued mainly through fusion. For this author's field (hand-object, RGB-D, occlusion), the sharper open problem is calibration-free cross-user continuous hand pose and contact force from wearables used as a complement to vision under occlusion. Relevance remains adjacent.

skeptics.reframe: Wearables used as a complement to cameras still have no calibration-free route to continuous hand pose or contact force. Gesture decoding with sEMG now transfers across users at product level. Continuous joint angles and per-finger forces do not: cross-user gains are only a few percent, and multi-user force estimation reaches only R2 = 0.57. Without an absolute reference from vision or UWB ranging, these estimates drift. The open problem is fusing wrist sensing with RGB-D so that it fills in hand pose and force during hand-object occlusion, and does so for unseen users without per-user calibration.

skeptics.reasons:
Artifact lens verdict: the bundle is mostly refuted, though a narrow part survives. The 17 supporting papers do come from different groups. They include Meta's emg2pose (NeurIPS 2024 D&B, 193 users), the mRI dataset (An, Li and Ogras, NeurIPS 2022, 20 subjects), OctoNet, HelmetPoser, the SLP in-bed dataset and Nymeria, so this is not one lab's quirk. The pain point, however, is an aggregation artifact: it joins seven modalities whose failure causes are unrelated (multipath for Wi-Fi, heat residue for thermal, the derivative relation for sEMG, integration for IMUs, contact-only sensing for pressure) under one heading.

(1) Treated as known or solved elsewhere: IMU drift has been understood physics in inertial navigation for decades. Commercial IMU suits handle it with magnetometers and biomechanical constraints. The sparse-IMU line treats drift and global translation as engineering targets with established remedies, such as foot-contact cues and physics-aware optimisation: TransPose (SIGGRAPH 2021) and PIP (CVPR 2022, Yi, Theobalt, Xu et al.). Camera-IMU fusion is standard practice. "Inertial drifts" is therefore not a new field-level finding.

(2) The non-transfer is not specific to these modalities. In the record's own OctoNet numbers, RGB degrades to 473.9 mm cross-scene, which is worse than Wi-Fi at 399.4 mm. That points to small lab rigs with few subjects, rooms and devices, not to non-visual sensing as such. emg2pose itself argues that sEMG generalisation needs, and improves with, hundreds of users and placements, which makes this a data-scale problem.

(3) The headline numbers are single-dataset values from small rigs: mRI has 20 subjects, rehabilitation exercises only and one radar setup. Its mmWave versus IMU MPJPE gap (163.3 mm versus 80.2 mm) is a property of that dataset, not a field constant.

(4) "Cannot yet replace cameras" argues against a claim few authors make. Most of these sensors are presented for privacy, darkness or occlusion niches, as complements to cameras rather than replacements.

(5) The privacy claim rests on one position paper (id 477).

(6) For the author's field (RGB-D hand-object and bimanual tracking), the topic is adjacent. The question that matters there is wearables as a complement to cameras under occlusion, and the record lists that only as "proposed".

What survives is a narrower point. Paired 3D ground truth for non-visual hand and body sensing exists only in small, single-site lab rigs. As a result, cross-user, cross-device and cross-room generalisation cannot be measured reliably, and no benchmark measures a wrist-worn sensor fused with a camera for hand-object manipulation under occlusion. Search budget note: WebSearch was exhausted (shared budget), so verification used WebFetch of arXiv abstract pages only. OctoNet, HelmetPoser and the privacy position paper were not independently verified.

skeptics.reasons:
Refutation attempt. As stated, P33 is a grab-bag across Wi-Fi, mmWave, thermal, IR arrays, acoustic, pressure mats, event cameras, sEMG and IMUs. Several of its parts have no research question that a top venue would take. (a) "Accuracy stays below RGB or IMU suits" is a performance-gap observation, not a question. (b) "Paired ground truth exists only in lab rigs with few subjects" is the cost of collecting data and calls for annotation money. (c) Electrodes detaching with sweat and pressure maps that cannot see limbs out of contact are physical limits of the hardware, not open learning problems. (d) "No privacy score" is a benchmark-definition wish. A single metric proposal would at best make a workshop or datasets-track paper, and it is far from the author's field. The modalities that dominate the evidence (Wi-Fi, mmWave, IR, in-bed thermal and pressure) are also marked adjacent. They do not touch hand-object or bimanual RGB-D tracking, so for this author most of the pain point is out of scope.

Why the refutation fails. One part survives and is a real research question rather than a resource gap. The question is how to learn the mapping from indirect, derivative-like signals (wrist sEMG, wrist and object IMUs) to articulated hand and object pose so that it does not drift and transfers to new users and new sensor units. The evidence shows the failure is in modelling, not in data volume. emg2pose (NeurIPS 2024 D&B, verified) reports cross-user degradation and 15.2 mm tracking error even with a ground-truth initial pose, because sEMG relates to pose derivatives. HelmetPoser (arXiv 2409.05006, verified, venue not stated) shows that the learned bias correction drops from about 91 percent to about 56 percent on a different IMU unit. More of the same rig's data does not obviously fix either problem.

The version a reviewer would find significant, inside the author's field, is complementary fusion under occlusion. During bimanual manipulation the camera loses the hands and objects during occlusion. The questions are whether wrist IMU or sEMG can carry the estimate through those gaps, and whether intermittent visual re-observations can recalibrate the wearable model online (test-time, self-supervised), so the system needs neither per-user calibration nor lab ground truth. The precedents show top venues accept this line. Physical Inertial Poser is CVPR 2022 and EgoLocate is SIGGRAPH 2023 (both verified): they constrain IMU drift with physics or with vision and SLAM. HOI-M3 (CVPR 2024, verified) uses object-mounted IMUs. DexEMG (arXiv 2603.05861, 2026, verified, no venue) uses emg2pose generalization for dexterous teleoperation, which ties the line to the robot-demonstration application. mmEgoHand (arXiv 2501.13805, under review, verified) fuses head-mounted mmWave with an IMU for egocentric hands.

Weaknesses that keep the score middling:
- Body-level IMU and vision fusion is already crowded (PIP, EgoLocate and their successors).
- The hand-level and object-level version needs custom hardware. That is costly for a small lab and drifts toward the "build a rig" kind of contribution.
- A careful reviewer could call cross-device and cross-user transfer standard domain adaptation unless the method exploits the structure of the signal: derivatives, contact events and visual anchors.
- I found no direct prior work on sEMG plus RGB-D for hand-object tracking under occlusion, but I could not run searches (the budget was exhausted), so the novelty claim is unverified.

skeptics.reframe: Wrist sEMG and wrist or object IMUs measure pose only through derivatives. Learned mappings from these signals to hand and object pose therefore drift, and they lose most of their accuracy on a new user or a new sensor unit. Meanwhile an RGB-D camera loses the hands and the object exactly during bimanual occlusion. The research question is whether intermittent visual observations can recalibrate a wearable pose model online, self-supervised and with no per-user calibration, so that the fused tracker bridges occlusion gaps without drift and transfers across users and devices. Success would be measured by error during occlusion and by cross-user and cross-device error, against camera-only and wearable-only baselines.

research_questions.question: Can intermittent, noisy 3D hand observations from an RGB-D (or egocentric) camera serve as the only supervision for adapting a cross-user wrist sEMG (plus wrist IMU) hand-pose decoder online? The goal is a fused tracker that needs no calibration session for an unseen user and keeps finger joint-angle error bounded through vision dropouts of 0.5-5 s.
research_questions.why_top_venue: Continuous cross-user sEMG hand pose is the part of P33 that no product has solved. emg2pose (NeurIPS 2024 D&B) reports 21.6 mm / 15.8 deg for held-out users, and 15.2 mm tracking error even when started from the ground-truth pose. REACT (arXiv 2605.30127) needs a supervised calibration of under 45 s and gains at most 3.9%. EgoEMG (arXiv 2605.05712, verified: 41 users, bilateral 16-channel EMG, 120 Hz IMU, egocentric RGB, external RGB-D, mocap ground truth, no objects mentioned) benchmarks only a static residual EMG-vision fusion. Three bounded arXiv listing searches (sEMG hand pose adaptation; electromyography vision fusion hand pose; inertial test-time adaptation pose) found no work that uses the camera as online, label-free supervision for the wearable. That absence is unverified, because the WebSearch budget was exhausted. A result showing zero-calibration adaptation that matches or beats supervised calibration, plus a drift-bounded bridge through occlusion, would be a new problem setting: test-time adaptation with intermittent, noisy, structured supervision. That fits CVPR and NeurIPS and the consumer EMG-band trend. It clears the bar only if the gains are clearly larger than REACT's few percent and the method uses the signal's structure (position versus velocity decoding, re-anchoring when vision returns) rather than generic test-time adaptation.
research_questions.method_sketch: (1) Base decoder: an emg2pose-style position decoder, following Hadidi et al. (arXiv 2603.08212), who found that position decoding beats velocity decoding on Tracking. Pretrain it on emg2pose with a small per-user or per-session parameter set (a FiLM user embedding as in REACT, or low-rank adapters); only this set is updated online. (2) Visual teacher: a frozen off-the-shelf 3D hand estimator (e.g., HaMeR or WiLoR) on the external RGB-D view. Lift its output with depth and fit it by IK to the same hand kinematic model to get joint-angle pseudo-labels. Give each label a confidence from keypoint scores, depth consistency and temporal smoothness. (3) Online loop: on high-confidence frames, update the user parameters with a robust (Huber) loss against an EMA-teacher-smoothed target, and replay pretraining data so the model does not collapse. When vision drops out or has low confidence, the EMG decoder runs alone. A per-joint error-growth model, fit on validation users as a function of time since the last visual anchor, gives a calibrated uncertainty. (4) Fusion: a per-joint Kalman filter or sliding-window smoother combines the vision and EMG estimates with these uncertainties and re-anchors when vision returns. Ablations: which parameters to adapt, confidence gating, pseudo-label noise level, position versus velocity heads, and with or without the wrist IMU.
research_questions.minimum_experiment: Main experiment on the EgoEMG cross-user and combined splits, if the data is released. Vision pseudo-labels come from its external RGB-D and egocentric streams; mocap is used only for scoring. Inject vision dropouts of 0.5, 1, 2 and 5 s covering 10-50% of frames. Compare: (a) generic EMG-only; (b) REACT-style supervised calibration with 45 s of ground truth; (c) EgoEMG residual fusion; (d) vision-only with hold or constant-velocity fill; (e) ours. Report joint-angle error inside gaps against gap length, the adaptation curve against seconds of visible hand, and the final held-out-user error. Scale check on emg2pose held-out users with simulated pseudo-labels: mocap plus a noise and dropout model fitted to real vision error on EgoEMG. Success bar: zero-calibration error at or below (b), and in-gap error below (d) for gaps of at least 2 s.
research_questions.data_and_hardware: Public data only: emg2pose (193 users; download size not checked, likely hundreds of GB) and EgoEMG (41 users, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 per its arXiv page; public release not confirmed). One workstation GPU (24-48 GB) is enough, because EMG decoders are small and the vision teacher runs once offline. The paper needs no new hardware. A live demo would need a research sEMG band (an open multi-channel board or a commercial armband); whether Meta's consumer neural band exposes raw sEMG is unverified. The demo is optional.
research_questions.risks: EgoEMG may not be released in time, or its non-commercial license may restrict use. It has no objects, so hand-object occlusion is simulated by dropout rather than recorded. Vision pseudo-labels are worst exactly when the hand is partly occluded, which invites confirmation bias. The gains may be as small as REACT's 3.9%. Meta Reality Labs and the emg2pose and EgoEMG groups have the data and hardware to do this first. Reviewers may call it standard test-time adaptation unless drift and re-anchoring are central to the method. Without an sEMG device there is no real-world demonstration, which weakens a vision-venue submission.

research_questions.question: Can one commodity IMU, stuck at an unknown place on an everyday object and self-calibrated online from intermittent single-view RGB-D observations of the object, keep the object's 6-DoF pose and the holding hand's pose measured through bimanual occlusion? The setting allows no per-object, per-user or IMU-mounting calibration. The second question is for how long this bridge stays more accurate than holding the last vision estimate.
research_questions.why_top_venue: Single-view hand-object trackers lose the object and the holding hand exactly during bimanual occlusion, which is a central failure in this field's own pain-point list. Prior wearable fixes need heavier instrumentation or lab ground truth. I'M HOI (CVPR 2024, verified) fuses an object-mounted IMU with monocular RGB for whole-body human-object capture and refines offline with a category-aware diffusion model. AVI-HT (arXiv 2605.21714, May 2026, verified, no venue) needs an IMU glove and trains on more than 100k mocap-labelled samples; it reports 16.1-24.2% lower keypoint error under heavy occlusion. KIWI (arXiv 2609.22809, Sept 2026, verified) uses offline IMU fusion to cut 360-camera tracking failures from 24.8% to 0.1%, but it tracks the wrist-mounted camera rig, not the object. VR controllers solve the problem only for purpose-built LED constellations (general knowledge, not checked here). A causal, calibration-free sticker IMU plus RGB-D, with an honest per-frame error bound, would be an enabling tool for robot demonstration capture and digital twins. At CoRL, ICRA or RSS it is a contribution if it shows downstream value for demonstration capture. At CVPR it would also need the learned inertial component and a public benchmark with real occlusion.
research_questions.method_sketch: (1) A sliding-window factor graph (GTSAM-style) per object. It combines IMU preintegration factors with visual object-pose factors from a model-based RGB-D tracker (e.g., FoundationPose, or fiducials where present); a visual factor is added only when the tracker is confident. The states include the IMU-to-object rotation and lever arm, gyroscope and accelerometer biases, gravity in the camera frame, and the camera-IMU time offset. All are estimated online from the first seconds of visible motion, with an observability check based on how much the object has moved. (2) Controlling translation drift is the hard part, and three constraints do it. Grasp persistence: the last visible hand-in-object transform is carried with the object until an IMU jerk or a visual cue signals a regrasp. Arm kinematic limits: forearm and upper-arm lengths, with the shoulder taken from body tracking. Zero-velocity events: the object resting, detected from IMU stillness. (3) Optional learned inertial-odometry head in the spirit of TLIO-style learned IMU displacement. Train it on synthetic IMU generated from object trajectories in public hand-object datasets (ARCTIC, HOT3D, DexYCB, OakInk2), plus a small amount of real data with visual pseudo-ground truth. (4) Per-frame labels and covariances: visually measured, inertially measured, constrained, held. Report the gap length at which inertial bridging stops beating hold. Ablation: a wrist-worn smartwatch-class IMU instead of, or in addition to, the object IMU, for the holding arm.
research_questions.minimum_experiment: Two parts. (A) Controlled scale: synthesize IMU streams with realistic noise and bias random walk from object trajectories in ARCTIC and HOT3D. Drop the visual track for gaps of 0.25-5 s and plot object rotation and translation error and holding-hand MPJPE against gap length. Compare vision-only hold, constant-velocity extrapolation, IMU-only, offline-calibrated fusion (an upper bound) and ours. (B) Real check: 8-12 participants, 6-8 objects, and bimanual handover, pour and reorientation tasks. Use one primary RGB-D camera plus one or two auxiliary consumer RGB-D views, which serve only to build reference poses where the primary view is occluded. Metrics: ADD-S and rotation and translation error inside occlusion gaps; holding-hand MPJPE in gaps; calibration convergence time; uncertainty coverage; and error across two different commodity IMU chips, to test the cross-unit drop HelmetPoser reports (about 90% to about 55% drift-correction retention). Optional: replay the captured trajectories on a borrowed robot arm to show they are usable as demonstrations.
research_questions.data_and_hardware: The hardware is cheap: the existing RGB-D camera, one or two extra consumer RGB-D cameras for reference views, 6-10 commodity 9-axis IMU boards or wearable IMU units with wireless streaming (prices not checked), and timestamp sync with online time-offset estimation. One GPU. Public data: object trajectories from ARCTIC, HOT3D, DexYCB and OakInk2 for synthetic IMU. No mocap is needed. A borrowed robot arm is optional.
research_questions.risks: Novelty pressure: reviewers may see this as visual-inertial odometry or VR-controller tracking applied to objects, and I'M HOI already fused object IMUs with RGB. Accelerometer translation drift grows fast, so the bridge may beat hold only for gaps under about 1-2 s unless the grasp and arm constraints carry most of the load; this must be measured, not assumed. Reference poses from auxiliary views are weaker than mocap and can themselves be occluded. An IMU on the object breaks the bare-object ideal that vision venues favour. Synthetic IMU from mocap trajectories has a sim-to-real gap. VIPose (IROS 2021) did visual-inertial 6D object tracking; whether its IMU was on the object was not verified. A realistic first venue is ICRA or RA-L; CVPR is a stretch.

fit.thesis_assets_help: Small but real for RQ2, none for RQ1 beyond familiarity with the pipeline. The ArUco-marked object with metric pose is a ready IMU carrier and gives both a free visual anchor and a reference: frames with the marker visible give ground truth for synthetic-gap evaluation without mocap. The object-conditioned recovery of the occluded holding arm is the grasp-persistence and arm-constraint prior that RQ2 needs to keep accelerometer translation drift in check. The measured/held/constrained honesty labels extend naturally with an 'inertially measured' class and give the per-label error reporting reviewers will ask for. The causal 30 fps chain supports a real-time claim, and the RGB-D desk setup matches EgoEMG's external RGB-D stream. The Unity twin helps only for demonstrations. The 28 single-subject recordings carry no IMU or EMG and cannot support cross-user or cross-device claims, so new multi-subject recordings with IMUs are required.
fit.what_a_small_lab_cannot_do_here: A small lab cannot collect paired wearable data with mocap ground truth at the scale the competing work uses: emg2pose has 193 users, EgoEMG 41 users with mocap, and AVI-HT more than 100k mocap-labelled samples from an IMU glove. Nor can it cover many rooms and sensor units. It cannot build or obtain research-grade sEMG hardware comparable to Meta's; whether the consumer neural band exposes raw sEMG is unverified. Wi-Fi, mmWave, thermal and multi-room transfer studies need many environments and subjects and lie outside this field anyway. Finger-level ground truth under real occlusion is out of reach without mocap or a dense multi-view rig. It also cannot outrun Meta Reality Labs, the ShanghaiTech group (Lan Xu, I'M HOI) or the ETH, Tsinghua and CMU IMU groups on body-level IMU-vision fusion, which is already crowded (PIP, EgoLocate, UMotion, Ultra Diffusion Poser). The privacy-metric sub-gap is a workshop or datasets-track item at best, and it is outside this field. A small lab can compete only where the contribution is a problem setting and a method: online self-calibration of wearables from visual anchors, or calibration-free object IMUs fused with RGB-D. It should be evaluated on public data or synthetic IMU, plus a modest real check with consumer cameras and commodity IMUs. Searches note: the shared WebSearch budget was exhausted, so the newer evidence (AVI-HT, KIWI, Wrist2Finger UIST 2025, I'M HOI CVPR 2024, EgoEMG details) comes from arXiv listing and abstract pages fetched directly. The absence of prior work on online visual-anchor recalibration is unverified.

painpoint.name: Parametric body templates break on bodies that deviate from them

evidence.latest_state: The best 2025-2026 work is a few dataset papers and topology-aware fixes, each built for one population. No body model handles residual limbs, prostheses, mobility aids and loose clothing together. ResiHMR (CVPR 2026 Highlight) adds topology-adaptive optimisation and explicit residual-limb termination geometry. On a curated set of real limb-loss images it cuts residual-limb 2D MPJPE from 73.61 to 23.19 with an HSMR backbone, and intact-joint 2D MPJPE from 41.32 to 37.40 with SMPLify-X. RSP3D (ECCV 2026, arXiv 2609.18406) is the first 3D mocap dataset of running-specific prosthesis users. It confirms zero-shot that model-based estimators cannot represent prosthesis geometry and that model-free methods fail under occlusion. Its hybrid baseline still reaches only about F@50 19.92 and Chamfer 288.44 on the prosthesis, with model-free MPJPE of 159.64-174.84 mm, according to the pain-point record. The 2D side is equally preliminary. ProPose (arXiv 2608.13047, Aug 2026) gains only 2-6% on long-tail prosthetic-joint classification, and ProGait (ICCV 2025) reports gait top-1 0.384 and Grounded SAM2 mIoU 0.358. AJAHR (arXiv 2509.19939, 2025) adds an amputation classifier and a synthetic amputee dataset to mesh recovery. On the template side, Anny (ECCV 2026) is a scan-free body model covering infants to the elderly, and Anny-Fit (CVPR 2026 Findings) reports large all-age shape gains. Both still assume a complete-limb topology. Loose-clothing avatars increasingly drop SMPL and linear blend skinning in favour of virtual bones, Gaussians or skeleton-free diffusion (RealityAvatar 2025, UNICA 2026, Latent Dynamics 2026). These are mostly unreviewed arXiv papers, evaluated on a few subjects in multi-view studio capture. None jointly recovers a body and an attached rigid device. I found no 2025-2026 work on hand-object or bimanual capture with prosthetic hands or atypical hands.

evidence.crowdedness: LOW: about five 2025-2026 papers address atypical limbs or prostheses, nearly all from three small groups: Xin Yu's team at the University of Queensland (ResiHMR, ProPose), Yusuke Sugano's team at the University of Tokyo (RSP3D) and Wei Gao's team at the University of Pittsburgh (ProGait), plus AJAHR. The loose-clothing avatar sub-problem is busier (MEDIUM), but it sits mainly in graphics groups and does not touch the joint recovery of a body and an attached device.
evidence.trend: rising: dedicated limb-loss and prosthesis benchmarks and methods appeared at top venues in 2025-2026 (ProGait ICCV 2025, ResiHMR CVPR 2026 Highlight, RSP3D ECCV 2026). New open body models also widen the template (Anny ECCV 2026, SOMA). The base is small, however, and the topic stays adjacent to hand-object and bimanual tracking.

skeptics.reasons: The pain point as stated is too broad to stand, but its core is not solved. Three of its parts have been substantially reduced by 2025-2026 work. (1) Loose clothing in avatars: several template-free or latent-dynamics methods claim to model loose garments without SMPL canonicalization limits (FreeCloth 2411.19942, PocoLoco 2411.04249, RealityAvatar 2504.01559, UNICA 2604.02799, Latent Dynamics for Full Body Avatar Animation 2605.21478). Most are person-specific or multi-view, so this is an engineering and data question rather than an open field-level problem. (2) Demographic and shape range: Anny (2511.03589), a scan-free model released under Apache 2.0 that covers infants to elders, and Anny-Fit (2605.04728), which adapts adult HMR pipelines zero-shot to all ages, cover the "children absent" part of the claim. Meta's MHR in SAM 3D Body (2602.15989) decouples skeleton from surface shape. (3) Limb loss: there is now a specific line of work. AJAHR (2509.19939) adds amputation classification and a synthetic Amputee 3D set, and ResiHMR (2604.28025) uses topology-adaptive residual-limb mesh recovery and cuts residual-limb 2D MPJPE from 73.61 to 23.19. Two parts remain open. First, joint recovery of a body together with an attached rigid device. RSP3D (2609.18406, September 2026, already in the evidence) says model-based estimators, including SAM 3D Body, hallucinate the amputated side, and that a hybrid of model-based and model-free recovery is only a baseline. Second, fidelity on bodies with atypical morphology. A 2026 analysis (2601.06035) finds SAM 3D Body regresses to the mean on muscle atrophy, scoliosis and pregnancy because MHR is low-dimensional. Cross-site clinical generalization (Care-PD) is a data-scarcity problem that none of these works addresses. Evidence limits: the WebSearch budget was exhausted, so I checked the arXiv export API (titles and abstracts only). I did not read full papers or check venue acceptance, and I found no product or saturated benchmark. For the author's hand-object, RGB-D, bimanual field, relevance stays adjacent.

skeptics.reframe: Narrow the pain point to this: template-based human reconstruction cannot jointly recover a body and a rigid device permanently attached to it (prosthesis, orthosis, cane, held tool) when the body's kinematic topology changes. Model-based methods hallucinate the template's missing limb, and model-free methods lose kinematic priors under occlusion (RSP3D 2026, ResiHMR 2026). Low-dimensional shape spaces also regress atypical morphology to the mean (2601.06035). Loose clothing and all-age shape coverage should be dropped from the claim because they are now largely engineering (template-free avatars, Anny/Anny-Fit). For a hand-object author, the transferable angle is a coupled body-plus-rigid-attachment model with an articulated, topology-adaptive template. It would be evaluated with RGB-D on prosthesis and tool-use captures, where no saturated benchmark exists.

skeptics.reasons: Artifact lens verdict: as stated, P34 is mostly an artifact of how the records were merged and counted. A narrower core does survive. (1) The headcount is inflated. Ids 438 and 1430 are the same paper (Codec Avatar Studio, with the Ava-256 and Goliath datasets). BEDLAM and BEDLAM2.0 (ids 1239 and 1240) come from one MPI group. MVHumanNet and MVHumanNet++ (ids 1434 and 1435) come from one group. So the 14 ids reduce to about 10 distinct papers. (2) The statement joins two unrelated problems from two source clusters (G2 atypical bodies and G5 tight-fit priors). (a) Loose clothing breaking SMPL or SMPL-X. Here the evidence is caveats that capture-dataset papers (Codec Avatar Studio, MVHumanNet x2, MVP-Human) and one avatar survey wrote about their own fitting pipelines. The avatar and graphics community has treated this as a known, actively addressed problem since about 2020: clothed-body offsets (CAPE), implicit clothed reconstruction (ICON, ECON), and template-free NeRF and 3DGS humans. It is not a new field-level pain, and it is a convention of the SMPL-fitting community, not a hard barrier. (b) Clinical cross-site collapse. Care-PD's 0.2 to 0.4 F1 drop and the cane joints in Text to Blind Motion are generic domain shift and data scarcity. They do not show that the body template is the cause. (3) The part that survives is the limb-deficiency and prosthesis evidence. It comes from at least four apparently independent groups in different settings: LDPose (ICCV 2025, 2D in the wild), ProGait (ICCV 2025, Pittsburgh, transfemoral gait video; verified on arXiv 2507.10223), InclusiveVidPose (ICLR 2026, video), and RSP3D (ECCV 2026, Wen, Sugano et al., UTokyo; verified on arXiv 2609.18406). TopoCap adds arbitrary-skeleton motion capture. So this is not a one-dataset artifact. It is a recent (2025-2026), small, inclusivity-driven niche whose benchmarks were built by the same papers that report the failure, and the measured failures are mostly 2D keypoint hallucination, not 3D body-object tracking. (4) Other communities partly handle it. Biomechanics builds subject-specific skeletal models that include prostheses (for example OpenSim). Graphics has topology-agnostic rigging and motion priors. What is missing is the monocular learned-estimation version, not the concept. (5) Relevance to the author's field (hand-object, bimanual, RGB-D) is weak. No supporting paper involves hands, MANO or object manipulation. The only body-object link is RSP3D's attached rigid prosthesis, a single paper. Unverified in this task: the author lists of LDPose and InclusiveVidPose (the CVF page returned 403 and the OpenReview search returned nothing), so overlap between those two groups cannot be ruled out. The web search budget was exhausted.

skeptics.reframe: Pose and mesh estimators that are learned for monocular or video input assume a fixed, complete-limb skeleton. When a residual limb or an attached rigid device (a prosthesis or cane) is present, they hallucinate the missing limb. They cannot jointly recover the body and the attached device as one articulated system with its own topology. The evidence is four independent 2025-2026 datasets (LDPose, ProGait, InclusiveVidPose, RSP3D). Loose clothing and cross-site clinical shift are separate, older or generic problems and should be dropped from this pain point.

skeptics.reasons:
The skeptic case is strong for most of P34. (1) The clinical half (Care-PD cross-site F1 drop of 0.2-0.4, scarce severe cases, cane and arm joints in BlindWays) is ordinary domain shift plus data scarcity. The record's own "why it persists" line says the data on atypical bodies are too small to learn new priors, which is a call for more data. (2) The loose-clothing half is not open in the sense the pain point implies. It has been worked on steadily since 2021: SHARP, TemporalUV (CVPR 2022), DLCA-Recon, PocoLoco (WACV 2025) and RealityAvatar (2025), all checked on arXiv. A loose-clothing paper now needs a new idea; the gap alone is not enough, so this part does not count as a fresh pain point. (3) The 2D keypoint findings mostly argue for new keypoint schemas and fine-tuning sets (LDPose, InclusiveVidPose), which is benchmark and annotation work. That work belongs in a datasets track, not a methods track.

One part survives as a research question. It is the structural mismatch between a fixed-topology, able-bodied template and a body whose topology changes, with a rigid or articulated device attached. RSP3D (arXiv 2609.18406, September 2026) shows that model-based estimators hallucinate the missing limb and that model-free recovery fails under occlusion (prosthesis Chamfer 288, F@50 about 20, MPJPE 160-175 mm). It also states that jointly recovering body joints and an attached rigid object is open. A known fix cannot solve this by adding resources, because collecting more amputee scans cannot cover every combination of amputation level, socket and device. A method has to handle missing segments and attachments the template does not contain. The question is how to recover such a body from monocular or RGB-D input with a template-derived kinematic prior. Concretely: model the residual limb plus device as a rigid or articulated object attached to the body at an unknown socket, keep the prior for the intact body, and infer the topology from few or no examples.

This can be framed as a generalisation of human-object reconstruction in which the object is permanently attached. In that framing CVPR, ICCV or ECCV reviewers would find it significant. A second, weaker question is how to adapt a body prior to a structural change without the accuracy trade-off reported for limb-deficiency-aware losses on COCO. LDPose reports an AP of 82.6 alongside physically impossible predictions.

Caveats. The relevant community is small, so reviewers may treat it as niche or fairness-motivated work. The likely first venue is a NeurIPS Datasets and Benchmarks or CVPR dataset paper rather than a method paper. Relevance to the author's field is adjacent unless the work is pointed at upper-limb prosthesis users manipulating objects. That variant connects directly to hand-object and bimanual tracking.

Score rationale: one significant, non-resource-bound question survives. The rest of the pain point is data collection or already-active work.

Search budget note: the shared WebSearch budget was already used up, so I checked papers through the arXiv API with WebFetch. LDPose, InclusiveVidPose and Care-PD are taken from the input record and I did not check them myself.

skeptics.reframe: Template-based human reconstruction assumes a fixed-topology, able-bodied kinematic tree. It cannot recover a body with missing segments and a permanently attached rigid or articulated device, such as a prosthesis, a cane or an assistive grip. The gap is not a lack of data, since no dataset can cover every amputation level and device combination. The open question is how to reconstruct such a body from monocular or RGB-D input. The proposed approach treats the device as an attached object at an unknown socket, keeps the template prior for the intact body, and infers the topology from few or no examples. The author's most relevant instance is upper-limb prosthesis users handling objects with both hands.

research_questions.question: Can a single RGB-D stream recover three things together while an upper-limb prosthesis user manipulates objects with both hands: the residual arm, the terminal device (hook or prosthetic hand), and the manipulated object? The proposed model is an intact-body template truncated at an inferred level, plus an articulated rigid device attached through an unknown socket transform that stays constant over the sequence. Does this beat (a) template estimators that hallucinate a hand, (b) model-free tracking of the device as a free object, and (c) an RSP3D-style hybrid baseline?
research_questions.why_top_venue: Three top venues have accepted work in this niche: ProGait (ICCV 2025), ResiHMR (CVPR 2026 Highlight, per its arXiv comment) and RSP3D (ECCV 2026, per its arXiv comment). RSP3D (arXiv 2609.18406) names joint recovery of body joints and an attached rigid prosthesis as open, and its hybrid baseline is weak: prosthesis F@50 is about 20 and model-free MPJPE is 160-175 mm. All three cover lower limbs or the full body from RGB or mocap. ResiHMR and AJAHR model the residual limb but not the device. My arXiv API queries on 2026-10-02 (prosthetic or amputee combined with hand, grasp, pose or markerless) returned no work on third-person 3D reconstruction of upper-limb prosthesis users or of prosthetic hands interacting with objects. Every vision-plus-prosthesis hit was eye-in-hand prosthesis control (for example 2503.00466, 2508.00491, 2608.31021). The framing generalises hand-object reconstruction to an object that is permanently attached at an unknown pose and whose host topology has changed. A main-track reviewer can treat this as a method contribution rather than only an inclusivity dataset.
research_questions.method_sketch: State per frame: SMPL-X or Anny arm chain truncated at a discrete level L in {partial hand, wrist, transradial, transhumeral}; the residual limb surface uses convex termination geometry as in ResiHMR. The device is a rigid body with 0-2 DoF (hook aperture, wrist rotator). Its geometry comes from CAD when available; otherwise it is reconstructed online from the RGB-D sequence with a neural SDF in the style of BundleSDF. The object 6DoF pose is tracked with FoundationPose. The key constraint: device pose = residual-segment pose composed with T_socket, where T_socket is one latent per sequence, estimated robustly over a sliding window and then frozen. The energy has these terms: depth and silhouette terms; a free-space carving term that penalises template or device volume where depth shows empty space (this suppresses a hallucinated hand); device-object contact and penetration terms; and intact-side hand-object terms from an existing bimanual tracker. L is chosen per sequence by comparing fit cost plus a complexity penalty across candidate levels (BIC or MDL style). Two variants: a causal sliding window for live use and a full-sequence offline refinement. No large learned prior is needed, because the intact body keeps the template prior and the device is either CAD or reconstructed.
research_questions.minimum_experiment: (1) Synthetic benchmark of about 100 sequences: retarget DexYCB, ARCTIC and GRAB grasps; on one side truncate the template at 3 levels and attach one of 3-4 open-source terminal-device CAD models (body-powered split hook, e-NABLE-style 3D-printed hand, a generic myoelectric hand); render RGB-D with a RealSense or Kinect depth-noise model. (2) Real able-bodied set: 6-8 participants wearing a 3D-printed bypass prosthesis simulator, a forearm brace with the device mounted distal to the hand. My understanding, not verified in this task, is that bypass simulators are standard in prosthetics research. Each participant performs 8 standardised bimanual tasks of the SHAP or AM-ULA type (open a jar, pour, carry a tray, cut, fold a towel), giving about 50 sequences of 30-60 s. (3) If a clinical partner is available, a test-only set of 3-5 real upper-limb prosthesis users. Metrics: device ADD-S and socket-transform error; elbow and shoulder error; object ADD-S; device-object contact F1; truncation-level accuracy; hallucinated-hand rate (fraction of frames in which predicted hand or limb volume falls in observed free space). Baselines: HaMeR or WiLoR plus FoundationPose; SAM 3D Body; AJAHR and ResiHMR if code is released (otherwise reimplement the core term); MoCapAnything V2 (arXiv 2604.28130) with the true skeleton given as an oracle; an RSP3D-style hybrid; BundleSDF on the device alone. Ablations: remove the constant-socket constraint, the free-space term, and L selection.
research_questions.data_and_hardware: One consumer RGB-D camera as the test input. Two or three extra cheap calibrated RGB or RGB-D cameras, used only to triangulate ground truth for elbow, shoulder and intact-hand keypoints. ArUco boards on the device, the socket and each object give metric 6DoF ground truth without mocap. A 3D printer and about USD 200-500 of parts for the bypass simulator and devices. One 24 GB GPU is enough: the method is optimisation-based and the only learned parts are off-the-shelf estimators. Public data: DexYCB, ARCTIC, GRAB, HO3D, SMPL-X, MANO, Anny (Apache licence, which makes topology edits easier), open terminal-device CAD. Human-subjects ethics approval is required. Real users need a prosthetics-clinic partner.
research_questions.risks: The gating risk is access to the population. Upper-limb loss is far rarer than lower-limb loss. Without a clinical partner the real evidence rests on able-bodied bypass simulators, and expert reviewers (the UQ, UTokyo and Pittsburgh groups) may discount them. Simulator validity is also limited: the full forearm plus the device makes an effective limb longer than a true transradial residual limb, so ground truth for the truncation level is ambiguous. Scooping: Sugano's RSP3D group states that joint body-plus-prosthesis recovery is its open next step, and Xin Yu's group (ResiHMR, ProPose) is moving toward body-device interaction. Both are lower-limb or full-body today, which leaves upper-limb manipulation as the defensible niche. ResiHMR, AJAHR and RSP3D code or data may be unreleased, so baselines would need reimplementation. Device geometry is highly varied, so CAD-free device reconstruction under heavy occlusion may fail. Some reviewers will see the work as niche or fairness-motivated. The counter-evidence also narrows scope: arXiv 2606.17427 found no significant HaMeR or WiLoR accuracy difference for cervical spinal-cord-injury hands (13 vs 15 participants). Impaired motion with intact topology is therefore not the problem; only topology change plus an attached device is.

research_questions.question: Can free-space evidence from depth infer, without topology-specific training, which template segments are absent and which unmodelled rigid bodies are permanently attached to a limb? Used as a plug-in on any body or hand estimator, does this suppress hallucinated limbs better than learned amputation classifiers (AJAHR) or structure-aware keypoint losses (ProPose), without falsely deleting limbs that objects merely occlude?
research_questions.why_top_venue: Hallucinated limbs are the shared failure in this niche: COCO-trained ViTPose places prostheses as natural ankles, video models propagate a complete limb across frames, and SAM 3D Body hallucinates the amputated side (per the record). The current fixes are learned from small, population-specific sets. ProPose gains only 2-6% on long-tail prosthetic joints, and limb-deficiency-aware losses trade off COCO accuracy (LDPose; I did not verify this myself). A geometric, training-free existence test that generalises across amputation levels and devices addresses the skeptics' point that no dataset can cover every combination. Separating 'absent' from 'occluded by a held object' and 'attached' from 'held' also ties the topic to mainstream hand-object reconstruction.
research_questions.method_sketch: Run a base estimator (SAM 3D Body or SMPLer-X for the body, HaMeR or WiLoR for hands). For each template segment, render its expected depth and classify every pixel as observed (depth agrees), occluded (measured depth in front) or contradicted (measured depth behind the predicted surface, i.e. space seen as empty). A per-segment Bayesian existence filter integrates this evidence over time, propagates absence along the kinematic chain (a missing forearm implies a missing hand) and adds a weak learned prior from AJAHR-style classifiers. Clustered depth points that no body part explains and that are adjacent to a segment end become attachment candidates. Each candidate is tracked as a rigid body relative to that segment, and a sequential test on the variance of the relative transform labels it attached (near-constant, never released) or held (released or regrasped). The output is a corrected topology plus per-segment provenance labels for downstream fitting (it feeds RQ1). For RGB-only public benchmarks, metric monocular depth (Depth Anything-class models) stands in for sensor depth, as a weaker variant.
research_questions.minimum_experiment: (a) Synthetic RGB-D renders of truncated bodies and hands with and without attached devices and held objects: segment-existence F1, hallucinated-limb rate, and attached-vs-held accuracy. (b) Non-regression on intact people under heavy object occlusion: DexYCB, HO3D and ARCTIC for hands; EMDB or 3DPW for bodies, with the metric being false absence rate and change in MPJPE or PA-MPJPE. (c) Cross-population check, if access is granted, on public RGB-only limb-loss data (ProGait clips; ProPose, LDPose or InclusiveVidPose images; RSP3D video) using monocular depth: hallucinated-keypoint rate against AJAHR, ProPose's ProLoss and fine-tuned ViTPose. (d) The author's own RGB-D captures with a strapped-on device or a long-held tool. Ablations: no temporal filter, no chain propagation, sensor depth vs monocular depth.
research_questions.data_and_hardware: Mostly public data plus synthetic renders. One RGB-D camera for own captures and one GPU. The data-use agreements of ProGait, ProPose, LDPose, InclusiveVidPose and RSP3D need checking; I did not confirm release status for any of them. No human-subjects recruitment is required for the core result, which makes this the cheapest RQ.
research_questions.risks: Monocular depth may be too coarse at limb ends, and loose sleeves can hide residual limbs (LDPose notes prostheses are often hidden by clothing), so the RGB-only transfer may be weak. Reviewers may call a visibility-reasoning filter engineering unless it clearly beats learned classifiers and generalises zero-shot. Public limb-loss sets are 2D and none has depth, so the strongest evidence stays synthetic. Self-occlusion and depth holes on dark or shiny prosthesis materials can create false 'contradicted' evidence. The result may end up as a strong section of RQ1 rather than a standalone paper.

research_questions.question: How far do current bimanual hand-object and body estimators fail on upper-limb prosthesis users doing standardised daily tasks? Can a single front RGB-D camera measure compensatory trunk and shoulder motion, together with device and object trajectories, to agree with multi-view ground truth?
research_questions.why_top_venue: No public 3D dataset covers upper-limb prosthesis users manipulating objects. The existing benchmarks are lower-limb or 2D: ProGait (4 transfemoral users, ICCV 2025) and RSP3D (running prostheses, ECCV 2026); LDPose, InclusiveVidPose and ProPose are 2D (unverified details). Benchmarks that expose a systematic failure of foundation models such as SAM 3D Body, HaMeR, WiLoR and FoundationPose on a new population have recently been accepted at top venues (ProGait at ICCV, RSP3D at ECCV). A dataset that pairs device and object metric ground truth with clinical compensation metrics would be a first of its kind.
research_questions.method_sketch: Record 10-15 upper-limb prosthesis users (body-powered and myoelectric, mainly transradial) and about 10 matched controls, using one front RGB-D camera as the test input and 2-3 extra calibrated cameras for triangulated ground truth. ArUco-tagged standardised objects and a marker plate on each socket give metric 6DoF ground truth for objects and devices. Tasks come from SHAP, AM-ULA and Box-and-Blocks style protocols. Proposed benchmark tracks: (i) intact hand, device and object 3D tracking; (ii) truncation and attachment recognition; (iii) clinical compensation metrics (trunk flexion and lateral lean, shoulder abduction, task time) measured from the single view and checked against the multi-view reference. Evaluate a baseline sweep zero-shot and after light fine-tuning, and include RQ1 and RQ2 as reference methods.
research_questions.minimum_experiment: At least 10 users by 8 tasks by 3 repetitions, about 240 sequences. The zero-shot baseline sweep should report per-population error gaps (users vs controls) for each track. Single-view compensation metrics should be reported against the multi-view reference with Bland-Altman limits. A data card should state consent scope, de-identification and the release licence.
research_questions.data_and_hardware: Same camera rig as RQ1 (one RGB-D camera plus 2-3 cheap cameras, ArUco boards). One GPU for the baselines. The deciding resource is a clinical partner: a prosthetics clinic or a university rehab lab with access to users, plus ethics approval for recording and public release of video of a vulnerable group, which I estimate at 3-6 months on its own (assumption).
research_questions.risks: Recruitment numbers and scheduling may not fit 12-18 months. Consent for public release may limit the dataset to features or blurred video, which reduces its value. With 10-15 subjects, reviewers will question generality, as with ProGait's 4 users. The UQ group may publish an upper-limb set first. Without the partner this RQ is infeasible, and the work would have to fall back to RQ1 and RQ2 with simulators only.

fit.thesis_assets_help: Moderate on engineering and ground truth; none on the gating item, which is access to prosthesis users. (1) The ArUco-marked object with metric pose transfers directly: marker plates on the socket, the terminal device and the task objects give metric 6DoF ground truth without motion capture, which RQ1 and RQ3 otherwise lack. (2) Object-conditioned recovery of an occluded holding arm is the closest existing module. A residual limb rigidly fixed to a device through a constant socket transform is a stricter case of an arm conditioned on a held object, so that conditioning carries over almost unchanged. (3) The measured/held/constrained labels map onto RQ2's per-segment states (observed, occluded, contradicted-absent) and onto honest reporting of clinical metrics. (4) The causal 30 fps chain gives RQ1 its live variant. (5) The Unity twin can render synthetic truncated bodies with attached devices, but it would need a depth-noise model. (6) The 28 recordings of one subject serve only as an intact-body regression and debugging set; they say nothing about the target population. Overall these assets give a few months' head start on rig and evaluation, not a scientific edge.

painpoint.name: Human demonstrations cannot be aligned to the robot's observations

evidence.latest_state: The visual side of the problem is being worked around at scale, but faithful alignment is not solved. Pipelines that robotize human video by inpainting and overlay (Phantom, Masquerade, HuRo) or by video diffusion (Mitty, H2R-Grounder, MimicDreamer, X-Humanoid, RoboEdit, disentangled cross-embodiment editing) now produce useful training data. HuRo (CoRL 2026) built 630K robotized episodes and 142M frames from five human-video sources; VLA pretraining on them raised completion on four real tasks from 51.5 to 80.3 percent, and OOD completion from 34.9 to 72.2 percent. Phantom reports up to 92 percent success with zero robot data. Masquerade gets 5 to 6x over baselines on bimanual kitchen tasks. RoboEdit releases 174K aligned human-robot video pairs (14M frames, seven embodiments), made by automatic 3D hand-object reconstruction and retargeting from RGB. The newest diagnostic, H2R-Bench (arXiv 2608.13049, August 2026), tests 11 video world models on two embodiments. Its conclusion is that leading models still fail on embodiment consistency, functional contact and task execution: H2RCore ranges from 30.0 to 84.6, and video-quality metrics barely track it. Real pixel-aligned pairs still cannot be captured. Paired datasets stay small or narrow (Human2Robot with VR teleoperation in mirrored workspaces; HRDexDB, 2026, limited to dexterous grasping), and every large pair set is synthetic. Cross-view and viewpoint alignment have had little dedicated progress: MimicDreamer canonicalizes ego viewpoints with a homography plus inpainting, and EgoExoLearn-style cross-view association accuracy stays near 50 percent. All of these methods depend on 3D hand pose and contact estimates that remain the weak link, which ties this pain point directly to hand-object reconstruction quality.

evidence.crowdedness: HIGH: I counted more than 13 arXiv papers from 2025-2026 on human-to-robot video robotization or editing alone (Stanford/Phantom-Masquerade line, HuRo at CoRL 2026, RoboEdit, Mitty, X-Humanoid, H2R-Bench, MimicDreamer, Pegasus), most of them from large robot-learning and video-generation groups. Real paired capture and the cross-viewpoint part get far less attention.
evidence.trend: Rising. Video world models and VLA pretraining on human video drove a surge from late 2025 through September 2026: new datasets, the H2R-Bench benchmark, and two 2026 surveys on robot learning from human videos (arXiv 2604.27621, 2606.00054).

skeptics.reasons:
I found no 2025-2026 work that solves P35 as stated. Several works do weaken its wording, and pixel-level conversion is getting crowded fast. Note: the shared WebSearch budget was already used up (200 of 200), so all evidence came from WebFetch of arXiv pages and project pages.

(1) Render-and-inpaint now works for policy learning, but it does not give real alignment. Phantom (CoRL 2025) trains policies from human video alone, using hand-pose estimation, arm inpainting and a rendered robot overlay. It reports 92% pick-and-place, 64% rope tying and 72-76% insertion and reorientation, with zero-shot real deployment. Masquerade (ICRA 2026) edits in-the-wild egocentric video the same way and reports large out-of-distribution gains. However, Masquerade still co-trains with 50 real robot demos per task. Both pipelines depend on accurate 3D hand pose and ignore contact fidelity. These works show that rough visual alignment is enough for some tasks. They confirm the pain point's own claim that such pipelines avoid the mismatch rather than solve it.

(2) 3D and keypoint representations sidestep pixel alignment. Point Policy (Haldar and Pinto, 2025) learns from human videos alone, uses keypoints that do not depend on robot shape, and by its abstract does not need identical cameras. So the claim that "working methods assume identical cameras or mirrored workspaces" is too strong and should be narrowed.

(3) Generative conversion is very active but not saturated. 2025-2026 examples: X-Humanoid (Dec 2025; trained on Unreal Engine pseudo-pairs, so it is supported only by user studies), Disentangled Cross-Embodiment Video Editing (May 2026; it lists contact, occlusion, viewpoint and real-robot success as open), Wh0, HandEdit, RoboEdit, Xiaomi-Robotics-U0 and GigaBrain-0 (claims view transfer). The 2026 benchmarks behind the pain point still show failure: H2R-Bench embodiment scores are near zero for strong video models, about 33% of HandEdit pseudo-pairs are rejected, and EgoExoLearn cross-view association is about 55% at best. No metric is saturated, and no product solves this.

(4) The stated root cause is accurate 3D hand-object reconstruction and contact under occlusion. That is still unsolved, and it is the author's own field.

Conclusion: not refuted. The broad statement should be narrowed, and the pixel-generation part is a crowded race dominated by large labs, which is a poor fit for a small lab.

skeptics.reframe: Human-to-robot transfer methods (Phantom, Masquerade, Point Policy, video-diffusion robotizers) already work when the hand pose is clean and the action is simple, such as pick-and-place. They break down when they need metric 3D hand-object pose and contact, under occlusion, from a demonstration camera that differs from the robot's. The open problem is reconstructing a 3D hand-object-contact state that is accurate enough and independent of viewpoint, from monocular or RGB-D human video, together with a way to check contact and embodiment fidelity after transfer. Generating convincing robot pixels is not the open problem.

skeptics.reasons:
P35 overstates the problem and is assembled from separate pieces. I am refuting it as worded, but a narrower version holds up.

(1) One community, mostly unreviewed work. All 14 papers sit in the robot-learning group. About 11 of them are arXiv preprints from April to September 2026: HuRo, RoboEdit, CosmoH2G, H2R-Bench, HandEdit, Wh0, HumanNet, EgoVerse, and the two surveys. They were listed as recent arXiv versions and have not been peer reviewed. The strongest numbers come from H2R-Bench (11 video world models, with an MLLM judge over EgoDex clips only) and HandEdit (a 33 percent rejection rate in its own pseudo-pair curation on ARCTIC). Both measure one paradigm, pixel-level human-to-robot video conversion, under that paradigm's own conventions.

(2) Three unrelated problems bundled together. The record merges three source clusters:
- paired capture (Human2Robot, CosmoH2G, RH20T);
- generative or edited robotization (H2R-Bench, HandEdit, RoboEdit, HuRo, Wh0);
- cross-view association (EgoExoLearn).
EgoExoLearn is a video-understanding benchmark about associating asynchronous procedural steps across ego and exo views. It does not align demonstrations to a robot's observations, and its "barely above random zero-shot" figure concerns activity association, not robot alignment. The "camera-robot alignment high-error tail" is a hand-eye or extrinsic calibration question, a mature topic in robotics.

(3) The statement says it cannot be done; peer-reviewed work does it.
- Phantom (CoRL 2025) converts human video to robot observations by estimating hand pose, inpainting the arm and overlaying a rendered robot. It deploys zero-shot on real hardware with up to 92 percent success on deformable, sweeping and insertion tasks.
- Masquerade (ICRA 2026) applies the same kind of editing to in-the-wild egocentric video and reports about 5-6x gains on bimanual kitchen tasks in unseen scenes. It does need 50 robot demonstrations per task for fine-tuning.
- RoVi-Aug (CoRL 2024 oral) synthesizes new viewpoints and embodiments and deploys zero-shot to unseen robots at different camera angles.
- EgoMimic (ICRA 2025), EgoBridge (NeurIPS 2025) and Point Policy (CoRL 2025) avoid pixel alignment altogether through aligned co-training, domain adaptation or keypoint representations.

So the community treats observation alignment as workable, with known engineering limits: occlusion, contact fidelity and runtime. The record admits this when it lists mirrored workspaces, re-enactment and compositing as fixes, then dismisses them as "by construction". Several of these fixes work in practice.

(4) Field relevance. The record itself marks P35 as adjacent. The part that touches the author's field (3D hand-object tracking and reconstruction) is narrower: monocular depth and scale error and missing contact in hand-object reconstruction. RoboEdit reports 42 mm wrist error and HuRo reports a 45 percent self-contact rate. These errors break occlusion-consistent, contact-preserving robot overlays. That sub-claim has support from several groups, but it overlaps existing pain points on metric hand-object reconstruction and contact, so it is not a new direction on its own.

skeptics.reframe: Robot overlays made from human video (render-and-inpaint editing, as in Phantom and Masquerade) already work for policy learning. Their fidelity is limited by monocular 3D hand-object reconstruction: metric depth and scale error, missing contact, and no model of how the robot occludes the scene. As a result the synthesized robot observations misplace contact and mishandle occlusion, and no benchmark scores them against real paired robot observations of the same act.

skeptics.reasons:
Not refuted as a no-research-question pain point, though it survives only in part. Two of its three sub-claims hold up as research, and they share one scientific core. The rest is engineering or a bundle of loosely related problems.

What does not survive this lens. (a) Collecting paired data at scale is not a money problem, because pixel-aligned human-robot pairs of the same act cannot be physically recorded (1394, 1495). For the same reason, more annotation budget does not fix it. Even so, the fixes listed (mirrored VR workspaces, UMI re-enactment, human screening, 1390/1495) are capture engineering. (b) Render-and-inpaint taking tens of minutes per clip is a speed and engineering issue. (c) Cross-view ego-exo association (EgoExoLearn, 23) is a separate video-understanding problem, merged in only through the word "viewpoint". Its numbers (zero-shot 21.7-33.3 against random 13-14) say nothing about robot transfer. (d) The pain point assumes pixel-space alignment is required. Embodiment-agnostic 3D intermediates, such as hand or end-effector trajectories and object pose or flow (EgoMimic, arXiv 2410.24221, is in this family), could sidestep visual alignment altogether. A reviewer could say the problem dissolves under a different policy input. (e) The area is crowded at top venues: Mirage (RSS 2024), RoVi-Aug (CoRL 2024 oral) and Phantom (CoRL 2025) already publish inpainting and generative conversion. Another conversion pipeline would be incremental.

What survives, with research questions a reviewer would take seriously.
RQ1: Can a human demonstration be converted into a robot-view observation that is physically consistent? That means preserved contact region and mode, the correct object trajectory, and correct robot-scene occlusion, conditioned on reconstructed 4D hand-object geometry rather than on 2D masks. How much does the error in 3D hand-object reconstruction and contact bound downstream policy success? This is non-trivial. H2R-Bench (1393) shows the strongest video models fail on embodiment correctness: HunyuanVideo near zero, Veo 3.1 at 0.100/0.227. It also shows contact scores near 0.185. The field's own explanation of why the problem persists names inaccurate 3D hand-object reconstruction and contact as the bottleneck, which is the author's own field.
RQ2: Which measurable property of converted data predicts its value for policy learning? Video quality spans only 0.73-0.81 and ranks weakly against H2R scores of 30-84.6 (1393). A transfer-validity metric grounded in 3D contact and geometry, validated against real policy success, is a significant evaluation contribution.
RQ3, weaker: viewpoint-robust transfer when demonstration and robot cameras differ. Mirage, RoVi-Aug and Phantom partly address it, so novelty is limited.

Net: the pain point yields at least one significant question (RQ1/RQ2), so it is not refuted. The publishable version is narrower than the statement: contact- and occlusion-faithful conversion grounded in 3D HOI reconstruction, plus a metric that predicts transfer. Pairing infrastructure, speed and the ego-exo association parts should be dropped. The "adjacent" relevance tag is fair. The thesis author's contribution would be the reconstruction side, not the policy side.

Evidence status. The paper titles come from the local digest, w3_digest/G4_robot_learning.jsonl. I did not fetch these during this task, and many are arXiv 2026 preprints whose venue status was not checked. I verified Mirage, RoVi-Aug, Phantom and EgoMimic on arXiv; no venue was stated for EgoMimic. WebSearch was unavailable because the shared budget was exhausted.
