skeptics.reframe: When a hand occludes the object it is manipulating, the object's pose can only be estimated from its visible parts, and its appearance can only be learned once its pose is known. Dynamic Gaussian and NeRF reconstructions do not get out of this loop: NVS-HO reports foreground PSNR around 16 and only marginal gains from pose refinement, and DiVa-360 scores interaction sequences up to 2.7 dB below object-only ones even with 53 cameras. The open research question is how to estimate hand articulation, the 6DoF pose of an unknown object, and its appearance together from a single RGB-D or monocular view, for example by using depth or physical contact constraints. A second requirement is that the reconstruction stays consistent over long sequences with regrasps and two-hand handovers, where contact keeps changing which parts are visible. Rendering fidelity alone is not the goal; the poses must be accurate enough for robot demonstration capture.

research_questions.question: When a hand hides much of an unknown hand-held object seen by one static RGB-D camera, does modelling the hand explicitly help? The proposal fits MANO-anchored Gaussians to depth, then uses the hand both as a known occluder and as a carrier of object pose, through a grasp transform that stays constant within each grasp segment. Does this break the pose-appearance loop well enough to beat (a) RGB-D methods that mask the hand out (BundleSDF, CVPR 2023; 6DOPE-GS, CVPR 2025) on object pose in heavily occluded frames, and (b) monocular prior-based methods (HOLD, BIGS, GHOST, Interaction-Aware 4DGS) on metric pose and on held-out-view appearance of the object surface that was actually observed?
research_questions.why_top_venue: The pain point holds up once narrowed to unknown hand-held objects under hand occlusion. NVS-HO (arXiv 2602.05822) reports a median foreground PSNR of about 16 and says pose refinement helps little. It captured with an OAK-D Lite but used only the RGB stream. On the RGB-D side, 6DOPE-GS (CVPR 2025, verified) masks the hand with SAM2 and says occlusion removes supervision. It reaches ADD 84.3 against 89.6 for BundleSDF on HO3D, at 0.24 s per frame against 2.1 s, and does not evaluate novel-view synthesis. The 2025-2026 hand-object 4DGS papers I checked (BIGS, GHOST, Interaction-Aware 4DGS, Grasp in Gaussians, CHOIR) all take monocular RGB. Interaction-Aware 4DGS ignores the depth that HOI4D provides, and its authors say it fails on fast motion and complex trajectories. Nothing I checked models the hand explicitly while using depth. The contribution would be the coupling mechanism, not RGB-D input as such: grasp rigidity as a latent constraint, plus occlusion reasoning based on depth ordering (a pixel whose depth is in front of the object is hand-occluded, not missing). Reviewers accept this kind of structural insight. It also matches the stated cause of the pain point, that canonical-plus-deformation and accurate-pose assumptions break under contact and occlusion.
research_questions.method_sketch: (1) Initialisation: SAM2 masks for hand and object; an off-the-shelf 3D hand estimator (for example HaMeR or WiLoR, which I did not re-check here) refined by ICP and silhouette fitting against the depth map. (2) Representation: rigid canonical 2D or 3D Gaussians for the object in its own frame; MANO-anchored Gaussians for the hand, used for occlusion and contact, not for photoreal rendering. (3) Pose model: object pose(t) = wrist pose(t) times G_k times a small residual during grasp segment k. G_k is estimated jointly with the object model. Segment boundaries (regrasp, slip, finger gaiting) are found by change-point detection on the depth-alignment residual of the rigid-grasp hypothesis and on changes in contact. (4) A keyframe pose graph across segments, BundleSDF-style, for loop closure when a side of the object is seen again. (5) Depth-ordered visibility: rendered object depth behind the measured hand depth counts as occluded and receives no photometric penalty. (6) A per-Gaussian evidence ledger (observed directly, propagated through the grasp, never observed). Generative completion is optional and reported separately, so measured and hallucinated surface are never mixed in one metric.
research_questions.minimum_experiment: (a) HO3D v3: the 13 test sequences used by BundleSDF and 6DOPE-GS, reporting ADD and ADD-S AUC overall and in frame bins by occlusion ratio (0-25, 25-50, 50-75, over 75 percent hidden). Ablations: hand masked (the 6DOPE-GS-style baseline), hand modelled as occluder only, and occluder plus grasp-rigidity prior. (b) DexYCB: 100 or more sequences selected for occlusion. Use one RealSense view as input and the other seven calibrated views as held-out views. Report object-region PSNR and LPIPS, split into observed and never-observed surface, and Chamfer distance against the YCB mesh. Compare with Interaction-Aware 4DGS or GHOST (whichever code is available) run on RGB only. Success criterion: a clear gain in ADD and ADD-S in the over-50-percent-occlusion bin with no loss elsewhere, and better observed-surface PSNR than the monocular baselines on held-out views. Expect small overall averages, because HO3D ADD-S is already about 95 percent.
research_questions.data_and_hardware: Public data only for the paper's numbers: HO3D v3 (RGB-D), DexYCB (8 RGB-D views, YCB meshes, MANO and 6D object pose), and HO-Cap (several RGB-D cameras plus a HoloLens; includes handovers; license not checked). If NVS-HO releases its data, use its board-sequence protocol; whether its depth stream is released is unverified. Compute: one 24 GB GPU is enough. Interaction-Aware 4DGS reports 1 h 20 min per sequence on one RTX 3090, and BundleSDF and 6DOPE-GS run at 2.1 and 0.24 s per frame. The consumer RGB-D camera serves only for qualitative and in-house checks. No motion capture or robot is needed.
research_questions.risks: (1) Getting scooped: NVIDIA (BundleSDF and HO-Cap authors), the Theobalt group (Grasp in Gaussians), ETH/Hilliges (HOLD) and KAIST/Baek (BIGS) are all one step away. (2) Reviewers may see RGB-D as niche next to monocular RGB plus foundation models. The robot-demonstration and metric-scale motivation has to be argued, and the RGB-only ablation shown. (3) Grasp rigidity fails under in-hand manipulation such as sliding or finger gaiting. If change-point detection is unreliable, the prior hurts. (4) Hand-estimator errors pass directly into object pose. (5) Headroom is small: DexYCB grasps are short pick-ups and HO3D pose metrics are near saturation, so the gain may show only in the occlusion bins. (6) Code for 6DOPE-GS and Interaction-Aware 4DGS may not be public (unverified), which would force re-implementation.

research_questions.question: Can a hand-object reconstruction stay pose-accurate and temporally consistent over minute-long sequences with repeated regrasps and two-hand handovers? The idea is to treat each change of contact state as a segment boundary of a rigid-object, articulated-hand model, and to close loops on the object across segments, instead of fitting one deformation field over the whole sequence. If this works, how do drift and object completeness scale with sequence length compared with deformation-field and per-segment baselines?
research_questions.why_top_venue: Long sequences with topology changes are a stated failure in the pain-point record: HumanRF drops from 30.30 to 29.05 PSNR between 20 and 1000 frames, and deformation fields struggle with rapid topology changes. The rq skeptic names regrasps and handovers, where contact changes what is visible, as an open question. Current hand-object 4DGS papers report short clips; Interaction-Aware 4DGS says it fails on complex trajectories. For robot demonstration capture, long, multi-grasp tasks are the target, so a method plus a length-stratified evaluation protocol is a defensible contribution. It is also less crowded than the short-clip setting.
research_questions.method_sketch: Build on the RQ1 representation. Contact state (left hand, right hand, both, or none, with contact regions on the object) is inferred from depth-aligned hand and object geometry. Each state change opens a new segment with its own grasp transform. The object keeps a single canonical Gaussian model that every segment updates. A global pose graph over object keyframes uses Gaussian-feature or render-and-compare matching for re-identification after full occlusion. Handovers are modelled as a short bimanual segment in which both grasp transforms are active, which over-constrains the object pose. Bounded memory comes from keyframe selection and pruning Gaussians by evidence count.
research_questions.minimum_experiment: On HO-Cap's handover and multi-step sequences, use one RGB-D view as input and the other cameras for held-out evaluation. Report, in bins of sequence length: object ADD and ADD-S, drift (pose error against time since last full visibility), the re-acquisition rate after full occlusion, consistency of geometry across segments (Chamfer between segment-wise partial reconstructions after alignment), and a temporal flicker metric (error of the rendered frame warped to the next frame). Baselines: BundleSDF; 6DOPE-GS if code exists; a single-deformation-field 4DGS baseline (for example Deform3DGS or SC-GS); and the RQ1 model without the segment and loop-closure logic. Optionally run on ARCTIC with RGB input to show the design is not tied to depth.
research_questions.data_and_hardware: HO-Cap is the main dataset (handovers and multiple RGB-D cameras; sequence counts and license not checked). ARCTIC (bimanual, RGB only) is optional. DexYCB has no handovers and so is not suitable. The author's 28 single-subject recordings with ArUco ground truth can serve only as an in-house drift check. One 24 GB GPU; per-sequence optimisation for sequences of 1-3 minutes is feasible offline if keyframes keep memory bounded.
research_questions.risks: HO-Cap annotations come from the same multi-camera pipeline that a reviewer might expect as the baseline, so ground-truth quality on handovers needs checking first. Inferring contact state from depth near the fingers is noisy, because RealSense-class depth is poor at fingertip scale. The gain may appear only on a few long sequences, which makes the statistics thin. Feed-forward 4D models (4DGT, Hand-4DGS) could take over long-sequence handling if they add hand-held objects within the project window.

research_questions.question: Can a causal, online RGB-D system track an unknown hand-held object's pose at camera rate (30 fps) on one GPU, grow its Gaussian appearance model, and keep per-region evidence labels (measured, propagated through the grasp, unobserved) while hands occlude it? Is that accuracy enough for downstream replay of robot demonstrations?
research_questions.why_top_venue: The best RGB-D model-free trackers checked run at 0.24 s per frame (6DOPE-GS) and 2.1 s per frame (BundleSDF), both offline-optimised and both masking the hand out. Real-time joint hand-object tracking from RGB-D dates from 2016 (arXiv 1610.04889) and does not build an appearance model of an unknown object. Robotics venues value a real-time capture system with calibrated uncertainty for demonstration data, and the evidence labels address the concern that diffusion or SDS completion hallucinates geometry a robot should not trust.
research_questions.method_sketch: Use a front end / back end split. The front end, at camera rate, propagates object pose with the grasp-rigid hand model and depth ICP against the current Gaussian model. The back end runs asynchronously and does keyframe pose-graph optimisation plus Gaussian densification and appearance refinement. Each Gaussian and each output pose frame carries an evidence label, and downstream consumers can filter on it. Latency and accuracy are exposed as a single tunable trade-off.
research_questions.minimum_experiment: Run on the HO3D and DexYCB sequences of RQ1 with strictly causal processing. Plot an accuracy-latency curve (ADD and ADD-S against per-frame latency) against BundleSDF and 6DOPE-GS. Report calibration of the evidence labels: the pose error conditional on each label. Show downstream value in simulation: replay the recovered object trajectories and grasp transforms in a simulator (Unity twin or an open-source robotics simulator) and measure kinematic replay error against ground-truth trajectories. Add a short real demonstration on a borrowed arm if one is available.
research_questions.data_and_hardware: The same public RGB-D datasets as RQ1, plus a live consumer RGB-D camera for timing and demonstrations. One GPU. A robot arm is optional; without one, the downstream claim stays in simulation, which weakens a CoRL or RSS submission but is acceptable for ICRA or RA-L.
research_questions.risks: Hitting 30 fps on one GPU while updating Gaussians may force a model coarse enough that appearance quality loses its point. Robotics reviewers may ask for a real-robot result. The idea overlaps with incremental Gaussian object SLAM work and with the authors of 6DOPE-GS and BundleSDF, who could ship an online hand-aware version first.

fit.thesis_assets_help:
A small to moderate edge, mostly in framing and engineering, not in data.

(1) The measured/held/constrained honesty labels map directly onto the per-Gaussian evidence ledger and the visibility-stratified metrics in RQ1 and RQ3. This is the asset most likely to set the work apart from prior-based methods (SDS, SAM3D initialisation) that hallucinate unseen surface.

(2) The object-conditioned recovery of an occluded holding arm is the mirror image of the grasp-rigidity idea (hand-conditioned object pose through occlusion). The occlusion logic and depth-ordering code can probably be reused.

(3) The causal 30 fps chain gives a starting front end for RQ3.

(4) The single RGB-D desk setup with an ArUco-marked object of known metric pose follows the same ground-truth protocol NVS-HO uses (ChArUco with solvePnP), but with depth. It supports in-house checks of pose under occlusion and qualitative figures.

(5) The Unity twin could produce synthetic occlusion stress tests or a simulated replay for RQ3.

The 28 recordings of one subject cannot serve as a benchmark. All headline numbers must come from HO3D, DexYCB and HO-Cap.
fit.what_a_small_lab_cannot_do_here:
A small lab cannot compete on the parts of P37 that need capture infrastructure or large-scale training:

- It cannot build dense capture rigs or new large multi-view benchmarks. DiVa-360 uses a 53-camera dome, GigaHands 51 views and Ego-1K a 12-camera head rig. Without such a rig, the lab also has no ground truth for egocentric photoreal NVS under head motion.
- It cannot train feed-forward 4D Gaussian models (4DGT, Hand-4DGS) or large generative priors (SDS or SAM3D-scale completion), which need large multi-view corpora and GPU clusters.
- It cannot address the avatar and light-stage half of the pain point (fast hair, OLAT sway, 1000-frame full-body video). That half is off-field anyway.
- It cannot collect a multi-subject, multi-object dataset with motion-capture-grade ground truth.
- It cannot win a pure PSNR race on photoreal dynamic NVS, where strong groups iterate quickly.

The feasible path is pose-first, per-sequence optimisation on a single GPU using public RGB-D datasets, with appearance quality as a secondary, visibility-stratified metric.

painpoint.name: Long-horizon and shifted conditions break learned policies

evidence.latest_state: Simulated long-horizon suites are close to saturated. PALM (CVPR 2026) reports 91.8 percent on LIBERO-Long and a 12.5 percent gain in average length on CALVIN ABC->D. SimpleVLA-RL reportedly lifts LIBERO-Long from 17.1 to 91.7 percent with one demonstration per task, but that number comes from a search snippet; the arXiv abstract I fetched gives no LIBERO-Long figure. The same models still collapse under shifted conditions. LIBERO-Plus (arXiv 2510.13626; a CVPR 2026 version is listed on openaccess.thecvf.com) shows success falling from about 95 percent to below 30 percent under modest camera-viewpoint and robot-initial-state perturbations, and OpenVLA falls from 76.5 to 1.1 percent under camera shift according to a secondary summary. Real-world results are much lower. UMI-Bench 1.0 (arXiv 2606.10382, June 2026) is the source of the pain point's 0 percent full success on its multi-stage and long-horizon tasks, and progress scores of 59.6 seen, 45.3 under position, layout, pose and dynamics shifts, and 40.2 under combined shifts. The fetched abstract does not state these numbers; they come from the pain-point record. PARTS (arXiv 2609.21788, September 2026) uses real-world subtask RL to raise complete-task success from 32 to 61 percent on bimanual YAM tasks and from 50 to 95 percent on Franka. LongBench (arXiv 2604.16788) finds that memory-based methods do not consistently help on context-dependent real-world long-horizon tasks, and RMBench (arXiv 2603.01229) also identifies memory limitations in existing policies. Gains now come from RL fine-tuning, progress or subtask tracking and memory, but no method recovers robustly from compounding deviations under geometric shift in the real world.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: PALM: Progress-Aware Policy Learning via Affordance Reasoning for Long-Horizon Robotic Manipulation
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Affordance representations plus continuous progress prediction for stable subtask transitions; 91.8 percent on LIBERO-Long, +12.5 percent average length on CALVIN ABC->D, about 2x over baselines in three real long-horizon settings.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: LIBERO-Plus: In-depth Robustness Analysis of Vision-Language-Action Models
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Benchmark of controlled perturbations along seven dimensions (layout, camera, robot initial state, language, light, background, noise); VLA success drops from about 95 percent to below 30 percent under camera and initial-state shifts, and the models largely ignore language.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: UMI-Bench 1.0: An Open and Reproducible Real-World Benchmark for Tabletop Robotic Manipulation with UMI Data
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Real-robot benchmark for UMI wrist-view policies (10 tasks, about 20k demonstrations, 50 evaluation episodes per task) with task-factor shift analysis; source of the 0 percent full success on multi-stage and long-horizon tasks.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: From Pretraining to Proficiency: Real-World Subtask RL for Long-Horizon Manipulation with Minimal Human Intervention (PARTS)
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Real-world RL concentrated on bottleneck subtasks on top of a frozen pretrained policy; complete-task success rises from 32 to 61 percent on bimanual YAM and from 50 to 95 percent on Franka, using tens of minutes of RL per task.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: LongBench: Evaluating Robotic Manipulation Policies on Real-World Long-Horizon Tasks
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Over 1,000 real episodes across fully observable and context-dependent regimes; six SOTA policies evaluated, and memory-based methods do not consistently help.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: RMBench: Memory-Dependent Robotic Manipulation Benchmark with Insights into Policy Design
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Simulation benchmark of 9 tasks at graded memory complexity, plus the modular Mem-0 policy with explicit memory components for ablating memory design.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: Don't Drop the BATON: Long-Horizon Robot Manipulation via Agentic Subtask Exploration and Transition-aware Memory
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Explores each subtask separately and adds transition-aware memory with verifier agents and handoff transitions; +37.7 percent task success over SOTA on RoboMemArena.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: SimpleVLA-RL: Scaling VLA Training via Reinforcement Learning
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: RL fine-tuning of OpenVLA-OFT that reaches SOTA on LIBERO. The search snippet claims LIBERO-Long rises from 17.1 to 91.7 percent with one demonstration per task, but this was not confirmed in the abstract.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: Bi-HIL: Bilateral Control-Based Multimodal Hierarchical Imitation Learning via Subtask-Level Progress Rate and Keyframe Memory for Long-Horizon Contact-Rich Robotic Manipulation
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Hierarchical imitation learning with subtask prediction, progress rate and keyframe memory for long-horizon contact-rich tasks.

attacking_papers_2025_2026.title: Trace-Focused Diffusion Policy for Multi-Modal Action Disambiguation in Long-Horizon Robotic Manipulation
attacking_papers_2025_2026.what_it_does: Diffusion policy that uses trace conditioning to resolve multi-modal stage ambiguity in long-horizon tasks.

evidence.crowdedness: HIGH: at least ten 2026 papers found with only six searches, from large groups (Fudan, HKU, PKU and others behind LIBERO-Plus, RMBench and UMI-Bench, plus many VLA and RL labs), with new benchmarks and methods every month.
evidence.trend: rising: attention has moved from saturated sim suites (LIBERO-Long, CALVIN) to real-world long-horizon and robustness benchmarks (UMI-Bench, LongBench, LIBERO-Plus, RMBench) and to RL fine-tuning and memory for VLAs, driven by the VLA scaling boom and the gap between sim and real results.

skeptics.reasons: Not refuted, but the broad form is weaker than stated. Work from 2025-2026 removes several parts of it. (1) Simulated chained-instruction suites (LIBERO-Long, CALVIN) are close to saturated. SimpleVLA-RL (ICLR 2026) raises LIBERO-Long from 17.1 to 91.7 percent with RL, so the CALVIN/VLABench evidence (paper 1401) no longer shows an open research problem. (2) Viewpoint shift on LIBERO-Plus is now cheap to fix. Li et al. (arXiv 2512.02902, revised 2026-03) restore camera-viewpoint success from 48.5 to 87.1 percent with a 4K-parameter feature-token modulation, and to 90.8 percent with 4.7M parameters. That undercuts the camera-perturbation evidence (paper 1385). (3) Recovery from compounding errors, the stated 'why it persists', is directly targeted by pi*0.6 with RECAP (Physical Intelligence, arXiv 2511.14759). It runs RL from on-policy rollouts and teleoperated corrections, reports 18 hours of continuous espresso making, 50 novel laundry items folded in a new home and 59 factory boxes assembled, and roughly halves failure rates on the hardest tasks. (4) Compositional object-centric skill chaining reaches 85 percent on 8 real long-horizon tasks (LiLo-VLA, arXiv 2602.21531), with zero-shot composition of novel long tasks. What survives: (a) these fixes depend on robot-side on-policy data, interventions, replanning modules or per-task RL, not on human or handheld demonstrations alone; (b) the UMI-Bench evidence still stands: zero full success on multi-stage and tight-tolerance long-horizon tasks, and larger drops under position, layout, pose and dynamics shifts than under appearance shifts. No 2025-2026 result I found shows geometric or dynamics-shift robustness saturating for policies trained only on human or handheld capture. LingBot-VLA-2.0 (2607.06403) still reports out-of-distribution degradation according to a search snippet; I could not confirm the numbers from the abstract. So the general claim 'long-horizon breaks learned policies' is being reduced to engineering (RL post-training, modular replanning). The narrower capture-side claim is still open. For this author the pain point stays peripheral: it is a policy-learning problem, and the overlap is only through what demonstration capture records.

skeptics.reframe: Policies trained only on human or handheld (UMI-style) demonstrations, with no robot-side on-policy correction, still fail on multi-stage, tight-tolerance tasks and under geometric and dynamics shifts (object position, layout, pose). Part of the cause is on the capture side: the recordings carry no explicit task-stage label and no metric 3D object and contact state. Simulated long-horizon suites and viewpoint robustness are now largely engineering problems (RL post-training, lightweight feature adaptation). The open question for a capture researcher is whether demonstrations that record stage and 3D hand-object state reduce the need for robot-side RL and interventions.

skeptics.reasons: The artifact attack fails on the core claim and succeeds on several sub-claims. Core claim survives: brittleness of imitation and VLA policies under distribution shift, and compounding error over long horizons, are not the product of one dataset or one group. The 15 supporting papers come from unrelated groups and settings: the TRI co-training study (709), the UMI-Bench and FastUMI real-robot UMI work (1372, 1369), the Urain et al. generative-models survey (1028), a VLA datasets survey (1401), and the WIYH, HuRo, CosmoH2G and tactile-pretraining papers. Independent benchmarks outside the cited set, which I verified, show the same thing. THE COLOSSEUM (Pumacay et al., RSS 2024, UW/NVIDIA) reports 30-50% success degradation per perturbation factor and at least 75% under combined perturbations, across five models. LIBERO-Plus (Fei et al., Fudan, arXiv 2510.13626) reports VLA success falling from 95% to below 30% under modest camera-viewpoint and initial-state perturbations. Compounding error under covariate shift has been named since Ross et al.'s DAgger work (2011, recalled from memory, not re-verified here). No other community treats it as solved; it is a standing open problem across imitation learning. Parts that are artifacts or overstated: (1) The headline zeros (0% full success on T3 and T9) come from a single benchmark, UMI-Bench 1.0 (1372), with only three policies on one wrist-fisheye UMI setup. (2) The "lost stage estimate under ambiguous views" mechanism is specific to UMI-style wrist-only observation (1369, 1372); conventional setups avoid it by adding a third-person camera or observation history, so it is a sensor-convention artifact rather than a field-level failure. (3) "Chain-of-thought gives no benefit" rests on one paper. (4) The absolute wording "cannot complete long-horizon multi-stage manipulation" is contradicted by pi0.5 (Physical Intelligence, arXiv 2504.16054), which reports end-to-end long-horizon cleaning of kitchens and bedrooms in unseen homes. That suggests the gap is one of reliability and data scale, not impossibility. (5) Relevance to the author's field (3D hand/body-object tracking and reconstruction) is peripheral. This is a G4 robot-learning pain point that sits downstream of demonstration capture, and only the "why it persists" clause (demonstrations lack explicit task-stage and 3D state structure) touches tracking and reconstruction. Net result: a real, well-known, multi-group problem, but an old and crowded robot-learning problem rather than a new field-level pain point for this author. The specific mechanisms cited are partly artifacts of the UMI wrist-camera convention.

skeptics.reframe: Policies learned from human or handheld demonstrations lose 30-75% of their success under geometric, viewpoint and combined shifts (COLOSSEUM, LIBERO-Plus, UMI-Bench), and errors compound across stages. One part of the cause is in reach of capture and reconstruction work: the demonstration data records wrist-view pixels and end-effector trajectories but no explicit 3D object state or task-stage structure, so policies cannot localize where they are in a task or recover from deviations. Robot learning broadly faces the policy problem. The capture-side gap is the part relevant to a hand-object tracking researcher.

skeptics.reasons: Default refutation attempt. One reading is that this is a resource problem: collect more and longer demonstrations, scale VLA pretraining, add cameras. The record argues against that reading. The attempted fixes include large-scale human-video and robotized pretraining, simulation co-training and tactile pretraining, and each gives only partial gains. Chain-of-thought conditioning gave no benefit. On LIBERO-plus camera perturbation the tactile-pretrained model (48.9) still scores below baselines (OpenVLA-OFT 56.4, pi0-Fast 65.1). UMI-Bench 1.0 (arXiv 2606.10382, verified) reports 0 percent full success for every model on T3 (multi-stage) and T9 (long-horizon rearrangement). Its progress scores fall from 59.62 to 45.33 under position, layout, pose and dynamics shifts and to 40.19 under combined shifts. The failure modes it names are concrete mechanisms, not data volume: the stage estimate is lost under ambiguous wrist views, and small placement errors compound until a tight final tolerance fails. Compounding error into off-distribution states and the mismatch between a density-estimation objective and task success are open learning-theoretic and algorithmic questions, so the solution is not known and simply waiting for resources. The refutation therefore fails on this lens: the pain point yields questions a CoRL, RSS or NeurIPS reviewer would find significant. Example: can policies keep an explicit, observable task-stage and 3D object-state estimate that is robust to aliased egocentric views, and does it measurably cut compounding error? Two caveats lower the score. (1) The area is crowded. Stage-aware reward modelling (SARM, arXiv 2509.25358), hierarchical sub-goal policies (GHOST, arXiv 2606.10025), one-shot long-horizon IL (ManiLong-Shot, arXiv 2512.16302) and MimicPlay (CoRL 2022) already attack it, so a generic 'better long-horizon policy' contribution needs strong novelty. (2) For this author the problem is peripheral: as a policy-learning problem it lies outside 3D hand-object tracking and reconstruction. The question survives for the author only when reframed so that the tracking and reconstruction output is the contribution. One version is to extract explicit 3D hand-object state, contact events and stage boundaries from monocular or RGB-D human demonstrations. Another is to test whether that structure reduces stage aliasing and geometric-shift failures. There is precedent for 3D hand-object reconstruction feeding policies (arXiv 2602.09013), which makes this a credible but contested niche.

skeptics.reframe: Policies learned from human or handheld demonstrations fail at long horizons and under geometric shifts. Two causes are named: the demonstrations carry no explicit task-stage or 3D object-state structure, so the stage estimate aliases under similar egocentric views, and small placement errors compound until a tight tolerance fails. Research question for this author: can stage boundaries, contact events and metric object pose be recovered from one camera or RGB-D tracking of bimanual human demonstrations, accurately enough to serve as a policy's observable stage and state signal? And does supplying that signal measurably lower full-task failure and shift-induced degradation on a real benchmark such as UMI-Bench T3/T9 and its Factor-B splits, compared with scaling demonstrations alone?

research_questions.question: RQ1 (main paper). Error budget for human-demonstration capture: how accurate must the capture of a human demonstration be (object 6D pose, hand pose, contact timing and stage-boundary placement) for policies built from it to keep working on multi-stage tasks and under geometric shift? Which error type, and which stage, dominates the compounding failure?
research_questions.why_top_venue: Human-video-to-robot-data pipelines are a fast-growing 2025-2026 line: VideoManip (arXiv 2602.09013), DexImit (2602.10105), Real2Render2Real (2505.09601), EgoWild2Dex (2609.23755, listing only) and DexMachina (2505.24853, listing only). All of them treat 3D hand-object reconstruction as a preprocessing step. In the abstracts I fetched (VideoManip, DexImit, R2R2R), none reports how reconstruction error propagates to policy success. The two mechanisms the pain point names, small placement deviations compounding until a tight tolerance fails and the stage estimate being lost, are both error-propagation claims that nobody has quantified. An empirical error budget, plus a per-stage compounding model that predicts full-task success from measured tracker error, would give both communities something they lack. It tells trackers what accuracy to aim for and tells policy builders which capture errors to fix first. Careful analysis papers of this kind have been accepted at CoRL before; robomimic's 'What matters in learning from offline human demonstrations' (CoRL 2021) is an example I recall from memory. Caveat: my search was limited (arXiv API queries only, because the shared WebSearch budget was used up), so a similar study may exist and has to be ruled out first.
research_questions.method_sketch: (1) Real error model. Run off-the-shelf trackers on public RGB-D hand-object datasets with ground truth: an object 6D tracker such as FoundationPose with CAD models, and a hand estimator such as HaMeR or WiLoR. Candidate datasets are DexYCB, HO3D v3, HOT3D and ARCTIC. Fit translation and rotation error distributions conditioned on visible fraction (from ground-truth masks), contact state, object symmetry and speed. Model temporal structure as jitter versus drift (an AR(1) or Gaussian-process residual), and add contact onset and offset timing error and stage-boundary offset. (2) Corruption harness. In public MimicGen and DexMimicGen simulation tasks, the source demonstrations come with object poses and subtask segments. MimicGen transforms object-centric segments relative to the object pose at each segment start; that description comes from the paper body as I recall it, not from the abstract I fetched. Replace the ground-truth object poses, segment boundaries and end-effector trajectory with samples from the error model, scaled from 0 to the 90th-percentile error under heavy occlusion. (3) Generate data with the MimicGen pipeline (CPU-bound). Train robomimic BC-RNN on low-dimensional state for the full sweep and a diffusion policy on images for a subset. (4) Evaluate on the default initial distribution and on the broader ones MimicGen ships (D1/D2), which serve as the geometric-shift test. (5) Fit P(success) = prod_k f_k(e_k) over stages k and test whether it predicts held-out error combinations. Report which error type, at which stage, accounts for most of the loss. (6) Optional real check: measure one real tracker error sample against a known metric object pose and place it on the budget curves.
research_questions.minimum_experiment: Three MimicGen tasks: one short task and two multi-stage tasks such as Coffee Preparation or Three Piece Assembly. Four error types: object translation, object rotation, stage-boundary offset and temporally correlated drift. Four levels spanning the measured tracker error range, three seeds, and 1,000 generated demonstrations per condition. Train low-dimensional BC-RNN policies and evaluate 50 rollouts each on D0 and D1, about 150 policies plus ground-truth baselines. The paper's claim stands if the curves show a clear nonlinearity or ranking that one could not guess beforehand (for example, stage-boundary or rotation error dominating translation error on multi-stage tasks) and the compounding model predicts held-out conditions within a few points. Extension for a stronger paper: one bimanual DexMimicGen task and an image-based diffusion-policy subset.
research_questions.data_and_hardware: No robot and no motion capture needed for the core study. Data: MimicGen and DexMimicGen source demonstrations and environments, which are public per their abstracts. DexYCB, HO3D v3, HOT3D and ARCTIC for the error model, plus object CAD models for FoundationPose. Hardware: one workstation GPU with 24 GB or more. Low-dimensional BC-RNN runs take roughly 1-2 GPU-hours each, which is about 10-15 GPU-days for the minimum sweep; this is my estimate, not measured. MuJoCo data generation runs in parallel on CPU cores. The consumer RGB-D camera is used only for the optional real error sample. A borrowed arm for 1-2 real tasks at about 20 trials each would greatly strengthen a CoRL or RSS submission.
research_questions.risks: (a) No real robot. CoRL and RSS reviewers may reject simulation-only conclusions, so a borrowed arm or a collaborator should be arranged by month 9. (b) The result may look obvious or depend on the consumer: MimicGen-style segment replay may be insensitive to some errors that end-to-end visual policies are sensitive to. Use two consumers (segment replay with BC, and a point-cloud or image policy) to make the conclusion general. (c) The embodiment and retargeting gap may outweigh tracking error, which would make the budget less relevant. Measure it as one more error term instead of ignoring it. (d) Error models fitted on lab datasets may not transfer to in-the-wild video. (e) A competing analysis may appear within months in a crowded area; my search for prior error-propagation studies was shallow (arXiv API only). (f) Compute: image-based sweeps will not fit on one GPU, so keep them to a subset.
target_venues: NeurIPS (Datasets and Benchmarks track, if released as a reusable harness)

research_questions.question: RQ2. Uncertainty-labelled demonstrations: can a causal single-view RGB-D hand-object tracker label each frame's object and hand state with calibrated uncertainty, as measured (directly observed), held (carried through occlusion) or constrained (inferred from grasp or kinematics)? And does using those labels to gate or weight generated demonstrations recover the policy success lost to occlusion-induced capture error?
research_questions.why_top_venue: The human-video-to-robot pipelines named above pass every reconstructed frame downstream as if it were equally trustworthy. In bimanual handling the object is most heavily occluded during the grasp and transport stages, which is exactly where placement deviations start to compound. Calibrated, coverage-guaranteed per-frame uncertainty under hand occlusion, shown to matter downstream, connects 3D hand-object tracking (CVPR/ICCV community) with demonstration capture (CoRL/ICRA community). Standalone pose-uncertainty work exists, for example conformal keypoint detection (recalled from memory, unverified), but I found no work that ties such uncertainty to data generation for long-horizon policies. The novelty is in that link, not in the uncertainty method itself.
research_questions.method_sketch: (1) Train a lightweight error regressor on top of a frozen tracker. Features: visible fraction from the tracker's rendered mask versus segmentation, depth residual, tracker score, hand-object distance and time since the last confident observation. Calibrate its intervals with split conformal prediction on DexYCB or HOT3D. (2) Map the intervals and the occlusion and grasp state to measured, held or constrained labels. (3) Downstream, in the RQ1 harness with real-error-model corruptions: (i) anchor each generated segment at the nearest measured frame instead of the nominal boundary; (ii) weight the behavior-cloning loss by inverse predicted error; (iii) reject source segments whose anchor frame is constrained only. (4) Compare against ground-truth demonstrations, untreated corrupted demonstrations and naive confidence thresholding.
research_questions.minimum_experiment: One object tracker (FoundationPose) calibrated on one dataset (DexYCB or HOT3D). Report empirical coverage and interval width per occlusion stratum, with coverage within 2 points of nominal as the target. Then two multi-stage tasks from the RQ1 harness at the realistic error level, three seeds. Success criterion: label-aware anchoring or weighting recovers a clearly significant share of the gap between corrupted and ground-truth demonstrations (for example, more than half), at equal demonstration count.
research_questions.data_and_hardware: The same public datasets and simulation harness as RQ1, one GPU, and no robot. The consumer RGB-D camera is optional, for a qualitative real demonstration of the labels on bimanual desk recordings.
research_questions.risks: (a) Uncertainty may be poorly predictable for symmetric or textureless objects, giving wide, useless intervals. (b) Gating may discard so much data that it costs more than the errors it removes. (c) Reviewers may call it an incremental combination of conformal prediction and MimicGen, unless the downstream gain is large and the labels clearly beat naive confidence thresholds. (d) It depends on RQ1's harness being built first. (e) Realistic venue level is ICRA or RA-L; reaching CoRL needs real-robot evidence.

research_questions.question: RQ3 (supporting; not a standalone top-venue bet). Can stage boundaries and contact events in bimanual human demonstrations be recovered causally from single-view RGB-D hand-object tracking, with frame-level accuracy under occlusion? Does the measured stage-boundary error fall inside the budget RQ1 derives?
research_questions.why_top_venue: The pain point attributes long-horizon failure partly to demonstrations that lack explicit stage structure, and DexImit already performs subtask decomposition from monocular video (its abstract gives no method details). Policy-side stage and memory modules are now crowded with September 2026 work: TaskAnchor (2609.23580, verified abstract), ActMem-VLA (2609.37307, listing only) and RB-VLA (2602.20659, listing only). A small lab should therefore not pitch a policy method. On its own, a capture-side causal stage and contact detector is an ICRA/IROS-level contribution. It adds top-venue value only as the measured stage-error input that closes the loop in RQ1.
research_questions.method_sketch: Derive contact events from tracked hand-mesh to object-mesh distance, depth consistency and object-motion onset (the object moves only when grasped). Decode a causal segment model (an HMM or online temporal segmentation) over primitive sequences. Train and test on OakInk2, which has bimanual sequences with affordance, primitive-task and complex-task levels (verified from its abstract). Use a single camera from its multi-view set to simulate one view. Use ARCTIC ground-truth contact for event timing. Report boundary F1 at 3, 5 and 10 frames, causal detection latency and contact-onset error. Feed the measured boundary-error distribution into the RQ1 harness.
research_questions.minimum_experiment: OakInk2 single-camera evaluation of boundary F1 and latency against an offline (non-causal) upper bound and an appearance-only temporal segmentation baseline. Then one RQ1 run that uses the measured boundary error instead of synthetic levels.
research_questions.data_and_hardware: OakInk2 and ARCTIC (public), one GPU, no robot.
research_questions.risks: (a) OakInk2 primitive annotations may not be precise enough at frame level to score boundaries finely; check this first. (b) Contact from mesh distance is noisy under occlusion, which is the very regime of interest. (c) Overlap with DexImit's decomposition stage and with policy-side stage modules makes standalone novelty thin. (d) The single-view setting may simply be worse than multi-view without a new insight.

fit.thesis_assets_help: Small. The pain point is peripheral to the author's field, and the core contribution (RQ1) depends on public simulation harnesses and public hand-object datasets, not on the thesis rig. Where the assets truly help: (1) The measured, held and constrained honesty labels plus the causal 30 fps chain are a working prototype of RQ2's per-frame state labelling. That saves design time, but the labels would need calibrated, coverage-guaranteed uncertainty to be publishable. (2) The ArUco-marked object with metric pose gives a real, in-house error sample for a tracked object under bimanual hand occlusion, which can be placed on the RQ1 budget curves as the optional real check. Its value is limited by one object, one subject and the marker itself altering appearance, and public datasets (DexYCB, HOT3D, ARCTIC) are better sources for the error model. Little or no help: the Unity twin (robot-learning work here uses MuJoCo/robosuite, ManiSkill or IsaacLab, and MimicGen and DexMimicGen run on robosuite), the 28 recordings of one subject (too small and too narrow for a dataset contribution; useful only for a qualitative figure), and the object-conditioned recovery of the occluded holding arm (object-centric data generation does not use human arm configuration).
fit.what_a_small_lab_cannot_do_here: Five things are out of reach. (1) Real-world long-horizon policy evaluation at benchmark scale, because UMI-Bench-style protocols need robot arms, scene resets and dozens of episodes per task and condition; without at least a borrowed arm the work stays in simulation, which CoRL and RSS reviewers discount. (2) The fixes that currently move the numbers: VLA pretraining, RL post-training and on-policy correction (pi*0.6 with RECAP, SimpleVLA-RL, PARTS), which need multi-GPU clusters and robot fleets or hours of real robot interaction. (3) Policy-side stage and memory modules for VLAs (TaskAnchor, ActMem-VLA, RB-VLA, BATON, all from 2026), where large groups publish monthly and fine-tuning a VLA does not fit on one GPU. (4) End-to-end human-video-to-robot pipelines validated on real dexterous or bimanual hardware (DexImit, VideoManip, EgoWild2Dex, R2R2R), which need robot hands, arms and multi-task real trials. (5) New large multi-subject capture datasets, which need motion capture or multi-camera rigs and many participants. The feasible niche is narrow: capture-side measurement in simulation using public data, namely the error budget, calibrated per-frame uncertainty and stage-event recovery. Even there the risk is real that a larger group publishes a similar analysis inside the 12-18 month window. Note on evidence: the shared WebSearch budget was exhausted before this task's first search ran, so the novelty checks relied on fetched arXiv abstracts and arXiv API keyword queries. Items marked "listing only" were seen only as arXiv API titles and summaries, and the lack of a prior error-propagation study is not exhaustively verified.

painpoint.name: Photoreal avatars of new people without studio capture

evidence.latest_state: The "studio capture per subject" part of P39 has largely been answered for heads since 2025. Feed-forward models trained on dome data plus synthetic identities now produce animatable Gaussian head avatars from one image or a phone video in about a second, with no per-identity optimization. The clearest numbers come from UIKA (CVPR 2026 Highlight; training data includes 7,500 synthetic identities). On NeRSemble-v2 monocular self-reenactment it reports PSNR 21.69, SSIM 0.867 and LPIPS 0.105, against GAGAvatar at 20.34 / 0.850 / 0.160 and LAM at 18.29 / LPIPS 0.206. In the multi-view setting it reaches PSNR 22.50 against 17.11 for GPAvatar. LAM reports VFHQ PSNR 22.65, SSIM 0.829, LPIPS 0.109 and HDTF PSNR 23.43, and renders at 35 FPS on an iPhone 16. For bodies, IDOL, LHM, GUAVA, FRESA, DiGS-Avatar (0.71 s) and Vid2Avatar-Pro reconstruct animatable avatars from a single image or monocular video, the last using a universal prior. HRM2Avatar (SIGGRAPH Asia 2025) builds avatars from monocular phone scans and renders them at 120 FPS on mobile and 90 FPS on VR headsets at 2K. Several problems stay open. Absolute fidelity is still well below studio level (around 22 dB PSNR, against more than 30 dB for per-subject dome avatars). Expressions outside FLAME are still not reproduced: LAM and UIKA both state that they cannot model tongue motion, dynamic wrinkles or micro-expressions. Relightable universal avatars (URAvatar, FiCA, LUCAS, HairCUP) come mainly from Meta and depend on private dome corpora of hundreds of subjects. UIKA notes demographic bias. Hands and full bodies interacting with objects are not covered by these feed-forward avatar models. No search turned up a paper that adds subjects to the 4-subject paired dome-headset-phone capture (Goliath-4), though this was not checked thoroughly.

evidence.crowdedness: HIGH. The arXiv listings alone show more than 15 feed-forward or universal-prior avatar papers in 2025-2026, from large, well-resourced groups: Meta Codec Avatars (FiCA, URAvatar, LUCAS, HairCUP, Vid2Avatar-Pro, Avat3r), Alibaba/Tongyi (LAM, LHM), Ant Research with Nanjing University (UIKA), plus TUM and many Chinese labs.
evidence.trend: Rising. Large reconstruction models, Gaussian splatting and video-diffusion synthetic data made one-shot animatable avatars feasible in 2025. New one-shot head and body avatar papers appeared every month through September 2026, along with CVPR 2026 highlights and work on mobile and VR deployment.

skeptics.reasons:
The pain point says photoreal, driveable head, hand and body avatars cannot be built for a new person from phone, headset or monocular input. That claim no longer holds in 2024-2026. Its own evidence comes almost entirely from 2022-2023 dataset papers (Multiface, RenderMe-360, HumanRF/ActorsHQ, Ava-256/Goliath), and the work since then answers each of its sub-claims directly.

(1) Studio capture per subject is not needed. URAvatar (SIGGRAPH Asia 2024) builds relightable Gaussian codec head avatars from a phone scan taken under unknown lighting, and they animate and relight in real time. Authentic Hand Avatar (CVPR 2024) builds a high-fidelity hand avatar from a short phone scan using a universal hand model. Vid2Avatar-Pro (2025) builds clothed full-body avatars from in-the-wild monocular video and animates them to novel motions.

(2) Per-identity fitting has been replaced by feed-forward models. All of these work from one image or a few images in seconds or less, with no test-time optimization: LHM (2025) for bodies; LAM (2025, real-time even on phones), Avat3r (2025, smartphone captures with inconsistent expressions) and FiCA (2026) for heads; HumanNOVA (CVPR 2026 Highlight) for full bodies in under one second; and UIKA and the two FFAvatar papers (2026). Reconstruction for an unseen identity is now a single forward pass.

(3) Headset driving now works for unseen users. Universal Facial Encoding of Codec Avatars from VR Headsets (SIGGRAPH 2024) drives photoreal avatars of previously unseen users in real time from consumer headset cameras, including extreme expressions.

(4) There is a shipping product. In visionOS 26 (2025), Apple Personas are created on the headset in seconds, with volumetric rendering, a full side profile and accurate hair. This is commodity-sensor avatar creation at product scale.

What survives is narrower than the stated pain point:
- The universal priors are still trained on dome or multi-view studio data (URAvatar on hundreds of light-stage scans, Vid2Avatar-Pro on a multi-view capture corpus, Avat3r on a large multi-view video dataset). Studio capture has moved from per subject to building the prior; it has not been removed.
- No public result shows quantitatively that phone-built avatars match personalized dome avatars on unseen identities, tongue or extreme expressions, or loose garments. FiCA itself says single-image avatars are limited by the visual information available.
- Distributing data at full fidelity is still an access problem, but that is a logistics issue, not a research gap.
- None of these systems models hands or bodies in contact with objects (contact deformation, occlusion by the object, object appearance), which is the only part that touches the author's hand-object field.

Overall: as stated, the pain point is solved or reduced to engineering, and its relevance to the author was already peripheral.

Verification: all papers listed were checked by fetching their arXiv abstract pages, and Personas by fetching the Apple newsroom page. Venue labels marked 'not verified' were not checked. The WebSearch budget was exhausted, so all lookups went through the arXiv API and WebFetch.

skeptics.reframe: Phone, headset and single-image avatar creation is solved through universal priors trained on studio data. What remains open is narrower. (a) There is no open benchmark that measures the fidelity gap between avatars built from lightweight input and personalized dome avatars on unseen identities and out-of-distribution expressions or poses; Goliath-4, with only 4 paired subjects, is the only paired reference. (b) Hands and bodies in contact with objects are not handled: universal-prior avatars model the person alone, not contact deformation, occlusion by the object or the joint appearance of hand and object. Only (b) touches the author's field.

skeptics.reasons:
P39 is not an artifact of a single group. The 12 paper ids (ids are 1-based into field_papers.json) resolve to 11 distinct papers, because 438 and 1430 are both Codec Avatar Studio (Ava-256/Goliath). They come from Meta Reality Labs (Codec Avatar Studio, Multiface, Auto-CARD), Shanghai AI Lab/SenseTime (RenderMe-360, DNA-Rendering), CUHK-SZ (MVHumanNet, MVHumanNet++), TUM (NeRSemble), Synthesia/UCL (HumanRF/ActorsHQ), MPI (HumanOLAT), plus SmartPortraits, MVP-Human and a survey. The statement as written still fails the artifact lens for four reasons.

(1) Every source is a dataset paper from one community: studio-dome avatars and neural rendering. Each states its own limitations in the dome-capture convention ("we need N cameras; error rises with fewer views"). This is a self-referential community framing, not a field-wide failure. It is also peripheral to the author's field, hand-object and bimanual tracking.

(2) The evidence is dated. About 8 of the 11 papers are from 2022-2023. Their "cannot yet" and "future work: generalize over identities" items have since been addressed head-on by feed-forward and universal-prior work: GAGAvatar (NeurIPS 2024, single image, unseen identities, real-time reenactment); URAvatar (SIGGRAPH Asia 2024, relightable and drivable Gaussian codec head avatars from a phone scan using a universal prior trained on hundreds of identities); Avat3r (2025, animatable head avatars from a few images, generalizing to new identities); and LHM (2025, an animatable full-body avatar from a single image in seconds). "Cannot yet be built from phone or monocular input" is therefore false as stated. What survives is a fidelity gap between phone-built and dome-built avatars, plus weak extrapolation to out-of-distribution expressions such as tongue-out and to rare poses and loose garments. That residual is real but incremental.

(3) Several evidence items describe one release's setup, not a field condition. "Only 4 subjects carry the full paired capture" and "petabyte captures cannot be distributed at full fidelity, so Ava-256 is downsampled" are facts about Meta's Goliath/Ava-256 release. "Experiments use 62% of the data" is MVHumanNet++'s own compute choice. "About one day on eight V100s per identity" is a per-identity-optimization convention that feed-forward methods have since dropped.

(4) The data-scarcity claim conflicts with the trend in the same evidence: MVHumanNet (thousands of identities), RenderMe-360 (500 identities), DNA-Rendering and Ava-256 (256 identities) were released precisely to scale up multi-view human data.

Verdict: the broad pain point is partly an artifact of the dome-capture community's dataset-paper conventions and an older snapshot. The narrower residual gap is not refuted.

Verification notes: the web-search budget was exhausted after the first search attempt, so counter-evidence was verified by fetching the arXiv abstract pages directly. Cao et al., "Authentic Volumetric Avatars from a Phone Scan" (SIGGRAPH 2022), another known counterexample, could not be verified in this session.

skeptics.reframe: Avatars of new people built in a feed-forward way from a phone, a single image or a few images (GAGAvatar, URAvatar, Avat3r, LHM) now exist. What remains open is a fidelity and extrapolation gap: these avatars still fall short of studio dome quality on fine detail, relighting, out-of-distribution expressions and loose clothing. The field also lacks a shared benchmark that pairs lightweight-sensor captures with dome captures across many identities. That residual concerns the avatar and graphics community, not hand-object or bimanual tracking.

skeptics.reasons: Skeptic 3 tried to refute P39 as having no research question. It is not refuted. Two parts of the pain point are only engineering and resources: petabyte-scale captures that cannot be distributed, and paired dome, headset and phone data that exists for only four Goliath subjects. Those two parts would yield no research question on their own. The core problem is different. Building a photoreal, driveable avatar of an unseen person from phone or monocular input, and driving it to expressions and poses outside those captured, is an open question about generalization and learned priors. More cameras or more annotation money do not settle it. The record's own benchmark evidence shows this. On RenderMe-360, methods lose more on unseen identities than on unseen expressions, and NeRFace, IMAvatar and PointAvatar fail on out-of-distribution expressions such as tongue out. These are method failures, not gaps in data size. Recent top-venue work confirms that the problem is open and publishable rather than solved. I verified three papers on arXiv. URAvatar (SIGGRAPH Asia 2024) learns a universal prior from dome captures and personalizes it from a phone scan. Avat3r and LAM (both 2025 arXiv; their venues were not verified here) regress animatable Gaussian head avatars feed-forward from a few images or from one image. Each still works only on heads, needs a per-user step or loses fidelity in rare cases, and leaves full-body, hand and interaction avatars largely open. A reviewer would rate the following questions significant. (1) How can a prior learned from a few studio subjects be transferred to phone or monocular captures, with guarantees about identity fidelity on the long tail? (2) Can one model be built that controls expression and pose outside the training range? (3) Can studio-quality supervision be replaced by self-supervision from in-the-wild video? Two things weaken the pain point. The head-avatar part is crowded, with groups at Meta, TUM and Alibaba competing on it. Its relevance to this author's field, hand-object and bimanual tracking, is peripheral. The score is held at 7 for those reasons. The angle that best fits the author's field and is least crowded is avatars of hands and arms that make contact with objects. Search budget ran out (0 of 6 searches used, both blocked), so the papers were checked with WebFetch only.

skeptics.reframe: Studio-trained universal priors do not carry over to new people captured on phone or monocular video. They lose identity on long-tail faces and bodies, and they cannot drive expressions or poses outside those captured. The open research question is how to learn priors that generalize across identities and control articulation outside the training range, supervised by in-the-wild video instead of dome captures. Heads are already crowded. For this author the open and relevant angle is hands and arms during object contact.

painpoint.name: Hair, thin structures and light transport are not modelled

evidence.latest_state:
Since 2025, Gaussian-splatting avatars have made clear progress on each part of P40, but no method yet covers all of it. For dynamic hair, strand-guided Gaussian methods learn hair motion from data or couple Gaussians to a physics simulator: DGH (NeurIPS 2025), PhysHead (CVPR 2026) and DynHair (arXiv 2607.23861, July 2026). This directly targets the 'deformation field cannot capture fast hair motion' failure. The abstracts I read give no numbers for these three, and none reports results on the RenderMe-360 curly-hair subset. For relighting, several 2025-2026 methods move away from per-subject OLAT data:
- BecomingLit (NeurIPS 2025) builds a low-cost light stage and adds an analytical specular term.
- Relightable Full-Body Gaussian Codec Avatars (arXiv 2501.14726) models non-local shadows and specular for the full body.
- RelightAnyone (arXiv 2601.03357) relights without per-subject OLAT capture.
- Relightable Holoported Characters (MPI, arXiv 2512.00255) relights in a single pass from random environment-map capture.
- D-Rex (arXiv 2604.27871) uses diffusion-based relighting.
- Large-scale Codec Avatars (CVPR 2026) reports zero-shot relightability after pretraining on 1M in-the-wild videos.
Self-shadowing gets explicit treatment in DNF-Avatar (ICCV 2025 Findings, 67 FPS, ambient-occlusion probes), Deep Gaussian Shadow Maps (arXiv 2601.01660) and ARS-Avatar (arXiv 2609.27600). Mouth interior and teeth are addressed by HyperGaussians (CVPR 2026), GeoAvatar (ICCV 2025), STAvatar (CVPR 2026), TexAvatars (3DV 2026) and CAG-Avatar. I found no 2025-2026 paper that models eye refraction or subsurface scattering explicitly in a dynamic avatar. HumanOLAT (ICCV 2025) remains the main public full-body OLAT benchmark, and I found no published number that beats its baselines. Relightable data stay scarce: the newer methods work around this with generative priors rather than more light-stage subjects. None of this work involves hands manipulating objects, so its relevance to the author's field stays peripheral.

evidence.crowdedness: HIGH. About 14 relevant 2025-2026 papers turned up from a few arXiv queries, many at CVPR, ICCV and NeurIPS, from well-resourced capture groups: Meta Codec Avatars, MPI Informatik, MPI-IS/Tuebingen, TUM, ETH. They own light stages and dome rigs that a small lab cannot match.
evidence.trend: Rising. Relightable and hair-dynamic Gaussian avatars are posting steadily from 2025 through September 2026 (ARS-Avatar, SAMIRA and Heartian all appeared in September 2026). Activity is shifting from per-subject OLAT fitting to large-scale pretraining and diffusion priors, and from rigid hair shells to simulated strands.

skeptics.reasons: Not refuted, but 2025-2026 work has cut it down, and it sits outside the author's field. Parts that no longer hold: (1) "Relightable data exist for only a few subjects." URAvatar (arXiv 2410.24223) trains a universal relightable Gaussian head prior on hundreds of multi-view scans lit by controllable point lights. BecomingLit (arXiv 2506.06271, 2025) builds a cheaper light stage and collects a new multi-subject relightable head dataset. RelightAnyone (arXiv 2601.03357, 2026) relights a new subject without capturing OLAT data for that subject. The scarcity that remains is about public access (the large sets are proprietary Meta captures), not whether such data can exist. (2) "No body relighting with self-shadowing." Relightable Full-Body Gaussian Codec Avatars (arXiv 2501.14726, 2025) explicitly handles non-local shadows between body parts with a shadow network and claims to generalize to unseen poses and lights. (3) Teeth, mouth interior and thin accessories get steady incremental gains: STAvatar (2511.19854) targets occluded mouth interiors and eyelids, HyperGaussians (2507.02803) targets teeth and eyeglass frames, CAG-Avatar (2601.14844) targets teeth, and Audio-Driven Universal Gaussian Head Avatars (2509.18924) models the mouth interior across identities. (4) Dynamic hair: DGH, Dynamic Gaussian Hair (2512.17094, Dec 2025), learns hair dynamics from data across many hairstyles. Parts that still hold: I found no 2025-2026 result that saturates the RenderMe-360 curly-hair subset or the HumanOLAT novel-light benchmark. I found no released model that models eye refraction, sharp shadows and specular highlights in dynamic capture together. Fast hair motion and refraction remain open. So this is still a research problem, but it is narrower than stated, and most of the frontier is driven by industry labs with light stages, which a small lab cannot reach. Relevance to the author's field (hand-object, bimanual RGB-D tracking) is peripheral. The only overlap is thin and specular or transparent objects in hand-object capture, and this record does not cover that. Verification limit: the WebSearch budget was used up, so every title was checked only through arXiv API abstracts. The claims above come from abstracts, not from reading benchmark tables.

skeptics.reframe: Relightable avatars now scale to many subjects and handle shadows between body parts, but only inside proprietary light-stage captures. What stays open is dynamic capture of fast or curly hair, eye refraction and sharp specular highlights, and the lack of open, multi-subject, dynamic OLAT data to benchmark them. This is peripheral to hand-object tracking; the nearest version in this field is thin, specular or transparent handheld objects under occlusion.

skeptics.reasons: P40 holds only inside one community: dense-studio head and body avatar capture. As a field-level pain point it is mostly an artifact. (1) The evidence is narrow and comes from one genre. Paper ids 438 and 1430 are the same NeurIPS 2024 Codec Avatar Studio paper, so there are 5 distinct papers, not 6. Two come from Meta Reality Labs (Multiface and Codec Avatar Studio). The other three are RenderMe-360 (Shanghai AI Lab), NeRSemble (TUM) and HumanOLAT (MPI/Saarland). All five are dataset papers from the head or full-body avatar community. Each reports failures of its own chosen baselines (NR-NeRF, IM Avatar, Instant-NGP, PRT-Gaussian, IC-Light) on its own new capture. That is the usual "limitations of the baselines" section of a dataset release, not independent confirmation across settings. None of the papers is about hand-object, body-object or bimanual tracking, RGB-D, or robot demonstration capture, which is the author's field. The record's own relevance tag is "peripheral". (2) The record bundles four separate problems into one statement: hair, thin structures, mouth and eye optics, and relighting/subsurface scattering. Each has its own dedicated literature, so treating them as one unmodelled problem is a framing artifact. Hair has strand-based and light-aware methods: Neural Haircut (ICCV 2023) and GaussianHair (2024). Subsurface scattering has Subsurface Scattering for 3D Gaussian Splatting (2024) and SSD-GS (2026). The graphics/light-stage community has long handled relighting with OLAT capture. These methods are not perfect, but the open problem is active and owned by graphics. (3) The most concrete and checkable sub-claim, that relightable data exist only for 21 static HumanOLAT subjects and 4 Goliath subjects, is out of date by 2026-10. POLAR (arXiv 2512.13192) releases an OLAT dataset with over 200 subjects, 156 lights, multiple views and expressions. 3DPR (arXiv 2510.15846) adds a multi-view 4K OLAT set of 139 subjects. URHand (CVPR 2024, Meta) trains on light-stage data from hundreds of hand identities. Relightable Holoported Characters (arXiv 2512.00255) and BodyReLux (arXiv 2605.21766) capture dynamic performances under time-multiplexed or interleaved lighting. These directly contradict "few subjects in static poses". The scarcity is a snapshot of the cited papers and of public release policy, not a lasting field limit. (4) The part that survives: public, dynamic, multi-identity relightable capture that includes hands and objects remains rare, and neural representations still blur specular highlights and sharp shadows. That residue belongs to graphics and avatar work, not to 3D hand-object tracking. Verdict: refuted as a field-level pain point for this author; at most a peripheral graphics issue.

skeptics.reframe: The part that survives is narrow: there is no public, dynamic, multi-identity relightable capture of hands manipulating objects, so relightable or physically based digital twins of hand-object interaction cannot be trained or benchmarked. Head-only OLAT sets (POLAR, 3DPR) and hand-only or static full-body sets (URHand, HumanOLAT) do not cover contact, objects or motion.

skeptics.reasons: P40 is only partly refuted. As written it bundles six separate effects: fast or curly hair, teeth and the mouth interior, eye specularity and refraction, subsurface scattering, sharp self-shadows, and the shortage of relightable data. Its own why_it_persists field puts the bottleneck in light stages with time-multiplexed illumination, which few labs have. That part is a wish for money and capture time, not a research question. The known fix also already exists and is being scaled by labs that do have the resources. Relightable Gaussian Codec Avatars (CVPR 2024), URAvatar (SIGGRAPH Asia 2024), RelightableHands and URHand all learn relightable universal priors from large light-stage captures and then personalise them from phone scans. A thesis author without a light stage would be competing with Meta Reality Labs on its own data, so the head-avatar version of P40 does not suit this author. That version is also peripheral to the field: none of the five evidence papers involves hands, objects, bimanual handling or RGB-D tracking. It does not fully reduce to engineering, though. Hair dynamics, eye refraction and mouth occlusion are open modelling problems, and they still appear in CVPR and SIGGRAPH papers. More importantly, when the light-transport part is moved into this author's field, it yields a question a reviewer would find significant. When a hand grasps an object, the two surfaces cast shadows on each other, reflect light onto each other and block each other at the contact points. These effects are lighting cues about the contact itself. Current hand-object trackers and digital-twin reconstructions bake them into the texture or treat them as noise, and the relightable hand models above (RelightableHands, URHand) model the hand alone, with no object. That gives three testable claims. First, modelling hand-object shading explicitly could serve as a cue for contact and depth that helps under occlusion. Second, it could make the reconstructed digital twin relightable for sim-to-real use. Third, thin, specular or transparent objects, which break RGB-D depth, may be recoverable through a light-transport-aware model. I could not verify, within the search budget, that no prior work already does this, so the novelty is unconfirmed. The score is held down by the bundled framing, the data-bound core, peripheral relevance and the fact that a capture rig may still be needed to supervise the model.
