evidence.title: Prior work on relightable or light-transport-aware hand-object reconstruction (mutual shadowing and interreflection at contact)

skeptics.reframe: Hand-object 3D reconstruction and digital-twin capture treat light transport as nuisance appearance, yet the shadows and reflections that a grasping hand and the held object cast on each other are a cue for contact and occlusion. Research question: from multi-view RGB-D under uncontrolled lighting, can a model that represents the hand and object shading jointly (visibility, cast shadows, interreflection, specular and transparent surfaces) improve contact and pose accuracy under occlusion? Can it also produce a hand-object digital twin that relights correctly, without the per-subject light-stage capture that current relightable hand and head models need?

research_questions.question: RQ1 (recommended first). Can one consumer RGB-D camera track the metric 6-DoF pose of transparent and specular hand-held objects (glasses, bottles, metal mugs, cutlery) during manipulation? The approach treats depth failure and refraction as structured evidence that light transport explains, not as noise, and uses the tracked hand both as a grasp constraint and as a known background seen through the object.
research_questions.why_top_venue: Current RGB-D object trackers and hand-object methods assume opaque surfaces with valid depth. Glass and metal objects are common in household demonstrations, yet existing transparent-object resources are static, synthetic or shape-only. ClearPose (ECCV 2022, verified) has 350K real RGB-D frames, but the scenes are static and not hand-held. HADR (arXiv 2408.14997, verified) does single-image depth restoration trained on the synthetic TransHand-14K. CHOC (arXiv 2211.10470, ICASSP 2023 submission) is a mixed-reality synthetic set of hand-occluded containers. StereoHO (arXiv 2412.07487, verified) reconstructs shape from stereo RGB and estimates no tracked metric pose. A real, dynamic benchmark of hand-held transparent and specular objects with metric ground truth, plus a tracker that explains the sensor's failure modes, is the in-field version of P40's 'light transport is not modelled'. It also matters directly for robot demonstration capture. Caveat: the WebSearch budget was exhausted, so novelty was checked only through arXiv API keyword queries. A 2025-2026 paper may have been missed.
research_questions.method_sketch: (1) Sensor-aware depth likelihood. For each pixel, render the object CAD at the current pose hypothesis and predict one of three depth outcomes: valid surface return, return from the background through the object (common on glass), or dropout or specular outlier (common on metal). Score the observed depth under this mixture instead of trusting or discarding it. Learn the mixture weights per sensor type (active stereo versus ToF) from a small calibration set. (2) RGB term. Silhouette and edge alignment, plus an environment-matting-style refraction term in which the reconstructed static background and the tracked MANO hand behind the object act as a known texture: their apparent displacement through the glass constrains pose. (3) Hand prior. The opaque hand is tracked reliably from RGB-D. Contact and non-penetration constraints with the object, and grasp-conditioned temporal smoothing, keep pose estimates going through frames where the object is nearly invisible. (4) A causal per-frame refiner, initialized from FoundationPose or a similar render-and-compare model, with a per-frame reliability flag that marks which pose components come from measurement and which are inferred. (5) Pretraining on Blender Cycles path-traced renders: public grasps (DexYCB, OakInk2) applied to transparent and metal meshes, under HDR environment maps.
research_questions.minimum_experiment: Use 8-12 objects: 4 glass, 4 metal and 2-4 opaque controls. Get CAD by scanning each object under vanishing scanning spray, or from manufacturer models. Record about 40 sequences with 2-3 subjects. One RGB-D test camera sees the clean object. A second RGB-D or RGB ground-truth camera sees ArUco markers on a small rigid clip on the hidden side, giving metric object pose without putting marker cues in the test view. Report ADD-S, BOP AR, translation error in mm, tracking-loss rate and hand-object penetration. Baselines: FoundationPose and BundleSDF on raw depth; FoundationPose after transparent depth completion (a TransCG- or ClearGrasp-style model, or HADR); RGB-only FoundationPose. Ablations: sensor model off, hand prior off, refraction term off. Run on both an active-stereo sensor (RealSense) and a ToF sensor (Azure Kinect or Orbbec), because glass behaves differently on each. Include the opaque controls to show no regression.
research_questions.data_and_hardware: Two consumer RGB-D cameras (about 300-500 USD each); printed ArUco clips; household glass and metal objects; scanning spray; one workstation GPU for Blender rendering and the refiner. Public data for pretraining and priors: DexYCB, OakInk2 and HO3D grasps; the ClearPose meshes where they match purchasable objects; HDR maps from Poly Haven. Hand ground truth is not available without motion capture, so claims are limited to object pose plus hand-object plausibility.
research_questions.risks: (a) The novelty is not fully verified. (b) The refraction cue is weak for thick-walled glass, glass filled with liquid, and frosted glass, so gains may come mostly from the sensor model and the hand prior. (c) An RGB-only render-and-compare baseline may already be fairly strong, which shrinks the margin. (d) The marker clip changes the grasp and can leak into the test view (mitigate by masking and by checking a no-clip subset qualitatively). (e) Depth artifacts are specific to each sensor, so a learned sensor model may not transfer across devices. (f) Hand pose without ground truth limits the hand-side claims.

research_questions.question: RQ2. When hand-object interaction is reconstructed from RGB-D video under uncontrolled indoor lighting, does explicitly modelling the mutual light transport between hand and object improve contact accuracy and hand and object pose under occlusion, compared with methods that bake these effects into appearance? The effects are cast shadows, ambient occlusion that vanishes toward the contact point, skin-coloured interreflection and specular highlights.
research_questions.why_top_venue: The closest prior work stops just short of this. DIR, 'Dynamic Inverse Rendering for Enhanced Material-Lighting Decomposition' (arXiv 2607.09329, ECCV 2026, verified), relights rigidly moving hand-held objects but masks the hand out with SAM3. It names 'Modelling hand occlusions and more complex near-field light interactions in real scenes' as future work. TexHOI (arXiv 2501.03525, CVM 2025 / IEEE TVCG, verified) models hand visibility through 108 MANO-fitted spheres and a constant skin interreflection term, but only to recover object texture. It reports no effect on pose or contact and takes about 14 h per stage. HARP (CVPR 2023, verified) shows that shadow-aware rendering refines hand pose, for the hand alone. Turning the light transport between hand and object into a cue for contact and occlusion is plausibly new and addresses contact, the weakest output of current hand-object capture. Novelty was checked only against arXiv abstracts.
research_questions.method_sketch: Representation: MANO hand plus an object SDF or 2D Gaussian surfels, with a per-sequence environment light (spherical Gaussians or split-sum) and simple BRDFs (Lambertian skin with a learned albedo map; object diffuse and specular). Light transport: object visibility under the hand comes from a sphere proxy (as in TexHOI) or screen-space ray marching through the fused depth. A one-bounce near-field interreflection term comes from the hand albedo. The contact-shading prior is that occlusion tends to full occlusion as the gap goes to zero, which ties shading gradients to the hand-object distance field. Optimization: photometric, depth and silhouette losses, with contact and penetration kept as free variables, so that shading consistency can pull fingers into or out of contact. Optional active variant: a handheld or motorized LED lamp, calibrated with a chrome ball, produces sharp shadows in a few frames, as a casual low-cost light stage.
research_questions.minimum_experiment: (a) Synthetic study with exact ground truth: Blender Cycles renders of DexYCB, ARCTIC and OakInk2 grasp sequences under HDR maps and point lights, sweeping light hardness from diffuse to a single spot to find where the cue helps. Metrics: contact F1, penetration depth, MPJPE on occluded joints, object ADD-S, and relighting PSNR under a held-out light. (b) Real: HO3D v3 and DexYCB (RGB-D) and ARCTIC (RGB, mocap ground truth), focusing on the heavily occluded frames. Baselines: HOLD (CVPR 2024), BIGS (CVPR 2025), the interaction-aware 4DGS of arXiv 2511.14540, DIR and TexHOI where code exists. The core ablation is the same pipeline with the light-transport terms disabled. (c) Optional: a small real set of about 10 sequences under one moving lamp, with object ground truth from markers.
research_questions.data_and_hardware: Public datasets only for the core claim: HO3D, DexYCB, ARCTIC, OakInk2. Blender for synthetic ground truth, Poly Haven HDR maps, one GPU; per-sequence optimization is acceptable. Optional: one LED lamp and a chrome ball (under 100 USD). No light stage is needed.
research_questions.risks: (a) Diffuse indoor light gives weak, low-frequency cues, so gains on HO3D and DexYCB may fall within noise. The synthetic sweep must show the regime where the cue matters, or the paper has no story. (b) Ground-truth contact in these datasets is derived from fitted meshes with a distance threshold, so contact metrics are noisy. (c) With RGB-D input, depth already gives proximity, which reduces the marginal value of shading; the cue matters most where depth is missing or occluded. (d) Competition: the DIR authors named this as their next step. (e) Joint inverse rendering is ill-posed and may need strong priors, such as hand material from a multi-subject prior like PALM (arXiv 2511.05403; whether it is publicly released is unverified).

research_questions.question: RQ3 (lowest priority). Can a hand-object digital twin reconstructed from one casual RGB-D capture be relit accurately enough that training data rendered from it makes a hand-object pose estimator, or a visuomotor policy, more robust to unseen lighting than 2D relighting augmentation or a non-relightable 3DGS replay does?
research_questions.why_top_venue: It links P40's relighting thread to the field's digital-twin and robot-learning applications. Re:InterHand (NeurIPS 2023 D&B, verified) showed that relit data helps two-hand pose estimation, but for hands only and from Meta's light-stage-trained relighting network. ViserDex (arXiv 2604.11138, verified) randomizes appearance in Gaussian space for in-hand object pose but does not decompose light transport between hand and object. A relightable twin covering hand and object, built from a casual capture, with a downstream robustness test, would interest CoRL, ICRA and RA-L. It is unlikely to reach CVPR level on its own.
research_questions.method_sketch: Reuse the RQ2 decomposition (hand albedo and BRDF, object BRDF, the light transport between them). Render the captured grasps under randomized HDR environments and point lights, with physically consistent shadows. Fine-tune an off-the-shelf hand estimator plus object pose estimator (for example a HaMeR-class hand model and FoundationPose) or a small visuomotor policy on these renders. Compare against color jitter, IC-Light-style image relighting and non-relightable 3DGS replay.
research_questions.minimum_experiment: Capture about 10 objects with a few grasps each under one lighting condition. Build a real test set of the same interactions under 4-5 distinct lighting setups (warm lamp, hard spot, window daylight, dim), with object ground truth from markers. Report object ADD-S and 2D hand keypoint error on each lighting split for each augmentation method.
research_questions.data_and_hardware: One or two consumer RGB-D cameras, household lamps, ArUco markers, one GPU, Blender or a Gaussian renderer. Public HDR maps.
research_questions.risks: (a) Incremental relative to Re:InterHand, ViserDex and DIR. (b) Downstream gains may come from more viewpoint and geometry diversity, not from the quality of the light transport, so the ablation must hold geometry fixed. (c) Relighting errors on skin may hurt more than they help. (d) The hand-side ground truth on the real test set is weak without motion capture.

fit.thesis_assets_help: Small, and limited almost entirely to RQ1. The marker-based metric object pose (ArUco-marked object, on the 45 mm scale) is a ready ground-truth protocol for transparent and specular objects, where RGB-D depth fails but the markers still give metric pose. Putting the markers on a clip seen only by a second ground-truth camera extends it cleanly. The measured, held and constrained honesty labels map naturally onto a per-frame reliability flag. When depth on glass is invalid, the tracker can mark which pose components are measured and which are inferred from the hand prior; this is a useful, reviewer-friendly output. The causal 30 fps chain gives a real-time baseline harness. Object-conditioned recovery of an occluded holding arm is reusable as the hand and grasp prior in RQ1, but only loosely. The Unity twin helps little: physically correct refraction and shadow ground truth need a path tracer (Blender Cycles or the HDRP path tracer), not the real-time scene. The 28 recordings of one subject (an opaque object under fixed lighting) contribute nothing to a benchmark here. For P40 as stated (hair, mouth, eyes and relighting of head and body avatars), the assets give no edge at all.
fit.what_a_small_lab_cannot_do_here:
P40 as stated is not a small-lab problem, and the verdict for that version is NO. The lab cannot build or borrow a light stage or OLAT dome, and cannot capture time-multiplexed, multi-identity, dynamic relightable data. That data is the bottleneck named in P40's own why_it_persists field, and the head- and body-avatar subfield is now driven by Meta Codec Avatars, MPI, TUM and ETH (URAvatar, Relightable Full-Body Gaussian Codec Avatars, Large-scale Codec Avatars pretrained on 1M videos, PhysHead, DGH, DynHair). The lab also cannot:
- Compete on hair-strand dynamics, eye refraction or subsurface scattering, which need dense multi-view capture plus polarized or OLAT measurement.
- Train large relighting or diffusion priors at the scale of the current state of the art.
- Obtain mocap-grade hand ground truth, so every hand-side claim must rest on public datasets (ARCTIC, DexYCB, HO3D) or on synthetic renders.
- Get physically exact ground truth for refraction or interreflection in real data; that must come from path-traced synthetic data.

What remains feasible is the in-field transfer of the light-transport idea:
- RQ1, light-transport-aware tracking of transparent and specular hand-held objects with a cheap two-camera ground-truth protocol. This has the best fit.
- RQ2, mutual light transport between hand and object as a cue for contact and pose, evaluated on public data plus Blender. This is more novel but its payoff is riskier.
